ANKARA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye is working to ensure investors in troubled investment funds receive payments as quickly as possible and at the highest possible level, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Thursday amid a probe into alleged market manipulation.

HANOI, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The economy of Vietnam's southern hub of Ho Chi Minh City grew 9.86 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, local news outlet VnExpress reported Thursday.
The services sector, which accounted for 51.9 percent of overall growth, expanded by 9.95 percent, while the industry and construction sector grew by 10.17 percent and the agriculture, forestry and fishery sector expanded by 3.4 percent.
The strong third-quarter performance brought the city's gross regional domestic product (GRDP) growth in the first nine months to 9.06 percent year on year, with services remaining the main growth driver, accounting for 51.8 percent of GRDP and contributing 53.6 percent to the overall expansion, the report added.
To achieve its full-year growth target of over 10 percent, the city's economy would need to expand by more than 13 percent in the fourth quarter, according to the report. ■

Proekt investigation finds Russian officials flying on private jets apparently provided by oligarchs whose industries they oversee
Proekt has published an extensive investigation into senior Russian officials’ use of private jets. Its journalists examined a database from the border service of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) that leaked in 2023. It contained records of more than 100 million people who left Russia by air or other means in 2014–2023. The reporters spent a year analyzing international flight records for 1,064 senior Russian officials. We briefly summarize the investigation’s most important findings.
- Of those 1,064 officials, 322 fly abroad on business jets. Most do so regularly. Flights cost an average of $32,000.
- Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) leader Leonid Slutsky and Tatarstan head Rustam Minnikhanov fly most frequently on business jets. In 2014–2023, each man and his relatives took a combined 350–360 such flights.
- A total of 101 senior officials fly at someone else’s expense on planes likely provided by prominent businesspeople. Officials also have no qualms about using business jets registered to state-owned companies for personal trips.
- Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov took the most flights with oligarchs. Sergey Kiriyenko, the Kremlin’s first deputy chief of staff, flew with his family to the Maldives on a Rosatom jet.
- Russian officials even travel to Mount Athos on private jets. These VIP pilgrims include Kiriyenko, Moscow Governor Andrey Vorobyov, and former Prosecutor General Yury Chaika.
- France is the most popular destination for Putin’s elite. Seven of the 10 countries officials visited most frequently in 2014–2023 were in Western and Southern Europe.
- Russian officials fly with relatives, businesspeople, and even figures from the criminal underworld. Communist lawmaker Boris Ivanyuzhenkov, who once belonged to the Podolsk organized crime group, flew abroad with leaders of the Izmailovo, Podolsk, Chekhov, and Balashikha criminal gangs.

Palermo, first coffee grown and harvested in Italy: warmer climate is changing farming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:04:20 UTC
02:04:20 KST

Rising temperatures now allow coffee to be grown in Italy. In Sicily, the Morettino family has completed its first harvest, showing how climate change is reshaping crops worldwide.
A plantation on the outskirts of Palermo has for the first time produced Arabica coffee beans grown and harvested entirely in Italy. The result, achieved on the Morettino family estate, has been made possible by climate change, which has effectively brought tropical temperatures to southern Italy.
While global warming had already enabled southern England to produce champagne-style sparkling wine, pushing the traditional growing areas of France and northern Italy further north, the jump made by coffee from equatorial zones to the Mediterranean is clearly even greater.
As the daily newspaper La Stampa reported on Thursday (source in Italian), the Sicilian plantation in the San Lorenzo ai Colli area, a few hundred metres above sea level, is currently producing around 100 kilograms of drupes (the fruit of the coffee plant, also known as cherries), which yield just over 15 kilograms of roasted beans.
The project, which involves the University and the Botanical Garden of Palermo (source in Italian) in studying how tropical crops adapt to the new Mediterranean climate, is still far from large-scale commercial production in terms of volume, but it already has considerable scientific and symbolic value.
Where coffee is grown: the world’s main producing countries
Traditionally, coffee is grown in the planet’s tropical and equatorial regions, where high temperatures, humidity and steady rainfall favour its growth.
For this reason, the world’s main producers and exporters are largely concentrated in Latin America, Africa and Asia, with the Arabica variety, which delivers higher quality, grown at higher altitudes than Robusta.
The leading producer countries include Brazil, Colombia, Peru and Costa Rica in Latin America; Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania in Africa; and Vietnam and Indonesia in Asia.
According to the promoters of the initiative, the coffee produced in Palermo develops distinctive aromatic notes reminiscent of raisins, a feature that sets it apart from beans grown in traditional coffee-growing regions.
Before the Morettino family’s venture, a local farm had already grown coffee entirely in greenhouses (source in Italian) in Terrasini, also in the Palermo area.
Similar experiments have been attempted in various forms elsewhere in southern Europe.
In Spain, particularly in the province of Granada, experimental projects have been launched to test the resilience of the plants, with results quite different from those in Gran Canaria where, thanks to its more southerly latitude, coffee has been grown since the 19th century, taking advantage of the fertility and humidity of volcanic soils.
On the Azores islands in Portugal, where numerous private plantations have been reported that benefit from the mild climate, the archipelago marks one of the northernmost points where coffee is grown.
How coffee consumption in Italy has changed
The growing interest in niche products such as the Sicilian coffee comes in a context in which Italy is the EU’s leading producer of roasted coffee, with over 400 tonnes produced in 2025.
The national coffee industry, although it relies on importing raw material from other producer countries (that is, unroasted beans, or "green coffee"), includes around a thousand roasters and generates an annual turnover of 5.9 billion euros.
The prospect of local cultivation, made possible by global warming, which is unfortunately also bringing more natural disasters, is in step with Italian consumption patterns, which remain robust and are growing, according to several studies published on 1 October to mark International Coffee Day.
According to a survey by AstraRicerche in partnership with the Segafredo brand, 82.6% of Italians consider the quality of the raw material decisive, while 71.8% pay attention to aromatic characteristics and 51.5% want to know the product’s origin and its journey along the supply chain.
Another survey, carried out by the Italian Coffee Committee of Unione Italiana Food and by Altroconsumo on more than 1,200 consumers, shows that three out of four Italians drink coffee regularly and almost one in two see it as one of the symbols of the country’s culture and lifestyle, on a par with pasta.
Among those who drink espresso, 83% have it every day, at home and at the bar, either with a moka pot or with modern capsule machines, which are now neck and neck in people’s habits.
Any commercial prospects must of course be weighed against environmental sustainability when growing coffee outside its traditional areas of origin.
Processing the beans after harvest can require between 50 and 200 litres of water for every kilogram of green coffee and produces wastewater which, if not properly treated, can affect local ecosystems.
And if, instead of the tropical rains that have always sustained coffee plantations, growing moves to areas where seasonal drought is becoming endemic, it becomes essential to match the agricultural challenge of coffee with a technological one, cutting the amount of water needed to grow and process the crop.

At a plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club he reminded that the more uncompromising the confrontation, the higher the risk of it escalating to the most severe phase, because "if a gun is hanging on the wall at the beginning of the play, it must inevitably fire by the end."

Elon Musk returns to Trump administration to co-lead Pentagon war study

Musk, who in 2024 threw his support behind Trump and helped his return to the White House, served as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he spearheaded sweeping job cuts across the US federal government.
Tech billionaire Elon Musk will make a return to officially advising US President Donald Trump's government by co-leading what the Pentagon called a study on the future of war.
Musk served as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he oversaw sweeping job cuts across the US federal government, before departing in May 2025.
In a speech Wednesday at the Quantico military base, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said "Project Meridian" will be "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare." "We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists", he added.
Musk will be a co-leader of Project Meridian alongside Palmer Luckey, the 34-year-old co founder of defence technology company Anduril Industries, and Newt Gingrich, the 83-year old Republican former House speaker.
No stranger to the Pentagon
Musk's companies are already major Pentagon contractors, including SpaceX building satellite networks for Trump's planned "Golden Dome" missile defence shield. His artificial intelligence firm xAI this year signed a deal allowing the military to use its Grok chatbot on classified systems.
In 2024, Musk threw his support behind Trump and helped his return to the White House, but the men later had a high-profile blow-up over the president's spending legislation.
The two have since reconciled, and Musk has again become a frequent presence at the White House, though less visibly than during his previous stint, when he often visited the Oval Office, most memorably with his young son on his shoulders.
On Tuesday he was seated next to Trump at a lunch with artificial intelligence executives, where he joined other tech leaders in signing a voluntary AI safety accord that the president described as "morally binding."
Last week, Musk attended the state dinner Trump hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in May he flew to Beijing on Air Force One as part of the business delegation accompanying Trump on his state visit to China.
Back among the big donors
He also resumed giving to Republican causes, including multimillion-dollar donations to individual candidates and conservative political groups. Musk, who spent more than $250 million backing Trump and other Republicans in the 2024 election, has given at least $90 million toward November's midterm elections, according to tallies of Federal Election Commission filings.
Hegseth said the project's purpose is to "creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master." Project members will include hand-picked private sector leaders and subject matter experts from across the innovation, academic and policy ecosystems. Hegseth said he has directed Project Meridian's findings to be completed and submitted within 120 days.

Ethiopia: Embassy shut in Eritrea, 10 diplomats expelled
October 1, 2026
Ethiopia on Thursday announced it was shutting its embassy in Eritrea and also declared ten Eritrean diplomats "persona non grata", accused them of involvement in activities that threatened national security.
The embassy in Eritrea had been reopened in 2018 as part of the rapprochement that culminated in Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize.
A statement issued by Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry said the action was being taken "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."
With regard to the expulsion of the Eritrean diplomats, Addis Ababa said that it was "for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security."
The Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave the country.
Reports of earlier blast at Ethiopian military headquarters
The measures came following reports of an explosion overnight at Ethiopian military headquarters in Addis Ababa.
The AFP news agency reported that the explosion took place at the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) headquarters between midnight and 1:00am local time, citing diplomatic and security sources with the information.
The sources could not provide further information relating to the nature of the blast or who was responsible, or if there had been any casualties.
The Associated Press, citing security sources, reported that there had been three blasts that came after the government banned the use of drones in the capital.
It's not clear whether the blasts were related to any attack or whether they had been part of training exercises.
Eritrea has denied allegations that it supports an armed alliance — which includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) — currently fighting Ethiopian government forces. The coalition is named Alliance for Survival.
Hundreds have been killed and wounded since last week's resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia.
Clashes have been ongoing and have have taken place along several fronts.
The United Nations has called for de-escalation of the fighting and for talks between the government and the recently formed alliance.

Google’s dream of AI data centers in space gets its first off-world test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:56:41 UTC
01:56:41 KST

When Elon Musk took SpaceX public in June, a big part of its value proposition came from promises of data centers in space. Skeptics were quick to list all of the hurdles. This afternoon Google’s Project Suncatcher is scheduled to launch hardware in pursuit of the same idea: it will send artificial intelligence processors into orbit onboard—of all things—a SpaceX rocket.
That doesn’t mean Musk’s pitch will become reality anytime soon. If anything, the gulf between Suncatcher and a working data center in orbit suggests how far off that future still is. But as AI’s appetite for electricity tests the patience of communities being asked to feed it, some of the richest tech companies are racing to source their energy needs from space instead.
The test satellite will carry just four processors, which will be used to run Google’s Gemini AI models for 15 minutes at a stretch before they need to shut down and cool off. The ultimate goal is to establish a full-fledged orbital data center, built from constellations of thousands of satellites that will share the work of running AI models and beam their responses back to Earth.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The whole effort has less to do with what could be accomplished out in space than with what’s getting harder to achieve down here on Earth. Data centers are projected to use around 3 percent of the world’s electricity by 2030, roughly double their share today, according to an International Energy Agency report. In orbit, sunlight is abundant and free, and Google says a solar panel there generates up to eight times as much power as it would on the ground. “We have direct access to a wonderful renewable source of energy,” says Alexander Wyglinski, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Worcester Polytechnic Institute.
There’s a political incentive to look beyond U.S. soil, too. As the data-center buildout grows more divisive, blasting that infrastructure into space and away from people’s backyards holds obvious appeal.
But scale is the main question, Google readily admits. The biggest AI data centers that are being built now pack in hundreds of thousands of chips and draw up to a gigawatt of power, several thousand times the output of the International Space Station’s solar arrays. Even getting enough solar panels into orbit would be a massive undertaking at that scale. “It’s going from arrays that are several meters on a side to arrays that are a couple of kilometers on a side,” says Kerri Cahoy, a professor of astronautics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “Launching enough mass to generate the power is huge.”
The problems don’t end once everything is up there, either. Though space is cold, its vacuum is a lousy place to dissipate heat, which is why Suncatcher’s chips must clock out to cool down and why the satellites require specialized radiators. The whole satellite network needs to be resilient to space debris. And the cosmic radiation that Earth’s atmosphere filters out can scramble calculations, forcing systems to catch and correct errors on the fly. “When we talk about satellite platforms, and you put a computer into them, you don’t put [in] a computer like the one you have on your desk,” Wyglinski says.
For months before today’s launch, Google has been anticipating those problems on Earth, shaking spacecraft to simulate the launch and bombarding its chips with proton beams to test their response to radiation. “It's about seeing what works, identifying points of failure and applying those findings to future missions,” says Travis Beals, a senior director at Google, who worked on Project Suncatcher.
Even so, scaling up could force Google and SpaceX to confront some stubborn physics. Every chip and solar panel has to be hauled into orbit, and every answer those chips produce has to come back down.
Satellites can transmit data to Earth, but doing so at scale is expensive and difficult. “We don’t have the convenient, easy way to get that data back to the ground,” says Alan George, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Pittsburgh, who heads a National Science Foundation center focused on space computing. During the Cold War, the problem was bad enough that U.S. spy satellites parachuted exposed film back to Earth.
Computers on Earth relay information easily, and lasers have made it possible to do the same between spacecraft. But getting information between Earth and space is another story entirely, so it is best to process some of the information gathered on satellites before it is sent down to Earth. “I like to tell my students the best data compression is answers,” George says. While that logic could apply to AI responses, too, his work putting computers in space tells him that the resource constraints make it hard to match what “you would put down the street in a building.”
Google’s engineers say they began from a similarly skeptical premise. “As a first step, we tried to find reasons that it was impossible,” Beals says, “but we gradually became convinced that it might actually work.”
And then there’s the question that may ultimately decide the whole thing: How will the limited bandwidth and energy savings make up the maintenance costs?
The cost of launching data center satellites and replacing them as they wear out, along with the bottleneck of getting data back down, may eat up whatever the free sunshine saves. The competitors in the first space race were nations jockeying for scientific dominance. Orbital data centers are mainly being pitched by corporations, which tend to prefer profitable ventures. So even if Project Suncatcher solves its technical challenges, those physical limitations could still kill the idea before Google gets anywhere close to a full-blown data center in space.
More often than not, space throws up more challenges than early movers expect. “It’s usually the late entrants who finally figured out how to do it effectively,” Cahoy says. SpaceX itself didn’t reach orbit until half a century after Sputnik.
If she’s right, the company that eventually gets data centers in space to scale may not even have booked its ride to orbit yet.

Market participants also identify geological exploration, joint ventures, and the petrochemical and oil-and-gas-chemical sectors as areas of interest.

US waives rights conditions for $320M in military aid to Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:55:36 UTC
01:55:36 KST

Breadcrumb
US waives rights conditions for $320 million in military aid to Egypt, letter shows
The US State Department has waived human rights conditions for more than $300 million of military aid to Egypt in light of Cairo's "helpful role" since the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a letter to US lawmakers obtained by Reuters.
Egypt started to get significant US support after signing a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, and has received about $1.3 billion a year in US military aid since the late 1980s.
A portion of that aid is subject to human rights and democracy-related conditions which can be waived on national-security grounds. The withholding of funds, including under former US President Joe Biden, has caused friction between Cairo and Washington in the past.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio "has made a determination to waive the certification requirement with respect to $320 million in FY 2025 Foreign Military Financing for Egypt," said a letter addressed to various congressional committees dated 21 September.
That portion of military aid was deemed "necessary for counterterrorism, border security, or non-proliferation programmes or is otherwise important to the national security interest of the United States," according to an accompanying memo justifying the decision.
"Exercising this waiver authority is essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities, particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," said the memo, which was dated 4 September and bore Rubio’s signature.
Operation Epic Fury is the name used by the US military for the campaign on Iran launched alongside Israel on 28 February. The State Department memo — which two sources in Washington familiar with the letter confirmed was authentic — did not elaborate on what it called Egypt's "helpful role".
War puts strain on Egypt's economy
The State Department's annual determination on Egypt's military aid typically deals with funds appropriated the previous fiscal year, which ends on 30 September.
The US State Department and Egypt's Foreign Ministry had no immediate comment.
The spillover from the Iran war has imposed a high cost on US security partners, including Egypt, which has seen its economy tested by surging fuel prices and other disruptions.
Hundreds of millions of dollars in cash assistance, as well as tanks, helicopters, missiles and fighter aircraft were held back after Egypt’s army ousted the country’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi, amid mass protests in 2013.
Under Biden, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation multiple times over Egypt’s human-rights record.
In 2024, after the Israeli war on Gaza began, the Biden administration overrode the human rights conditions and granted the full $1.3 billion allocation to Egypt for the first time in his administration.
Egypt has played a central role in ceasefire negotiations over conflicts in Gaza, including a truce deal agreed in October 2025, but has been less prominent in mediation over the Iran war.
Rights groups have long accused Egypt of widespread human rights abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, including torture and enforced disappearances.
This week Egyptian police arrested six journalists from a fact-checking and investigative media outlet, accusing them of spreading misinformation on behalf of the banned Muslim Brotherhood, which the publication denied.
Egyptian authorities say they have taken steps to address rights. Sisi says stability is paramount and the government is promoting rights by trying to provide for basic needs.

"Russia attacks Ukrainian ports, blocks Ukraine's grain exports, and then looks for new routes for its own grain," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on X. "Estonia will not provide one."
Kyiv fears that once Russia completes the satellite constellation, Moscow could use the network to obtain real-time information for strikes against Ukraine.

The Syrian Postal Corporation, also known as Syrian Post, announced Thursday the resumption of international parcel shipments from Syria to countries worldwide through the Universal Postal Union (UPU) network, after a prolonged suspension.
The Syrian news agency SANA cited the corporation’s head, Imad al-Din Hamad, who said the service went into operation Thursday, reconnecting Syria’s postal system with the international postal network.

The Syrian Postal Corporation announced in June that it would reactivate the receipt of international postal parcels beginning July 1 through the postal exchange office at Damascus International Airport.
With the resumption of outbound shipments Thursday, international parcel services through the corporation are now available in both directions, from abroad to Syria and from Syria to countries worldwide.

Anti-Zionism is not antisemitism, US rights commission finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:54:39 UTC
01:54:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Anti-Zionism is not antisemitism, US rights commission finds in rebuke to Trump
A bipartisan US civil rights commission has challenged President Donald Trump's crackdown on pro-Palestinian activism at American universities, finding that opposition to Zionism does not constitute unlawful antisemitic discrimination.
The US Commission on Civil Rights, in a report published on Monday, also questioned the legality of the Trump administration's decision to withhold billions of dollars in federal funding from universities over alleged failure to protect Jewish students.
The findings challenge a central argument used by the White House to justify its crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrations following the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The report distinguishes between discrimination against Jewish people and criticism of Zionism, the political movement that underpinned Israel's establishment and the mass expulsion and dispossession of Palestinians from historic Palestine.
It found that Zionism was not automatically protected under US civil rights law simply because some Jewish people identify with it.
The commission explained that criticizing political beliefs or institutions does not, by itself, constitute discrimination against people who support them.
Its findings challenge the Trump administration's treatment of some forms of anti-Zionist activism and criticism of Israel as evidence of antisemitism.
The report also found that 97% of campus protests against Israel during the 2023–2024 academic year were peaceful, challenging claims that pro-Palestinian demonstrations were overwhelmingly violent.
The commission stressed that Jewish students must be protected from genuine discrimination, harassment and threats, and that universities have a responsibility to address such incidents without restricting freedom of expression.
Trump's university crackdown under scrutiny
The commission further criticised the Trump administration's decision to freeze billions of dollars in federal funding to universities, including Harvard and Columbia, over allegations that they had failed to tackle antisemitism.
Under US law, the government must investigate discrimination complaints and follow a series of legal steps before withdrawing funding from an institution.
The report found that the administration had bypassed or accelerated parts of that process, imposing sweeping financial penalties that went beyond the university programmes under investigation.
It also highlighted court rulings that questioned the legality of some of the administration's actions, raising concerns that the funding cuts were being used to pressure universities into restricting speech critical of Israel.
The crackdown has prompted criticism from civil rights advocates and legal experts, who argue that the administration has used allegations of antisemitism to target pro-Palestinian activism and undermine academic freedom.
The commission also raised concerns about the Trump administration's decision to cut resources from the very government office responsible for investigating discrimination against Jewish students.
In March 2025, seven of the Education Department's 12 regional civil rights offices were closed, despite having handled 90% of the antisemitism complaints resolved by the department in 2024.
The report also criticised the departments of Education, Justice and Health and Human Services for failing to provide information requested during the investigation, raising concerns about the administration's lack of transparency.
Commission chair Rochelle Garza stressed that efforts to protect Jewish students must follow the law and respect constitutional rights, including freedom of speech.
Bipartisan findings challenge White House policy
The commission's eight members, four Democrats and four Republicans, unanimously approved the report after an investigation that included testimony from Jewish students, university officials, legal experts and civil rights organisations.
The commission unanimously authorised the investigation in January 2025, held a public hearing in February 2026 and approved the final report in July, before its publication earlier this week.
Commission chair Rochelle Garza welcomed the unanimous findings, saying they had demonstrated what the commission could achieve by working across party lines and taking difficult civil rights issues seriously.
"Antisemitism has no place on our college campuses. Students should be protected from discrimination and harassment while colleges and universities also respect free speech and expression," she said.
However, Republican commissioner J. Christian Adams, who was appointed by Trump, issued a separate statement criticising the report for not endorsing the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism.
The definition has drawn criticism from free speech advocates because some of its examples involving Israel can be used to classify certain forms of anti-Zionism and criticism of Israeli policies as "antisemitic".
Adams also objected to the report's discussion of Republican attitudes towards Israel and Jewish identity, although he did not challenge its broader legal findings.
Democratic commissioner Mondaire Jones, who helped lead the investigation alongside Republican Peter Kirsanow, criticised the administration for pursuing its crackdown without adequately consulting the Jewish students it claimed to be protecting.
The commission called for stronger protections against antisemitism on university campuses, but stressed that these must not come at the expense of students' right to protest, criticise Israel or express opposition to Zionism.

The State Secretary for International Cooperation, Eva Granados, highlighted on Wednesday in Mexico City the renewed impetus for cooperation between Spain and Mexico, following a working meeting with the Executive Director of the Mexican Agency for International Development Cooperation (AMEXCID), Alejandra del Moral.

“Spain and Mexico have entered a new phase of cooperation, based on trust, dialogue between equals and the determination to transform our common priorities into concrete results for our citizens,” said Granados.
The Joint Fund will strengthen collaboration between the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID) and AMEXCID and will facilitate the implementation of both bilateral actions and triangular cooperation initiatives with other countries in Latin America and the Caribbean. The Fund builds on the work carried out by the AECID through other instruments, in line with the priorities of Spanish Cooperation in Mexico, such as gender equality and social cohesion, the environment, climate change, and drinking water and sanitation.
The reactivation of this mechanism comes against a backdrop of intensifying cooperation relations between Spain and Mexico. Spanish Cooperation currently has 35 projects underway in the country, worth over 29 million euros, representing a 20.8 per cent increase in funding compared with the previous year. This growth reflects the commitment of both governments to expand their collaboration tools and move towards a more horizontal, innovative and results-oriented form of cooperation.
Subsequently, the State Secretary discussed with the Mexican Government collaboration to strengthen the capabilities of the National Search Commission in locating and identifying missing and unaccounted-for persons. Spain is thus supporting a key priority for Mexican institutions and society, based on respect for the victims and a commitment to human rights.
The State Secretary also expressed her gratitude for Mexico’s constructive participation in the preparatory work for the forthcoming Ibero-American Summit in Madrid, one of the key milestones of which will be the adoption of the Ibero-American Cooperation Strategy 2027–2030. Granados highlighted Mexico’s contribution to the initiatives being promoted within the framework of the Summit in areas such as care, artificial intelligence, academic mobility and disaster risk reduction.
Cooperation projects with an impact
Following her schedule in Mexico City, Granados will travel to Yucatán to visit several Spanish Cooperation projects on the ground and meet with state authorities, institutions and participating communities.
In Mérida, the State Secretary will hold a meeting with the Governor of Yucatán, Joaquín Díaz Mena. She will then inaugurate a project in Tekax to provide access to drinking water and sanitation in rural indigenous communities. The project combines resilient infrastructure, institutional strengthening and community participation, based on the principle that access to water is a human right essential for health, dignity and sustainable development. Finally, she will visit the archaeological site of Uxmal, as part of Spain’s commitment to understanding and protecting the heritage of Mexico’s indigenous peoples.
Cultural cooperation also plays a central role in strengthening relations between the two countries. Spain and Mexico share a desire to deepen their understanding of their common history and to recognise and promote the richness of indigenous peoples and cultures. Initiatives such as the exhibition ‘Half the World. Women in Indigenous Mexico’ have demonstrated culture’s ability to build bridges, foster dialogue and forge a bilateral relationship based on respect and a shared vision for the future.
In Progreso, Granados will meet with representatives of fishing communities and the Mexican Institute for Research into Sustainable Fisheries and Aquaculture to learn about the progress of a project that combines scientific research, governance, training and sustainable techniques for containing and harvesting sargassum.

These projects reflect a comprehensive approach that seeks to turn a serious environmental and economic challenge for the Caribbean into new solutions based on the circular economy, innovation and the creation of opportunities for coastal communities.
Through this visit, Spain and Mexico reaffirm their commitment to continuing to build, together, a transformative, horizontal and solidarity-based partnership, capable of strengthening institutions, improving people’s lives and providing joint responses to major regional and global challenges.

After 2 years in office, how has Claudia Sheinbaum changed Mexico?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:48:00 UTC
01:48:00 KST

After 2 years, Sheinbaum's Mexico sees incremental change
October 1, 2026
Since Claudia Sheinbaum first took office in 2024 as Mexico's first female president, she has largely adhered to the political agenda of her mentor and predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador.
But she has also had to contend with several problems that go far beyond Mexico's borders: violence inflicted by drug cartels, tens of thousands of missing persons and the growing political pressure from US President Donald Trump.
Fewer murders — but more missing persons
Sheinbaum has been able to report some progress when it comes to the security situation in Mexico. In her second government report, presented in September, she touted a 51% drop in the daily homicide rate since 2024.
To what extent this progress can be attributed to Sheinbaum's administration is, however, a matter of debate. While the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy has also noted progress in the effort to reduce homicides, the Mexico Evalua think tank has said there isn't enough statistical evidence to attribute the decline directly to measures taken by Sheinbaum.
And other indicators highlight a problematic trend. Mexico Evalua, referring to the government's own figures, pointed out that the number of recorded cases of kidnapping and enforced disappearances has surged by 127% over the last decade, "crimes against life" by 197% and femicide by 53%.
As of June 2026, the national register recorded a total of 135,271 missing persons. At the start of Sheinbaum's time in office in October 2024, that figure stood at around 115,000, according to an analysis by Red Lupa, a citizen-led network dedicated to monitoring disappearances.
"There is a lack of political will [to address the issue]," said Edgar Cortez, a project coordinator at the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy in Mexico City. On the one hand, he said, the government sees little political benefit, while at the same time it's lacking the technical expertise to coordinate the varied measures implemented at the state and federal levels.
Displacement — another consequence of violence — is also disrupting the lives of millions across the country. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Geography, violence or crime forced at least one member in 510,000 households — some 1.6 million people — to change their place of residence between October 2020 and October 2025.
Selective crackdown on corruption
Eduardo Bohorquez, director of civil society organization Transparencia Mexicana, told DW he has noted a shift in the government's strategy when it comes to fighting corruption. Two years on, he said the government is now focusing on the links between federal employees and organized crime.
As example he gave Operacion Enjambre, during which more than 100 public officials of varying political affiliation were arrested — including mayors, former mayors and police commanders, according to Mexico's security chief Omar Garcia Harfuch.
Critics, however, have accused the government of taking a selective approach. To date, no incumbent or former governor of Sheinbaum's ruling Morena party has been either prosecuted or detained for corruption or alleged links to organized crime.
Shienbaum has announced a package of reforms to tackle corruption, and Bohorquez said that will show whether or not her administration will actually chart a different course than that of her predecessor.
Placating Trump a top priority
Domestic and foreign policy have been closely linked during Sheinbaum's two years in office. Most of that time has been shaped by Donald Trump's return to the White House in January 2025, and his administration's increasing pressure on drug cartels, migration and trade.
Trump has accused Mexico of not doing enough to tackle the cartels, with Washington classifying several Mexican criminal organizations as terrorist groups. The US president has repeatedly threatened to take unilateral action against the cartels. Sheinbaum, however, has opposed any US military actions on Mexican territory, calling instead for "cooperation without subordination."
At the same time, Mexico and the US have been cooperating closely — especially when it comes to migration. Between 2024 and 2025, the number of migrant contacts registered by US authorities along the US-Mexico border dropped by more than 84%, from 1.5 million to around 238,000.
Economic cooperation is also key to the cross-border relationship. Mexico and the US are currently negotiating several trade issues, including the future of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as USMCA. For its part, Mexico is hoping to reduce Trump's tariffs on steel, aluminum and automobiles.
After talks with Trump in September, Sheinbaum said both sides were working toward a trade deal. It remains a tricky balancing act for the Mexican president — developing the closest possible trading relationship with her country's most important economic partner, while at the same time not giving the impression that Mexico is giving up its political sovereignty under pressure from Washington.
Progress on social rights
The outlook is brighter when it comes to economic and social rights, with Cortez of the Mexican Institute of Human Rights and Democracy singling out the increase in minimum wage and government benefits for older people and those living with disabilities.
When it comes to other human rights concerns, however, he hasn't seen "any progress or setbacks." Alongside the staggering number of missing persons, Cortez also pointed out attacks on human rights defenders and journalists, along with a failure to sufficiently consult with Indigenous groups and rural communities when it came to major construction projects.
Sheinbaum has announced a plan to introduce a nationwide law against femicide that would align the various regulations on the local and state level, said Cortez. "That could end up being a positive, but the problem will be to put it into practice," he added.
Transparency without 'accountability'
The government's record on transparency remains problematic, according to observers, with Sheinbaum doing away with the National Institute for Transparency, Access to Information and Protection of Personal Data, or INAI. The responsibilities of the independent agency, which had been in place for two decades, have since been divided among several state entities.
"Instead of making things easier, everything has become fragmented," said Bohorquez of Transparencia Mexicana. Anyone looking for information from Congress, the judiciary, the military or local authorities now needs to go directly to the source.
Bohorquez also gave a mixed reaction to Sheinbaum's daily press conference, saying that while it was "a very effective political communication tool it didn't provide accountability."
For Cortez, that reflects a fundamental question of Sheinbaum's political priorities. New social programs bring "instant political benefits," he said, while advancing on civil and political rights required long-term effort and didn't allow the government to "immediately capitalize on political gains."

Google rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concerns

16:47:29 UTC
01:47:29 KST

Google on Wednesday said it would withhold its most powerful artificial intelligence model from the public for now, releasing Gemini 4 Argon only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts to avoid misuse by hackers.
“Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach,” wrote Koray Kavukcuoglu, Google’s chief AI architect, in a blogpost announcing the model.
Google said it was voluntarily giving the US government early access to the model and would gather feedback from testers before making it widely available.
The cautious rollout mirrors the approach of rival Anthropic, which has kept its most advanced model, Claude Mythos Preview, restricted to a small number of trusted organizations.
Washington briefly forced Anthropic to suspend access to its publicly released Claude Mythos and Claude Fable models in June, and has since set up a voluntary process for vetting the most powerful AI models before release.
The announcement came a day after Donald Trump hosted top tech executives, including the Google chief, Sundar Pichai, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, at the White House, where they signed a voluntary accord pledging to police the risks of their own AI systems.
Cybersecurity experts fear the state-of-the-art technology could be used to hack banks, hospitals and government systems.
Google said Argon excelled at complex tasks in software engineering, legal and financial work and cyber-defense, with a leading ability to find and fix critical software flaws.
Early testers used Argon to uncover a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information – something other advanced models had missed, Google said.
Google said Argon was designed to refuse requests that could help carry out cyber-attacks or develop chemical, biological or nuclear weapons.
Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI have built similar safeguards into their most advanced models.
Google said it was monitoring the model’s reasoning to stop it from straying beyond what users intended, a risk researchers call misalignment.
The issue has taken on new urgency since OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its models, including one not yet released, broke out of a sealed test environment during a cybersecurity evaluation and hacked into the servers of the AI company Hugging Face.

EU, Ukraine agree to accelerate €45B loan payout in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

(From L) European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrive to attend the EU Summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on June 18, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The European Commission and Ukraine have reached a deal to accelerate the disbursement of €45 billion earmarked for Kyiv in 2027 under the EU’s €90 billion loan program, they said Thursday in a joint statement.
Russia has in recent weeks escalated its drone and missile attacks against Ukraine, while the country is running out of funds to buy weapons to defend itself.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi warned journalists this week that Ukraine faces a $27 billion (€23 billion) defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that if the gap isn't plugged in the next two months, Kyiv risks being unable to buy weapons early next year.
Advertisement
At a recent meeting of EU defense ministers, "many called for front-loading parts of the €90 billion loan allocated for 2027," meaning disbursing part of the 2027 loan this year instead, the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said last month.
But the Commission preferred to instead speed up the disbursement of the 2027 loan next year itself, meaning Ukraine would get that money faster, diplomats said.
"Our dialogue with the European Commission has delivered good results in addressing Ukraine's financial and defense needs for 2026 and 2027," Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. "We have agreed on the format, timeline, and steps needed to ensure full coverage," he added.
"For 2027, we have agreed to move forward swiftly with the allocation of €45 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan, subject to the established conditions," the two sides said, referring to the reforms Ukraine must carry out to receive the money. Once Ukraine meets the conditions, the funds will be immediately disbursed, according to a senior EU official.
The two sides also agreed that they will "begin work on identifying additional budgetary and defence needs" and meet monthly to coordinate their efforts.
The €90 billion EU loan was agreed by leaders last December to provide financial support to Ukraine in 2026 and 2027. It includes strict conditions for Kyiv, including adherence to the rule of law and the fight against corruption. A large share of the loan — €60 billion — is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense needs.
Advertisement
The loan has been split evenly, with €45 billion earmarked for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027. It was designed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's external financing needs over the two years, with the rest expected to be covered by other countries, particularly G7 partners.
The joint statement also calls on those partners to step in.
"All sides agreed that other partners should also fulfil their financial commitments and step up their efforts in light of the significant challenges Ukraine is facing," it says.

A 27-year-old dual British and Iranian national has been arrested in London over the activity near RAF Fairford at the weekend, on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, according to Counter Terrorism Policing.
The man was detained on Thursday afternoon in the borough of Westminster under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. A second man, aged 26 and a British national, has been questioned under caution, and two properties in the same area have been searched.
Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles, including possible foreign state involvement. I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation.”
The five men in their twenties arrested on Sunday remain on police bail. They were detained in the early hours after Gloucestershire Constabulary received a report of suspicious vehicles near the airfield, initially on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later of preparation of a terrorist act. A major incident was declared and properties were evacuated in the village of Whelford beside the base.
Counter Terrorism Policing said on Tuesday that no improvised explosive devices had been found in the three vehicles examined, although a quantity of petrol was recovered, and that searches of properties in London had concluded. All five of those arrested on Sunday are London residents, four in Westminster and one in Camden, as we reported.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, who heads National Counter Terrorism Policing, said earlier in the week that officers were keeping an open mind on whether the current international situation had any bearing on the case, and that they were considering whether the activity might have been committed by proxies or by individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state. Evans has now repeated that possible foreign state involvement is among the lines being pursued.
Fairford, in Gloucestershire, is a United States Air Force forward operating location rather than a flying station of the Royal Air Force, and its long runway has made it the standing European base for American strategic bombers. B-1B Lancers have been operating from the airfield, and the base moved to its highest force protection condition before the arrests were made.
Nobody has been charged in connection with the investigation, and Counter Terrorism Policing has asked anyone with information that might assist to report it through gov.uk/ACT or by calling the Anti-Terrorist Hotline on 0800 789 321.

Olena Fidanyan, head of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Education and Science, told Hromadske that some schools have been hit repeatedly.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
UNITED24 Media previously reported that Russian attacks have damaged 4,650 educational facilities across Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, with 423 completely destroyed. 01:42:36 KST

Sahin Demir
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Energy ministers from Algeria, Tunisia, Italy, Austria and Germany signed the Algiers Ministerial Declaration on Thursday on the SoutH2 Corridor project to transport green hydrogen from Algeria to Europe.
The declaration was signed following the second ministerial meeting of the five partner countries in the Algerian capital.
The project will transport 4 million tons of green hydrogen annually from Algeria to Austria, Germany and Italy along a roughly 3,000-kilometer *1,864-mile) route, equivalent to about 10% of Europe’s projected demand for the clean fuel by 2040.
The project is expected to use existing natural gas pipeline infrastructure, which would be upgraded and adapted for hydrogen transportation.
Work on the project began in October 2024 in Oran, where Algeria’s Sonatrach and Sonelgaz signed a memorandum of understanding with Germany’s VNG, Italy’s Snam and SeaCorridor and Austria’s VERBUND Green Hydrogen to conduct studies on the feasibility and profitability of an integrated project to produce green hydrogen in Algeria and export it to Europe.
The first ministerial meeting was held in Rome in January 2025 and resulted in the signing of a declaration of political intent on the strategic project, with the parties agreeing to strengthen cooperation through a five-country working group.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune also received the energy ministers of Austria, Italy, Germany and Tunisia following Thursday’s meeting.

The Russian government has submitted a draft federal budget for 2027–2029 to the State Duma, Meduza reported on 30 September, citing TASS. In all three years, Russia's expenditures will exceed its revenues, the outlet noted.
Russia's finances have been eroding since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. To keep paying for the war, the Kremlin has drained its reserves, borrowed more, and pushed tax burdens onto residents and businesses, while the wider economy stalls.
The government listed social obligations, including aid to those who fought in its war against Ukraine and their families, along with defense needs among the budget's priorities, while its press release left out the planned cuts to social spending and the rise in military spending, Meduza noted, citing The Bell.
Spending will exceed revenue by about 2% of GDP a year
Russia's federal budget for 2027 sets spending at 48.8 trillion rubles ($585 billion) and revenue at 43.3 trillion ($519 billion), the Russian government stated, leaving a deficit of 5.5 trillion rubles ($66 billion). It claimed the draft is "balanced" and that healthcare spending will rise compared with 2026.
Deficits of 5.1 trillion rubles ($61 billion) in 2028 and 5.3 trillion ($64 billion) in 2029 are also planned, about 2% of GDP a year, Meduza noted.
This year's deficit is now set to reach a record 7.345 trillion rubles ($88 billion), nearly double the previous forecast of 3.785 trillion ($45 billion), The Moscow Times reported on 1 October. To help close the gap, Moscow plans an array of tax hikes for 2027–2029 to fund military spending. Already by May, its four-month deficit had run 50% above what it had planned for the whole year.
Even as the deficit widens, Russia plans its highest defense spending since the full-scale invasion began: 17.1 trillion rubles ($202.58 billion) in 2027, 27% more than the 13.5 trillion originally planned.
Only 2.3 trillion rubles ($28 billion) of that sum is itemized in public documents, and 34.9% of all 2027 spending will be classified, the highest share in at least 12 years, exiled outlet Vyorstka reported. The Duma is expected to hold the first of three readings on 29 October, the date proposed by Budget Committee chairman Andrei Makarov, Interfax reported.

US Congress ought to fix the flawed Saudi nuclear deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:15 UTC
01:41:15 KST

The confusion surrounding a proposed civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia has not exactly disappeared: The White House is still claiming it depends on the country normalizing relations with Israel, even if that is not part of the written agreement. At least the US Congress now has the text for review. Having seen its flaws, legislators should demand changes.
The 30-year nuclear cooperation pact would allow US companies not only to build new reactors in the kingdom, but possibly also a uranium enrichment facility — needed to produce the fissile material for a bomb. The two governments would have up to two years to decide whether an indigenous enrichment program makes sense, both commercially and in terms of US national interests. If so, the US would introduce, but restrict the sensitive technology, keeping it in a metaphorical “black box” to prevent transfer to the Saudis. Congress has 90 days in session to decide whether to oppose the deal; otherwise, it will go into effect automatically.
Proceeding on such terms would be risky. For decades, the US and other nuclear suppliers have refused to provide customers with the technology to enrich uranium or reprocess spent fuel, precisely so they could not assemble the working materials for a bomb. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman has already said his nation would “have to” match Iran if it develops a nuclear weapon; the mere possibility that the Saudis might do so would encourage other countries in the region to pursue one as well. Any restricted facilities would be vulnerable to leakage, if not outright seizure.
It is unclear why the US even needs to offer such a concession. Other suppliers are not threatening to provide the same access to enrichment technology; Russia and China compete mainly on cost. Besides, the Saudis have been pursuing access to US nuclear technology for nearly two decades. They have had plenty of time to seek alternatives if they wished. Breaking with precedent, on the other hand, could liberate US rivals to do the same. (Russia is already leading major reactor projects in Egypt and Turkey.) It would also dramatically weaken the US case against allowing Iran a domestic enrichment program.
While a joint resolution opposing the agreement seems unlikely to muster a veto-proof majority, Congress should still use this chance to press for greater clarity and stronger safeguards against proliferation.
At minimum, lawmakers should thoroughly scrutinize the classified documents linked to the deal, including two secret side letters, and insist on answers to unresolved questions such as whether the Saudis would be allowed to pursue an independent enrichment program if the joint study decides against one. Congress should insist on input into that study, to ensure the arguments against allowing nuclear fuel-making are fully absorbed.
Legislators should continue to push for the Saudis to sign an Additional Protocol with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), allowing for expanded international inspections. Failing that, they should press the administration to work with the IAEA on expedited procedures to investigate any suspicions that the Saudis might be pursuing a hidden enrichment or weapons program. Perhaps most important, Congress should lay out severe consequences for such cheating — including asset freezes and cutting off access to other US technology.
The administration should be commended for looking for ways to boost US nuclear exports, but that goal should not be pursued at any cost — and Congress should say so clearly.

The new underground Tainan Railway Station was unveiled to the public for the first time yesterday ahead of its official opening next month.
The Tainan City Government said that train operations are scheduled to officially move to the new underground station on Oct. 18.
The Railway Bureau said that the existing Tainan Railway Station, a designated national heritage site, would be closed for restoration once the new underground station becomes operational.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Train passengers would access the new underground facility through a different entrance while the train station is being restored, it said.
The bureau invited news media to see the facilities inside the newly built station, including the train control room, central monitoring room, telecommunications equipment room, tunnel ventilation plant room and ballastless tracks.
The station would be equipped with the Taiwan Railway Corp’s fourth-generation ticketing machines, which have eliminated the function for processing magnetic-stripe tickets and would be equipped with QR code scanners.
The Tainan underground railway station is equipped with a range of new rail, signaling and safety systems designed to improve train operations and passenger safety, the bureau’s Southern Region Engineering Branch said in its briefing.
The underground railway has 10 ventilation rooms equipped with 19 tunnel ventilation fans, silencers, control dampers and power-supply equipment. The systems provide routine air circulation and can be switched to emergency ventilation mode during fires to remove smoke and maintain airflow, making it possible for personnel to evacuate within 900 seconds of critical period.
The station’s train control room is equipped with signaling control units, control panels, train information displays, overhead power control switches, closed-circuit television cameras, and wired and wireless dispatch communications.
The equipment enables dispatchers to monitor train locations, track conditions and switch status in real time, and adjust train operations or respond to incidents as needed, the bureau said.
A central monitoring room serves as the control hub for the underground railway tunnels and station.
It monitors tunnel ventilation, power supplies, access control, lighting, fire alarms, elevators and escalators, while CCTV provide views of the station concourse, platforms and underground tunnels.
The train control room and central monitoring room are considered the “brains” of the new underground railway station.
Railway Bureau Deputy Director-General Liu Yun-sheng (劉雲生) said the station combines architectural elements reflecting Tainan’s history with rail, electrical and safety technologies to support safe and stable operations.
The bureau said that it is to hold open-house tours for the public this weekend and on Tuesday next week, led by professionals.

Manufacturing PMI rises to five-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:14 UTC
01:41:14 KST

Taiwan’s manufacturing sector expanded at its fastest pace in more than five years last month, as robust demand for artificial intelligence (AI) hardware continued to drive growth, despite easing new orders and mounting supply and cost pressures, the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER, 中華經濟研究院) said yesterday.
The manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI) climbed to 63.4 from 61.7 in August, its highest level since August 2021, with all six major industries reporting improved business conditions, the institute said.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA
“AI demand continues to drive manufacturing growth, with the benefits gradually extending to nonmanufacturing sectors,” CIER president Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明) told a news conference in Taipei.
The expansion remained particularly strong in technology-related industries, although its pace moderated somewhat, Lien said.
The new orders index, a leading indicator of future activity, fell 2.9 points to 63.6. Manufacturers reported shortages of some materials, excess inventories of others and longer delivery times, all of which were complicating production schedules, the institute said.
The combination suggests manufacturers are shifting some focus from expanding output to managing inventory and supply-chain pressures, it said.
AI-related demand remains the main support for manufacturing, while rising energy costs amid heightened tensions in the Middle East have sharply increased raw material prices and prompted companies to reallocate orders, Supply Management Institute in Taiwan (中華採購與供應管理協會) adviser Jerry Pai (白宗城) said.
Petrochemical producers are facing higher raw material and transportation costs, while demand remains relatively firm for advanced semiconductor materials, specialty chemicals and materials used in precision medical products, Pai said.
Manufacturers are also reviewing products and production plans for next year, while new product trials and testing are competing for capacity already strained by long lead times, potentially weighing on some short-term PMI readings, he said.
Still, the six-month business outlook remained firmly in expansion territory at 59.5 last month, the highest reading since May 2024, with all six major industries expecting growth, the institute said.
Meanwhile, the nonmanufacturing index rose for a 19th consecutive month to 56.9, indicating that the manufacturing boom is gradually extending into services, including stock-related and tourism businesses, the CIER said.
Service sector companies also became more optimistic about fourth-quarter activity, although persistent cost and delivery pressures remained a concern, it said.
Lien cautioned that the expansion remains uneven, with a pronounced gap between technology and non-technology industries.
“We hope other industries can gradually catch up as the tech sector expands, narrowing the gap across the economy, but so far, the tech sector remains exceptionally strong,” Lien said.

Woman hospitalized after surviving execution twice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

A Tennessee woman convicted of murder yesterday survived two lethal injection doses and was hospitalized, her lawyers said, marking the state’s second failed execution in months and prompting it to halt capital punishment this year.
Hours earlier on Wednesday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for Christa Pike, 50, to become the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in 200 years — but the attempt failed.
“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” Death Penalty Information Center executive director Robin Maher said. “There is no precedent.”
Photo: Tennessee Department of Correction via REUTERS
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol.”
Her attorneys said she was transported to a nearby hospital, adding they have not been informed as to her condition.
“Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution,” the attorneys said in a statement.
Tennessee halted the execution by lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after medical staff were unable to tap a vein.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee called for a “comprehensive, third-party review” after Pike’s failed execution.
“The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year,” Lee said — apparently referencing the execution of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton scheduled for Dec. 3.
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer’s body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike’s lawyers said she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
“She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill,” they said.
The US Supreme Court on Tuesday rejected an application for a stay of execution, which said that Pike’s history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause “needless suffering.”

Advocates call for research into owls at Shalun park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:13 UTC
01:41:13 KST

Environmental advocates called for an investigation into the pre-breeding population size of eastern grass owls, the population density of rodents and the preservation of habitats for the critically endangered bird species in the Shalun Science Park development project.
Based in the Shalun (沙崙) area around Tainan High Speed Rail Station in the city’s Gueiren District (歸仁), the 507-hectare project is part of the government’s Southern Taiwan Silicon Valley Program, which aims to build a semiconductor industry S-corridor in southern Taiwan.
The project’s second scoping meeting was held at the Ministry of Environment in Taipei yesterday.
Photo: CNA
Environmental groups focusing on different fields yesterday attended the meeting to express concerns over the project’s public health risks, carbon emissions, water usage plan and biodiversity preservation plan.
Of all the discussed issues, the habitat conservation for eastern grass owls was at center of debate.
The critically endangered bird species has an estimated population size of 200 to 500 nationwide, with its population highly restricted to southern Taiwan.
Apple Bird Satoyama Conservation Foundation representative Tseng Lung-yung (曾瀧永) said that roadkill is the leading cause of eastern grass owl deaths while rodenticides are a sublethal factor for the rodent-eating raptor.
Eastern grass owls need large, undivided grassland covering at least 200 hectares for habitat and an area of 20 hectares to 70 hectares for nest range, he said.
“Micro shelters” planted with white cogongrass and covering only 10 hectares or less might not help preserve eastern grass owls at the project site, Tseng said.
Tseng also called for a rodent population density survey to ensure that eastern grass owls have sufficient food without excessive rodenticide intake.
“Eastern grass owl conservation does not conflict with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co setting up fabs at the science park,” he said, adding that the disagreement lies in different conservation thinking.
Tseng said that owl habitat preservation should be established before the project started construction, which could happen in 18 months.
“Creating an eastern grass owl habitat requires two years,” he said, adding the habitat preservation effort is falling behind.
Tainan City Wildlife Conservation Association executive director Tseng I-shuo (曾翌碩) said it might be difficult to establish the causal link between rodenticide intake from the project site and eastern grass owl deaths.
While wildlife could have trace elements accumulating in their body just like humans, eastern grass owls have an activity range of up to 300 hectares, making it difficult to identify their exact forage locations, he said.
Tseng Lung-yung said that if a causal link cannot be established between the project’s rodenticide use and its eastern grass owl population size, then it cannot be built between the government’s regional eco-friendly farming practices and the bird species’ population growth.
He called for an investigation to ensure eastern grass owls have a pre-breeding population size of at least 100 adult birds.
Taiwan People’s Party Legislator Chen Gao-tzu (陳昭姿), who also attended the meeting, asked the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency to designate major wildlife habitats for eastern grass owls at the project site.
She said she would list the issue as a resolution for review by the legislature.

Old masters, wider worlds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:41:11 UTC
01:41:11 KST

Van Gogh once said that he would starve himself to spend time with Rembrandt’s The Jewish Bride.
“I should be happy to give 10 years of my life if I could go on sitting here in front of this picture for a fortnight, with only a crust of dry bread for food,” van Gogh said.
The quote can be found at “Old Masters From Rembrandt to Goya,” an exhibition of 52 masterpieces from the Toledo Museum of Arts at the Fubon Museum in Taipei.
Photo: Bonnie White, Taipei Times
Rembrandt’s deep influence on van Gogh is a central theme to the exhibition which shows how European artists not only influenced each other, but were also influenced by their society and foreign cultures.
It is Rembrandt’s mastery of chiaroscuro and his unmatched ability to portray the emotional depth of his subjects that inspired van Gogh to spend hours looking at his paintings in Dutch museums.
In the section titled “Painting and Power”, monastic depictions and Napoleonic propaganda show how royal patrons and wealthy elites sought influence by wielding artistic commissions.
In The Oath of the Horatii (1786) commissioned by King Louis XVI, Jacques-Louis David contrasts determined male postures with women slumped in desperation to frame militaristic ambition as a moral virtue.
Seventeenth-century Dutch painters fractured this dynamic. Bypassing church and royal patrons, artists catered to a rising middle class.
Rembrandt embraced this shift to paint uncommissioned character studies. Two of his tronies displayed by van Gogh’s commendation, portray anonymous characters in theatrically flamboyant costumes.
The portraits, from his early and late period, offer a transfixing repertoire of his ability to grasp evocative facial expressions and capture light and shadow.
Yet, this emancipated merchant market still demanded structure. Thomas de Keyser’s portrait of authoritative Dutch guild officers debunks the lone genius trope to reveal how production markets actually sustained painters such as Rembrandt.
This new market based on a flourishing colonial economy also brought new artistic focus, introducing painters to imported commodities and turning bustling ports into landscape studios.
In the “European Art in a Global Context” section, Chinese porcelain, rare Turkish tulips and shells from the Indonesian archipelago in van der Astat’s Fruits, Flowers and Shells (1620s) reveal the Dutch East India company’s vast colonial expeditions.
Across the room, van Goyen’s View of Dordrecht (1649) shows billowing clouds above fleets of boats in the bustling Dutch port, capturing the momentum of a nation securing dominance over trade routes.
By the eighteenth century, artistic influence spread beyond colonial conquests and stolen luxuries. Genre work was popularized as painters elevated as subject matter ordinary people and everyday life.
In the “Everyday Beauty” section, Jean-Simeon Chardin paints textured surfaces and light effects in The Washerwoman and The Woman Drawing Water at the Cistern (1733-39), to transform laborious domestic settings into harmonious scenes.
“We have learned from Chardin that a pear is as living as a woman, that an ordinary piece of pottery is as beautiful as a precious stone,” said French writer Marcel Proust.
This elevation of feeling over form laid the groundwork for nineteenth-century Romanticism, during which artists rejected the order, logic and classical restraint of the Enlightenment to portray emotions.
In the “Capturing Nature” section, Theodore Rousseau’s Under the Birches, Evening (1842-43), shows an idyllic summer evening in the countryside by contrasting a darkening dusk sky with colorful autumn trees set ablaze by fading light.
Using impressionist-like brushstrokes and dabbed highlights John Constable brings movement to his landscape Arundel Mill and Castle (1837). Shifting clouds, the rustle of trees and dappling sunlight seemingly extend beyond the canvas.
While Rousseau and Constable searched for emotional resonance, Francisco Goya was inspired by the human condition.
Often remembered for his work consumed by the dark, psychological depths of his permanent deafness and the brutal French invasion of Spain, the exhibition anchors Goya in an earlier, unshadowed chapter of his life.
In his tapestry cartoon Children in a Cart (1778), Goya captures an optimistic world with playful and smiling youth before the political and personal upheavals that would eventually shatter his life and alter European art.
For art enthusiasts, this is a unique opportunity to map the societal shifts and cultural revolutions that transformed European painting from the Renaissance to Neoclassicism.
Sept. 28 to Oct. 4 Opening in 1971, Singapore’s Wisma Theatre (海燕歌劇院) was entirely modeled after Taiwanese live variety shows, combining singing, dancing and drama. Even its performers were recruited from Taiwan. The formula was an instant hit, selling out on the third night with the crowd fighting outside for tickets. Among its key figures was 31-year-old Chi Li-nan (紀利男), an acclaimed saxophonist and band leader who had entered Taiwan’s live entertainment scene at age 19 with zero musical training. Chi wasn’t even supposed to be there. He had accompanied his girlfriend, pop singer Shang Kuan Ping (上官萍), to negotiations with Wisma’s agent.

Initially titled the Free China Review, and later rechristened as the Taiwan Review, the magazine published its final issue in March. Former editor Richard Vuylsteke has described the magazine as Taiwan’s “landmark foreign language publication going abroad.” The magazine was not universally respected.
