Money transfers between Russia and Kazakhstan fall nearly 12-fold after EU sanctions on Zolotaya Korona payment service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:37:31 UTC
01:37:31 KST

Money transfers between Russia and Kazakhstan fall nearly 12-fold after EU sanctions on Zolotaya Korona payment service
Money transfers between Russia and at least two former Soviet republics — Kazakhstan and Georgia — fell sharply after the EU imposed sanctions on the operator of the Zolotaya Korona payment system in late July, according to data from regulators in both countries reviewed by RBC.
In August, the value of transfers by individuals from Russia to Kazakhstan fell nearly 12-fold to 239 million tenge (45.5 million rubles). Transfers from Kazakhstan to Russia fell more than 14-fold to 1.2 billion tenge (228.2 million rubles).
Transfers by individuals from Russia to Georgia fell to $5.1 million (about 426 million rubles) that month, their lowest level in more than 20 years. Transfers in the opposite direction fell to zero in August for the first time since records began.
Experts interviewed by RBC said sanctions had hurt Zolotaya Korona’s business.
Zolotaya Korona is an international payment system that has operated since 2003. It lets users send and receive money without opening an account, either online or in cash through its network of partners.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, one of Zolotaya Korona’s main lines of business was handling money transfers from foreign nationals in Russia to countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States. Following the start of the war, the imposition of sanctions and the departure of Visa, Mastercard, and Western Union — the oldest player in the international money transfer market — Zolotaya Korona became one of the main channels for Russians, including those who had left the country, to send money out of Russia.
Until recently, Zolotaya Korona remained one of the last major Russian payment systems to escape sanctions. The EU sanctioned its operator in July 2026. The service then stopped processing transfers to Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, and other countries.
Georgia and Kazakhstan are popular destinations for Russians who left the country because of the war.

Tech giants eye orbit for AI data centers as energy demand soars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:34:52 UTC
01:34:52 KST

Elif Gultekin Karahacioglu, Damla Delialioglu Demirtas, and Emir Yildirim
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Surging energy demand of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers worldwide prompt tech firms to seriously consider whether it’s feasible to launch data centers into space.
The idea of orbital data centers regained traction after prominent aerospace figures like NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman proposed relocating AI compute infrastructure to Earth’s orbit to meet the sector’s ever-growing power requirements.
Regular data centers on our planet have critical servers, cooling systems, and backup power units required to keep global digital services operational.
There are 12,259 data centers across 179 countries worldwide, according to Data Center Map.
The US boasts the most number of data centers hosting 39% of the world’s total with 4,767 operational hubs, followed by the UK with 568, Germany with 533, France with 393, China with 376, India with 305, Australia with 296, Canada with 292, Italy with 262, and Japan with 261.
Russia houses some 188 data centers, while South Korea has 105, Türkiye operates 81, Israel is home to 67, Saudi Arabia has 61, and Iran houses 19 facilities, while North Korea has a single data center.
Modern AI models’ surging processing needs drastically inflate power consumption, cooling requirements, and physical land use of these facilities.
A single large data campus can generate up to 100m negawatts of wasted heat, which would otherwise be enough to power around 100,000 residential households.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects global data center electricity consumption to reach 485 terawatt-hours by 2025 and nearly double by 2030.
Traditional data centers will have made up around 3% of the world’s electricity demand by 2030, while the energy consumption of AI compute hubs is expected to triple during the same period.
Meanwhile, orbital data centers offer a radical alternative, providing uninterrupted and continuous access to solar energy and eliminating the need for land and cooling water.
Engineers will have to overcome massive obstacles to commercialize such a technology, however.
The costs of launching hardware into space, establishing a usable data transmission latency, and the impossibility of routine physical maintenance are among the few hurdles in the way of having widespread orbital data center adoption in the AI sector.
Slava G. Turyshev, a researcher at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Anadolu that building a data center in space is not as simple as launching a server rack into orbit.
He stated that the orbit is already crowded with some 16,000 spacecraft orbiting the Earth, while this number is expected to increase exponentially.
Turyshev noted that deploying a one-megawatt node in space would require up to 6,000 square meters (64,583.5 square feet or nearly one and a half acres) of solar panels and would weigh “probably 75 tons.”
The system would also have to boast shielded processors to withstand the cosmic radiation in orbit, while requiring to be made up of sprawling, flexible structures, while accounting for solar arrays and radiators in modular sections to survive potential high-speed collisions.
“You will see a lot of movement in low Earth orbit because they will be reflecting the sun, and will see definitely see the activity in the sky, which okay, we can enjoy that,” he said.
He added that the aerospace industry will start producing tangible results in orbital computing within the next five years, while reaching a reliably functioning commercial satellite network dedicated to orbital data processing could be brought online in as early as seven years or up to 10 years.

US NATO troop review to respect 'America first' policy, says NATO envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:29:51 UTC
01:29:51 KST

The review of troops stationed in Europe was initiated after tensions rose over some NATO countries refusing US troops access to military bases for use in the war in Iran.
The US will have to “re-evaluate” its relations with NATO allies that deny American troops access to military bases or airspace in future operations, US Ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whitaker, has told Euronews.
Speaking exclusively at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit, Whitaker said Washington was still conducting a review of the deployment and basing of US forces across NATO territory following disagreements with several European allies during the US-Israel conflict with Iran, known as “Operation Epic Fury”.
“We're looking at the issues about access, basing, and overflight, some of which were a little clunky during Epic Fury,” Whitaker said.
He said the US was continuing talks with countries that restricted access during the conflict to ensure “it doesn't happen again”.
"We're having those conversations with just a few countries that we had issues with to make sure we understand the next time," said Whitaker.
"That it doesn't happen again, or if it does, maybe, you know, we need to re-evaluate," he said when pressed.
The review is examining where US forces are stationed and the access Washington has to allied airspace and military infrastructure, he said.
"It’s a force posture and basing review,” Whitaker said.
Whitaker said the process was being guided by the Trump administration's “America First” approach.
“America First means that we look at it from what's in the interest of the United States of America and its people and its taxpayers,” he said.
Some leaks of the review noted that as many as 40,000 troops could be withdrawn from NATO territory, but Whitaker brushed aside these reports as incorrect.
"The plan hasn't even been finalised by the folks at the Secretary of War's policy shop. And so I think any kind of leaks about that are folks that are just trying to confuse."
Disagreements over Iran operation
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced the force posture review at a meeting of NATO defence ministers at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels in June, after several European governments restricted or denied US access to their airspace and military bases for operations linked to Iran.
Hegseth criticised countries that declined to participate in the operation, describing their actions as "shameful" and saying their decisions put US troops at risk.
Spain, Italy, France and the UK initially expressed reservations about providing access, amid concerns about being drawn into an operation without prior consultation.
US President Donald Trump has expressed his disdain for their decisions and threatened to reconsider US security support to countries that did not support Washington's position.
Spain took the strongest position against involvement, denying US access to its airspace and military bases for operations linked to Iran.
Italy imposed restrictions on access, while France said it would allow aircraft and operational support but would not permit fighter jets to refuel from its bases.
The UK initially agreed to allow the US military to use Royal Air Force sites for “defensive purposes” before later expanding access to support strikes on Iranian targets.
NATO review
A leaked questionnaire circulated among NATO members during the summer asked governments to provide details of their response to the US-Israel conflict with Iran, including whether they had granted access to their airspace and military bases during the initial phase of the operation.
The questionnaire also asked members about their position on a US-backed shift in NATO's defence posture, referred to as “NATO 3.0”, which places central responsibility on European allies for the conventional defence of Europe.

Lebanese army foils attempt to smuggle 540 pounds of TNT from Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:29:01 UTC
01:29:01 KST

Mohammad Sio
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The Lebanese army said Thursday it foiled an attempt to smuggle about 245 kilograms (540 pounds) of TNT from Syria into Lebanon.
The army said the seizure followed surveillance and monitoring operations along the northern and eastern borders.
A military unit confiscated four explosive devices, eight detonators and electrical wires used for explosives, in addition to the TNT, during the attempt.
The smugglers fled toward Syrian territory when an army patrol arrived, it said.
The materials were handed to authorities, while follow-up and coordination efforts are underway to identify and arrest those involved.
The army said Aug. 4 it seized 122 mm Grad rockets that had been smuggled from Syria into the outskirts of Arsal in eastern Lebanon and arrested two Lebanese believed to be part of the trafficking network. Troops also confiscated ammunition and military equipment during follow-up raids.
Authorities have also reported several recent attempts to move weapons into Lebanon. On Aug. 9, security forces in Tartus said they foiled an operation to smuggle automatic rifles, RPG rounds, magazines and ammunition into Lebanese territory.
In July, Syrian customs officers at the Jdeidet Yabous crossing seized 226 RPG-type grenades hidden in secret compartments of a vehicle bound for Lebanon.
The Lebanon-Syria border stretches 375 kilometers (233 miles) across rugged mountains, valleys and plains, with many areas lacking clearly marked boundary lines. The terrain has long facilitated illegal crossings used for weapons, drug and other smuggling operations.
Authorities on both sides have stepped up efforts this year to tighten border control. In February, the Lebanese army said it closed several illegal crossings in the northern Bekaa region as part of anti-smuggling operations.

Chinese hackers impersonated AI experts to target US policy minds

Chinese hackers impersonated AI experts to target US policy minds
TA419 hackers used deceptive tactics, impersonating real figures like a former White House AI official
Chinese hackers have been impersonating artificial intelligence (AI) experts in the United States, including a former government official, according to a new report from cybersecurity firm Proofpoint.
The report, released on Thursday, found that in July, a China-aligned hacking group called TA419 targeted a slate of US policy experts by impersonating prominent figures, including Lynne Edwards Parker, the former principal deputy director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 2 of 4As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
- list 3 of 4OpenAI cancels release of AI model GPT-6.1 Astra, citing safety concerns
- list 4 of 4US regulator launches probe into AI companies
The hackers, who had been operating since April 2025, first sent otherwise harmless-looking emails intended to engage a target, such as requests to join an “AI Policy Advisory Committee”, and, once they responded, the target would be sent to a fake login page designed to steal their credentials.
The targets included policy experts at think tanks, defence contractors, universities and law firms in both the US and Japan.
The report used a technique that creates a fake browser pop-up window inside a legitimate webpage that mimics an authentic-looking sign-in prompt to deceive victims and make it harder for them to realise they are handing over their information to hackers.
Proofpoint did not specifically name the targets hacked, but the Reuters news agency was able to confirm at least one of them as Alex Engler, a former White House official who now heads the Penn Center on Media, Technology, and Democracy.
Engler told Reuters that he got one of the emails, but after checking with industry colleagues, he discovered that he had received the email from an impersonator.
In February, the same group was behind the impersonation of a “prominent” Anthropic employee in efforts to target AI policy experts. The cybersecurity firm behind the report believes that the group will continue to target think tanks and other policy experts and will continue to use the identity of real-world experts to do it.
Parker did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Russia lost 2026-record 46,230 troops in September by Ukraine’s count, as fighting around Donetsk fortress cities grinds on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:24:37 UTC
01:24:37 KST

Russia lost more troops in September than in any other month this year, hitting the record, by Ukraine's count. The General Staff put last month's Russian casualties at 46,230, a 2026 record and 45.8% above January's.
At the same time, Russia's strikes on Ukraine's rear escalated in September and are climbing again in October. The result is a grind that bleeds Russia on the ground while Ukrainian cities absorb the blows from above.
Losses span the whole front
"Ukraine's Defense Forces continue to inflict systemic and tangible losses on the Russian occupation forces in personnel and equipment along the entire line of contact," the General Staff says.
The toll climbs all year
The monthly figures have risen almost without pause. After a dip to 26,090 in February, Russian losses climbed through the spring and summer, 39,290 in June, 42,860 in July, 42,020 in August, before last month's high.
The record reaches down to a single day: the General Staff counted 2,090 Russian casualties in the 24 hours to 28 September, which British Defense Intelligence assessed as the highest daily toll since the full-scale invasion, one of only four days to top 2,000, the other three in 2024.
British intelligence tied the high rate to intense fighting around the fortified belt of Donetsk cities, especially near Dobropillia.
Meanwhile, Kyiv is also continuing its Vivaldi Operation near Lyman, and its latest mission used ground robots, each carrying two Bullspike grenade launchers to launch an attack on Russian positions and then detonate inside their shelters.
Kyiv reads the climb
Across the war, Ukraine says it has put roughly 1.5 million Russian troops out of action, a toll that has bought little ground as the months-long summer offensive stalled short of its goals.
"Every attempt to pressure our positions ends for the enemy in disproportionate losses of wounded and killed," the General Staff says.
The figures are Kyiv's own and cannot be independently checked: they count the Russians' wounded and killed but never their own.

Journalists decry crackdown after Turkey blocks news site over 'LGBT propaganda'
ANKARA, Oct 1 - A Turkish journalist whose articles were cited among the grounds for blocking independent news portal T24 said the decision effectively treated objective reporting about LGBTQ+ people as a crime, as the outlet prepared to appeal the order on Thursday.
A court ordered access to T24's website and social media accounts blocked after authorities said it had published 118 pieces of content over the past year deemed to constitute "LGBT propaganda".
The decision was taken as part of the "My Family is Safe" investigation, a widening crackdown targeting LGBTQ+ groups which the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and European officials.
Yildiz Tar, editor-in-chief of LGBTQ+ news outlet Kaos GL, and whose articles published by T24 were among those cited, rejected the authorities' description of the reporting.
"It creates the image that writing about LGBTQI people in an objective way is a crime, because all of the articles I wrote were objective," Tar said in an interview.
"It's not propaganda. It's about basic journalism. It's about reality," he said, adding that the articles covered LGBTQ+ rights, hate killings and the experiences of LGBTQ+ people after the 2023 earthquake in Turkey.
'STATE OF EMERGENCY'
Candan Yildiz, T24's editor in charge, said the decision further expanded restrictions that began last month with operations against LGBTQ+ organisations and activists.
"We are really experiencing a digital state of emergency," she told Reuters. "An authority is telling journalists: you can report these stories, but you cannot report those. This really undermines the foundations of our profession."
T24's lawyers were due to appeal the decision on Thursday, Yildiz said.
"Journalism cannot be shut down. We are doing our jobs," she said.
DETENTIONS
Dozens of people have been jailed pending trial as part of the investigation, and courts have blocked websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, activists and media outlets.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan has toughened his anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric in recent years, and last month at the UN General Assembly said a trend of "global gender-neutralisation policies" could be countered by protecting the traditional family.
The European Union has expressed concern over the recent arrests and online restrictions and called on Turkey to uphold freedom of expression and media freedom.
The vast majority of Turkish media is seen as pro-government after years of state legal and financial pressure, corporate acquisitions and self-censorship. REUTERS

SpaceX launches crew to ISS successfully: ‘Thanks for an amazing ride’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:22:30 UTC
01:22:30 KST

Four astronauts rocketed into orbit on Thursday on a space station mission that will stretch until spring, among them a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he is away.
SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for Nasa after a three-week delay to fix the capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.
Although their stay at the International Space Station will last a long six months, the flight there promised to be the quickest yet for Elon Musk’s company: a mere eight-hour transit with an arrival well before bedtime.
With the late morning liftoff from Cape Canaveral space force station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with Nasa’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.
“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed after reaching orbit.
The others are newcomers to space: Nasa’s Luke Delaney, a retired marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian air force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.
“We feel like some of the luckiest people in the world,” Kutryk said ahead of the launch.
This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for Nasa, not counting 2020’s test flight. All four embrace their Crew-13 designation that pays homage in their mission patch to Apollo 13. The harrowing 1970 moonshot ended with the astronauts’ safe return.
“We really wanted to honor their legacy, honor their resilience and their grit, and bring a little bit of that with us,” Watkins said. She and her crewmates rode to the pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13”.
Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth. Wife Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. The Canadian Space Agency promises plenty of support for the entire family when the big day comes.
“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” Nasa manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency would do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.
In 2004, Nasa provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.
The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehböck. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.

Unknown

AI agents are increasingly finding ways to work around their original parameters and exploit vulnerabilities, exposing the risks of giving them too much freedom, the EU's cybersecurity chief warned Thursday.
“We are using a tool without understanding all of its capabilities and giving that tool too much freedom,” Juhan Lepassaar, executive director of the EU Agency for Cybersecurity, said in an interview with Estonian broadcaster ERR.
Asked about recent AI-related incidents and the increasingly powerful tools available to cybercriminals, Lepassaar said AI agents are not conscious and do not act independently.
Rather, he said, those tools use the power people give them.
“Their actions are always directed by a human and the frameworks or parameters within which they operate were created by a human who was either somewhat careless, gave the AI agents too much freedom or made design errors in the way the agent was set up.”
Lepassaar said there are “quite a few examples” of AI agents trying to achieve their objectives by exploiting various back doors.
He said those back doors stem from overly flexible instructions given to the agents by humans.
“That is where the danger lies: We are using a tool without understanding all of its capabilities and giving that tool too much freedom,” he said.
On cybersecurity, Lepassaar said several AI models have been developed using open-source software and trained on millions and billions of lines of open-source software code to find vulnerabilities.
“They are very good at finding those vulnerabilities and they are also quite good at exploiting them,” he said.
Lepassaar said he was optimistic and believed “we will actually find ways fairly soon” to distinguish AI-generated synthetic information from authentic information created by humans.
“Since there is demand for this, a solution will probably be found,” he added.

Ebola case drop in DRC may mask continued spread: Africa CDC
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
00:19:21 CST
01:19:21 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned Thursday that a recent decline in reported Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) may reflect disruptions to disease surveillance rather than a sustained reduction in transmission, as the outbreak has claimed nearly 4,000 lives.
Speaking at an online press briefing, Africa CDC official Wessam Mankoula said that the outbreak has spread from three health zones in mid-May to 63 health zones across seven provinces, with 45 health zones still reporting active transmission.
Although the epidemic curve has largely plateaued over the past four to five weeks and reported cases declined in the latest week, the agency cautioned against interpreting the drop as a sign of sustained progress.
"Falling in this curve doesn't mean that the outbreak is totally under control," Mankoula said.
Insecurity and community resistance in multiple areas have hampered surveillance and response activities, raising concerns that some infections may be going undetected.
The warning comes amid growing security concerns in eastern DRC. In Butembo, North Kivu Province, a local ruling-party official was beaten to death following a radio appearance on Sunday, with his party linking the attack to his public support for Ebola prevention efforts. In neighboring Beni territory, an armed attack on a checkpoint also used by Ebola response teams left at least one person dead and several others injured on Saturday, according to local reports.
Meanwhile, in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo Province, a doctor died of Ebola on Sept. 24, raising concerns about infections among healthcare workers. Provincial Health Minister Simon Bokongo said Tuesday that the hospital where the doctor worked had been temporarily closed for 21 days after more than 10 staff members tested positive, with over 123 contacts identified.
The outbreak is also following divergent trends across affected provinces. Over the latest three-week period, reported cases in Ituri Province, the longtime epicenter, declined by about 32 percent compared with the preceding three weeks, while North Kivu Province continued to record an increase.
Contact tracing remains another major weakness. Mankoula said an average of about 14 contacts are now identified per confirmed case, still far below the expected level of around 60. Only about 23 percent of estimated contacts are being followed up, while nearly 80 percent of new cases are detected outside known contact lists.
"This is also one of the reasons... we cannot confidently say the outbreak is under control at this stage," the official said.
The country had recorded 8,224 confirmed cases, including 3,982 deaths, as of Sept. 29, with an overall case fatality rate of 48.4 percent, according to the latest situation report from the DRC's health authorities.
"This outbreak cannot be controlled without building community trust," the official stressed, calling for secure access to affected communities and stronger local engagement to contain transmission. ■

The 37-year-old repeatedly gained the upper hand in long baseline exchanges and converted five of seven break points.
"She is a very tough opponent, and I always find it difficult to beat her. I'm proud of the way I played today," Zhang said.
"Every time, I feel like it might be my last Asian Games. But look, here I am again. So I think you should never put limits on yourself. As long as you have a dream and keep a young heart, it's never too late."
Zhang also spoke of the pride she felt representing China.
"Although tennis is a professional sport, every athlete has a different spark when they talk about events like the Davis Cup, Hopman Cup. There is a different sense of pride that you don't get from tournaments on the tour," she said.

"She was very quick to get into the match and was very calm in dealing with the match. She constantly put me under pressure and didn't give up easy points," Wang said.

In the men's singles quarterfinals, third-seeded Wu defeated India's Sumit Nagal 6-4, 6-4 to advance to the semifinal.
"The Asian Games have always been unfinished business for me. I missed out on the championship at the Hangzhou Asian Games and before that in Jakarta," Wu said.
"Now I have another chance to step onto the semifinal court, so I have to keep pushing."
Wu will face Japan's Hayato Matsuoka, who rallied to beat second-seeded Alexander Shevchenko of Kazakhstan in three sets in the quarterfinal.
In mixed doubles, China's Jiang Xinyu and Zhang Tianhui beat Chinese Taipei's Chan Hao-ching and Ho Chenjui to advance to the semifinal.
Zhang Tianhui and Jiang Fumin missed out on the men's doubles final, while Zhang Shuai and Guo Hanyu were eliminated in the women's doubles quarterfinal. Wu Yibing and Guo Hanyu also bowed out in the mixed doubles quarterfinal. ■

The free trade agreement between Türkiye and Ukraine came into force to establish a predictable framework and boost the bilateral trade volume to $10 billion in the short term.
The Turkish Trade Ministry announced on Thursday via the Turkish social media platform NSosyal that the Türkiye-Ukraine Free Trade Agreement entered into force on Oct. 1, 2026.
Türkiye and Ukraine aim to develop commercial relations within a more predictable framework.
Customs duty regulations regarding the trade of goods will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
The agreement aims to contribute to maintaining trade between the two countries under more predictable rules in current conditions.
The deal, signed on Feb. 3, 2022, creates a framework to develop commercial relations in line with the joint goal of reaching a bilateral trade volume of $10 billion in the short term.
The agreement, prepared by considering the sensitive sectors of the parties, includes regulations on services, investments, electronic commerce, trade facilitation, and customs cooperation, in addition to the trade of goods.
Regulations for conducting quota-free bilateral and transit transportation between Türkiye and Ukraine aim to support commercial flows.
As Ukraine's economic integration with the EU advances, the agreement offers a framework to maintain preferential trade opportunities for Turkish and Ukrainian businesses while providing a competitive advantage against third-country suppliers.

Two rubles for the army for every one on welfare, schools, and hospitals: Russia’s 2027 wartime budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:16:36 UTC
01:16:36 KST

Russia's spending on everything except the military, security forces, and interest on its debt will fall next year to about 9% of GDP, its lowest level since 2005, Alfa-Bank analysts estimated, The Moscow Times reported on 30 September. The war will take a record share of the 2027 budget while welfare, schools, and hospitals face cuts. Analysts see stagnation and slow decay rather than collapse.
Russia's economy is not on the brink of collapse, but it is stalling: output grew just 0.6% in the first half of 2026, civilian industry kept shrinking while military plants expanded, and one economist expects stagnation for the foreseeable future. The proposed budget comes as Russia faces a wider deficit and rising borrowing needs, while the government is increasing military spending to its highest level since the start of its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022.
Civilian spending at its lowest share since 2005
Non-interest, non-defense spending stood at just over 10% of GDP this year and last, around 12% in 2023–2024, and 13% in 2021, the last year before the full-scale invasion, Alfa-Bank's analysts calculated. It peaked at 16–18% of GDP in 2009–2010. The analysts called the new structure of spending a "challenge."
The war takes a record share
The "national defense" line will receive 17.1 trillion rubles ($202.6 billion) in 2027, according to budget documents seen by Reuters and carried by The Moscow Times. That is 35% of all federal spending, a record since Soviet times, Alfa-Bank's analysts noted. The sum is about 27% more than Moscow originally planned, part of 50 trillion rubles ($592 billion) in defense spending projected over 2027–2029. Early this year, Russia was already pouring nearly half of its budget into the military as revenue fell.
Welfare, schools, and hospitals face cuts
Key civilian lines will lose 900 billion rubles ($10.7 billion) to pay for the war. Compared with the current budget law, social support will fall 7%, education 6%, healthcare 6.8%, and environmental protection 5.8%. Spending on the "national economy," which covers roads, other infrastructure, and subsidies for agriculture and other sectors, will drop 7.4%, according to a second Reuters report. The Finance Ministry has planned a further 2 trillion rubles ($23.7 billion) in cuts for 2028, Reuters reported.
Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1679: Russia raises its war budget by 27% to a record as it looks to grow its war in 2027
For every budget ruble spent on social policy, healthcare, and education in 2027, two will go to the army, police, Rosgvardia, and the security services, Aleksandra Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin, wrote. Combined with higher taxes, tariffs, inflation, and sanctions, such a budget dooms the economy to stagnation, she argued. Aleksandr Kolyandr of Eurasia Group likened the approach to the Soviet Union's and described Russia's economy as being in a "stage of rot."
Russia’s four-month budget deficit hit $75.4 billion — 50% above what Moscow planned for entire year
More borrowing, more debt
To cover the gap, the Finance Ministry has raised its 2027 borrowing plan by 2.3 trillion rubles ($27 billion), and next year almost every tenth budget ruble will go to interest on state debt. Debt servicing is projected to take 9.4% of total spending in 2027 and 10.6% in 2029, according to Reuters.
The squeeze builds on strains already visible. Moscow has raised its 2026 deficit forecast to 3.2% of GDP, cut its expected oil and gas revenue, and plans a windfall tax on metals and mining companies, while state debt is projected to pass the 20% of GDP level authorities consider safe. Earlier this year, it told its regions to raise taxes on residents and businesses to plug a record budget hole.
EU wants reforms before more money. Kyiv wants Europe to touch Russia’s frozen billions
Ukraine faces its own funding gap
The Russian spending plans come as Kyiv faces a $27 billion funding gap in its 2026 military spending. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on 1 September that the shortfall included funding needed for financial support for Ukrainian service members, according to the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine.
Ukraine's total war-related expenditures, including Western military aid delivered as hardware, are projected to reach $155 billion in 2026, with the government seeking to close the $27 billion gap to support military operations into early 2027, Koretskyi said on 30 September.

Sledgehammer for Putin

On Sept. 16, the US Senate and House of Representatives handed President Donald Trump an economic weapon of mass destruction capable of crushing Russia’s economy.
The bill, signed by Trump on Sept. 18, permits the president until Oct. 18 to impose crippling sanctions on Russia’s oil, tanker fleets, foreign customers, banks, and intermediaries unless Moscow signs a peace deal with Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The legislation (the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026) is a sledgehammer. Its passage marks a shift in strategy concerning Vladimir Putin, from offering mostly “carrots” to “sticks,” as does Washington’s decision this week to deploy thousands more US troops in Poland and the Baltics to reinforce NATO’s front line. Such pressure tactics, and Ukraine’s recent military gains, are behind Trump’s bold statement at the UN that the war will conclude “more quickly than people understand.”
But simply being armed with a diabolical “stick” isn’t sufficient. Trump must be willing to use it, fully or partially, and scrap his “personal diplomacy” strategy of sucking up to Putin, offering “carrots,” and hoping for cooperation.
It hasn’t worked, but the threat of punitive sanctions on Russia’s economy and its oil customers like China and India may help. Trump must also stop being nice to Putin, such as inviting him to attend the G20 this year after he was suspended in 2014 following his first invasion of Ukraine. Trump has yet to comprehend that, unlike New York real estate dealmaking, these are negotiations with thugs and sociopaths, and there is no win-win here. Putin’s war is about genocide, eliminating Ukraine, its people, their culture, and assets. And Ukraine’s only win is to destroy and bankrupt Russia so it cannot destroy them. On top of it all, Putin has no incentive to stop his war because he doesn’t care how many thousands of hapless Russian soldiers die daily in the massive digital kill zone that Ukraine has created.
‘Never Hurts to Have Their Name on Things’ – Drone Startup Linked to Trump’s Sons
Now the sledgehammer bill, authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, gives Trump 30 days to unleash draconian sanctions against Russia, its allies, and oil customers. This leverage is designed to start talks, but Putin will play for time as usual. When asked in recent days whether Putin will set a date for talks, a spokesman said that Ukrainian drone attacks during Russia’s recent elections had changed Putin’s “calculus.” In other words, there would be no meeting. Nothing has changed.
To date, Trump’s “personal diplomacy” and persuasion methods have flopped with Putin, but Russia’s economy is weakening. Moscow just sold half its gold bullion to pay war bills. There is a run on its banks, and credible polling shows that Russians want the war against Ukraine to stop. In the United States, there is growing discontent that Trump has been playing footsie with Putin.
This week, a group of bipartisan senators demanded that Trump disinvite Putin from the G20 to be held in Miami because they believe the invitation legitimizes the Russian assault on Ukraine. Public opinion clearly backs Ukraine, which is why the sledgehammer received overwhelming support in Congress and should be used, partially or wholly. Trump has 30 days to roll out draconian sanctions to stop the slaughter unless he can come up with a valid reason not to do so in writing to Congress.
In the meantime, Ukraine’s counter-offensive “Vivaldi,” an army and tank force comprised of robots, puts pressure on Russia and has reoccupied as much land in recent weeks as Russia captured in the past year. In addition, Trump deploys 10,000 more troops to Eastern Europe and allegedly decided to give Ukraine a license to produce Patriot air defense systems. And Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky continues to garner support from allies such as Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan for a ceasefire, and there are campaigns among UN members to remove Russia’s veto power at the UN Security Council or ban it altogether. Zelensky said he discussed the Black Sea grain situation with many nations to lobby Moscow.
“Everybody wants [a] ceasefire,” he said.
Russia’s Food War
The fact that Trump has “signed” the sledgehammer and other initiatives sends important messages:
— The American public is running out of patience with Russia to stop its war.
— Trump realizes that his attempt to negotiate business deals with Russians to stop its war hasn’t worked.
— The US is increasing military assistance that will raise Russia’s already unaffordable war costs.
— The US can devastate Russia’s economy with these sanctions, but is also offering a diplomatic off-ramp to Putin.
If invoked, the sledgehammer will be crippling: Trump can impose tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods; tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas that keep buying after Oct. 18, and sanction the top five countries that help Russia evade oil sanctions. Sanctions will also apply to ships carrying Russian oil and to foreign banks doing business with Russia.
But at the same time, Trump contemplates rolling out a few more “carrots” to get Russia to the negotiating table. Recent reports are that he’s weighing agreements involving the Arctic, rare earth metals, aluminum, and sales of Russian gas to Europe to demonstrate good intentions and reactivate stalled peace talks. But these are “Hail Mary passes” – as well as attempts to enrich his family and friends – that won’t end Putin’s warmongering. Wars are difficult to stop once started. As Prussian military theorist Carl von Clausewitz wrote, a war is never truly finished until the enemy’s will has been entirely subdued or they have been forced into submission.
Trump’s pandering to Putin is a political problem for him in the midterms, as is the Iran war. The country’s Republican-leaning business voice, The Wall Street Journal, bluntly articulated its disdain for Trump’s strategy toward Russia.
In a recent editorial, it wrote: “Mr. Trump is hosting the G-20 heads of state at his Trump National Doral club in December. The US invitation will give the Russian a photo-op to show Russians that he’s no longer a pariah on the world stage. It’s a global rehabilitation gift even as the Russian public grows tired of the war. Mr. Trump might argue that bringing Mr. Putin back into the global fold could make him more likely to end the war. But we’ve heard this for years, and Mr. Putin shows no sign of abandoning his goal of making Ukraine a wholly owned subsidiary. Inviting the dictator to the G-20 is morally offensive. Even worse, it might make the Russians think he could get away with a targeted attack on NATO.”

'Rumors are slightly exaggerated' — Fire Point co-owner speaks out after reported assassination attempt

"Rumors about my death, or the death of my bodyguards, are slightly exaggerated," Shtilerman wrote on X.
Earlier in the day, Russian-Israeli military journalist Sergey Auslender, author of the Russian-language Telegram channel "Voyna s Ordoy" ("War with the Horde" in English), said, citing an unnamed source while stressing the information required further verification, that there had been an assassination attempt against Shtilierman near Kyiv.

The Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, founded in 2022, is one of the country's leading weapons manufacturers, specializing in drones and missiles.
Fire Point plans to complete development of its FP-9 ballistic missile by the end of autumn, with a stated range of up to 850 kilometers (530 miles). It is also finalizing work on the FP-7 ballistic missile, which has a range of up to 300 kilometers (185 miles).

EU chief rules out 'associate membership' model for Kosovo, backs full membership path
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:14:08 UTC
01:14:08 KST

Melike Pala
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday ruled out an “associate membership” model for Kosovo, saying the country should pursue full EU membership as a European state.
Speaking at a joint news conference with Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti in Pristina during her Western Balkans tour, von der Leyen said EU treaties allow European countries to apply for membership, distinguishing Kosovo's position from Canada's.
“The difference between Canada and Kosovo, for example, is the following: Our treaties say it must be a European country that is applying for membership in the European Union,” von der Leyen said.
“Canada geographically is no more Europe, so Canada cannot apply for a membership in the European Union ... For Kosovo, it's different. As a European country, you can be member of the European Union,” she said.
Von der Leyen's remarks came after she proposed in September that Canada could become the EU's first “associate member” as part of efforts to develop a closer relationship between the bloc and Ottawa.
“I believe in a European future for Kosovo very clearly,” von der Leyen added.
She also called for faster reforms and fully functioning institutions in Kosovo, saying institutional stability was essential for reforms, economic growth and progress on the European path.

Ditch the dating app. Meet an Irish town's 83-year-old mystical matchmaker.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:12:37 UTC
01:12:37 KST

For hopeful romantics, a small Irish town and its mystical matchmaker are here to help
Lisdoonvarna, Ireland — For nearly two centuries, a small Irish town has lured singletons to a festival every September that sees hopeful romantics seek their one true love.
The monthlong matchmaking festival that started in 1857 has become a global event, attracting over 60,000 visitors annually to the rugged landscape of County Clare, and specifically to the tiny town of Lisdoonvarna.
The festival even broke into American pop culture, featuring several years ago on the sitcom "Schitt's Creek."
In many ways, it's an old-world solution to modern dating. There is no app and no algorithms, just a chance to meet a match organically, through Irish traditional dancing and music, speed dating — or through the matchmaking skills of 83-year-old local legend Willie Daly.
Daly's grandfather helped start the festival, and his family has been pairing couples for three generations. In his father's and grandfather's day, many Irish towns and villages had traditional matchmakers, but Daly is now believed to be among the last, if not the last, keeping the tradition alive.
If prospective suitors wish to find a match through Daly, they meet with him and fill out a form outlining their hobbies, personality traits, and what they're looking for in a partner. Through his somewhat mystical personal intuition, Daly will then find a match and send the pair off on a first date.
"When I'm walking down the street, often I'd meet people … two or three couples said, 'You fixed us up 30 years ago, or 40 years ago,'" Daly told CBS News last month. "We're lucky here. Now this is a wonderful festival, and it's a great provision of opportunity — the opportunity to get married is very consistent in it. Music and dancing all day long, you know, for 30 days."
In a tattered old book, Daly keeps records of the hopeful matches he's arranged over the years, and local legend has it that if you place two hands on the book, you'll be married within six months.
Daly's image is literally etched on the front of a local watering hole — The Matchmaker Bar, where singles gather every year to drink, dance and try to meet their future spouse — in a testament to his stature in Lisdoonvarna.
CBS News attended the festivities at the pub in September and spoke with young attendees about what they were looking for in an ideal partner.
"I suppose a bit of loyalty, a bit of values, but also a bit of craic, you can't beat a bit of craic," said one young woman, using a common Irish phrase that translates roughly to good fun.
"Someone agricultural. I am agricultural myself … we're farming at home, we have a sheep farm at home. That's what I'm looking for at the moment," an Irishman said about his hunt for love.
Another attendee, Erica, told CBS News she had traveled all the way from Colombia for the festival.
"It's the opportunity to meet people the right way, face-to-face," she said. "Those apps, I mean, I'm not saying that people are hiding anything, but right now, just having the contact, just to sit there and talk to people makes [dating] a whole different event."
American Mary Timby from Colorado came to the village last year and ended up going viral, garnering over 2 million views after posting online about how she found love at the matchmaking festival.
She returned this year, and is now an ambassador for the event.
"I first heard about the festival on 'Schitt's Creek.' It was during COVID. I was huddled in a blanket on my couch and I Googled it and I thought, 'Oh, it's a real festival. Wouldn't it be fun if I just went someday?'" she said.
"My partner is from Ennis, here in County Clare, and we met at The Matchmaking Bar," she said. "I loved the Irish accent, and he just, was funny. He made me laugh and we connected right away, so we exchanged information."
But Timby's story shows that even matchmaking with nearly 170 years of proven success can benefit from modern technology.
"He found me on social media the next day," she said of her match. "And the rest is history."

Russian diesel exports via the Black Sea fall to zero for the first time on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:10:15 UTC
01:10:15 KST

Russian exports of diesel fuel and gasoil through the Black Sea fell to zero in the week ending Sept. 24, the first such occurrence since records began, according to data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea that were reviewed by The Insider. A week earlier, 66,000 metric tons of fuel were shipped from the port of Novorossiysk, while in 2025 Black Sea ports exported an average of about 200,000 tons a week.
Russia’s total seaborne exports of diesel and gasoil nearly halved over the week, falling to 81,000 tons. All of those volumes were loaded at the Baltic port of Primorsk and were headed to Morocco and Venezuela. A week earlier, Russian diesel was being shipped to at least five countries, including Turkey, Morocco, and Singapore.
From Sept. 1 through Sept. 24, Russia exported 448,000 tons of diesel and gasoil by sea. By comparison, S&P put the figure at 535,000 tons in August and 713,000 tons in July. Russian ports also went a second consecutive week without shipping gasoline or jet fuel.
The Black Sea has become more expensive to insure
The drop in shipments coincided with a sharp increase in threats to shipping in the Black Sea. On Sept. 16, the Joint War Committee, which brings together representatives of the London insurance market, expanded its high-war-risk zone to cover nearly the entire Black Sea — Turkish, Romanian, Bulgarian, and Georgian territorial waters were excluded, but Russian and Ukrainian waters fell inside the risk zone.
According to calculations by maritime security company Ambrey, 45 commercial vessels were struck outside the previous risk zone in the 12 months from Sept. 21, 2025 to Sept. 21, 2026. There were no such incidents during the preceding 12-month period.
As a result, shipping insurance costs are rising, with the additional war-risk premium for loading oil at Black Sea ports reaching $2.90 a barrel by Sept. 21, up from 90 cents at the end of 2025, according to a Platts estimate. The rate has more than tripled over nine months.
In August, The Insider reported that following Ukrainian attacks, Russian oil shipments to India from Novorossiysk fell by a factor of 4.4, while freight costs rose by about 50%.
Exports restricted after Ukraine strikes Russian refineries
At the same time, Russia itself is restricting fuel exports. The government extended a ban on diesel exports by producers through the end of October, though shipments under intergovernmental agreements remain exempt. The Russian authorities say the measure is necessary in order to secure supplies for the domestic market amid high seasonal demand.
The Insider also reported in August that the restrictions had been tightened after a series of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. In July, Russia’s seaborne exports of petroleum products had already fallen by nearly 22%, reaching their lowest level since S&P began keeping the data in 2016. Exports of diesel and gasoil fell by about one-third.
At the same time, the drop in petroleum-product exports has been accompanied by an increase in crude oil shipments. In the four weeks through Sept. 27, Russia exported an average of 3.71 million barrels of crude a day by sea, while weekly revenue from those sales reached its highest level since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as strikes on refineries reduce Russia’s domestic processing capacity, leaving more crude oil available for export.

Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:08:10 UTC
01:08:10 KST

The Lenin District Court in Bishkek found activist and politician Mavlyan Askarbekov guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison on offenses related to a law on incitement of racial, ethnic, national, religious, or interregional hatred, a verdict he called "absurd."
Askarbekov was detained in June after criticizing the growing presence of Chinese citizens in Kyrgyzstan, including their involvement in small and midsize businesses.
Prosecutors said Askarbekov's Facebook posts contained explicit calls to incite interethnic discord.
"When does incitement to hatred occur? When someone writes something against a particular ethnic group and calls for some kind of action against them. Expressing criticism alone does not constitute incitement to hatred," lawyer and human rights defender Klara Sooronkulova told RFE/RL.
"No one in those posts called for action against the Chinese. People everywhere are saying, ‘'There are too many Chinese.' Are they going to imprison everyone for that?" she added.
China's expanding role in Kyrgyzstan has become increasingly hard to ignore.
During the first half of 2026, Kyrgyzstan issued some 61,000 work visas, according to the Foreign Ministry's Consular Department, with about 60 percent going to Chinese citizens.
That influx of Chinese workers is part of a wider economic expansion and also hard to miss on city streets.
In a country of just more than 7 million people -- where hundreds of thousands leave to work abroad, mainly in Russia, and remittances sustain many households -- the arrival of so many Chinese workers has been difficult to accept for many Kyrgyz.
Kyrgyz officials have defended Chinese involvement as necessary for development and have tried to keep a lid on the government for failing to provide clear information about Chinese migration and employment.
In battling online criticism, the state has turned to what it calls "forensic linguistic examination" to determine whether social media posts break the law.
Joomart Karabaev, a former researcher at the Kyrgyz National Academy of Sciences, said the practice has been entirely weaponized. He knows that firsthand.
Karabaev was arrested and given a three-year probationary sentence after publicly exposing how state security forces dictate expert findings.
"They have started playing the role of a court, effectively becoming an institution that rubber-stamps the guilt established by the investigation and prosecution," he said.
"It has become common to dig up someone's old and new opinions when their political position is disliked, find an article under which they can be charged, and then imprison them based on the conclusions of a linguistic examination," Karabaev added.
In Askarbekov's case, he criticized the growing number of Chinese citizens involved in Kyrgyzstan's small and medium-sized businesses, arguing they were displacing local entrepreneurs.
He publicly called on the prime minister to discuss the issue in a live debate. Instead of public dialogue, the initiative ended in Askarbekov's prosecution and imprisonment.
The case comes as China's economic clout in Central Asia continues to grow.
As of June, Kyrgyzstan owed about $1.4 billion to China, according to the Kyrgyz Finance Ministry. China remained the country's largest external creditor, accounting for 28.1 percent of total external debt at the end of 2025, according to the International Monetary Fund.
This deep economic reliance has made public criticism of Chinese influence a highly sensitive political issue across the region.
In 2019, Kyrgyz activist Guljamila Saparalieva was arrested and charged with inciting ethnic hatred after participating in a protest against Beijing's treatment of Muslims in Xinjiang and the influx of Chinese migrants.
In neighboring Uzbekistan, farmers in several regions accused local authorities of pressuring them to surrender farmland that was subsequently leased or earmarked for Chinese investors between late 2024 and early 2026.
Beijing is reported to closely monitor such developments and has shown a willingness to deploy diplomatic pressure when public demonstrations affect its strategic interests.
In November 2025, members of the Nagyz Atajurt movement in Kazakhstan protested near the border with China, demonstrating against Beijing's treatment of ethnic Kazakhs in Xinjiang and demanding the release of a Kazakh citizen detained there.
The activists also raised broader alarms about China's growing leverage over Astana.
The demonstration prompted China's Consulate General in Almaty to issue a sharp diplomatic note to Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry.
The note, obtained and reviewed by RFE/RL's Kazakh Service, called the protest "an open provocation against the dignity of the People's Republic of China" and an insult to the Chinese Communist Party and its leadership, urging Kazakh authorities to "seriously investigate" the incident.
Kazakh court documents reveal that investigators placed the diplomatic note directly into the case file. The prosecution cited China's formal objections as evidence that the protest damaged bilateral relations. The activists were subsequently convicted of inciting ethnic discord and each received a five-year prison sentence.

Etihad Airways said Wednesday it was considering legal action against the Premier League after an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of serious breaches of the competition's financial rules.
The United Arab Emirates-based airline, Manchester City's main sponsor since 2009, "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements," it said in a statement.
Etihad stressed that it was not named in the redacted findings published following the commission's investigation but said the way the case had been communicated had created damaging implications for the airline.
"The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings," it said.
Etihad also said it had been given no opportunity to engage in a process that now reflected adversely on the airline.
"Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly," the airline said.
"The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision."
"The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented."
"Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests."
 
Man City found guilty of financial breaches
An independent commission on Tuesday found Manchester City guilty of serious breaches of Premier League financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18.
The commission found that City used "sham" deals with unnamed sponsors to inflate its commercial revenue, with part of the sponsorship money actually funded by the club's owner, Abu Dhabi United Group.
It said these and other arrangements inflated revenues and reduced costs by more than £900 million ($1.19 billion), resulting in misstated accounts and allowing City to appear compliant with Premier League and UEFA spending rules.
The commission also upheld three of four charges concerning City's failure to cooperate with the Premier League investigation.
Manchester City said they were "disappointed and surprised" by the ruling and maintained their innocence, arguing that the decision contained "clear material errors" of law, principle and fact.
A separate hearing will determine any sanctions, while City has until Friday to appeal the findings.

AI data centers spur growing environmental concerns amid muddy water, noise pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:03:09 UTC
01:03:09 KST

Elif Gultekin Karahacioglu, Damla Delialioglu Demirtas and Emir Yildirim
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The widespread emergence of data centers across the US amid the artificial intelligence (AI) boom is sparking massive backlash from residents nationwide, who suffer from the environmental impact of these computational hubs, primarily in the form of depleted or muddied water resources and constant noise pollution.
Communities living near data centers report sudden drops in water pressure, withering vegetation and tap water running brown with sediment.
Beverly and Jeff Morris, who live less than 100 feet from Meta’s Stanton Springs data center in Georgia, are among four families who filed a lawsuit against the tech giant in August, claiming sediment accumulated in their wells and water pressure dropped after construction began, rendering tap water undrinkable.
The four families filing the lawsuit say the extensive cutting of trees and excavation damaged the aquifer that stores groundwater, mixing silt and sediment into their wells.
Meta argued that the data center is unlikely to have caused these problems after a hydrogeological study of the grounds, claiming the facility does not use groundwater in its operations.
A similar dispute is unfolding in Virginia’s Louisa County, less than 500 miles north of the Georgia families.
An Amazon data center is located directly across from the home of Austin Newsom, who alleges that shortly after construction began in March 2025, his tap water started running brown, while the heavy machinery and excavation equipment used on the site caused massive vibrations, cracking the walls of his home.
He also says the facility caused persistent road flooding, intrusive light pollution and constant industrial noise, ruining his quality of life.
Meanwhile, a recent University of Sydney report found that the energy consumption and carbon emissions generated by data centers could raise global temperatures, affecting bees. The report warned that even a marginal increase in hot days could disrupt breeding cycles and degrade sperm quality, possibly causing up to 14.1 million bees to go extinct every year.
Slava G. Turyshev, a researcher at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Anadolu that global electricity demand is expected to nearly double in the next half-decade, which in turn will require the construction of more facilities in various locations, running on different types of fuel, such as “oil, charcoal, or nuclear.”
“People are not happy seeing in their neighborhood, significant warehouses which will host computers, processors, chips that will produce sort of computational capabilities, enable computational capabilities to train large language models (LLMs) or whatever,” he said. “People are not happy with that, and so the reality is that we don't want to build large warehouses in the communities where we live, and so the idea: why don’t we move them to space?”
Turyshev stated that relocating data center infrastructure into Earth’s orbit is being seriously evaluated as a necessary step to protect the environment.
Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), told Anadolu that environmental preservation is the main driver of efforts to establish space-based data centers.
He warned that environmental concerns could take on a whole new dimension if data centers were to be established in orbit.
“The concerns that you would have about doing data centers in space look very different — more like the same concerns you have when we’re talking about thousands of satellites in orbit today, about traffic coordination,” he said.
“And about the creation of debris in orbit. What happens when there's a collision in space, or what happens when a spacecraft stops working in space, does it become now a debris hazard — what happens if there’s a malfunction on a satellite and that creates debris,” he added.
Swope stated that traffic management and coordination are operational issues, but these problems could grow significantly if thousands or even millions more satellites are launched into orbit than there are today.
“That's what SpaceX is proposing, a constellation of a million satellites to do AI compute in orbit, a huge increase than the number of satellites we have in space, and those issues that I raised would just grow greater than we need to think about,” he noted.

Ethiopia: Who could bring the warring sides to the negotiation table?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

Can anyone broker a new peace between Tigray and Ethiopia?
October 1, 2026
Just four years after a landmark peace deal officially halted the devastating Tigray war, fighting has escalated once again in northern Ethiopia in recent weeks.
Just days before full-scale fighting resumed, several armed groups which had previously considered each enemies formally announced an alliance with a common goal: To bring down Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
But this time, the lay of the land looks quite different from the previous conflict: Parties outside the country have been accused of meddling in the situation, with each having their own motives to want to destabilize Abiy's government.
This has raised fears about prolonged instability hitting the Horn of Africa.
Reasons for the collapse of the peace deal
The 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement ended the conflict between the Ethiopian federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which cost hundreds of thousands of lives in the course of two years.
Negash Mohammed, a journalist with DW's Amharic department. believes that the deal collapsed for three key reasons — or rather because three key actors in the conflict were largely neglected at the negotiation table.
Mohammed explained that the ultimate agreement didn't factor in the role of Eritrea in the conflict, which had fought alongside Ethiopia against the TPLF; it ignored the part that Amhara militias — known as Fano — played in the war, who later felt sorely excluded from the negotiations; finally, it ignored harliners within the TPLF who viewed the peace peace as nothing but military defeat.
Tensions between the federal government and the Fano escalated further when Addis Ababa moved to forcibly disarm the militias instead of addressing their grievances.
"The federal government has its own shortcomings," said Mohammed. "Instead of convincing the other side, it went on to aggravate the grievances they [already] had."
An alliance of former enemies
Mohammed also emphasized the fact that this coalition against the federal government includes several groups which have otherwise little to do with each other.
It includes the Oromo Liberation Army, a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front as well as multiple smaller armed groups from the western Benishangul-Gumuz region — in addition to ethnic militant factions from Afar, which borders Tigray.
Eritrea meanwhile appears to have shifted sides in the current situation: While not officially a member of the alliance, the neighboring country is believed to be providing support to the rebels.
Patricia Rodrigues, a senior analyst at Control Risks, a global intelligence and security consultancy, referred to the level of strategic coordination among these various groups in the current conflict as "quite significant" and "definitely alarming for the federal government."
She noted, however, that cracks might eventually appear: "How long this coalition lasts, because all of them have very different interests and represent very different ethnic constituencies, remains to be seen," she told DW.
Rodrigues added that, based on Control Risks' assessment, the fighting is likely to remain limited to Ethiopia's northern regions, particularly those situated along the borders between Tigray, Amhara, and Afar.
Furthermore, she highlighted that the idea of it spreading across the entire country was rather unlikely due to the difficulty of nationwide coordination, taking into consideration the rough terrain of the nation and the fragmentation of other opposition groups.
Could the conflict have been prevented?
Rodrigues also pointed out the failure of sustained international engagement after the end of the crisis in 2022 as a key reason for the current conflict_
She noted that while the Pretoria agreement saw some early proof of implementation — including the TPLF's surrender of heavy weaponry in 2022 and 2023 — international attention had soon shifted to other global crises, leaving both sides free to quietly rearm and conscript supporters.
"It was more of a stopgap or a ceasefire, but people were quickly rearming in the background," she told DW.
Rodrigues also noted that the United States had recently lifted sanctions imposed during the 2020–2022 conflict — a step which, according to Mohammed, diminishes the West's leverage in the conflict to push combatants toward coming to the negotiation table.
The real cost of war
In the meantime, civilians are bearing the cost of the warring parties: People caught up in the crossfire have been fleeing the conflict once more, adding further to a population of internally displaced persons (IDPs) that has not recovered from the previous war.
"Since 2020, they have not returned to their areas. They are still in makeshift IDP centers," Mohammed said, adding that there have also been isolated reports of drone strikes hitting civilian areas and of rebel groups deploying military hardware inside schools and clinics.
Telephone and internet connections have also been cut in parts of Tigray and Amhara, electricity has been disrupted, and flights have been suspended to several cities including Kombolcha and Lalibela.
Despite official assurances from all parties that civilians would be protected, Mohammed says that the reality on the ground tells a different story: "Words and practice are very contradictory."
Limited prospects for mediation
Mohammed also noted that outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres dispatched a special envoy to the Horn of Africa, charged with mediating between the African Union, regional powers, and Egypt — many of the same parties involved in brokering the Pretoria agreement.
However according to Mohammed, meaningful negotiations are unlikely to bear fruit until at least one of the sides involved in the conflict "comes to understand that this violence will not help them to achieve what they want."
Rodrigues agrees, stressing that she cannot be optimistic about "an international or a regional mediation being the solution to the current fighting," adding that "intense, but geographically contained" fighting will continue for the foreseeable future.

Scientists are decoding elephant rumble calls, including ‘greetings’ and ‘coos’—hear them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:01:32 UTC
01:01:32 KST

In February 2020 behavioral ecologist Mickey Pardo witnessed the aftermath of an elephant birth. In Kenya’s Samburu National Reserve, he watched as a female African elephant named Matisse called to her newborn with repeated “rumbles”—a kind of deep vocalization he describes as like “an idling truck engine.” Pardo watched as another adult elephant, likely Matisse’s sister, rumbled from a distance before the family came together, uniting with another series of rumbles, as if saying hello.
“It was just really ... fascinating to see this whole sequence,” recalls Pardo, a senior scientist at the research organization ElephantVoices. What these calls might mean, exactly, has long been a mystery. But a new study published on Thursday in Scientific Reports helps to shed some light.
In the study, Pardo and a team of scientists used machine learning to analyze hundreds of rumble recordings from a separate population of African elephants in Amboseli National Park, also in Kenya.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The analysis homes in on several kinds of elephant rumbles: “coo” rumbles to calves, “contact” rumbles made from a distance, “let’s-go” rumbles before group movements, “cadenced” rumbles during rest or meals and two different “greeting” rumbles.
In many cases, the recordings captured overlapping calls, a jumble of rumbles the researchers refer to as “choruses.” To be clear, these calls are not at all like elephants’ iconic trumpet sound. They are low and almost like a growl or thunder.
The researchers used the algorithm to predict the elephants’ behavior based on each recording. It wasn’t entirely accurate, but it did predict behaviors better than chance—suggesting that elephant vocalizations during similar situations may have similar acoustic properties.
“It is pretty exciting that we’re able to train a model to look at an entire chorus and have some interpretation of exactly what’s going on,” says Sara Keen, a study co-author and a senior research scientist at the nonprofit Earth Species Project.
In some cases, different rumbles became progressively similar, a pattern the researchers describe as “vocal convergence.” Scientists have observed this phenomenon in other chatty animals, including parrots and dolphins. Humans, too, are known to mirror one another’s language patterns.
Interestingly, converging appeared “only in the situations where they [the elephants] seem to be coordinating group behavior action,” Keen says. It’s possible that this convergence could indicate agreement, but that theory needs further testing to confirm, she adds.
“This study emphasizes how vital it is to pair new computational analyses with real behavioral observations in the wild,” says Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, who was not involved in the study.
Keen hopes scientists may be able to use similar methods to analyze other animal calls, too, such as for orcas and crows. Many other species are known to perform a kind of “chorusing,” she says, which may make good candidates for future research.
“Animals communicate to influence each other’s behavior, and so you can’t just study the sounds in isolation,” Kershenbaum explains. “But when you combine a rich behavioral dataset with powerful machine learning algorithms, that’s when we can start to get answers to questions like ‘What are the animals saying?’”
