People found not guilty by reason of insanity show a surprisingly mixed criminal risk profile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:49 UTC
01:00:49 KST

People who experience severe mental health conditions are frequently overrepresented in the criminal justice system, but their psychiatric symptoms alone do not always explain their legal troubles. A recent study found that standard criminal risk factors, such as antisocial attitudes and having friends involved in crime, are strongly linked to whether a psychiatric patient has been involved in the legal system. The research was published in Law and Human Behavior.
In the past, intervention programs aimed at reducing repeat offenses among people with mental illness focused almost entirely on treating psychiatric symptoms. These medical interventions routinely failed to keep people out of jail. Researchers began to realize that most people with mental illness do not commit crimes because of hallucinations or delusions.
Instead, their criminal behavior is closely linked to the same risk factors that drive crime in the general population. In the fields of criminology and psychology, experts often refer to the central eight criminogenic risk factors. These include a history of antisocial behavior, antisocial personality traits, antisocial friends, substance abuse, family or marital problems, school or work difficulties, a lack of positive recreational activities, and criminal attitudes.
Researchers have consistently found that these non-clinical factors outperform traditional mental health variables in predicting criminal behavior. This means that mental illness alone does not necessarily increase an individual’s risk of breaking the law. Instead, some people with mental illness happen to have co-occurring antisocial tendencies that lead to legal trouble.
While this pattern holds true for general psychiatric patients, a unique subset of individuals occupies a gray area between the mental health and legal systems. These are patients who have been found not guilty by reason of insanity. In these specific cases, a court has determined that the person is not legally responsible for a crime because a mental disease or defect impaired their actions at the time of the offense.
Because their crimes are legally attributed to mental illness, one might assume these individuals lack the general criminal risk factors seen in other offenders. To test this idea, psychology researchers Angelea Bolaños, Faith Scanlon, and their colleagues set out to compare different groups of psychiatric patients. They wanted to see how insanity acquittees stacked up against other patients in terms of criminal attitudes, social support, and psychiatric distress.
The researchers gathered data from 349 participants across three distinct groups. The first group consisted of 74 psychiatric patients who had a history of misdemeanor or felony convictions. The second group included 68 psychiatric patients who had no history of criminal involvement. Both of these groups were recruited from a short-term, private inpatient psychiatric hospital in Texas.
The third group was made up of 207 forensic patients residing in the California state hospital system. These individuals had been found not guilty by reason of insanity and were institutionalized for mandatory psychiatric treatment. To compare the groups, the research team administered a series of self-report questionnaires designed to measure attitudes toward crime, social support networks, and current mental health.
One survey assessed general criminal tendencies, conduct problems, and antisocial personality traits. Another measured the participants’ number of criminal friends and their level of agreement with antisocial attitudes, such as feelings of entitlement or the belief that violence is justified. A third questionnaire evaluated how much support the participants felt they received from family, friends, and romantic partners.
Finally, the participants completed an inventory that measured the severity of their current psychiatric symptoms over the previous week. This included looking at markers for anxiety, depression, and paranoia. The researchers then used statistical models to see if the combination of these traits could accurately distinguish the three types of patients from one another based solely on their survey answers.
The team discovered that patients with mental illness and a history of typical criminal involvement scored the highest on almost all indicators of criminal risk. This group reported having the most criminal associates and the strongest antisocial attitudes. They also reported the lowest levels of perceived positive social support from their families and friends.
The patients found not guilty by reason of insanity presented a more mixed profile. They showed some shared criminal risk factors with the traditional criminal group, scoring higher on general criminal tendencies than the patients with no legal history. However, they did not display the same elevated levels of antisocial attitudes as the group with typical legal involvement.
When it came to social networks, the insanity acquittees actually resembled the patients with no criminal history. Both of these groups reported feeling a comparable level of social support. The researchers suggest that friends and family might remain more supportive of someone whose crime is attributed to a mental health crisis, compared to someone who engages in standard criminal behavior.
In an unexpected twist regarding psychiatric symptoms, the insanity acquittees reported the lowest severity of current mental health distress among all three groups. The researchers suspect this is due to the nature of their hospitalizations. The Texas patients were in a short-term, acute crisis facility, while the California forensic patients had likely been living in a stable, long-term therapeutic environment for an extended period, allowing their symptoms to subside.
Overall, the data showed that criminal risk factors and social support metrics successfully sorted roughly two thirds to three quarters of the participants into their correct legal categories. This predictive accuracy reinforces the idea that criminal attitudes and social environments are defining features of justice-involved populations. The results highlight the need for treatment programs to target these specific criminal risk factors alongside standard psychiatric care.
For example, specialized rehabilitation programs exist to address the concurrent mental health and criminal needs of people in the justice system. Providing this kind of dual-focused therapy could assist forensic patients in developing necessary life skills to optimize their recovery. Preparing these patients for eventual release requires treating the whole person, rather than viewing them solely through a psychiatric lens.
While the study offers a detailed look at forensic and non-forensic patients, the research design relies on data collected at a single point in time. This cross-sectional approach prevents researchers from determining exactly how a person’s mental illness and criminal behavior evolved over time. It is impossible to know whether a patient’s antisocial attitudes developed before or after their psychiatric symptoms began.
The reliance on self-reported questionnaires also introduces the possibility of response bias. Participants might have underreported their antisocial attitudes or exaggerated their mental health symptoms based on what they thought the researchers wanted to hear. Corroborating these self-reports with official legal records or clinician observations in future studies could yield a more comprehensive picture of their behavior.
The sample composition limits how broadly the results can be applied to the general population. The patients from the Texas hospital lacked demographic diversity, being predominantly White and male. Comparing patients across two different states also introduces variations in how different legal systems define and handle insanity acquittals, meaning a patient in California might be treated differently than one in Texas.
A final complication is that 85 percent of the forensic patients in the California sample had additional criminal convictions on top of the charges that led to their insanity acquittals. This high rate of prior criminal behavior blurs the boundary between the strictly psychiatric and the strictly criminal groups. Future investigations could separate insanity acquittees based on their past criminal histories to better understand this unique population.
The study, “Psychiatric Symptoms and Criminogenic Risk in People With Mental Illness: Comparing Patients Across Forensic and Nonforensic Settings,” was authored by Angelea D. Bolaños, Faith Scanlon, Robert D. Morgan, Sean M. Mitchell, and Darci Delgado.

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Western nations – representing a minority – continue to seek to arrogate governance functions to themselves, for instance within the UN, thereby creating an increasing imbalance. However, the West's actual influence in the world is visibly declining today, Russian President Vladimir Putin noted at a plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club.
He pointed out that a group of Western countries currently enjoys disproportionately large influence within the UN.
"This group, while clearly a global minority, seeks to arrogate governance functions to itself," the Russian leader observed. "As the real influence of these states wanes – giving way to an increasingly independent and self-confident global majority – the imbalances in the UN's structure are becoming ever starker."

Putin, against the backdrop of nuclear threats, made a statement on international conflicts and "catastrophic scenarios"
Kyiv • UNN
Putin said that international conflicts would likely continue due to global changes. He called for "avoiding catastrophic scenarios."
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin said on Thursday that international conflicts are likely to continue amid changes in the world, but that the situation will improve as the so-called Western hegemony weakens, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
According to Putin, catastrophic scenarios must be avoided.
"Regardless of what scenario unfolds in the world in the coming years, the continuation of international conflicts is, unfortunately, quite likely. This is partly due to the fact that prolonged fundamental shifts — and the opportunities they open up — fuel ambitions and a willingness to take risks for the sake of what appears to be an enormous payoff," Putin said.

Hong Kong invests billions to accelerate innovation of impactful solutions as an AI-powered future comes into focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:16 UTC
01:00:16 KST

Hong Kong invests billions to accelerate innovation of impactful solutions as an AI-powered future comes into focus
•    The HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme aims to accelerate the transformation of AI R&D projects into impactful practical solutions.
•    Over 30 projects have been approved, backed by a total of HK$1.7 billion.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Artificial intelligence has rapidly evolved from an emerging technology into a cornerstone of Hong Kong's economic transformation strategy. Under the Government's AI+ initiative, further reinforced by the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the HKSAR (2026-2030), the city is stepping up efforts to integrate AI across industries, public services, scientific research, healthcare, finance and smart-city development, with the ambition of becoming a leading innovation hub in the Greater Bay Area and beyond.
At the heart of this strategy is the HK$3 billion Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme (AISS), a three-year programme that supports universities, research institutions, enterprises and government departments in harnessing the immense computing power of Cyberport's Artificial Intelligence Supercomputing Centre, the city's largest AI computing facility and a key piece of digital infrastructure. Hong Kong's total computing capacity has now surpassed 5,000 petaFLOPS.
The scheme marks a strategic shift from supporting AI research alone to accelerating real-world applications capable of generating tangible economic and social benefits. .
Against this backdrop, a new generation of researchers, scientists and innovators is translating cutting-edge breakthroughs into practical solutions.
Since the launch of AISS in 2024, more than 50 applications have been received and over 30 projects approved, spanning local universities, R&D centres, government departments, technology companies and start-ups. Total subsidies granted have exceeded HK$1.7 billion.
Speaking at a sharing session featuring approved AISS projects, Daniel Cheung, Acting Commissioner for Digital Policy, highlighted the scheme's role in supporting Hong Kong's broader development goals. "The AISS closely aligns with the National 15th Five-Year Plan by advancing ‘industries for AI’ and ‘AI for industries,’ promoting the transformation and upgrading of traditional sectors such as finance and healthcare. Since its launch, the AISS has received enthusiastic responses, with subsidised projects demonstrating immense potential in technological innovation and industrial application," he said.
 
Echoing this view, Hendrick Sin, Chairperson of the Committee of AISS, said: "The approved projects not only showcase scientific breakthroughs but are steadily being transformed into practical applications that benefit society and industry, enhancing citizens' quality of life and exemplifying the power of collaborative innovation among government, industry, academia and research."
One of the highlights of the sharing session was a multimodal large language model for medical diagnosis and surgery developed by the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (CAIR) under the Hong Kong Institute of Science & Innovation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Focused on advancing innovation at the intersection of AI and life and health sciences, CAIR has built a comprehensive medical AI ecosystem centred on CARES 3.0, a multimodal medical model equipped with continual learning and trustworthy decision-making capabilities. The platform pioneers a new "copilot" approach to intelligent healthcare.
Among its innovations is EchoCare, an ultrasound foundation model trained on four million ultrasound datasets. Adaptable across a wide range of clinical applications, the model can accurately identify lesions in more than 50 organs. CAIR's technological advances have helped overcome critical technical bottlenecks.
Financial innovation
AI is also reshaping Hong Kong's financial sector. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Cyberport launched the first and second cohorts of the GenA.I. Sandbox in 2024 and 2025 respectively, focusing on use cases in anti-fraud operations, risk management and customer experience enhancement.
Trial results demonstrated significant operational gains across the banking sector. Participating institutions recorded a 30 to 80 percent reduction in preparation time for suspicious transaction reports, while document processing times were cut from one day to approximately five minutes. The technology also reduced risk assessment report production time by 60 percent, enabled more comprehensive risk analysis workflows, and resulted in more than 70 percent of GenAI-generated credit assessments being regarded as useful references by adopting institutions.
Building on this momentum, the HKMA joined forces with Cyberport, the Securities and Futures Commission, the Insurance Authority and the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority to launch GenA.I. Sandbox++ in March 2026, with a strong emphasis on exploring Agentic AI applications.
Moving beyond content generation, selected use cases under Sandbox++ are examining how AI systems can responsibly take on greater autonomy across end-to-end processes, including customer onboarding, payments, insurance claims and customer interactions.
Collaborative Generative AI Platform
Another project demonstrating the breadth of Hong Kong's AI ambitions comes from InfiX.ai, which has independently developed the Collaborative Generative AI (Co-GenAI) Platform. It enables enterprises, research institutions and industry partners to train domain-specific AI models using their own datasets at significantly lower computing costs. By avoiding the centralisation of proprietary data while safeguarding privacy and intellectual property, Co-GenAI allows specialised intelligence distributed across organisations and devices to be connected and integrated into a continuously evolving collaborative intelligence network.
This approach enables AI technologies to be co-created, co-developed and shared among participating organisations. Supported by high-efficiency computing resources, model engineering, knowledge bases and application workflows, the platform offers capabilities ranging from local deployment and model fine-tuning to evaluation, inference services and multi-model collaboration.
Designed as a scalable, secure and controllable AI infrastructure, the platform has applications across sectors including manufacturing, public administration, finance, healthcare and education, helping drive digital transformation and strengthen the broader AI ecosystem.
These three projects illustrate how government support, world-class computing infrastructure and research excellence are converging to address pressing challenges, unlock new opportunities and demonstrate the transformative potential of artificial intelligence for Hong Kong's future.
The city's ambitions are set to grow further with the planned commissioning of the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster in the Northern Metropolis by 2032. Once fully operational, the facility is expected to propel Hong Kong into the ranks of the world's leading centres for computing capacity, strengthening its position as a regional and global AI powerhouse.

Supreme Court to review Trump administration’s mandatory immigration agency detention policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:08 UTC
01:00:08 KST

Diyar Guldogan
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The Supreme Court agreed Thursday to review the Trump administration’s policy of mandating detention for certain immigrants in removal proceedings without allowing them to seek release on bond, setting up one of the term’s most significant immigration cases.
The case, Rhoney, Acting Director v. Barbosa da Cunha, No. 26-104, was among three cases added to the court’s docket in an order issued Thursday.
The justices will consider whether federal immigration law authorizes the government to detain certain noncitizens throughout their removal proceedings without providing them an opportunity for a bond hearing.
The dispute centers on a policy implemented by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency after President Donald Trump returned to office. Under the policy, immigrants subject to certain removal proceedings can be placed in mandatory detention rather than receiving an individualized hearing before an immigration judge to determine whether they should be released while their cases proceed.
Before the policy change, many immigrants who were arrested while living inside the US could seek a bond hearing before an immigration judge. A successful request could allow them to remain outside detention while their immigration cases were pending.
The administration's policy has instead resulted in prolonged detention for immigrants who might otherwise have sought release on bond. Immigration advocates and attorneys have challenged the policy in federal court, arguing that relevant immigration statutes do not require detention in the circumstances at issue.
The Supreme Court's review will focus on the interpretation of several federal immigration statutes governing detention during removal proceedings.
The case was brought by Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national who challenged his continued detention. The federal government appealed after the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled in his favor.
The administration has argued that the immigration laws require mandatory detention for the class of noncitizens covered by the policy. Barbosa da Cunha's side disputes that interpretation and has argued that eligible immigrants are entitled to an opportunity for an individualized bond determination.
The case comes as the Trump administration has dramatically expanded immigration enforcement and detention as part of its broader immigration crackdown.
The Supreme Court's decision could determine whether the administration can continue requiring detention without bond hearings for a large group of immigrants facing removal.

Tim Heidecker Is Bringing His Joe Rogan Parody Show to The Onion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

As satirical news outlet The Onion continued to wage a legal battle to acquire the assets of Infowars out of bankruptcy this summer, it launched a streaming program that spoofed the brand and its bellowing conspiracist ringleader, Alex Jones.
Comedian Tim Heidecker took the reins of the operation, adopting Jones’ guttural and paranoid bluster as he investigated, among other unconfirmed reports, whether Jones himself had exploded in his car after eating too much Whataburger.
But Heidecker wasn’t about to stop there in his quest to transform the Infowars brand into a gonzo comedy network along the lines of Adult Swim. Now he’s taking aim at another high-profile target: Joe Rogan, the bro podcaster whose rambling, misinformed conversations with everyone from Vice President JD Vance to [checks notes] Yakov Smirnoff have somehow kept his long-running series, The Joe Rogan Experience, at the top of the charts for years. Heidecker’s companion show, The Tim Heidecker Podcast, premieres at 8 pm ET on Thursday night, and WIRED can exclusively reveal that the debut episode includes lots of complaining about pronouns, wildly dumb speculation around AI, and plugs for a supplement called “Crab Salts” that makes your “head hurt” and causes you to shout.
A representative for Rogan did not immediately return a request for comment.
Heidecker first lampooned Rogan’s discursive and disorganized interviews in 2021, with a viral 12-hour podcast (in reality, one hour of footage looped a dozen times) covering topics including psychedelics, cancel culture, and whether Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson would run for president. His guests for that show, comedy duo and Onion contributors Rajat Suresh and Jeremy Levick, return for the new episode, offering their “expert” takes on hot-button topics. (The pair have essentially perfected the art of fake celebrity web content and once even got Justin Theroux in on the joke for a mock Hollywood Reporter-style actors roundtable.)
“What is essentially happening is, in place of Christianity, we have the 10 commandments of woke,” Levick says during a discussion of DEI policies on the first episode of The Tim Heidecker Podcast. The chat veers into concerns that bearded men are dressing as princesses to visit Disneyland. Heidecker then abruptly informs the boys that he’s planned a weekend trip to Glasgow “for Scotch wrestling.”
In 2026, it’s more difficult than ever to exaggerate the absurdities of the right-wing media ecosystem, with its fact-free moral panics and bizarre alternative medicines. Though if anyone is up to the task, it’s the endlessly inventive Heidecker—who will have no shortage of grifters and lunatics to go after once he’s done with his run as a Rogan type. Luckily for him, few of those potential impressions are as rough on the voice as Alex Jones.

Putin expects global conflicts to continue in near future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:59:07 UTC
00:59:07 KST

Elena Teslova
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that he expects the continuation of conflicts around the world in the near future.
Putin told a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow that he sees the probability as "high."
“The continuation of international conflicts in the coming years is very likely. I would very much like to be mistaken,” he noted.
He also said there were reasonable concerns about the functioning of the UN, which he said was operating in "a less collegial and democratic manner" than originally intended.
"Russia supports the idea of a fair reform of the UN, but it is impossible now without an internal consensus," he said.
He also advocated for reforming the structure so that it reflects the diversity of the world.
"Asia, Africa and Latin America should play an increasingly significant role in the UN," he said.
Turning to artificial intelligence, Putin said experts were increasingly warning that its spread could lead to people being stripped of their individuality and reduced to a common denominator.
He warned that the development of AI could result in "digital totalitarianism."
"Possible ‘digital totalitarianism' in the development of AI will become just as dead-end, bleak and anti-human as the totalitarian societies of the past," he said.

David Sullivan sues BBC for £150m over Panorama’s sexual misconduct claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:57:49 UTC
00:57:49 KST

David Sullivan is suing the BBC for £150m over multiple claims of sexual misconduct made in a documentary.
Lawyers acting for Sullivan, who remains West Ham United’s co-owner, have lodged a high court claim against the corporation over its Panorama investigation Predator: The Billionaire Football Boss, which was broadcast in June.
It featured three women who alleged Sullivan had abused his power as the owner of the Sport newspapers to prey on them for sex when they were seeking work.
A further four women accused Sullivan of exploitative and predatory behaviour, including allegations he had tried to pressure them into sex during business meetings.
As part of a joint investigation, the BBC and the Times said their reporters had spoken to dozens of former models and industry insiders, with some sources alleging Sullivan was known for “casting couch” behaviour.
The former pornographer vowed to take legal action against the BBC even before the programme had aired. In a statement in which he also resigned as West Ham’s co-chair, he said the accusations were “factually incorrect and entirely false”.
“The false allegations levelled against me have been sensationalised by the media,” he said. “After a lifetime spent building businesses in the adult industry in which I have met thousands of women, it is sadly inevitable that a small number of improper conduct claims are being made against me. I categorically deny these claims.”
Sullivan’s high court claim, first seen by the Telegraph, accuses the BBC of “libel and malicious falsehood” in airing the documentary. It states the show caused Sullivan “grave, catastrophic, and irreparable harm” to his reputation and business interests.
It states that the programme’s claims opened the 77-year-old up to “profound public hatred, universal ridicule, and global opprobrium”, as well as “immediate and severe commercial alienation, banking disruption, and quantifiable financial destruction”.
The BBC declined to comment.
While Sullivan has resigned as West Ham’s co-chair, he remains the Championship club’s largest shareholder, owning 39% of its shares.
It has also emerged that Sullivan has faced restrictions on his contact with West Ham’s women’s and youth teams since 2023 because of a safeguarding investigation.
The Football Association began an inquiry three years ago after receiving a complaint, which the Guardian understands involves an allegation of sexual misconduct unrelated to football.
Sullivan said through lawyers that the restrictions were part of a “negotiated and temporary agreement” and that the safeguarding investigation related to a “single anonymous complaint” from an event in 1981. He said the alleged incident “never happened”.
After the BBC documentary, the presenter Tony Livesey stepped back from the broadcaster. Earlier in his career, Livesey had been the editor-in-chief of Sullivan’s Sport newspapers. The BBC investigation raised questions for the 62-year-old, with one alleged victim saying he had arranged a meeting between her and Sullivan.
Livesey has said he has “no recollection” of introducing the young woman to Sullivan and that it was “not part” of his job to do so. He said he had had “practically zero” contact with anyone appearing in the paper, such as female models.
Another high-profile legal case would be a blow for the BBC, which is already fighting a claim brought against it by Donald Trump. The US president has taken legal action over an episode of Panorama that spliced together two parts of a speech.
The BBC has apologised for the edit, but has always maintained the programme did not defame Trump.

During the meeting following the presentation ceremony, Ambassador Saar-Isop and President Connolly discussed relations between Estonia and Ireland, European security and support for Ukraine.

Saar-Isop has served at the Estonian embassies in Paris and Washington. From 2022 to 2026, she was Director General of the Ministry’s Department for Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid.

Tochytskyi: 15 more ratifications needed to launch Claims Commission for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:56:00 UTC
00:56:00 KST

Tochytskyi: 15 more ratifications needed to launch Claims Commission for Ukraine
Ukraine's Permanent Representative to the Council of Europe, Mykola Tochytskyi, said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the PACE session in Strasbourg.
"We would like this process to move faster and more efficiently. Since our previous meeting, the agreement has been signed by 40 countries and the EU, but only ten have ratified it. We need at least 25 ratifications for it to enter into force," the diplomat said.
According to him, the main reason for the delay is the different domestic procedures for approving international documents. In some countries, ratification requires several parliamentary stages and may depend on the electoral cycle.
"For example, in one of the Scandinavian countries, the law must pass through two successive compositions of parliament: first it is approved by one parliament, then elections are held, and only after a vote by the newly elected parliament does the document enter into force. Therefore, it is necessary to take into account not only the procedures but also what the political climate will be in the next parliament," Tochytskyi said.
At the same time, he said, around ten countries have already assured the Ukrainian side that they will complete ratification in the near future.
He added that the chairmanship of the Conference of Participants of the Register of Damage for Ukraine had passed from the United Kingdom to Sweden, so the Swedish ambassador is now working with Ukraine and other signatory states to speed up the ratification process.
Tochytskyi also drew attention to the imbalance between progress in the work of the Register of Damage for Ukraine, which has already opened all categories of claims, and the delay in completing the establishment of the entire compensation mechanism under the auspices of the Council of Europe.
"The number of claims submitted does not correspond to the actual scale of the damage. There are many more people who have suffered, including our fellow citizens. For every citizen who has suffered damage, the main question is when compensation will be paid. So, of course, people expect to see at least the first actual payment. Until that happens, confidence in the mechanism will not grow," he added.
As reported, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that Germany would complete the ratification of its accession to the International Claims Commission for Ukraine by the end of 2026 and was working to establish a Special Tribunal for Russia's Crime of Aggression against Ukraine as soon as possible.

PACE Declares Russia’s New State Duma Illegitimate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:55:36 UTC
00:55:36 KST

Lawmakers from 46 European countries refused to recognize Russia’s new parliament, ruling that the Sept. 18-20 election – held even in occupied territories of Ukraine – was neither free nor fair.
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) adopted the resolution on the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, with 59 voters in favor and none against at a plenary session in Strasbourg.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The so-called ‘elections’ to the State Duma on Sept. 18-20 did not meet the fundamental conditions of free and fair elections and cannot be considered a genuine expression of the will of Russian citizens,” Yevheniya Kravchuk, a Ukrainian lawmaker and member of Ukraine’s permanent delegation to PACE, said in a statement.
Ukraine’s key demands accepted
The Assembly adopted three amendments that Kravchuk proposed.
- They affirm that occupation is temporary and does not transfer sovereignty to the occupying state;
- condemn the coercion of Ukrainians in occupied territories into Russian “electoral” processes;
- and call for immediate sanctions against anyone attempting to “represent” those territories.
“Participation obtained under conditions of occupation, coercion or pressure cannot be interpreted as free political expression or used to legitimize an attempted illegal annexation,” Kravchuk said, echoing Ukraine’s previous warnings to the European officials ahead of the elections.
PACE’s resolution calls on member states to refrain from engaging with the new Duma, maintaining Russia’s political and diplomatic isolation.
It also calls for greater sanction of Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC), as well as regional election commissions and those who organized, participated in or “observed” the vote in occupied Ukraine.
‘Never Hurts to Have Their Name on Things’ – Drone Startup Linked to Trump’s Sons
The resolution urges Schengen-wide restrictions on the movement of Russian diplomats and officials, limits on tourist visas for Russian citizens, and the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s defense and reconstruction.
Kravchuk noted that President Volodymyr Zelensky imposed sanctions last week, on Sept. 26, against 44 individuals involved in the vote in occupied territories, and urged its Western allies to follow suit.
Voting under armed guard
Russia began early voting in occupied parts of Ukraine in early September, as election officials visited rural settlements with portable voting booths and ballot boxes.
According to Euronews on Sept. 14, members of Russia’s Central Election Commission, armed servicemen and police monitored the process in Russian-controlled Donetsk, without independent observers from the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) present at the scene.
The vote was organized in occupied Crimea and Sevastopol, as well as Russian-controlled parts of the Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. According to a separate report from Euronews, the voting for Russian-installed legislatures had already concluded on Sunday, Sept. 13.
Over the three days of voting, officially held during Sept. 18-20, voters elected the 450-member Duma along with 39 regional parliaments and 11 governors.
It was Russia’s first national parliamentary election since the full-scale invasion launched on Ukraine in February 2022.
Ahead of the vote, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) urged residents of occupied territories not to take part, warning that organizing or promoting the process may carry criminal liability. Under Part 5 of Article 111-1 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, the penalty includes up to 10 years in prison and confiscation of property.
However, some residents had no choice as the voting process was heavily monitored by armed Russian servicemen and policemen. Others embraced the Russian authorities’ political efforts, describing it as familiar under years of occupation.
Outcome expected
On Aug. 10, Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko, the country’s only registered liberal party, after Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov granted a lawsuit by the nationalist Rodina party accusing it of “extremism” and receiving foreign funding.
The court upheld the ban on Aug. 17, the same day a court sentenced Yabloko deputy chairman Lev Shlosberg to 11 years and one month in a penal colony because of his anti-war statements.
With Yabloko excluded, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party was widely expected to win.
According to near-final results, the ruling party took 57.83% of the vote and 355 of the Duma’s 450 seats, preserving its constitutional majority. The figures surpassed the 343 seats won in 2016, according to NV.
Kyiv and Brussels condemn the results
“Putin has ruled Russia for 26 years – longer than Joseph Stalin. During this time, his regime has systematically dismantled anything that resembled democracy,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 7, saying that the process is a farce.
On Sept. 21, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement on behalf of the bloc that the EU will never recognize the vote in occupied Ukraine or its results, and warned that organizers and candidates there would face sanctions.
The bloc also criticized Moscow for not inviting OSCE observers.
A week later, the Council of the EU sanctioned 10 individuals over Yabloko’s exclusion, including three Supreme Court judges and an official in the Prosecutor General’s Office.
“No Russian ‘elections’ can change Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders,” Kravchuk wrote.
Meanwhile, 51 European countries separately issued a joint statement backing Ukraine and urging Russia to agree to an unconditional ceasefire on Sept. 23.
So far, the Kremlin has not accepted a full ceasefire and has continued its offensive, with seizing the rest of the Donbas widely seen as its main military objective.

Ethiopia closes embassy in Eritrea, expels 10 Eritrean diplomats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:55:35 KST

Zehra Nur Celik
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Ethiopia on Thursday announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats in Addis Ababa persona non grata.
In a statement, Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry said it has decided to close its embassy in Asmara in response to Eritrea's “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence” against Ethiopia.
According to the statement, 10 Eritrean diplomats had been involved in activities that posed a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security, in breach of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.
The diplomats were ordered to leave Ethiopia within 48 hours.
The ministry called on the Eritrean government to cease what it described as acts contrary to the principles governing relations between sovereign states.
“Ethiopia values its strong historical, cultural and people-to-people ties with Eritrea and remains committed to peaceful coexistence, regional stability and integration,” the statement said.

According to a Reuters report, the US defense startup Powerus which was formed in Florida a year ago and is run by a former US Army Special Operations intelligence analyst said it plans to import drone technology from Ukraine and other foreign partners to help meet rising Pentagon demand.
He said the business is about to go public later this month when it intends to merge with Nasdaq-listed Aureus Greenway Holdings, a golf course operator backed by two of the sons of President Donald Trump – Donald Jr. and Eric – via their American Ventures investment fund.

Powerus president and CEO, Brett Velicovich, a former US Army Special Operations intelligence analyst, said he wants the firm to serve as a “one-stop solution” to supply the Pentagon with foreign technology that has an “American face.”
Powerus is just one example of the growing portfolio of defense technology investments backed by the brothers that includes XTEND AI Robotics, an Israeli drone maker that went public in early September after merging with a construction firm in which American Ventures also held a stake.
While Powerus said that the brothers are passive investors with no operational role in the drone firm, Keith Kellogg, a retired US Army lieutenant general, Trump’s former envoy to Ukraine and now an advisor to the Powerus board said, “It never hurts to have their name on something.”

Following lessons learnt from the war in Ukraine there is a surge in demand from investors seeking to fill the global demand for unmanned vehicles, particularly from the Pentagon. They see domestic manufacture of technology obtained by acquisitions and partnership as the best way to shortcut the usual R&D process.
Powerus may already have a head start as Velicovich was praised by the US President, saying “he really knows his stuff” in a July 2025 Truth Social post.
The company is still very much a startup, despite showing promise and announcing recent deals including acquiring access to aerial and maritime drones earlier this year. In March, it unveiled its “Guardian” interceptor drone, which it said was a “joint US-Ukrainian development.”
Another Powerus product, the MatrixFold attack drone was entered into the Pentagon’s $1 billion Drone Dominance program, intended to rapidly acquire large quantities of low-cost attack drones, but failed to reach the second round. Velicovich suggesed that the competition’s electronic warfare requirements were especially challenging.

Meet Thor Hammer: Ukraine’s $25,000 Strike Drone Built to Reach 600 Km
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:53:08 UTC
00:53:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Meet Thor Hammer: Ukraine’s $25,000 Strike Drone Built to Reach 600 Km
Ukrainian defense company SkyFall has unveiled Thor Hammer, a new middle-range strike drone already in combat use that can fly as far as 600 kilometers, carry a warhead weighing up to 50 kilograms, and cost as little as $25,000 per aircraft.
SkyFall disclosed details of the system to Militarnyi on October 1, revealing two primary versions with ranges of up to 350 and 600 kilometers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Depending on configuration, each drone costs approximately $25,000 to $30,000 and can reach speeds of up to 180 kilometers per hour.
The drone has a 3.5-meter wingspan and measures roughly three meters long. Its maximum operating altitude reaches about 4,000 meters, while crews can prepare the system for launch in approximately 18 minutes.
Thor Hammer can carry fragmentation, high-explosive fragmentation and other warhead configurations depending on the target.
Launch options include a catapult or rocket-assisted takeoff, allowing the system to operate from fixed sites or mobile launchers mounted on trucks and other vehicles. Mobile crews can therefore relocate quickly after launching.
The drone can also be equipped with Starlink or other protected communications systems depending on mission requirements.
Its navigation suite combines satellite, inertial, and backup positioning systems designed to keep the aircraft flying even in areas affected by intense Russian electronic warfare.
Thor Hammer follows its programmed route autonomously while transmitting live video to its operator.
As the drone approaches its target, the system alerts the operator, who makes the final decision on whether to engage.
Once the target is confirmed, onboard artificial intelligence and computer-vision algorithms can automatically correct the drone’s final trajectory.
SkyFall says terminal guidance can continue even if radio and video communications are completely lost, giving the drone a degree of autonomy during the final stage of the strike.
Much of Thor Hammer’s core electronics was developed internally by SkyFall. The company’s R&D team is also working on domestically developed engines for the middle-strike class, reducing reliance on externally sourced propulsion systems.
Thor Hammer is integrated into SkyFall’s remote-control architecture, allowing missions to be managed from a distant command post.
The company says it provides not only serial production but also its own software, operator and technician training, and around-the-clock technical support.
And SkyFall is already planning to scale the platform aggressively.
By the end of 2026, the company aims to expand production capacity to as many as 5,000 Thor Hammer drones per month.
At the same time, engineers are developing an even longer-range variant designed to fly more than 1,000 kilometers.
Previously, Ukraine’s DevDroid has put its combat unmanned ground vehicles through trials with the Italian Army, testing how Ukrainian battlefield robotics can operate alongside Italian systems and plug directly into a NATO tactical network.

TAF Industries Brings Ukraine’s Battlefield Drone Experience to New European Production Partnership
Ukrainian defense company TAF Industries and Luxembourg-based LUXUAV have signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation in unmanned technologies, TAF Industries told Militarnyi .
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the agreement, the companies plan to jointly develop new unmanned solutions, accelerate their development, and establish industrial-scale production in the Benelux countries.
The partnership is intended to combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience with the technological and industrial capabilities of European partners, while expanding production capacity in Europe.
“This partnership will help accelerate innovation and expand production capacity in Europe,” TAF Industries CEO Volodymyr Zinovskyi said.
TAF Industries is participating in the “Build with Ukraine” initiative, which focuses on developing Ukrainian defense production in partner countries, according to Militarnyi. The cooperation with LUXUAV will form part of this effort, with the companies seeking to establish joint manufacturing and technological capabilities in Europe.
LUXUAV is developing a European UAV ecosystem encompassing communications systems, artificial intelligence-powered software, and manufacturing capabilities, the outlet reported.
TAF Industries, meanwhile, develops and manufactures strike and reconnaissance UAVs, interceptor drones, fiber-optic drones, unmanned ground systems, and AI-based technologies.
The agreement comes as Ukrainian defense companies increasingly cooperate with European partners on integrating battlefield-tested technologies into European defense systems. Ukrainian defense company DevDroid, for instance, recently tested its combat unmanned ground vehicles with the Italian Army, assessing their interoperability with Italian systems and integration into a NATO tactical network.
During an intensive training exercise, DevDroid demonstrated its Droid TW 7.62 and heavier Droid TW 12.7 platforms alongside Italian troops, the company said in a press release shared with UNITED24 Media on October 1.

‘Thank you, Andy’: Farage gloats as Burnham reopens Brexit fight
The Reform UK leader used a speech in a Brexit-supporting Labour heartland to claim reopening the EU debate presents the “biggest boost” to his career.
LONDON — Nigel Farage told Andy Burnham to “bring it on” if he wants to fight a general election on rejoining the European Union.
The Reform UK leader, a veteran Brexiteer, claimed in a speech on Thursday that the British prime minister has given him the “biggest boost in my career” by reopening the EU debate.
Burnham used his first conference address as Labour leader this week to open up the possibility of Britain trying to rejoin the bloc it left after the 2016 referendum.
Advertisement
Polling has suggested a shift in public support towards rejoining the EU since then — but it remains a deeply divisive issue in U.K. politics.
Farage claimed that Burnham will be “in for a shock” — and tried out his arguments against trying to rejoin the bloc.
Those include a claimed £25 billion annual price tag for re-entry, a wave of immigration under freedom of movement, and a claim that Britain would be forced to join the Euro.
Each of these will doubtless be disputed by the government if Burnham does choose rejoining as one of several options he’s floated for a reboot of European ties after a general election.
But it shows the attack lines that Farage would relish fighting a campaign on.
“It’s just so contradictory,” the Reform UK boss told supporters at Doncaster racecourse.
Advertisement
“He says he wants to unite the country,” Farage said of Burnham. “A second referendum will divide the country bitterly in a way perhaps we’ve never seen before.
“If Andy Burnham — the ‘King of the North’ — wants a fight in Doncaster and the Red Wall with me on rejoining the European Union, then bring it on, I say.”
The choice of Doncaster for the speech was no coincidence. The northern city strongly voted to leave the EU, and lies in the so-called “Red Wall” that was once Labour’s industrial heartlands.
“He might have just given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy,” Farage added.
Return to campaigning
The Reform leader used the speech to kick off a promised stretch of constant campaigning.
Farage acknowledged he had been “relatively absent” from the limelight during a summer in which his party has been dogged by questions over the probity of donations to Reform.
Advertisement
He launched what he dubbed a “100 Days to Save Britain Tour” — billing it as the start of Reform’s general election campaign.
“And I will be out on the road every week between now and the general election, whether it happens this year or next spring or in three years’ time, we are back out actively campaigning and fighting,” Farage said.
A spokesperson for the Reform leader promised he’d be making stops on this tour “at least twice a week” up until the election — barring holiday periods.
Farage still believes an election will be called as early as the spring, but it’s in Burnham’s power to call one as late as August 2029, and the prime minister has spent the past few days publicly damping down expectation of one.

Oil Exports Find A Way Past Iranian Attacks, But Refinery Bottleneck Persists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:51:38 UTC
00:51:38 KST

Exports of crude oil from the Middle East hit their highest level in September since the war with Iran began, reinforcing a trend of increased supplies despite Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, according to analysis of shipping and commodity market data by industry observers.
But while crude levels have risen, the refinery bottleneck that has caused a global spike in diesel prices persists. European Union figures published on October 1 showed diesel pump prices at record levels. Prices have also surged in the United States despite the recovery in oil exports.
"More oil is coming out of the Middle East Gulf than many expected that would be possible even just a few months ago," Richard Meade, chief editor of Lloyds List, told an online briefing on October 1.
Roll Out The Barrel
Lloyds List data shows a steady upward curve of crude tanker transits through the Strait of Hormuz since mid-July, following a sharp fall that coincided with the collapse of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the conflict, now in its eighth month.
Investment bank JP Morgan said Middle East crude exports in September were at 98 percent of pre-war levels, describing it as "a remarkable recovery for a region still at war."
Commodities analytics firm Kpler reported Saudi oil exports were at average levels for 2025, while maritime intelligence company Windward said Saudi terminals loaded four times more oil than in August -- a big increase but still nearly 40 percent lower than in January.
There appear to be a number of factors behind the revival, including the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, the use of oil shuttles and ship-to-ship oil transfers, and a willingness by some in the industry to accept higher risk.
The Saudi pipeline, which pumps its crude to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, was damaged in an attack by Iran-aligned Houthi militants on September 10. An uptick in shipments from Yanbu later in the month, however, suggested the pipeline had regained at least some of its lost operational capacity.
The United Arab Emirates has found a similar solution, using its pipeline to the port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman. It has been targeted in Iranian attacks but is far less vulnerable than Hormuz.
Another route to market has been to use smaller shuttle vessels to transport crude through the Strait of Hormuz, using a route hugging the Omani coastline patrolled by the US Navy. These ships, often traveling in a convoy, pump their cargoes onto tankers in the safety of the Gulf of Oman.
Meanwhile, refineries in India have reportedly begun commissioning tankers to use the route directly.
Attacks Continue
The risks to shipping have not disappeared. In the latest incident, three Liberian-flagged tankers were struck by unknown projectiles when transiting the Strait of Hormuz on September 30. Industry analysts suggest the dangers have simply been priced in.
"Higher exports do not necessarily mean that the Strait of Hormuz has become safe. They simply show that the oil industry has become accustomed to working around that danger," Meade said.
Crude prices have retreated from recent highs, but refinery bottlenecks remain a global issue. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), much of this is in the Persian Gulf.
Iranian attacks on refineries combined with Hormuz shipping disruption have led to a collapse in output, the IEA said.
"In 2025, Middle East producers exported 3.3 million barrels per day of refined oil products. But since the conflict began, as much as 3 million barrels per day of refining capacity has been unavailable," the IEA wrote in a note on September 21.
This global diesel shortage has been compounded by Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, leading the Kremlin to impose a diesel export ban.
"Refineries around the world are already stretched to capacity," the IEA said. "This leaves few available options to prevent a further tightening of supplies and higher prices in the coming months."

Diesel américain : la France et quatre autres pays européens s’accordent sur une réponse “ferme”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:50:05 UTC
00:50:05 KST

Diesel américain : la France et quatre autres pays européens s’accordent sur une réponse “ferme”
Ces pays et la Commission européenne ont tenu jeudi une réunion d’urgence pour répondre aux appels lancés par les Etats-Unis en faveur d’un déblocage des réserves de carburant.
BRUXELLES — Cinq pays européens, dont la France, ont convenu lors d’une réunion d'urgence jeudi de répondre “d’une seule voix” aux pressions croissantes exercées par le gouvernement américain pour qu’ils libèrent leurs réserves stratégiques de gazole, a appris POLITICO auprès de plusieurs personnes au fait des discussions.
La France, l’Allemagne, la Grande-Bretagne, l’Italie, l’Irlande et la Commission européenne ont pris part aux discussions visant à déterminer comment réagir face aux pressions exercées par l’administration Trump pour qu’ils réduisent leurs stocks de pétrole, sous peine de voir les exportations américaines de gazole interdites, ont relaté trois responsables européens à POLITICO.
Tous ces pays ont subi des pressions en coulisses de la part des Etats-Unis pour qu’ils réduisent leurs stocks de pétrole, sous peine de se voir imposer un embargo sur les exportations américaines de gazole, ont indiqué deux de ces responsables.
Advertisement
Ces pays, ainsi que l’exécutif européen, se sont mis d’accord sur trois points, selon ces mêmes interlocuteurs : réagir à la pression d’une “voix coordonnée”, veiller à ce que “toute décision concernant la libération des stocks soit portée au niveau de l’AIE [l’Agence internationale de l’énergie]”, et s’efforcer d’“apaiser les tensions dans les échanges avec les Etats-Unis”.
L’AIE, dont le siège est à Paris, coordonne la politique énergétique des pays développés et a supervisé le déblocage de stocks pétroliers en début d'année, à la suite de la fermeture du détroit d'Ormuz.
L’idée, c’est de “désamorcer” la situation, a expliqué l’une des sources mentionnées plus haut. “Il s’agit d’adopter une attitude à la fois ferme et positive dans la communication […] Quand on a affaire à un lion affamé, on ne lui joue pas forcément des mauvais coups.”
Un groupe plus large de pays, dont certains ont également subi des pressions de la part de l’administration Trump, se réunira vendredi pour discuter de la réponse à apporter, a ajouté cette source.
POLITICO avait précédemment rapporté que le secrétaire américain à l’Energie, Chris Wright, avait mis sur la table une alternative : plutôt qu’un embargo sur les exportations de diesel — dont dépend fortement l’UE —, il demandait que des stocks stratégiques de pétrole soient mis sur le marché.
Les prix du diesel s’envolent aux Etats-Unis en raison des guerres en Ukraine et en Iran. Et la pression s’accentue sur Donald Trump pour qu’il fasse baisser les prix à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat, qui s’annoncent décisives.
Il n’est pas question pour le président américain d’exclure une interdiction des exportations, malgré la forte opposition du secteur pétrolier américain. “J’y réfléchis”, a déclaré Donald Trump lors d’un événement à la Maison-Blanche. Après avoir assuré en parler régulièrement avec d’autres membres de l’administration, il a déclaré que ceux-ci “pensent, en quelque sorte, que cela aiderait le diesel, mais que ça pourrait faire augmenter le prix d’autres produits”.
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Alexandre Léchenet.

European Greens urge EU leaders to back UK's potential return to bloc

Aysu Bicer
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The European Greens on Thursday called on European leaders to support the UK's potential return to the EU, saying there was new momentum behind the idea.
“Britain’s place is in the European Union. Our shared prosperity and security rely on it,” Ciaran Cuffe, co-chair of the European Green Party, said in a statement.
He said that if Europe was serious about “peace, security, and autonomy,” the EU should expand both eastward and westward.
The European Greens said leaders of European Green parties agreed in May that they would be ready to welcome the UK back if British people chose to return to the EU in the future.
Cuffe said the possibility of Britain rejoining the EU was now being “discussed openly at the highest level of British politics.”
He said the idea had been received positively by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and French President Emmanuel Macron.
“We now hope that all the European political families and governments that support the UK’s eventual return to the European Union will make their position equally clear,” he said.
The European Greens also linked a potential UK return to the EU with the issue of Irish unity.
Cuffe said rejoining the EU would help “move further along the road to Irish unity,” arguing that there would be no need for an “Irish Sea Border.”
He said this would eliminate the need for customs checks between the UK and Ireland and mean that all parts of Ireland and the UK would be subject to the same EU regulatory controls on trade.
The European Greens said they were the first European political family to explicitly invite the UK to rejoin the EU, making the call in a declaration by the Green Leadership Council in May 2026.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that he wanted to see Britain rejoin the EU during his lifetime, while stressing that rejoining was not necessarily the option that should be pursued now.
Speaking at the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Burnham said Britain could not have “the clear path we need into the rest of this century” without deciding on its future relationship with the EU, which he described as “still our largest market.”
The UK left the EU in 2020, four years after a referendum in which about 52% of voters chose to leave.
Burnham said he would use the opportunity around the summit to set out the choices available to Britain.
“And there are different options, and I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in,” he said.

Nigel Farage has claimed that Andy Burnham has given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate, which the Reform UK leader said had reopened a “huge flank” to his party.

Looking tanned and relaxed before his party’s first major rally since its conference last month, Farage indicated to reporters that he was relishing a return to the playbook that he and others deployed during the 2016 referendum.
Dismissing polls showing that as much as 59% of the public favoured rejoining the EU, Farage told the Guardian: “Of course they do, until you tell them it’ll cost 25bn quid a year, until you tell him it’ll mean joining Schengen [the area of Europe that has open borders], until he tells them it will mean actually having to recommit to joining the euro.
“Remember that the leavers haven’t made their arguments since 2016. The ‘remoaners’ have made their arguments every single week. I mean, do you know what? I actually think that Burnham has made a very big political mistake here.”
Farage was speaking before a rally in the South Yorkshire city of Doncaster, the first of a series Reform is holding around Britain on the theme of what the party would do in its first 100 days of government.
While the Reform UK leader said he believed Burnham had calculated that new language on the EU might help win back voters from the Greens in big cities, Farage added: “Here in Doncaster and across the ‘red wall’ in the north and Midlands, I think he’s opened up a huge flank to us.”

“He might just have given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy, if you’re watching.”

However, Reform sources claim that the prime minister’s intervention has energised them and that specific donors are already discussing how they can fund a rerun of the 2016 campaign.
Meanwhile, Farage strongly hinted that Reform’s internal inquiry into the donations controversy that has overshadowed the party this year would absolve two key aides and that legal action would be launched against journalists involved.
Indicating that he had already seen the report and knew its conclusions, Farage said its release was “imminent”.
“It’s been done. It’ll be out in public very soon and I think some of your co-conspirators might find themselves with one or two legal challenges,” he told a Channel 4 journalist among reporters who questioned him.
Reform was rocked on the eve of its party conference after some of Farage’s team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.
A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.
In Channel 4 News’s investigation, footage showed that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.
In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.
Jukes has denied “any wrongdoing” while Orr has said he would cooperate with the party’s internal investigation “fully”.
The Metropolitan police are carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform over allegations it broke foreign funding laws.

Flydubai attack gives Netanyahu new security message ahead of Israel vote
Motive behind Flydubai incident still unclear, but Israeli PM is framing it within his warnings of threats to Israelis.
Many questions about the apparent attempted hijacking of flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv remain unanswered. What was the motive of the attacker, the flight’s unnamed co-pilot, who stabbed the captain before being overpowered? What were the aims of his attack?
And yet, in contrast to the ambiguity that still exists, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – amidst his appearances greeting returning passengers – has been quick to frame the attack as the almost inevitable outcome of the “propaganda” he says continues to vilify Israel.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump amazed that an ‘Israeli plumber’ helped land Flydubai flight

- list 3 of 4UAE investigates possible ‘terrorist’ link in attack on flight to Israel

While conceding it was too early to establish a motive, Netanyahu nevertheless pointed to Iran – which Israel and the United States launched a war against in late February – and its proxies as intent on stepping up attacks on Israelis abroad. “It’s probably too early to say how this will pan out politically,” said former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy, speaking to Al Jazeera.
“But it could have the advantage of removing many things that Netanyahu doesn’t want to see on the country’s front pages, such as the approaching anniversary of October 7 [2023 attacks on Israel], and replacing them with a story hinting at Iranian involvement, at the same time as other claims of possible Iranian operations are surfacing,” he said, referring to accusations of Tehran’s potential involvement in an incident near a US Air Force base in the United Kingdom.
“That would certainly give fresh impetus to the outcome that Netanyahu is pushing for – namely the resumption of intensified strikes against Iran, which also helps distract from Netanyahu’s domestic difficulties and could be touted as vindicating his warnings of earlier this week,” he said.
Netanyahu on Tuesday published a video statement in which he warned of “indications that, ahead of the elections, our enemies will try to attack us”, a warning his opponents swiftly dismissed as unevidenced fearmongering.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, who called the plane attack an “attempted jihadist terror attack”, also appeared to refer back to the earlier warning, saying: “When the prime minister and I issue security warnings and alerts based on intelligence, everyone would do well, both our enemies abroad and uninformed former officials at home, to listen and take them seriously.”
However, Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid – who had received a security briefing from Netanyahu on Tuesday night – was quick to reject such a connection, saying on Wednesday that “nothing even resembling [the plane attack] appeared in the security briefing with the prime minister last night”.
Political gain
For some observers who have followed Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – for years, his actions following the attempted hijacking have been part of a long-running method of ensuring the aftermath of crises works in his favour.
“Netanyahu is trying to gain politically from the event,” said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London. “You could see him, soon after the passengers landed in Israel, chatting with one of the Israeli heroes [who had subdued the co-pilot].”
But Bregman doesn’t necessarily think that Netanyahu, who polls predict may narrowly be beaten in the elections, will benefit.
“There is no political gain for him,” Bregman said. “[The attack] surprised him as it surprised all of us.”
Bregman added that Netanyahu’s only hope might be if a connection to Iran is established, leading to further escalation in the conflict with Tehran, which the US has appeared to be backing away from.
“There was clearly a security glitch which will be investigated,” Bregman told Al Jazeera. “It could have ended in another 9/11, but thanks to some brave passengers, and a massive amount of luck, it was averted.”
Persecution
Speaking to US media on Wednesday, Netanyahu said that while it was “too early to say” who was behind the failed attempt to seize control of the plane, the co-pilot’s actions were the result of what he described as “fanaticism and hatred of an incalculable level”, sentiments that he suggested were tied to anti-Semitism because of international criticism of Israel.
Netanyahu’s claims of victimhood and persecution have ramped up in tandem with the rising tide of anger among many in the international community over Israel’s genocide in Gaza – in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians – its multiple strikes on neighbouring states, and widespread accusations of state complicity in the increasingly violent settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which has led numerous countries to impose restrictions on trade with Israel’s illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.
Addressing the sense of global outrage that he has since blamed for the attempted hijacking, Netanyahu told the United Nations General Assembly last month that Israel was fighting an “eighth front”, in addition to the seven fronts on which he said it was already fighting.
“It’s the war for truth. It is waged in the world’s media, and most perniciously, in social media,” he said, blaming the world’s media, including Al Jazeera, which sought to “brainwash young minds to hate Israel, hate America and hate the West”.
Al Jazeera Media Network has rejected Netanyahu’s attack, calling it the latest example of Israel’s “sustained campaign against Al Jazeera and its journalists”, which has resulted in the killing of 12 of its team in Gaza.
Israel’s government “will want to position the [attempted hijacking] attack against the backdrop of Netanyahu’s speech at the UN,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House.
“It just feeds into the sense of insecurity that many in Israel feel, as well as the trauma that has held since October 7,” he said, adding that it would also feed the sense of hypocrisy many in Israel feel at the sanctioning of a state for taking action against those it frames as intent on its destruction.

Unknown

2026-10-01

Halis Sunnetci
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
LaLiga President Javier Tebas on Tuesday called FIFA's handling of US striker Folarin Balogun's World Cup red card the “most serious incident in the history of football,” criticizing the governing body's management.
Balogun was sent off during the United States' 2-0 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina in the World Cup round of 32 for a challenge on Tarik Muharemovic.
He was due to serve an automatic one-match suspension.
However, FIFA's disciplinary committee later converted the punishment into a one-match suspended ban with a one-year probation period, allowing Balogun to face Belgium in the round of 16.
US President Donald Trump subsequently confirmed that he had called FIFA President Gianni Infantino and asked him to review the suspension, while saying he had not told Infantino what decision to make.
FIFA maintained that its disciplinary committee made the decision independently.
“We have FIFA, which has overturned a red card because the president of a country called the FIFA president,” Tebas said at a FIFPRO event in London.
“This is the most serious incident in the history of football. I think that, for this to be resolved, the issue of governance has to be addressed clearly.”
Balogun subsequently played against Belgium, but the US was eliminated following a 4-1 defeat in the round of 16.
 
'Infantino era is over'
Tebas had already called for new leadership and governance at FIFA in an interview with French newspaper Le Monde published on Aug. 9.
His comments followed controversy over a plan to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors.
FIFA abandoned the plan on Aug. 1.
“For me, Gianni Infantino's time has long since passed,” Tebas said, arguing that his concerns went beyond the recent controversy and reflected what he described as a long-standing style of management at FIFA.
“Gianni Infantino is not someone who contributes to the growth of football,” he said.
“On the contrary, his projects are destroying the very essence of the sport: the national leagues.”
“Football is not limited to the elite. For me, the Infantino era is over.”

dune-inspired promenade brings sand and vegetation into comillas’ waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:45:11 UTC
00:45:11 KST

dune-inspired promenade brings sand and vegetation into comillas’ waterfront
hector navarro + arkhitekton rework the seafront of comillas, spain, using sand, vegetation, permeable surfaces, and limestone.
Sand Becomes Part of Comillas’ Seafront Landscape
Located on Spain’s northern coast, Comillas is a small Cantabrian town with a rich architectural heritage, including El Capricho, one of Antoni Gaudí’s few buildings outside Catalonia. Against this historic backdrop, the transformation of the town’s seafront by Hector Navarro + arkhitekton addresses its changing relationship with the Cantabrian Sea. Instead of treating sand as something to be removed, the intervention incorporates it into the everyday functioning of the promenade. Carried inland by wind and beachgoers, sand settles within planted areas and permeable paving, becoming part of the public space.
Dune-Inspired Landscape Connects Town and Coast
Through this strategy, the design team extends into a new landscape inspired by the dune ecosystems of the Cantabrian coast. The promenade creates a transition between the built fabric of Comillas and the beach, using vegetation, permeable surfaces, and mineral materials to accommodate the changing conditions of the coastline. Limestone riprap reinforces the connection with the rocky coastal landscape, while permeable surfaces allow water and sand to remain part of the ground.
Benches and Open Space Reframe Comillas’ Waterfront
Individual benches are distributed along the promenade, providing places to stop and look toward the sea without creating a continuous line of conventional street furniture. By reducing the presence of cars and expanding pedestrian areas, the intervention gives greater space to everyday public use. Rather than introducing an autonomous object on the coastline, the project works with processes already present on the site: wind, sand, vegetation, water, and movement, to shape a new public landscape for Comillas.
project info:
name: Comillas Waterfront Promenade
 architect: Hector Navarro | @hectornavarro + arkhitekton
location: Comillas, Spain
landscape designers: Héctor Navarro, Diego Jardinería (Diego Cuartas & Adolfo Vila)
photographer: Imagen Subliminal (Miguel de Guzmán + Rocío Romero) | @imagensubliminal

Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments stir fresh tensions with Premier League
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:40:49 UTC
00:40:49 KST

Andy Burnham’s intervention in the Manchester City debate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister. Government officials are understood to be unhappy they were not given notice that the independent commission’s damning judgment of £900m of financial manipulation and “sham contracts” would be published this week and Burnham’s response has not gone down well with several Premier League clubs concerned by his relationship with City’s owners.
The Premier League published a redacted 40-page version of the commission’s report on Tuesday, not long after Burnham’s first keynote speech as leader at the Labour party conference.
Burnham responded in a series of interviews on Wednesday by saying he would be “really concerned” if City’s owners were forced to sell after being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules, although he did add he could not intervene more in the process, which remains subject to appeal.
City’s disciplinary fate lies in the hands of an independent commission and pending its final judgment the owners’ suitability to remain running the club could be assessed by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), with no role for the Premier League or government.
The Times and Daily Mail have reported that City’s appeal will be based on evidence the club claim proves their sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government and not the club. The commission rejected that argument as “untrue”.
Paragraph 77 of the judgment states: “We concluded that it was an ‘explanation’ that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme.”
Burnham brought up his previous criticisms of the Premier League over the prosecution of his club, Everton, for financial rule breaches after they were docked 10 points – reduced to six on appeal – by an independent commission three years ago.
In November 2023, Burnham, when mayor of Greater Manchester, wrote to the Premier League chair, Alison Brittain, accusing the league of an “abuse of process” and claimed Everton were being used as a pawn in efforts to show an independent regulator was not required in football.
Burnham made similar complaints on Wednesday despite Everton having admitted breaching profitability and sustainability rules, with the club contesting only the extent of the breach and sanction. “I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled,” he said. “I still hold the view very firmly that they weren’t fairly treated in that process.”
The Premier League was unhappy with Burnham’s behaviour in 2023, particularly as his office posted on X two letters of complaint he sent to the league, but did not publicise replies sent by Brittain that explained the competition’s financial regulations governance process.
His apparent expression of sympathy for City, with a warning about jumping to conclusions and praise for the owners’ investment in Manchester, has also raised eyebrows at the Premier League, although it does not intend to respond.
The IFR chief executive, David Kogan, has made clear he will not tolerate political interference in his role, telling the Times last year that he would resign if he sensed government pressure.
The City case has the potential to present an early test of his mettle and the IFR’s powers, given Burnham’s previous working relationship with the club’s owner, the Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), and the £25bn annual UK-Abu Dhabi trading relationship. One of Burnham’s first calls after he succeeded Sir Keir Starmer in July was with Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, president of the United Arab Emirates and the ultimate owner of ADUG.
Kogan confirmed the IFR was monitoring the case and has powers “to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives” to protect “honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals”.
City’s owners are unlikely to fall foul of the licensing system that will be introduced next season, because that is an assessment of financial sustainability and separate from the new owners, directors and senior executives test, which the IFR uses to examine honesty and integrity.
The Premier League and IFR declined to comment.
