vollebak turns thousands of tiny slate tiles into a flexible rock jacket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:39:40 UTC
00:39:40 KST

vollebak turns thousands of tiny slate tiles into a flexible rock jacket
the rock jacket uses thousands of 5mm slate tiles, neoprene and cordura to turn geological time into flexible outerwear: somewhere between material experiment and a harrington built from the earth’s crust.
VOLLEBAK ROCK JACKET TURNS SLATE INTO FLEXIBLE OUTERWEAR
Vollebak takes its material experiments underground with the Rock Jacket, a one-off garment built from thousands of tiny pieces of slate. The British clothing brand has previously worked with copper, wood, aerogel and electromagnetic shielding, but its latest prototype goes considerably further back in the material timeline: stone. Rather than treating it as a rigid shell, the project sets out to make rock behave more like fabric.
Each 5mm x 5mm slate tile sits on a neoprene backing, forming a gridded surface that can twist and bend while retaining the uneven texture of natural stone. From a distance, the jacket reads almost like pixelated armor; up close, its fragmented surface reveals the layers and variations of the slate itself. The result lands somewhere between geological sample, digital texture and something a particularly well-dressed space miner might keep by the door.
STEVEN LEPRIZÉ ADAPTS WOOWOOD MARQUETRY TO STONE
The material was developed with French designer, material technologist and experimental cabinetmaker Steven Leprizé, whom Vollebak initially approached to explore a more wearable version of its earlier Wooden Jacket prototype. Leprizé adapted WooWood, his elastic marquetry technique that bonds hundreds of small wooden tiles onto a flexible rubber membrane, replacing timber with thin squares of slate.
Producing the new surface is a precision-heavy exercise. The slate arrives in sheets measuring 100 x 50cm and just 0.5mm thick before being cut into clean-edged squares half a centimeter wide. According to Leprizé, making the material involves around 50 individual steps, with the cutting process determining whether the final grid can move cleanly without losing the visual character of the stone.
SLATE TILES AND CORDURA SHAPE VOLLEBAK’S CROPPED HARRINGTON
Vollebak turns the flexible sheets into a cropped, minimalist Harrington jacket with a deliberately stripped-back silhouette. The slate panels are laser cut and joined with visibly taped seams, while Cordura pockets and a conventional zipper bring a few recognizably garment-like details back into the equation. The contrast is part of the appeal: an everyday jacket typology, except its surface happens to be made from rock.
The Rock Jacket currently exists as a one-of-one piece, with Vollebak positioning it as the beginning of a longer investigation rather than a finished material system. Co-founder Nick Tidball suggests that rock could eventually be explored as a construction material for clothing in much the same way it has long been used in architecture. Whether stone ever becomes wardrobe staple is another question, but a jacket made from a fragment of the Earth’s crust certainly makes the usual seasonal turnover feel rather hurried.
project info:
name: Rock Jacket
 designer: Steven Leprizé for Vollebak | @vollebak
 location: London, UK

Estonian Ambassador to Hungary Jana Vanamölder presents credentials

The conversation following the presentation of credentials focused on bilateral relations between Estonia and Hungary and European security.

Vanamölder stressed that relations between Estonia and Hungary have deep historical roots. “We are ready to open a new chapter in relations between our two countries, deepen our dialogue and develop cooperation in areas where we have shared interests. It is important for Estonia to build a close and trusted partnership with Hungary,” she said.
Speaking about security cooperation, Vanamölder highlighted Hungary’s contribution to protecting Baltic airspace. “We are grateful to Hungary for its contribution to protecting Baltic airspace. Allied solidarity and cooperation are extremely important for ensuring the security of our region,” she said.
Ambassador Jana Vanamölder has worked at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs since 1995. She has worked in the Ministry’s Policy Planning Department, Press and Information Department, Political Department and Human Resources Department. She has also served as Deputy Head of Mission at the Estonian Embassy in Moscow and at Estonia’s Permanent Representations to the European Union and NATO. From 2022 to 2025, Jana Vanamölder served as chargé d’affaires at the Embassy of the Republic of Estonia in Moscow. The IDF on Thursday published the names of 170 Palestinians killed in Gaza during the war who were presented internationally as journalists or media workers but who the military says also served as members of terrorist organizations, primarily Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad.
The move comes after the IDF said it had identified a recurring pattern in recent months in which Hamas and Islamic Jihad themselves published information after the deaths of some media workers acknowledging that they had also served in the organizations’ military wings.
“Following an extensive research effort, the IDF is now revealing that 170 Gazans who were killed during the war and presented as journalists and media personnel actually served as terrorists in terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, primarily Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad,” the IDF said.
The military said it was publishing what it described as verified evidence, including images and documents produced by the terrorist organizations, some of which were recovered in Gaza, that it says demonstrate the individuals’ affiliations and roles.
The IDF said 118 of the 170 were members of Hamas’ military wing, 49 belonged to Palestinian Islamic Jihad, one was affiliated with Adonei HaShmama and two with the Popular Resistance Committees.
According to the military, 17 of those on the list participated in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel. The IDF said more than 40 of the deaths on the list prompted condemnations of Israel from the United Nations.
Some of those named had also worked for major international media organizations, according to the IDF, including Reuters, CNN, ABC News, The Associated Press, Agence France-Presse, the BBC, Le Monde and Australia’s ABC.
The military said the disclosures were intended to challenge accusations that Israel has deliberately and systematically targeted journalists during the Gaza war.
“Throughout the war, various media organizations in the international community repeatedly accused the State of Israel and the IDF, without presenting verified findings, of deliberately harming journalists,” the military said.
It added that in some cases, “the terrorist organizations themselves presented those individuals as terrorists in their ranks and even claimed them as their own.”
The military said the material illustrates what it describes as a gap between how some of the dead were portrayed internationally and their alleged roles on the ground.
“The information now being revealed illustrates the gap between the picture presented around the world and the reality on the ground, and provides additional conclusive evidence that the IDF does not deliberately and systematically operate against journalists, but against terrorist organizations and their members, in accordance with international law,” the military said.
International media outlets, human rights organizations and international institutions have repeatedly cited the number of journalists and media workers killed in Gaza while criticizing Israel’s conduct during the war. The IDF argues that such figures often fail to distinguish between journalists carrying out media work and people who were simultaneously serving in terrorist organizations.
Among the cases highlighted by the military was Amro Nahid Abdel Rahman Abu Odeh, who worked for Reuters and Turkey’s Anadolu Agency.
According to the IDF, Abu Odeh was also a team commander in the photography unit of Hamas’ military wing. The military published images showing him both carrying a camera and holding a Kalashnikov rifle.
Another man named by the IDF, Hassan Majdi Ibrahim Abu Warda, worked for the Barq Gaza news agency but was also, according to the military, a sniper in Palestinian Islamic Jihad’s Northern Gaza Brigade.
The IDF said its new website was created to make the underlying material publicly accessible, including the individuals’ alleged organizational affiliations and military positions as well as evidence that the military says can be released publicly.
The military also addressed controversy surrounding the documentary NAZA, after IDF representatives viewed the film.
“The film presents a distorted, misleading and unrealistic picture,” the IDF said. “We never planned, approved or carried out a strike in which 500 civilians were expected to be killed.”

Finland to provide EUR 50M loan for Ukraine's reconstruction
The Finnish Foreign Ministry said this in a press release, according to Ukrinform.
"The loan will be provided for the Special Program for Ukraine Recovery 2.0 (SPUR 2.0), a new financing program established by IDA to respond to Ukraine's substantial reconstruction and recovery needs," the statement said.
According to the World Bank's latest estimate, the cost of Ukraine's reconstruction and recovery will amount to almost $588 billion over the next decade. Financing provided through the SPUR 2.0 program will bolster Ukraine's economic stability, help maintain the functioning of society and contribute to reconstruction efforts as Russia continues its war of aggression.
"Supporting Ukraine is both a matter of values for Finland and an investment in European security and stability. Russia's war of aggression has caused immense damage, and the international community must therefore continue its determined support to ensure the resilience of Ukrainian society and to rebuild the country," said Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Ville Tavio.
Financing provided through the program can mobilize substantially more funding for Ukraine on more favorable terms than usual, owing to IDA's strong balance sheet and AAA credit rating. The EUR 50 million loan granted by Finland will consequently enable the World Bank to channel significantly more funding to Ukraine.
The loan decision requires the consent of parliament.
In 2023, Finland participated in IDA's previous SPUR program in support of Ukraine and Moldova. At that time, Finland allocated a EUR 50 million loan and a EUR 12 million grant for the program as part of a larger contribution to IDA Crisis Facility.

Ukraine’s steel output fell 57% and may hit zero next month. Expert says saving it comes down to four steps, and they’re Brussels’ to make
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:32:42 UTC
00:32:42 KST

Ukraine's steel industry, one of the pillars of its wartime economy, may produce almost no steel at all next month. Output fell 57.3% in August under Russian strikes and could approach zero in October, and the recovery of giants like Zaporizhstal and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih depends less on Kyiv than on Brussels, says Stanislav Zinchenko, director of the GMK Center, the center for industrial, mining, and metals sector expertise, in an analysis for ThePage.
Steel is Ukraine's second-largest foreign-currency earner and a prop for the hryvnia, employing more than 70,000 people directly and another 250,000 in related industries, and paying close to $1 billion a year in taxes.
Russian missile strikes on the big plants, compounded by an energy crisis, closed ports, and EU competition, have cut production to a fraction and threaten to halt it, Zinchenko says.
He calls it the worst crisis the industry has faced since independence, "a perfect storm" that has struck all at once. The sector supplies 6% of Ukraine's GDP and 13% of its foreign-currency earnings.
Output could hit zero
The fall has been precipitous. In August, steel output dropped 57.3 percent year on year to 277,000 tonnes and pig iron 65.6%, Zinchenko says. Across eight months, the decline is 12.5%, and he warns that October could bring output to zero. Exports have cratered too: iron ore down 27% over eight months, long rolled steel down 45.8%, semi-finished products down 76% in a single month, and pig-iron exports halted entirely.
September may yield just 100,000 to 150,000 tonnes of steel, he says. Four producers bore the brunt: Zaporizhstal, Kametstal, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, and Interpipe.
Rebuilding breaks new ground
"No one in the world has learned how to rebuild metallurgical giants after missile strikes," Zinchenko says.
In reality, it means technical audits, clearing rubble, and ordering unique new equipment, at a cost the plants cannot meet after four and a half years of war spent at a loss or at zero margin, their reserves gone.
Three steps for Kyiv
Zinchenko sets out three moves the state could make at once to stabilize the industry:
- Frontline rail. Give steelmakers priority access to locomotives from the state railway Ukrzaliznytsia within 150 kilometers of the front, so the product can still be moved out.
- Energy parity. Scrap or soften the rule forcing industry to import 80% of its electricity, which leaves plants paying European prices they cannot match.
- Market protection. Tax scrap-metal exports to keep raw material for decarbonization at home, and curb Turkish imports that undercut Ukrainian steel.
However, the recovery depends not on Kyiv, but on Brussels
Recovery is impossible without international funds and guarantees. No one will provide loans to enterprises on foreign capital markets during the war. No one will invest in recovery "into a void," the expert says.
He names four steps that would support the industry:
- A recovery fund. A dedicated fund for the steel industry, modeled on those partners built for Ukraine's energy sector, to pool grants and cheap loans.
- A safe sea corridor. Reopen the deepwater ports, as Ukraine managed in 2023 and 2024; without them, rail costs make exports unprofitable.
- No EU quotas. Remove the European Union's restrictive quotas and tariffs on Ukrainian metal.
- A CBAM exemption. Free Ukrainian steel, for the duration of the war and reconstruction, from the EU's carbon border levy, which Zinchenko says would otherwise finish off its competitiveness.
Meet those, he says, and bringing the plants back to baseline could take three to six months, with a full rebuild one to two years.

Here’s how brain-eating amoebas may infect people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

Some deadly amoebas may be primed to invade the brain.
Naegleria fowleri, known widely as the brain-eating amoeba, typically dine on bacteria in ponds. But the amoeba’s meal-seeking skills might make it uniquely suited to crawling up people’s noses and into their brains.
Naegleria amoebas are intrepid explorers, probing nooks and crannies in the lab — and they’re persistent, too. When creeping down narrow passageways, the amoebas charge relentlessly forward, almost never turning back, researchers report September 10 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. “They’re like robots,” says Lillian Fritz-Laylin, a cell biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. “They just go and go and go.”
Such persistence might help these tiny, single-celled creatures make the marathon journey from the nostrils all the way to the brain. Fritz-Laylin’s work helps flesh out a largely skeletal picture of Naegleria behavior. “We know almost nothing about the basic biology of these organisms,” she says.
N. fowleri amoebas don’t routinely harm humans. They usually dwell in warm bodies of fresh water, where they squirm through sediment and mind their own business. But on rare occasions, the creatures can be washed up a swimmer’s nose. As the amoebas migrate through the nasal cavity and into the brain, they destroy and eat tissue. Then they begin to reproduce, usually with lethal consequences. The United States typically sees fewer than 10 Naegleria infections each year, often at summer swimming spots, but nearly every one is fatal.
In the lab, Fritz-Laylin’s team tested Naegleria amoebas’ ability to move through different environments. They focused on N. gruberi, a harmless species that shares behaviors with its brain-eating relative. “It’s a lot safer to work with something that can’t kill you,” Fritz-Laylin says.
The researchers placed the amoebas on glass-bottom dishes containing narrow microchannels and watched them move under a microscope. They squeezed through channels smaller than themselves and seemed to be interested in exploring. When the amoebas encountered a channel opening, they very rarely left it, Fritz-Laylin says. Confinement sometimes sped them up, too. Inside the largest channels tested, the amoebas still zipped along twice as fast as cells on the outside.
Naegleria’s persistence and need for speed may make it unique. The team didn’t observe the same behaviors in a different type of amoeba tested. Such attributes probably make Naegleria well-adapted to hunting bacteria in pond sediments, says Fritz-Laylin, who is also a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator. But those innocent behaviors could also explain N. fowleri’s dark side. Put one at “the wrong place at the wrong time,” she says, “and it can cause devastating infection.”

Argentina rejects UK criticism about Falkland Islands arbitration
Unknown

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Argentina rejected British criticism Thursday of its decision to seek international arbitration about oil exploration around the Falkland Islands, which Buenos Aires calls Islas Malvinas.
It said an independent international tribunal is the appropriate mechanism to resolve the dispute peacefully.
“Nothing has to be feared from submitting a dispute to an impartial international tribunal,” Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said in a statement on US social media platform X.
Quirno said Buenos Aires rejected Britain's characterization of the arbitration as an attempt to “undermine” the rights of Falkland Islanders.
Argentina said resorting to arbitration under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) is a legal procedure accepted by both countries and argued that international legal mechanisms provide the appropriate framework for resolving disputes.
The statement came one day after British Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Overseas Territories Uma Kumaran defended London's position on the Falkland Islands.
“The Falkland Islands are British,” Kumaran said on X, reaffirming the UK's support for the islanders' right to self-determination.
She described Argentina's decision to pursue arbitration on the Sea Lion oil project as an attempt to “undermine” the rights and livelihoods of Falkland Islanders.
Kumaran also said the islanders have the right to develop their natural resources without intimidation, coercion or interference.
Argentina rejected the application of self-determination in the Falkland Islands sovereignty dispute and said unilateral British oil and gas exploration activities in the disputed area violate UN resolutions.
Buenos Aires also reaffirmed its willingness to resume negotiations with London to address the sovereignty dispute through diplomatic channels.
Argentina announced Monday that it had initiated arbitration proceedings under UNCLOS because of the Sea Lion project, involving oil exploration in waters around the Falkland Islands.
The government said the proceedings seek to challenge what it considers unlawful British exploitation of hydrocarbon resources in the disputed area.
The UK maintains that its activities around the islands comply with international law and has defended the rights of the islanders to determine their own political future and develop their natural resources.

A court in Lviv sentenced 20-year-old Viacheslav Zinchenko to life imprisonment on Thursday, Oct. 1, after finding him guilty of murdering Ukrainian linguist and former lawmaker Iryna Farion outside her home in July 2024.
The verdict was delivered by a panel of judges at the Shevchenkivskyi District Court of Lviv, Suspilne Lviv reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zinchenko was convicted of intentionally killing a person in connection with the performance of her public duty, motivated by national intolerance, as well as illegally possessing a firearm.
He pleaded not guilty and denied involvement in Farion’s killing throughout the proceedings.
Court points to forensic and digital evidence
The court said evidence established that Zinchenko was the person repeatedly seen in disguise near Farion’s apartment building before the shooting.
“The evidence clearly established that the person recorded in the courtyard of the building on Masaryka Street wearing a disguise was Zinchenko,” one of the judges said while reading the verdict.
An odor examination found a 99.999% match between a sample taken from Zinchenko and traces collected from a bench where prosecutors said the attacker waited for Farion. All three dogs involved in the examination produced the same result, according to the court.
Judges also cited a facial-comparison examination, surveillance footage documenting Zinchenko’s movements through Lviv and digital evidence recovered from his devices.
'Watering the Desert': EU Pushes Back as Ukraine Seeks More Money Despite €90B Aid Package
Investigators found that Zinchenko had searched for Farion’s personal information, obtained her telephone number and saved identifying details about her. He also searched for electricity outage schedules covering Masaryka Street, where she lived.
According to the verdict, Zinchenko researched ammunition, silencers and ways to convert firearms. The court said he purchased a converted Stalker 2906 pistol online in April 2024, although investigators did not recover or conclusively identify the weapon used to kill Farion.
Prosecutors also presented records showing that Zinchenko purchased clothing and accessories resembling those worn by the suspect, including a Panama hat, glasses, gloves and a camera. He traveled from Dnipro to Lviv on July 8 and rented several apartments in the city before the attack.
Farion shot outside her Lviv home
Farion was shot in the head near the entrance to her apartment building on Masaryka Street in Lviv on July 19, 2024.
Witnesses heard the shot and saw a young man run from the courtyard. Farion was taken to St. Panteleimon Hospital in critical condition and underwent emergency surgery but died several hours later at age 60.
Farion had been attacked shortly after leaving her home.
Police detained Zinchenko at his family home in Dnipro on July 25 following a nationwide search. He was 18 at the time of his arrest.
A court subsequently ordered him held without bail while investigators examined surveillance footage, witness statements and evidence collected during searches. Authorities believed the killing had been carefully planned.
Prosecutors said the investigation involved more than 60 forensic examinations, interviews with over 1,500 people and the analysis of extensive surveillance-camera footage.
Who was Iryna Farion?
Farion was a linguist, professor and prominent advocate for the Ukrainian language. She taught at Lviv Polytechnic National University and represented the nationalist Svoboda party in the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine’s legislature, from 2012 to 2014.
Her uncompromising statements about the use of Russian in Ukraine frequently generated controversy, particularly after Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Thousands attended her funeral in Lviv on July 22, 2024. She was buried at the city’s historic Lychakiv Cemetery.
Zinchenko’s defense maintained that prosecutors had failed to prove he fired the fatal shot. The verdict was issued by a court of first instance and can be appealed.

"Now, local growers can transport cash crops like cassava and corn smoothly to regional markets," she told Xinhua.

"This road has greatly benefited our farmers, who can now transport produce like cassava and corn without worrying about their vehicles getting bogged down like before -- it is bringing happiness and progress to our district," she said.

"National Road 10 is very beautiful. I used to live in a remote area plagued by many hardships, so seeing this modern road completed makes me absolutely thrilled."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said the highway marks a monumental leap forward for Cambodia, stitching together regional connectivity while transforming daily life across Battambang, Pursat, and Koh Kong.
"By linking agricultural hubs directly to seaport logistics, this strategic corridor empowers rural communities with faster market access, while seamless border-to-port transport enhances our trade competitiveness," he told Xinhua.
"Supported by our partnership with China under the Belt and Road Initiative, National Road 10 stands as a practical deliverable of the 'Diamond Hexagon Cooperation,' translating bilateral friendship into tangible, sustainable economic growth for the Cambodian people," Mengdavid said. ■

Trump Offers Russia Sanctions Relief Using His Belarusian Model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:25:00 UTC
00:25:00 KST

The negotiations between the US and Russia over the release of political prisoners appear to be a humanitarian mission. But if you set aside the humanitarian rhetoric and look at the timing, the price of the exchanges, the people conducting the negotiations, and the parallel economic decisions, a very different picture emerges.
There are enough signs to suggest that political prisoners are being used as a cheap and politically attractive asset to cover up reputation-damaging deals.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This is not a “humanitarian track” at all. It is potentially a sanctions-arbitrage mechanism using prisoners as currency.
In the current US-Russia track, Russia appears to have played its hand skillfully: it seized on the argument the US administration uses to save face and turned it into a tool of its own.
The first story is about Belarusian potash and 250 political prisoners – but in reality, it is about pressure on Canada and a potential deal with Gazprom. John Coale called the release of 250 Belarusian political prisoners a “significant humanitarian milestone,” while also describing it as the result of “direct, hard-nosed diplomacy.” But let’s look at what is actually happening.
In March 2026, Lukashenko released 250 people, and the US lifted sanctions on Belarusian potash producers. By September, the US economic interest had become clear: President Trump started talking about a “massive deal” to buy Belarusian potash at a lower price than Canadian potash, explicitly linking it to the interests of American farmers and ranchers.
Ukraine Rejects Australia’s Ageing Tiger Helicopters
Canada supplies the vast majority of US potash imports, so Belarusian potash gives Washington additional leverage in its trade relations with Ottawa. At the same time, the US is not facing a potash shortage – the interest lies primarily in lower prices, diversification, and strengthening Washington’s negotiating position with Canada.
At the same time, the deal creates an economic bridge to Russia. Because sanctions restrict transit through Lithuania, Belarusian potash is routed through Russian infrastructure. The chain therefore becomes broader: sanctions relief → Belarusian potash returns to the market → Russia’s involvement → a new US-Belarus-Russia trade and economic channel. Political prisoners provide the reputational cover.
And on Sept. 29, Lukashenko proposed the next step: a joint US-Belarusian nitrogen fertilizer plant, with the project already preliminarily agreed with Gazprom.
The second story is about creating and consolidating a Russia-US negotiating channel.
February 2025. The US gets Marc Fogel, an American teacher imprisoned on drug charges. Russia gets Alexander Vinnik. But Vinnik is an entirely different kind of asset. He ran BTC-e, one of the world’s key cryptocurrency money-laundering platforms. More than $9 billion in transactions passed through BTC-e, with US authorities linking the platform to ransomware, hacking, narcotics, identity theft, and other criminal activity.
Now look at the timing. Fogel was released on Feb. 11, 2025. On Feb. 18, one week later, US-Russia talks took place in Riyadh, launching Ukraine talks, diplomatic normalization, and economic cooperation. The following day, on Feb. 19, Dmitriev was already talking about the return of American companies to Russia.
Moscow got a valuable Russian national back. President Trump got a powerful television image: “American brought home.” And Witkoff gained a personal channel to Moscow.
In practical terms, the Fogel-Vinnik exchange functioned as an opening ritual for a direct Trump-Putin/Witkoff negotiating channel.
In the exchange of Ksenia Karelina for Artur Petrov, Russia’s gain was far more concrete. Karelina, a Russian-American citizen, was sentenced to 12 years in prison over a small donation to an organization helping Ukraine. In return, Moscow got Petrov back – a participant in a network designed to circumvent technology sanctions.
According to the US Department of Justice, he worked for Electrocom VPK, which used shell companies to purchase microcontrollers and integrated circuits in the US for Russian weapons manufacturers. Such components are used in missiles, drones, electronic warfare systems, and military communications.
So Russia did not simply get one of its citizens back, but rather an operator in a procurement network serving its defense industry, while also ending his criminal prosecution in the US. Washington, meanwhile, got a politically powerful case: the release of a young American citizen sentenced to 12 years for donating to Ukraine.
Moscow got an operationally valuable person – Washington got a politically valuable release.
The release of Robert Gilman in August 2026 is interesting precisely because the US officially said it made no concessions to Russia. Yet Moscow still gained a diplomatic asset: Witkoff publicly thanked Putin for his “personal engagement,” while US officials linked the decision, among other things, to the personal relationship between Putin and President Trump.
Russia gave up a prisoner who no longer held much value for it, while allowing the Trump administration to demonstrate another result of personal diplomacy.
The timing makes this gesture particularly revealing. On Sept. 5, Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin, Dmitriev held a separate three-hour discussion with them, and later that month he traveled to Washington for talks, including contacts with the Treasury Department and Department of Energy regarding future US-Russian energy projects.
Gilman’s release can therefore be viewed as a cheap signal of goodwill aimed at sustaining the personal Putin-Trump/Witkoff/Kushner channel: Moscow received no material concession, but invested an asset of little value to itself in political capital in Washington.
The third story is about sanctions relief and economic cooperation with Russia.
Once the negotiating track has been established and legitimized, the Trump administration faces another problem: how to begin easing sanctions and economically normalizing relations with Russia while Russia continues its war against Ukraine. This is where the Coale-Muratov initiative on Russian political prisoners comes in.
The Atlantic explicitly writes that the release of political prisoners could give Washington grounds for sanctions relief that would open the way for financial transactions and business deals with Russia. Potential areas include Russian oil, diesel, rare-earth metals, and other commodities.
For the Kremlin, such an arrangement is particularly advantageous because it allows Russia to obtain sanctions concessions without making concessions on Ukraine. Russia can release people it imprisoned itself, Washington can present this as a diplomatic achievement and use it to justify limited sanctions relief, and that, in turn, can make broader financial, energy, and raw materials deals possible.
This is not a “humanitarian track” at all. It is potentially a sanctions-arbitrage mechanism that uses prisoners as currency. And the most interesting part is that the American side does not deny it.
In an interview with RFE/RL, Coale is asked directly: Lukashenko is trading prisoners for sanctions relief – does that not encourage further arrests.
Coale’s answer is essentially that if Lukashenko trades prisoners for sanctions relief, “that’s fine with me.” What is particularly notable is that Coale himself selects which sanctions to propose lifting and then clears them with the Secretary of State or the President.
In negotiations with Russia, prisoners, sanctions, and energy are already moving through the same negotiating channel involving Dmitriev, Witkoff, and Kushner. This is especially revealing given Dmitriev’s role: he is not a humanitarian negotiator, but the head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund and one of Moscow’s key representatives in talks on restoring economic relations with the US.
The release of prisoners increasingly looks like a justification for launching the normalization of relations with Russia – the real strategic objective for part of the American negotiating team.
For the Kremlin, this is an almost ideal transaction: release people it imprisoned itself and try to convert that cheap domestic resource into much more valuable external concessions – sanctions relief, access to capital, technology, and energy markets – without ending the war or making concessions on Ukraine.
For the Trump administration, the same releases create visible diplomatic victories and a political justification for sanctions exemptions and economic deals it has already shown interest in.
Belarus has demonstrated how this model works: the regime creates hostages, releases them in batches, and receives real economic concessions in return.
If this mechanism is applied to Russia, political prisoners will become the currency with which the Kremlin will pay for normalization with the US without changing its behavior in the war.

Ex-Hungarian Minister Detained in $53 Million Graft Probe
Unknown

Reported by
Black-masked law enforcement officers escorted Balázs Hankó, a former Hungarian culture minister, into a district court on Thursday, where a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention over allegations that he masterminded the widespread misappropriation of state funds to benefit the party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
Hankó was taken into custody after Hungary's Parliament voted 139 to 0 on Monday to strip his legislative immunity. Before surrendering to prosecutors later that evening, he spent the day inside the Parliament building surrounded by his family, framing his pending arrest as political persecution.
"My conscience is clear; this is a political show trial," Hankó said in a video broadcast live on Orbán’s Facebook page before walking out alongside relatives and lawmakers from Fidesz, Orbán's right-wing party, which is now in opposition.
Prosecutors allege that Hankó misused 17.3 billion forints (about $53 million) during his concurrent tenure as president of the National Cultural Fund. According to the prosecutor’s office, between September 2025 and March 2026, Hankó and his associates established a "dual decision-making system" that bypassed legal evaluation procedures to distribute public grants across 1,079 separate instances along electoral and political lines.
The investigation was launched after whistleblowers alleged that the cultural fund was secretly channeling state grants to artists and organizations loyal to Fidesz. In one instance, public money was allegedly used to book a circus for a Fidesz campaign rally, which officials registered as a cultural event. Police previously raided offices housing Fidesz’s internet servers in July as part of the inquiry.
The court order marks one of the most high-profile moves yet in a sweeping anti-graft drive led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose administration took power after defeating Orbán and ending his 16 years in office. Magyar has estimated that systemic corruption under the prior government cost Hungary 8 to 10 percent of its gross domestic product. Writing on social media, Magyar declared that "millions of Hungarians had experienced for the first time what true regime change and equality before the law mean."
Fidesz leaders have fiercely denounced the proceedings, accusing Magyar’s government of authoritarian overreach. János Bóka, the leader of the Fidesz parliamentary group, pledged that the party would hold anyone involved in the prosecution answerable "in court, in politics, and in their finances."
The anti-graft inquiry has expanded beyond Hankó. On Monday, authorities also detained Miklós Seszták, who served as national development minister under Orbán from 2014 to 2018, in connection with a separate bribery investigation. Seszták has denied any wrongdoing.
Prosecutors have not formally charged Hankó beyond the initial suspicion of misappropriation, and he has not been convicted of a crime.
Lawmakers also voted to strip Prime Minister Péter Magyar of his immunity in an unrelated case that predates his time in office.

Woody Allen presents new film in Madrid, funded with €3m in public money
Unknown

2026-10-01
15:24:26 UTC
00:24:26 KST

The 90-year-old American director has unveiled in the capital his 51st film, due to start shooting on 5 October with public funding, as past scandals still shadow his career.
Woody Allen is stepping behind the camera once again. The American director presented his next film in Madrid on Thursday, the 51st of his career, which will start shooting on 5 October and will be filmed mainly in the Spanish capital and Aranjuez.
At 90, Allen was joined at the launch by the president of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, and the mayor of the capital, José Luis Martínez-Almeida. The project is being financed by both authorities: the City Council and the regional government will each contribute 1.5 million euros, 3 million in total, through sponsorship contracts linked to promoting Madrid. The film has a budget of around 12 million euros, so public support will cover roughly a quarter of the overall cost.
The film, still without a final title and provisionally known as 'Wasp 2026', will be a contemporary comedy blending romance, intrigue and infidelity in a diplomatic atmosphere. The cast includes Alexi Wasser, Jemima Kirke, Peter Vives, Marton Csokas and Jakob Oftebro, while much of the technical crew will be Spanish. Filming will run for around six weeks and will span more than 30 locations in Madrid and Aranjuez.
The sponsorship agreement also stipulates that Madrid must appear in the title of the film and that the city should have a clearly recognisable presence on screen. The City Council justifies its contribution as a tool to strengthen Madrid's international profile as a cultural, tourist and film-making destination.
Allen steers clear of current politics
During the presentation, Allen was also asked about the protests linked to the housing crisis taking place in Madrid. The director declined to comment on the situation, saying he has never seen himself as a filmmaker driven by political causes and that his films have focused mainly on human relationships and existential and romantic questions.
He did say he is "deeply" concerned about the rise of fascism and stressed that he has always opposed it in all its forms, whether in government or in areas such as theatre, censorship or literature.
The new production marks Allen's return to Spain after works such as 'Vicky Cristina Barcelona' and 'Rifkin's Festival'. The filmmaker again raised the possibility of retiring. During the event he said making films is exhausting and recalled that he had previously expressed his intention to give up cinema, although the chance to shoot this story in Madrid proved too tempting to refuse.
The controversies that follow Woody Allen
The director's return to Spain is also bringing renewed attention to the controversies that have defined his public image in recent decades. The main one concerns accusations of sexual abuse made by his adopted daughter Dylan Farrow, who alleges that Allen abused her in 1992, when she was seven. The filmmaker has repeatedly denied the allegation.
Allen has never been formally charged or tried over these claims. In 1993, Connecticut state prosecutor Frank Maco said there was probable cause to bring charges, but decided not to do so, arguing that putting Dylan Farrow through a court case could harm her. Meanwhile, a team of specialists at the child sexual abuse clinic of Yale-New Haven Hospital concluded after its assessment that Dylan had not been sexually abused. Allen has maintained ever since that the accusation is false.
The controversy flared up again decades later, particularly with the #MeToo movement and following the release in 2021 of the documentary series 'Allen v. Farrow'. Several Hollywood figures publicly distanced themselves from the filmmaker, and his professional relationship with Amazon ended up before the courts. Allen sued the company for 68 million dollars after it cancelled its agreement to produce several films. The two sides later reached an out-of-court settlement, the terms of which were not made public.
Another widely debated episode in his private life has been his relationship with Soon-Yi Previn, the adopted daughter of Mia Farrow and André Previn. The relationship between Allen and Previn became public in 1992, when the filmmaker had long been in a romantic relationship with Farrow. Allen and Previn married in Venice in 1997, when he was 62 and she was 27, a 35-year age gap.

====================================================================================================

Orbital data centers become new frontier in global AI race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:24:07 UTC
00:24:07 KST

Elif Gultekin Karahacioglu, Damla Delialioglu Demirtas and Emir Yildirim
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The race to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centers in space could change the global tech race at a foundational level as the computational demands of AI models continue to expand, turning the already heated competition into a geopolitical power struggle over digital sovereignty, experts say.
The US-China rivalry in the AI scene gained a whole new frontier with the emergence of space-based computing infrastructure, which sparked debate over which country will control what will ultimately become the foundation of the global internet.
Attorney Joao Lupi, a space law specialist, told Anadolu that the commercial race had already kicked off, with American tech giants like SpaceX, Google and Nvidia advancing their off-planet capabilities, while Beijing designated space-based data centers as one of the priorities in its 2026-2030 development plan, having approved a 2,800-satellite “Three-Body Computing Constellation,” 12 of which are already in orbit.
“More than a commercial race, the real contest is on the control dimension: who will own the next layer of global digital infrastructure — whoever operates the dominant orbital compute infrastructure could selectively provide or withhold processing services,” he said.
Lupi stated that modern satellites already make up the backbone of “communications, intelligence, and power generation command-and-control,” while commercial space data centers are expected to be “eventually caught up in strategic calculations and geopolitical tensions” on our planet, and data centers will become “a node of the data economy” in orbit.
He noted that the 1967 Outer Space Treaty requires the peaceful use of orbit and bans weapons of mass destruction, warning that there are currently no binding global agreements prohibiting the use of anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons and that the US, Russia, China and India conducted over 20 ASAT tests over the past 20 years.
“When serving both civilian and military users, which virtually all constellations may, the lines of distinction between civilian objects and military objects, when directing attacks as international humanitarian law requires, turn blurred,” he added.
He warned that moving computing networks into orbit also exacerbates the growing physical hazards of orbital congestion and space debris, alongside the potential for such orbital data centers to be targeted by kinetic ASATs, co-orbital systems, directed energy and other electronic warfare methods.
While the relocation of data centers into space led to a wave of applications for national and international legal rules over jurisdiction, data protection, cybersecurity and AI regulations, significant gaps in the current legal framework remain.
Slava G. Turyshev, a researcher at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Anadolu that a single large piece of debris striking a data satellite could result in the “Kessler effect,” which creates a catastrophic chain reaction of high-speed collisions, damaging multiple satellites.
He stated that private firms and governments are preparing to launch tens of thousands of new spacecraft into low and medium Earth orbits, requiring strong global information-sharing mechanisms to prevent accidental disasters.
Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), told Anadolu that only a handful of countries have clear legal frameworks to govern spacecraft or mandate liability insurance for orbital operations, revealing an unprecedented legal vacuum in relocating massive data reserves into space.
Swope warned that the international community must decide how privacy and intellectual property (IP) protections will be enforced when data is processed and stored in the largely unregulated and legally ambiguous expanse of space.

“Why is it too much?” Boxer replied. “You saved dozens of lives. You saved three families from Ness Ziona who were on that plane, and the entire country is thanking you.”
Among previous recipients of the city honor is retired Brig. Gen. Avigdor Kahalani, one of Israel’s best-known heroes of the 1973 Yom Kippur War and one of the few soldiers to receive both the Medal of Valor and the Medal of Distinguished Service.
Hayun said he was not sure what he had done could be called courage. “In moments like that, you operate automatically,” he said.
Boxer said that when he first heard what had happened, he wondered about Hayun’s military background. “Those are actions that come with experience and background,” he said. “To function like that isn’t natural. It’s inconceivable.”
Hayun’s wife, Meital, said people kept asking what her husband did for a living. “I told them, ‘He unclogs sewers,’” she said.
The couple recalled the moments when they felt the aircraft suddenly descending. “At first we thought it was turbulence,” they said. “The plane shook a little at first. Something crazy.”
“This isn’t a joke. It’s a historic event,” Hayun added. “When you think about it, it’s unbelievable.”
He returned to the same thought that had stayed with him since the flight landed safely. “This should be the passengers’ birthday,” he said. “We were all born again.”
‘I’m an upgraded plumber’
Hayun, 38, was among the Israelis who overpowered the Omani co-pilot alongside Tzvika Mans and Assaf Reguan.
He also responded Thursday to U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks about his role in the incident. Trump had described Hayun as an Israeli plumber with virtually no aviation experience who recognized what was happening and acted.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun joked. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with filthy pipes, and he was right. It didn’t offend me.”
Hayun said all he wanted now was to return to his normal life. “In my wildest dreams, I never thought Trump would talk about me and refer to what I did,” he said. “I actually like his humor. The way he described it was funny.”
“I’m no Bruce Lee,” he added. “But I managed to overpower the terrorist with a few other Israelis, pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Netanyahu admits Flydubai security ‘loophole’
Separately, Netanyahu acknowledged in a Fox News interview that the incident had exposed a loophole in the security procedures governing pilots operating flights to Israel.
“The first thing is you want a background check on pilots,” Netanyahu said. “Even if you have metal detectors, they’re usually for the passengers, and it’s quite possible that pilots just don’t go through that. So obviously, that’s a loophole that has to be corrected.”
Netanyahu also said the Omani co-pilot had undergone radicalization. “We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” he said.
Meanwhile, Indian media reported that Machchhar, the Indian captain attacked in the cockpit, apparently with an emergency axe, had been transferred from Saudi Arabia to Dubai for further medical treatment.
The government of Gujarat announced that it would honor Machchhar for his actions. Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel praised his “unwavering courage,” saying the captain’s actions helped save the lives of the passengers.

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:23:32 UTC
00:23:32 KST

SpaceX launches 13th long-duration astronaut crew to International Space Station
- SpaceX launched its 13th long-duration astronaut crew to the International Space Station, carrying two US astronauts, one Canadian, and one Russian for a mission on human health in orbit.
- The Falcon 9 rocket successfully delivered the Crew Dragon capsule into orbit, with a reusable booster returning safely to Earth after launch from Cape Canaveral.
- Crew 13 will conduct biomedical studies on microgravity's effects and join seven ISS occupants, continuing research aboard the US-Russian-led space station operating since 1998 and planned until 2030.
AI generated
CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida - A SpaceX rocket lifted off from Florida on Oct 1 with a crew of two US astronauts, a Canadian astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut headed to the International Space Station (ISS) for a science mission devoted to human health and performance in orbit.
The two-stage Falcon 9 rocket, topped with an autonomously operated Crew Dragon capsule carrying the four-member crew, was launched from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, along Florida’s Atlantic Coast.
A live webcast showed the 25-storey-tall rocket thundering off the launch pad as its nine Merlin engines roared to life in billowing, incandescent plumes of vapour.
Falcon 9’s reusable lower-stage booster separated from the rest of the vehicle within three minutes of launch and flew itself back to Earth for a return landing.
The rocket’s upper stage climbed higher and released into orbit the Crew Dragon carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
“Dragon separation confirmed. Jessica, Luke, Josh, Sergey, welcome to orbit,” SpaceX mission control in Hawthorne, California, told the crew.
The capsule is thrusting itself along an eight-hour orbital voyage to the space station and is set to dock with the orbiting laboratory platform some 400km above Earth around 7pm EDT (7am on Oct 2 in Singapore).
The mission marks the 13th long-duration space station team that NASA has flown aboard a SpaceX launch vehicle since the rocket venture founded in 2002 by Elon Musk began sending US astronauts to orbit in May 2020. The company went public in a record-breaking IPO in July.
The launch also comes days after SpaceX launched its next-generation Starship spacecraft on its first trip to orbit and first commercial satellite deployment, marking the vehicle’s 14th uncrewed test flight since 2023.
Crew 13 is led by geologist-turned-astronaut Watkins, 38, making her second voyage to space and becoming the first NASA astronaut to fly twice aboard a Crew Dragon.
Seated beside her in the pilot’s chair is Delaney, 47, a former test pilot and fighter pilot making his debut in space.
Rounding out Crew 13 are two other spaceflight rookies ranked as mission specialists - Kutryk, 44, a former test and fighter pilot, and Teteryatnikov, 37, an engineer who specialised in the operation of submarines.
The four crewmates are to be welcomed aboard the space station by seven current occupants of the orbital outpost, including the four members of Crew 12 who are due to fly back to Earth as soon as their seven-month-plus mission comes to an end.
The latest arrivals are expected to focus their attention on a series of biomedical and human performance studies, including research on how microgravity affects blood circulation and clotting, and gathering health data to inform future space missions.
The ISS, which spans the length of a football field and ranks as the largest human-made object in space, has been continuously operated by a US-Russian-led consortium that includes Canada, Japan and 11 European countries.
The first hardware for the outpost was launched more than a quarter-century ago. NASA has said it is committed to keeping the space station operating through 2030. REUTERS

FACTBOX: Key takeaways from Russia's draft federal budget for 2027-2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:21:16 UTC
00:21:16 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Fiscal and monetary policy measures implemented to cool inflationary pressures have proven highly effective, according to the explanatory note to the draft federal budget for 2027-2029 submitted to the State Duma's electronic database.
TASS has summarized the key highlights of the document:
Economic situation
- Fiscal and monetary policy measures designed to cool inflationary trends were quite effective.
- Russia's federal budget deficit for 2026 is projected at 3.2% of GDP, or 7.335 trillion rubles ($87.79 billion).
- Russia's total public debt is forecast to reach 53.9 trillion rubles ($645.08 billion) by the end of 2027, 61.1 trillion rubles ($731.24 billion) by the end of 2028, and 67.9 trillion rubles ($812.63 billion) by the end of 2029.
- The share of domestic debt within the country's total public debt is set to rise progressively to 89.1% in 2027, 89.9% in 2028, and 91.3% in 2029.
Finance Ministry plans and National Wealth Fund replenishment
- The Finance Ministry plans to issue ruble-denominated bonds totaling 7.72 trillion rubles ($92.39 billion) in 2027, 7.43 trillion rubles ($88.92 billion) in 2028, and 8 trillion rubles ($95.74 billion) in 2029.
- The ministry will allocate 51.5 billion rubles ($616.35 million) annually from 2027 to 2029 to purchase precious metals and gemstones for the State Fund (Gokhran).
- The National Wealth Fund will be replenished by 1.082 trillion rubles ($12.95 billion) in 2027, 345.7 billion rubles ($4.14 billion) in 2028, and 379 billion rubles ($4.54 billion) in 2029.
- Plans also include issuing foreign-currency government bonds worth up to $1 billion annually between 2027 and 2029.
Budget revenues
- Gambling tax revenues are projected at 36.6 billion rubles ($438.03 million) in 2027, 38.1 billion rubles ($456.00 million) in 2028, and 39.5 billion rubles ($472.74 million) in 2029.
- Total oil and gas revenues flowing into the federal budget in 2027 are forecast at 7 trillion rubles ($83.78 billion).
- The Finance Ministry expects budget revenues from state-company dividends to reach 838.4 billion rubles ($10.03 billion) in 2027, 914 billion rubles ($10.94 billion) in 2028, and 986 billion rubles ($11.80 billion) in 2029.
- Value-added tax (VAT) revenues will amount to 20 trillion rubles ($239.36 billion) in 2027, 21.3 trillion rubles ($254.92 billion) in 2028, and 22.7 trillion rubles ($271.67 billion) in 2029.
- Personal Income Tax revenues will total nearly 2 trillion rubles (nearly $23.94 billion) in 2027, and 1.3 trillion rubles ($15.56 billion) and 1.4 trillion rubles ($16.76 billion) in 2028 and 2029, respectively.
- The Finance Ministry does not expect any revenue from the Bank of Russia's profits this year, whereas in 2027, such revenue could reach 216 billion rubles ($2.59 billion).
- National Wealth Fund (NWF) assets held in accounts at the Bank of Russia are projected at 5.16 trillion rubles ($61.76 billion) by the end of 2027, 5.98 trillion rubles ($71.57 billion) in 2028, and 6.62 trillion rubles ($79.23 billion) in 2029.
- Foreign borrowers may repay 193 billion rubles ($2.31 billion) to Russia in 2027, 209 billion rubles ($2.50 billion) in 2028, and 248.9 billion rubles ($2.98 billion) in 2029 toward the settlement of outstanding sovereign loans.
- Budget revenues from state asset privatization will amount to 3.05 billion rubles ($36.50 million) in 2027, dropping to 231.6 million rubles ($2.77 million) in 2028, and 231 million rubles ($2.76 million) in 2029.
- Non-repayable receipts from non-state organizations are expected to amount to 1.9 trillion rubles ($22.74 billion) annually from 2027 to 2029.
- Revenues from fines, sanctions, and damage compensation are projected to rise to 397 billion rubles ($4.75 billion) in 2027, 446.7 billion rubles ($5.35 billion) in 2028, and 464.1 billion rubles ($5.55 billion) in 2029.
Social sector spending
- Approximately 1.78 trillion rubles ($21.30 billion) is earmarked for the "Education" sector for 2027.
- Nearly 1.82 trillion rubles (nearly $21.78 billion) is allocated for the "Healthcare" national category for 2027.
- The 2027 budget of the Federal Compulsory Medical Insurance Fund (FOMS) indexes salaries for doctors and mid-level medical personnel.
- Insurance pension payments through the Social Fund will amount to 12.9 trillion rubles ($154.39 billion) in 2027.
Mortgage programs
- Subsidies for family mortgages are set at 785.8 billion rubles ($9.40 billion) for 2027, 471.7 billion rubles ($5.65 billion) for 2028, and 389.7 billion rubles ($4.66 billion) for 2029.
- Subsidies for mortgages with rates of up to 8% are set at 232.5 billion rubles ($2.78 billion) for 2027, 107.1 billion rubles ($1.28 billion) for 2028, and 91.4 billion rubles ($1.09 billion) for 2029.
- Subsidies for IT mortgages are set at 64.8 billion rubles ($775.53 million) for 2027, 41.1 billion rubles ($491.88 million) for 2028, and 35 billion rubles ($418.88 million) for 2029.
- Subsidies for rural mortgages are set at 32.9 billion rubles ($393.75 million) for 2027, 21.9 billion rubles ($262.10 million) for 2028, and 18.8 billion rubles ($224.99 million) for 2029.
- Subsidies for Far East and Arctic mortgages are set at 135.3 billion rubles ($1.62 billion) for 2027, 121 billion rubles ($1.45 billion) for 2028, and 130 billion rubles ($1.56 billion) for 2029.
Shipping
- Over 100 billion rubles ($1.20 billion) from the federal budget will be allocated for the development of the Greater Northern Sea Route between 2027 and 2029.
- Plans are in place to allocate 388 million rubles ($4.64 million) in 2027, 408.2 million rubles ($4.89 million) in 2028, and 408.2 million rubles ($4.89 million) in 2029 for organizing regular shipping services along the Northern Sea Route.
- Over 1.069 billion rubles ($12.79 million) will be allocated from the budget in 2027 to replace decommissioned vessels.
- More than 26.7 billion rubles ($319.55 million) from the budget will be directed toward the construction of the lead nuclear-powered icebreaker of the "Leader" project in 2027.
Security and Defense
- Plans call for allocating over 17.147 trillion rubles ($205.22 billion) from the budget for national defense in 2027, nearly 16.608 trillion rubles ($198.76 billion) in 2028, and nearly 16.296 trillion rubles ($195.03 billion) in 2029.
- The 2027 budget includes 11.7 billion rubles ($140.03 million) for allowances for contract military personnel and law enforcement officers.
- Over 1.5 trillion rubles ($17.95 billion) is slated for allocation from the budget in 2027 to cover pensions for military personnel and their families.
- Additionally, more than 1.5 billion rubles ($17.95 million) will be allocated from the budget in 2027 to support the operation of the unified registry of individuals liable for military service.
- Plans are in place to allocate over 4.6 billion rubles ($55.05 million) next year to ensure Russia's chemical and biological security.
- Over 5 billion rubles ($59.84 million) in budget subsidies are planned to be allocated to the Russian Voluntary Society for Assistance to the Army, Aviation, and Navy over the next three years: 2,385.8 million rubles ($28.56 million) in 2027, 1,377.1 million rubles ($16.48 million) in 2028, and 1,370.9 million rubles ($16.41 million) in 2029.
- More than 62.5 billion rubles ($748.00 million) is planned to be allocated from the budget to the Defenders of the Fatherland Foundation during the 2027-2029 period.
-The budget earmarks 3 billion rubles ($35.90 million) for a subsidy to Rosoboronexport for the 2027-2029 period.
Space industry development
- A budget allocation of over 337.646 billion rubles ($4.04 billion) is proposed for the development of space activities in 2027.
- The government plans to allocate approximately 38.6 billion rubles ($461.96 million) from the budget in 2027 for the creation and operation of the Russian Orbital Station (ROS). A total of 136.72 billion rubles ($1.64 billion) is planned for this purpose over the 2027-2029 period.
- Approximately 112.46 billion rubles ($1.35 billion) is proposed to be allocated from the budget in 2027 for the "Manned Spaceflight" federal project.
- Also in 2027, a proposal has been made to allocate approximately 14.16 billion rubles ($169.47 million) for the development of space systems for lunar exploration.
- Plans are in place to allocate over 20.4 billion rubles ($244.15 million) for the creation of a heavy-class space rocket complex at the Vostochny Cosmodrome.
- Approximately 22.5 billion rubles ($269.28 million) is proposed for the development of Russian space nuclear power technologies in 2027.
Information Technology Development
- Approximately 1 billion rubles ($11.97 million) will be allocated from the budget in 2028-2029 for the development of critical technologies for 5G Advanced/6G communication network equipment.
- The "Data Economy" national project may receive over 470 billion rubles ($5.63 billion) in budget allocations during 2027-2029.
Transport
The government plans to allocate funds for the implementation of the "Efficient Transport System" national project as follows: 185.139 billion rubles ($2.22 billion) in 2027, 118.9 billion rubles ($1.42 billion) in 2028, and 122.2 billion rubles ($1.46 billion) in 2029.
Plans also include allocating over 1.75 trillion rubles ($20.94 billion) in 2027, 2.1 trillion rubles ($25.13 billion) in 2028, and 1.75 trillion rubles ($20.94 billion) in 2029 for the implementation of the "Development of the Transport System" state program.
Regional Development
- Over 269 billion rubles ($3.22 billion) will be allocated from the budget for the socio-economic development program for Crimea and Sevastopol during 2027-2029.
- Over 865 billion rubles ($10.35 billion) will be allocated from the budget for the restoration and development of the Donbass and Novorossiya regions during 2027-2029.
- Over 28 billion rubles ($335.10 million) will be allocated from the budget for investment projects in the Arctic during 2027-2029.
Food Security
Funding for the Technological Support for Food Security national project is planned at 22.59 billion rubles ($270.36 million) for 2027, 24.622 billion rubles ($294.68 million) for 2028, and 24.737 billion rubles ($296.05 million) for 2029.

The EU and Ukraine have agreed on funding for defense and budgetary needs for 2026 — official statement and details

Ukraine and the EU have agreed on sources of funding for budgetary and defense needs for 2026. They plan to allocate €45 billion for 2027.

Greece pitches suspension of the EU’s right to asylum during migration crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:20:06 UTC
00:20:06 KST

A special regime would be activated in case of a rapid increase in arrivals and migrants flows used as a hybrid threat by third countries. Several EU governments seem open to the proposal, which could feature in the Commission’s new Emergency Response.
Greek Migration and Asylum Minister Thanos Plevris on Thursday proposed suspending the right to apply for asylum in the EU in cases of a mass influx of irregular migrants.
The controversial measure would mark a major shift in the bloc's migration policy, allowing migrants to be returned without an individual assessment of their asylum claims, potentially resulting in “collective pushbacks”, which are prohibited under current EU law.
Greece is pushing for the proposal to be included in the “European Emergency Response Framework”, a new law the European Commission is presenting in the coming months to tackle irregular arrivals and the instrumentalisation of migration at the EU’s external borders.
Athens has proposed a mechanism called the “Special Derogation Regime”, which would be triggered only in exceptional circumstances. The criteria would include a rapid increase in irregular arrivals, pressure on local infrastructure and evidence that migratory flows are being organised or facilitated by non-EU countries.
If triggered, the mechanism would allow the temporary suspension of asylum applications, the use of accelerated return procedures and immediate assistance from the EU border agency Frontex.
The discussion was brief after Plevris presented the proposal at the Home Affairs Council in Luxembourg, according to diplomats.
But several EU countries appear open to backing the measure.
"There was a clear willingness to look into this matter and see what is possible", an EU diplomat told Euronews.
Poland, Germany, Austria and Denmark are among the countries showing support.
“Normal asylum procedures cannot take place when it is clear that [a mass influx of migrants] is not a humanitarian situation, but one caused by smuggling and disinformation acts,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters on arrival.
“If 70,000 people, especially young men, come in one day, that obviously has nothing to do with asylum [...] and then you cannot work with the previous rules,” Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said.
Belgian Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt also said there should be “no taboos” when considering measures to make the return of irregular migrants more effective.
Earlier this week, the European People’s Party backed suspending the right to seek asylum in response to “hybrid attacks”, in which third countries facilitate large-scale migration to destabilise an EU border.
The proposal has been criticised by left-wing politicians, migration experts and civil society groups, who argue that suspending a fundamental right would be unprecedented and could undermine existing safeguards.
Some EU countries have temporarily suspended the processing of asylum claims in the past.
Greece suspended the processing of asylum claims for one month in March 2020 and again for three months in July 2025, following a sudden increase in sea arrivals from Libya. Poland introduced a similar measure for migrants crossing its border from Belarus in March 2025.
At EU level, however, suspending the right to seek asylum remains under consideration. Under current rules, people present in an EU country have the right to apply for asylum, with claims assessed individually.
Asylum applications in the EU have been falling since 2023. In the first half of this year, around 332,000 people applied for asylum in EU countries plus Switzerland and Norway, 17% fewer than during the same period in 2025.
During the same meeting, EU ministers gave a final green light to the "Return Regulation", a law aimed at speeding up the return of migrants with no legal right to remain in the EU. It allows EU countries to set up deportation centres outside the bloc, known as return hubs, through agreements with non-EU countries.

Ukraine Rejects Australia’s Ageing Tiger Helicopters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

Ukraine has withdrawn its request for Australia’s retiring Eurocopter Tiger attack helicopters, deciding that their maintenance and logistical demands would outweigh the benefits of receiving the aircraft as military aid.
Ukraine’s Ambassador to Australia Vasyl Myroshnychenko confirmed the decision to Defense Express, which reported it on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We have withdrawn our interest in the Tiger helicopters. So we are no longer pursuing them,” Myroshnychenko said.
Ukraine initially requested the Australian helicopters in 2024 but formally withdrew its interest in early 2026 after military specialists evaluated the aircraft and the resources required to operate them.
Australia had reportedly been prepared to transfer its retiring Tigers to Ukraine. Although the helicopters themselves would have been provided without charge, Kyiv would still have needed to finance pilot and ground-crew training, repairs, spare parts and continued maintenance.
Why Ukraine turned down the Tiger
According to Defense Express, Ukraine considered several factors, including the helicopters’ technical condition, their remaining service life, the cost of each flight hour and the availability of replacement parts.
Australia’s Tiger configuration also contains US-made equipment, potentially requiring Washington’s approval before the helicopters could be transferred without removing those systems.
Introducing another aircraft type would have created an additional maintenance and supply chain for Ukraine, whose army aviation already operates several Soviet-designed helicopter models under wartime conditions.
Media Report Assassination Attempt on Fire Point Co-Owner – ‘Somewhat Exaggerated,’ He Says
The Tiger entered Australian service in 2004 but faced long-running reliability and availability problems. Australia’s 2024-25 defense report acknowledged that the fleet’s reliability and serviceability remained under pressure as the military prepared to phase out the aircraft.
Australia formally ended Tiger flying operations in September. Its Defense Department said the retirement reflected the aircraft’s planned 20-year service life and the challenges posed by modern air defenses, precision weapons and unmanned systems.
The aircraft’s history does not mean the Tiger lacks combat capability. It can conduct armed reconnaissance and ground-attack missions using a cannon, rockets and guided missiles. However, keeping a small foreign fleet operational during a high-intensity war would require substantial long-term investment.
Australia replaces Tigers with Apaches
Australia is replacing its 22 Tigers with 29 US-made AH-64E Apache Guardian attack helicopters purchased through the US Foreign Military Sales program.
Six Apaches had been delivered by May, while the entire fleet is expected to arrive by 2029. Australia conducted its first domestic Apache live-fire exercise in July.
The AH-64E offers more advanced sensors, communications and targeting systems and is supported by a considerably larger international supply chain than the Tiger.
Myroshnychenko previously said Ukraine was interested in obtaining Apaches from the United States, rather than receiving aircraft from Australia’s newly purchased fleet.
Apache may not be frontline survivable in Russian air defense threat environment
Ukraine does not currently operate Apache helicopters. As Kyiv Post previously reported, their effectiveness over Ukraine would depend on suppressing Russia’s extensive air defense network and integrating the aircraft with reconnaissance and electronic-warfare systems.
Ukrainian Ground Force Aviation has also identified the multipurpose UH-60 Black Hawk as a possible foundation for its future fleet as Kyiv considers how to replace its aging Soviet-designed helicopters.
The decision contrasts with an earlier dispute over Australia’s retired MRH-90 Taipan transport helicopters.
Ukraine requested those aircraft, but Canberra dismantled the fleet after concluding that restoring it to operational condition was impractical.
Earlier, Australian Federation of Ukrainian Organizations co-chair Stefan Romaniw also said that Ukraine had appealed to Australia to transfer the Taipans rather than scrap them.

Greece: Human rights defenders Tommy Olsen and Panayote Dimitras on trial for their work supporting refugees and migrants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Ahead of the trial of human rights defenders Tommy Olsen and Panayote Dimitras on 6 October in Rhodes on charges relating to their work in support of refugees and migrants Dinushika Dissanayake, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for Europe said:
“The criminal charges against Panayote Dimitras and Tommy Olsen are a gross misuse of anti-smuggling legislation and are not backed by evidence. Both are being targeted for their work documenting serious human rights violations against migrants and refugees.
“The Greek authorities have a long-standing record of going after human rights defenders and criminalizing human rights work, but this is a new low. For the first time, human rights workers are being referred to trial for helping people access asylum procedures. Construing this as ‘smuggling’ is not only a distortion of international and domestic law but a dangerous vilification of NGOs’ valuable work.”
In July 2021, Dimitras and Olsen were supporting people seeking asylum on the island of Kos including helping them to access the asylum procedure. They also documented and reported cases of pushbacks by the Greek authorities – the illegal and often violent practice of summarily returning people across borders, a practice that Greece has been found guilty of by the European Court of Human Rights.
The authorities accuse Dimitras and Olsen of establishing and participating in a criminal organization and jointly facilitating the “unlawful entry” and “unlawful stay” of third country nationals in Greece. Based on information available to Amnesty International, there is no indication that Dimitras’ and Olsen’s work went beyond the legitimate activities of assisting people in legally exercising their human rights and documenting the situation.
If convicted they face up to 20 years in prison.
Tommy Olsen said: “When human rights defenders face criminal prosecution for documenting what happens at Europe’s borders, while pushbacks and other serious human rights violations continue with impunity, it sends a powerful message to everyone doing this work: stay silent, or risk becoming the accused yourself.”
Panayote Dimitras said: “This prosecution had the sole aim to harass us and severely limit our work documenting human rights violations at Greece’s borders. It has left me stigmatized and has prevented me from travelling abroad to continue our human rights advocacy at an international level for more than three years.”
“The charges brought against Olsen and Dimitras send an alarming message that supporting people in need of protection to exercise their rights can be misconstrued as complicity in smuggling. This doesn’t just harm refugees and migrants who have undertaken dangerous journeys at sea, as it discourages the provision of assistance, but has a chilling effect on civil society a whole,” said Dinushika Dissanayake from Amnesty International.
Background
Tommy Olsen is a Norwegian human rights worker who founded the NGO Aegean Boat Report in 2017 to monitor arrivals to the Greek islands and document rights violations. Panayote Dimitras is the legal administrator and representative of the NGO Greek Helsinki Monitor, an organization that documents racist violence and racist speech including pushbacks of asylum seekers by Greek law enforcement officers at borders.
Since 2023, the Greek authorities have imposed extremely onerous pretrial measures on Dimitras, including a ban on leaving the country, a duty to regularly report to the police station, and a bail payment of €10,000.
Tommy Olsen is currently living in Norway. Earlier in the year, Norway’s authorities rejected an extradition request from Greece, finding that the actions for which Olsen had been prosecuted in Greece are not illegal in Norway and represented a real risk for Olsen’s right to freedom of expression.
Amnesty International has repeatedly highlighted shortcomings in Greek anti-smuggling laws, noting that the legislation is based on broad and vague language, and does not adequately protect human rights defenders and humanitarian actors from criminal prosecution.

DUSHANBE, October 1. /TASS/. Russia remains Tajikistan’s leading economic partner, accounting for more than 20% of the republic’s foreign trade turnover, Prime Minister of Tajikistan Kokhir Rasulzoda said.
"Russia confidently maintains its status as Tajikistan’s leading economic partner, accounting for over 22% of our country’s total foreign trade turnover," he said at an expanded meeting of the intergovernmental commission on economic cooperation between the two countries. "In 2025, mutual trade reached a record high of $2.5 bln, an increase of nearly a quarter," the premier added.
