Europäische Länder vereinbaren „entschlossene“ Reaktion auf Diesel-Druck aus den USA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:15:35 UTC
00:15:35 KST

Europäische Länder vereinbaren „entschlossene“ Reaktion auf Diesel-Druck aus den USA
Die Länder, darunter Großbritannien, Frankreich und Deutschland, hielten am Donnerstag eine Krisensitzung ab, um auf die Forderungen der Trump-Regierung nach einer Freigabe ihrer Dieselreserven zu reagieren.
BRÜSSEL — Fünf europäische Länder haben sich am Donnerstag bei einem Krisentreffen darauf geeinigt, „mit einer Stimme“ auf den wachsenden Druck der US-Regierung zu reagieren, europäische Dieselreserven freizugeben. Das erfuhr POLITICO aus Kreisen, die mit der Angelegenheit vertraut sind.
Frankreich, Deutschland, Großbritannien, Italien, Irland und die Europäische Kommission nahmen an den Gesprächen teil, um zu entscheiden, wie auf den Druck aus Washington reagiert werden soll, wie drei europäische Beamte gegenüber POLITICO erklärten.
Alle teilnehmenden EU-Länder seien von den USA hinter verschlossenen Türen unter Druck gesetzt worden, ihre Dieselreserven auszuschütten, andernfalls drohe ein Verbot von US-Dieselexporten, sagten zwei der Informanten.
Advertisement
Die Länder einigten sich gemeinsam mit der Kommission auf drei Punkte, wie die Informanten angaben: auf den Druck mit einer „koordinierten Stimme“ zu reagieren, sicherzustellen, dass „jede Entscheidung über die Freigabe von Vorräten auf die Ebene der IEA [Internationale Energieagentur] gehoben wird“, und zu versuchen, „die Spannungen im Gespräch mit den USA abzubauen“.
Die in Paris ansässige Internationale Energieagentur koordiniert die Energiepolitik der reichen Industrieländer der Welt. Die IEA leitete Anfang dieses Jahres nach der Sperrung der Straße von Hormus die Freigabe von Ölvorräten, an denen sich auch Deutschland beteiligte.
„Es geht darum, die Situation zu ‚deeskalieren‘“, sagte einer der Beteiligten an den heutigen Krisengesprächen. „Man soll in der Kommunikation zwar selbstbewusst, aber positiv auftreten … Wenn man es mit einem hungrigen Löwen zu tun hat, spielt man mit ihm besser keine schmutzigen Spielchen.“
Eine größere Gruppe von Ländern, von denen einige ebenfalls unter Druck seitens der Trump-Regierung stehen, wird bei einem Treffen am Freitag über ihre Reaktion beraten, fügte die Person hinzu.
POLITICO hatte zuvor berichtet, dass US-Energieminister Chris Wright von mehreren EU-Staaten die Freigabe von Dieselvorräten als Alternative zu einem Exportverbot forderte. Europa ist von Diesel aus den Vereinigten Staaten in hohem Maße abhängig. Infolge der Kriege in der Ukraine und im Iran steigen die Dieselpreise in den USA rasant an, was den Druck auf US-Präsident Donald Trump erhöht, die Preise noch vor den entscheidenden Zwischenwahlen zu senken.
Trump hatte sich am Mittwoch geweigert, ein Exportverbot auszuschließen, trotz heftigen Widerstands seitens der US-Ölindustrie. „Ich denke darüber nach“, sagte Trump bei einer Veranstaltung im Oval Office zum Thema Exportverbot. „Ich spreche oft mit [Energieminister] Chris [Wright] und [Innenminister] Doug [Burgum] darüber – sie glauben irgendwie, dass es dem Diesel helfen würde, aber es könnte die Preise für andere Dinge in die Höhe treiben.“
Dieser Artikel erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO. Er wurde von Josh Groeneveld auf Deutsch übersetzt.

Sweden Ready to Take the Fight Into Russia if NATO Attacked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:13:00 UTC
00:13:00 KST

Since its accession to NATO, which was a sudden reversal of its century’s old tradition of neutrality, Sweden’s armed forces are also revisiting its long-held strategy of engaging in purely defensive operations.
As Colonel Karl Bergqvist, head of the Swedish Air Force’s Air Warfare Center, made clear in an interview with the Aftonbladet newspaper on Monday, Stockholm is adopting a more offensive approach to air operations.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bergqvist said that in the event of a Russian attack, Sweden will target objectives deep within enemy territory. He added that Moscow must become aware that: “An attack will come at a high cost.” He made it clear that this strategy was one of deterrence and that any future conflict would not remain confined to Swedish territory.
The strategy was based on lessons from the war in Ukraine, particularly the start of the 2022 full-scale invasion, when air superiority played a key role in Moscow’s early success. At the same time, Sweden continues to emphasize its ability to rapidly disperse aircraft and operate from highways and other improvised airstrips, a concept central to the design of its JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets.
Bergqvist said another key factor in the new strategy was the capability of the Gripen to use air-launched Taurus KEPD 350 cruise missiles – a concept that was successfully tested in use in August and September.
Russia Strikes Kyiv Nuclear Institute Housing Reactor
Its range, more than 500 kilometers (310 miles), would enable deep strikes against logistics, command centers, and air bases where its MEPHISTO dual-stage penetrating warhead can defeat even hardened targets, disrupting Russian operations at an early stage.
Sweden is also in the process of acquiring longer-range cruise and ballistic missile systems capable of engaging targets of up to 2,000 kilometers (1,250 miles).
As well as increasing its ability to take the fight to the enemy, Sweden is strengthening its conventional air defenses, its ability to counter drones, and expanding its intelligence-gathering capabilities – part of the alliance wide enhancements announced by US Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, SACEUR, on Saturday.
That same day, Denmark said there was a “small but growing risk” that Russia might launch a limited military offensive against one or more neighboring NATO countries in the near future.

US jobless claims fall to lowest since mid-July
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices
The number of people applying for US unemployment benefits dipped last week to the lowest level since mid-July as lay-offs remain low and most American workers enjoy job security.
The Labor Department said on Thursday that initial jobless claims ticked down to 197,000 from a revised 198,000 the week before. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, dropped by 2,500 to 200,000.
Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for lay-offs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. So far this year, claims have mostly stayed below 220,000 – historically low.
The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher energy prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began February 28.

Greece to set up a new national dementia centre for patients, families and caretakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:11:17 UTC
00:11:17 KST

The new centre in Athens will provide cognitive training, occupational and music therapy, plus services for prevention, diagnosis and ongoing patient monitoring.
Greece is creating a new integrated care model for people living with dementia and Alzheimer's disease, for their families and caretakers. The new National Dementia Model Centre will be located in Peristeri, Athens.
The Centre aims to become a key reference point for the prevention, diagnosis, monitoring and care of people with dementia and related disorders, and a blueprint for similar services across the country.
Services for patients and carers
The new facility will offer cognitive stimulation, occupational therapy and music therapy programmes, as well as services for prevention, diagnosis and systematic patient follow-up.
The services will include counselling and guidance for families and carers, including via telemedicine, while training programmes will be developed for health professionals, carers and young researchers.
The Centre will provide free services to up to 160 people a day, reaching around 5,000 people a year.
Setting standards nationwide
Beyond services, the Centre will also develop quality standards and evaluation tools to continuously upgrade the facilities that provide services to people with dementia in Greece.
At the same time, it is expected to support volunteering, information and awareness-raising initiatives, contribute to educating civil society and promote dementia research.
Presenting the project, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis stressed that the Centre will serve as a source of expertise for similar facilities throughout Greece, while also contributing to research and public information. Mitsotakis said that the aim is also to reduce the social stigma that still surrounds the disease.
The prime minister also referred to the importance of cooperation between the state, civil society, local government and the Church in delivering the project.
The National Dementia Model Centre is set to open in September 2027. A pilot phase is planned, with full operation of the facility scheduled for spring 2028.
Partnership between the state, foundations and institutions
The creation of the Centre is the result of cooperation between the public sector, the National Bank of Greece and 12 charitable foundations that participate in the "Initiative '21'", with the involvement of local authorities and the Church.
Renovation of the space, procurement of equipment and funding for the first two years will be covered by a donation of €4.49 million from the members of the "Initiative '21'".
Deputy Health Minister Irini Agapidaki described the project as an opportunity for a broader change in how dementia is addressed, with an emphasis on prevention, early diagnosis and patient support. She placed particular emphasis on the need to train informal carers, who shoulder a significant part of the daily care of people with dementia.

Why Are Modi Government Critics Now Targeting India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

“You must have heard of Dharmendra Pradhan,” student leader Neha Bora said in a video message on September 30, two days before a series of agitations is scheduled to start in major Indian cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Kolkata, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.
“Gyanesh Kumar, it’s your turn now. We are coming,” Bora said with a cheeky smile. A leftist student leader, Bora was part of the youth agitation in July that forced the Narendra Modi government’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, out of office.
Now, students and youth are rallying around the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties against a new target: Gyanesh Kumar, who has been at the center of political controversies since his appointment as chief election commissioner about a year and a half ago.
Kumar has been accused of speaking political language and giving undue advantage to India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). He is being compared with Adolf Eichmann, the central operational manager of the Holocaust.
The latest trigger for the nationwide protests that will begin on October 2 was an investigation by The Indian Express, which reported that two members of the Election Commission, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns with Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months, only to be overlooked. Some decisions were reportedly taken without their knowledge. The objections concerned electoral roll decisions and orders.
Notably, Kumar is the first chief election commissioner appointed under a new law that the Modi government brought, overturning a mechanism recommended by India’s Supreme Court. This new law gives the government the authority to pick election commissioners of its choice. The law also gives immunity to the election commissioner for any action they take with regard to conducting elections.
The opposition’s challenge to the law has not made much progress in the Supreme Court yet, with a five-judge constitutional bench expected to start hearing it.
The Indian Express report dropped like a political bombshell. Opposition parties jumped in to claim that the report vindicates what they have been alleging for a long time: that the BJP government is using Chief Election Commissioner Kumar to manipulate elections in favor of the BJP, starting with the voter roll.
Trying to downplay the internal rift, the commission’s reply was measured: differences are normal in any institution. Despite the concerns raised at different stages, the final decisions were unanimous, the commission said.
Its defense has not calmed the room. The Indian Express disclosures landed amid the highly contested overhaul of the voter roll, the Special Intensive Revision, which has removed millions of names from the electoral rolls. Several opposition leaders and civil society personalities, including Rahul Gandhi of the Congress, India’s main opposition party, have alleged that the electoral roll revision process is being used to steal votes.
A dispute inside a constitutional body has thus become evidence, for opponents, not only of a wider institutional failure, but also of “sabotage” of an institution that is most critical for the smooth functioning of an electoral democracy.
The CJP, a youth movement that spearheaded the July agitation, moved quickly. “Gyanesh, it’s done bro,” CJP leader Abhijit Dipke wrote on social media the day the Indian Express report was published. The CJP gave Kumar 48 hours to quit. In the national capital of New Delhi, the Jantar Mantar premises, the site of the June-July protests, were heavily barricaded on September 25 as organizations and activists, mostly leftists, marched. Several protesters were detained.
Opposition parties echoed the demand for Kumar’s resignation, accusing him of sidelining his fellow commissioners. Kumar, as expected, did not oblige.
Therefore, protests are expected in different parts of the country over the coming days, some led by the CJP, some by opposition parties. Over the past few days, Congress workers demonstrated in different states, with a rally outside the Election Commission’s office in the national capital.
The tension can perhaps be sensed from the fact that after some Congress workers defaced the gates and walls of Kumar’s residence in the BJP-ruled north Indian state of Uttar Pradesh, police booked them under charges of attempt to murder.
While Kumar is the visible immediate target, the movement’s demands go further than one man’s exit. The CJP and opposition parties also want the entire SIR exercise to be scrapped. Gandhi asked people not to forget that it was Modi who appointed Kumar, which means the prime minister cannot escape responsibility for Kumar’s deeds and misdeeds.
BJP supporters argue that cleaning the rolls is a legitimate duty of the government. Some BJP leaders have even demanded that Kumar be awarded some of India’s highest civilian awards for his service in electoral reforms.
As a target, Kumar is much tougher to unseat than Pradhan. A minister serves at the government’s pleasure, and a prime minister can sacrifice one minister to defuse a larger crisis. A chief election commissioner’s position is designed to be harder to dislodge, because the office’s independence depends on that insulation. Article 324(5) gives the CEC the same removal protection as a Supreme Court judge.
That means a parliamentary motion on the grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity must be passed by special majorities in both houses of parliament. No such move has ever succeeded. Earlier this year, the chairpersons of both the upper and lower houses of Parliament rejected the opposition’s notice for Kumar’s removal.
Understandably, the Modi government would likely wait for the proceedings at the apex court, even as the ruling party is expected to garner public sympathy for Kumar and his “bold actions.”
The CJP and different student organizations and youth forces, on the other hand, seem to believe in the power of the street protests. To what extent the CJP, the student organizations, and opposition political parties manage to build sustained pressure through street protests remains to be seen. October being a month when festivals will be celebrated in most parts of the country, it would not be easy for them to maintain the momentum.

‘Releasing strategic reserves is a possibility,’ EU energy chief tells Euronews as diesel squeeze bites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:10:10 UTC
00:10:10 KST

Member states are discussing a coordinated release through the IEA, as the US pressures Europe to put more oil on the market. The Energy Commissioner told Euronews that Brussels can help coordinate the effort.
The European Union is contemplating a fresh emergency oil-reserve release, with Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen telling Euronews strategic stocks could be drawn down again to bolster supply and ease mounting price pressures.
The war in Iran and reduced refining capacity have squeezed supply, driving a sharp rise in prices for companies and consumers. Diesel prices at the pump have surged over the past month, prompting the US to pressure EU member states to release emergency stocks in a move that could put an additional 120 million barrels on the market.
“We are discussing with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the United States, when the right time is to release, because this is one of the opportunities that we have. We've used it before, and we'll likely use it again,” the Danish commissioner told Euronews on Thursday.
US diesel has surged to $7 a gallon, while Brent crude has traded between $97 and $102 a barrel since late September — up $25 to $30 from pre-war levels.
Jørgensen said EU countries are discussing a coordinated release through the Paris-based IEA, although the decision ultimately rests with individual member states.
"We coordinate via the EU and our positions in the IAE. But this is a decision of each member state; do they want this or not?" he told Euronews.
"And this is something that is being discussed as we speak."
An EU source told Euronews that the Commission held a call on Thursday with several countries, including the UK, to assess different scenarios.
Releasing reserves can quickly add diesel and other petroleum products to the market, potentially easing tight supplies. But emergency stocks are finite: once drawn down, they must be replenished, and governments may be reluctant to reduce their buffers while the geopolitical crisis remains unresolved.
The IEA said in August that global observed stocks had fallen by about 410 million barrels since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran on 28 February, while tight diesel and jet-fuel supplies had pushed refining margins to record levels.
EU emergency stocks remain high and are available in the event of market disruption, although diesel and jet-fuel markets remain tight and prices elevated, according to the latest 2026 Eurostat figures.
The EU already participated in a major coordinated release in March, when the IEA oversaw the release of 400 million barrels. EU countries contributed roughly 20% of the total, although a significant portion had yet to reach markets as of last week.
IEA chief Fatih Birol urged EU countries to use the remaining March allocations at an informal meeting of energy ministers in Dublin on 29 September.

The UAE’s attorney general has also ordered the formation of a team to investigate the attempted hijacking.

Karl Lagerfeld's beloved cat was left without his inheritance — who will share the millions
Kyiv • UNN
Karl Lagerfeld's inheritance will go to his assistant, godson, and former muse. Choupette will not inherit any money, but has financial support.
The famous cat of designer Karl Lagerfeld, Choupette, will not receive a cent from his estate. Seven years after the fashion designer’s death, it became known who is listed as the beneficiary of the inheritance. Contrary to all expectations, neither the cat nor her new owner is among them, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
According to the publication, Lagerfeld’s fortune is estimated at approximately €260 million. The heirs named are his longtime assistant Sébastien Jondeau, his godson Hudson Kroenig, his father — model Brad Kroenig — and the designer’s former muse Baptiste Giabiconi.
During his lifetime, Lagerfeld repeatedly spoke of his special affection for Choupette. The cat traveled with the fashion designer for years on a private jet and in a Rolls-Royce. She was cared for by a team consisting of two personal maids, a chef, and a bodyguard, and every year she celebrated her birthday with lavish parties.
After Lagerfeld’s death, the cat continued living with his former housekeeper, Françoise Caçot, in Paris. Under French law, animals cannot directly inherit money or property. However, Lagerfeld had made provisions for Choupette’s care in advance: financial support was set aside for her, while Caçot received a house with a garden in the suburbs of Paris.

Civil Protection Unit in Ottawa: Solidarity and Cooperation Between Italy and Canada
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:07:27 CEST
00:07:27 KST

In recent days, the Civil Protection Operational Unit (NOPC) carried out a new, delicate international mission in Ottawa, ensuring the transport to Italy of hematopoietic stem cells from a compatible donor identified in Canada, intended for an Italian patient suffering from acute myeloid leukemia and awaiting a transplant at a specialized center in northern Italy. 
     A special container provided by the Rotary Club of Bergamo was used to transport the cells, a testament to the network of solidarity that actively supports these delicate missions. The mission to the Canadian capital by NOPC volunteer Dr. Sabrina Foti coincided with a visit to Ottawa by Minister for Persons with Disabilities Alessandra Locatelli. During a meeting held at the residence of Ambassador Alessandro Cattaneo, Locatelli thanked the NOPC for its important work, emphasizing that it is an Italian organization founded on solidarity, volunteerism, and the ability to build concrete connections between people and healthcare systems—even thousands of kilometers apart.
                                    
                                       
				     Thanks to the work of approximately 140 volunteers, the Unit has so far assisted 16,348 people in receiving transplants, carrying out 1,061 missions in 2026 alone. Canada represents an increasingly important hub in this international network. In 2025, the Unit carried out organ retrievals in Calgary, Ottawa, Quebec City, and Toronto, while in 2026, transports have already been conducted from Toronto, Ottawa, and Vancouver. The recent mission in Ottawa is thus yet another example of the deep human bonds that unite Italy and Canada and of how international cooperation can translate into a concrete gesture of solidarity and hope.

What we're learning about the FlyDubai co-pilot who allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to crash the plane
One day after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the passenger aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about his identity and motive continued to swirl Thursday.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
There were 174 people aboard the plane. No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries, and the co-pilot remained in custody on Thursday.
Who was the FlyDubai co-pilot?
The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified.
An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
Co-pilot's motive unknown
The co-pilot's motive in the alleged attack remains unknown.
Netanyahu speculated to CBS News on Wednesday that the incident looked "like a suicide attempt," referring to witnesses who said the co-pilot had tried to jam the plane's equipment instead of stabilizing the aircraft. After passengers subdued the co-pilot, he shouted for someone to kill him, Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday.
In the same interview with Fox, Netanyahu said "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning had led Israel to the conclusion that the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination." He did not offer more information.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday called the incident "an attempted jihadist terror attack," and referred to the co-pilot as a "terrorist."
An Israeli security official told CBS News that authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and whether the attacker was working alone. Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Co-pilot to be questioned in UAE
The co-pilot was placed under arrest immediately.
He was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities" on Wednesday, Netanyahu said.
A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Netanyahu Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the co-pilot to the UAE for questioning.
Netanyahu said Israeli authorities would "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly," but did not say when that might happen.
He did not say whether the questioning that led investigators to believe the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination" was carried out by Saudi or Israeli authorities.

Comment les patrons de Meta et Nvidia ont œuvré en coulisses pour l’accord de la Maison-Blanche sur l’IA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:06:46 UTC
00:06:46 KST

Comment les patrons de Meta et Nvidia ont œuvré en coulisses pour l’accord de la Maison-Blanche sur l’IA
Mark Zuckerberg et Jensen Huang ont cherché à mobiliser des soutiens en faveur des accords “moralement contraignants”, signés par Donald Trump et des dirigeants de la tech.
Le président des États-Unis Donald Trump, assis aux côtés du PDG de Nvidia Jensen Huang et du PDG de Meta Mark Zuckerberg, lors d'une réunion portant sur l'intelligence artificielle à Washington, DC, aux États-Unis le 29 septembre 2026. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images
Le PDG de Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, a été l’architecte en chef des accords “moralement contraignants” sur l’IA issus du déjeuner organisé mardi à la Maison-Blanche avec le président Donald Trump, le président de la Chambre des représentants Mike Johnson et plus d’une douzaine de dirigeants de la tech, selon cinq personnes au fait de cette réunion à huis clos.
Mark Zuckerberg, avec l’aide du PDG de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, a présenté ces accords sur l’IA à de hauts responsables de la Maison-Blanche et à plusieurs des plus grands noms de la tech pendant le déjeuner, ont indiqué trois de ces personnes. Jensen Huang et des responsables de l’administration Trump ont contribué à élaborer ce texte avant la réunion, selon deux d’entre elles.
Advertisement
Ces cinq sources s’expriment sous couvert d’anonymat, car elles n’étaient pas autorisées à révéler les détails des discussions.
Dans le cadre de cet accord volontaire, les signataires s’engageraient à reconnaître l’importance de mettre en place des garde-fous pour atténuer les risques potentiels liés aux modèles avancés d’IA. Mais en l’absence de mécanisme clair de mise en application, on ne sait pas quelles conséquences, le cas échéant, ils pourraient subir s’ils ne respectaient pas leurs engagements.
Cet épisode témoigne de l’influence croissante de Mark Zuckerberg et Jensen Huang sur la politique de la Maison-Blanche en matière d’IA, alors que l’administration continue de privilégier une approche peu interventionniste dans la régulation de cette technologie. Le Congrès n’a pas encore adopté de loi fédérale pour encadrer l’IA.
Contactée, Meta a refusé de commenter. Nvidia et la Maison-Blanche n’ont pas répondu immédiatement à une demande de commentaire.
L’idée serait née lors d’un dîner d’Etat organisé en l’honneur du président chinois Xi Jinping, au cours duquel Mark Zuckerberg l’aurait présentée à Mike Johnson, selon l’une des sources mentionnées plus haut. Peu après, le patron de Meta aurait échangé avec celui de Nvidia, qui a ensuite contribué à rallier les dirigeants des principaux laboratoires d’IA au projet, selon deux de ces sources. Entre ce dîner d’Etat et le déjeuner de mardi, les dirigeants ont communiqué régulièrement afin de finaliser le document.
Le site d’information américain Semafor avait précédemment révélé certains détails sur la rédaction du document.
Advertisement
Les accords engagent les entreprises à “mettre en œuvre des contrôles internes rigoureux” pour surveiller les capacités des modèles d’IA, à collaborer avec des auditeurs externes et à créer des comités indépendants chargés d’examiner leurs rapports. Certains démocrates et défenseurs de la sécurité de l’IA les ont critiqués, estimant qu’ils sont inapplicables et reposent principalement sur un accord mutuel.
“L’idée n’est pas que ce soit la seule chose que nous ferons”, a souligné Mark Zuckerberg aux journalistes devant la Maison-Blanche mardi. “C’est un début, un accord auquel toute l’industrie pourrait adhérer.”
La régulation de l’IA fait débat
Donald Trump s’est montré réticent à imposer de nouveaux garde-fous à cette technologie. Il considère que les lois existantes suffiront à en atténuer les risques potentiels. “Le seul contrôle ou les seuls ‘garde-fous’ dont l’IA a besoin, c’est un PRÉSIDENT FORT ET INTELLIGENT (QI élevé !), et les Etats-Unis en ont un qui en a à revendre”, a-t-il posté mi-septembre sur son réseau social Truth Social.
Alors que la Maison-Blanche réfléchissait à la meilleure façon de réguler l’IA, Mark Zuckerberg s’est prononcé en faveur d’une approche moins interventionniste. Au téléphone avec Donald Trump en août, le patron de Meta s’est opposé à une proposition visant à créer un organisme de régulation indépendant inspiré de la Financial Industry Regulatory Authority pour les marchés financiers.
Jensen Huang se présente en fédérateur du secteur. Lundi, Nvidia a dévoilé un nouveau système de sécurité pour l’IA qui, selon l’entreprise, aiderait à prévenir les piratages menés par des agents d’IA autonomes, comme ceux qui se sont produits récemment et qui ont été largement médiatisés.
D’autres grands dirigeants de la tech, notamment Dario Amodei, d’Anthropic, et Sam Altman, d’OpenAI, ont appelé le gouvernement à intervenir davantage pour réguler cette technologie et à ralentir son développement.
Mark Zuckerberg et Jensen Huang, eux, ont largement balayé les critiques selon lesquelles l’IA pourrait représenter un risque existentiel pour l’humanité.
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Airborne T-7 Links Up with Simulators in Air Force First
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:05:14 UTC
00:05:14 KST

Three T-7A Red Hawks flew together at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas, on Sept. 16—but only one was a real aircraft in the air. The other two jets were virtual, controlled from simulators on the ground. All three shared a single, common operating picture.
The demo marked the first time Air Education and Training Command has demonstrated live, virtual, and constructive simulation with its future jet trainer, the T-7 from Boeing. The demo inserted physical and digital assets into one synthetic environment, in which all three could communicate and work together.
“Think of it as a gaming area,” said Steven “Stein” Dobrinski, a Boeing flight simulator design engineer, in a January interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “If I’ve got everything programmed and I’m in the data link, now I’m able to have all the entities, the sims and the airplanes, that are all talking to each other in the same gaming area.”
Using LVC, the simulators and jets can fly as if equipped with missiles, bombs, or pods attached, and when employed by a pilot, others will “see” the effects play out on their displays. The simulators can also “inject” adversary aircraft or threats into a scenario, with threats appearing on everyone’s displays.
The Sept. 16 flight aimed to test and validate the “foundational digital architecture” for LVC to work with the T-7, according to a release from AETC.
The real T-7A was crewed by Col. Michael Trott and Lt. Col. Phillip Bourquin of the 99th Flying Training Squadron, while the simulators were controlled by civilian instructors with the 12th Training Squadron: Robb Erickson, a retired Air Force colonel, and Ryan Sparkman, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel.
“Through secure, high-bandwidth tactical data links, ground-based flight simulators communicated directly with the airborne T-7A maneuvering across local military training airspace,” according to the release.
Boeing and the Air Force refer to the T-7 simulator as the Ground-Based Training System and see it as integral with the new trainer aircraft. The ability to pair simulators with real planes and inject virtual opponents into a scenario opens up a whole range of trainin capability that legacy T-38 Talon trainers could not support.
Officials envision future fighter pilots collaborating with manned and unmanned systems, along with automation, to manage enormous information streams, as they face off against high-level threats that will be difficult if not impossible to simulate in the physical world.
The most advanced versions of the T-7 GBTS simulator resemble an egg shell, with a 360-degree field of view, cockpit controls that mirror the real T-7 exactly, a seat that moves based on users’ inputs, and even an associated G-suit.
Trott, commander of the 99th and one of the first Airmen to be qualified as an instructor pilot on the T-7, praised the simulator to Air & Space Forces Magazine, calling it far more realistic than existing systems for the T-38 and F-15E, both of which he has used in the past.
The Sept. 16 flight is not the first time the T-7’s LVC capabilities have been tested—Dobrinski told Air & Space Forces Magazine in January that Boeing tried it out in a series of test flights last year. As one of the jets flew to Eglin Air Force Base, Fla., for climate testing, Boeing officials paired it with a simulator in St. Louis and inserted constructive entities.
“It worked like a champ on the way out,” Dobrinski said. “When it came back, we intercepted it again, and I was in one of [the simulators]. We had a four-ship, so we had four pilots in the sims, and we rejoined on the live aircraft and flew with them until they got sick of us, because we were talking on the radio. And we locked them with the radars, and that worked really, really well.”
More test flights followed, expanding up to a six-ship flight, Dobrinski said.
Training officials say live, virtual and constructive training is the future, not only for the T-7 but for other new aircraft, as well. The F-35 is starting to add elements of LVC through its highly advanced Joint Simulation Environment and new F-35 Emulated Non-Operational Flight Program Interoperability Experience, or FENIX, simulators. Air Force aviators used FENIX during Exercise Valiant Shield this summer to connect crews across the Pacific, according to a service release.

Moroccan intelligence uses surveillance to ‘silence’ journalists: Amnesty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:04:21 UTC
00:04:21 KST

Moroccan intelligence uses surveillance to ‘silence’ journalists: Amnesty
Probe finds spyware, hidden microphones and pre-infected phones used to surveil journalists, activists, rights defenders.
Amnesty International has denounced Morocco’s intelligence agency for using spyware, hidden microphones and pre-infected phones in the “unlawful surveillance” of journalists and human rights defenders.
Moroccan authorities host an “expansive and vast” surveillance apparatus that they use to “ultimately silence journalists, activists and other critical voices”, the rights NGO said in a report published on Thursday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mahsa Amini death four years on: Iranians reflect on ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’
- list 2 of 3Palestine Action protesters arrested outside UK Labour Party conference
- list 3 of 3‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days
The report, Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine, is based on the testimony of a former employee of the Moroccan domestic intelligence service (DGST), as well as leaked documents and journalistic investigations.
NGOs, including Amnesty, have for years accused Morocco of using Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli NSO Group, to monitor journalists, activists and political figures.
Rabat has repeatedly denied using spyware against its citizens. Amnesty said it wrote to Moroccan authorities four weeks before publication and received no response. Al Jazeera could not immediately reach Moroccan officials for comment.
In its report, Amnesty identified the DGST as the body responsible for deploying Pegasus in Morocco, saying the agency used the spyware against activists and journalists between 2017 and 2021.
Amnesty said Moroccan authorities combined “high-tech tools” like Pegasus with more traditional techniques like tailing and wiretapping.
“People are secretly videoed and audio recorded in detention, in their own offices and cars, and even in their own bedrooms,” the report says, citing the whistleblower.
“Phone calls are systematically recorded and spied upon,” and “shops sell mobile phones pre-infected with malware by DGST agents”.
The personal data collected on activists and human rights defenders is used to fuel public smear campaigns against them, according to the NGO.
The whistleblower said the agency infected internet cafes with remote-controlled spyware, and that devices were physically compromised at airports. He added that microphones were hidden in the light fixtures of the apartment of journalist Omar Radi, who was later imprisoned.
Amnesty said it matched 103 Moroccan phone numbers entered into the Pegasus system between September and December 2017 to specific individuals. Of these, 65 were civil society members, including 34 human rights defenders and 22 journalists and media workers. Another 25 were political figures or officials, and five were diplomats or representatives of international organisations.
“These records show the phone numbers of prominent human rights defenders and journalists were among the first to be entered into the Pegasus system,” said Donncha O Cearbhaill, head of Amnesty’s Security Lab.
Amnesty said it also found evidence of spyware delivered over the state-owned Maroc Telecom network, and that Morocco bought tools from companies based in Israel, the European Union and the United States.
“Morocco has wholly embraced techno-authoritarian practices,” Amnesty Secretary-General Agnes Callamard said.
Amnesty called on Morocco to end the surveillance and on states to halt spyware exports to the country until human rights safeguards are in place.
The investigation was part of a collaboration with 14 media organisations coordinated by Forbidden Stories.

Council of Europe assembly calls for frozen Russian assets to be used to compensate Ukraine

Council of Europe assembly calls for frozen Russian assets to be used to compensate Ukraine
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has called on member states to take action to redirect frozen Russian assets to pay compensation to Ukraine under European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) rulings.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda, citing a PACE resolution
Details: PACE noted that Russia owes over EUR 3.3 billion in unpaid compensation awarded by the ECHR but continues to ignore its legal obligations, refusing to comply with ECHR rulings and cooperate with the Council of Europe's supervisory mechanisms.
Quote from the resolution: "In this Resolution, the Parliamentary Assembly calls on member and observer States to take concrete steps to address this unprecedented situation, including repurposing frozen Russian State assets to compensate Ukraine and Ukrainian victims once the Court delivers its judgments in inter-State cases, and ensuring that national legal frameworks allow for the domestic enforcement of the Court's awards."
Details: The Assembly also called on member states and the European Union to impose targeted individual sanctions on specific individuals who have committed the most serious human rights violations recorded in ECHR rulings.
Furthermore, the Assembly urged the preservation of all case files relating to complaints against Russia, the protection of the personal data of illegally deported Ukrainian children, and the provision of full information about these children through the appropriate international mechanism.
Background:
- The Ukrainian delegation to PACE previously noted that it would use plenary debates, committee meetings and bilateral meetings to draw attention to the massive Russian attacks on civilian targets and critical infrastructure, the humanitarian situation in occupied Oleshky, and Ukraine's needs ahead of the winter. They also intended to focus on the payment of compensation under ECHR rulings.
- The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe had previously proposed a way to transfer frozen Russian funds to Ukraine based on decisions of the European Court of Human Rights.

Michael Jordan ‘Last Dance’ jersey sells for record $12.26M
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:03:22 UTC
00:03:22 KST

Dilara Hamit
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
A jersey worn by basketball legend Michael Jordan during his final championship season with the Chicago Bulls has sold for $12.26 million, according to auction house Joopiter.
Jordan wore the white No. 23 jersey during Game 3 of the 1998 NBA Finals against the Utah Jazz, part of the season later immortalized as “The Last Dance.”
The jersey was offered by entrepreneur Ryan Gough and sold through Joopiter, the digital auction platform founded by musician Pharrell Williams. Its estimated value before the sale was between $10 million and $15 million.
The June 7, 1998, game was played at Chicago’s United Center with the series tied at 1-1. Jordan recorded 24 points, three rebounds, two assists, one steal and one block as the Bulls defeated the Jazz 96-54.
Utah’s 54 points remain the lowest total recorded by a team in an NBA Finals game. The victory gave Chicago control of the series, which the Bulls eventually won 4-2 to claim their sixth championship in eight seasons.
Jordan was named NBA Finals Most Valuable Player for a sixth time.
Joopiter described the jersey as one of the most significant pieces of game-worn sporting history to reach the market.
“Few objects in the history of sport embody greatness as completely,” the auction house said, adding that the jersey represented the end of an era that helped transform basketball into a global cultural phenomenon.
According to Joopiter, only four jerseys from Bulls victories in the 1998 Finals exist. The Game 3 jersey is the only publicly known white game-winning jersey from the series to have surfaced.
The sale surpassed the previous record for Jordan memorabilia, set in 2022 when the red jersey he wore during Game 1 of the same Finals sold at Sotheby’s for $10.091 million.
Jordan’s customized 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello was also sold by Joopiter for $2.7 million. The vehicle, which was reportedly out of public view for 24 years, had specially modified seat rails to accommodate Jordan’s 6-foot-6-inch frame.
Despite setting a record for Jordan's memorabilia, the Game 3 jersey remains well below the highest price paid for game-worn sports memorabilia.
That record belongs to the jersey worn by baseball great Babe Ruth during his celebrated “called shot” appearance in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series. It sold for $24.12 million in 2024.

Flydubai stabbing: How safe are planes if a pilot turns violent?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:03:08 UTC
00:03:08 KST

Flydubai stabbing: How safe are planes if a pilot turns violent?
Civil aviation changed after 9/11 to keep attackers outside the cockpit. The Flydubai scare now flips the dilemma: what if a pilot turns violent?
On Wednesday morning, a co-pilot aboard a Flydubai plane stabbed the captain in what is believed to have been a foiled attempt to crash the flight with more than 170 people on board, en route from Dubai to Israel’s Tel Aviv.
As the plane plunged, within a minute, to half its altitude amid the commotion as it approached Jordanian airspace, the captain managed to unlock the door to the cockpit, and a group of passengers and crew members stormed inside and overpowered the attacker, who was reportedly attempting to damage the controls.
The aircraft also emitted an emergency distress signal during the incident.
Another pilot on board managed to take control of the aircraft and land it safely in Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk.
While the United Arab Emirates, the airline’s host country, has begun an investigation into what happened, Saudi authorities are questioning the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain. The attacker was also injured and is now in Saudi custody. Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country would follow the investigation and “possibly participate”.
Israel has claimed the incident on board the plane, the majority of whose passengers were Israeli, was a “terrorist” attack and an attempt to crash the aircraft.
Meanwhile, the incident on board Flydubai flight FZ1073 has raised a host of uncomfortable questions in the civil aviation industry, chief among them: how safe is a commercial aircraft when one of its own pilots turns violent?
How has aviation changed since the attacks of 9/11?
Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks on the United States, which killed nearly 3,000 people, changed the civil aviation industry.
That day, al-Qaeda-affiliated hijackers took control of four commercial planes as they were in the air, crashing two into the twin towers of New York’s World Trade Center on Manhattan island, and another into the Pentagon. A fourth crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers overwhelmed the hijackers.
The attacks transformed aviation security, which stepped up its focus on preventing unauthorised access to aircraft flight decks, as well as strengthening security and boarding procedures within airports.
Within months, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) had overhauled the global aviation rules, extending security measures for domestic flights and introducing bulletproof, reinforced cockpit doors, personnel vetting and airport identity checks.
The most consequential physical change was the reinforced, lockable cockpit door, designed to resist forcible intrusion, followed by a mandatory 100 percent screening of checked baggage.
Airports increased employee screening, baggage and cargo security, and aircraft protection, while ICAO introduced mandatory security audits to assess how countries were implementing the new global standards.
In 2015, Germanwings Flight 9525’s first officer Andreas Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the Airbus A320 they were piloting into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board.
France’s BEA determined that the aviation industry’s medical-certification system had failed to prevent a pilot experiencing a serious mental disorder from operating with a licence.
Following that incident, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) temporarily recommended that at least two authorised people remain in the cockpit at all times. But the following year, the EASA moved the rule to a risk-based approach only, allowing airlines to adopt equivalent safeguards based on operational risks.
The Germanwings incident also triggered broader measures in Europe: from 2018, airlines were required to conduct psychological assessments before pilots began flying and introduce psychoactive substance and alcohol testing.
Some flights also carry air marshals – or “in-flight security officers” – who are generally covert, armed law-enforcement officers placed on selected flights depending on a country’s threat assessment.
How secure are cockpit doors?
Cockpit doors are made to be particularly difficult to penetrate, as standard. On modern commercial aircraft, the cockpit door is built to be a heavy-duty composite structure mounted inside a reinforced frame, and electronically controlled, designed to resist forcible intrusion and penetration by small firearms. The cockpit door can usually only be opened from the inside.
On Boeing 737 aircraft, the flight-deck access system normally remains in AUTO mode during the flight, keeping the reinforced cockpit door locked. Cabin crew can ask pilots to grant them entry through the access system.
ICAO standards require that such doors can be locked or unlocked from either pilot station.
An emergency keypad also allows crew to initiate an emergency entry sequence to enter the cockpit. If a functioning pilot does not cancel the emergency request, the system would permit emergency access, but only after a built-in delay.
These systems are designed to keep an attacker out of the cockpit – not to stop a threat already inside it.
On the Flydubai flight on Wednesday, the Indian pilot who had been stabbed reportedly managed to open the cockpit door during the attack, which “enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic midair disaster”, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who hailed the captain as a “hero”, told the media.
What happens once a pilot raises the alarm?
It depends on the type of emergency in the aircraft. Under ICAO procedures, a crew can declare an emergency by radio using the signal “MAYDAY”.
In cases of medical or technical issues, pilots use the transponder code 7700 to alert air traffic control that they need to land as soon as possible, said Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, a London-based aviation consultancy. “Often, passengers are oblivious to this as there’s no need for alarm,” he added. This is the code that the Flydubai craft emitted as it was descending sharply, according to the flight monitoring service Flightradar24.
If the emergency is an attack or hijacking, the aircraft can transmit transponder code 7500, which flags the flight to air traffic controllers as being subject to unlawful interference, added Ahmad. “The crew can also communicate the nature of the threat and their intentions in plain language,” he said. The Flydubai craft switched to this code a few minutes after issuing the first code, according to flight data.
If code 7500 is the input, air traffic control is alerted to an “interference with the flight or a possible hijack in progress, and often ATC will divert other jets away so that the squawking jet can land”.
Flydubai’s 7700 emergency warning was sent at 5:28 GMT, followed by 7500 at 5:35 GMT, according to FlightRadar24, leading to the initial reports of a possible hijacking of the flight en route to Israel.
The cabin crew’s duties in such emergencies cover pilot incapacitation and security threats, including protecting the flight deck and communicating with the operating pilot.
But the nature of violence in or near the flight deck can vary, Ahmad said, as “often the strategy is to open the door so that other crew members can assist”.
Violence between the pilots inside the cockpit leads to a worst-case scenario, he said: “Where both pilots are unable to fly, the consequences are pretty self-evident if no one is flying the airplane.”
The Flydubai aeroplane was ultimately safely landed by two other pilots who were on board. That is the equivalent of lightning striking once, Ahmad suggested. “It is frightening to think of what the outcome would have been if those additional pilots were not there to take control.”
What checks do pilots undergo?
Before being granted a Class 1 medical certificate necessary for their licence, pilots undergo an aeromedical assessment covering vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, and other conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.
Aviation security rules also require background checks for all personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.
“Frequency of health checks varies, but standard health checks like height, weight, blood pressure, psychological testing, psychometric testing, as well as fitness, are minimum evaluations that all pilots undergo, as well as drug and drink testing,” said Ahmad of StrategicAero Research.
After the Flydubai incident, Ahmad said that “Israel will probably insist on specific nationalities for flight crew going forward” as well.
Israel has already said it will ramp up security checks on pilots flying into the country. “Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, said.
“I can see Israel demanding details of flight crews before a flight even departs, with full and even more invasive security checks and ensuring pilots who fly there are from nations where diplomatic relations with Israel exist,” Ahmad told Al Jazeera.
“This sort of cross-vetting isn’t usually a thing, but after this Flydubai incident, it makes sense now to explore whether wider sharing of pilot details and backgrounds to other aviation regulators in other countries could be standardised to further advance safety measures,” he added.
Pilot-on-pilot violence is not completely unheard of. There have been punches thrown, collars grabbed and arguments. But a co-pilot stabbing his captain in mid-flight in an attempt to seize the aircraft is an extraordinarily rare form of aviation security incident, analysts said.

European leaders must stop calling Russian attacks “hybrid,” according to Estonia's foreign minister. They are “terror attacks” and “sabotage attacks,” Margus Tsahkna told POLITICO in an interview, and part of a systematic Russian effort against Europe that amounts to “some kind of war."
Tsahkna was speaking after Estonia’s announcement Tuesday that Russian special services were behind an August arson attack on a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which supplies unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine. Three Latvian citizens suspected of starting the fire have been handed over to Estonia and will face the full force of the law, Tsahkna said.
The Milrem Robotics attack was one of a spate of similar incidents, including August drone attacks at Leipzig-Halle airport, which German authorities also attributed to Russia.
Advertisement
“Easy money,” rather than ideology, motivates many of Russia's recruits for drone and arson attacks, and European countries must make clear that such saboteurs will be harshly punished to deter future incidents, the foreign minister said.
“The message is that if you collaborate with the Russian secret services, you will be caught and sent to prison,” Tsahkna said. “Think many times before” taking part in such operations, he warned.
European governments should gather and share evidence so they can publicly attribute attacks to Russia, coordinate their intelligence and security services more closely, and make clear that those who collaborate with Moscow will face tough consequences, Tsahkna said.
The Kremlin aims to “divide our societies, divide our unity, and play with fear,” he said, warning that more serious attacks, including ones that claim multiple European lives, are more likely if Russian President Vladimir Putin believes the EU is not responding collectively.
The EU is working on a new security strategy, expected later this year. Tsahkna said it should improve intelligence sharing, invest in security services and give countries the ability to respond rapidly to unconventional warfare.
Currently, “Russia is not able to wage any military full-scale aggression or attacks against NATO,” Tsahkna said. “But it doesn't mean that it may not happen in the future. So let's use this time for preparation.”
“We must coordinate our intelligence services, secret police,” he said. “We need to take Putin very seriously; he's a terrorist. He is using all the different opportunities to attack us already, so we need to understand that the business as usual is not coming back.”
Governments also need to communicate clearly with the public, he said, so people know what to do in the event of an emergency without panicking.

Margot Robbie changing her name to her husband’s hurts my beautiful lesbian brain. Here's why | Rebecca Shaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:00:56 UTC
00:00:56 KST

Being a lesbian in a heretofore heteronormative society means having to go along with lots of things that don’t make sense to your beautiful lesbian brain. One such thing for me is the ongoing expectation that women who marry men should change their surname to their husband’s.
Last week my tolerance was tested again when it was revealed that after a decade of marriage, Margot Robbie has changed her surname to that of her husband, Tom Ackerley.
Margot Ackerley – it simply rolls off the tongue. She will remain Margot Robbie in her public life, and we don’t know why she has done this, but it has nonetheless caused a stir. We got the usual discourse of blah blah tradition, blah blah patriarchy, blah blah women’s individual choice and so on.
We all know how it goes and Margot is not alone in doing this, of course. The statistics are hard to pin down (bearing in mind I dropped out of psychology at uni because of the statistics part) but I think it’s safe to say that in the overwhelming majority of straight marriages, the woman changes her name to the man’s. I see this in every part of my social life, from friends back home who married directly out of high school to my cabal of highly educated urban feminist friends. I play my part by putting all my married male friends in my phone under their wives’ surnames.
Of course I have no personal sense of the societal pressure and systems that inform such decisions, which is why I don’t flip a table every time it happens – but I actually do mind when it’s the default decision with no discussion.
There are plenty of reasons a woman might want to change her name. She might hate her dad. She might feel no attachment to her name. Her husband might have a meaningful attachment to his and so she might just think it’s a nice thing to do.
I’m not an unreasonable lesbian. My issue isn’t with women taking their man’s surname, the problem comes when there is no choosing. When it’s a foregone conclusion, when it hasn’t been actively decided. That’s your name!
If there is discussion, if there is equal respect for both people, if someone has a reason, then that’s fine with me. I once had a colleague whose future husband told her it was a dealbreaker if she didn’t take his name. That’s not a reason. That should have been the dealbreaker itself.
I don’t really care about the reasoning, I just care that there is a reason. That said, when it comes to which surname a baby gets, that’s when I really get irritated. If we really have stopped considering a man’s wife and children his property, why on earth is giving them his name still the default? Women carry and birth the babies. Women are still far more likely to do the lion’s share of childcare. Hello?? The lesbian mind boggles.
But never fear, because I have a solution. And you may be surprised that it doesn’t involve any gender politics whatsoever! My solution is that we throw tradition out the window and that if a couple wants to share a name, we make the decision based on … which surname is cooler. Which surname sounds better, which surname will offer more success – that’s the one you should both use.
In an ideal world, this would be done in a courtroom setting, where each couple comes in and sees me sitting high above them like Judge Judy, ready to bang my gavel. Congratulations, Mr Brown, you are now Mr Beaumont. Sorry, Mrs Jones, you’re now Mrs Wilder. Mr Cheeseman, I release you from your prison.
No longer would awesome surnames be swallowed by the crap oesophagus of patriarchy. No longer would it be considered weak or weird for a man to take his wife’s last name – instead it would be cool and wise. Even though my loyalty always lies with women, I am willing to maintain neutrality in the courtroom.
And sorry, Mr Ackerley, which sounds a bit like a cat throwing up – you’re now Mr Robbie.

Western militaries are undermining Ukraine’s defence, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:00:44 UTC
00:00:44 KST

Western militaries are undermining Ukraine’s defence, experts say
A combination of rigid Western military attitudes and regulatory paralysis in Kyiv is leading to fewer weapons at the front.
Mundane regulatory problems in Kyiv and unimaginative institutional thinking in Europe’s militaries are holding up joint weapons production. And that is undermining Ukraine’s battlefield performance and leaving Europe’s armed forces unprepared for modern warfare.
Those are the conclusions of a new report from the Centre for Statecraft and National Security (CSNS) at King’s College London, and experts who spoke to Al Jazeera.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why has Putin added 15,000 new soldiers to Russia’s army?
- list 2 of 4Russian attacks on Kyiv region kill four people, target power grid
- list 3 of 4Russian drone hits school in Ukraine’s Kyiv as Moscow presses air assault
- list 4 of 4Russia warns NATO of possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off
For two years, Kyiv has sought to scale up its weapons production by inviting Western partners to fund new production facilities in exchange for battlefield testing. Kyiv receives weapons, Western partners receive know-how.
That formula has led to at least 180 business-to-business partnerships between Ukrainian and foreign partners, but 22 percent of them are stalled, according to the report, Beyond Aid: Making Ukraine Defence Cooperation Work.
One of those stalled ventures is an artillery shell factory that German defence giant Rheinmetall announced a year ago, which should now be starting production. Yet ground has not been broken on the project, because Ukrainian authorities have delayed permits and the government then moved the factory’s site.
There are other legal and bureaucratic problems.
“The process of registering intellectual property is lengthy,” Chris Pool, a visiting fellow at the CSNS, told Al Jazeera. “Iteration cycles move so quickly, often what’s registered and protected is obsolete.”
Former CIA Director General David Petraeus recently discussed how Ukrainian drone manufacturers “can make software changes once a week as required by what the Russians are doing to counter their systems. They can make hardware changes every three or four weeks.”
That is a dizzying speed of innovation by the West’s peacetime standards.
“What happens If the product ends up with a Ukrainian brigade and that brigade then modifies it and adapts it to new developments? Who then owns the intellectual property in the improved product? Does the Ukrainian state have a stake at that point?” said Pool.
Export rights are another problem.
“While focusing exclusively on the Ukrainian market may be viable at the initial stage, the absence of a clear export mechanism may later constrain companies’ ability to … integrate Ukrainian-based facilities into wider international supply chains,” said the report.
‘Not relevant to us’
The problems sometimes lie in Europe’s rigid approach to land warfare, said Pool, who has spoken to Ukrainian teams looking for Western partners.
In 2022, both Russia and Ukraine were fighting exclusively with classic battlefield artillery and heavy armour. Ukraine defeated Russia’s initial attacks with effective use of defensive weapons.
But when Ukraine went on the counteroffensive in 2023, it was unable to compete with Russian scale and production capacity, and quickly adapted.
It designed cheap, long-range drones and missiles to stanch the flow of Russian weapons and fuel to the front, and to destroy Russian refining capacity. It also began to design and build its own first-person view (FPV) drones as a form of artillery.
Ukraine reportedly invested $1bn in drone warfare in 2023, 10 times what it spent in 2022. A New York Times video analysis found that it struck as many Russian armoured vehicles in three months this year as in all of 2022.
In 2024, Ukraine produced a million FPV drones. In 2025, the production was more than 3 million. This year, Ukraine will produce an estimated 8 million – 16 for every 10 that Russia fields – achieving localised air superiority.
The new weapons came with new tactics and new command structures.
“The most important thing is decentralised command. Ukraine has implemented this more than anyone else,” said Konstantinos Grivas, who teaches advanced weapons systems at the Hellenic Military Academy.
“Units don’t wait for commands from upstairs. They harvest their own information and make their own decisions … You need very capable junior commanders,” he told Al Jazeera.
That dispersed command runs counter to classic military hierarchies and tactics.
“In the UK, there’s a certain amount of arrogance that the British army wouldn’t fight like this, and this is all very interesting, but ultimately, not relevant to us,” said Pool. The Ukrainian teams he spoke to were told, “’Couldn’t you just partner with [defence companies British Aerospace] or Babcock and then we can deal with the faces with whom we’re used to dealing,’” he said.
Ukraine has demonstrated the challenges of this approach.
In wargames dubbed Combined Resolve in August, Ukrainian drone operators destroyed a US tank brigade by simulating their tactic of dropping armour-piercing artillery directly onto tanks. They did the same to a British brigade in February.
“Faced with teams who are presenting a new technology or navigation that doesn’t rely on GPS, for example, there isn’t that curiosity to find out what’s going on and how this could be adapted to the British Army,” said Pool.
Western militaries have “not even started to shift all of the land forces units into drone infantry,” said Oleksandr Danylyuk, a former senior adviser to Ukraine’s Ministries of Defence and Foreign Affairs, now a land warfare expert at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a London-based think tank.
“If you actually don’t use drones as the main weapon of your infantry, they are obsolete,” he told Al Jazeera. “These people, you recruited and trained to fight with assault rifles, they will never see the enemy. They will be all killed with drones.”
Perhaps the biggest problem of all is money.
The US stopped funding Ukraine last year, and far-right leaders in France and Germany want to follow suit. The European Union is providing the bulk of Ukraine’s military and financial aid for now, but Kyiv overspent in the first half of this year to finance two counteroffensives that took back at least 870sq km of land Russia had occupied, and is impatient for more funds.
Those funds, too, are tied up in European regulations, and Ukrainians feel that with current political trends, receiving them over the long term is an increasingly precarious proposition.
“I don’t see any real chance for any positive transformations in the West,” said Danylyuk.
“Instead of actually using this miracle, which was given by God to the West, and using this Ukrainian heroism and this readiness to sacrifice themselves and the nation, it was just wasted.”

Rapid AI adoption poses systemic risks to financial sector, ECB chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:00:04 UTC
00:00:04 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
European Central Bank (ECB) governor warned that rapid artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in financial markets creates systemic risks, calling for enhanced macroprudential monitoring and global cooperation to protect economic stability.
Speaking at the 10th annual conference of the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) on Thursday, Christine Lagarde, president of the ECB and chair of the ESRB, highlighted three critical areas where AI could disrupt the financial system: market trading, cyber resilience, and geopolitics.
Lagarde noted that nearly nine out of 10 significant euro area banks already use generative AI, while 70% of EU securities market firms plan to increase investments in the technology.
She warned that autonomous AI agents in financial market trading might pursue goals in ways human overseers neither intended nor could detect, raising concerns over market manipulation and price distortion.
Addressing cyber resilience, the ECB chief stressed that recent frontier AI models possess advanced capabilities that allow automated attacks to escalate from an initial breach to widespread exploitation in hours rather than weeks.
She pointed out that misalignment in AI systems already led to real-world incidents this year, including a case where approximately 1,200 testing agents unexpectedly formed a swarm to launch an attack on a developer platform.
Highlighting geopolitical vulnerabilities, Lagarde cited a June incident where a US export-control directive abruptly cut off European access to two advanced AI models, underscoring Europe's heavy dependence on technology controlled in the US and China.
She urged Europe to build independent AI capabilities to prevent external actors from controlling vital financial tools and called for international cooperation on frontier AI governance similar to historic nuclear capability limits between the US and Soviet Union during the Cold War.
Lagarde concluded by emphasizing that European authorities must update cyber defenses and enforce proactive risk management as AI continues to reshape the global financial landscape.

CX2 turns FPV drones into hunters of enemy drone pilots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:59:04 UTC
23:59:04 KST

- CX2 launched Vadris SDR, a software-defined version of its FPV-mounted RF direction-finding payload that adds TBS Crossfire and DJI OcuSync detection.
- The company says more than 450 Vadris systems have been fielded to the U.S. Department of War.
U.S.-based defense technology firm CX2 has released a new version of Vadris, a small radio sensor that rides on an FPV drone and steers it toward the source of an enemy drone’s control signal, now able to pick up several of the most common drone control systems instead of just one.
CX2 announced Vadris SDR on Oct. 1. The original Vadris was built to detect ExpressLRS, an open-source radio control link widely used on first-person-view drones by hobbyists, commercial users and militaries. The new software-defined radio version adds TBS Crossfire and DJI’s OcuSync, two other widely used control links, and CX2 says it can add more through software updates as new links appear, without fitting new hardware each time.
Vadris is mounted directly on an FPV drone. It detects radio activity, works out the direction it is coming from, and overlays directional cues on the operator’s video feed, letting the pilot fly toward the transmitter. CX2 describes the goal as “Hunt the Archer, Not the Arrow,” meaning the system goes after the ground station or pilot controlling an enemy drone, rather than chasing the drone itself.
“Drones speak different languages. If you want to hunt drones, you need sensors that can speak all of those languages. Vadris does that. Moving ahead, Vadris can speak any language for counter-UAS,” said Porter Smith, CEO of CX2.
The company says more than 450 Vadris systems have already been fielded to the U.S. Department of War. It did not say which units have them, how they have been used, or whether any customer has ordered the new SDR version. It also did not give prices, detection ranges or a delivery date.
The pitch rests on cost. Attaching a cheap sensor to an expendable FPV drone gives small units their own way to find and strike enemy drone teams, a task that otherwise requires larger, dedicated electronic warfare equipment. CX2 calls Vadris a low-cost, attritable payload, meaning the military can afford to lose it.
The update targets a problem seen on the battlefield in Ukraine, where both sides change drone radios, frequencies and control links quickly to stay ahead of jamming and detection. A sensor tuned to a single protocol can become far less useful once the other side switches. Radio-based hunting also has a clear limit: drones guided over fiber-optic cable, now common on the front in Ukraine, give off no control signal for a sensor like Vadris to follow.

UK tells OSCE Russia chose war and can choose to end it
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:55:55 BST
23:55:55 KST

Britain has, in a statement to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, set out what it called the fundamental facts of Russia’s war against Ukraine, arguing that Moscow began the conflict by choice and has the power to end it, according to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.
The statement was delivered in Vienna on Thursday by James Ford, the UK’s Deputy Ambassador to the OSCE, at a meeting of the organisation’s Permanent Council. Ford told delegates he intended to “step back and return to first principles and undeniable facts,” before tracing Russia’s actions towards Ukraine back more than three decades.
He began with the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom gave security assurances to Ukraine as Kyiv surrendered the nuclear arsenal it had inherited from the Soviet Union. Ford said Russia had committed under the agreement to respect Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and existing borders. He then pointed to the seizure of Crimea in 2014 and the eight years of fighting in eastern Ukraine that followed, accusing Moscow of undermining the Minsk Agreements “while presenting itself as their guarantor.”
Turning to the full-scale invasion of 24 February 2022, Ford said: “Ukraine did not attack Russia. Russia’s invasion was unprovoked and a deliberate choice made in Moscow.” He recalled that Russian representatives had dismissed Western warnings of an imminent attack in the same forum, quoting them as having described those warnings as “unsubstantiated conjectures” and “scare stories.”
According to Ford, the invasion breached the UN Charter, the Budapest Memorandum and “every single principle of the Helsinki Final Act,” the 1975 accord that forms the founding basis of the OSCE. “States are sovereign. Borders cannot be changed by force. Disputes must be resolved peacefully,” he said, adding that Russia had negotiated and freely accepted those principles.
The deputy ambassador said the war had reached its 1,681st day and that Russia was on course to set new wartime records for missile and drone attacks against Ukraine this year. He cited findings by the OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, United Nations bodies and experts appointed under the OSCE Moscow Mechanism, which have reported grave violations of international humanitarian and human rights law. Ford said those bodies had identified conduct they say may amount to war crimes and crimes against humanity, and that evidence from the killings in Bucha, the town outside Kyiv occupied by Russian forces in the opening weeks of the invasion, formed part of that record.
On the question of ending the conflict, Ford called for “a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire” followed by serious negotiations towards a just and lasting peace. He said Ukraine had accepted such a ceasefire proposal and remained ready for meaningful talks, while Russia had so far refused. Kyiv agreed to a US-proposed 30-day ceasefire during talks in Jeddah in March 2025, a proposal Moscow did not accept.
Ford closed his remarks with what he described as one final fact: “Russia will not deter us from supporting Ukraine and its legitimate right to self-defence.”
