Russia Can Still Finance Its War, but Costs and Risks Are Rising, KSE Institute Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:52:52 UTC
23:52:52 KST

KSE Institute’s new study, “Assessing Russia’s War-Financing Capacity,” examines how Russia can sustain war financing as the federal budget deficit widens, fiscal buffers are depleted, and pressure on the financial system increases. Russia has so far financed the war without acute fiscal or financial instability, but the study finds that its room for maneuver is narrowing. A sharp decline in global energy prices or a loss of confidence in the financial system could quickly destabilize the current fragile equilibrium.
Russia’s financing model has shifted since 2022. During the first years of the full-scale war, the government relied on NWF withdrawals and domestic borrowing while pushing part of the war’s costs off budget through rapid corporate credit growth. That wartime credit boom has largely run its course, shifting more of the burden back onto federal and regional budgets, supported by domestic borrowing and substantial liquidity provision from the Central Bank of Russia (CBR).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Traditional budget-financing channels remain available but are increasingly constrained. The federal budget deficit reached RUB 5.8 trillion in January–August 2026, 48% higher than in the same period of 2025 and already 20% above the revised full-year target. Liquid NWF assets have fallen by around 60% compared with February 2022. Domestic borrowing remains the most important source of financing, but bond issuance resumed in September only at considerably higher costs.
Russia Strikes Kyiv Nuclear Institute Housing Reactor
The banking system is also under growing pressure from government financing needs, a structural liquidity deficit, and the legacy of rapid wartime credit expansion. Banks are carrying larger corporate loan books while absorbing more government debt, and their reliance on CBR refinancing has increased markedly. Reported capital adequacy, profitability, and asset-quality indicators remain relatively strong, but the study warns that they may obscure emerging stress because of regulatory forbearance, provisioning and valuation practices, and state support.
Russia still retains substantial capacity to extend war financing, but the measures required are becoming increasingly costly and potentially destabilizing. The least disruptive path is continued market-based domestic borrowing on more attractive terms, backed by additional CBR liquidity; fiscal adjustment or more coercive measures could extend financing further, but at growing economic, financial, social, and political costs. The authors argue that Ukraine’s allies should reduce Russia’s energy revenues, limit foreign participation in sovereign debt, target banks that play a disproportionate role in absorbing government debt, keep Russian reserves immobilized, and constrain sovereign gold liquidation.

Trump aims to leverage US aircraft-part exports to China in trade negotiations, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:52:26 UTC
23:52:26 KST

The Trump administration has been taking steps to turn China's dependence on US aviation suppliers into leverage for trade negotiations, according to people familiar with the matter.
Efforts to slow vital goods to China show how the US is working to strengthen its hand in trade talks as Washington works to loosen Beijing's grip on rare earth minerals needed for a wide range of US industries, including vehicle manufacturing, chipmaking and aerospace. Two sources said the US Department of Commerce is positioning itself to increase pressure on Beijing, should the administration call upon it to do so.
The slowdown has taken several forms. The Commerce Department slowed export licensing for airplane parts bound for China in recent weeks, two other sources told Reuters.
Officials have also expressed interest in issuing an export regulation that could make it easier to restrict landing gear and other aircraft parts to China, two sources said. A draft version included a new licensing requirement on aviation hydraulic fluid shipped by US suppliers like ExxonMobil, one of the people said.
And the Commerce Department has been limiting the number of parts licensed to be shipped to China's state-owned planemaker, COMAC, to keep the company from stockpiling, another source said.
The Commerce Department and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Chinese embassy in Washington also did not immediately respond, but after the US imposed export restrictions amid trade tensions last year, an embassy spokesperson accused the US of abusing export controls.
US and Chinese officials met in September in New York and Washington to negotiate key economic issues between the two countries, including US access to Chinese rare earth minerals, agricultural trade and issues around increasingly powerful AI.
Trade truce extended to January
With Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington last week, the two countries entered a new period of detente, agreeing to reduce tariffs on a variety of goods imported from each other and extend a trade truce set to expire on November 10, giving negotiators until January 10, 2027, to tackle tougher issues.
The effort to constrain the flow of commercial aircraft parts between the world's two largest economies, after a heated tug of war over parts last year, has raised industry concerns over planes as weapons for trade talks.
Aerospace has been largely unscathed by US President Donald Trump's tariffs, which have been slapped on multiple sectors and trading partners globally. But the industry has wrestled with shortages of parts and materials due to geopolitical tensions. Producers of thermal coating sprays used to protect jet engines, for example, continue to struggle with Chinese controls of rare earth materials that have led to delays.
China seeks guarantees on jet supplies
Meanwhile, China has sought several years' worth of spare parts for 200 Boeing jets it agreed to purchase last spring, sources said, in what would be the US planemaker's first major deal with Chinese carriers in nearly a decade. But the US has been reluctant to provide guarantees, seeing the parts as leverage that could be used to secure future concessions, the sources said.
It is unclear where China's request for the spare parts stands.
A spokesperson for Boeing said, “Consistent with US export requirements, Boeing is committed to supporting Chinese airlines with the parts and services they need as we have done for decades.”
Planes are not generally sold with guarantees on parts. China’s stance reflects industry-wide concerns about parts shortages as well as political concerns about a new flare-up of trade tensions.
Last October, in fact, Trump said the US could impose export controls on Boeing plane parts as part of Washington's response to Chinese export limits on rare earth minerals.
US suppliers are critical to Chinese aviation
Access to parts manufactured by US aerospace suppliers is critical for Boeing and Airbus jets operated by Chinese carriers, as well as COMAC, which wants to ramp up production of its own commercial jets.
The US imposed new export restrictions on aircraft products last year as the trade war between Washington and Beijing intensified. In late spring, the US suspended licenses for GE Aerospace's jet engines, Honeywell Aerospace navigation systems and other parts for COMAC. It also sent letters to manufacturers of hydraulic fluid used in airplanes in China, saying the fluid was subject to a new - but ultimately short-lived - export license requirement.
The 2025 restrictions extended to a broad swath of items beyond aerospace, including ethane and electronic design automation software, and appeared aimed at preventing China from getting products necessary for key sectors. But they lasted only a few weeks.

International Coffee Day: the history of the holiday, the origin of the beverage, and the arrival of coffee in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
17:52:21 EEST
23:52:21 KST

International Coffee Day: the history of the holiday, the origin of the beverage, and the arrival of coffee in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
International Coffee Day has been celebrated on October 1 since 2015. We рассказываем about the origin of coffee and its path to popularity in Ukraine.
On October 1, International Coffee Day is celebrated around the world. This holiday is dedicated to one of the most popular beverages, which over the centuries has become part of the daily life and culture of many countries. More about when this day was established, where coffee originated, and how it gradually became popular in Ukraine will be told by UNN.
When International Coffee Day was established
International Coffee Day was officially first celebrated on October 1, 2015. The decision to hold the first official International Coffee Day was made by the International Coffee Organization in 2014. The first celebration took place in Milan during Expo 2015. Since then, October 1 has been dedicated each year to coffee and the people involved in its production and consumption. The holiday also became an opportunity to draw attention to the coffee industry and its importance for farmers and entire communities.
Where coffee originated
Ethiopia is considered the homeland of legendary coffee. There are many legends about how people discovered the properties of the coffee tree, but one of the best-known tells of a shepherd named Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became more active after eating the leaves of a coffee tree. Thus, it seems that goats were the discoverers of coffee. The first accounts of the stimulating properties of coffee fruit date back to the 6th century, and later coffee berries became known in the Arab world, particularly in Yemen, while the beverage made from roasted beans began to be consumed much later, approximately from the 15th century.
Coffee gradually spread beyond Arabia. It was drunk in the Middle East, and later the beverage began to gain popularity in Europe as well. The first coffeehouses became places where people not only drank coffee, but also socialized, discussed the news, concluded trade agreements, and simply spent time.
How coffee came to Ukraine
People began drinking coffee in the territory of modern Ukraine as early as the 16th century. At that time, the beverage was known to the inhabitants of the Crimean Khanate and the Black Sea coastal territories, which were under the influence of the Ottoman Empire. Coffee was also familiar to Ukrainian Cossacks, and references to it have survived in historical sources from the 17th century. In particular, coffee beans were among the gifts that Patriarch Macarius III of Antioch brought to Bohdan Khmelnytsky in 1654.
In Kyiv, however, coffee was known no later than 1679. That year, Scottish soldiers led by Patrick Gordon arrived in the city. Gordon enjoyed the beverage and served it at his parties, but even then coffee was not yet a mass beverage. It became much more popular among Kyiv residents in the second half of the 19th century, when confectioneries and coffeehouses began operating actively in the city. Such establishments gradually became places for meetings, relaxation, and socializing, while coffee became part of urban life. Moreover, Kyiv coffeehouses differed not only in their menus but also in their clientele: some establishments were frequented by representatives of business circles, while others were mainly visited by writers, artists, and the urban bohemian community. A coffeehouse could be a place where, over a cup of coffee, people read the latest newspaper, discussed the news, or played chess.
One well-known example was the Semadeni confectionery in Kyiv, located near Khreshchatyk. Brokers and bankers met there, and the fresh press was an important part of the establishment’s atmosphere, while in other coffeehouses visitors were attracted by cheaper beverages and the opportunity to spend a great deal of time at a table.
What kinds of coffee are there
The most widespread commercial varieties of coffee beans are Arabica and Robusta. The Robusta plant is hardier and has a bitter taste, while Arabica has traditionally been more popular due to its milder flavor characteristics. Liberica also exists, but it is much less widespread.
Roasting plays an important role in the taste of the beverage. During this process, green beans change color and increase in volume, while numerous aromatic compounds develop inside them. Depending on the roasting method, several levels are distinguished—from light to very dark—and different degrees of roasting are used for different methods of preparing coffee.
Coffee as part of global culture
Over the centuries of its existence, coffee spread far beyond the regions where it was first cultivated. Along with the beverage, traditions of preparing and serving it developed, and Americano, latte, cappuccino, and other coffee drinks became an integral part of modern life. Today, October 1, International Coffee Day reminds us not only of the popular beverage but also of the long history of its spread.
Interesting facts about coffee
Coffee is a fruit. Coffee "beans" are actually seeds that grow inside berries called coffee cherries.
Brazil ranks first in the world in coffee production. Vietnam and Colombia follow on the list.
The world's most expensive coffee is called Kopi Luwak and costs hundreds of dollars. This coffee is roasted after it has been eaten, digested, and excreted by an Asian palm civet. Thanks to natural fermentation, this coffee acquires a distinctive sweet flavor.Coffee is one of the most popular beverages in the world. Every year, people drink about 400 billion cups.
Coffee has a centuries-old history and has been known to humanity for more than seven centuries.
There are more than 200,000 coffee shops in Italy because coffee is an important part of Italian culture. Italians even have their own traditions regarding when to drink different types of coffee.
Water, juice, coffee: what to drink in the heat, and what to avoid25.06.26, 16:25 • 73610 views
As brewed coffee cools, it releases more than 700 chemical compounds that create its aroma.
Coffee came to Brazil through smuggling. In 1727, coffee-tree seedlings were secretly taken from France to Brazil.

Reporter's notebook: Hezbollah's flags no longer intimidate Metula's residents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:51:50 UTC
23:51:50 KST

In Metula, northern Israel, a new mural has appeared. In large red numbers, it says “7.10” in memory of the Hamas attack on October 7. The mural is a bit jarring as it now appears on the historic main road of the town, among pretty homes and restaurants.
The mural demonstrates the history of the community. However, that history moves from the beauty of early Israel to the horrors of October 7. It shows rockets targeting an Israeli home from all directions. Then it shows destruction and ruin, and soldiers taking shelter.
Metula is on Israel’s northern border, the northernmost community. Throughout the war, it was exposed directly to Hezbollah attacks. Many homes were damaged. More than 2,000 residents here were evacuated. Only a few remained. The IDF moved into the town. Today things have changed again. Now people are returning. On Sukkot, there were tourists and visitors. Several restaurants and small hotels appeared open.
A drive through the community and its pretty historic main street, which dates from the late 19th century, takes a visitor to the border. There is a fence.
Beyond the fence is another fence. There is a bunker that is reached from a concrete entranceway at the rear. Inside the bunker, one can see into Lebanon. Peering through the fence, one can see a large blue can, the size of an oil drum, perched on top of a pole. The blue can says “UN.” Apparently, this is some marker that UNIFIL installed.
'We are coming,' was Hezbollah's threatening presence over Metula
A bunker is reached through a concrete entranceway at the rear. Inside the bunker, one can see into Lebanon. Peering through the fence, one can see a large blue can, the size of an oil drum, perched on top of a pole. The blue can says “UN.” Apparently, this is some marker that UNIFIL installed.
Before 2023, you could see the UN on the other side. Their white vehicles were sometimes visible. In addition, you could see Hezbollah flags. Hezbollah had also installed a large Palestinian flag on a hill on the other side. A giant billboard showed the Al-Aqsa Mosque. The message was clear. Hezbollah was saying, “We are here, and we are coming.” Hezbollah could look over Metula and wait for their chance.
On October 7, Hezbollah did not attack Israel. However, it did choose to join the war on October 8, 2023, with some shelling of the border. In the days the followed, Israel and Hezbollah traded fire, but the major Hezbollah invasion did not occur. Nevertheless, Israel was so worried it would be unable to prevent a large Hezbollah invasion that it evacuated the border communities such as Metula, Kiryat Shmona, and many other places. Tens of thousands of Israelis were displaced, joining some 100,000 people displaced across the country, on the northern border and Gaza border.
For a long time it was unclear if Israel would be able to bring peace and protection to Metula. Drones would fly over the border from Lebanon, striking various sites. Rockets rained down. Houses were damaged. When Israel finally began to seriously strike back in September 2024, Hezbollah suffered major losses. A ceasefire followed in November 2024. Later, the conflict grew again in March 2026 in the wake of Israel and US strikes on Iran. This time, the IDF moved further into Lebanon and cleared Hezbollah from villages, destroying many of the villages in the process.
Symbols of Israel's victory visible from Metula
From Metula today, the Hezbollah flags are gone. The Palestinian flag and Al-Aqsa billboard are gone. This is a symbol of the victory here. Hezbollah can no longer sit on the border and provoke Israel. The privilege it had since 2006 is not longer. For years, it felt it could do what it wanted. It believed Israel was deterred. Iran also felt it had deterred Israel. The fear in Israel over the years was that Hezbollah would launch a major invasion. It also had some 200,000 rockets, and this was seen as such a large number that it would be hard to stop them all.
The IDF’s innovations and Israel's intelligence operations, including the pager attack, weakened Hezbollah. Hezbollah is not defeated or gone from Lebanon. However, it is no longer on the border. Its forts and also its underground facilities have been found and destroyed. There must be more work to be done. Over two nights in the northern Galilee near Metula, I could hear explosions that appeared to come from Lebanon. Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure still exists in Lebanon. Lebanon has not disarmed the group.
It remains to be seen what comes next in northern Israel with Hezbollah. However, what is clear is that communities such as Metula have a chance to recover. Visitors are coming back, slowly. People are back on the hiking trails. Restaurants are open.
This is the beginning of an attempted return to more peace and quiet. The removal of the Hezbollah flags and banners on the other side of the border is a symbol of getting rid of a threat that loomed over the north for years. That threat often thrived amid the UN vehicles that failed to document the Hezbollah presence.
Whether the UN presence will be replaced with a new force is unclear. Whether the Lebanese army can ever disarm Hezbollah or successfully secure this area is unclear. It has also abandoned southern Lebanon for decades. Now the area near the Israeli border is primarily cleared of Lebanese. Some Lebanese homes appear in the distance from Metula. However, no one seems visible on the other side of the border. What is visible are the IDF Humvees and bulldozers, and the feeling that Israel has firm control now.

Antisemitism watchdogs reported that online conspiracy theories accusing Israel of orchestrating a false flag operation began circulating on social media just over an hour after an attempted terrorist attack aboard an Israel-bound flydubai flight on Wednesday.
The incident began at 1:21 AM ET when a Boeing 737 MAX 8 flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv with 174 passengers transmitted emergency distress signals after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the second pilot and attempted to crash the aircraft. Passengers and crew intervened to subdue the attacker before the plane diverted safely to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
According to a monitoring report from the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM) Antisemitism Research Center (ARC), the first post declaring the event an Israeli false flag appeared on X just 67 minutes after the emergency signal.
"What’s striking here isn’t just the volume; it’s the speed," said ARC Research Associate Oliver Marks.
"67 minutes is all it took for the near-downing of a commercial airliner by a terrorist pilot to become fodder for antisemitic conspiracy theorists across the globe. It’s clear this isn’t a narrative that forms in response to an incident. Rather, it’s part of a script that already exists, sitting ready for use whenever opportunities arise."
Conspiracies spread online that Netanyahu staged the flydubai incident
The ARC study tracked 4,136 posts containing the phrase "false flag" over a 12-hour monitoring period, identifying 2,963 hostile posts that blamed Israel, the Mossad, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Zionists, or Jews for the incident. Conspiracy content escalated rapidly from the initial post, reaching 100 posts by 3:07 AM ET, 500 posts by 5:42 AM ET, 1,000 posts by 7:35 AM ET, and 2,000 posts by 9:36 AM ET, with volume continuing to rise until collection ended at 10:43 AM ET.
About 72% of all tracked false flag posts promoted these conspiracy theories, rising the 82% in the final hour. Peak hourly volume occurred between 9:00 AM and 10:00 AM ET, recording 623 posts.
Examples documented in the report included social media posts alleging that Netanyahu staged the event to cancel elections or distract from criminal charges, alongside posts explicitly drawing comparisons to September 11 and claiming the incident was an Israeli false flag operation akin to October 7.
The ARC study’s concluding assessment noted, “The pattern mirrors the influence operations that hostile states, Russia foremost among them, use to destabilize Western societies: sowing social division, exploiting breaking news events, and portraying Israel and Jews as the ‘hidden hand’ behind them.”
CyberWell also responded to the proliferation of false flag narratives spreading online following the attack.
CyberWell Founder and CEO Tal-Or Cohen Montemayor said, “Today’s horrific attack aboard a flydubai flight from the UAE to Israel is an ugly reminder of how quickly online antisemitism can distort the facts of an unfolding event. After a co-pilot allegedly stabbed the second pilot and attempted to take control of the aircraft, Israeli passengers helped restrain him and keep the injured pilot alive before the plane diverted safely to Saudi Arabia."
Cohen Montemayor added, "As news of the incident spread, ‘false flag’ claims quickly emerged on social media, alleging that Israelis had hijacked the plane or staged the attack. These claims reflect a broader pattern of conspiratorial self-victimization, an antisemitic conspiracy that falsely accuses Jews or Israelis of orchestrating attacks against themselves to manipulate public opinion. It is a contemporary expression of Jew-hatred and a form of misinformation aimed at spreading hatred, distrust, and disgust toward Jews."
Cohen Montemayor stated, "Platforms and LLMs cannot rely on poisoned knowledge sources or automated systems that fail to recognize these rapidly evolving forms of antisemitic conspiracy. They need real-time expertise from organizations like CyberWell that can identify emerging narratives, understand the context behind them, and help platforms respond effectively."
"‘False flag’ conspiracy theories are particularly corrosive because they do more than deny an attack," Cohen Montemayor concluded.
"They recast victims as perpetrators and can perpetuate violence by fueling hatred and encouraging further violence against Jews."

EU turns page on Ukraine's $27 billion deficit, says all needs are covered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:50:05 UTC
23:50:05 KST

The mystery surrounding Ukraine's $27 billion shortfall abruptly ended on Thursday as the European Commission confirmed the country's financial and military needs for 2026 are fully covered.
The European Commission has concluded that Ukraine's financial and military needs for this year are fully met, one month after Kyiv flagged a $27 billion (€23.92 billion) shortfall in its Ministry of Defence that caught Brussels off guard.
"Today, through coordinated joint efforts, we have identified the means to cover Ukraine's budget and defence needs for 2026," the Commission said in a vaguely worded statement shared by President Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday.
"We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release."
With this, the executive closes the debate that began in late August when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on allies to fill the $27 billion gap, warning essential weapon deliveries were at risk.
"We need more money, much more," Zelenskyy said.
Since then, the Commission has been engaged in technical talks with the Ukrainian government to pin down the exact scope of the financing hole.
From the outset, EU officials were reluctant to validate the $27 billion figure, later reduced to $20 billion, which they considered unexpected and unexplained.
Instead, they shifted the focus to the €90 billion loan, the bloc's main line of assistance. It foresees €45 billion for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027.
At first, Zelenskyy suggested that a share of the loan earmarked for next year be moved to this year, but the request was never formalised.
As technical talks dragged on, Brussels dialled up the pressure on Kyiv to advance the reforms necessary to unlock the support loan and the Ukraine Facility, a prior assistance envelope. The Commission is frustrated by the slow legislative pace.
The loan and the facility have roughly $37 billion still available until the end of the year, which EU officials insist is enough to keep Ukraine on a solid footing.
With 2026 settled, attention now turns to the much direr 2027.
In its statement, the Commission promised to "swiftly" allocate the loan's second €45 billion half to ensure fast disbursements, "subject to the established conditions".
Brussels and Kyiv will "begin work on identifying additional budgetary and defence needs", it added, urging allied nations to increase their contributions.
"All sides agreed that other partners should also fulfil their financial commitments and step up their efforts in light of the significant challenges Ukraine is facing."
In response to the Commission's statement, Zelenskyy praised the "good results" of the bilateral consultations about the 2026 and 2027 needs.
"We have agreed on the format, timeline, and steps needed to ensure full coverage," he said. "Going forward, we will coordinate this work and align our actions every month, ensuring continuous coordination."
Earlier this week, Ukrainian Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said the country faces a staggering $78 billion hole in 2027: $32.6 billion on the budget and $45 billion on military expenditures. (The Commission has not yet validated the numbers.)
Marchenko warned that Russia's non-stop attacks, targeting data centres, telecoms, power grids, factories and railways, coupled with the blockade in the Black Sea, threaten to paralyse the Ukrainian economy and cripple tax collection.
The wartime costs for 2027 could exceed Marchenko's estimates, says Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategy in Kyiv.
"These are the realities of war. When the €90 billion support loan was adopted, the partners understood that Ukraine would still need to seek additional resources to meet all its necessary needs. And we did indeed expect that part of the defence needs would be covered by in-kind support," Myronenko told Euronews.
"Unfortunately, that in-kind support has decreased, increasing the need for additional funding. Moreover, the war is indeed becoming more expensive and more intense."

Syngenta moves to close Grangemouth plant, 377 jobs at risk
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:49:04 BST
23:49:04 KST

Agrochemical manufacturer Syngenta has begun a formal consultation with trade unions and employees over the proposed closure of its site at Grangemouth, placing 377 jobs at risk.
The company stated that no final decision has been taken and that alternatives will be considered during the consultation period.
Syngenta said it had been reviewing its Grangemouth operations for some time against a backdrop of growing international competition and difficult energy conditions. According to the company, the site costs significantly more to run than its other production facilities, a gap that has persisted despite sustained efforts to narrow it.
The Grangemouth plant produces active ingredients used in crop protection products and has a long history in the town’s chemical sector, having previously operated under ICI and later Zeneca before Syngenta was formed in 2000 from the merger of the agribusiness divisions of Novartis and AstraZeneca. The Swiss-headquartered group was acquired by ChemChina in 2017 and is now ultimately owned by Chinese state company Sinochem following the merger of the two state-owned firms. The site received more than £2 million in Scottish Enterprise funding a little over a year ago.
Responding to the announcement, Scotland’s Cabinet Secretary for Economy, Tourism and Transport Stephen Flynn said in a statement issued by the Scottish Government: “My thoughts are with the workers, their families and the local community who will be affected by this decision.”
Flynn said ministers had told the company’s board of their opposition to any reduction or closure at the site. “We made clear to Syngenta’s board our strong opposition to any potential scale down or closure of their Grangemouth site,” he said, adding: “It is therefore extremely disappointing to hear that the board has taken the commercial decision to enter a consultation period on the closure of the site despite the Scottish Government’s commitment to exploring support for its continued operations.”
The cabinet secretary also turned his attention to Westminster and the £200 million pledged by the UK Government for Grangemouth in 2024. “During this period of consultation, I sincerely hope that the UK Government will now provide some of the £200 million committed to Grangemouth, since not a single penny has yet been allocated from that fund promised in 2024. I will continue to press the UK Government on this,” he said.
Grangemouth’s industrial base has come under sustained pressure in recent years. Petroineos ended crude oil refining at the town’s refinery in 2025, converting the facility into a fuel import terminal with the loss of around 400 jobs. The UK and Scottish governments subsequently commissioned Project Willow, a study published in 2025 that identified a range of potential low-carbon projects intended to secure the long-term future of the industrial cluster.
According to the Scottish Government, its Partnership Action for Continuing Employment (PACE) initiative, which supports workers facing redundancy, is ready to assist those affected at Syngenta. “Our priority now is to ensure that the affected workers receive support, which is why the Scottish Government’s initiative for responding to redundancy situations, PACE, stands ready to help those who may be affected by redundancy,” Flynn said.
He added that he had been briefed by the company and intended to meet trade unions, local MSPs and UK Government representatives later on Thursday. “I have been briefed by the company, and aim to meet with the trade unions, local MSPs, and the UK Government later today,” he said.

Algerian parliament approves death penalty for arson, child kidnapping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:48:16 UTC
23:48:16 KST

Abbas Maimouni and Ikram Kouachi
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Algeria’s lower house of parliament approved a bill Thursday amending the penal code to introduce the death penalty for those convicted of deliberately setting fires and kidnapping children.
The bill is the first legislation approved by lawmakers in the People’s National Assembly during the new parliamentary session and follows directives from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune after wildfires swept across parts of the country in August, causing human and property losses.
The death penalty would apply to those convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests and fields, as well as the deliberate destruction of public or private property on behalf of foreign parties as part of treason, espionage or organized crime.
The penalty would also apply to anyone attempting to undermine public security and order, national unity, or economic and environmental stability, according to the bill.
One of the newly approved provisions introduces the death penalty for those who kidnap children by any means, with harsher penalties when the crime involves torture, sexual assault or abuse.
The bill also stipulates that individuals convicted of offenses related to arson or attacks against children would not be eligible for mitigating circumstances provided for under the penal code.
The legislation will take effect after approval by the Council of the Nation, the upper house of parliament, by a three-quarters majority of its members, followed by promulgation by the president and publication in the official gazette.
The death penalty remains part of Algeria’s criminal legislation for a number of offenses, although executions have been suspended since 1993.
Between Aug. 27 and 30, major wildfires broke out in several eastern provinces, causing significant human and property losses, particularly in Jijel province, which continues to receive aid and relief convoys.
Interior Minister Said Sayoud said at the time that 12 people had died in the wildfires.

China’s Stake in the Russian Duma Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:47:00 UTC
23:47:00 KST

What did observers in China think about the Russian State Duma election on September 20? While retaining a veneer of democratic procedure, Vladimir Putin has steadily eliminated potential rivals and term limits, much like Xi Jinping has done. In past Russian election cycles, Chinese officials and experts by large have emphasized the importance of outcomes reinforcing political stability in Russia.
In terms of the latest election, most Western commentary criticized the unfair process preventing Putin’s primary opposing party, Yabloko, from running. Yabloko – which means apple in Russian but actually is an acronym for the last names of its three founders – is the only pro-democracy and anti-war party in Russia. By contrast, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun congratulated Russia for the “smooth conclusion” of the process and hailed the elections for representing “the will of the Russian people.”
Chinese media commentary did note that Yabloko was prohibited from participating in the election as a party, although some Yabloko candidates were still running in single-member districts (and all lost). Given the lack of real electoral competition, a Hong Kong media outlet, China Review News Agency, pointed out that the 59 percent turnout (7.6 percentage points higher than the previous Duma election in 2021) reflected “the state’s mobilization capabilities,” not increased political participation.
Putin’s televised address in the lead-up to the election framed it as an opportunity for Russians to express their support for the war in Ukraine and as “a collective response to those who seek to weaken Russia,” Chinese commentary reported. More than 200 Russian veterans of the war in Ukraine ran for the Duma and election commission chair Ella Pamfilova reported that 46 of them won seats – 41 of whom belonged to United Russia, the ruling party that has dominated the Russian political landscape throughout Putin’s leadership.
With the elections held against a background of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian soil and rising prices, Ma Bin, deputy director of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Fudan University, called the Duma election a major test and demonstration of Russian political stability. Chinese military analyst Shi Hong agreed that United Russia’s overwhelming victory demonstrated that for Russia “stability was paramount” and would support continuity in Russia’s military strategy and appropriations. Zhang Yanjun, a research fellow at the Institute of International Studies in Shanghai, predicted that the results of the election (held for the first time on occupied Ukrainian territory) would make Putin more intent on demonstrating strategic resolve and less likely to make concessions on Ukraine.
Since the failed coup attempt by the (since deceased) Wagner Group chairman, Yevgeny Prigozhin, in 2023, Chinese officials have made some efforts to reach out to officials beyond Putin’s inner circle. Wu Dahui, deputy director of the Russian Research Institute at Tsinghua University, emphasized that the Sino-Russian partnership has become institutionalized in a dense network of 60,000 channels at all levels of society, which he likened to the “blood vessels” sustaining the partnership.
Nevertheless, recently Chinese and Russian officials have emphasized the importance of top leader ties for their partnership. Following their most recent summit in May 2026, a Chinese diplomat hailed the relationship between Xi and Putin as “the fundamental guarantee” of the partnership. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov credited the “diplomacy of leaders” for codifying progress in the partnership in concrete agreements.
With the Russian ruling party, United Russia, capturing the majority of seats in the latest election (349 out of 450), Guo added that China would continue to work with Russia to implement “the important common understandings between the two presidents to make fresh progress and bring bilateral relations to new heights.”
A 2019 article by Professor Wang Zhihua in the Rule of Law Forum of the Shanghai University of Political Science and Law about the role of the Duma in the Russian political system noted that in the Russian system the president has “absolute power” and constitutionally outlined checks and balances are “merely nominal, resulting in a unique presidential system with Russian characteristics.” Wang concluded that “In short, in Russia’s political system, the president has too much power, the parliament has less power, and the judiciary is also weak.”
In Wang’s view, the configuration of the Russian political system based on a strong president with personal charisma may be expedient in the short term for the country’s revival and rise. However, he cautioned that the expansion of presidential power may ultimately lead to a crisis and undermine the long-term development of legally based governance.
Such conclusions could easily be applied to China and it is not surprising that this article, which I obtained on September 11, 2026, is no longer accessible on the CNKI database of academic articles and or on the Baidu search engine.
Chinese scholars’ assessments of Russian political developments also contribute to our understanding of Chinese views about the long-term viability of the Sino-Russian partnership. An analysis of the Duma election by a Chinese military blogger emphasized the importance of Putin’s continued hold on power and his ability to restrain hardline factions from even more escalatory actions in Ukraine. The blogger wrote: “For China, while the specific choice of Russian leader is important, Russia’s ability to maintain stability and policy continuity is even more crucial. This is why Sino-Russian relations have been continuously strengthening institutional ties in recent years.”
The results of the Russian Duma election startled no one in Beijing, but Chinese observers followed them closely. The topic is a controversial one in China due to the obvious parallels between the Russian and Chinese political systems and the stake the Chinese leadership has in the stability of their neighbor.

Why is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:45:49 UTC
23:45:49 KST

A British Border Force vessel arrives at Ramsgate after picking up people trying to cross the Channel in a small boat. Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreenA British Border Force vessel arrives at Ramsgate after picking up people trying to cross the Channel in a small boat. Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersExplainerWhy is the UK-France ‘one in, one out’ migration deal being scrapped?Agreement expected to end on Thursday after running for 423 days, during which it has been beset by problems UK politics live – latest updates The UK government’s “one in, one out” deal with France, which was supposed to help deter small boat arrivals, is expected to expire on Thursday, government sources have said.What was one in, one out?The deal involved returning to France one asylum seeker who had arrived in the UK in a small boat, in exchange for another brought legally to the UK from France. It lasted 423 days – from 10 July 2025 until 1 October 2026.Why didn’t it work out?The UK’s official explanation was that it had not been able to scale up the numbers of asylum seekers involved as much as it would have liked to. However, the scheme was beset with problems. Scores returned to the UK during the scheme because they felt unsafe in France. Some were returned to France a second time while others were allowed to remain in the UK to have their claims processed here. Many were believed to have vanished after being returned to France. Asylum seekers said they were threatened by smugglers because they owed them money and feared being sent back to their home countries or to another European country they had passed through on their journey.How many people were sent back under it and how many returned to the UK?Approximately 1,500 asylum seekers were returned to France, with a similar number brought legally from France to the UK. The numbers removed under the scheme were fewer than the total who arrived in small boats over seven days in the second half of last month. More than 40,000 have arrived in Britain in small boats during the period the deal has been in place.What do the French say about the scheme?It is understood France wanted to end the deal because it did not want to carry the weight of accepting small boat arrivals back from the UK alone and instead wanted the rest of Europe to also get involved. Other European countries have so far not agreed to join the scheme. “Why do we have to manage this border on our own?” the French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said at a parliamentary hearing this year. “We believe that France should not have to bear the burden alone, and that it would be better to incorporate it into an agreement between the European Union and the United Kingdom.”What do the British say?The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said at a recent session of the Commons home affairs committee that it was difficult to pinpoint exactly why there had been a reduction of more than 40% in the number of people crossing the Channel so far this year compared with the same period last year. Others say that lower levels of irregular migration into the UK from France in the first five months of this year compared with the same period last year are likely at least partially to be due to a drop in arrivals of irregular migrants to Europe overall. The Home Office said it would continue to remove as many small boat arrivals as possible. But it is not possible to forcibly remove people to unsafe countries such as Iran, Eritrea, Sudan and others, where many on small boats come from.What do critics of the scheme say?NGOs such as Medical Justice have condemned the trauma they have documented due to the detention of this group, many of whom are survivors of trafficking or torture. Force was used against one in 10 of 224 asylum seekers during their removal to France in the first three months of this year, according to Home Office freedom of information data. Both the NGO Médecins Sans Frontières and the French health organisation Samusocial, which provides treatment for returnees to France, documented physical and psychological injuries. At the home affairs committee the home secretary suggested these injuries may have been self-inflicted. The Labour MP and committee member Bell Ribeiro-Addy accused the home secretary of “victim blaming” and said there was independent evidence of injuries sustained as a result of use of force.What could the UK government do now?Successive prime ministers and home secretaries have vowed to stop small boats crossing the Channel. So far none have succeeded. For as long as people flee war and conflict a percentage of them are likely to turn up in the UK by one means or another. The use of return hubs in third countries is under discussion by some European countries although no details have been confirmed.How do asylum seekers feel about the end of one in, one out?In a word, overjoyed. “Thank God. You gave me the best news,” said one asylum seeker forcibly returned to France, after hearing the news. He is now considering returning to the UK. Another who is also hoping to return said: “That’s good news. European countries agree on ‘assertive’ response to US pressure on diesel
Unknown

European countries agree on ‘assertive’ response to US pressure on diesel
The countries, including Britain, France and Germany, held an emergency meeting Thursday to respond to calls from the Trump administration to release fuel reserves.
BRUSSELS — Five European countries agreed at an emergency meeting Thursday to respond with "one voice" to growing pressure from the U.S. government to release reserves of diesel, according to people familiar with the matter.
France, Germany, Britain, Italy, Ireland and the European Commission joined the talks to decide how to respond to pressure from Washington to draw down oil stockpiles or face a ban on U.S. exports of diesel, three European officials told POLITICO.
All these countries have been privately pressured by the U.S. to draw down on their reserves, two of the people said.
Advertisement
The countries, along with the EU's executive arm, agreed three things, according to the people: To react to the pressure with a "coordinated voice," to make sure that "every decision about releasing stocks should be elevated to the IEA [International Energy Agency] level," and to seek to "decrease the tension when speaking to the U.S."
The Paris-based IEA coordinates energy policy among rich countries, and oversaw a release of oil stocks earlier this year following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The idea is to "de-escalate," one of the people said. "To be sort of assertive but positive in the communication ... When you're dealing with the hungry lion, you do not necessarily play dirty games with him."
A wider pool of countries, some of which have also faced pressure from the Trump administration, will discuss how to respond in a meeting on Friday, the person added.
POLITICO reported earlier that U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright was asking for oil releases as an alternative to imposing a ban on exports, on which the EU is heavily dependent. The requested release of 120 million barrels of diesel over six months would account for well over a third of the EU's total reserves of the essential transport fuel.
Diesel prices are soaring in the U.S. as a result of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, heaping pressure on U.S. President Donald Trump to bring down prices ahead of critical mid-term elections. The U.S. is a major diesel exporter, and currently provides more than half of the EU's imports — meaning a ban would have serious implications for the European economy.
Trump has refused to rule out an export ban despite vociferous opposition from the U.S. oil sector. “I’m thinking about it,” Trump said of the export ban at an Oval Office event. “I speak to [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it a lot — they sort of think it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things.”

Ukraine solves riddle of metal “whiskers” on new Russia’s drones. They aren’t clever sensor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:43:39 UTC
23:43:39 KST

Ukraine has cracked the riddle of strange metal "whiskers" that appeared on Russian jet-powered drones striking Kyiv, and they don't appear to be some clever new sensor. They are a simple mechanical detonator, a metal tube, and a rod that, on impact, closes a circuit to set off the warhead, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, presidential adviser, says, ending online guessing about the strange devices.
Photos of Russian drones with long metal prongs jutting from the nose had set off speculation about what they were for. The answer, Flash explains, is low-tech: when the prong hits something, the contact closes, and the charge goes off, with no sensors or electronics.
That simplicity sits against a more worrying trend: Russia is steadily upgrading what its drones carry, from the mix of warheads on the jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 to a new charge designed to sever power pylons.
A contact closes the circuit
"It's all mechanically simple, no sensors or complex detectors," Flash says, commenting on the "whiskers".
It is the kind of crude, cheap fuze that suits a weapon meant to be built and spent in the thousands, where cost matters more than finesse.
Russia upgrades the warheads
Russia's jet drones, now built at roughly 3,000 a month, have become the dominant threat in its nightly campaign. The day when Flash published his "whiskers" post, Russia hit Kyiv with another round of drone strikes, hitting a school, a café, and warehouse buildings across the capital. The children inside the school were in its shelter. Fires broke out across two districts, and one person in the city was wounded.
On 28 September, Russia struck Kyiv's Academy of Sciences, which has a century-old history.
On the same day, Dmitry Peskov, Kremlin spokesperson, said Ukraine must "pay a price" for its actions in recent months and calls Russia's intensified strikes "part of this price."

Source: Serhii Derkach, First Deputy Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine, in an interview with Radio Liberty

The implementation timeline depends mainly on manufacturers' capacity
Quote: "We hope to provide all border crossing points with shelters by the end of this year. The only issue is production. Production of the shelters in Ukraine takes time because there are currently many facilities that need them."

NEW DELHI, October 1. /TASS/. Russian Urals crude oil accounted for 35% of India's total hydrocarbon imports in September, The Times of India reported, citing data from Kpler analytical firm.
Last month, Russia continued to rank first in Indian oil imports, which stood at 5.4 million barrels daily. This is the highest level of energy supplies to India since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February, achieved due to improved logistics through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Kpler statistics, India received nearly 40% of its oil, over 60% of its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), and 47% of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Iran last month. In August, oil supplies from Middle Eastern countries averaged 25%. Deliveries of LPG and LNG stood at 29%.
An increase in imports from Oman and the UAE allowed India to reduce its costly LPG imports from the US to 16%, which had accounted for nearly one-third of such total deliveries to the country during the peak escalation of the Middle East conflict.

System sprang into action within seconds: Behind the scenes of the Flydubai terror drama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:37:43 UTC
23:37:43 KST

A single distress signal sent from the cockpit of a Flydubai plane carrying 174 passengers was enough to send Israel’s security establishment into one of its most tense and complex operations in recent memory.
The activation of various security bodies follows an orderly, almost automatic mechanism linking events aboard the aircraft directly and immediately to IDF command centers, putting the system on maximum alert within seconds.
At first, there was genuine concern that an aircraft bound for Israel had been hijacked. Even before the full picture became clear, the first contingency plan was activated — the protocol for a suspected hijacking. The plan’s code name is barred from publication.
Two Israeli Air Force fighter jets were scrambled to intercept the aircraft, escort it and isolate the surrounding airspace. At the same time, Home Front Command units were placed on alert and General Staff negotiation teams were put on full readiness in case the plane landed in Israel.
Within minutes, however, the situation changed dramatically.
The “hijacked” plane made a sharp U-turn and moved away from Israel’s borders, heading back toward Saudi Arabia. Initial reports sent to the operations command center indicated that a violent confrontation had erupted inside the cockpit between the captain and the co-pilot — a fierce struggle during which passengers and crew members managed, with considerable resourcefulness, to overpower the attacker.
As the aircraft headed for an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, Israel’s course of action shifted completely.
At that stage, a second contingency plan was activated — a readiness order for a complex hostage-rescue operation in a foreign country. The code name of that plan is also barred from publication.
Once the alert was received that the aircraft was expected to land in Saudi Arabia, Israel’s security forces raised their readiness further. Air Force transport aircraft, including three Hercules planes, were prepared for immediate takeoff, and additional steps were taken as part of hostage-rescue procedures.
Shortly afterward, the IDF Operations Directorate and the broader security establishment concluded that the aircraft was landing in Saudi Arabia without having been hijacked and that its passengers were not being held hostage.
A senior military official said the options were examined with great caution, and three main alternatives were prepared for bringing the Israeli citizens home.
The first was a direct military evacuation using three Air Force Hercules aircraft that were standing by as part of the hostage-rescue order. The second was dispatching a designated civilian aircraft carrying military rescue teams. The third was relying on a civilian Flydubai flight.
In the end, after detailed assessments and complex coordination behind the scenes, officials decided to use what they considered the fastest and safest option for the passengers: evacuation aboard a civilian flight.
Security officials said the main consideration for decision-makers was to avoid unnecessary diplomatic friction on Saudi soil.
At the same time, security officials stressed that all physical and operational systems were fully prepared to carry out any of the other options, including a direct military landing, if difficulties or security risks had emerged.
Senior Israeli security officials said the Saudi government’s conduct during the tense hours was very positive.
“Behind the scenes, there was a great deal of willingness on the Saudi side,” senior Israeli officials said, “and in the end, they took very significant action from our perspective.”
Although military officials have avoided describing the incident as a diplomatic breakthrough and have left such interpretation to the political leadership, the ongoing and positive coordination in such a sensitive setting demonstrated the ability of the two sides to work together in real time.
The IDF said afterward that the operational orders and automatic mechanisms designed to protect Israeli airspace functioned adequately. The General Staff is expected to carry out a routine lessons-learned process in the coming days to further improve the system, with an emphasis on responding appropriately to rapidly developing and changing events.
Still, much remains unclear about the investigation, and difficult questions remain for Israeli security mechanisms that work with international airlines.
Officials will have to determine how an Omani pilot came to be flying Israeli passengers and entering Israeli airspace, and how the relevant security authorities were unaware of his recruitment by an airline that operates extensively in Israel, particularly in recent years.
Another question is whether he was part of a terrorist infrastructure or cell capable of deploying attackers in similar scenarios against Israelis abroad.
The investigation into the apparent security gap comes against the backdrop of the Shin Bet having barred Israeli airlines for months from landing in Dubai because of security concerns. However, the scenarios officials had considered were not similar to what ultimately unfolded aboard the Flydubai flight.
The expectation is that, following the unusual incident, changes will be made primarily behind the scenes in the relationship between the airline, similar carriers and Israeli security bodies.
The screening, questioning and vetting mechanisms relating to pilots carrying Israelis to Israel and other destinations are expected to undergo significant review and overhaul.

“With sincere regret,” Say Agency said on Telegram that the concerts would not be able to proceed on the scheduled dates.
The company said it would issue a further statement regarding the status of the project and its future plans.

"The number one issue was Islamophobia, and the issue around the political atmosphere is really the rhetoric online and within political parties."
He cited comments by Conservative MP Nick Timothy, who described Muslim prayers held in Trafalgar Square during an iftar event in March as "an act of dominance", as an example of the political rhetoric contributing to these concerns.
The concerns come amid a sharp rise in anti-Muslim hate across Britain. According to Home Office figures, 3,199 religious hate crimes targeting Muslims were recorded in England and Wales, excluding the Metropolitan Police, in the year to March 2025, a 19% increase on the previous year.
Anti-Muslim hate has surged across Britain in recent years, with anti-Muslim hate rising by 165% between 2022 and 2024, reaching a record 6,313 in 2024, according to TELL MAMA. In London alone, reported incidents increased more than sixfold between 2021 and 2025.
Salik also welcomed the government's introduction of a definition of Islamophobia earlier this year but stressed that the policies accompanying it needed to be "fast-tracked and implemented".
"That's the key thing. We need to see leadership we heard yesterday," he said, referring to Ed Miliband's remarks on Monday acknowledging that pro-Palestinian protesters had been right to demonstrate against Israel's actions in Gaza.
"I think this kind of narrative needs to apply across the board and on issues like this as well, and we welcome that approach."
Devolution offers hope for marginalised communities
This year's Labour conference has been dominated by the message of "hope again", as the party seeks to change course following the ousting of Keir Starmer in June.
Addressing the conference on Tuesday, Burnham said it was "time to draw a line, to move beyond a decade of drift and division", urging the public to imagine "a Britain for everyone, no matter who we are or where we're born".
Asked whether this message of hope was resonating with Muslim communities, Salik said the atmosphere at the conference had been encouraging.
"I think there has been a positive atmosphere. I think there's been lots of conversations about things that need to happen, that haven't happened for a long time [and] that are starting to happen."
Sajid Mohammed, executive director of the social justice organisation Himmah, also welcomed the shift in Labour's rhetoric but warned that the party had yet to translate its promises into meaningful change.
"I think it was refreshing to see Ed Miliband and Andy Burnham use the language that they do. I think it cuts very clearly and connects with the communities," Mohammed said.
"Unfortunately, we have not yet seen it in action and it being delivered," he cautioned, calling on Labour to reflect on the deprioritisation of racial equality and, by extension, Muslim communities in recent years.
Mohammed argued that Burnham's devolution agenda, a cornerstone of his premiership, could give marginalised communities greater influence over the decisions affecting their lives.
"I think there's a real big opportunity with devolution and how marginalised communities, socially and economically marginalised communities, can interact and shape policy," he said, adding, "it's all in the details and how it's delivered."
He said giving communities greater ownership and a meaningful say in local decision-making could help strengthen their sense of belonging and counter far-right narratives that portray different groups as competing for limited resources.
"There's a saying, 'an Englishman's home is his castle'. Ownership is belonging, that's meaningful belonging, and unless communities have ownership, have a real say [in] what happens, I think there's that erosion and space given to far-right narratives of zero [sum] gaming where there's winners and losers, and that's what needs to be tackled."
The scale of the problem is particularly evident in London, where Tell MAMA recorded 1,909 reports of anti-Muslim hate in 2025, compared with 313 in 2021. A further 1,031 incidents were reported in the first six months of 2026, highlighting the growing pressure on local authorities to respond to anti-Muslim hostility.
Shabna Begum, chief executive of the Runnymede Trust, a race equality think tank, also identified devolution as a potential tool for tackling Islamophobia, arguing that the problem requires action at multiple levels because it is both structural and political.
"In terms of aspirations and values, there's a desire [from Muslim communities] and an aspiration to belong," Begum told The New Arab, adding, "but at the same time, we've got kind of a material environment that inhibits that belonging and actually makes that more difficult."
She urged the government to challenge the increasingly normalised portrayal of Muslims as a "deviant community", arguing that devolution could help policymakers better understand how Islamophobia manifests in different parts of society.
"I think the devolution piece is an opportunity to really surface what is happening at that closer level, and to examine what those experiences are at the city level, the country level, whatever the devolved level happens to be."
Beyond the government's devolution agenda, Begum said this year's Labour conference had marked a noticeable shift in the atmosphere, with organisations that had previously worked in separate spaces increasingly finding common ground and pursuing shared objectives.
"There is a sense of much more collective effort, and that actually, we may not be joined up in a really intentional and coordinated way, but I get the sense that people feel we are are pushing towards something, more hopeful, more optimistic, more progressive," Begum said.
"From my view, it's felt more productive and positive than it's felt recently."

This is the story of only Turkish village that dislikes smoking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:32:47 UTC
23:32:47 KST

Whether you're in a crowded alley in Istanbul or near a beach resort in Antalya, you’ll likely come across a Tekel shop. These roadside stores, mostly with blue-painted exteriors, are remnants of the State Tobacco Monopoly (Tekel). That’s where you go to buy cigarettes.
Tekel was created in the mid-1920s as the young Turkish state took control of the lucrative tobacco business from foreign companies, which had captured the market in the final years of the Ottoman Empire.
Türkiye was already a tobacco producer. Even the image of the camel that became synonymous with the Camel brand has Turkish roots. RJR, the American behemoth that made Camels, used a blend of Turkish tobacco in its cigarettes. So someone in the company’s marketing department thought it fit to emboss a camel as a logo — even though Türkiye is not known for these humpy-backed mammals.
It was a pivotal moment for the Turkish cigarette industry.
But right around that time in Tazlar, a tiny village in the Sinanpasa district of Türkiye’s western province of Afyonkarahisar, another revolution was taking place.
Led by a village elder, Ahmet Aga, the villagers took a vow not to smoke and set an example for future generations.
That decision permanently transformed Tazlar Village into a smoke-free sanctuary nearly a century before modern public health legislation existed.
It has been almost a hundred years, and the village, with its population of roughly 2,000 people, still boasts a reputation as a place where the sight of smokers is almost nonexistent.
Tazlar’s story is all the more relevant now as the Turkish government is pushing hard to curb smoking. Ankara is considering a law that will impose a lifetime ban on smoking for people born after January 2015.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is known for his strong opposition to smoking. He reportedly told the Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to quit, which she did earlier this year.
Multiple studies show Turks rank among the highest consumers of cigarettes. But that’s not a problem in Tazlar.
How did it all start
History has mostly forgotten Ahmed Aga, and the Tazlar residents can recall only what they were told by their parents. But as the story goes, Aga was driven by a desire to protect both the physical health and the limited financial resources of his people. In 1928, when the villagers took a collective oath against tobacco, Aga was able to capitalise on a moment when only a handful of villagers smoked, and he successfully persuaded them to quit.
“We grew up without people smoking around us,” says 66-year-old Mehmet Aydogmus, who serves as village preacher and is also an accountant. “In a sense, not smoking was not a decision we made later in life. It became directly part of our lives and our culture.”
That distinction is central to understanding Tazlar’s experience.
Rather than relying solely on individual decisions, the village appears to have developed a collective culture in which smoking never became normalised.
Aydogmus says the principle was not presented to children as a rule imposed from above. Instead, it was something they absorbed by watching their parents, grandparents and neighbours.
“When I was a child, seeing someone smoking in the village was not something we were accustomed to,” Aydogmus recalls.
Tazlar is a village of red-bricked houses, surrounded by fields of yellow tomatoes and sugar beets. Villagers here follow a set routine. They wake up early and go to bed after sunset. Here, everyone knows each other.
The villagers’ opposition to smoking is rooted partly in health concerns, but Aydogmus says the tradition cannot be explained by health alone.
“Our elders would constantly tell us about the damage smoking causes to human health,” he says. “But they would not stop at saying that it was harmful to health.”
They also spoke about the effects of harmful habits on families, communities and individual willpower.
“We gradually learned this,” he says. “Even when we were children and did not fully understand what it meant, we knew from the attitude of our elders that this was an important issue for us.”
The village’s approach combined family responsibility, religious values and communal solidarity, says Aydogmus.
Families looked after their children. Older people warned younger generations. Neighbours knew one another. And behaviour was understood not only as an individual matter but also as something that could affect the wider family and community.
If a child begins to develop what the family considers a harmful habit, relatives and neighbours do not necessarily remain passive.
“If a young person makes a mistake somewhere, people do not say, ‘It has nothing to do with me,’” Aydogmus says. “People know one another in the village. Everyone knows whose child and whose grandchild someone is.”
But how do you preserve a culture if there are no young people to follow in your footsteps?
Dispersing like smoke
Murat Karasogut, 29, who grew up in Tazlar, always gets a cultural shock when he travels to other parts of the country.
“When we see someone smoking outside, sometimes we think, ‘We do not have something like this in our village.’”
In Tazlar, he says, not smoking became the expected norm. Young people did not necessarily need to be repeatedly told to reject smoking because cigarettes were already outside the village’s everyday culture.
“Not smoking is something that is customary in our village, so young people adopt it more easily,” he says.
That difference, he believes, remains significant even as young people encounter cigarettes more frequently elsewhere.
But more and more young people from Tazlar are moving to cities, raising concerns that the steadfast opposition to smoking might fade over time.
More than two-thirds of the village’s young people now live in cities such as Istanbul and Bursa, lured by better education and employment prospects.
For both Aydogmus and Karasogut, the future of Tazlar’s tradition ultimately depends on whether younger generations choose to carry it forward.
Karasogut believes young people have a particular responsibility.
“We do not want to remain in the past,” Aydogmus says. “But we do not want to lose our past either.”

Collapse of diagnostic system in Gaza masks hundreds of breast cancer cases: Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:32:26 UTC
23:32:26 KST

Jomaa Younis and Mohammad Sio
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The collapse of breast cancer screening and early diagnosis services in the Gaza Strip is concealing the true scale of the disease, with hundreds of cases believed to be undiagnosed, the Health Ministry said Thursday.
It issued the warning in a statement marking the start of “Pink October,” the global breast cancer awareness month dedicated to early detection and support for patients.
Women with breast cancer in Gaza are living through a “catastrophic health and humanitarian reality” amid the loss of even the most basic requirements for medical care and treatment, according to the statement.
Screening and early diagnosis services have become “extremely limited and virtually suspended,” it added, citing severe shortages and repeated breakdowns of mammography machines as well as the lack of laboratory reagents and medical supplies.
It said the situation is depriving women of opportunities for early detection.
The treatment system for breast cancer patients is suffering from a “near-total absence of approved treatment protocols.”
It said oncology departments lack chemotherapy drugs, hormonal treatments and targeted therapies, while radiotherapy services are completely unavailable inside Gaza.
Operations to remove advanced tumors have also stopped because of the lack of specialized medical capabilities, it said.
Before Israel’s genocide began in late 2023, the enclave recorded 360 new breast cancer cases annually, according to the ministry.
It said 250 cases were diagnosed in 2024 and around 260 in 2025, while based on the pre-war rate, more than 1,000 new cases would have been expected over roughly three years.
“The most dangerous thing we face today is not only the number of patients who are diagnosed, but the number of women who may have the disease without it being detected early,” it said.
It added that the suffering of cancer patients is being compounded by movement restrictions and the closure of crossings, which prevent hundreds of urgent cases from traveling to specialized oncology centers outside Gaza.
“Pink October from Gaza is not merely an awareness campaign, but a humanitarian distress call to save the lives of patients struggling against death amid the absence of basic treatment requirements,” it said.
Gaza’s health system has suffered severe damage since October 2023, with hospitals and medical facilities destroyed or rendered inoperable and shortages of medicines, medical supplies and fuel severely limiting care, particularly for cancer and chronic disease patients.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza by Israel since October 2023.

New Delhi voices alarm as Indians continue to join Russian army amid Ukraine war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:31:06 UTC
23:31:06 KST

India has warned its citizens against being recruited into the Russian army amid the Ukraine war, calling it a “dangerous path".
The country’s external affairs ministry said in a statement on Thursday that it continues to see reports of Indian nationals being recruited into the Russian armed forces and has repeatedly underlined the risks and dangers inherent in this course of action.
The ministry said it has come across numerous instances where individuals are willingly “seeking out offers to join the Russian armed forces with an understanding that they would be able to avail concomitant monetary benefits" and later “secure release” by approaching the Indian government.
“It is reiterated that this is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government,” the ministry said.
It said there are several cases in which “individuals have approached Indian authorities to willingly give up their Indian citizenship, avail a Russian passport and then get recruited into the Russian armed forces.”
“It is advised that individuals should consider the gravity of such actions and understand the mortal dangers they are exposing themselves to,” the ministry said.
The Indian government, the statement said, remains “continuously engaged with the Russian side to ensure the safety, well-being and early discharge of all Indian nationals in the Russian armed forces.”
Last month, India said that it asked Russia to end the practice of recruiting its nationals in the military.
According to figures released last month, 227 Indian nationals have been recruited into the Russian army since the beginning of the war in 2022.
Of them, 139 had been discharged from service, while 51 people died.
“This is an issue that we are in constant discussions with the Russian side,” Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri told reporters in New Delhi last month.
In July this year, the Indian parliament was informed that there were 127 Indian nationals in the Russian armed forces, out of whom the services of 98 individuals were discontinued.
The ministry said 13 Indian nationals remain in the Russian armed forces, of whom 12 individuals have been reported missing by the Russian side.
Before that, in March, the Indian government had said 12 Indian nationals had lost their lives during the ongoing conflict.

Two Russian drones have hit one of Kyiv's main bridges, bringing public transport in the Ukrainian capital to a halt and signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks.
The Pivdennyi or Southern bridge came under fire as a metro train was travelling across. Passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.
The Pivdennyi bridge is one of the main arteries across the Dnipro river dividing western and eastern Kyiv.
Kyiv's bridges had not been hit before Thursday's strikes - and despite a dramatic explosion close to a main support section, city authorities said preliminary checks "did not find any critical damage to the structure".
For the people of Kyiv, the drone strikes were another powerful reminder that Russia has their city firmly in its sights and is doing everything it can to disrupt life in the capital.
Kyiv had just suffered its first co-ordinated attacks on the city's energy grid since the end of last winter, and commentators believe Russia has stepped up its campaign seeing that Ukraine is suffering from a shortage of air defences.
Strikes on Wednesday also heralded a return to power cuts in the capital. Although Kyiv authorities have spent months constructing smaller-scale power plants to counter Russia's anticipated winter campaign, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a combined strike on such a scale had not taken place since the end of spring.
- Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine 
  - Published18 hours ago
The first big attack on the capital on Thursday came when a Russian drone slammed into the third floor of a school at about 09:00 local time (10:00 GMT).
Although more than 100 students had been at the school at the time, they had all reached a shelter when the drone hit. One of the school's walls partially collapsed.
"[The shelter's] structure is strong, so none of the children were hurt, neither were any staff," said head teacher Valentyna Chorna. "They just kept on with their lessons."
Russia denies targeting civilians, but Chorna said that to destroy her nation "they need to destroy children". President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had to be held fully accountable.
Later in the morning, two drones hit the Pivdenny bridge, one hitting the base of a central stanchion.
Ukrainian 5 Kanal TV reporter Mariana Mykytenko described how one of the passengers on her metro train shouted the word "Shahed", referring to Russia's Iranian-designed drones, before the blast sent dust pouring into their carriage.
No-one in her compartment was hurt, she said, and "the train took people to Vydubychi station on the right bank, then it didn't go any further". The right bank is on the west side of the Dnipro river.
Metro trains were suspended but road traffic was eventually allowed to resume.
It is not yet clear what kind of drone was used in the Kyiv bridge attack, but Ukrainian officials say a new design of Russia's jet-powered drones came into operation for the first time on Wednesday.
The drone has a 40kg warhead and is especially designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons and iron bridge structures, according to Zelensky's technology adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash.
In recent weeks, Russia has had considerable success with jet-powered drones and Ukrainian air force officials say that, during September, at least 3,177 were launched. Their high speed has caused problems for Ukraine's beleaguered air defences.
Kyiv's Institute of Nuclear Research came under drone attack on Wednesday night and, earlier in the week, one person was killed when a drone targeted the National Academy of Sciences.
