‘Set-jetting’ trips: How to holiday like the Gilmore Girls in Stars Hollow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:29:50 UTC
23:29:50 KST

From the fictional Connecticut town of Gilmore Girls' Stars Hollow to destinations closer to home in Europe, the set-jetting trend continues to turn film and TV locations into travel experiences.
Rather than watching re-runs of your favourite TV show from the sofa this winter, what if you could step onto the set instead?
This is exactly what Gilmore Girls fans could do thanks to a new “holiday” experience launched by Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood. Taking place from 12 December 2026 to 3 January 2027 (with the exception of 25 December) fans can swap the living room for the seasonal holiday event.
The new attraction weaves visitors through familiar locations from the show’s fictional Connecticut town of Stars Hollow, transforming Warner Bros.’ Burbank studio into “the most expansive and immersive Gilmore Girls holiday fan experience ever created”.
Visitors will be able to stroll through Lorelai Gilmore’s house and Luke’s Diner, the haunt of the protagonist's on-again, off-again love interest – Luke Danes. Other recognisable settings will include The Dragonfly Inn as well as Miss Patty's School of Ballet.
Iconic storefronts from the show will also house gift shops with collector items, while fan-favourite foods on offer will include Luke’s cold brew, Jojo’s burgers, Caesar’s chilaquiles nachos and Gazebo pretzel.
Centred on the lives of Lorelai and her daughter Rory, Gilmore Girls first aired in 2000, with the series now featuring on The New York Times list of The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century.
Where else can you set-jet to?
Warner Bros.’ decision to expand on its previous Gilmore Girls-themed holidays taps into the growing set-jetting trend. The phrase was coined to describe holiday itineraries based on the shooting locations of films or TV series – turning on-screen scenes into real life experiences.
Closer to home, Europe’s cinematic coastlines and iconic locations have long served as the backdrop for major film and TV productions. Dubrovnik, for instance, became a major draw for Game of Thrones fans after the Croatian city doubled as King’s Landing.
In Lavenham, England, guests can check into Harry Potter's “childhood home”. Listed on Airbnb, the 15th-century Vere House featured in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part One and is replete with four en-suite bedrooms, a private guest sitting room with log fire and courtyard garden.
One of the biggest movie releases this year was Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. For travellers keen to plan their own odyssey, the film’s locations ranged from Sardinia and the Strait of Messina in Italy, Ithaca in Greece, Troy in Türkiye as well as Gozo in Malta.
Madrid also has a long history of being a sought-after location for productions. The Spanish capital’s portfolio includes scenes in the popular Netflix series La Casa de Papel (Money Heist), The Cold Light of Day, and Terminator: Dark Fate.
Woody Allen's "WASP 26" – an acronym for ‘Woody Allen Summer Project’ – is also in the works to be shot in and around Madrid and is earmarked to be completed by the end of 2027. In 2025, as part of efforts to promote local tourism, the Madrid Regional Government pledged to invest three payments totalling €1.5 million into Allen's upcoming picture.
Beyond Europe, Netflix's adaptation of John Steinbeck's "East of Eden" was filmed entirely in New Zealand, despite being set in US destinations, like California’s Salinas Valley, alongside San Francisco, Connecticut, and Washington.
Harbour Street in Oamaru, a town on New Zealand's South Island, was an ideal choice for the period production thanks to its preserved limestone buildings. Dunedin also features in the series, including its Queen’s Garden and Railway Station.

The force said in a statement: “The Helsinki police department is working closely with the national bureau of investigation in clarifying the matter. The inquiry is at an early stage, and the police have nothing further to comment on at this time.”

France's Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure looks on during a press conference in Paris on May 19, 2026. | Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — The French government on Thursday proposed a 2027 budget with €43 billion in savings that seem designed to appease Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, the National Rally, and reassure markets frightened over France’s increasingly dire fiscal outlook.
“In 2027, we will return to the path of consolidation,” Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure told reporters Thursday as he presented the budget that lawmakers will debate in the coming weeks.
The government is betting that €9 billion in state spending cuts, a freeze on adjusting pensions for inflation and the extension of a temporary tax on big companies — which is expected to bring in €5 billion — will be enough to reduce the budget deficit from an estimated 5.4% of gross domestic product this year to 5% in 2027. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said last month that the government was seeking to squeeze the budget by €54 billion, but Lescure said measures already adopted this year would save the government €11 billion in 2027.
Advertisement
The government also committed to upping its annual contribution to the European Union budget by €2.5 billion as required by the bloc’s rules.
But Paris’ proposal to delay access to welfare outlays and make key provisions easily modifiable by the next government were seen by lawmakers across the political spectrum as an olive branch to Le Pen, the front-runner in the spring race to replace term-limited President Emmanuel Macron.
Since snap elections delivered a hung parliament in 2024, the budget process has become treacherous territory. Lecornu’s two predecessors lost their jobs trying to pass their spending plans in parliament by year-end.
Lawmakers of all political colors told POLITICO that the National Rally could play ball on the budget, allowing Le Pen to look like a responsible player who avoided a financial crisis while being able to still change the text if she wins.
“The only party that can afford not to topple the government is the National Rally,” said a lawmaker and former minister from Macron’s camp who was granted anonymity to speak candidly.
France Unbowed MP Eric Coquerel, the president of the National Assembly finance committee, told POLITICO he has “the impression that for now the prime minister is banking on the National Rally not to topple him.”
Advertisement
Le Pen pledged at POLITICO’s Playbook Paris Live event last week to amend the budget rather than just block it. But centrist veteran Charles de Courson cautioned that while the National Rally is “showing some openness” now, the party could very well topple Lecornu later — as Le Pen did with former Prime Minister Michel Barnier.
There is plenty of time for Lecornu to change his strategy, but a protracted and contentious budget debate would further fuel concerns of a sovereign debt crisis given the number of economic indicators pointing in a worrying direction.
Borrowing costs are now their highest since 2008, and the premium investors demand to hold French 10-year bonds over their German equivalent crossed 130 basis points Thursday — a level not seen since the 2012 eurozone debt crisis.
Statistics agency INSEE reported Wednesday that inflation hit 3% in September as energy prices spiked. The day before, INSEE said French debt reached a record-high of 119% of GDP at the end of June.
However, Lescure on Thursday dismissed warnings of an impending financial crisis as the work of “prophets of bad luck.”

Ferry service on Lake Constance in Germany suspended due to low water levels
Kyiv • UNN
The water level in Lake Constance fell to 251 cm, which is 108 cm below average. Ferry service was suspended for safety reasons.
The low water level in Lake Constance has forced the suspension of boat services on one section of the body of water. DW reports this, citing the municipal utility company of the southern German city of Constance, UNN writes.
Details
It is reported that the Bodensee-Schiffsbetriebe (BSB) ferry operator announced that it had suspended services in the Untersee area until further notice.
In a statement by BSB, the company’s head, Frank Weber, said: "We maintained the ferry service down to the last centimetre. Now we have reached the point where the risk of getting stuck at the harbour entrance has become too high."
The company added that the service had to be suspended for the safety of passengers and vessels.
The lake, known in German as Bodensee, borders Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
The water level in the lake currently stands at 251 cm—108 cm below the average of 359 cm for this day of the year, calculated on the basis of many years of observations.
A prolonged period of dry weather has forced tourist and cargo vessels on other German waterways to reduce or suspend operations.
Cargo shipping on the Rhine has been particularly badly affected, negatively impacting several industries that depend on the supply of raw materials by river transport.

Revenues from windfall tax projected at over $7 bln in 2027-2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:24:01 UTC
23:24:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Revenues from the windfall tax on companies operating in the mining and metals sector will amount to 200 bln rubles ($2.4 bln) per year in 2027-2029, according to an explanatory note to the draft federal budget for the next three years. The document has been uploaded to the lower house of parliament’s electronic database.
The tax rate on windfall profits for companies in the mining and metals sector will be 20% for gold and 30% for other commodities.
The tax base will be determined on the basis of the volume of the mineral resource extracted in the corresponding year and the amount by which its average global market price exceeds the average price for 2025, considering readjustment provided for in the bill.
The obligation to pay the tax arises when the average price for 2026 exceeds the 2025 level by 10% or more.

An alliance against invisibility: Prado and Rijksmuseum unite for women in art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

Madrid's Prado Museum and Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum are joining forces in a strategic alliance to explore women's role in history and reassess the shared heritage between Spain and the Netherlands.
Madrid's Prado Museum and Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum have joined forces to restore the memory of women in art. The two major European galleries are pooling efforts to revisit the shared history between Spain and the Netherlands and to give women artists, patrons and key figures the prominence they have always deserved in their rooms.
The centrepiece of this agreement is an international postdoctoral fellowship that will start in 2027. The aim is to delve into the collections and shed light on women's roles during the Habsburg era, with findings that will inform upcoming projects at both museums and culminate in a major exhibition at the Rijksmuseum in 2029.
This step consolidates a path both institutions had already been following separately. On one side is the initiative 'El Prado en Femenino', which, after returning centre stage to names such as Clara Peeters and Sofonisba Anguissola, two of the most important painters in the history of European art, is now preparing an exhibition on Mariana of Austria for this autumn.
On the other side is the 'Women of the Rijksmuseum' project, which since 2021 has analysed hundreds of works and added to its catalogue pieces by previously overlooked artists such as Gesina ter Borch, Maria van Oosterwijck and Marlow Moss.
Key facts about the postdoctoral fellowship
- Call for applications: The selection process opens in October 2026.
- Programme start: September 2027.
- Research focus: Work with the collections of the Prado Museum and the Rijksmuseum on the role of women in the Habsburg era.
- Final project: The selected researcher will play an active role in the major exhibition on this topic to be hosted by the Amsterdam museum in 2029.

Nicolas Cage, whose recent work includes the Sony and Marvel series "Spider-Man: Noir" (Spider-Noir), criticized the Marvel Cinematic Universe, calling it an overfunded and shameful spectacle, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
"I say this with love," Cage said at a fan convention in Texas. "When I see these actors—who are over 50, who are intelligent and extraordinarily talented people—putting on these ridiculous costumes and getting ready for a fight (and ultimately, everything comes down to a fight anyway), it's hard for me not to think that the Marvel Cinematic Universe is turning into lavishly funded and 'glamorized' wrestling (WWE)."
Cage's collaboration with Marvel—the company headed for many decades by comic-book creator Stan Lee—includes not only the series "Spider-Man: Noir" (which was canceled after its first season), but also two films in which he played the superhero Ghost Rider.
Marvel unveiled trailer for new "Avengers"15.08.26, 09:00 • 104353 views
The 62-year-old Cage told Variety that his interest in the "Spider-Man: Noir" project was primarily aesthetic. Robinson—and I built my performance so that it would suit the black-and-white format."

Russia expels Hungarian diplomats as Budapest breaks with Orbán era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:18:58 UTC
23:18:58 KST

Moscow ordered Hungarian embassy and consulate staff out just weeks after Budapest expelled 10 Russian diplomats on national security grounds in September, the first such move by Hungary since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russia expelled a group of Hungarian diplomats on Thursday after Hungary ordered 10 Russian diplomats out last month, marking a sharp break from the era of former Premier Viktor Orbán, who maintained closer ties with Moscow than any other EU leader.
Hungary's chargé d'affaires Gábor Gergics was summoned to Russia's foreign ministry and informed that staff from the Hungarian embassy in Moscow and consulates in St Petersburg and Kazan had been ordered to leave within two weeks.
Moscow described Hungary's original 8 September expulsion as a "baseless and openly unfriendly" act.
Budapest acknowledged Moscow's decision but said it stood by its position.
"Hungary is not interested in an escalation of diplomatic tensions. But we stand by our decision, taken on national security grounds. Our missions continue to operate in full, and Hungary will maintain its diplomatic presence in Russia," the Hungarian foreign ministry wrote on X.
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said at the time of the initial expulsion that the Russian diplomats "had been engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention."
The mutual expulsions follow a shift in Hungarian foreign policy since Prime Minister Péter Magyar took office earlier this year.
At the end of August, the new government's guidance to its delegation at the UN General Assembly officially described Russia as a threat to Hungary and to the "global order," condemned its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and affirmed support for Ukrainian sovereignty and its right to self-defence.
Hungary is also seeking to improve relations with Kyiv, although Budapest is blocking the opening of new EU accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine to secure concessions on the rights of the country's Hungarian minority.
Orbán, who was in power for 16 years until his party Fidesz' loss in general elections this April, openly sympathised with the Kremlin and refused to join other EU member states in expelling Russian diplomats after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He made multiple visits to Moscow after the invasion and repeatedly used Hungary's veto in the European Council to block Ukraine-related initiatives.
Magyar has promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow during his tenure.

Belgium will send three F-16 fighter jets, but maintenance delays may keep Ukraine from using them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:15:46 UTC
23:15:46 KST

Less than 50% of the F-16 fighter jets delivered to Ukraine may be operational, Defense Express reports, citing a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) editorial published on 29 September. On the same day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Belgium would deliver three F-16 fighter jets this year.
F-16s are used extensively to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones. As the number of Russian attacks has increased, these aircraft have become particularly important for Ukraine. However, the jets Ukraine receives are old, and keeping them flying takes regular maintenance, extra work, and hard-to-find parts.
Routine inspections are taking as long as 40 weeks in Belgium, retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery told the WSJ.
The maintenance process for these aircraft for Ukraine is lengthy
A likely reason for the problem is the lengthy maintenance process handled by Belgian company Sabena Aerospace Engineering, according to the WSJ, whose questions the company declined to answer. This process, according to Defense Express's estimates, takes 6–20 times longer than maintenance in the United States, which usually takes between 2 and 6 weeks. Ukraine uses the services of the Belgian company, meaning its F-16s are not being serviced quickly enough.
Delivering three additional fighter jets will not significantly help the Ukrainian military until the issue with aircraft maintenance times is resolved, Defense Express notes. The lengthy turnaround may be caused by a large maintenance backlog at the company, limited capacity, or logistical constraints, and older jets may need extra work and scarcer parts.
The delivery is part of an earlier commitment. Belgium plans to provide seven fighter jets this year: three for operational use and four for spare parts, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken said in June.
"I'll propose to the government to send all our F-16s to Ukraine in the coming years. It depends on having the F-35s in place because, of course, we have DCA [dual-capable aircraft] capacity. We have our role in the nuclear doctrine of NATO," Francken said.
Belgium has pledged its entire F-16 fleet of 53 aircraft as F-35s replace them, according to Defense Express.
F-16s in Ukraine have already shot down several thousand Russian aerial targets
F-16s operated by Ukrainian pilots have shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets. These include 666 cruise missiles and around 2,500 drones of various types. The aircraft have also carried out more than 650 strikes against Russian ground targets, Lieutenant General Anatolii Kryvonozhko, Commander of the Ukrainian Air Force, said during a meeting between a Ukrainian Air Force delegation and representatives of Lockheed Martin on 29 September.
At the meeting, Conor McGuire, Lockheed Martin's head of F-16 capability development, highly praised the combat use and operation of F-16s by Ukrainian pilots and the entire ground aviation personnel. He also expressed his intention to help Ukrainians enhance the capabilities of the existing platform, the statement said.

The construction of a Fire Point plant in Denmark helps protect both the country and Europe, Prime Minister Frederiksen says

The construction of a plant belonging to the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point in Denmark is not only a way to support Ukraine, but also part of protecting Denmark itself and Europe. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said this in a comment to DR, UNN reports.
Details
According to her, Europe must increase its defense capabilities and produce more weapons on its own territory.
If we do not increase our defense capabilities quickly enough to be able to protect both the country that is currently under attack and other parts of Europe that may come under attack, then the risk will be much greater—both from a Danish and a European perspective. Therefore, when we produce Ukrainian weapons in Denmark, when we support Ukraine, we do so in order to protect ourselves
This refers to a solid rocket-fuel plant that Fire Point is building in Denmark.
Mette Frederiksen emphasized that peacetime for Europe had ended because Russia does not want peace and poses an increasing threat to Denmark and NATO. Last week, Denmark presented a new threat assessment, which stated that Russia would intensify its hybrid warfare through "more frequent attacks" against the West and NATO.
That is why, under the current circumstances, Denmark must be ready to defend itself.
Europe must ensure the necessary strengthening of its defense capabilities. Therefore, we will have to produce more weapons, including on our own territory. That is why I am pleased that we are now launching Ukrainian production in Denmark
She also noted that she could not say that Denmark's support for Ukraine would ever end.
I do not view the funds we spend on Ukraine as the defense of Ukraine. I view them as the defense of ourselves and Europe. Ukraine is the "first line of defense." I cannot say that our support will ever end. I can say that I do not believe Russia should win this war, and I do not believe Russia should determine what our security architecture in Europe will be
"Ukraine's largest export to Europe is time" — Fire Point CEO12.09.26, 11:20 • 12928 views
Reminder

This is the first case within NATO in which a member state has allowed a Ukrainian defense company to establish a production site on its territory.
As Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh reported, the plant's total area will exceed 120,000 sq. m, with capacity ranging from 800 to more than 4,100 missiles per year depending on requirements. The construction process required a review of regulatory standards and expertise related to the construction of facilities of this scale. In addition, the Danish authorities removed more than 20 legislative barriers overall.
During the war in Ukraine, the plant will operate to meet the needs of our Defense Forces; later, it is planned that the fuel will also be supplied to European partners.

Russian drone strikes Kyiv nuclear institute housing research reactor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:13:40 UTC
23:13:40 KST

A Russian drone struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv on Sept. 30, where a research nuclear reactor is located, Ukraine's State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said on Telegram on Oct. 1.
The strike, which occurred at around 6:18 p.m. local time, sparked a fire that was quickly extinguished. No one was injured in the attack, according to the statement.
The VVR-M research reactor itself and systems important for its safety were not damaged, according to the regulator. Radiation levels remained within the normal background range of 0.16-0.20 microsieverts per hour.
The reactor has been shut down since February 2022, when its core was fully unloaded to reduce radiation risks following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. It is currently used only for maintenance of safety-related systems.
The institute is part of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences and conducts research in nuclear physics, atomic energy, and radioecology.
"The drone strike on the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research was an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility used exclusively for scientific and research purposes," the regulator said.
The strike on the Kyiv institute is the latest incident to put a Ukrainian nuclear facility at risk. Russian attacks have repeatedly threatened the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant and the infrastructure supplying it with electricity. The latest such incident occurred in June 2026, when Russian drone strikes damaged a spent nuclear fuel storage facility at Chornobyl.
The attack came amid a sharp increase in Russian strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks. Russia has intensified its use of drones around the clock, striking residential buildings, businesses, transport infrastructure, and other civilian sites.
Two Russian drones also struck Kyiv's Southern Bridge on Oct. 1 as cars and a metro train were crossing it.
A day earlier, Russia launched its first mass attack on Kyiv's energy infrastructure since the previous heating season, causing emergency power outages in the capital and other regions.

Russia's methodical use of starvation in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:11:08 UTC
23:11:08 KST

Russia's methodical use of starvation in Oleshky
An aerial view of Oleshky, a Russian-occupied town in Kherson Oblast, Ukraine in a photo published on May 2, 2026. (UAOleshki2026 / Telegram)
Elise Lauriot Prevost
Conflict, Business and International Crimes Lead at Global Rights Compliance
The town of Oleshky and the surrounding district in southern Kherson Oblast in Ukraine are under a total blockade imposed by Russian occupation forces.
Since May 26, 2026, no humanitarian aid has reached Oleshky.
Residents are hanging signs on their fences reading "no food, we're starving too," emaciated animals have disappeared from the streets, and a three-liter jar of preserved bread crusts has become, in the words of one resident, worth its "weight in gold."
Reports of civilians eating weeds draw harrowing parallels with the sieges of Yarmouk and Mariupol, both used by Russia to refine its use of starvation as a weapon of war. Following in their genocidal Holodomor in the 1930s, Russia is again using starvation to punish, terrorize, and humiliate Ukrainians.
Estimates of how many civilians remain trapped range from around 2,000, including some 50 children in Oleshky town, to more than 6,000, including 200 children across the wider district.
The dead are left in the streets for weeks and buried in plastic bags marked with serial numbers as Russia refuses to allow residents either access or the means for proper or dignified burials.
Russia has continuously occupied Oleshky since the full-scale invasion's first hours, and five of the community's thirteen settlements, Krynky, Pishchanivka, Pidstepne, Sagi, and Zaplava, were destroyed in the fighting, according to local officials, "ceasing to exist."
The Antonivka bridge, the town's last link to Ukrainian-held territory, was destroyed by Russian forces in November 2022. The June 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka dam by Russian forces unleashed a flood that submerged much of Oleshky, killed an unknown number of residents, and destroyed what remained of the town's water, electricity, and gas infrastructure.
Oleshky still has no centralized power, gas, or running water. Residents also lost most of their administrative documents in the flood; the hospital only has one department functioning, and residents are unable to obtain health or hygiene services or products.
By February 2026, any attempt to evacuate or deliver aid meant traveling down what locals call "the road of death" — a route littered with landmines and terrorized by Russian drones. On Feb. 12, at least four people were killed attempting to deliver food.
The last delivery that reached Oleshky arrived on May 26, 2026. Every attempt since has ended in death or injury at the behest of the so-called liberation forces: a convoy struck a landmine on June 2, and a food convoy was destroyed by first-person-view (FPV) drones in early September. On Sept. 20, two civilians were killed by a drone while attempting to bring food from a neighboring town.
Ukrainian authorities have tried to coordinate humanitarian access and evacuation with the ICRC. As usual, Russia has so far failed to cooperate, underlining its intent to starve the town's civilians.
Russia's cruelty and their intent are self-evident: their forces have delivered "humanitarian aid," condensed milk, to Oleshky twice - but only to those who held Russian passports.
Starvation as a method of warfare
Article 54 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, reflecting customary international law, prohibits starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, including by attacking, destroying, removing, or rendering useless the objects indispensable to survival (OIS). Starvation is also criminalized by the Rome Statute and Article 438 of Ukraine's Criminal Code.
In the case of Oleshky, the material element of the crime has been confirmed multiple times.
Civilians have been deprived of OIS since 2023, when Russia's deliberate destruction of the Kakhovka dam cut off water, power, and gas. That deprivation is now compounded by the Russian intentional collapse of the food supply, their refusal to allow humanitarian aid, and a consequential lack of medical personnel and services.
The mental element, which requires a specific intent to starve rather than mere indifference to a side-effect of war, is glaringly obvious in the case of Oleshky.
The attacks against humanitarian aid, the complete blockade of the town, and the discriminatory distribution of food to Russian passport holders all point towards an intent to starve Ukrainian civilians with the aim of terrorizing Ukraine into submission.
Oleshky's occupation, now in its fifth year, makes the conduct particularly egregious.
Since the first days of the occupation, Russia has had this positive obligation to feed the population of Oleshky, and has continuously breached it. Under the law of occupation, Russia is not only prohibited from starving the population; it also has a positive duty to feed civilians.
Article 55 of the Fourth Geneva Convention requires an occupying power, to the fullest extent of the means available to it, to ensure the population's food and medical supplies, bringing in what is needed if local resources fall short.
Article 59 goes further: where a population is inadequately supplied, the occupying power must agree to relief schemes proposed by states or impartial organizations such as the ICRC, and facilitate them by all means at its disposal. This is not discretionary. Once the supply is shown to be inadequate, the duty to accept such offers is unconditional.
An occupying power may impose reasonable technical conditions on how aid is delivered, but it may not arbitrarily refuse, delay, or obstruct it; doing so constitutes the war crime of wilfully impeding relief supplies, a sister war crime to starvation in the Rome Statute.
The duration and consistency of the violations in Oleshky are particularly heinous.
Oleshky has been occupied since the first day of the invasion; Russian forces destroyed the bridge linking it to unoccupied Ukraine; the attack on the Kakhovka dam destroyed the town’s infrastructure; and, year after year, Russia has systematically refused to let food and medicine in or let people evacuate.
This pattern of starvation is the method Russia uses repeatedly to force the capitulation of a people who refuse to disavow their Ukrainian identity and swear allegiance to the Kremlin.

Bangladesh quota reform sees women lose out on government jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:11:00 UTC
23:11:00 KST

Bangladesh’s 2024 student-led uprising that toppled a government and replaced a public sector job quota system for a merit-based hiring, has drastically reduced civil service opportunities for women in the Muslim-majority nation.
Tothapi Azad, a 25-year-old Dhaka University graduate, supported calls to end quotas but says she should have supported retaining them for women.
"For me, who had my family's support, a quota might not have been essential – but for an average woman, it was essential," she said.
"A job is a tool for women's empowerment. For rural women, it is more than that – a survival tactic, a shield to resist domestic violence."
Data shows the share of female government recruits has fallen since quotas were cut, shrinking an already limited number of civil service roles held by women.
Until 2018, quotas accounted for 56% of Class I posts, the top-ranking civil service and public sector jobs.
That included 10% for women, as well as 30% for descendants of those who fought for Bangladesh's independence from Pakistan in 1971.
Another 16% was reserved for underprivileged regions and people with disabilities.
In 2018, after student protests, the then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina scrapped quotas.
In 2024, it was proposed to reinstate quotas, sparking student protests. That escalated into a mass uprising and Hasina was overthrown.
Today, 93% are filled on merit. Around 7% are for those related to freedom fighters and other smaller groups and there is no quota for women.
The Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC), which runs the recruitment examinations, has around 300,000 applicants each year for 2,500 to 3,000 Class I jobs.
Before the quota was scrapped in 2018, women accounted for up to 35% of recruits, including both quota and merit-based appointments.
That has dropped to 19%, according to figures from the last exam round.
A BPSC official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the body "finds the outcome uncomfortable," but that its "duty is limited to conducting the examination."
AKM Abdul Awal Majumdar, a former bureaucrat, backs merit-based recruitment but advocates coaching to help women compete.
"My female colleagues were unparalleled," he said.
The government elected in February also backs merit-based recruitment.
Md Abdul Bari, a public administration minister, described it as a "rational reform" in parliament.
But some officials fear the decline in female recruitment will become increasingly visible.
"At this moment, at least 21 women are leading 21 districts," said a female bureaucrat with 20 years of experience, speaking on condition of anonymity.
"In 10 years' time, there won't be this many women in the service."
The impact goes beyond the civil service.
Police data shows only 267 women out of 2,651 candidates qualified as constables this year.
Only six of the 184 candidates who qualified as police sub-inspectors were women. No women qualified as sergeants, compared with 96 men.
"We can't continue without them," a police officer said, noting every station has dedicated desks for women and children.
Bangladesh previously had 60% quotas for women in primary teaching positions. That has also ended.
Asif Shahan, a Dhaka University professor of Development Studies, said fewer women in government would impact policymaking.
"Their issues get reflected in policy," he told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The debate has split students.
Md Mazharul Islam, a Dhaka University students' union career advisor and a supporter of the opposition Jamaat-e-Islami, backs a merit system.
"Society was much more conservative before and girls were not allowed to pursue higher education," he said. "That has changed."
Philosophy student Adity Islam said abolishing the women's quota was wrong.
"We measured women across all walks of life with the yardstick of female students at Dhaka University," said Islam, who is involved in leftist politics.
"Cutting the quota for women would eventually impact the overall governance system. We have already seen that in some districts. So aspiring candidates in many other places will lose hope."

EU gives final green light to stricter rules for migrants, return hubs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:10:40 UTC
23:10:40 KST

Melike Pala
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The European Council on Thursday gave final approval to new rules aimed at strengthening the return of non-EU nationals who have no legal right to stay in the bloc.
The rules, which complement the EU's Pact on Migration and Asylum, include allowing member states to establish return hubs in third countries, according to an EU statement.
They outline procedures for returns and additional measures for people considered to pose a security risk.
Under the new framework, non-EU nationals subject to a return decision will be required to leave the member state concerned and cooperate with national authorities.
Failure to comply could result in sanctions, including reduced benefits and allowances granted under national law, the loss of incentives for voluntary return, financial penalties or criminal sanctions where provided for under national legislation.
The legislation also introduces a European Return Order, which will contain key elements of national return decisions and is intended to facilitate their recognition by authorities in other EU member states.
Mutual recognition of return decisions will initially remain voluntary.
The system will be reviewed three years after the rules enter into force, after which the European Commission may propose legislation to make recognition mandatory.
The new rules provide additional measures for non-EU nationals considered a security risk.
Member states may impose an indefinite entry ban where it is justified and proportionate to the security risk posed.
They may also detain such individuals for longer than 24 months under the conditions established by the regulation.
The legislation also allows member states to transfer people subject to return decisions to return hubs in non-EU countries.
Such arrangements will require an agreement or arrangement with the third country concerned.
The EU said these agreements may only be concluded with countries that respect international human rights standards and international law, including the principle of non-refoulement.
Unaccompanied minors are excluded from such return hub arrangements.

Wie Trumps Energieminister die EU zur Freigabe von Dieselreserven drängt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:10:33 UTC
23:10:33 KST

Wie Trumps Energieminister die EU zur Freigabe von Dieselreserven drängt
Mehrere EU-Staaten – darunter Deutschland – wurden von Chris Wright mit dem Angebot kontaktiert, entweder ihre Dieselreserven anzuzapfen, oder ein Exportverbot von US-Diesel zu riskieren.
U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright attends an announcement made by President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington on Sept. 28, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
BERLIN — Die Trump-Regierung hat europäische Regierungen aufgefordert, einen Großteil der strategischen Dieselreserven der EU freizugeben, um so die stark steigenden Kraftstoffkosten zu dämpfen. Das sagten vier Regierungsvertreter aus der EU und den USA gegenüber POLITICO.
Der von US-Energieminister Chris Wright vorgelegte Vorschlag wurde als Alternative zu der Drohung von Präsident Donald Trump präsentiert, ein pauschales Verbot für Dieselexporte aus den USA zu verhängen (POLITICO berichtete). Dem Vorschlag zufolge würden die EU-Regierungen über einen Zeitraum von 180 Tagen 120 Millionen Barrel Diesel aus ihren nationalen strategischen Reserven freigeben, wie ein Regierungsvertreter eines europäischen Landes gegenüber POLITICO erklärte.
Das würde laut Eurostat-Zahlen weit über ein Drittel der rund 315 Millionen Barrel Diesel ausmachen, die die EU-Länder im Juni dieses Jahres in Reserve hielten. Unter den EU-Ländern verfügen Deutschland, Frankreich, Italien, Spanien und Polen über die größten Dieselvorräte.
Advertisement
POLITICO hatte bereits am Dienstag berichtet, dass das Weiße Haus erwägt, die EU zu bitten, ihre Dieselreserven einzusetzen, um die weltweite Versorgung zu stärken und damit die Preise zu senken. Die Vereinigten Staaten hätten Berlin in dieser Angelegenheit bereits kontaktiert, hieß es am Donnerstag aus deutschen Regierungskreisen.
Die Bundesrepublik ist jedoch nur einer von mehreren EU-Staaten, an den sich die USA gewandt haben, heißt es von einer Person, die mit den Plänen der Trump-Regierung vertraut ist. So berichtet ein hochrangiger europäischer, für Energie zuständiger Regierungsbeamter eines großen EU-Landes, sein Land sei vergangene Woche bilateral in den USA angesprochen worden.
„Es war sehr hypothetisch: ‚Was halten Sie davon, wenn Europa einen Teil seiner Reserven freigibt, um die Preise zu senken und Druck auf das Angebot auszuüben?‘“, beschrieb der Beamte die Gespräche. Das könne auch dabei helfen, die Diskussion über ein Diesel-Exportverbot nicht weiterzuführen, soll es aus der US-Regierung geheißen haben. „Ich antwortete, das könnte die transatlantischen Beziehungen sehr belasten.“
Auch die britische Regierung befinde sich in „nach vorne gerichteten und offenen Gesprächen“ mit den USA, sagte ein Regierungsbeamter aus Großbritannien auf die Frage hin, ob sein Land ebenfalls angehalten worden sei, seine Dieselreserve anzuzapfen oder von einem Exportverbot betroffen zu sein.
US-Energieminister Wright lehnt – ebenso wie die US-amerikanische Öl- und Gasindustrie – ein Exportverbot für US-Diesel ab. Sein Vorschlag, dass EU-Länder Diesel aus ihren Reserven ausschütten, wird als Versuch gewertet, eine Alternative zu einem Exportstopp zu finden.
Auf einer Pressekonferenz am Donnerstag wollte eine EU-Kommissionssprecherin nicht bestätigen, ob die EU Wrights Anfrage erhalten habe. Sie erklärte jedoch, dass mögliche Freigaben von Lagerbeständen ausschließlich – und wie bereits im Sommer – über die Internationale Energieagentur (IEA) vereinbart würden. Die Kommission stehe in engem Kontakt mit den EU-Mitgliedstaaten und Washington, so die Sprecherin.
Advertisement
Unterdessen bestätigte US-Präsident Donald Trump am Mittwoch, dass ein von seiner Regierung geplantes Exportverbot für Diesel weiterhin im Raum stehe. „Ich denke darüber nach“, sagte Trump bei einer Veranstaltung im Oval Office. „Ich spreche viel mit [Energieminister] Chris [Wright] und [Innenminister] Doug [Burgum] darüber – sie glauben irgendwie, dass es dem Diesel helfen wird, aber es könnte die Preise für andere Dinge in die Höhe treiben.“
Trump wollte eine Beschränkung der Diesellieferungen nicht ausschließen. „Das ist etwas, worüber wir jeden Tag nachdenken und sprechen“, sagte er. „Aber es scheint einfach so, als hätte das negative Auswirkungen auf Benzin, sodass dessen Preis ein wenig steigen würde, während der Dieselpreis ein wenig sinken würde.“
Wright, der am Mittwoch mit Trump im Oval Office war, erklärte, die Regierung werde in Kürze Maßnahmen ankündigen, die darauf abzielen, die Dieselpreise zu senken. Auch Europa würde Maßnahmen ankündigen, um das Angebot auf dem Markt zu erhöhen, sagte er.
„Sie werden von unseren Partnern in Europa Ankündigungen über neue Diesellieferungen hören, die auf den Markt kommen und die Dieselpreise deutlich nach unten drücken werden“, sagte Wright.
Ben Lefebvre, James Bikales, und Charlie Cooper haben zu diesem Artikel beigetragen.Dieser Artikel erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO, und wurde von Johanna Sahlberg ins Deutsche editiert.

Russia’s Supercam S180 recon UAV successfully operates under attacks — company
Unknown

2026-10-01
14:07:52 UTC
23:07:52 KST

BAKU, October 1. /TASS/. Russia’s new high-speed reconnaissance unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) Supercam S180 is capable of conducting photographic reconnaissance in the conditions of jamming and attacks by FPV drones, Unmanned Systems Group Spokeswoman Yekaterina Zgirovskaya told reporters at the ADEX 2026 exhibition.
"The latest Russian high-speed reconnaissance UAV, the Supercam S180, is equipped with various systems that allow it to successfully conduct photographic reconnaissance and transmit intelligence data during flight even under jamming and attacks by interceptor drones," Zgirovskaya stated.
According to her, its high cruising speed and "afterburner" (brief acceleration) mode help it overcome such countermeasures. "The UAV’s autonomous flight, with positioning accuracy of up to 50 meters, is ensured by three complementary systems that operate without relying on GNSS signals: an inertial navigation system, an optical navigation system, and a local positioning system," she added.
Zgirovskaya specified that the approach of enemy interceptor drones is detected by the optical and radio detection system. "It alerts the operator to the danger, an evasive maneuver is performed automatically, and once the threat has disappeared, the Supercam S180 continues to carry out its mission," she said.
The ADEX 2026 International Defense Exhibition is being held in Baku from September 30 to October 2.

Ukraine called on the U.S. to impose sanctions for supporting the &quot;Rassvet&quot; network - Russia&apos;s equivalent of Starlink
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

17:07:43 EEST
23:07:43 KST

Ukraine called on the U.S. to impose sanctions for supporting the "Rassvet" network - Russia's equivalent of Starlink
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv is asking Washington to impose sanctions against participants in Russia's "Rassvet" satellite network. Ukraine also needs 300 Patriot missiles by winter.
Ukraine is calling on the United States to impose sanctions on several Russian organizations that, according to its information, are helping develop Moscow’s "Rassvet" satellite network, a national alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink. Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in the United States, Denys Sienik, made the statement on September 30, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Sienik said that Russia is rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network, stating that its goal of beginning operations in 2027 would pose serious risks to Ukraine.
"If they launch Rassvet by the end of 2026, they will be able to strike Ukrainian targets in real time on our territory," Sienik said, adding that he would share with the U.S. government and Congress details about the companies and individuals involved in facilitating Rassvet.
"If these organizations are not sanctioned, this will effectively make the program possible for Russia, and it will be a game changer," Sienik said.
He also emphasized Ukraine’s urgent need for approximately 300 additional Patriot interceptor missiles by winter, saying that Russia produces more than 100 ballistic missiles per month.
The U.S. Treasury Department did not comment on Ukraine’s call for new sanctions.
Russia plans to begin operating Rassvet, a scaled-down version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system, in 2027, Alexei Shelobkov, CEO of Iks Holding, the company developing the service, said in June. The company launched its first 16 low-Earth-orbit satellites in March and plans to reach 900 within several years.
SpaceX currently has more than 10,000 satellites in orbit. Starlink is banned in Russia, and use of its equipment is punishable by fines.
Western countries have targeted the infrastructure behind Russia’s space communications efforts, but gaps remain. Kyiv is pressing Washington to expand sanctions against a broader group of Russian companies and individuals, the publication reports.
Ukraine has insisted on access to expanded Starlink satellite internet coverage so that it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located on Russian territory; this position was supported last week by Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
Sienik also questioned the lack of a U.S. response when Russian strikes hit American companies in Ukraine.
"Washington remained silent when it came to sending a message to Moscow after American companies in Ukraine were affected, while officials were even reluctant to name the companies that were hit," he said.
Last week, Sienik published details about American companies affected by Russian missiles in Ukraine, including offices of Boeing, Flex, and Bunge. A Coca-Cola facility in Kyiv region was also hit in September, as was a logistics facility serving McDonald’s, he said in his post on X.
"This is not accidental; Russia knows what it is doing when it attacks ordinary businesses operating in Ukraine that are backed by American investment and serve civilian needs," he wrote.
"While Russia must be deprived of the ability to cause more deaths and destruction through strong sanctions, Ukraine must have sufficient air-defense capabilities to protect itself and also ensure the safety of American businesses operating and investing in Ukraine," the diplomat stated.

For a second time in a week, the White House has unilaterally removed CNN from its assignment as the primary television pool representative covering Donald Trump.

Focus on Saada: Yemen's Houthis amass forces near Saudi border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:06:49 UTC
23:06:49 KST

Breadcrumb
Saada becomes focus of Yemen war as Houthis amass forces near Saudi border
Attention is turning to Saada province, the Houthi stronghold in northernmost Yemen, as the group steps up its military mobilisation and moves weapons and equipment to areas bordering Saudi Arabia.
These movements, confirmed by military and local sources to The New Arab, put the possibility a border confrontation, particularly as the group increases its threats against Saudi Arabia.
Saada has featured prominently in recent military statements by Majed Al-Nazili, spokesman for the armed forces affiliated with the internationally recognised government.
He included the Kataf and Al-Buqaa front and the Alab axis among the operations. These are important fronts because of their location along the Saudi border. Kataf and Al-Buqaa districts, the largest district in Saada by area, stretch along the Najran region and contain the Al-Buqaa border crossing. The Alab axis is located in Baqim district on the border north of Saada and is one of the advanced border fronts.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree referred to Saudi strikes on Saada, while government military sources said the group was preparing to seek a breakthrough across the border.
A government military source familiar with the situation told The New Arab that the Houthis "are preparing for a confrontation on the border" with Saudi Arabia and are heavily mobilising for it, adding: "A border war is coming; it is only a matter of time."
The source said the group is seeking to launch an attack that would allow it to make an incursion into Saudi territory.
The source's account corresponds with information from other military and local sources in Saada, who told TNA that the Houthis have stepped up the moving fighters, weapons and equipment to border areas in recent days.
According to the government source, these transfers go beyond reinforcing the group's defensive positions and amount to preparations for an offensive, at a time when its forces and positions are being targeted on several fronts.
In this context, posts on Al Masirah, the Houthi's affiliated channel, two days ago included reports of strikes on the districts of Sahar, Al-Safra, Al-Dhahir and Majz, alongside rocket fire on Sahar.
The channel had reported the previous day that two strikes hit Al-Dhahir and that four rockets targeted eastern Saada city.
These areas are spread between the border strip, the vicinity of Saada provincial centre and routes connecting to the border—Al-Dhahir lies on the Saudi border, Al-Safra extends north to the border with Najran, Sahar surrounds Saada city and includes its outskirts, and Majz is connected to the road leading to Baqim and the Alab border crossing.
This distribution gives the strikes significance beyond pressure on the front lines, extending to pressure on the group's positions deep inside the province and areas connecting them to the border, and could disrupt the movement of reinforcements and supplies.
Saada, as the focus
Al-Nazili announced for the first time since the start of the latest escalation that Saada fronts were included in the operations.
In a statement posted on his account on X on 27 September, he said the forces had carried out 756 targeting operations during the previous 72 hours, covering Kataf and Al-Buqaa and the Alab axis, alongside the fronts in Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda and Lahj and Taiz, using air forces, drones, snipers, field artillery and rocket launchers.
Al-Nazili reiterated in a statement on 28 September that Saada fronts were included in the operations, announcing 356 operations during the previous 24 hours, and also included the coast, Haradh and Al-Tuwal in neighbouring Hajjah, as well as other fronts.
He said the operations overall targeted Houthi reinforcements and military capabilities, destroying command and control centres, weapons depots, artillery and vehicles.
A military source in government forces in the border areas told TNA, in response to a question on 26 September, that the latest escalation had also included Saada.
However, operations there were less intense at the time than on the active fronts in Taiz, Marib, Hodeidah and Al-Jawf, the source said.
The source explained that the Yemeni air force launches occasional strikes against Houthi reinforcements and targets in Saada districts, alongside artillery, drone and rocket-launcher operations.
The succession of reports coming from Saada reflects the province's growing presence in the military scene.
Targeting reinforcements, depots and vehicles has gained additional importance in light of the mobilisation because it could disrupt Houthi preparations for a potential confrontation on the border, and pressures Saada's role in mobilising fighters and supplying the group's other fronts with fighters and equipment.
The current mobilisation recalls the experience of the border fronts after Operation Decisive Storm began on 26 March 2015, when the Saudi-led coalition intervened at the request of then-President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi.
In May that year, Houthi shelling extended to Najran and Jizan, turning the border into a confrontation zone and forcing Saudi Arabia to deal with a direct threat to its border areas.
The Houthis and their allies announced incursions at the time into positions inside Saudi territory and released footage they claimed showed breaches they had carried out there.
That precedent shows how a border incursion can provide a propaganda gain and a tool for putting pressure on Riyadh, even if the group's ability to hold territory is limited by military standards.
The group is betting more on the political and security impact of an incursion than on maintaining long-term control.
Houthi rhetoric
The current mobilisation has coincided with an explicit escalation in the group's rhetoric, as Houthi media outlets have recently intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The presenter of an Al Masirah report on 27 September, whose political and mobilisation-focused rhetoric reflects the group's positions and the messages it seeks to convey, spoke of moving from "restraint to deterrence through attack".
The presenter threatened to put Riyadh into "a state of unprecedented all-out war" and hinted at options that "had remained ruled out but are now possible, painful and decisive", without specifying the nature of these options.
Since the start of the latest round of fighting on 10 September, the Houthis have justified their attacks by referring to what they describe as the "Saudi blockade", citing airports and ports and what they said were restrictions on movement.
They later added almost daily accusations against Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on Yemeni provinces and targeting civilians.
This sequence allows the group to present any expansion of the confrontation as a response to Riyadh.
The Al Masirah account on Telegram published more than 90 breaking news reports about Saada during the past month, most attributed to its correspondent in the province.
They included reports of civilian injuries, including five shoppers in the Al Thabet area of Qatabir on 24 September, according to the channel.
Saree continued to include Saada in his statements, announcing on 28 September that 38 airstrikes and rocket strikes had taken place in Saada, Taiz and Hajjah.
The following day, he reported 35 strikes on Saada, Taiz, Al-Jawf, Amran and Hodeidah, adding that the strikes had hit telecommunications networks, schools and other civilian sites.
He raised his cumulative figure to 1,158 missiles since the start of the escalation across various provinces.
While the Houthis attribute these strikes to Saudi Arabia, government forces attribute the announced operations to their own forces.
The military source in the border areas said in a statement on 26 September that the Houthis combine government forces' operations with limited artillery strikes carried out by Saudi border guards against smuggling operations, then attribute them all to the kingdom.
Military and local sources said artillery fire linked to smuggling routes is known to residents and that its frequency had not increased recently, according to their monitoring.
The motives behind Houthi pressure on Saudi Arabia go beyond battlefield needs to the group's efforts to push Riyadh towards a direct agreement that would consolidate its position and limit support for the Yemeni government by raising the cost of confrontation for Saudi Arabia.
These calculations are specific to the group but overlap with Iranian interests in putting pressure on Riyadh and energy and trade routes in order to ease the pressure of the US war on Iran, according to observers.
While Yemeni army operations are putting pressure on Houthi positions and reinforcements in Saada, the mobilisation towards the border gives the group's threats a military dimension.
If these preparations turn into an attack on Saudi territory, according to the scenario anticipated by military sources, the group may be betting on an incursion that imposes a direct security and political cost on Riyadh and strengthens its ability to extract concessions from it, even if its ability to hold territory remains limited.

Japan's premier says stronger economy to help maintain confidence in yen

14:06:43 UTC
23:06:43 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Thursday that strengthening the economy and improving international competitiveness would help maintain confidence in the yen following coordinated Japanese-US intervention to support the currency.
Speaking to Nippon Television, Takaichi said her government would expand domestic investment to strengthen supply capacity and raise potential growth.
“Economic and fiscal policy is not conducted for the purpose of steering exchange rates,” she said.
“I believe strengthening Japan’s international competitiveness through these efforts will ultimately also help maintain confidence in the yen.”
Takaichi confirmed that US President Donald Trump raised concerns about yen weakness during their Sept. 22 meeting in New York.
“The other side said that the weak yen was making trade difficult for the United States. In response, I said, strictly as a general observation, that the yen’s undervaluation is a problem,” she said.
Japan’s Finance Ministry purchased yen in coordination with the US Treasury on July 31 to counter excessive volatility and disorderly currency movements, according to a ministry statement.
Japan spent 15.4 trillion yen ($97.45 billion) on foreign exchange intervention between July 30 and Aug. 26, ministry data showed. No intervention was recorded between Aug. 27 and Sept. 28.
Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reaffirmed during a Sept. 25 call that the yen’s undervaluation was a concern and pledged closer cooperation.
Addressing fiscal concerns, Takaichi pledged to control annual government bond issuance and secure funding while pursuing spending consistent with steadily lowering Japan’s debt-to-GDP ratio.
She said ministries’ budget requests would not automatically become next year’s budget, promising to review spending and revenue and prioritize effective policies before year-end.

Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
15:05:55 BST
23:05:55 KST

Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
- Published
An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.
Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.
His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.
Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.
Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.
Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.
Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.
"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."
Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.
He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.
The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.
He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.
A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said.
It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world.
Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said.
The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro.
All five remain at large, the Justice Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

Latvia Arrests Two Accused of Collecting NATO Intelligence for Russia’s GRU
Latvia detained two citizens suspected of collecting intelligence on the country’s defense sector for Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, Latvia’s State Security Service reported on September 30.
The pair were arrested on June 28 in cooperation with Latvia’s Military Intelligence and Security Service. A criminal case had been opened the previous day over the alleged collection and transfer of non-public information to a foreign intelligence service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian hybrid operations across Europe have included sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, drone incursions, disinformation, and surveillance of military and critical infrastructure. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how these tactics have intensified across the continent, often using recruited local operatives while remaining below the threshold of conventional war.
Investigators determined that the suspects gathered and passed information to the GRU about Latvia’s defense system, NATO-allied activity, and different forms of support for Ukraine, the State Security Service noted.

The pair are additionally suspected of carrying out activities intended to support potential intelligence and sabotage groups operating inside Latvia.

Both suspects remain in custody while Latvia’s State Security Service and Military Intelligence and Security Service continue the investigation.
Lithuania recently moved to restrict Russian and Belarusian citizens from buying property near strategically important sites, including those with valid residence permits. Similar restrictions have already been introduced in Latvia and Finland, while Estonia is preparing its own measures.

Australia as an AI Middle Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:05:00 UTC
23:05:00 KST

Australia’s role in the frontier world of artificial intelligence was the focus in Canberra last month, with two events bringing together hundreds of defense, diplomacy, development, and industry experts. The Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) gathered the national security and defense community for an AI Masterclass on September 14. The next day, the Development Intelligence Lab’s Situation 2026 explored how AI can solve Indo-Pacific development challenges.
The events revealed a country grappling with what it means to be a middle power in the age of AI. As ClearAI founder Jisoo Kim put it, at a time when AI is developing at breakneck speed and reordering economies and societies, “Where in this ecosystem, where in this global economy is Australia going to sit?”
Judging from opinion polling, many Australians would probably prefer that AI had never been invented. But now that the cat is out of the bag, Australia needs to think about what it means for its security and prosperity, and the risks and opportunities it brings.
As a middle power, with a range of assets and resources, Australia is not powerless in the face of these changes. It has some capacity to influence the new world that AI is making.
Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton addressed this openly. Asking how middle powers manage AI, he identified four plays: alignment with a superpower, leverage in the value chain, competition through different models and capabilities, and sovereign capability. Charlton stated that Australia is pursuing all four simultaneously.
Shadow Minister for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie broadly agreed, particularly emphasizing the U.S. relationship as Australia’s “line to sovereignty.” Hastie suggested using Australia’s relationships in Washington to encourage a hyperscaler to invest in Australia.
Without data centers, frontier labs, and talent, Australia remains dependent on what comes through submarine cables, and this may make Australia a “supplicant state” – with Hastie using the analogy of the nuclear race, where once the U.S. convinced Australia to withdraw, it has been reliant on Washington ever since. He gave a sense of the stakes for Australia: countries with AI will pull ahead and Australia will fall further behind.
According to Minister for Industry and Innovation Tim Ayres, the government’s “aim is not to do everything, but to make ourselves the indispensable country.” That is, to find what Australia can excel at in this new ecosystem and make it the country’s comparative advantage.
Australia brings assets in policy expertise, talent, and trust. Ayres also highlighted capabilities in chip packaging, quantum computing, and specialized datasets, alongside institutional advantages such as firms and unions working together in the national interest.
Throughout the discussions, there were multiple calls for Australia to work with other countries including the United Kingdom, Canada, Japan, South Korea, and India.
As the American Enterprise Institute’s Ryan Fedasiuk put it, middle powers have a path forward if they “conceive of AI as a global megaproject which everyone can contribute to.” Importantly, “Sovereignty doesn’t mean autarky. Sovereignty means being able to choose your own dependencies rather than having them foisted on you.”
Aditya Maheshwari of the Indian Institute of Management Indore outlined how middle powers could energize their own ecosystems through talent, research, joint projects, and shared computing facilities, rather than competing with the United States and China on frontier models.
Australia also has considerable opportunities to shape international standards. Australian Signals Directorate Director-General Abigail Bradshaw argued that having a place in the AI industry strengthens Australia’s sovereignty and gives it a voice in global standards.
Australian AI Safety Institute head Kate Conroy highlighted Australia’s ability to punch above its weight internationally, drawing on its experience in developing standards adopted globally.
Australia’s Ambassador for Cyber Affairs and Critical Technology, Jessica Hunter, argued that Australia has the assets, relationships, and agency to be a shaper of the AI world rather than merely a consumer.
It’s interesting that this proactivity is being actively encouraged by frontier labs, including OpenAI Vice President Ann O’Leary and Anthropic Special Envoy and former U.S Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich.
An important element of being an AI middle power is to think about how it contributes to development outcomes. As Minister for International Development Anne Aly put it, “The value of technologies lies in the way that people’s lives are improved.” The challenge is “to ensure the benefits of emerging technologies are shared widely rather than used to widen inequalities.”
Through this lens, Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sponsored a competition on what Indo-Pacific development challenge AI could solve in the next five years, gathering more than 100 proposals. From disaster warning systems to healthcare and protecting Pacific maritime zones, there are countless ways Australia can use AI to contribute as a development partner.
Times of change are generally good for middle powers, enabling them to play an entrepreneurial role. These discussions demonstrated the benefits of Australia inserting itself into the AI economy, shaping global safety standards and enabling positive diffusion of technology across the region.

Russian Drone Hits Kyiv Nuclear Research Institute Housing VVR-M Reactor
A Russian drone struck the grounds of Ukraine’s Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv, where the VVR-M research reactor is located, Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate reported on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the regulator, citing the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the strike occurred at 6:18 p.m. local time on September 30. A fire broke out following the attack but was quickly extinguished, with no casualties reported.
The reactor itself and systems important to its safety were not damaged. Authorities recorded no changes in radiation levels, which remained within the natural background range of 0.16 to 0.20 microsieverts per hour.
An investigation into the incident is ongoing, while specialists continue to assess the extent of the damage caused by the strike.
The VVR-M reactor has remained shut down since February 2022 as a precaution aimed at reducing radiation risks. Its core has been fully unloaded, and operations at the facility are currently limited to routine maintenance of systems important to nuclear safety.
“Thus, the drone strike on the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research constitutes an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility used exclusively for scientific and research purposes. It is yet another cynical disregard by Russia for internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety and constitutes a war crime,” the regulator concluded.
The incident follows another recent Russian strike on a facility belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. On September 28, a Russian drone hit an academy building in central Kyiv, sparking a fire in the capital’s Shevchenkivskyi district.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said emergency crews were deployed to extinguish the blaze and search for people who may have been inside the building.

SpaceX Crew-13 Takes Canadian Astronaut With Ukrainian Roots on His First Flight to Space
SpaceX is set to launch its Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on October 1, carrying four astronauts, including Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, whose family roots trace back to western Ukraine, according to TSN.
The mission is scheduled to lift off aboard a Crew Dragon spacecraft on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida, at 6:10 p.m. Kyiv time. It will mark Kutryk’s first flight to space.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Crew-13 team will be commanded by NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, with fellow NASA astronaut Luke Delaney serving as pilot. Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergei Teteryatnikov will serve as mission specialists.
During their approximately six-month stay aboard the ISS, the crew will conduct a series of scientific experiments and technology demonstrations, TSN reported. Research will include studying how spaceflight affects blood circulation and clotting, examining stem cells for potential applications related to cardiovascular disease and Parkinson’s disease, and growing plants to support future long-duration missions.
NASA also stated that the crew would conduct scientific research and technology demonstrations aimed at preparing humans for future missions to the Moon and Mars while also contributing to research with potential benefits for people on Earth.
Crew-13 is part of NASA’s Commercial Crew Program, under which SpaceX conducts crewed missions to the ISS. The launch was initially scheduled for September 12 but was postponed after a leak was detected in the Dragon spacecraft’s attitude-control propulsion system.
Following its arrival at the ISS, Crew-13 will join the station’s 75th long-duration expedition. The crew is expected to return to Earth approximately six months after launch.
The mission comes as Ukraine has also reported space-related activities during the full-scale war. Ukrainian lawmaker Fedir Venislavskyi, who chairs the parliamentary subcommittee on state security and defense, told RBC-Ukraine on April 13 that Ukraine’s military intelligence had conducted two successful rocket launches into space since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
According to Venislavskyi, military intelligence units successfully sent rocket carriers beyond Earth’s atmosphere on two occasions during the full-scale war.

A Shahed With “Whiskers” Just Appeared in Ukraine—And They Have a Very Specific Purpose
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:04:27 UTC
23:04:27 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
A Shahed With “Whiskers” Just Appeared in Ukraine—And They Have a Very Specific Purpose
Russia appears to be turning its jet-powered Shahed drones into specialized weapons for hunting Ukraine’s power grid, adding unusual whisker-like rods designed to trigger the warhead when the drone touches something as thin as a high-voltage cable.
The previously unseen modification was highlighted by Defence Blog on October 1 after Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko published footage of the drone.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The rods extend forward from the nose of the aircraft and appear to function as contact triggers, allowing the warhead to detonate the instant they touch a wire.
“And this is a whiskered Shahed with a specialized warhead for attacks on high-voltage power lines. Most likely the whiskers were added to close a contact and initiate the warhead when hitting small targets such as power lines,” Sternenko wrote.
According to Defence Blog, a similar configuration has been observed at another location, suggesting the modification may not be limited to a single experimental drone.
The reasoning behind the design is straightforward. A conventional impact fuse works best when the drone hits a solid object. A power cable, however, presents an unusually difficult target: it is thin, suspended in open space and may simply be clipped by the aircraft without producing the kind of impact needed to detonate the warhead.
A transmission tower poses a similar challenge because much of the structure consists of open latticework.
The forward-projecting rods effectively make the drone’s contact area much larger, allowing a cable to trigger the weapon before the fuselage passes through it.
And the “whiskers” appear to be only one part of a broader Russian effort to adapt jet-powered drones specifically for Ukraine’s electricity network.
A day earlier, presidential defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov reported that Russia had used a specialized shaped-charge cutting warhead, known as KRSN, on a jet-powered drone for the first time.
The payload is designed not primarily to create a large blast, but to cut through strong metal structures.
According to Beskrestnov, the KRSN consists of a 40-kilogram, or 88-pound, main charge accompanied by four additional strike modules.
That makes it particularly suited for severing the steel legs of high-voltage transmission towers or structural elements of bridges.
Earlier, reports emerged that nearly 100 foreign-made parts have been recovered from jet-powered strike drones used during attacks on Kyiv and other regions, according to Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine’s presidential commissioner for sanctions policy.
The identified parts include hardware produced in the United States, China, Taiwan, European countries, Germany, and Japan.
