HIV prevention drug hailed as breakthrough, but who gets access?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:54:50 UTC
22:54:50 KST

HIV prevention drug hailed as breakthrough, but who gets access?
Lenacapavir, a twice-a-year injection could transform HIV prevention, but it will not be available to all.
A medicine injected just twice a year could transform the fight against HIV.
In a 2024 clinical trial involving more than 2,000 young women in South Africa and Uganda, no participants who received lenacapavir contracted HIV.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4An AIDS-free generation is within reach, but not guaranteed
- list 2 of 4US funding cuts deal blow to global HIV treatment: Report
- list 3 of 4In Senegal, a mother’s ordeal exposes a health system under strain
- list 4 of 4It’s the ‘closest thing to an HIV vaccine’, but who gets access?
Developed by United States pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences, the injectable drug can be used to prevent HIV.
“It’s the most innovative tool that has reached the HIV arena for the last decade, because it’s the closest we have [to] a vaccine,” Carlota Baptista da Silva, global HIV lead at Doctors Without Borders (known by its French initials, MSF), told Al Jazeera.
The World Health Organization has recommended the long-acting injectable as an additional form of pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP – medicine to reduce the risk of getting HIV.
But the arrival of the drug comes at a challenging juncture in the global fight against HIV.
International funding for HIV fell 18 percent in 2025, to $7.3bn, its lowest level in nearly two decades, according to the United Nations programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS). The squeeze has already hit prevention programmes: The number of people receiving medicine to reduce risk fell from 1.4 million in 2024 to 1.1 million in 2025.
That makes the arrival of a highly effective, twice-yearly prevention option significant. The question of who can access it is now more urgent.
For MSF, the scientific question has largely been answered: lenacapavir can prevent HIV with remarkable efficacy.
The fight now is whether the rules governing manufacture, price and supply will allow that scientific breakthrough to reach the people who need it.
Why some countries are excluded
In the United States, lenacapavir costs about $28,000 per person annually. Generic versions are expected to cost about $40 a year.
A generic version is a copy of the original drug made by another manufacturer after the patent holder licenses the technology. It contains the same active ingredient, but it can be produced and sold at a much lower price.
In June 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved lenacapavir for HIV prevention, giving people the option of an injection twice a year. But in several low- and middle-income countries, access to cheaper versions is not expected at scale until 2027.
Gilead is supplying its own version of lenacapavir at no profit for programmes supported by the Global Fund and the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), with rollouts under way in countries including South Africa, Kenya, Zambia, Nigeria and Eswatini.
These are not the cheaper generic versions expected to cost about $40 per person a year. Gilead has licensed six manufacturers to produce those, with large-scale generic rollout expected in 2027.
At least 26 middle-income countries are excluded from Gilead’s generics agreement, MSF says, including countries with rising HIV infections and some that helped test the drug. Among them are Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Peru.
“People should not really help generate the evidence for breakthrough medicine and then find that their country is excluded from affordable generic access,” da Silva said.
According to MSF, countries excluded from the licence accounted for close to 23 percent of new HIV infections globally in 2023.
Gilead has since announced a separate agreement with the Pan American Health Organization, creating an access pathway for 14 Latin American and Caribbean countries outside its generic licensing territory, including Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Peru.
MSF argues that leaves those countries dependent on Gilead rather than able to automatically buy the cheaper generics.
MSF says it still cannot buy the drug
For more than a year, MSF says it has sought permission to purchase lenacapavir directly from Gilead for its medical programmes, without demanding a discounted price.
“Despite those requests, Gilead has not allowed MSF to purchase this medicine directly,” da Silva said.
That matters particularly in humanitarian emergencies, she argues. People displaced by conflict or disaster may struggle to take a prevention pill every day, while sexual violence and other vulnerabilities can increase the risk of HIV.
Daily PrEP pills are already available as an alternative to the injection. But unlike lenacapavir, they need to be taken consistently to provide protection. An injection offering six months of protection could be particularly valuable.
“People living through conflict [and] humanitarian crises cannot be the last in line for medical innovation,” da Silva said.
Gilead declined Al Jazeera’s request for an interview due to scheduling constraints. In its emailed statement, it said its access strategy combines no-profit supplies, royalty-free licensing and regional agreements. It didn’t reply to questions about why it won’t sell its drug to MSF, or why certain countries were excluded from its generics agreement.
The company plans to provide enough lenacapavir for up to three million people through 2028 as generic manufacturers scale up production, with large-scale generic rollout expected in 2027.
MSF says that is nowhere near the scale required, pointing to projections that close to 20 million people worldwide need access to PrEP to substantially reduce new HIV infections. That includes all forms of PrEP, not just lenacapavir.
But countries left outside Gilead’s generic licensing deal may have another option.
Can governments bypass the patent barriers?
World Trade Organization (WTO) rules allow governments, in some cases, to bypass a drug company’s patent so cheaper versions of a medicine can be made or imported without the company’s permission.
They can also authorise government use of patents and challenge patents they consider weak or unjustified. The 2001 Doha Declaration affirmed WTO members’ right to use such safeguards to protect public health.
Brazil has used them before in the fight against HIV. In 2007, after negotiations with pharmaceutical company Merck over the price of the HIV drug efavirenz failed, Brazil issued a compulsory licence allowing it to access cheaper generic versions of the medicine.
Nearly two decades later, activists are urging Brazil to consider using those powers again for lenacapavir if patent barriers prevent affordable generic access.
MSF says governments excluded from Gilead’s licence could consider those same legal safeguards for lenacapavir, including compulsory licensing, government-use authorisations and challenges to patents.
It is also calling on Gilead to ensure its agreements with generic manufacturers do not prevent them from supplying countries where patent barriers have been removed through such measures.
For MSF, the stakes go beyond lenacapavir. The way the drug is made available could determine whether one of the greatest advances in HIV prevention in decades reaches people based on need, rather than where they live or what their health systems can afford.
“For a humanitarian medical organisation, we should not have to spend more than a year trying to find a way to buy a WHO-recommended medicine,” da Silva said.

Denmark happy with Greenland deal but wary Trump could change course: Lawmaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:54:17 UTC
22:54:17 KST

- NATO can play a much bigger part in defending and surveillance of Greenland, he says
- Major opposition parties in Denmark's parliament, the Folketing, have broadly supported the deal
Denmark is "happy and relaxed" with the newly signed Greenland agreement with the US, but remains aware that circumstances could shift when dealing with President Donald Trump, a senior Danish lawmaker said.
“We are very happy and relaxed but we are very much aware that things can change when it comes to dealing with Trump," Karsten Honge told Anadolu.
“It is a good deal but as long as President Trump abides by it," he added.
Honge, chair of the Danish parliament's Foreign Policy Committee, was in New York as part of the Danish prime minister's delegation to last week's UN General Assembly. He was also present at the signing of the agreement on the sidelines of the gathering.
The agreement, signed in late September by the US, Denmark and Greenland, updates a 1951 defense pact and expands the US military presence in Greenland, while also strengthening NATO's role in Arctic security.
It came after months of tensions sparked by Trump's repeated calls for US control or ownership of Greenland.
The lawmaker said that the Danish delegation is proud of the Greenland agreement as it shows that “small states like Denmark and Greenland could match the US when it comes to negotiations.”
The Kingdom of Denmark (Danish Realm), consists of Denmark, Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
Denmark is the sovereign state, while Greenland and the Faroe Islands are self-governing parts of the Realm, each with its own parliament and government and extensive authority over domestic matters. 
Greenland has had self-government since 2009 but Denmark retains responsibility for areas such as foreign policy, defense and security.
 
Military bases and NATO role
The Danish lawmaker said that the most important part in the agreement is that the sovereignty of Denmark and Greenland remains untouched.
“The other very important part is that now NATO can play a much bigger part in defending and surveillance of Greenland. It is now a written agreement that it is in the interest of the US, Denmark, Greenland and NATO and world peace that we have to match Russia and China,” he said.
On US military bases in Greenland, he said the new agreement does not create a US military presence from scratch.
US military presence in Greenland dates back to 1951, when Denmark and the US signed the Greenland Defense Agreement, allowing Washington to maintain three main bases — Thule, Narsarsuaq and Sondrestrom — and establish additional “defense areas” if NATO deemed necessary.
The US later closed all its bases in Greenland except Thule, now known as Pituffik Space Base. In 2004, the Igaliku Agreement amended the 1951 pact and gave Greenland greater influence over matters concerning the base.
The latest agreement allows the US to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik and establish additional defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig.
 
Greater say in economic matters
The latest deal with Trump also gives Washington greater control over Greenland, in particular sensitive foreign investments.
“Now the US has the right to oversee what kind of investments will happen in Greenland," Honge said.
He said the agreement introduces US screening of companies and countries seeking to invest in Greenland’s mining sector, including provisions barring US adversaries from establishing a military presence on the island.
 
Broad support from opposition
Major opposition parties in Denmark's parliament, the Folketing, have broadly supported the deal.
Denmark's Liberal Party's (Venstre) leader Troels Lund Poulsen called it "an exceptionally good agreement” and a happy day for Greenland, Denmark and the Realm.
Conservative leader Mona Juul praised it in a Facebook post, crediting the diplomatic work behind it.
Denmark Democrats leader Inger Stojberg, a vocal critic of the government, also praised the deal for safeguarding Danish sovereignty and cementing NATO's presence.
The Danish People's Party was more guarded.
Leader Morten Messerschmidt said it remains "dangerous for a country like Denmark to submit to threats," a reference to his earlier criticism of the January working group. Days later he softened his tone, saying that he hopes it closes the chapter between Trump and Denmark.
The agreement will soon be put to vote in both Inatsisartut, Greenland's parliament, and the Folketing.
 
Thanking friendly nations
Honge gave credit to the countries who stood up for Denmark in the tense negotiation period with the US.
“Denmark succeeded in building a lot of alliances along with Greenland and in doing that European countries and Canada stood up and showed solidarity.
“That made a big impression in the public opinion in the US because now they say that it was not just Greenland and Denmark but countries like Canada, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom.
“If Trump had taken Greenland as he had threatened to do it would have been really dangerous for all small states,” he said.
On the months-long negotiations leading to the deal, he said: "All I can say is that it was tough work, it took a long time, and nobody knew where this would end.”
The negotiations began after a diplomatic crisis in January and continued for about eight months.
He said there were doubts about whether the negotiations would ultimately succeed. 
However, he noted that one positive development during the tense negotiations was that Denmark was able to successfully build alliances with a number of countries.
The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement on Sept. 22 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with the deal aimed at strengthening security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump said it gives the US “permanent control over security and all other needs” in Greenland, while Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen stressed that the agreement reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
The agreement also allows for consideration of a US Golden Dome missile defense system in Greenland, although Frederiksen said no decision had been made on its scope.

ynet Global to broadcast Awake Jerusalem live as Christian leaders from 51 nations gather in Israel

More than 550 Christian leaders from 51 nations have arrived in Israel for a major gathering of international faith leaders, culminating this week in Awake Jerusalem, a night of music, prayer and solidarity at Jerusalem’s Tower of David.
ynet Global will broadcast Awake Jerusalem live on October 3 on its website and social media channels, bringing the event to audiences in Israel and around the world.
The concert is part of a 10-day delegation organized by Eagles’ Wings and led by its founder and president, Bishop Robert Stearns. Taking place during Sukkot and in the days leading up to the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks, the visit brings Christian leaders, dignitaries and officials to Israel for meetings, briefings and encounters with Israelis directly affected by the past three years.
For Stearns, who has been coming to Israel since 1992, this visit feels markedly different.  “I feel that nationally there is a greater sense in the nation of dependence on God for help, and a spiritual component that has renewed,” he said on an interview ahead of the events. But he said the change he sees is not only spiritual. He has also noticed Israelis taking greater personal responsibility for explaining their country and experiences to the outside world.
Stearns recalled having lunch with three Israeli businessmen who had nothing to do with politics, yet each was thinking about what role he could play in Israel’s struggle over international public opinion. Israelis, he said, understand the military battles being fought by the IDF, but increasingly recognize another arena as well: what he describes as an “eighth front” - the battle over Israel’s story.  “I sense a tremendous level of personal responsibility that Israelis are taking for telling the story and being a ‘shaliach’, a messenger,” he said.
‘Come and see for themselves’
That idea lies at the heart of the Eagles’ Wings delegation.
Among those participating are senior Christian leaders whose churches and networks collectively reach tens of millions of people worldwide, including Bishop Dr. David A. Sobrepeña, founder and senior pastor of Word of Hope Christian Church in the Philippines; Rev. Ricardo Castillo Medina, general superintendent of the Assemblies of God in Costa Rica and president of the World Hispanic Assemblies of God; and Brazil’s Rev. Dr. Reinaldo dos Santos.
Delegations from Kenya and Nigeria are also participating. They include Kenya’s First Lady Rachel Ruto; Ogiame Atuwatse III and Olori Atuwatse III of Nigeria’s Warri Kingdom; and Nigeria’s Minister of Defence, Gen. Christopher Gwabin Musa.
Stearns said the delegation represents networks reaching some 100 million people globally. “We are here to pray. But to act,” he said. “We are not just here to sing. We are here to become educated, empowered, and go back to our nations.”
During their stay, delegates are scheduled to meet Israeli leaders, IDF and Foreign Ministry officials, faith leaders, returned hostages and bereaved families. Strategic briefings are also intended to give participants a deeper understanding of Israel’s security challenges and the impact of the past three years.
Stearns believes there is still a significant gap between the support Israel receives from evangelical Christians and Israelis’ understanding of that community. “There’s very little bridge of connection,” he said, noting that Israelis sometimes approach evangelical support with uncertainty or suspicion.
His answer is direct engagement. Eagles’ Wings says it has brought some 45,000 people to Israel over the years, including thousands of pastors and influencers. Stearns said that when participants are asked afterward about the most memorable part of their visit, the answer is often surprisingly simple: Shabbat.  “When we saw women lighting candles, fathers blessing sons and daughters, when we saw the phones go off, traffic die down, and the beauty and power of the simplicity of family and friends coming together,” he said, describing what visitors tell his organization.
Such experiences, he argues, can have more impact than political arguments. He recalled speaking recently with a German businessman visiting Israel for the first time. His reaction, Stearns said, was straightforward: “This place is nothing like the media says.”
“That’s just a human being experiencing the land,” Stearns said. “Israel tells its own story.”
Prayer - followed by action
Asked what prayer can accomplish at a time of war, division and rising antisemitism, Stearns said prayer without tangible action is insufficient. “Prayer is everything. And prayer must have with it action,” he said, citing the Bible’s teaching that “faith without action is dead.”
“We must pray, but we must become the answer to the prayer that we are praying.” For Stearns, that means participants returning home better equipped to speak about Israel, confront antisemitism and engage their own communities.
He also sees the current moment as an opportunity to deepen Christian-Jewish relations while acknowledging the real differences between the two faiths.  “We have genuine theological differences, and they should be respected, mutually,” he said. “But we are united in 95 percent in our view, and we must build this gesher for the sake of humanity, so there is a brighter future.”
Music from the Tower of David
That bridge will take a musical form on October 3. Awake Jerusalem will bring Christian artists from around the world to the Tower of David for an evening centered on Jerusalem, faith and solidarity with Israel.
According to Stearns, public interest was immediate. “We opened to sell tickets, and we sold out in four hours. Gone,” he said. The vision, he explained, is deliberately youthful and joyful, using music to rise “above the noise” at a moment dominated by conflict and political division.
“David was not only a warrior, he was also a musician,” Stearns said. “So the City of David should put the music” at the center. He hopes Awake Jerusalem will continue to grow, with ambitions for an even larger event at Sultan’s Pool next year.
Engaging younger Christians is becoming an increasingly important part of that effort. Stearns said Eagles’ Wings recently brought 100 college students to Israel, part of a broader attempt to expose a new generation to the country beyond what they encounter through social media, campus activism and international news coverage.
Many evangelical Christians grow up with a strong connection to the biblical Israel, he said, but often know far less about the complexities of the modern state and the conflict surrounding it.
Bringing them to Israel allows them to encounter that reality themselves. “You shape people’s views by telling stories,” Stearns said. “Israel and the land of Israel tell a story that the nations can learn from.”
For Stearns, the events of the coming days are part of something larger than a single delegation or concert. After more than three decades of bringing Christians to Israel, he believes the challenge now is turning affinity into meaningful relationships,  and relationships into action. “It’s time for tachles,” he said, using the Hebrew and Yiddish expression for getting down to practical matters. “We have to stand together shoulder to shoulder.”
And on October 3, that message will begin with music in the heart of Jerusalem.
ynet Global will broadcast Awake Jerusalem live from the Tower of David on October 3 on our website and across its social media channels.

UK PM Burnham says Iran likely behind RAF base incident: Is there evidence?
UK, US and Israeli officials point to Iranian involvement but remain tight-lipped on details.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK’s security services have “strong indications” of Iranian involvement in the incident at a British Royal Air Force (RAF) station near Fairford this week in which five men were arrested before they were released on bail.
The five British men were spotted near the airbase and arrested on Sunday on suspicion of “terrorism” and explosives offences, before they were released.

list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘Strong indications’ Iran linked to suspected UK airbase plot
- list 2 of 3Is Iran losing its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz?
- list 3 of 3Iran parades Shahed drones through capital
The United States has used the British base to carry out operations in various conflicts, including to deploy bombers in its war against Iran.
Iran has strongly denied any involvement with the airbase incident, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying British authorities are “barking up the wrong tree”.
So, what do we know about the incident, and is there evidence Iran played a role?
What happened at the airbase?
Authorities were alerted to suspicious activity near the base early Sunday morning, including three vans parked oddly and a group of hooded, masked men.
Police responded and arrested five British men in their early 20s in the nearby Whelford area, saying they were suspected of explosives offences. Counter Terrorism police later took over the probe and said the men were suspected of preparing “a terrorist act”.
The suspects were released on bail Monday, but remain subject to “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others,” according to the United Kingdom’s head of counter terrorism policing, Laurence Taylor.
On Tuesday, after three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said they had found no explosives in the vehicles that were parked the near the base, but had retrieved a “quantity of petrol”.
Who is linking the incident to Iran, and have they cited evidence?
Officials in the UK, the US and Israel have all pointed to Iran but offered no details.
Burnham on Wednesday spoke of “strong indications” of Iran’s involvement and said an “ongoing, complex and serious police investigation” is continuing.
However, the prime minister did not give any details on what the suspects were planning or why the UK thinks Iran was involved, saying only that he would “update people more in due course”.
In the US, President Donald Trump said the case “might be” Iran-linked and that the US had been keeping tabs on the suspects “for a long time”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the case “clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor”, without naming a specific state.
In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had forewarned the UK about a potential “Iranian-sponsored attack”.
How has Iran responded?
Iran has firmly denied involvement.
In a statement on Monday, Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” any attempts to link Iran to the individuals arrested near the airbase.
It said the spread of such “fabricated speculations” fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” and that Iran reserves the right to “take appropriate legal measures”.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the UK was “barking up the wrong tree” by pointing to potential Iranian involvement.
Why has the UK released the suspects on bail?
It is unclear. Under British “counterterrorism law”, police can hold suspects for up to two weeks before charging them. However, if authorities find little evidence to support their initial suspicion of “terrorism”, they would have far less time – usually 24 to 36 hours, said Chris Phillips, a former head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Security Office.
“If it’s not an actual terrorist attack, then the police don’t have anywhere near as long to keep them in custody,” said Phillips. “I think the police just need more time to do their enquiries.”
Andrew Silke, professor of criminology at Royal Holloway, University of London, said the suspects could have also been released on bail while under suspicion of “terrorism” if “authorities feel relatively confident that these individuals do not pose an imminent danger of either carrying out or organising a terrorist attack”, such as if they had “peripheral” or “unknowing involvement”.
Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University and a former senior Royal Air Force officer, said the bail release does not necessarily indicate that the “Iranian-involvement hypothesis has been rejected” but it does mean “police have judged that these individuals did not present any immediate danger”.
Taylor, the head of counter terrorism policing, said the men’s release on bail was an “investigative decision” based on “experience and careful considerations of policing powers.” He stressed that the men are bound by “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others” as the investigation into them continues.
But their release drew backlash in the US from Trump, who said British authorities “should not have done that”.
“How do you give bail to a terrorist?” Trump asked.
Iran’s Araghchi appeared to suggest that the suspects’ release supported Iran’s position that it was not involved.
“I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all,” wrote Araghchi in a post on X.
What questions about the case are still unanswered?
Questions remain about the circumstances in which authorities were initially alerted to suspicious activity near the base, the extent to which they believe the suspects are linked to Iran and what the suspects may have been planning.
According to the BBC, police received two early-morning calls on Sunday regarding suspicious vehicles near the base, the first of which the media understands was made by one of the suspects themselves.
The Times of London reported that police are looking into the suspect’s motives for making such a call, including “whether he got cold feet or whether it was part of the plan”.
Authorities are also probing whether the incident was a form of “surveillance, a ‘dry run’ to test security or a stunt to send a message to the British government”, reported The Times.
Meanwhile, police have suggested they are looking into whether the suspects could have been unwittingly acting on Iran’s behalf.
In an updated briefing on Tuesday, Taylor said officials were examining whether the activity could have been “committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”.
He also spoke more generally about the “increasing breadth and complexity” of threats facing the UK, saying threats often emerge first as small-scale criminal activity, “committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain”.
Phillips told Al Jazeera he believes the suspects could have been recruited online to carry out some type of malicious activity that falls short of a “terrorist attack”.
“It sounds as though these people have been paid online to do some naughty work”, such as “setting fire to something”, said Phillips.
He said both Russia and Iran have allegedly paid “stooges” to carry out such acts in recent years. “At first glance now, it seems that that may be the case, but time will tell,” Phillips added.
Royal Holloway’s Silke also said he believes the evidence suggests “a proxy explanation”.
“Certainly, there have been recent cases in Europe where individuals have been used unwittingly as proxies by foreign governments to carry out activities which have a hostile intent,” he said. “The UK authorities in this case may have assessed that something similar had happened here, and that the individuals involved had no inherent terrorist motivation themselves, but had been caught up unintentionally in a larger plot.”
Has Iran previously been accused of plots in the UK?
Yes. MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said in October 2025 that the agency had tracked “more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots” in the UK within a year.
McCallum alleged that Iran, along with Russia, has resorted to “ugly methods,” such as “surveillance, sabotage, arson or physical violence”.
British Security Minister Dan Jarvis has said Iran often uses criminal proxies to “obfuscate” its involvement in attacks, which have targeted Iranian dissidents and Jewish and Israeli people in the country.
In March this year, British police arrested four people on suspicion of helping Iran spy on the local Jewish community. The month after, police said they were probing possible Iran links to a series of arson attacks on Jewish targets in London.
In June, two Romanian men whom British prosecutors said had acted as proxies for Iran’s government were handed lengthy jail terms for stabbing a British journalist of Iranian origin who wrote for an Iranian media outlet critical of Iran’s government.
Iran’s government has repeatedly denied involvement in any illegal plots or attacks on British.

A new Libya is possible, but it needs economic reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:45:03 UTC
22:45:03 KST

Breadcrumb
A new Libya is possible, but it needs economic reform
Libya should be one of the most prosperous countries in the Mediterranean. It has Africa’s largest proven oil reserves, around 48 billion barrels, a relatively small population, and an enviable geographical position between Europe and Africa's rapidly growing markets.
Yet for many Libyans, the reality is very different. Living standards are under pressure, public services struggle to function, and young people increasingly look abroad for opportunities.
It is tempting to blame all this on the political turmoil that has engulfed Libya since 2011. Political division certainly makes the situation worse. But the roots of Libya’s economic problems go deeper.
For decades, the country has operated an economic model built on an overwhelming dependence on oil revenues and a political economy initially introduced by Muammar Gaddafi in the 1970s, when he nationalised private businesses and greatly expanded the state's role in the economy.
Libya has never properly reformed that model. It now needs to take steps to create a more modern, liberalised, Western-style economy.
Meanwhile, Libya remains heavily dependent on oil for its income, and equally reliant on imports. Despite its extraordinary oil reserves, years of political conflict, blockades and underinvestment have constrained production and investment. This leaves the country dangerously exposed to oil price fluctuations.
The consequences of perpetuating this economic model are particularly serious for younger Libyans. The state has invested in educating doctors, engineers and other professionals, only for many to conclude that their prospects are better overseas.
Libya is losing precisely the skills it needs to build a more productive economy in a 'brain drain'.
There is no easy solution. Libya will eventually have to confront the need for economic reform, including encouraging private enterprise. The real choice is whether that transition is carefully managed or whether an economic crisis eventually forces change on the country.
That cannot happen without political change. Libya’s competing governments and institutions did not create the underlying economic model, but they make reforming it more difficult. Tough decisions require institutions capable of making them and, crucially, carrying them through.
Greater decentralisation should be part of the answer too. Libya is a vast country. Trying to manage its political and economic life almost entirely from the centre has failed. Municipalities should have greater responsibility for decisions affecting their own areas.
Diversification is also essential. Libya has clear opportunities to extract more value from oil through refining and related industries, though it needs to be realistic about where its advantages lie. Water scarcity limits the potential for large-scale agriculture, while a small domestic market constrains some forms of manufacturing.
The greatest opportunity, however, may be trade. Libya sits in the centre of the Mediterranean, immediately south of Europe and on the northern edge of a continent of more than 1.5 billion people. Free trade zones along its borders with its North African and Sahel neighbours could encourage investment, commerce and employment.
Libya could become an important trading and logistics hub connecting Africa and Europe.
A more prosperous Libya could also provide employment for workers from neighbouring countries, support regional economies through wage remittances, and help address some of the economic pressures driving irregular migration towards Europe.
With a credible government, greater transparency and economic reform, Libya could look dramatically different within five years. The alternative is to keep managing decline until the existing system can no longer sustain itself.
Libya has the resources to become one of the Mediterranean’s new economic success stories. What it truly needs now is the political will and structures to use them properly.
Hamza M Bait Elmal is a diplomat and economist from Libya.

New “plant armor” more than triples strawberry yields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:43:15 UTC
22:43:15 KST

New “plant armor” more than triples strawberry yields
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- North Carolina State University
- Summary:
- A new protective fabric boosted strawberry yields by as much as 3.56 times while blocking insects and still allowing sunlight, rain, and airflow to reach the plants. Originally inspired by research on military clothing, Plant Armor could also help farms reduce pesticide and water use.
- Share:
A newly developed textile covering helped strawberry plants produce more than three times as much fruit in tunnel field trials, while showing no harmful effects on plant health. Researchers say the technology may also offer a way to reduce water use and reliance on pesticides in strawberry production.
The fabric, called Plant Armor, is designed to be placed directly over strawberry plants. Its three dimensional structure creates a barrier that keeps insects from reaching the plants, while the layered material still allows sunlight, rain, and air to pass through.
In tunnel field tests, strawberries protected by Plant Armor produced yields as much as 3.56 times higher than uncovered plants. The fabric did not reduce light availability or negatively affect relative humidity.
A Fabric That Protects Without Blocking Sunlight
"To produce fruit, plants need sunlight," said Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant at North Carolina State University and lead author of a paper on Plant Armor. "We expected that Plant Armor's seemingly opaque fabric would lead to an increase in vegetative biomass at the expense of fruiting -- because reduced sunlight would trigger a 'shade-avoidance' response, making the plant divert energy toward stem and leaf growth rather than fruit production. However, we found the fabric did not impede access to light at all, and fruit production increased significantly."
Researchers also found that Plant Armor created a steady warming effect throughout the three growing seasons. According to Olawuyi, that extra warmth helped covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier than plants grown without the textile.
"Plants require a certain amount of accumulated heat, calculated as 'growing degree-days,' to progress through developmental stages including fruiting. Our plant cover has proven to enhance these," Olawuyi said. "The plants were in a condition whereby the warmth they need to go through each phenological stage to their production was given to them optimally, and they produced far more than the uncovered plants."
Because Plant Armor physically prevents insects from feeding on the plants, Olawuyi said the technology could also reduce the amount of conventional pesticides needed in agricultural fields.
From Military Textiles to Strawberry Fields
The idea behind Plant Armor did not begin with farming. The technology emerged from research focused on making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites and improving comfort for soldiers wearing body armor.
That unexpected path from military clothing research to agriculture demonstrates the value of collaboration across scientific fields, said co-author R. Michael Roe, William Neal Reynolds Distinguished Professor at NC State.
"The path to Plant Armor started with trying to make a cloth to go on a soldier's chest to make body armor more comfortable," said Roe. "Then, through trial and error, we arrive at a product which could triple the output of strawberry farms here in North Carolina.
"We couldn't have predicted that when we started. Without all these people here doing research and following the science, we wouldn't have arrived at this product."
Study Details and Support
The paper, "Knitted 3-D, Porous Textile Cover to Enhance Strawberry Fruit Production and Prevent Insect Feeding," is published in the journal Agriculture. Co-authors include James Clothier, Matthew Bertone, Grayson Cave, Reuben Garshong, Andre West, Loganathan Ponnusamy and Clyde Sorenson of NC State University.
This project was supported by a grant from the North Carolina Agricultural Foundation (grant number AG00463770). The work was also supported by the Research Capacity Fund (HATCH), project award no. 02853, from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Institute of Food and Agriculture. The Plant Armor Gen 2 fabric studied in this paper was patented by North Carolina State University (US Patent No. 11,582,968 B2; 21 February 2023) and is licensed for commercial development by the University. This work was a collaborative project between the NC State College of Natural Resources, Wilson College of Textiles and College of Agriculture and Life Sciences.

Trump's Board of Peace: Can it deliver a future for Gaza?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:39:09 UTC
22:39:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump's Board of Peace: Can it deliver a future for Gaza?
Khan Younis - Nearly a year after a ceasefire halted the heaviest fighting in Gaza, Palestinian analysts say the recovery plan unveiled last week by the US-led Board of Peace will not make any progress before Israelis vote on 27 October.
Its fate, they argue, will depend largely on the next Israeli government and the positions it takes on Gaza, and still faces a series of political and security obstacles before it can move from paper to the ground.
The Board presented the six-month, $2.45 billion program on 23 September on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. It sets out 66 costed programs across six clusters: infrastructure, human development, economic acceleration, digital transformation, legal recovery, and peace and security.
Chaired by US President Donald Trump, the Board operates under a UN Security Council mandate adopted in November 2025. The program was drawn up under its supervision by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the Palestinian technocratic body meant to take over the Strip's daily affairs.
The plan hinges almost entirely on Hamas handing over its weapons and its control of Gaza to the new administration. Meanwhile, Israel's military still controls more than 60 percent of the territory.
Experts who spoke to The New Arab expect the plan to be amended and doubt it will be implemented in its current form or at the announced pace. Some believe its success depends on full Israeli approval.
Others describe it as a "major deception" intended to prolong Gaza's catastrophe and push its people to ask the world to let them emigrate.
Meanwhile, Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, has described three possible paths for the Gaza Strip. The Palestinian territory could remain in its current state, Israel could expand its military operations and reoccupy it, or the parties could implement the Board's roadmap.
He warned that failure to move forward could make a two-state solution practically impossible.
Waiting for the Israeli elections
Israeli affairs expert Ismat Mansour argues that implementation of the plan is "definitively linked to the Israeli elections," saying Netanyahu is postponing major decisions until after the vote because he does not want to appear to have withdrawn from Gaza, eased pressure on Hamas, or ended the war without achieving what he can present as a victory before the election.
“Until then, Netanyahu will keep political options open,” he told The New Arab. “He is not allowing any concessions or even allowing the NCAG to intervene.”
Board officials describe a similar picture. Netanyahu largely cooperated with the Board for most of the past year, one Israeli official said, but stopped entirely about two months ago when the election campaign officially began.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board's high representative for Gaza, acknowledged in New York that talks with Israel have been difficult during the campaign.
Abu Rahma agrees that the plan is heavily tied to the vote, because the current government treats Gaza as both a security file and a domestic political issue.
He warns, however, against assuming that a new government would transform the situation.
"It cannot be said that a change of government will automatically improve the situation in Gaza. A change could open a new political space, but it will not be sufficient on its own," he told The New Arab.
Much will depend on the composition of the next government and its positions on withdrawal, disarmament, Palestinian administration, an international presence, and reconstruction.
The opposition is led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose centrist Yashar party is running alongside the joint list of former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. A government led by Eisenkot or Bennett could open more room for the Board.
Such a government would be less dependent on settler and ultra-Orthodox partners. It would therefore likely find it easier to accept the full sequencing of the disarmament and reconstruction plan, including withdrawal to the original Yellow Line.
“The outcome of the election will determine the course ahead,” says Mansour. “Netanyahu is more hardline than Eisenkot, so what happens after the election will be crucial.”
A Jerusalem Post column argued that a new government would create an immediate opening for the Palestinian technocratic committee to take over civilian authority and for reconstruction to begin.
Mansour agrees with this position, seeing more room for change. A new Israeli government, he argues, could give the Palestinian Authority a broader role, explore ways to strengthen the Board if international forces cannot be secured, or draw on the Palestinian Authority's security capabilities in Gaza.
But so far, the outcome is far from certain. Israel faces a real possibility of a stalemate in the 27 October vote, which would complicate efforts to advance the recovery program even further.
The vote looks set to end in deadlock. Neither the bloc led by Netanyahu's Likud, which includes the far-right Religious Zionism and Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) parties and the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism, nor the opposition, is close to the 61 seats needed to govern.
The Palestinian-majority parties could tip the balance, but a 23 September ban by Israel's Central Elections Committee, which voted to bar Ra'am and the Joint List from running, despite the attorney general's opposition to barring Ra'am. The Supreme Court, which has overturned similar bans before, must rule by 4 October.
Without their roughly 12 seats, the opposition's path to a majority narrows. Even with them, much of the Zionist opposition has ruled out governing with Palestinian parties, and Eisenkot has said Ra'am will not be part of his government.
For Netanyahu, the campaign leaves little room to show any flexibility on Gaza. His far-right partners have campaigned against any withdrawal from the Strip, any public sign he would reduce Israel's control there, or make concessions to Hamas, would likely cost him his voter base.
Hamas weapons or Israeli withdrawal first?
Hamas accepted the Board's disarmament plan on 30 July, but its implementation stalled after Israel rejected it. The plan linked disarmament to a phased Israeli withdrawal, while Netanyahu insists Hamas must give up its weapons before Israeli forces pull back.
In August, Netanyahu said Israeli forces would stay in their current positions until Hamas had fully disarmed. After meeting him, the Board hardened its position and tied any pullback beyond the Yellow Line to the complete decommissioning of light weapons, heavy weapons, and tunnels, dropping the phased approach it had presented days earlier.
Mansour says the election is the plan's main obstacle but not its only one. Other unresolved questions include how withdrawal and disarmament would be synchronised, how and when weapons would be collected, which areas Israel would leave, how Hamas would be removed from government, and when and where the Board would assume its responsibilities.
The Yellow Line itself has become part of the problem. It is the demarcation set by the October 2025 ceasefire as the position to which Israeli troops would initially withdraw. Israel's military has since confirmed that it controls 60 percent of Gaza, up from the 53 percent agreed in the ceasefire talks. In July, Israeli control had reached nearly 70 percent.
The International Crisis Group (ICG) said this month that Israeli forces are levelling neighbourhoods behind the line and enforcing it as a no-go zone as they push it toward the sea.
“I do not expect a complete or rapid Israeli withdrawal from the areas behind the Yellow Line without a binding US decision involving all parties and a clear political agreement on disarmament and security arrangements,” Abu Rahma says.
He also warns against a piecemeal approach, adding that continued reconstruction in some areas but not others would be a major problem, as it would create geographically fragmented reconstruction and make Gaza appear as if it consisted of multiple areas in terms of administration, security, and services.
"The most stable solution is for the Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction to take place as a synchronised and gradual process," he told The New Arab.
Board of Peace: A strategic deception
Academic and political analyst Talal Abu Rokba reads the plan very differently. He believes that "everything that is happening is an attempt to deceive the world into believing that solutions are coming for Gaza while Israel continues with its plans to displace its people".
The killing has indeed continued. Gaza's Health Ministry said on 26 September that 1,145 Palestinians had been killed since the ceasefire took effect, bringing the war's toll to around 74,000 killed and 175,000 wounded, although the unofficial death toll is thought to be much higher.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly on 24 September, Netanyahu rejected accusations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and ruled out Palestinian statehood under present conditions.
Mansour shares part of Abu Rokba's concern. He links the success of the recovery plan to Israel's intentions for Gaza's population, saying that "the displacement issue remains on the table and will remain so as long as the recovery phase does not genuinely begin".
Israel's defence minister has confirmed the government's intention to move large numbers of Palestinians out of Gaza "at the right time and in the right manner”.
“It’s like throwing dust in the eyes to cover up the ongoing genocide, a strategic deception carried out by the Board of Peace to sustain Israeli policy in Gaza,” says Abu Rukba.
He also argues that the Board was designed to meet Israel's core demand that Gaza should not come under any genuine Palestinian rule, with the Board and the technocratic committee serving as alternatives to the Palestinian statehood Netanyahu seeks to eliminate.
“Israel is not allowing the committee to operate. They meet with the Americans, Europeans and Arabs, issue statements, and are in contact with the UN and even officials in the Palestinian Authority, but they have no presence on the ground,” says Abu Rokba.
Mansour expects changes after the Israeli vote, and within the Palestinian Authority and its structures as well, including possible elections for the Palestinian Legislative Council.
Palestinian elections and any reconciliation within Fatah, he says, could change the course of Gaza as a whole, and could transform the recovery plan completely.
Mohamed Solaimane is a Gaza-based journalist with bylines in regional and international outlets, focusing on humanitarian and environmental issues

Trump’s energy chief asked Europe to release more than a third of its diesel reserves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:38:55 UTC

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright attends an announcement made by President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington on Sept. 28, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
BERLIN — The Trump administration has circulated a proposal to European governments asking them to release a large portion of the bloc’s strategic diesel reserves to ease soaring fuel costs, according to four officials in European and U.S. governments.
The plan, put forward by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, was pitched as an alternative to President Donald Trump's threat of a blanket ban on diesel exports from the U.S.
Under the proposal, EU governments would release 120 million barrels of diesel from their national strategic reserves over 180 days, a government official from a European country told POLITICO. The official, like others in this story, was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the proposal's details publicly.
Advertisement
That would account for well over a third of the approximately 315 million barrels of diesel EU countries held in reserve as of June this year, according to Eurostat figures. Among EU countries, Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland hold the largest reserves of the essential transport fuel.
POLITICO reported Tuesday that the White House was floating the idea of asking the EU to use its diesel reserves to bolster global supply and thus lower prices. A German government official on Thursday confirmed that the United States had contacted Berlin in the matter.
Multiple countries in Europe were approached for a coordinated release, according to a person familiar with the Trump administration's plans. One major EU member was approached bilaterally in the U.S. last week, according to a senior European energy official.
"It was very hypothetical: ‘What do you think about Europe releasing some of the reserves in order to decrease prices, put pressure on supplies?'" the official said. "'It could also help our government not to continue the discussion on the export ban.'"
Wright, along with the U.S. oil and gas industry, opposes an export ban on one of the world's most in-demand petroleum products, and the proposal is seen as an attempt to find an alternative to such a drastic measure.
At a press conference Thursday, Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen wouldn’t confirm whether the EU had received Wright’s request but said that any stock releases would only be agreed through the International Energy Agency, a Paris-based institution which coordinates energy policy among rich countries and oversaw an earlier stock release this year. She added that the Commission was in close contact with EU member countries and Washington.
Advertisement
Meanwhile, President Trump on Wednesday confirmed that a diesel export ban by his administration was still on the table. “I’m thinking about it,” Trump said of the export ban at an Oval Office event. “I speak to [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it a lot — they sort of think it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things.”
Trump declined to rule out restricting diesel shipments. “It’s something that we think about and we talk about every day,” he said. “But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline, so that would go up a little bit, and diesel would come down a little bit.”
Wright, who was with Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said the administration would soon announce measures aimed at bringing down diesel prices. Europe would also be announcing moves to add supply to the market, he said.
“You will hear announcements from our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that’ll come to the market that’ll meaningfully push diesel prices down,” Wright said.

ADL report finds systemic exclusion of Jewish, Israeli artists across US cultural institutions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:38:48 UTC
22:38:48 KST

A comprehensive body of research released by the Anti-Defamation League on Thursday documents the systemic exclusion and marginalization of Jewish and Israeli artists across American cultural life.
The initiative, titled “State of the Arts: Advancing Jewish Inclusion in Arts, Entertainment and Culture,” examines institutional practices across art museums, the publishing sector, and live performance venues alongside a companion investigation into activist networks.
"Jewish artists are being canceled, blacklisted, and pushed out of American cultural life. We knew the situation was bad; we just didn't know how bad, and no one had documented it this way before," ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said.
"Forty leading museums, not one includes Jewish identity in its DEI commitments. Authors are being told to strip Hebrew words and change Jewish character names just to get published. Jewish and Israeli performers are being harassed off stages and dropped from lineups. This is antisemitism and anti-Israeli discrimination, plain and simple, and the arts and culture sector needs to wake up before Jewish voices are silenced entirely."
The museum sector report, titled “Behind the Frame: A Quiet, Systemic Erasure in America's Museums", evaluated antisemitism and Jewish representation across 40 leading US art museums, grading institutions on policies, artist representation, and programming.
Of the 40 museums invited to review their assessments, 20 participated. The findings showed that only one museum, the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, achieved the gold standard, while 12 museums received the lowest rating of "critically deficient," including the Whitney Museum of American Art and The Broad.
Additionally, only one of the 40 museums recognized Jewish American Heritage Month in May 2026, even though 60% continued recognizing other heritage months during the same period.
Jewish, Israeli cultural motifs discouraged in publishing
The publishing sector report, titled “Missing Chapter: Suppression of Jewish Voices in Publishing", identifies seven anti-Jewish trends reshaping the industry since October 7, 2023, based on secondary research and more than 30 interviews with authors and publishing professionals.
These trends include the suppression of books with Jewish, Israeli, or Zionist characters at the acquisition stage, where manuscripts dealing with Jewish identity or contemporary Israel are increasingly treated as commercially risky. Authors face editorial pressure to remove Hebrew words, Israeli settings, and Jewish-sounding character names before their works can be considered for publication.
Blacklistings and boycotts of authors have also proliferated across online reader communities and social media platforms like BookTok, Bookstagram, and X. This is highlighted by a viral May 2024 Google spreadsheet titled "Is your fav author a Zionist?" that sorted writers by political affiliation and urged readers not to buy, review, or promote their work.
Additionally, transnational boycotts have targeted Israeli publishing institutions and translation rights. This includes a 2024 PalFest letter signed by more than 1,000 writers urging a total boycott of Israeli publishers, literary agencies, and festivals.
Other documented trends include author-level exclusion from literary festivals and events, as well as struggles to secure and keep literary agents who view Jewish or Zionist identity as too risky for the market. The report also highlights an institutional failure by major literary bodies to name antisemitism directly rather than grouping it under generalized anti-bigotry.
The report documents cases of review-bombing, coordinated waves of negative ratings and reviews on public book platforms such as Goodreads, which function as critical marketing and discovery tools within the publishing industry. These malicious campaigns often occur months before a book is published and before reviewers could plausibly have read the work, damaging an author's commercial viability, retail visibility, and professional standing based on identity or perceived politics rather than the book's content.
ADL: US cultural institutions failing Jewish, Israeli artists
The entertainment sector report, titled “Dark Stage: Jewish and Israeli Performers Are Being Canceled, Harassed and Silenced", alongside its accompanying case archive, catalogs 65 incidents across 41 US locations detailing the rising hurdles faced by Jewish, Israeli, and openly Zionist artists in live music, comedy, theater, dance, film, and campus events.
The findings highlight how political demonstrations have increasingly shifted away from standard advocacy and toward targeted campaigns aimed at excluding Jewish and Israeli performers from the stage entirely, utilizing petitions, boycotts, and organized protests to block appearances.
Venues frequently lean on safety rationales to enact a security veto, where the mere prospect of public outcry or disruption, rather than any confirmed danger, is enough to scrap a show. This environment also fosters informal cultural boycotts and quiet professional distancing, where bookings silently vanish.
Furthermore, artists encounter frequent mid-performance harassment and audience heckling, exemplified by comedian Judy Gold facing hostile remarks during two separate shows in April 2026, including an audience member shouting "You're a Jew," and singer-songwriter Regina Spektor being interrupted by a protestor during a concert in Portland.
Compounding these pressures is widespread institutional inconsistency, where venues and cultural organizations respond unpredictably to controversies without clear standards, leaving performers unable to anticipate how their events will be handled and forcing administrators into reactive decision-making that frequently leaves Jewish and Israeli artists to absorb the professional and reputational fallout alone.
To accompany these sector analyses, the ADL Center on Extremism released an investigation into how external activist organizations target cultural spaces, detailing how groups work to pressure venues and museums to isolate Jewish and Zionist creators through coordinated demonstrations, blacklists, and confrontational tactics.
To examine public attitudes toward these dynamics, the ADL Ratings and Assessments Institute fielded an online survey through Prolific in July 2026 with an analytical sample of 951 US adults.
The survey found that 88% of respondents somewhat or strongly agreed they would visit an art gallery exhibiting work by Jewish artists, 87% would attend a performance featuring Jewish performers, and 84% would buy an interesting book even if it included Jewish topics or characters.
Support remained robust for Israeli-identified work, with 77% saying they would visit a gallery exhibiting Israeli artists, 75% attending a performance featuring Israeli performers, and 73% buying a book with Israeli topics or characters.
Furthermore, 85% of respondents somewhat or strongly agreed that excluding Jews or their work from cultural spaces contributes to anti-Jewish hate, while 72% said the same about excluding Israelis.
Despite this widespread recognition of harm, 32% somewhat or strongly agreed it was understandable for people to avoid art galleries showing work by Jewish artists, and 46% said the same regarding Israeli artists.
"This research shows a clear and consistent gap between perceived market risk, what Jewish and Israeli authors are being told, and actual audience demand," said ADL Vice President of Public Affairs and Special Initiatives Shira Goodman.
“The interview ADL carried out with literary professionals for this research surfaced a recurring pattern of authors being told by agents and publishers to strip Jewish and/or Israeli themes and characters from their work over fears it won’t sell or is too much of a risk," she added. "The survey findings suggest this risk aversion is a misperception, not a market reality, and something that urgently needs to be addressed by the industry.”
The ADL is calling on cultural institutions, museums, publishers, literary agents, and venue operators to close these gaps by naming antisemitism explicitly in policies and DEI commitments, recognizing Jewish American Heritage Month alongside other heritage observances, resisting pressure campaigns rooted in identity-based exclusion, and trusting data that shows American audiences want and will support Jewish and Israeli inclusion in the arts.

Connecticut man sentenced to over seven years in prison for attempting to join ISIS

2026-10-01
13:38:47 UTC
22:38:47 KST

A 29-year-old Connecticut man who intended to join the Islamic State (ISIS) terrorist organization was sentenced to over seven years in prison on Wednesday for attempting to provide material support for a designated terrorist organization.
According to the US Justice Department, starting in 2018, US citizen Ahmad Khalil Elshazly began expressing interest in traveling to the Middle East to fight on behalf of ISIS.
Online and in person, Elshazly swore allegiance to ISIS. He created and administered a pro-ISIS Discord server used to spread hundreds of ISIS memes and videos, along with other extremist propaganda.
On December 14, 2019, Elshazly paid $500 to an individual he believed was an ISIS facilitator to smuggle him to Turkey by boat. He planned to connect with an ISIS member in Turkey who would then assist him with traveling to Syria to join ISIS.
The next day, Elshazly arrived in Stonington, Connecticut, where he expected to begin his journey to Syria, and was arrested.
He remained in detention since his arrest and pleaded guilty to attempting to provide material support to a designated terrorist foreign terrorist organization in 2022. Elshazly was sentenced to 92 months in prison and lifetime supervised release for the offenses.
US citizen extradited from Georgia to face charges of supporting ISIS, ANF
On September 23, a 41-year-old citizen of Uzbekistan and naturalized US citizen was arraigned on charges of conspiring and providing material support to ISIS and the then-al-Qaeda-affiliated al-Nusra Front (ANF) terrorist organization after being extradited from Tbilisi, Georgia.
ANF was led by Ahmed al-Sharaa, who split from al-Qaeda in 2016 to form Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham, and overthrew the Assad regime in December 2024, becoming the Syrian president.
Davud Ansariy, also known as “Kozimjon Gafurov” and “Kozim,” is suspected of leading a group of radicalized individuals who planned to travel to Syria to fight for ISIS or ANF and financed such travel.
According to the Justice Department, Ansariy’s group was based in Brooklyn, New York, and was referred to by the group's associates as “chayxona,” the Uzbek word for “tea party.”
An investigation uncovered that the “tea party” group raised money to fund the travel of individuals seeking to join terrorist organizations and to support the families left by the individuals.
Ansariy and the “tea party” group funded the travel of at least three individuals who joined terrorist organizations in Syria in 2013. It is believed that the three individuals were killed in Syria, according to the Justice Department.
In May 2016, one of Ansariy’s co-conspirators was arrested, prompting Ansariy to flee the US for Turkey.
Ansariy arrested, extradited to New York
He remained a fugitive until authorities arrested him in Georgia in August 2026 and extradited him to New York in September.
If Ansariy is convicted of the charges, he faces a maximum penalty of 35 years in prison.
US Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, Joseph Nocella Jr., thanked the FBI Office of the Law Enforcement Attaché in Tbilisi and the Prosecutor’s Office of Georgia for their cooperation in extraditing Ansariy.
“As alleged, the defendant facilitated an expansive network that sought to finance the travel of foreign fighters to wage violent jihad,” Nocella said of Ansariy. “His extradition and prosecution should serve as a reminder that our Office and our law enforcement partners will work relentlessly to hold accountable those who would provide support to terrorists seeking to harm the United States.”

The co-pilot of a passenger jet who stabbed the captain in an apparent attempt to hijack and crash a flydubai plane as it flew to Israel had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly suicidal, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday.
Disaster was averted on Wednesday's flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv after the wounded captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers to subdue the attacker. A reserve crew that had been aboard landed the plane, which had more than 170 people on board, at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.
"We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination. That appears to be something we are gathering from his personal information," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News.
Two Israeli security officials said Israel's initial assessment is that the co-pilot, identified by Israeli officials as an Omani national, was likely acting alone, though the investigation was still ongoing.
The flight plunged more than 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds during the incident as it flew over Saudi Arabia on the journey from the United Arab Emirates to Israel, according to the flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
"It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane," Netanyahu said. Coupled with "the Islamist tendencies, that radicalization that are found in his background, I think that's... a pretty good clue," he said, without elaborating.
"But again, I don't make final conclusions yet. But that's the indications we have now," he added.
The United Arab Emirates has started investigations seeking to establish the circumstances and motives and determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction," the UAE state news agency reported on Thursday.
Israel's Ambassador to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, earlier told Reuters it was too early to draw conclusions and no motive had been determined.
Another Israeli official said Israel was not receiving all the information it sought from the Saudis and that Israeli intelligence services, Mossad and Shin Bet, were investigating the incident as well.
The Saudi government's media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment, and Saudi Arabia has issued no statements on its investigations.
Israeli officials have identified the attacker as an Omani national. Omani authorities have not commented.
In a separate interview with Fox News, Netanyahu said the attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia, and he believed that he would be taken to the UAE.
'Too early to tell' if co-pilot was linked to Iran
Asked if there was any indication of Iranian involvement, Netanyahu said it was too early to say. "We'll get to the root of this attacker, whether he had accomplices, whether Iran was behind it. I think we'll find out very soon," Netanyahu said.
There have been no official suggestions from Israel of Iranian involvement.
The two Israeli security officials said Israel had not identified any Iranian involvement so far.
Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Wednesday that Israel's preliminary information indicated that the co-pilot aimed to crash the plane, describing him as a terrorist, though Netanyahu only described it as "a serious security incident."

The U.K. government's upcoming ban on social media for children under 16 is only a "staging post" toward a more interventionist regulatory framework for technology companies, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has warned.
Speaking to British daily The Guardian ahead of a Labour Party conference, Nandy vowed to expand state oversight of digital platforms beyond the restrictions set to take effect by March.
"We shouldn’t accept that this is the end," Nandy said. "This is a staging post to what must be a very active interventionist state, policing and regulating the online space so that people are safe."
The upcoming ban targets high-risk apps, including TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, and Instagram. Subsequent measures aimed at 16- and 17-year-olds will restrict features such as infinite scrolling, harmful recommendation algorithms, and weak age-verification checks.
A public consultation on the ban drew over 116,000 responses, with 85% of parents agreeing that the risks of social media outweigh the benefits, The Guardian reported.
Comparing digital platforms to physical public areas, Nandy criticized the necessity of removing children from social media altogether.
"If we were in a situation where we were saying our town centers are now so unsafe that we’ve decided that every child is going to have to stay in their bedrooms, people would rightly be up in arms," Nandy said.
"How have we got to a point where we’re saying these social media sites are so harmful and dangerous that we cannot conceive of any way of protecting our children except to remove them altogether? This ends now," she added.
Nandy highlighted a "step change" in policy under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office in July, succeeding Keir Starmer.
She noted the U.K. is willing to diverge from Washington on technology policy, citing plans to guarantee established broadcasters greater prominence on platforms like YouTube and TikTok.
"That is a difference of opinion with the U.S. administration, but we do reserve the right to take a different approach," Nandy said, adding that digital infrastructure should not be "entirely outsourced to the private sector."
"It’s not acceptable to outsource this to Musk or anybody else," she said, revealing that representatives from X failed to attend a recent meeting she called with tech executives.
Nandy also acknowledged enforcement challenges with the regulatory body Ofcom regarding the Online Safety Act, saying, "Laws are only as good as the ability to enforce them."
She also expressed support for a proposal by BBC Director-General Matt Brittin to develop a "public service algorithm" to compete with major tech platforms.

Damen’s lawyer Peter Gauweiler sent a letter to members of the Bundestag’s budget and defense committees demanding €4,679,663,394, according to the report.
Gauweiler argued that the figure concerns payments the federal government committed to under the contract, rather than an additional claim for damages.

Allegations against ministry
The correspondence reportedly included a letter dated Sept. 22 addressed to Pistorius, alleging that suspicions of abuses of authority by senior Defense Ministry officials had intensified.
Damen requested a legally binding commitment from the ministry to cover existing and future losses arising from the alleged breaches.
The allegations are part of an escalating dispute about the cancellation of a program to build six F126 frigates, one of the navy’s largest modernization projects.
Although Damen was the main contractor, the ships were to be built entirely at German shipyards in Wolgast, Kiel and Hamburg.
Pistorius halted the project on June 24, citing severe delays, rising costs and unpredictable risks. Completing the program could have cost as much as €18 billion, according to the ministry’s calculations cited in the report.
Germany considers counterclaim
