Cornell Sex Assault Case Raises Questions About Title IX Accountability and New York’s Intoxicated Consent Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Two years after a woman alleged a gang rape at Cornell University, renewed attention to the case and the limited consequences faced by the alleged perpetrators has raised questions about what higher education owes students who experience sexual assault on campus as well as how consent and intoxication are understood under New York law.
A woman identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging that she was sexually assaulted, gang-raped, and pressured to take drugs and drink alcohol by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024. The lawsuit is filed against the fraternity, Doe’s sorority chapter, and Cornell University; it names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar as defendants. Prosecutors said this week they were reopening a criminal investigation into the case after declining to press charges originally.
Separate attorneys for Kretzschmar and Lopes denied the allegations in statements to ABC, while Norris, via an attorney, denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use but acknowledged that he sent a message included in the complaint.
When sexual assault allegations of this kind occur on campus, they can be addressed in three distinct ways: through school disciplinary proceedings, criminal proceedings, and civil lawsuits.
Doe’s civil lawsuit alleges that Cornell failed to protect her. Her attorney has separately criticized authorities’ handling of the criminal investigation, although observers say what’s known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law could limit what prosecutors are able to charge.
Here’s what to know about how the case was handled—by Cornell and the criminal justice system—before, and what could happen next.
How Cornell responded when the alleged assault was reported
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police in November 2024. According to her complaint, Cornell began its Title IX investigation on Jan. 14, 2025.
Title IX is a law dating back to 1972 that is meant to, among other things, ensure that a college investigates when there is sexual assault on campus. Central to this premise is that Title IX is meant to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
Doe’s attorney has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students. Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but has not disclosed individual outcomes. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.
Cornell responded in a statement last week, saying that it could not confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes due to student privacy laws. However, the university clarified on Monday that “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
“We take sexual violence extremely seriously,” the Sept. 21 statement said. “The Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault was launched shortly after this incident and issued a REPORT in March 2026.”
In a statement Monday, Kyle Kimball, Cornell’s vice president for university relations, said Chi Phi’s Cornell chapter closed in 2024 and the fraternity remains barred from campus.
But women’s rights advocates believe that the school might not have fulfilled its legal obligations in investigating the incident and taking appropriate actions toward those involved.
What does Title IX require universities to do about sexual assault?
Title IX is a federal civil rights law meant to prohibit sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
Since Title IX was introduced, courts have found that the law requires institutions to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
“The reason why Title IX addresses sexual harassment, including sexual assault, is because of the very real impact that has on students’ ability to access education,” Shiwali Patel, a Title IX expert with the National Women’s Law Center, tells TIME.
According to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), students who experience sexual assault are more likely to earn lower GPAs in school and are more likely to drop out of school altogether.
Patel points to Doe’s attorney’s account of her efforts to leave Cornell after the alleged assault. In a Sept. 28 interview with CNN, Thomas Giuffra—Jane Doe’s lawyer—said Cornell refused her family’s tuition-refund request, leaving her to spend another semester on campus.
“She was trying to leave the institution; she didn’t want to be there,” Patel says.
Cornell told People that it works with students seeking to take leave or withdraw and “regularly refunds payments if students are no longer enrolled.”
Giuffra also told CNN that Doe is no longer in college as of 2026.
Universities also have obligations to offer support regardless of a formal complaint or a finding of culpability. These can include counseling, academic adjustments, and housing or schedule changes. Patel says it remains unclear whether Cornell fully complied with its Title IX obligations because the supportive measures it provided Doe are not publicly known.
Regardless, the situation raises questions about what more schools can do for students, Patel says, providing some examples of the types of questions that a university might ask in the aftermath of this kind of incident: “Does she need extensions on exams? Does she need some time off, some leave? Does she need a housing shift if the fraternity house and her sorority house are close together? Does she need counseling? Did they provide a stay away order? What kind of support were they giving her to make sure she wouldn’t have to be retriggered and traumatized by running into them?”
Title IX also requires schools to investigate allegations through a reliable, impartial process—independently of criminal court systems, and using a lower burden of proof to determine if a student violated campus policy.
Cornell University publicly disclosed that it was investigating the allegation on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe went to the police, according to the lawsuit. The university sent an alert to students regarding a report of sexual assault and coercion into taking drugs at a fraternity house. The same day, Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity.
In response to an inquiry from TIME, Cornell said that its “Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated the allegations against the individuals and the fraternity consistent with university policies and Title IX.”
“The university’s Title IX investigation was conducted over several months and included hearings where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days,” the university’s statement continued. “The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence in the university’s investigation.”
How did Trump change Title IX rules?
Cornell’s handling of the case unfolded amid shifting federal rules on campus sexual misconduct. A court vacated the Biden Administration’s Title IX rule on Jan. 9, 2025—five days before Cornell began its formal investigation, according to Doe’s complaint. The university held hearings that May, making the rules it applied a key question in assessing its response.
The Biden Administration had expanded Title IX regulations in April 2024—taking effect in August 2024—broadening the definition of sexual harassment and extending federal protections.
On Jan. 9, 2025, however, a federal district court issued a decision vacating the 2024 Biden rule nationwide. This week, the Trump Administration formally restored the 2020 Title IX regulations to the Code of Federal Regulations. Those rules, introduced during President Donald Trump’s first term, had already been enforced since January 2025.
“The Trump rule essentially narrowed the definition of sexual harassment to make it more burdensome for a complainant to actually complain of something that meets a definition,” Patel says of the differences between the Biden-era and Trump-era Title IX rules.
The 2020 rule requires hostile-environment sexual harassment to be “severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive,” a narrower standard than the Biden-era rule. Sexual assault, however, is covered separately and does not have to meet that threshold—and a direct link between recent revisions and the Cornell case has not been established.
“It also sets limits on what schools can respond to under Title IX based on the location of the assault, harassment, and based on the complainant’s status,” she adds. “This is going a huge step backwards because it is allowing schools to do less in the face of sexual assault.”
Another difference between the 2020 and 2024 rules was that the latter required schools to proactively monitor educational programs for sex discrimination, identify and address barriers to reporting, and take prompt, effective steps to prevent discrimination from recurring.
Patel argues that a university’s ability to prevent and respond to sexual assault is hindered by this “ping-ponging of Title IX protections based on the administration that’s in power.”
“We need to have a legislative fix,” she argues. “There needs to be some clarity through legislation to prevent this type of thing from happening.”
Nancy Cantalupo, an assistant professor at Wayne State University Law School, says that this type of case highlights issues within the government itself—what she describes as “failures of those in the current administration and certain previous administrations, as well as the courts—led by the U.S. Supreme Court—to interpret and enforce Title IX in a manner that is consistent with Title IX’s purposes.”
Namely, she says, that involves preventing gender discrimination in education.
How do Title IX investigations differ from criminal cases?
Survivor advocates describe Title IX as an alternative form of recourse to the criminal legal system, emphasizing its capacity to address other harms of sexual violence, including its impact on educational access. In written testimony to a Senate roundtable discussion of Title IX in 2014, the Victim Rights Law Center said the law “is a mechanism to enforce a victim’s civil rights and not a tool of the criminal justice system.”
Where prosecutors are tasked with focusing on the accused’s accountability and the community’s interests, the Victim Rights Law Center said Title IX is meant to address victims’ equal educational rights.
The two processes also apply different standards of proof, at times leading a prosecutor to decline charges because they do not believe the evidence can support a criminal conviction.
“The View” co-host Sunny Hostin, who said she prosecuted sex crimes for a decade, defended the initial decision not to prosecute. On the show’s Tuesday episode, the former assistant U.S. attorney said, “under New York law, voluntary intoxication or drug use that merely impairs judgment does not legally constitute an inability to consent to sexual activity.”
“There is no way,” she added, “according to [Doe’s] statement in 2024, that any prosecutor would have brought charges.”
What does New York law say about intoxication and consent?
Under the state’s rape laws, lack of consent can be established through force, an explicit refusal of sex, physical helplessness such as unconsciousness, or mental incapacitation. The definition of mental incapacitation excludes incapacity caused by voluntarily consuming drugs or alcohol, leading to a restriction that lawmakers and advocates call the “voluntary intoxication loophole.”
“The current law sees it in black and white: Either you’re stone cold sober or you’re totally comatose,” says Ann Olivarius, an attorney who represents victims of sexual misconduct and discrimination in employment. “Life is not like that, and certainly not in college. We all know how easily our faculties are undermined by drugs and alcohol.”
Even if, under the law, you’re too impaired to operate heavy machinery or be responsible for children, Olivarius says, “if you’re slurring, stumbling, or visibly disoriented, you are still considered capable of giving consent for sex.”
The law’s limitations have been a focal point of the debate over whether the prosecutor should, or could, have brought charges in 2024.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reopened the investigation and said the case would be presented to a grand jury for their consideration. But he defended his initial decision not to charge the alleged perpetrators in a statement on Monday, citing New York state laws on intoxication and consent.
According to Van Houten, Doe’s sworn statement in November 2024 “did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.”
The civil lawsuit, however, states that she was incapacitated when frat members sexually assaulted her and thus incapable of consenting. It also claims that she was “pressured” and “plied” with drugs, and that certain acts were done “without her consent” as well as some “forced” on her.
Olivarius, who was also a plaintiff in the landmark Alexander v. Yale case nearly half a century ago that established sexual harassment is a form of sex discrimination under Title IX, tells TIME that the nature of the law can also lead to victim-blaming questions: “They say to her, ‘Were you drunk? Why did you drink?’ … It’s all on her.
The New York Times reported in May that people who voluntarily drank or took drugs faced a high burden when pursuing rape charges.
Legal advocates have for years argued that the law’s limitations underscore the need for reform, especially as advocacy efforts have increasingly spotlighted how intoxication can impair a person’s ability to consent to sex.
Have there been efforts to change the law?
The New York State Assembly is forming a working group to review the state’s rape laws in light of the civil lawsuit, State Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie, a Democrat, announced on Wednesday. The group, composed of 14 Democratic Assembly members, will be expected to report its findings and legislative recommendations to Heastie and the Assembly Democratic majority conference by the end of the year.
A bill addressing the voluntary intoxication exclusion passed the state Senate unanimously in June, but remains stalled in the Assembly. Earlier versions passed the Senate in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024, and 2025, but none passed the Assembly. The proposals to change the law date back to legislation introduced by then-Sen. Alessandra Biaggi, a Democrat, in 2019.
New York is one of 19 states whose rape or sexual assault laws recognize intoxication as mental incapacitation only when the person became intoxicated without their knowledge or consent, according to research by the Associated Press and a report published in the Journal of the American Academy of Psychiatry and the Law.
Several states have changed their laws in recent years to also protect victims incapacitated by voluntary intoxication.
In 2021, lawmakers in Minnesota expanded the definition of mental incapacitation to include voluntary intoxication, after the state Supreme Court overturned a sexual assault conviction under the narrower definition.
Michigan also revised its laws in 2023 to broaden its definition of mental incapacitation. Last year, Texas expanded its law to cover sexual acts committed when the perpetrator knows the other person is too impaired to consent, regardless of how that person became intoxicated.
California also tightened its sentencing laws in 2016 following the sexual assault case involving Stanford student Brock Turner. The state barred probation and suspended sentences for certain sexual offenses involving victims who were incapable of consenting because of intoxication.
What happens next in the Cornell sexual assault case?
There are three possible ways that this case may move forward.
Van Houten said his office plans to present the criminal case to a grand jury, which would determine whether an indictment is warranted. “Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence,” Van Houten said in his Monday statement. He told ABC that his office wanted to determine whether additional evidence, not considered at the time, would change its assessment, potentially including a screenshot included in the civil complaint of an alleged Snapchat message between the fraternity members that referred to Doe as “free p-ssy.”
After the woman’s initial police report, she reportedly told police a week later that she was “completely and totally incapacitated,” and could “say with 100% confidence I was raped.” A transcript obtained by CBS of a police interview on Nov. 14 and 15, 2024, showed that the woman described being “physically hit very, very hard,” and describing the incident as “coercion.” Van Houten told CBS that he had not seen the transcript of the interview, and that his office had relied on the sworn statement when it declined to bring charges.
Separately, Doe’s civil lawsuit seeks monetary damages from the seven men and other defendants, including Cornell University. A court date has not been set.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Tuesday also called for an independent investigation into how Cornell University handled the allegations when they arose in 2024.
“The allegations in this case are nothing short of horrifying. For any student to come forward after an experience like this takes extraordinary courage. No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act,” the governor’s statement said. “That is why I am calling for outside counsel to conduct a transparent, independent review of the university’s response to determine whether Cornell met every obligation to protect its students and pursue justice.”
The individuals who might be tasked with such an investigation have yet to be named; however, the outcomes could help shape how similar investigations into sexual assault cases are handled on campuses both in and beyond New York.
“This case,” Olivarius tells TIME, “ may change the conversation.”

Zehra Nur Celik
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Thursday said the "Terror-Free Türkiye" initiative has already created new momentum in the region.
Speaking at the Turkish parliament on the opening of the new legislative year, Erdogan said the initiative has strengthened Türkiye's position amid regional turmoil.
"In an environment where our region has turned into a ring of fire, the 'Terror-Free Türkiye' efforts have already had a deterrent effect on Türkiye's adversaries, have further strengthened Türkiye's power, and ushered in a new momentum in our region," he said.
"On matters concerning Türkiye's national interests, politics must be able to reach a full consensus," Erdogan said, referring to the recent initiative as the "Great Türkiye Consensus."
Erdogan stressed that the "Terror-Free Türkiye" process is aimed at building this "national consensus."
 
Türkiye maintains growth despite regional wars, crises
Speaking on the Turkish economy, Erdogan said: "Despite the wars and crises that have erupted one after another in our region, we have managed to keep Türkiye on a path of development and growth."
Türkiye's economy grew 2.5% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, he said, adding that annualized national income exceeded $1.7 trillion.
The country's exports hit a record $280.3 billion on an annual basis in August, he added.
"Following the agricultural frost and drought last year, our agricultural sector has made a rapid recovery," he said.
Türkiye maintained a strong performance in tourism despite regional conflicts, Erdogan said, adding that tourism revenues reached $25.7 billion in the first six months of the year.
"We strengthened our national defense industry with new products while also becoming a country that exports defense products to the world," he said.
Erdogan said Türkiye's defense and aerospace exports increased 16.2% to $6.3 billion in the first eight months of the year.
"We are at a sustainable point in terms of our external balance. We expect the current account deficit to remain at 2.6% of GDP this year," he added.
 
Ongoing fund investigation
Turning to an ongoing fund investigation in the country, Erdogan said: "We are also successfully overcoming the issue that has emerged in a certain segment of the funding markets."
"In accordance with the capital market regulations, we are swiftly resolving this matter while upholding fairness and justice and ensuring that no one's rights are infringed upon," he said.
"We will not allow this issue to turn into a threat to our economic security and social peace," Erdogan added.
Türkiye's banking regulator decided Wednesday to transfer the management of three investment banks and two factoring companies to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund following developments linked to an ongoing fund investigation.
The decisions cover Tera Investment Bank, Destek Investment Bank, Hedef Investment Bank, Destek Finance Factoring and Tera Finance Factoring, according to the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency.
The regulator said its board adopted the measures following assessments of recent developments related to the process publicly known as the "fund investigation."
The three banks account for 0.22% of the banking sector's total assets, while the two factoring companies represent 1.45% of total factoring sector assets, according to the regulator.

Boeing wins contract for new American naval fighter
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:28:55 BST
22:28:55 KST

Boeing has been selected to design, build and deliver the US Navy’s F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter under a multi-billion-dollar contract, with the aircraft intended to replace the service’s F/A-18 Super Hornet fleet, according to the company.
The award gives Boeing responsibility for the Navy’s next-generation carrier-based combat aircraft and follows its selection in 2025 for the US Air Force’s F-47 programme, meaning the manufacturer is now working on two separate sixth-generation fighter programmes for the American military.
Technical and programme details surrounding F/A-XX remain classified under US national security and export regulations. Boeing said the aircraft will incorporate an open mission systems architecture, advanced mission systems and increased operational reach and capacity, although detailed performance information has not been released.
The US Navy has also released an artist’s rendering of Boeing’s F/A-XX design, describing it as the service’s planned sixth-generation replacement for the Super Hornet.
According to a company announcement, Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said: “It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform. Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program.”
The F/A-XX programme is intended to provide the Navy with a new carrier-based fighter as its existing Super Hornet fleet approaches the later stages of its service life. The F/A-18E/F remains the principal strike fighter aboard US aircraft carriers, operating alongside the F-35C Lightning II.
Although both aircraft are carrier-capable, F/A-XX is being developed as a new generation of combat aircraft rather than a direct derivative of either existing type. The Navy has kept most details of the programme classified, including the aircraft’s final configuration and many of the systems expected to form part of it.
Boeing’s selection also gives the company two major future combat aircraft programmes running concurrently. The US Air Force selected Boeing in 2025 to develop the F-47 as part of its Next Generation Air Dominance effort.
Parker said: “Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly. We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs.”
Work on the two programmes is expected to draw heavily on Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis, Missouri, where the company is constructing a new secure manufacturing site for future combat aircraft production.
Boeing described the facility as the largest secure manufacturing development of its kind in the United States and said it will form part of an all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system. The company has been expanding its infrastructure in St. Louis as it prepares for future military aircraft production.
Parker added: “Investment in facilities is just one part of the story; we’re also investing in technology and people so that we can deliver for our customers.”
The award places Boeing at the centre of both the U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy’s next-generation fighter efforts, while the two services continue to pursue separate aircraft designed around their respective operational requirements. For the U.S. Navy, F/A-XX is planned as the eventual successor to the Super Hornet aboard its aircraft carriers, with the programme’s technical and operational details remaining classified.

Tennessee governor suspends all executions after Christa Pike’s lethal injections fail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:27:34 UTC
22:27:34 KST

Tennessee’s governor on Thursday said it was “deeply disturbing” that his state botched the execution of a death row prisoner who remained alive and snoring 40 minutes after receiving a double dose of the lethal drug that should have quickly killed her.
Bill Lee, a Republican, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry after Wednesday night’s failed attempt to put to death Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder, at the execution chamber in Nashville.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday morning, Lee said he had spoken with Frank Strada, secretary of the Tennessee department of correction, but did not have an update on the condition of Pike, who was taken to an off-site medical facility after surviving two doses of pentobarbital.
“This is a tragedy,” Lee said, adding that he had not yet spoken to the families of Pike or the teenager she killed in 1995. “There is no one that wanted what happened last night to happen. It shouldn’t have happened.
“It’s the most difficult of circumstances as it relates to the sentence that should have been carried out by the state. It’s a tragedy, and it’s deeply disturbing that that has happened in this state. The people deserve better than that.”
Lee added, in comments reported by the Tennessean, that he had not yet chosen an investigator to lead a “comprehensive, third party review” he announced in a statement late Wednesday.
“There are a lot of questions,” he said. “The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered. I’m highly disappointed, along with Tennesseans, about what happened.”
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, called the botched execution attempt “singular and unparalleled”, according to the Associated Press.
She said her group was aware of seven other people that have survived medical problems due to an execution team’s failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but nobody had remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions.
In May, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, another convicted murderer, after failing for more than an hour to place an intravenous line into his arm.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death for the brutal 1994 killing of a teenage classmate, was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
The execution attempt was allowed to proceed only after the US supreme court intervened late on Wednesday to lift a federal court stay issued earlier in the day, a delay it said was necessary to assess whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her 1996 sentencing.
Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion to the Tennessee supreme court after the second pentobarbital dose was administered asking to halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony”, and that the state was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.
In a later statement, they said: “Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.
“We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy,” the statement said.
“Christa is being treated at a nearby hospital. We have not been informed as to her condition.”
A representative of the state corrections department defended its handling of the unsuccessful execution attempt.
“The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office,” the spokesperson, Dorinda Carter, said in a statement.
“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility.”
According to the AP, Tennessee’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Seven journalists who were present at the Riverbend maximum security institution as witnesses described what they saw during a livestream hosted by WVLT television station soon after curtains in the execution chamber were lowered for the final time.
They said Pike was snoring as corrections officials escorted them out.
John North, of ABC News affiliate WBIR, said: “It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go. When we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive.”
Pike and her boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp were 18 and 17 when they and another female friend tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in January 1995, using boxcutters and a rock.
The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of those involved and the brutality of the murder, in which Shipp carved a pentagram into their victim’s chest and Pike later showed a friend a fragment of her skull.
Pike never denied the killing, and was later diagnosed with mental health disorders.
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” she said in a clemency petition that Lee and the US supreme court denied.
Lee’s suspension order affects the only other execution set in Tennessee this year. Gary Wayne Sutton has been on death row since 1996 for the murder of a friend, and was scheduled to be put to death on 3 December.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

Trump doesn’t rule out sending ICE to polling sites; US supreme court to review policy to detain immigrants challenging deportation – live
Justices will consider whether immigrants have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation
Supreme court says it will review whether Trump administration can detain immigrants while they challenge deportation
The supreme court today said it will review whether the Trump administration can enforce its policy of denying bond hearings for immigrants to determine whether they should remain detained while their cases are adjudicated.
The novel move to impose mandatory detention is another feature of Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown during his second term in office, and has now made its way to the top court after several appeals court judges ruled that the policy violated federal law and fails to provide immigrants with due process.
However, those decisions conflict with rulings by the fifth and eighth circuits – which ruled that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the US must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.
The case that will be part of the supreme court’s docket for the 2026-27 term focuses on Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a citizen of Brazil, who authorities say he entered the US illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016 and was granted a work permit.
He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory after his September 2025 arrest. After Barbosa da Cunha sued, a federal judge ordered that be provided a hearing or released. An immigration judge found that Barbosa da Cunha did not present a flight risk or danger to persons or property, and ordered him released on bond. The administration appealed against the decision.
The number of people in immigration detention has shot up since Trump returned to office. It was more than 65,000 in July 2026, up from about 40,000 at the end of Joe Biden’s administration.
Donald Trump spoke to reporters briefly earlier, as he departed the White House for Texas and Oklahoma.
The president was asked about his comments to Time that Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh should’ve voted against the board of governors (which unanimously voted to raise interest rates earlier this month) and whether he had spoken to Warsh since the vote.
“No, I want him to vote the way he wants,” Trump told reporters, adding: “I personally would’ve voted against the raise because we’ve got inflation totally under control … The problem is interest rates will hurt our growth.”
In the Time interview, Trump was asked if he regretted nominating Warsh, to which he skirted: “Well, he’s controlled to a certain extent by the board.”
Asked if he still had confidence in Warsh, the president added:
We have a lot of people on [the Fed board of governors] that would love for our country to do badly. It’s become very political. I don’t blame you, Kevin. I think it’s too bad. Not fair. Look, our nation is going through a growth explosion like no nation’s ever seen. We’re blowing through the interest rates. But if we didn’t have to, it would be great.
Compared to his frequent personal attacks on Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, over the Fed refusing to cut interest rates, Trump has so far refrained from publicly criticizing his handpicked chair, and instead directed his ire towards the Fed “board” more generally.
Family of Renee Good sues ICE agent who shot her and top Trump officials
Alba Asenjo Domínguez
The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, have filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration.
In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers.
Good was a US citizen and mother of three who, on 7 January, joined her wife in protesting against the deployment of thousands of ICE agents in their city as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation policy.
The 37-year-old was shot and killed in her car by an agent who claimed he acted in self-defense and the Department of Homeland Security claimed that she had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”. Multiple video clips of the encounter, however, show that Good was steering her vehicle away from the agent as she tried to drive away.
Her death and that of Alex Pretti, an American nurse who was also shot and killed by an immigration agent during Minneapolis protests two weeks later, sparked outrage and a wave of anger across the country.
Shortly after Good’s killing, Todd Blanche, then deputy attorney general, said he saw no grounds for opening a civil rights investigation. Days later, the justice department opened an investigation into the relationship between Becca Good, the deceased’s partner, and protest groups. At least 10 prosecutors resigned following the fatal shootings.
Now, these lawsuits have become some of the first major civil lawsuits filed against Trump’s deportation campaign in Minnesota.
In one of them, the attorneys for Good’s wife and brother allege wrongful death and seek damages for the “immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family”.
“The complaint also seeks to recover for Becca Good, who was standing feet from the couple’s vehicle when Ross fired three rounds into it, and she watched her partner die,” the complaint says.
“Peaceful assembly, speech and even dissent are protected rights. However, the government has distorted the exercise of these rights as violence against our republic and acted with extreme and unconstitutional force, causing egregious harm. Many of these illegal uses of force resulted in death – including the death of an American mother of three, Renee Good […] Today’s legal actions demand accountability for countless violations of the law, the Constitution and the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) own rules governing the use of force,” the lawsuit says.
The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials and federal immigration enforcement agents, and names Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who shot Good, the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem, the White House deputy chief of staff and architect of hardline US immigration policies, Stephen Miller, and former US border patrol officer Gregory Bovino, among others, for their “roles in Renee Good’s death”.
Trump refuses to commit to not demolishing Kennedy Center
Donald Trump also refused to rule out demolishing the Kennedy Center without the consent of Congress. Amid the ongoing high-stakes legal battle over the institution’s name and proposed renovations, the president told Time: “I’m not committing to anything. We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”
He added: “But if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I’m going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people … then I think the Trump administration should be recognized.”
A reminder that Trump has threatened to block proposed renovations to the Kennedy Center and suggested it could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it the “Trump-Kennedy Center” without congressional approval.
Per my colleague David Smith, Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way. Kerry Kennedy, JFK’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president.
“It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job.”
Trump also said earlier in the Time interview that he would be “willing to save it, but it’s in terrible, terrible shape.”
Attacking the judge who ordered his name to be removed from the facade of the building as a “radical-left Trump hater”, the president added:
Well, why would I want to stick with something that’s going to lose hundreds of millions of dollars, and I’m not even recognized? It’s not me; it’s the administration.
The Trump-appointed board voted for the closure of the facility for two years earlier this month, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. But as David notes in his piece, Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and senator Sheldon Whitehouse have alleged that the proposed closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales following Trump’s takeover of the center when he returned to office.
The president remained convinced that Republicans chances of retaining control of Congress this midterm cycle remain strong.
“I think we’ll do OK if I campaign, and I intend to. If I campaign … you don’t give me enough credit. When I campaign, I give people a lot,” Trump told Time. “If I campaign for people, those people are going to win.”
At the GOP midterm convention last month, the president implored voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, in an effort to boost turnout. However, many Republican candidates running in battlegrounds where the president’s approval rating has cratered due to animus around Trump’s handling of the economy and ongoing war in Iran.
Trump doesn't rule out sending ICE agents to polls in upcoming midterms
In his interview with Time magazine, Donald Trump did not rule out the possibility of sending federal immigration agents to polling sites in the upcoming midterms.
When asked, the president said: “Haven’t thought of it” and said that he “could” use the Insurrection Act to declare a national emergency. “A lot of people think I should use it sometimes,” he added.
However, it’s worth noting that legal experts say the law – which would allow the president to deploy troops domestically – doesn’t override the constitution, which prevents them from interfering with elections and appearing at polling sites.
Nonetheless, the administration has hinted at the idea of sending militarized federal agents to polls in recent months. In September, homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said that ICE officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country “to enforce specific threats”.
“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.”
Supreme court says it will review whether Trump administration can detain immigrants while they challenge deportation
The supreme court today said it will review whether the Trump administration can enforce its policy of denying bond hearings for immigrants to determine whether they should remain detained while their cases are adjudicated.
The novel move to impose mandatory detention is another feature of Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown during his second term in office, and has now made its way to the top court after several appeals court judges ruled that the policy violated federal law and fails to provide immigrants with due process.
However, those decisions conflict with rulings by the fifth and eighth circuits – which ruled that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the US must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.
The case that will be part of the supreme court’s docket for the 2026-27 term focuses on Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a citizen of Brazil, who authorities say he entered the US illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016 and was granted a work permit.
He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory after his September 2025 arrest. After Barbosa da Cunha sued, a federal judge ordered that be provided a hearing or released. An immigration judge found that Barbosa da Cunha did not present a flight risk or danger to persons or property, and ordered him released on bond. The administration appealed against the decision.
The number of people in immigration detention has shot up since Trump returned to office. It was more than 65,000 in July 2026, up from about 40,000 at the end of Joe Biden’s administration.
Donald Trump also claimed that “today” was the first he had heard of reports that Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, was warned prior to 7 October 2023 that there would be a likely attack by Hamas.
When Time pushed back, noting that Trump has “access to the highest intelligence”, the president dismissed concerns that Egypt and the United Arab Emirates altered Netanyahu in late September of that year that Hamas was planning a major operation.
“I can’t imagine this,” Trump said. “I don’t think so … I think if he would have known, he would have done something about it. Certainly, he would have had people at least alert.”
However, the president failed to give a clear answer on whether Netanyahu should serve for another term, ahead of Israel’s October elections.
Trump says that it’s ‘possible’ that strikes on Iran will increase after the midterms
Donald Trump defended the ongoing war with Iran, which appears to have little end in sight after the president rejected the latest ceasefire proposal from Tehran, which he described in his Time interview as “not good enough”.
When asked whether he plans to ramp up bombings on Iran after the midterms, Trump said it was “possible”. The president also dismissed concerns from the Pentagon about munitions shortages as the war enters its seventh month.
“I would say it was mostly fake news,” Trump said. “Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms. We have that middle grade and upper middle grade, which is very powerful, which is stronger than it’s ever been before. There is ammunition that President [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy wouldn’t take, but it’s very powerful ammunition.”
Capping off his tirade against the media during his interview with Time magazine, the president made sure to insult CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins, one of the many female reporters Trump has taken aim at during his second administration.
“I can name 100 great things I’ve done. I never get good press. I never get fair press. Doesn’t have to be good. All it has to be is fair,” he told Time. “So at a certain point, you say, ‘what’s the purpose of like this crazy Kaitlan Collins?’ She’s a very average person. She’s the most unhappy young person I’ve ever seen.”
In that same interview, Trump insisted that he wasn’t defying the judge’s order by still preventing these outlets from covering the president at certain events.
“I don’t have to go out of my way, these people write only bad stories,” he said. The White House communications director, Steven Cheung, added that the judge’s order required the president to restore the newsrooms’ access to the White House, “but that’s different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One”.
If you recall, there is ongoing litigation about the Associated Press’ access to these so-called “intimate spaces” after Trump banned the outlet from them last year for refusing to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.
Trump continues to take aim at media in wide-ranging Time interview
Donald Trump doubled down on his attacks on the outlets he’s trying to ban from the White House in a wide-ranging Time magazine interview.
“I believe in an honest press, but I don’t believe in fake news,” he said, without providing any evidence about the areas of coverage he believes to be incorrect.
The president also said that Timothy Kelly, the federal judge who temporarily blocked the president’s ban on CNN, Politico and MS Now, was “very anti-Trump”. However, Trump actually appointed Kelly during his first term in office. When the Time interviewer reminded the president of this fact, he simply replied: “Yeah, he was. He was. It’s one of those things.”

South Korea on Thursday protested Washington’s unilateral announcement suggesting that its investment in the Alaska liquefied natural gas (LNG) project had been finalized, stressing that participation remains conditional on commercial viability and domestic legal requirements, according to The Korea Times.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said he raised the issue with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick after President Donald Trump presented the Alaska project and eight nuclear reactors as part of South Korea’s strategic investment package.

The proposed development involves a pipeline transporting natural gas from northern Alaska to the south and an LNG export terminal.
President Lee Jae Myung separately said on US social media platform X that the Alaska project must demonstrate commercial viability and comply with South Korean legal procedures. Each nuclear plant would also require its own commercial assessment, according to The Korea Times.

The agreed framework envisages two South Korean-designed APR1400 reactors and six AP1000 reactors. Meanwhile, the approved Texas project comprises a $22.3 billion, 6,472-megawatt gas-fired plant supplying AI data centers, with initial operations targeted for 2029 and full operation for 2032.
Seoul also secured an annual investment ceiling of $20 billion and an overall cap of $200 billion, according to the ministry.

Blasts heard in Addis Ababa as Ethiopia conflict widens in the north
Government forces close in on Tigray’s capital amid renewed accusations of Eritrean involvement.
Explosions have been heard in the Ethiopian capital as fighting between federal forces and a coalition of armed opposition groups widens in the country’s north.
The violence comes as Ethiopia said on Thursday that it will close its embassy in neighbouring Eritrea.

Three diplomatic sources told the Reuters news agency that blasts were heard overnight in Addis Ababa, hours after the government banned drone-flying over the capital city and surrounding areas. A source linked to Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival told the agency the rebel alliance had carried out several drone strikes in Addis Ababa, including some targeting the military’s headquarters.
The alliance unites seven armed groups, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and groups from the Amhara, Afar, Somali and Benishangul-Gumuz regions, in an effort to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
Alliance fighters have also clashed with government forces in the neighbouring Afar region, where the authorities have renewed accusations of an Eritrean incursion.
Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement that it will close its embassy in Eritrea’s capital, Asmara, after it ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats in Addis Ababa to leave the country within 48 hours.
The ministry accused Eritrea of “direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia”. The Eritrean diplomats were expelled on Thursday over activities that pose “a direct threat to Ethiopia’s national security” in breach of the United Nations Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, the ministry said.
The ministry urged Eritrea to “cease all acts that are contrary to the principles governing relations between sovereign states”, saying it remains committed to “peaceful resolution of disputes” and regional integration in the Horn of Africa.
Eritrea has denied allegations that it is supporting the opposition alliance fighting Ethiopian government forces since last week.
Reporting from Afar on Wednesday, Al Jazeera’s Muhammed Taha Tawakel said fighting had moved from the Amhara region deep into Tigray as government forces advanced north, reaching within about 40km (25 miles) of Mekelle, its regional capital.
The TPLF, meanwhile, had pulled its fighters back to new positions, and some of its leaders had moved out of Mekelle, Tawakel said.
They were joined by thousands of civilians who fled the city fearing clashes, he said. Electricity and internet services in the region had been cut.
Last week, Tigrayan forces mounted a large offensive, which the TPLF calls a “defensive war” against federal drone and artillery strikes. Government troops and allied fighters have since launched a counteroffensive.
The federal government has accused neighbouring states of backing the coalition, which they deny.
The Afar front
In Afar, government forces told Reuters they have recaptured the towns of Erebti and Abaala near the border with Tigray. The claim remains unconfirmed.
On Wednesday, Al Jazeera’s Tawakel reported that the fight to control the towns was ongoing, and escalation in the northern region threatened to drag Ethiopia and Eritrea into a wider war.
He said mediation efforts by locals to persuade forces controlling Abala and Erebti to withdraw failed, and the situation of more than 80,000 Afar residents trapped in the area remains uncertain.
Tawakel said the fighting in Afar carries the risk of regional repercussions, potentially bringing Eritrea and Ethiopia into a wider war and poses a risk to food security if routes between Ethiopia and Djibouti are disrupted.
Fighting had also reached areas along Ethiopia’s borders with Eritrea and Sudan, he said, increasing the risk of regionalising the conflict.
Ahmed Hussein, Afar’s deputy governor, told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that Ethiopia had come under an unprecedented attack which he said sought to undermine the regional administration and install figures loyal to Eritrea.
He called on Asmara to withdraw from Afar territory and held it responsible for the safety of civilians in areas controlled by opposition groups.

The current pressure on energy prices, however, is a global issue, particularly in oil markets, which are less regulated and inherently global, she said.

2077: The Palestinian play asking who gets to survive the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:24:02 UTC
22:24:02 KST

Breadcrumb
2077: The Palestinian play looking beyond occupation to imagine a future of technological control
How many of us have thought as far ahead as the year 2077? In an age of climate-emergency-linked catastrophe, unbridled AI development, and drastic bio-optimisation, perhaps the future in its bleakest form is already hurtling towards us, faster than thought.
As such, the backdrop for the play 2077: Who Wants to Survive, running as part of this year’s PalArt Festival of Palestinian arts and culture, will sound familiarly dark, inspired by a dystopian present and near-future in Palestine and elsewhere.
In 2077, ordinary people are held prisoner in walled enclaves in which they face poverty, disease, and hunger, while elites pursue biotechnical perfection and immortality.
Here, private detective Harold Harrison, played by Palestinian actor Emile Saba, makes some disturbing discoveries.
First performed in Germany in 2021, a year that already feels technologically like aeons ago, 2077 was written by Palestinian playwright Bayan Shbib and co-produced by Ashtar Theatre, where Emile is now Artistic Director, and Germany-based arts organisation Bridgeworks.
"I really liked the idea of the play from the beginning. It felt new and fresh," Emile tells The New Arab.
"At the time, AI wasn’t as present in our everyday lives as it is now. Of course, we had all grown up watching films and imagining artificial intelligence through movies like Blade Runner and The Matrix, but I hadn’t really seen those ideas explored in theatre, especially not in Palestinian or Arab theatre," he explains.
Beyond the lens of occupation
Palestine has long been used as a site of experimentation for some of dystopia’s darkest tools, and has been used to test new kinds of weaponry, surveillance, and biometrics-led security, primed for use elsewhere at the cost of Palestinian life.
For many in the audience, 2077’s walled enclaves and oppressive living conditions will scream Palestine – but the country is never explicitly mentioned in the play.
"There are many similarities, but we are not trying to make it a like-for-like representation of Palestine," Emile says of the world created in 2077.
"One of the most interesting comments I received was from people who said: 'We didn’t hear Palestine in the play, but you are Palestinian, and we can see the parallels'," Emile recalls.
"I think that is very meaningful, because sometimes people look for Palestinian identity in a very direct way when they watch Palestinian theatre or see a Palestinian actor. But when the connection isn’t obvious, it can sometimes be even more interesting. It allows people to think beyond the expected images and discover the deeper connections between the story, our reality, and the wider world," Emile adds.
"Sometimes there is an expectation that Palestinian theatre will always speak about Palestine through the traditional lens of occupation, conflict, or our direct political reality. But this play goes beyond that. It deals with a global topic that anyone, regardless of nationality or background, can connect with," he continues.
A stage without borders
Ashtar Theatre, established in 1991 in Jerusalem before moving to its current base in Ramallah four years later, is one of several Palestine-based theatre companies whose productions are being staged at PalArt Festival, which runs from 23 September to 3 October.
"One of the things that distinguishes Ashtar is that we are a very critical theatre," Emile explains.
"We raise social and political questions that are not always welcomed by people in positions of power, regardless of which side they are on.
"We don’t necessarily echo a mainstream ideology or the political ideology of any particular party. That often puts us on the margins – sometimes we feel like the black sheep. But we actually see that as one of our strengths. It gives us the freedom to question, to challenge, and to remain critical," he adds.
Ashtar’s critical nature extends from the stage to its administration, with the theatre giving up some of its much-needed funding since the start of the genocide, Emile says.
"Since the war on Gaza, Ashtar was one of the first theatres to boycott some funders that we felt were complicit in the genocide or unwilling to speak up for the Palestinian people. That pushed us to look for other resources and develop new fundraising methods," he adds.
"In some ways, this has been positive because it forced us to discover new channels and become more creative and independent in how we raise resources, but it has not been easy."
Despite this and other adversity the theatre has faced, Ashtar is refusing containment. They have almost finished building themselves a new home in Birzeit, near Ramallah, and hope to start an academy programme next year in collaboration with the Palestinian Circus School, to formally train students in the performing and circus arts.
The theatre also intends to keep putting on a breadth of genres and forms, reflecting the diverse tastes of theatregoers in Palestine.
"Audiences are very open to different theatrical forms. It can be physical theatre, text-based theatre, fantasy, or something more experimental. I don’t think the Palestinian audience is limited in terms of the style of theatre they are willing to see," Emile says.
"The subject is what is always very important. What is the play trying to say? Does it speak to something that people are experiencing, questioning, or feeling? I think that remains one of the most important things for Palestinian audiences," he continues.
A dystopia built from reality
Ashtar’s creative risk with a dystopian sci-fi like 2077 has been rewarded, with the play winning the Jury’s Award for Most Exceptional Performance at the Cairo International Festival in 2023 – a sign that the play’s message and warning translate internationally.
"The world of the play… is built from things that already exist around us: systems of control, surveillance, separation, and the increasing power of technology over our lives. The question is not only what machines can do, but what happens when we allow them to make decisions about human lives," Emile says.
"I see the play as a reflection of our current reality and a warning about a possible future. It is almost saying: if we don’t question the way we use technology and the way power is distributed, machines may not only serve humans – they may eventually begin to control them."
2077: Who Wants to Survive runs on 2 and 3 October as part of PalArt Festival 2026 at the Pleasance Theatre in north London
Shahla Omar is a freelance journalist based in London
Follow her on Instagram: @shahlatan

Could settler violence, Al-Aqsa incursions spark a new intifada?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:22:15 UTC
22:22:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Could settler violence, Al-Aqsa incursions spark a new intifada?
Twenty-six years after the Second Intifada, escalating Israeli military raids, settler violence and incursions into the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound have raised concerns about another Palestinian uprising.
The anniversary comes amid Israel's ongoing war on Gaza, mounting violence in the occupied West Bank and growing incitement against Palestinians ahead of Israel's general election on 27 October.
On Wednesday, 2,474 Israeli settlers entered the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound under police protection during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, according to the Jerusalem Governorate. It said 52,277 settlers had entered the compound since the beginning of 2026.
Israeli forces also carried out raids across the occupied West Bank, arresting Palestinians, searching homes and turning residential buildings into military positions. Meanwhile, settlers attacked Palestinian communities, damaged property and targeted agricultural land.
The developments have revived memories of the uprising that erupted in September 2000 following a visit by then Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon to Al-Aqsa, accompanied by a large security presence.
In the first days of October, Israeli police killed 13 Palestinian citizens of Israel while suppressing demonstrations.
For the families of those killed, the anniversary is a reminder of both their loss and the failure to secure justice.
The victims of the Second Intifada
Among those killed was Ahmad Siam, from the village of Muawiya, whose parents were returning from Jordan when they began receiving calls about their son.
"My wife, Ahmad's mother, and I were returning from a visit to Jordan when we were flooded with calls on the way. We felt that something involving us had happened. Then my brother told me that Ahmad had been injured and was lying in hospital," his father, Ibrahim Siam, told The New Arab.
"But when his mother placed her hand on his chest in the intensive care unit, she realised that he had been killed. She addressed him, saying, 'Congratulations on your martyrdom, Ahmad.'"
Ahmad had been deeply affected by the killing of Palestinian child Muhammad al-Durra in Gaza shortly before his own death. He had also participated in demonstrations defending Palestinian land and was among those protesting in support of Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa when he was killed.
His family has preserved his room and belongings for the past 26 years.
An Israeli commission of inquiry, known as the Or Commission, was subsequently established to investigate the October 2000 killings. Although it issued recommendations, no officers were ultimately prosecuted over the deaths.
"We realised that they were not interested in bringing the criminals to justice, so we withdrew from the court. This was even though they knew who the killers were, and we also had indications of their identities," Siam said.
Israel's shift to the right
Palestinian historian Professor Mahmoud Yazbek believes the events of October 2000 marked a turning point in Israel's treatment of Palestinian citizens.
"What many people believed were sudden events reflected the beginning of a new phase in Israeli society's attitudes and Israeli policies towards our community," he told The New Arab.
Yazbek argued that Israeli society has shifted further to the right since then, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu increasingly dependent on figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
He also accused Israeli institutions of attempting to weaken ties between Palestinian citizens of Israel and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.
The struggle over land remains another major source of tension. Yazbek pointed to recent attempts by settlers to establish a presence on land belonging to the Palestinian village of Majd al-Krum in the Galilee.
"It seems that we will witness another chapter of events starting from this period, concerning land, geography and demographics. But we will not leave for anywhere," he said.
Could another uprising erupt?
Lawyer Fouad Sultani, who helped organise legal assistance for Palestinians arrested during the Second Intifada, warned that growing incitement and the arming of settlers and sections of Israeli society could lead to another violent confrontation.
"The scenes from the beginning of the second intifada affected us deeply. The Arab public was ready to protest, and young people were prepared to rise against the injustice inflicted on us as Palestinians," Sultani said. "But perhaps we did not expect protesters to be shot."
Sultani said the events had exposed the vulnerability of Palestinian citizens of Israel despite their formal citizenship.
"We realised that Israeli institutions do not distinguish between a Palestinian inside Israel and a Palestinian in the West Bank, for example, and treat us in the same way," he said.
He also described increasing pressure on Palestinian lawyers and activists, including disciplinary proceedings against him over social media posts.
"More broadly, all of us inside Israel are being targeted. As lawyers, we no longer know the boundaries of the red lines they have drawn for us," he said.
Sultani warned that the ease with which Israeli police opened fire on Palestinian protesters in October 2000 could be repeated, particularly amid continued incitement and the proliferation of weapons.

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. The BRICS+ Fashion Summit in Moscow has brought together representatives from more than 100 countries over its four seasons, the press service of the Moscow Department of Culture said.

Previous editions of the summit also resulted in invitations for 23 Russian designers from across the country, including Moscow, St. Petersburg, Murmansk, Ulan-Ude, Yakutsk and Komsomolsk-on-Amur, to take part in industry events in different countries. They have already visited India, Tunisia, Costa Rica, South Africa and Ethiopia. In 2024, participants signed a declaration on establishing the International BRICS Fashion Federation, which includes 60 countries.
The BRICS+ Fashion Summit was held as part of Moscow Fashion Week. TASS is the event’s general information partner.

Gaza documentary NAZA tops Italian box office ahead of 'Avengers Endgame: Encore'
Award-winning Gaza documentary NAZA, directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has beaten Avengers Endgame: Encore to top the Italian box office at number one.
The documentary, which examines the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza through testimonies from Israeli military and intelligence personnel, topped the Italian box office during its first two days in cinemas.
Its debut marked its first theatrical release following its premiere at the Venice Film Festival, with ticket sales reaching nearly €1.1 million ($1.24 million) by Tuesday, according to Italian box office tracker Cinetel.
Meanwhile, Avengers Endgame: Encore, an extended re-release of the 2019 Marvel film, grossed €356,000 ($404,000) over the same period in Italy.
NAZA was initially released as a three-day cinema event across 515 cinemas in Italy, with many screenings selling out.
However, strong demand has led to screenings continuing beyond the initial run.
More than 150 cinemas have extended the film’s programming, according to The Guardian, which produced the documentary, with further extensions expected.
Interest in Italy was already high ahead of the film’s release after it won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, with a premiere that was followed by a 25-minute standing ovation, a festival record.
NAZA features testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel whose identities, voices and appearances were digitally altered for allegedly for their protection.
The interviews were conducted over three years and focus on the use of AI-powered surveillance and targeting systems in Gaza, including how targets were identified and struck despite expected civilian casualties.
According to reports about the documentary, some of those interviewed describe witnessing Palestinian civilians being killed and residential areas used as shelters being set ablaze.
The film’s title is derived from an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate the number of civilians expected to die in an airstrike, according to The Guardian.
The documentary has faced significant backlash from senior Israeli officials since its Venice win.
Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for Abraham and Szor to have their citizenship revoked, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar posted on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently said he would pursue legislation allowing citizenship to be revoked in cases involving people who "defame" Israeli soldiers abroad.
Netanyahu also proposed a second bill that would increase damages in defamation cases involving the Israeli military or state.
Simiarly, Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir said the military was examining possible legal measures over the film.
Israeli media subsequently reported that the military was considering a leak investigation and seeking assistance from the Shin Bet.
Abraham and Szor were among the co-directors of the 2025 Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land, which focused on Israeli settler violence and the destruction of Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank.

U.S. surrogate for Chinese billionaire says she trusted agency, as questions arise

U.S. surrogate for Chinese billionaire says she trusted agency to "protect surrogates" amid questions surrounding its CEO
A surrogate carrying a child for Chinese billionaire Xu Bo — a man reported to have over 100 children — said she trusted her agency to "protect surrogates." Now, the business practices of California-based Patriot Conceptions and its CEO are facing fresh scrutiny.
Stanford University's Hoover Institution, where the company's CEO Haotian Bai formerly served as a fellow, cut ties with him last week, shortly after a CBS Sunday Morning investigation featuring the surrogate put a spotlight on loopholes and accusations of questionable practices in the commercial surrogacy industry. A subsequent story in the New York Post looked at Bai's background.
"He is no longer affiliated with the Hoover Institution," the institution said on its website. "In light of recent media reports, it is clear that Mr. Bai misled the Institution on the nature of his businesses."
During his 2024-25 fellowship, Bai focused on veterans' access to in vitro fertilization. He frequently advertises his surrogacy agency as veteran-founded.
Bai said in a 2019 court declaration, filed in a dispute with a former business partner, that he served in the U.S. Army in Afghanistan until 2017 and that he'd been diagnosed with PTSD.
A U.S. Army spokesperson confirmed to CBS News that Bai served as a chemical operations specialist from November 2013 to October 2017. However, the Army said that while he assisted with units that were preparing to deploy, he never deployed himself.
"He had no deployments and left the Army in the rank of specialist," said Christopher Surridge, a U.S. Army spokesperson.
After leaving the military, Bai co-founded another surrogacy agency in 2018. He ended up in a court battle with his co-founder a year later. The case was later voluntarily dismissed. Bai founded Patriot Conceptions in 2019
The Hoover Institution said it would conduct "a full internal review" of the application process for the Veteran Fellowship Program. CBS News reached out to Patriot Conceptions, and in a written response, Bai said he went through "a normal application process as a U.S. Army veteran for a Hoover Institution fellowship in 2023 and was selected through what appeared to be their usual channels and protocols to be a fellow." The statement said there was "no point at which Mr Bai 'misled' the Hoover Institution about his research or his intentions."
Bai's surrogacy agency caters to international clients, who make up 40% of its business — with an emphasis on intended parents from China.
The U.S. is the only developed country where commercial surrogacy is widely legal, attracting foreign nationals who don't have the option in their country, with a large percentage coming from China.
It remains unclear how Patriot Conceptions initially agreed to provide a surrogate for Xu Bo, a video game executive who is well known in China. Patriot Conceptions partnered with a global surrogacy agency representing the intended father.
The surrogate, whom CBS News is calling Judy to protect her identity, said she first learned who the intended parent was on the night before her embryo transfer in April, after traveling from her home state to California for the procedure.
Documents obtained by CBS News showed that the intended father was Xu, who has boasted online about his desire to father large numbers of children.
A single mother, Judy said she decided to become a surrogate because she wanted to use the payment to create a better life for herself and her daughter. She said she also liked the idea of helping someone build a family — but added that she never imagined it would be that large.
"You don't think to ask … 'Oh, do they have, like, over 100 babies already?'" she said in an interview.
In an earlier phone conversation with CBS News, Bai asked whether Judy's surrogacy records had been offered for sale on the dark web. CBS News obtained the records from whistleblowers concerned about irregularities in the surrogacy industry.
During the call, Bai dismissed media reports detailing the scale of Xu's family.
Xu, a reclusive billionaire who is rarely seen in public, made his fortune as founder of Guangzhou Duoyi Network, one of China's largest mobile game companies. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the number of children Xu is said to have fathered via surrogacy, as well as other Chinese billionaires building mega-families.
His company said in a December statement that Xu had 12 children born in the U.S. via surrogates, but acknowledged a larger overall total: "Regarding the rumors about the number of children … the actual number is only a little over one hundred."
Six months later, Xu posted a photo of young children seated in rows alongside a statement: "Mr. Xu Bo believes in the philosophy that more children bring more blessings, and he wishes for all his words and actions to benefit the long-term development of the Chinese nation."
CBS News reached out to Xu directly and through representatives but received no response.
Addressing media coverage in a recent statement, Xu wrote: "Overseas media outlets have previously produced numerous misinterpretations and unfriendly reports about China, as a Chinese citizen safeguarding China's interests, Xu stands on the same side as the Chinese government and avoids granting interviews to overseas media unless necessary."
Following the publication of the CBS News report on Sept. 13, Patriot Conceptions said the firm's employees had encouraged Judy to terminate her contract after public reports about the size of Xu's family surfaced in December.
A statement issued by Patriot Conceptions stated that "it did not know the wider scale of Xu's family described in later public reporting." Patriot Conceptions declined to be interviewed on camera.
Judy disputed this account, stating that the agency "never" advised her to terminate the agreement. She said agency representatives visited her hotel room following her embryo transfer in April to bring her "flowers and snacks."
Judy said the agency told her after she matched that the intended parent was a "single father looking to expand their family."
"I felt like I trusted this agency to kind of protect surrogates and match them with people with good intentions," Judy said.
Judy said when the agency mentioned a large family, she was picturing something from a movie.
"'[The] Sound of Music.' Do you know that movie? My immediate first thought, 'Oh, that would be really cute,' like a family of 10 kids," she said.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

They include three shadow fleet vessels, two ships providing bunkering services, and three Russian-owned ice-class vessels. The ships will face sanctions on shipping and trade, while designated individuals and entities will face asset freezes and other restrictions.
