A new East-West divide: Current political crisis and state of the union in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:17:57 UTC
22:17:57 KST

- Ulrich Schlie is Henry Kissinger Professor at University of Bonn and Joint Research Professor at University of St. Andrews.
Germany's National Day on Oct. 3 has for years been the moment in the nation’s annual cycle when Germans pause to reflect on the state of the union and the country’s inner unity. Reunification in peace and freedom came in 1990 as a gift from history. It was the result of earth-shattering political upheavals that brought down the bipolar system, the order of Yalta and Potsdam. In a defining moment for German diplomacy, Chancellor Helmut Kohl, with tact, a clear sense of direction, and a stroke of luck, made the seemingly impossible possible: the reunification of Germans in East and West with the consent of neighbouring countries. What was a resounding success in external terms reached its natural limits internally. Biographically diverse experiences -- indeed, fundamentally different life experiences shaped by opposing political systems -- and unequal starting points in 1990 in terms of state and society could not be erased overnight through transfer payments, infrastructure projects, the development of administrative structures, and administrative assistance alone. Germans have never been truly united since 1990. This is hardly surprising, given that the country has a strong federal character and significant differences in mindset. Even in the West, the contrasts between people from Holstein, Upper Swabia, and Lower Bavaria were striking, and this was all the more true once people from Saxony, Thuringia, and Mecklenburg joined the mix.
 
Wealth, faith, and the lingering gap
Above all, the economic disparities resulting from the wealth gap between West and East have never completely disappeared. Nor has party loyalty in the East ever been able to develop the strength that had long characterized the old Federal Republic. The Protestant Church was unable either to maintain its unique position in the GDR as the "Church under Socialism" or to translate this into political influence in reunified Germany. The Catholic Church in the GDR was a diaspora church; it never really emerged from this position, and both churches have steadily lost influence across Germany as a whole.
Since 1990, a general sense of dissatisfaction has been more prevalent in the East than in the West, despite many impressive success stories. Politics and the media have played their part in perpetuating cliches and exaggerating differences in mentality into deep rifts. Dissatisfaction is now widespread throughout Germany; confidence in politicians’ ability to find solutions has hit rock bottom, and the reputation of institutions has suffered as a result. Whilst voters expressed their frustration in the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin -- resulting in a significant rise in support for the far-right parties and a collapse for the former mainstream parties, with double-digit losses in the vote -- this phenomenon cannot be explained solely as an East-West issue. It is true, however, that traditional party loyalties in Eastern Germany are now significantly less pronounced than in the West. That said, the issue of the political parties’ standing extends far beyond a comparison of Germany’s East and West.
 
Polarization and the failure of mainstream politics
The latest election results -- with the rise of the AfD, the collapse of the former mainstream parties, the disappearance of the Liberals and, in major cities such as Berlin, a significant share of the vote for the Left Party -- reveal the crisis in the German party system particularly clearly in the East. In the East, voters’ dissatisfaction with the current state of affairs is even greater than in the West; confidence in the political parties’ ability to find solutions is even lower; and the willingness to engage in experiments with an uncertain outcome -- partly as a consequence of the two aforementioned trends -- is particularly strong. The forthcoming anniversary of the national holiday will, in the reflections it provokes, highlight these worrying developments particularly clearly. Despite all the differences between East and West, however, the emerging trends are not contradictory, but merely manifest themselves in different shades. The difficulties in forming a government in Magdeburg, where the AfD is reliant on some form of cooperation with the left-wing populist BSW, and in Berlin, where the SPD and the Greens are now showing a tendency to elevate an openly anti-Semitic and anti-Israeli far-left party to the office of Governing Mayor, will lead to further polarisation of the political system. The former mainstream parties have so far failed to draw any real lessons from the crisis. They are proceeding according to the mottos "close your eyes and carry on" and "carry on as before."
The grand coalitions of the past two decades, which have been a major factor in the political malaise, are continuing with their usual tug-of-war rituals over supposed territorial gains, a situation exacerbated by the lack of distinction between their policy proposals. They merely increase frustration and strengthen the political fringes. The current situation in Eastern Germany, too -- where the CDU and SPD have, in some regions, sunk to the level of the almost defunct FDP -- is partly attributable to misguided political priorities, excessive bureaucracy, the neglect of support for rural areas, and a lack of effective regional and industrial policies. For some time now, Germany has been grappling with problems relating to its geographical structure and the contrasts between urban centres and rural areas -- problems that have long dominated the political agenda in countries such as the UK or Italy. The East-West divide will continue to deepen as the political crisis persists and the general mood in Germany remains gloomy. Despite certain implementation errors, the real roots of this lie not in the country’s internal reunification, but in a political crisis that has much to do with misguided compromises, a lack of courage, excessive bureaucracy, and the absence of an intellectual compass for the country.
*Opinions expressed in this article are the author's own and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Anadolu.

French government proposes $48.5B in fiscal consolidation measures for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

Ilayda Cakirtekin
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The French government unveiled its draft budget bill for 2027 on Thursday, proposing €43 billion ($48.5 billion) in new fiscal measures, according to daily Le Figaro.
The government aims to bring the budget deficit down to 5% of GDP in 2027, particularly through the implementation of "€43 billion in fiscal consolidation measures," according to the draft bill seen by the French outlet.
The government plans to supplement the €43 billion with "the ramping up of fiscal consolidation measures adopted in 2026" and "previously," bringing the total fiscal effort in 2027 to €54 billion ($60.9 billion).
The draft reportedly projects higher value-added tax and income tax revenues, while revenues from businesses are expected to fall.
The government also expects the extension of the tax on high-income households to generate €600 million ($677 million) in revenue next year.
The Economy and Finance Ministry further said the number of state employees would be reduced by around 1,076 full-time equivalent positions in 2027, excluding the planned increase in the defense sector.
The government also aims to make renewable energy financing more efficient by ending "excessive remuneration" under the oldest renewable energy support schemes.
It also proposes freezing family benefits in 2027 in the draft Social Security financing bill.
The freeze is projected to save €500 million ($564 million).
"The amount of family benefits will be maintained in 2027 at its current level," the document seen by Le Figaro said.
Spending on the back-to-school allowance is also planned to be cut by €600 million.
The draft budget bill also proposes a tax on kerosene suppliers to finance the development of sustainable aviation fuel projects.
The government aims to cut the Social Security deficit from €21.8 billion ($24.6 billion) in 2026 to €12.7 billion ($14.3 billion) in 2027 through measures focused primarily on reducing spending.
It further plans to freeze the 2027 budget for personal housing assistance at its 2026 level and consider reforms affecting housing benefits and tax advantages for students from wealthier families.
The draft budget bill comes as France faces soaring public debt of €3.596 trillion ($4.06 trillion), according to recent figures cited by Le Monde.
The figure represents 119% of the country's GDP, a level France has not experienced since 1945.

This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:17:13 UTC
22:17:13 KST

This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough
- Date:
- October 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Surrey
- Summary:
- A proposed qubit made with superfluid helium could cut quantum computing error rates by around 100 times by shielding quantum information from common forms of electromagnetic noise. If experiments confirm the predictions, the technology could eventually work alongside today’s superconducting qubits or serve as a new kind of quantum memory.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a new kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.
The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.
Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors
Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.
Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.
In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.
Their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.
A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates
According to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.
Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, said:
"We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.
"The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test."
Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.
That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.
A Possible Role as Quantum Memory
One longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.
Dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, said:
"We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.
"Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system."
The Next Step Is Building a Prototype
The team now plans to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.
The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.
The project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Surrey. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Priya Sharma, Jens Koch, Eran Ginossar. Towards a micromechanical qubit based on quantized oscillations in superfluid helium. npj Quantum Information, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41534-026-01355-3

The New Development Bank Quietly Delivers During India’s BRICS Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

As India hosted the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026, a familiar question returned: does the grouping produce anything beyond summit statements? The New Development Bank (NDB) offers the clearest evidence in the affirmative. India first proposed the bank at an earlier BRICS summit in New Delhi in 2012, and its 2026 chairship of BRICS brought that idea full circle.
Judging a development bank is not simple; big announcements matter less than the money that actually reaches projects. The NDB’s record can thus be evaluated on three broad counts. The first is how much it has lent and how much of that money has actually been paid out. The second is whom the bank lends to. The third is how it raises the money it lends. On all three, the picture is more encouraging than the NDB’s low public profile suggests.
By the end of June 2026, the NDB had approved loans worth about $44 billion for 141 projects in clean energy, transport, water systems and digital infrastructure. Of that amount, roughly $25 billion had already been paid out to borrowers. The second figure is especially important. Many development banks approve large loans but pay out much less, and much more slowly. A bank that has paid out more than half of what it approved is doing real work, not just signing agreements.
The NDB’s public figures show what this money is building: 2,400 megawatts of clean energy capacity under way, 1,400 kilometers of tunnels and canals, 43 schools built or upgraded and a large increase in sewage treatment capacity.
The bank’s reach has also grown. Its founding members were Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa. It has since added Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, and Uzbekistan. Its members now stretch from South and Central Asia to Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America.
India’s place in the NDB is unusual. It helped create the bank, it owns an equal share of it, and it is one of its biggest borrowers. Each founding member holds about 18.7 percent of the bank’s capital. This was designed so that no single country could control it. Even so, India has used the bank’s loans more than most members.
Since 2016 the bank has approved 32 initiatives for India, worth close to $9.5 billion, in transport, social development, and clean energy. Lending has continued into 2026 also. Recent approvals include a $300 million clean energy project involving REC Limited and an affordable housing project backed by the Housing and Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO). Earlier, the bank provided $500 million towards the 82-km long rapid transit line between Delhi and Meerut. This is not aid. It is an ordinary lending relationship.
Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has described the NDB’s value less in terms of money and more in terms of shared knowledge. In August 2026, she said development banks should help countries plan cities and infrastructure better, not just pay for them. NDB President Dilma Rousseff, a former president of Brazil, replied by pointing to India’s Viksit Bharat development plans as a model for other members. It is a small but telling detail: the bank India proposed is now led by a Brazilian who uses Indian policy as an example for everyone else.
The third count, how the bank funds itself, is where India’s chairship of BRICS this year has left its clearest mark. In August 2026, the bank and the Indian government held a joint meeting on bringing more private money into development projects. Rousseff called this a key priority, as members look for ways to fund large infrastructure beyond what governments alone can pay for. Sitharaman’s point was simple: development banks can make projects safer and more predictable for private investors, which brings in more private money.
Two more steps followed. On September 10, two days before the BRICS summit opened, the bank raised 7 billion Chinese yuan through a bond sale in China. This gave it a new source of funds, separate from its usual channels. On the same day, it launched a BRICS-NDB knowledge portal linked to India’s chairship.
These steps will not make headlines outside financial circles. But they matter. A bank that can raise money in different markets and attract private investors does not have to wait for its member governments to put in more capital. That makes it a more reliable lender for developing countries. At the same time, however, relying more on Chinese bond markets may raise questions about whether the bank’s funding is spread evenly across its members.
The NDB can be an important source of finance for the Global South, helping countries build power plants, transport links and water systems. But development lending is slow work. It needs steady funding, careful planning, and trust between members. India’s chairship year has pushed the bank toward a broader funding base. Whether that shift lasts will become clearer in 2027, when India will host the bank’s annual meeting and this year’s results can be measured against what follows.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

Ahmad Adil
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
India on Thursday warned its citizens against being recruited in the Russian army amid the Ukraine war, calling it a “dangerous path.”
The External Affairs Ministry said in a statement that it continues to see reports that Indian nationals are being recruited into the Russian armed forces, and has on several occasions underlined the risks and dangers inherent in this course of action.
The ministry said it has come across numerous instances where individuals are willingly “seeking out offers to join the Russian armed forces with an understanding that they would be able to avail concomitant monetary benefits,” and later “secure release” by approaching the Indian government.
“It is reiterated that this is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government,” the ministry said.
It said there are several cases in which “individuals have approached Indian authorities to willingly give up their Indian citizenship, avail a Russian passport and then get recruited into the Russian armed forces.”
“It is advised that individuals should consider the gravity of such actions and understand the mortal dangers they are exposing themselves to,” the ministry said.
The Indian government, the statement said, remains “continuously engaged with the Russian side to ensure the safety, well-being and early discharge of all Indian nationals in the Russian armed forces.”
According to figures released last month, 227 Indian nationals have been recruited into the Russian army since the beginning of the war in 2022. Of them, 139 had been discharged from service, while 51 people died.
“This is an issue that we are in constant discussions with the Russian side,” Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri told reporters in New Delhi last month.

Issued on:
In an interview with FRANCE 24, UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix said the US continues to be "a very significant partner", despite owing $3 billion to peacekeeping. With the UN forced to cut about 25 percent of its capacity, Lacroix defended missions that cost just 0.2 percent of global military spending: "Peacekeeping is a good deal really."
Speaking to FRANCE 24 at UN headquarters in New York, Lacroix insisted the US "is and will be and has been a critical partner to peacekeeping", despite Washington owing $3 billion in past dues and Congress yet to decide on future funding. He stopped short of any prediction, saying simply: "I'm hopeful that this will continue to be the case." To those who find peacekeeping too expensive, Lacroix pointed out that its total cost this year will be "0.2 percent of military expenditures in the world". He said he is asking only for resources "that would be commensurate to the mandates that are given to us by the Security Council", warning that missions leaving too early are "very bad news for the population", as seen in Mali, Haiti and Darfur.
With UNIFIL, the UN's peacekeeping mission in Lebanon, due to shut down at the end of the year, the UN has submitted to the Security Council an option for a continued presence in Lebanon, at the request of the Lebanese authorities – a move opposed by Israel.
"The main point is that Lebanon needs international support," Lacroix said.

Travelodge guests are still at risk, finds review launched after sexual assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:10:40 UTC
22:10:40 KST

An independent review into Travelodge after a serious sexual assault has found that guests are still at risk, with room intrusions reported at nearly one in 10 of its hotels this summer.
The damning findings were published in a 70-page report on Thursday, which was commissioned earlier this year after a man was convicted of a serious sexual assault against a Travelodge guest in Maidenhead in 2022.
The perpetrator was handed a copy of the victim’s room key, having falsely claimed to be her boyfriend, and sexually assaulted her in her hotel bed. The victim – referred to as “Lily” in the report – was later offered what she described as an “insulting” £30 refund.
The incident prompted further reports of security failings at the hotel chain, eventually leading to the resignation of Joanna Boydell as chief executive in August.
Paul Greaney KC, the barrister who led the review, said Lily “was treated by Travelodge in a way that was inappropriate and unfair; indeed, it was disgraceful” He said the hotel’s response to her complaint “was driven by a desire to get rid of the complaint as quickly and cheaply as possible”.
The report said: “Travelodge’s treatment of Lily, following her complaint in writing, fell short of every standard the public would expect of an organisation such as Travelodge. It was simply appalling.
“Overall, these failings are extremely serious and rest principally with the organisation, rather than with any individual [member of staff].”
Greaney acknowledged that Travelodge had been trying to improve its room security policies and training since March. However, he said not enough had yet been done to ensure guests were safe.
Despite Travelodge strengthening its key security policy, Greaney found it was “not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground. In other words, it has not sufficiently embedded.”
“Even in this period of strong improvement, there were reports by guests of room intrusion across nearly one in 10 of Travelodge hotels, which represents around 60 hotels,” the report said.
“I am not satisfied that enough has yet occurred to make guests as safe as they should be when staying in a Travelodge,” Greaney added.
Although the review was focused on the budget chain’s failings, the KC said guests were suffering unacceptable security breaches in hotels across the country and room intrusions “are a problem across the hotel sector”.
The review put forward a series of recommendations, including:
- 
  Creating a new policy to address violence against women and girls.
- 
  Improving safety policies for staff working alone.
- 
  Introducing body cameras for all reception staff.
- 
  Installing consistent CCTV systems across all its hotels.
- 
  Introducing mystery shoppers to test its key security policy.
Travelodge said it welcomed the report’s recommendations, had put together a new board committee to ensure they were implemented and planned to track their progress over the next six to 12 months.
In a statement released alongside the review, Travelodge’s interim chief executive, Ray Reidy, said: “I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed, and particularly to Lily. We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go.
“We are working hard to transform our customer service so we respond appropriately when things don’t go right. We will continue to improve so customers get the right level of support and empathy when they need it most.”

Armenian premier says planned modular nuclear power plant may not meet growing energy needs
Unknown

2026-10-01

Burc Eruygur
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said on Thursday that the country’s planned modular nuclear power plant may not meet his country’s growing energy needs, state news agency Armenpress reported.
The premier told a press briefing that discussions continue within the government on the construction of a new nuclear power plant, and the country had an electricity surplus over a year ago.
But “one year later, Armenia has become a country with an electricity deficit. The fact that two AI factories have been established is not the issue. The issue is that the investment programs that have already been approved are of such a scale that Armenia now has an electricity deficit,” he said.
He said it has become necessary for Armenia to consider the “possibility of importing electricity and generating electricity from our sources,” recalling that previously he said they need “nothing more” than a modular nuclear power plant, which is small and can be rapidly deployed compared to a nuclear power plant.
“That has been our position. But now, due to this change, we have to understand that, most likely, a modular plant will not be enough for us,” Pashinyan added.
Armenia currently has one nuclear power plant, the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant (ANPP), which was commissioned in 1976.
The ANPP, which is also the South Caucasus region’s sole nuclear power plant, is about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) west of the capital and around 16 kilometers (10 miles) from border with Türkiye. The plant currently has a single operational power unit.
Another was shut down following a 6.8 magnitude earthquake in 1988 that killed at least 25,000 people and left hundreds of thousands homeless.
In recent years, Yerevan has been looking into the possibility of building a modular nuclear power plant to replace the ANPP, while also working to extend the already operational plant's life cycle.
Last month, Pashinyan said negotiations were continuing with several countries, including the US and Russia, for a new nuclear power plant.

Kremlin says states hosting nuclear weapons near Russian borders fuel escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:10:07 UTC
22:10:07 KST

Elena Teslova
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned on Thursday that countries deploying nuclear weapons near Russia's borders are adding fuel to escalation and tension.
Speaking at a press briefing in Moscow, Peskov said states agreeing to deploy nuclear weapons near Russia’s borders are deeply mistaken if they believe this will enhance their security.
"Those countries that reassure themselves by saying, ‘Let’s install and deploy nuclear weapons near the Russian borders,’ are deeply mistaken. This will not bring them any security, on the contrary, it will further lead to escalation and increased tensions,” he said.
Commenting on Putin’s recent letter to NATO warning of consequences from a blockade of Russia’s Kaliningrad region, Peskov said the message should not be viewed as confrontational.
"The letter and its publication should not be perceived as a confrontational statement," he said, drawing a parallel with Putin’s 2007 speech at the Munich Security Conference, which he said had also been widely perceived in the West as "confrontational."
Peskov said Kaliningrad is an integral part of Russia, and Moscow would ensure the security of the region in accordance with Russian law.
The official noted that Putin's warning came amid rapid militarization across Europe and the involvement of most European countries in the Ukraine conflict through arms and ammunition supplies and the provision of military instructors.
"If you take part in a war on someone’s side, you cannot avoid consequences of various kinds," he said.
Peskov said neither Ukraine nor Europe had moved closer to negotiations, adding that European countries continue to hinder the resumption of the negotiating process.
At the same time, he welcomed recent remarks by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on the need to use every opportunity for dialogue with Russia.
"Such a manifestation of political will for dialogue is undoubtedly a very positive phenomenon, we note and register it," he said, adding that such calls had so far not translated into practical steps or changed Europe’s anti-Russian and confrontational policy.
Peskov said European countries were developing their own security arrangements after concluding that NATO, led by the US, could no longer guarantee their security.
The official noted that Europe was building those arrangements on the same model as NATO.
"NATO was created in its genesis as a confrontational mechanism, it is not a mechanism aimed at ensuring security," he said.
Turning to contacts between Russia and US representatives, Pesko said they are continuing, with envoy Kirill Dmitriev discussing economic issues and the possibility of launching major projects in various sectors with his American counterparts.
"Indeed, implementing economic projects in various areas, including major ones, would be highly beneficial for both Russia and America," he said.
He said Washington continues to link such cooperation to a settlement in Ukraine.
Russia, meanwhile, believes economic projects could begin without waiting for a settlement, but dialogue with US representatives remains ongoing, he said.
"Americans, unfortunately, still link this entire process with the settlement in Ukraine, saying -- first the settlement, then the implementation of projects," he said. "We believe we could work for our mutual benefit right now and not wait, but contacts and dialogue are continuing, and this is quite a lengthy process."
Asked whether Russian citizens were aboard a Flydubai flight that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday while traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Peskov urged journalists to await information from the special services investigating the incident.
"The event happened only yesterday, and an investigation is now underway. We should show a little patience, and we will receive the information that the investigation considers possible to publish," he said.

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Brent oil prices will gradually decline to the range of $60-70 per barrel in 2027-2029 after the sharp increase this year driven by the Middle East situation, the Russian Finance Ministry said in the prepared guidelines for budget, tax, and customs and tariff policy for 2027 and the 2028-2029 planning period.

The long-term balance is also shifted toward lower prices due to the expected contraction in demand as vehicle fleet electrification expands and the role of renewable energy sources strengthens within the global energy balance structure, the ministry added.

====================================================================================================

Burnham is right that ‘hope comes from honesty’. That’s why Labour must make the case for rejoining the EU | Sadiq Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:04:31 UTC
22:04:31 KST

Hope again. That was the prime minister’s message to the country this week. A national social care system, greater public control of water and energy, help for first-time buyers and a crackdown on rogue landlords and empty homes. With clarity and conviction, Andy Burnham set out a bold plan to put Britain on a new path, steeped in Labour values.
It felt like a conference speech that would be remembered for years to come, marking a decisive break with a broken political model that has let British people down for decades. And perhaps most encouraging of all was the prime minister’s promise to rethink Britain’s relationship with the EU.
Burnham’s words were simple but stark: “Brexit has done more harm than good.” He is right – and the reality of the vote’s impact on the UK is sobering. Research commissioned by City Hall in 2024 showed that London’s economy was £30bn smaller than it would have been without Brexit and that there were nearly 2m fewer jobs overall in the UK as a result of us leaving. Earlier this year, we set out new analysis showing that our country has grown more slowly than our comparable European counterparts since 2016. If that trend continues, our economy could be £250bn smaller than similar EU countries’ by 2030.
Ten years after the referendum, the sunlit uplands promised by the Brexiters have proven to be a total fiction. Instead, Britain finds itself battling an economic and geopolitical storm.
Earlier this year, I warned that Donald Trump’s bombing of Iran could have catastrophic consequences for Londoners, and it gives me no pleasure to be proved right. The folly of this reckless war of choice is now clear for all to see. The conflict is sending shock waves through the global economy, hiking up mortgage costs and pushing up fuel prices. The price of diesel has hit an all-time high at nearly £2 per litre, while energy bills are forecast to rise 25% this winter, piling unbearable pressure on many households across the UK already grappling with a cost-of-living crisis.
At the same time, Trump’s fondness for unilateralism has shaken the foundations of the transatlantic alliance on which our national security depends. As Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, persists with his illegal and unconscionable full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Trump’s unpredictable actions and unsettling ambivalence towards European security can no longer be ignored.
In this geopolitical storm, Europe offers us not just a safe harbour, but a huge opportunity for growth. The EU is our biggest trading partner and our most reliable ally. That’s why, at the UK-EU summit in November, I will call on the government to lay the groundwork for Britain’s swift return to both the customs union and the single market – a move that should happen within this parliament.
Rejoining the customs union and the single market would deliver an immediate boost to economic growth, improving living standards for communities across the country and helping to grant Londoners some respite from the most acute cost of living pressures. In the long term, however, we must raise our ambitions higher still. Our party must immediately start making the case for rejoining the EU, so we can fight and win a general election with EU membership effectively on the ballot paper in 2029.
The brutal truth is that leaving the EU was the biggest act of economic and geopolitical self-harm in our country’s history. Rejoining is the only viable path to long-term prosperity and security. Anything less will fail to undo the severe damage that’s been done.
For far too long, the Labour party’s debate about Europe has been constrained by “red lines” that make rebuilding our relationship with the EU impossible. But Burnham has now recognised that these lines were drawn up for a different world.
In Canada, Mark Carney has set out his plan to partner much more closely with the EU on defence, critical minerals and energy security, with the country now on the path to becoming the bloc’s first associate member. In this multipolar world, middle powers such as Canada, the UK and our European neighbours must come together, both to safeguard our own security and economies and to stand up for free trade and our liberal democratic values.
Deeper integration can – and will – unlock a new age of growth and productivity, but it will also provide us with a louder voice on the world stage. From bolstering our military defences to safely developing AI and combating the climate crisis, if we are to make ourselves heard, we must speak as one. And in a world whose superpowers appear ever more comfortable with throwing their weight around, the EU is the only organisation with the economic and geopolitical heft to hold its own.
For me, the most memorable line in Burnham’s speech came a couple of minutes in: “Hope comes from honesty.” They were the words of a leader unafraid to change the terms of Britain’s dysfunctional political debate by taking on the seemingly intractable problems that too many would be inclined to avoid.
Today, Brexit is foremost among those problems. If we are to bring back hope, we must be honest about the disastrous costs of our decision to leave the EU. And we must be honest about the fact that reversing it is the best chance we have to get Britain back on track – and get the country firing on all cylinders again.
- 
  Sadiq Khan is mayor of London

Beneath Türkiye’s blue: A window into the region’s ancient maritime heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:03:19 UTC
22:03:19 KST

For a country better known internationally for its Byzantine and Ottoman landmarks and for ancient ruins scattered across its landscape, the scale of what lies beneath its waters is far less familiar to outsiders.
Shipwrecks, cargoes of copper ingots, ancient amphorae and bronze weapons are among the finds recovered from Türkiye’s waters, which for millennia carried ships between the civilizations of Anatolia, the Aegean, the Levant and Egypt.
The country has more than 8,300 kilometers (5,157 miles) of coastline bordering four seas — the Mediterranean, Aegean, Marmara and Black seas — placing it at the intersection of several major maritime routes.
Its southern and western shores in particular were part of the ancient Eastern Mediterranean trading world.
We have detected and documented more than 430 shipwrecks along Türkiye's Mediterranean coast alone, said Hakan Oniz, an underwater archaeologist at Akdeniz University in Antalya, southern Türkiye.
"This is an amazing number of documented shipwrecks all over the world, not only for Türkiye," he said.
The modern history of underwater archaeology is closely tied to Türkiye’s coasts.
First spotted by a Turkish sponge diver in the 1950s, the Cape Gelidonya shipwreck off Antalya was excavated by American archaeologist George Bass in 1960.
It is regarded as the first scientific excavation of an ancient shipwreck conducted on the seabed.
But Oniz argues that the story may go back further.
“In a way, Türkiye is the birthplace of underwater archaeology,” he told Anadolu. “However, the Ottoman Empire conducted underwater excavations 70 years before George Bass.”
In the 1890s, Osman Hamdi Bey -- the Ottoman painter, archaeologist and founding director of the Istanbul Archaeology Museums -- ordered archaeological work around Farmakonisi, known today as Bulamac Island, in the Aegean.
Ottoman archival research records the hiring of divers to search for antiquities there in 1891, with finds subsequently sent to Istanbul. Some of the gold coins recovered there are still kept in Istanbul’s collections.
Just as significant, Oniz argues, was the legal framework Osman Hamdi Bey helped put in place.
The Ottoman antiquities regulation of 1884, known as Asar-i Atika, represented one of the world’s earliest state legal frameworks explicitly addressing archaeological material found underwater.
The regulation was a response to the large-scale extraction and export of antiquities by foreign excavators.
By legally declaring antiquities found in Ottoman territory -- including those recovered from the sea -- as state property, the regulation effectively banned their unauthorized removal from the empire.
Off Kas, the Uluburun wreck is one of the best known.
Discovered in 1982 and excavated over 11 years, it yielded one of the richest and most diverse Bronze Age cargoes ever found: about 10 tons of copper and 1 ton of tin ingots, glass ingots, ebony logs, elephant and hippopotamus ivory, and a gold scarab bearing the name of the Egyptian queen Nefertiti.
A very different kind of discovery came to light in Istanbul, and not by diving at all. Construction of the Marmaray rail project led archaeologists to the buried remains of the Theodosian Harbour at Yenikapi, a Byzantine-era port that had gradually filled with sediment and disappeared from view.
Archaeologists eventually recovered 37 shipwrecks dating from the 5th to the 11th centuries, constituting the biggest collection of medieval ships uncovered at a single excavation site, along with traces of a Neolithic settlement dating back roughly 8,000 years.
Oniz and his team are now working on three shipwreck sites along the Antalya coast, using research vessels equipped with remotely operated underwater vehicles, or ROVs, to reach sites tens of meters down.
The oldest of those sites lies near the Kekova islands, an area more familiar to visitors for its partly submerged ancient ruins than for what sits deeper down. There, an Early Bronze Age wreck carrying Levantine-type amphorae is being investigated.
Not far away, off Kumluca, a second Bronze Age ship, roughly 3,600 years old, was found carrying copper ingots believed to have come from the island of Cyprus.
Oniz maintains that both the Kekova and Kumluca wrecks predate the two Bronze Age ships that first put Türkiye on the map for underwater archaeologists, Uluburun and Cape Gelidonya, both of which are dated to several centuries later.
The third site, known as the "Ceramic Wreck" off Adrasan, belongs to a much later period. Oniz's team has dated it to the late Hellenistic or early Roman era, saying it was carrying hundreds of plates, trays and bowls, each packed in raw clay to survive the journey from the port of Rhosus near Antioch toward Rome.
Oniz said a coin recovered recently from the site helped narrow the ship's date to the middle of the first century B.C., placing it in the years when the Roman statesman Cicero governed the nearby province of Cilicia.
"It's very exciting," he added.
On Monday, Turkish Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced the new discovery of 122 different forms and sizes of plates, bowls and trays at the excavation site, reflecting the period’s luxury dining culture.
The excavations are also part of a broader expansion of archaeological work under the Culture and Tourism Ministry's Legacy to the Future program, launched in 2023.
By 2025, the program covered 255 excavation sites in 65 provinces, with more than 15,000 finds brought into the scientific record.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy himself has also joined archaeologists underwater, diving to several shipwreck sites to see the work firsthand.
The growing number of underwater excavations is also prompting new efforts to preserve and display the finds on land.
The Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology, established in 1964, remains the country's main museum dedicated to the field. Its collections include finds from major wrecks such as Uluburun, Yassiada and Serce Limani.
New museum projects are also planned in Istanbul and Antalya.
In Antalya's Kemer district, construction is underway on a Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum at the ancient site of Idyros, designed to bring discoveries from the region's seabed together.
In Istanbul, the redevelopment of the historic Haydarpasa railway station is also incorporating a “Four Seas Museum” concept centered on Türkiye's maritime heritage across the Mediterranean, Aegean, Marmara and Black seas.
The museum would be curated by Luca Molinari, a former Venice Biennale curator, and would display artifacts from all 81 of Türkiye's provinces across roughly 10,000 square meters of exhibition space, alongside an archaeological park on the station grounds.
Türkiye is also working to recover cultural artifacts smuggled abroad.
Since 1980, more than 26,000 cultural artifacts have been repatriated to Türkiye.

On Wednesday, a Russian drone struck the grounds of Kyiv’s Institute for Nuclear Research, where a research nuclear reactor is located, Ukraine’s nuclear regulator said.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A fire caused by the attack was quickly extinguished, with no casualties reported. Investigators and specialists continued assessing the damage.
Reactor undamaged and radiation levels normal
The VVR-M research reactor and systems essential to its safety were not damaged, according to the regulator.
Radiation monitoring recorded no changes following the strike. Radiation levels remained within the natural background range of 0.16 to 0.20 microsieverts per hour.
The reactor has been shut down since February 2022 as a precaution against wartime nuclear risks. Its active zone has been completely unloaded, meaning it currently contains no nuclear fuel.
Operations at the facility have since been limited to scheduled maintenance of systems important for nuclear and radiation safety.
“An attack by a [unmanned aerial vehicle] UAV on the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research is an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility that performs exclusively scientific and research functions,” the regulator said.
It described the strike as another violation of internationally recognized nuclear and radiation safety principles, characterizing it as a war crime.
UAE Government Used Sanctioned Russian ‘Shadow’ Airline
Institute conducts peaceful nuclear research
The Institute for Nuclear Research of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences is one of the country’s leading research institutions in nuclear physics, nuclear energy, and radioecology.
Its VVR-M reactor serves as a neutron source for fundamental and applied nuclear physics research.
The institute also operates particle accelerators and laboratories used for research in radiation physics, nuclear technologies, and reactor materials.
Russia continues attacks on Kyiv
The strike on the institute occurred during an extended series of Russian attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions.
On Wednesday, Russia launched its first mass combined attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since the end of the previous heating season, using missiles and drones against facilities in Kyiv, the surrounding region and elsewhere. The assault affected 11 regions, killing five people, including a child, and injuring 14.
Russian attacks on the capital continued into Thursday. A drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while children were sheltering during an air raid alert, damaging the third floor and causing a fire. The children were not injured, and firefighters extinguished the blaze. Russian forces also struck warehouse facilities in the same district.
Later on Thursday, two Russian drone strikes hit near the supports of Kyiv’s Pivdennyi (South) Bridge, forcing authorities to suspend metro and surface public transport across the bridge. Municipal specialists began inspecting the structure, while social media claims that a drone struck as a metro train was crossing, blowing out windows in one of its cars.
Previously, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that Russia has launched a renewed campaign of mass assaults against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter.
“Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day when the enemy did not attack energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack took place for the first time since the end of the previous heating season,” he said.
The strikes damaged and destroyed energy equipment, although Koretskyi did not disclose which facilities were hit or the extent of the damage. He said he was awaiting a detailed report on the condition of the equipment and the expected timeframe for repairs.
The attacks also disrupted electricity supplies in the capital and the surrounding Kyiv region. DTEK said emergency power cuts were introduced in Kyiv on Ukrenergo’s instructions, meaning regular schedules temporarily did not apply. The capital was later returned to scheduled stabilization outages, while planned power-cut schedules were also introduced across the Kyiv region on Wednesday.

US and Royal Navy crews train for sea rescue off Scotland
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:02:23 BST
22:02:23 KST

Royal Navy helicopter crews have trained with the Kentucky Air National Guard off the Scottish coast in a multinational search-and-rescue exercise involving US C-130J Super Hercules aircraft and Merlin helicopters, according to the Royal Navy.
Personnel from 814 Naval Air Squadron joined the US unit during a deployment to Prestwick Airport, where four C-130J aircraft, around 60 personnel and approximately 62,000lb of equipment were based for a series of training events with UK and Canadian forces. The Kentucky Air National Guard deployment was intended to test its ability to operate alongside NATO partners in unfamiliar terrain and airspace, with activities including aerial refuelling, formation flying, low-level flying and rapid-reaction departures.
Prestwick also provided the unit with immediate access to maritime training areas. The Kentucky Air National Guard is based in Louisville, well inland from the US east coast, while Prestwick’s runway lies close to the Firth of Clyde. That allowed the Americans to conduct open-water personnel recovery training with Swordfish Flight from 814 Naval Air Squadron.
During the exercise, C-130 crews first located personnel in a life raft before dropping an inflatable motorboat nearby. Special Tactics Airmen then entered the water, deployed the boat and provided first aid before coordinating with the Royal Navy helicopter crew to recover the casualty by winch. The training gave both sides an opportunity to practise maritime personnel recovery procedures while working with different aircraft, equipment and operating methods.
According to a news update from the Royal Navy, Lieutenant Colonel Reinke, a C-130 pilot and mission commander, said: “The integration with the Royal Navy was one of the highlights of the exercise.”
A pararescue flight chief from the Special Tactics team said conditions off Scotland differed substantially from those normally encountered during training in the United States.
“It’s a lot colder here, and the salt water is an unusual factor for us,” he said. “The Royal Navy also uses different geolocation methods, and they have different tactics and techniques than we typically employ.”
The US personnel also encountered differences in aircraft behaviour, including the stronger rotor wash generated by the Merlin compared with the Black Hawk helicopters they more commonly work with.
“Those are the kinds of things you don’t anticipate, but we were able to work through them and figure out what worked best for their guys and for us,” the Airman said. “We had to be flexible on the spot to get the mission done.”
814 Naval Air Squadron is normally associated with anti-submarine warfare operations, with its Merlin helicopters deployed from Royal Navy frigates and Royal Fleet Auxiliary vessels in support of maritime task groups.
Swordfish Flight Commander Lieutenant Cass said: “This complex personnel recovery and search and rescue training ensures crews remain proficient in recovering those in need during challenging conditions.”
He added: “Swordfish Flight thoroughly enjoyed training with the Kentucky Air National Guard. This vital training strengthens our ability to work with each other and reinforces the close defence relationship between NATO allies.
“We hope to continue working with our friends across the pond in the years to come.”

From breakfast pancakes to dinner sides and pudding: Alissa Timoshkina’s apple recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:00:51 UTC
22:00:51 KST

Few ingredients are as familiar as apples, yet few carry such symbolic weight. Peaking just as the season’s begin to turn, they are the ultimate symbol of nature’s abundance, imbued with a sense of nostalgia for the retreating sunlight. The symbolism became unexpectedly tangible to me during a recent autumn apple-picking trip with my family: surrounded by branches heavy with fruit, I found myself seeing the humble apple with fresh awe. It looked nothing short of nature’s miracle. Native to the mountains of central Asia, near the modern Kazakhstan-China border, it has travelled further than perhaps any other fruit, becoming at home in cuisines from Normandy to New York, Caucasus to Kashmir. Sweet or savoury, everyday or celebratory, the apple is truly universal. Its versatility always reminds me of the simple joy of cooking with the seasons.
Breakfast apple oladky (pictured top)
Prep 10 min
 Cook 25 min
 Makes 24, to serve 6
200g plain flour, sifted 
1 shy tsp baking powder
  ¼ tsp bicarbonate of soda
  A pinch of cinnamon 
  A pinch of fine sea salt 
  1 medium egg (50g)
  200ml whole milk
  50g unsalted butter, melted, plus extra for frying
3 sweet apples, cored, then 1 grated and 2 thinly sliced on a mandoline 
2 tbsp runny honey, plus extra for serving 
Neutral oil, for frying 
Greek yoghurt, for serving
In a bowl, mix all the dry ingredients together, then in a separate bowl whisk the wet ones, including the grated apple.
Gently fold the wet and dry ingredients together with a silicone spatula – make sure you don’t over mix it. Leave to rest at room temperature for five minutes, or until you see bubbles appear.
Heat a frying pan on a low-medium heat, and add enough oil to coat it evenly. Scoop up the batter (about 15-20g per oladky) and drop it into the pan – it should start sizzling straight away. Depending on the size of your pan, you should be able to cook around four oladky at the same time.
Fry them on one side for 40 seconds, adding a few slices of apple on top halfway through cooking.
Flip them over, adding a teaspoon of butter to help the apples soften and caramelise, and continue cooking undisturbed for 90 seconds to two minutes, until the pancakes have puffed up and the apples are caramelised.
Repeat with the remaining batter and apple slices. Serve with Greek yoghurt and a drizzle of honey.
Roast chicken salad with kale, fennel, pickled apples and tahini ‘mayo’
Prep 20 min
Rest 30 min
 Cook 15 min
 Serves 4
For the salad
150-200g kale, washed and stalks removed
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil 
Flaky sea salt and black pepper
Juice of ¼ lemon
  1 granny smith apple, thinly sliced on a mandolin
2 celery sticks, sliced diagonally into long wedges 
1 small fennel bulb, trimmed and thinly sliced on a mandoline
25g flat-leaf parsley, leaves picked, plus extra to garnish 
1 roast chicken breast (about 200g), or equivalent chicken meat leftover from a roast, shredded 
2 tbsp toasted sunflower seeds, to garnish 
 For the pickle 
  4 tbsp apple cider vinegar 
  Juice of ½ lemon
1 tbsp runny honey 
  A pinch of flaky sea salt 
1 granny smith, finely diced 
For the tahini mayo 
150ml tahini 
  3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  Juice of ½ lemon
  1 tbsp runny honey
  1 tbsp apple cider vinegar
Flaky sea salt, to taste 
Pickle brine (see above) 
  1 ice cube, or 2 tsp of ice-cold water 
Start by making the pickle. In a medium jar, mix two tablespoons of cold water, the vinegar, lemon juice, honey and salt. Add the diced apple and shake well to combine. Leave to rest in the fridge for about 30 minutes.
Next, prep the kale. Massage the kale with the olive oil, salt and lemon juice in a large bowl until wilted. Set aside.
 To make the tahini mayo, add the first six ingredients into a mixing bowl, finishing with all the apple pickle brine. Start mixing slowly with a fork; if the paste gets too thick or splits, add an ice cube or ice-cold water and continue stirring gently, until you reach a silky consistency (you will!).
Back to the salad. To the bowl with the kale, add the fresh and pickled apples, celery, fennel, parsley and chicken. Add a third of the tahini dressing and give everything a gentle toss.
Transfer the salad to a large bowl or sharing platter, drizzle over the tahini sauce in wriggly lines, then scatter over the sunflower seeds and extra torn parsley leaves. Finish with an extra sprinkle of sea salt and a generous crack of black pepper. You will have some tahini dressing left over; serve this in the jar alongside.
Duck legs with braised sauerkraut, apples and cranberries
Prep 10 min
 Cook 2 hr
 Serves 4
1-2 tbsp duck fat
  4 duck legs, at room temperature
Sea salt and black pepper
2 red onions, peeled and thinly sliced 
1 tsp caraway seeds 
  1 tsp dried thyme 
  200ml red wine 
½ small red cabbage, shredded 
650g jar sauerkraut with brine 
  3 red apples, sliced into chunky wedges (about 6-8 each)
1 orange, zest and juice 
2 tbsp dried cranberries 
  1 tsp sugar 
  4 bay leaves
  400ml stock (vegetable or chicken)
Melt a tablespoon of the duck fat in a heavy-based casserole. Pat the duck legs dry and salt on both sides, then place them in the casserole skin side down and sear on a medium-high heat for 10 minutes, to achieve a seductive crispy skin. Transfer the legs to a plate and set aside while you get on with the rest.
Depending on how fatty the duck legs are, add another tablespoon of duck fat to the casserole. Lower the heat to medium, and fry the onion with a pinch of salt, the caraway and thyme for eight to 10 minutes.
Deglaze the pan by adding the wine and scraping off any delicious bits of fat and onion that might be stuck to the pan. Cook with the lid off for a minute. Next, add the remaining ingredients, stir well to combine and bring to a gentle simmer.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the duck legs on top of the cabbage, skin side up, cover with a lid, and put in the oven for 90 minutes, or until tender.
The dish goes down a treat as is (with a glass of red wine, of course), or add some creamy mash or roast potatoes for an extra comforting autumnal meal.
Fermented apple salsa
This is a very versatile ferment: add it to salads or egg mayo (instead of capers), use it to top avocado or layer into a cheese toastie filling.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 15 min
 Ferment 3 days+
 Makes 1 x 1.5L jar
For the apple salsa
3 large granny smith apples, cored and diced
2 spring onions, trimmed, white and green parts finely sliced
100g white grapes, quartered
2 celery sticks, diced 
1 jalapeño, seeds and pith removed, flesh finely diced
10g fresh dill, stems and fronds finely chopped
1 tsp fennel seeds
For the brine
  7g fine, non-iodized sea salt (roughly 1½ level tsp)
350ml filtered water
 Sterilise a 1.5L jar by running it through the dishwasher, then let it cool down before handling. Mix all the apple salsa ingredients in a bowl to make sure everything is well distributed. Make the brine by dissolving the salt in the water.
Pack the jar tightly with the apple mix, and top with the brine, leaving about two fingers’ worth of space at the top (for the weight). Put a fermentation weight on top, close the lid and place in a small bowl to catch any leakages. Leave at room temperature and out of direct sunlight for three to six days, depending on how warm the room is.
The salsa is ready when the brine becomes effervescent and the apples acquire a pleasant, piquant, sour quality. At this point, remove the weight, and transfer to the fridge. The salsa will keep in the fridge for up to three months.
Ukrainian baked rice pudding with apples, cinnamon and raisins
Prep 5 min
 Cook 1 hr
 Serves 4
200g long-grain rice
  750ml whole milk
  A pinch of salt
  50g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing and dotting
2 medium apples (gala, cox’s, braeburn, for example), cored and diced
50g raisins
Zest of 1 medium orange
1 tsp ground cinnamon, plus extra for dusting
2 large eggs
50g caster sugar
1 tsp vanilla extract
Rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear. Then, in a saucepan, combine the rice with the milk and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 18–20 minutes, until the rice is soft and creamy and most of the milk has been absorbed. It might feel like a lot of milk at first, but it will work.
Meanwhile, melt the butter in a frying pan and saute the diced apples with the raisins, orange zest and cinnamon for five to seven minutes, until slightly softened. In a large bowl, beat the eggs with the sugar and vanilla extract.
When the rice is cooked, let it cool slightly before stirring it into the egg mixture, followed by the sauteed apples, raisins and orange zest, until well combined.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6 and grease a 20cm × 30cm ovenproof dish with butter. Pour the rice mixture into the dish, smoothing the top and dotting with small pieces of butter. Bake for 30–40 minutes, until the top is golden and set. Cool slightly before serving, dusted with extra cinnamon, if desired.

Losing deep belly fat may slow brain aging and protect memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:00:40 UTC
22:00:40 KST

Losing deep belly fat rather than just overall body weight is linked to slower brain aging and better cognitive function years later. The research, published in Nature Communications, suggests that targeting this specific type of fat might help protect the brain from age-related decline.
Visceral fat wraps deep around internal organs, while subcutaneous fat sits just beneath the skin and is more visible. Visceral fat is highly metabolically active and frequently releases inflammatory molecules that can travel and affect the whole body, including the brain. Previous research linked high visceral fat to cognitive decline, but it remained unknown if actively losing this fat could protect brain structure over the long term. Scientists needed to determine if reducing this specific fat depot offered lasting neurological benefits.
Lead authors Dafna Pachter and Hadar Klein, along with corresponding author Iris Shai and colleagues from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev in Israel, conducted the research. They wanted to understand if sustained reductions in specific fat depots could preserve brain health. To investigate this, they utilized a wealth of long-term data from several earlier clinical trials.
The researchers first looked at 533 adults who had participated in four dietary and lifestyle trials five to sixteen years earlier. These participants, who were mostly male and in their early sixties, underwent magnetic resonance imaging to measure both their brain volume and abdominal fat. They also completed the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, a standard test used to detect cognitive impairment.
The team found that individuals with lower amounts of visceral fat scored consistently higher on the cognitive tests. This relationship was heavily influenced by brain volume, with the negative association between visceral fat and cognitive scores appearing most pronounced in people who had relatively preserved brain structures. Body mass index, a standard measure of weight relative to height, did not show these same relationships with cognitive performance or brain structure. This suggests that body mass index alone might not capture the specific neurodegenerative risks posed by deep abdominal fat.
Next, the team examined a subset of 295 participants who had complete abdominal fat data across three time points. These measurements were taken at the start of their original trial, at eighteen months, and at a final follow-up several years later. The researchers calculated the cumulative exposure to abdominal fat over the years for each individual.
The results showed that long-term exposure to high levels of visceral fat predicted lower cognitive test scores. In contrast, cumulative exposure to subcutaneous fat did not show this negative relationship with memory and cognition. This difference highlights the unique metabolic risks associated with visceral fat compared to fat stored under the skin.
The researchers then analyzed whether the initial fat lost during the eighteen-month trials predicted later brain health. For 297 participants, they compared the change in fat during the intervention to brain scans taken five to ten years later. A greater reduction in visceral fat during the trial predicted higher total brain volume at the long-term follow-up.
Reductions in visceral fat also predicted greater gray matter volume. Gray matter contains most of the brain’s neuronal cell bodies and is highly involved in processing sensory information, muscle control, and decision making. The analysis also showed that reductions in the proportion of visceral fat were associated with a healthier hippocampus. The hippocampus is a brain region central to learning and memory, and it is often one of the first areas affected by cognitive decline.
Reductions in superficial and deep subcutaneous fat during the intervention showed no such relationship with later brain structure. The relative change in body mass index during the intervention also did not predict long-term brain volume. This points to the specific role of visceral fat in neurodegeneration.
The team also evaluated 188 participants who underwent repeated brain scans at baseline, eighteen months, and five years. They tracked the rate at which the brain shrank over time, comparing it to the participants’ cumulative visceral fat exposure. People with higher long-term visceral fat experienced a faster rate of brain atrophy across multiple regions.
These individuals also showed a faster expansion of the brain’s ventricles. Ventricles are fluid-filled spaces in the brain that grow larger as surrounding brain tissue is lost. To understand the biological mechanism at play, the researchers tested various blood markers to see how they related to longitudinal brain changes.
They found that baseline levels of fasting blood sugar and a marker of long-term blood sugar control were the only metabolic factors related to the long-term brain changes. Lipid and inflammatory markers did not show this relationship over time. This suggests that the way visceral fat disrupts blood sugar regulation and insulin sensitivity may be the primary path through which it harms the brain. When visceral fat levels drop, improved glycemic control might alleviate stress on brain tissues.
Readers should note that the study population was eighty-six percent male and mostly overweight or obese. This might limit how well the findings apply to women or individuals with lower body weight. While the initial fat loss occurred during randomized controlled trials, the long-term follow-up was observational.
Because the participants’ habits after the trials ended were not strictly controlled, the study cannot definitively prove cause and effect for the long-term data. The researchers accounted for the participants’ diets during the follow-up period, but post-trial lifestyle choices could still influence the outcomes. The study also did not measure fat accumulation in organs like the liver and pancreas, which could play a role in brain health.
Future studies incorporating these measurements and specific biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s will help clarify the exact biological pathways linking abdominal fat to brain aging. These findings address a gap in the field, identifying visceral fat as a distinct, modifiable risk factor for neurodegeneration.
The study, “Sustained visceral fat loss is associated with attenuated brain atrophy and improved cognitive function in late midlife,” was authored by Dafna Pachter, Hadar Klein, Omer Kamer, Dana Tamar Goldberg Toren, Liav Alufer, Noa Ebstein Karamani, Tomer Atlas, Amit Yaary, Idan Hagbi, Yoash Chassidim, Ilan Shelef, Moti Salti, Frauke Beyer, Veronica Witte, Assaf Rudich, Uri Yoel, Gal Ben-Arie, Anat Yaskolka Meir, Alon Kaplan, Gal Tsaban, Hila Zelicha, Carmi Bartal, Lu Qi, Matthias Blüher, Michael Stumvoll, Uta Ceglarek, Berend Isermann, Dong D. Wang, Meir J. Stampfer, Frank B. Hu, Galia Avidan, and Iris Shai.
