Mike Flanagan's Timely Carrie Is the First Worthwhile Adaptation in 50 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

Everyone knows what happens in Carrie. Fifty-two years after its publication, the novel that ignited Stephen King’s career has so thoroughly engulfed the culture, you’d have to be almost as sheltered as Carietta White herself not to have absorbed its most indelible images. The locker-room tampon gauntlet and “Plug it up!” chant. Carrie’s smothering holy-roller mom, locking her up in prayer-closet solitary confinement. The eerily unlikely prom date. The swinging bucket that has haunted every coronation of school-dance royalty in film and TV since Brian De Palma first adapted the book in 1976.
It’s a tale as old as time: Warped by her mother’s zealotry and scapegoated since childhood by her classmates, 16-year-old Carrie has a late, traumatic menarche that reactivates her latent telekinetic abilities. Then, after accepting a pity date to the prom, she’s crowned queen and immediately gets pig’s blood dumped on her head by a resentful bully. The humiliation causes her to lay waste to the school and then the town, using her powers to exact revenge.
King’s book and De Palma’s film became classics of the horror genre. No less venerable a critic than Pauline Kael wrote of Sissy Spacek’s Oscar-nominated portrayal: “I don’t see how this performance could be any better.” Yet in the 21st century, new interpreters keep trying to improve upon it. With platforms scrambling to capitalize on popular IP, it’s no mystery why this would sound like a good idea to Hollywood executives. But something else must be inspiring high-minded filmmakers like Boys Don’t Cry director Kimberly Peirce, who released a divisive remake in 2013, to keep resurrecting Carrie.
The fourth screen adaptation of the novel (unless you count the pitiful 1999 sequel, The Rage: Carrie 2) is an eight-episode Prime Video series created by Mike Flanagan, who is known both for riffing on horror touchstones in Netflix hits like The Haunting of Hill House and The Fall of the House of Usher and for his features based on King novels like Gerald’s Game and Doctor Sleep. Premiering Oct. 7, his ambitious Carrie is the first that manages to fully get out from under the shadow of De Palma’s. Yet it confirms a gradual shift in how the story is being told. What was once an account of an abusive mother and an evil bully unwittingly uniting to create a lethal monster has become, with each new incarnation, more like an indictment of society as a whole.
All three Carrie movies are mostly faithful to the novel, dutifully reproducing every major plot point and set piece, as well as a lot of dialogue. King’s writing is remarkably cinematic, which is probably why he’s our most adapted living author. But every Carrie is also a product of its time. De Palma, whose masterfully crafted version turns 50 in November, seems to lust after and fear the female body in equal measure—a common response within what was then a male-dominated genre to the feminist upheavals of the ’70s. It’s hard to imagine a contemporary adaptation pairing its opening credits with a steamy, slow-motion parade of nude high school girls in their locker room. A 2002 made-for-TV movie written by cult creator Bryan Fuller (Hannibal) is a relic of an era when the only things teen girls loved more than low-rise denim were movies where female misfits get glow ups (She’s All That, 10 Things I Hate About You, Jawbreaker). Just over a decade later, Peirce incorporated smartphones and YouTube, as well as an emerging pop-feminist sensibility that traced the derangement of Carrie’s mom, Margaret (played here by Julianne Moore), to childbirth trauma and found a palpably empowered Carrie actively choosing who to kill and who to save.
You can find support for each of these readings in King’s own reflections. “The book is, in its more adult implications, an uneasy masculine shrinking from a future of female equality,” he wrote in his 1981 nonfiction book Danse Macabre. “For me, Carrie White is a sadly misused teenager, an example of the sort of person whose spirit is so often broken for good in that pit of man- and woman-eaters that is your normal suburban high school. But she's also Woman, feeling her powers for the first time and, like Samson, pulling down the temple on everyone in sight.” In her influential 1992 study Men, Women, and Chain Saws: Gender in the Modern Horror Film, the scholar Carol J. Clover suggests that this tangle of intentions explains the broad and, in some ways, contradictory appeal of Carrie across genders. Its protagonist is, at once, a projection of female power and male fear and the universal horror of bullying.
Despite feeling mostly redundant, the two features released after Clover’s book shared a new emphasis. De Palma’s stylish ’70s chiller played up the ghoulishness of Margaret (a bellowing, vicious Piper Laurie) and of Carrie’s chief tormentor at school, the sadistic mean girl Chris Hargensen (Nancy Allen), as well as the otherworldly oddness of Spacek’s lead. But Fuller’s and especially Peirce’s films sand down those characters’ excesses, revealing motivations and vulnerabilities that make them harder to hate or fear. (The latter faced criticism for casting the conventionally beautiful, preternaturally confident Chloë Grace Moretz in the title role.) At the same time, we see the condescending assumptions behind the actions of ostensibly heroic figures like Sue Snell, the popular girl who tries to atone for hazing Carrie by sending her boyfriend to the prom with her. In these movies, Carrie’s reign of terror is the ultimate expression of the school’s brokenness. As the critic Matt Zoller Seitz wrote in a favorable review of the 2013 version: “The first Carrie was horror. This is tragedy.”
If the 21st century Carrie movies spoke to a post-Columbine era of school shootings, then Flanagan’s series is a product of the Trump decade, in which seemingly every aspect of American life has fractured along bipartisan political lines. The educational realm has become a crucible for debates around censorship, technology, parental rights, gun control, LGBTQ inclusion, critical race theory, the teaching of science vs. religion, social media. Which explains how Flanagan and his creative team, which includes many female writers and directors, found in this slight story eight episodes’ worth of material.
Without omitting any of the moments King fans will anticipate, they depart pretty boldly from the text. This Carrie opens with the death of Carrie’s conspiracy-theorist father (who, in previous versions, she never got to know) in a bizarre accident on his construction site. Somehow, no one knows he had a wife (Flanagan regular Samantha Sloyan, locating the wounded soul of a character who’s always been more of a caricature) and daughter (a movingly fragile Summer H. Howell) until they’re found cowering at home, in the closet where they pray. The previously homeschooled Carrie is forced to enroll at the local public high school while Margaret gets a job at a soulless big-box store, where her refusal to ring up a sex toy gets her demoted to cleaning toilets.
An almost saintly figure who believes in kindness most of all, Carrie develops complicated friendships with smart, benevolent Sue (Siena Agudong) and Chris (Alison Thornton)—who has been spiraling since her mom moved in with a classmate’s dad and her own father’s financial woes have jeopardized her college plans. What she doesn’t know is that Chris is behind an anonymous social media account that posted footage of her locker-room nightmare before expanding to target practically everyone at school, teachers included. A constant nuisance to the administration, Margaret harangues Principal Grayle (Matthew Lillard) to intervene. But he dithers, questioning whether the free speech of kids on a platform external to school is his jurisdiction.
The problem isn’t that Grayle doesn’t care; he’s a kindhearted guy who wants the best for his students. So do other adults, like the girls’ young gym teacher (Amber Midthunder), who’s horrified by the “Plug it up!” incident, and empathetic school counselor (Somebody Somewhere sweetheart Tim Bagley). Even Margaret, an archetypal Karen with MAHA tendencies who becomes a vlogging parents’ rights crusader, is sincerely trying to help a daughter she cherishes. She’s not wrong to point out that a world where, for example, children are shot in their classrooms is an abomination. But meaning well is not enough. Fights, protests, and parental panics ensue. By prom night, whose carnage is now so unsurprising that Flanagan flashes forward to it in the opening scene, the place has already metaphorically exploded. Carrie only makes it literal.
For everything of value it adds to the story, Flanagan’s take can still feel a bit cluttered. There are too many interconnected framing devices, from on-camera interviews with survivors of Carrie’s massacre to history lessons on Joan of Arc. If you watched House of Usher, which filters the downfall of a Sackler-like family of opioid profiteers through the sieve of Poe’s Gothic tale, you’re probably aware that Flanagan’s social commentary can be blunt. His Carrie can get bogged down in meetings and assemblies where characters representing different facets of Trump-era vitriol and complacency monologue on what’s really wrong with the world today.
Yet at the core of this series is a perceptive diagnosis of that problem. More than individual bad actors who need to be brought down, there are people like Grayle and Margaret and Sue, whose pure intentions are undermined by complacency, indecision, disinformation, conformity, fear—all of it amplified to a potentially global scale by social media. Even Chris is lashing out as a direct result of her family’s dissolution and her father’s money troubles, which erode the class privileges to which she feels entitled. Amid extreme rhetoric, Flanagan implies, everyone who doesn’t work hard to avert atrocities is complicit in them. And there's precious little evidence that most of us are doing much to examine that complicity. Tragedy becomes, specifically, a tragedy of the commons as selfishness metastasizes into a scourge on the entire town. And Carrie becomes something between Frankenstein’s monster and Jesus Christ: an innocent persecuted for the sins of all mankind, but one whose all-too-human impulse to seek retribution incinerates any hope of forgiveness.

Amazon Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft 2026: Specs, Price, Release Date
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.
On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.
The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.
It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:
Lighter and Premium
The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.
The base Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster page turns than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. The screen refreshes 30 percent faster than the base Kindle, and the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.
Amazon says the new Kindles are also compliant with the European Union’s new battery regulations, meaning they should be easier to remove and replace.
Upgrading to the Signature Edition for both nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.
Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.
Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.
Kindle Ablaze
The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of product, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.
At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.
Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).
While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.
Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.
“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”
For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook) saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.
Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.
“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”
For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.
“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.
As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.
“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”
So, probably not.

Amazon's Prime Day has returned for its fall edition, and the Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?
There's already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it's a question of whether the sales are more of a mind game than a real discount. That's thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case to recommend it. Some devices are already on sale right now ahead of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days for $40 off, but went up in price by $20 just a few weeks ago, cutting that discount into something that feels barely worth the spend.
If you're interested in Amazon's device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I've got you covered. I've been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED's resident Kindle tester, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here's my full breakdown.
Which Amazon Devices Are on Sale Already, and Which Aren’t
Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. They do seem to be permanent price changes, though, so if you're certain you want one of these models, this is the best time to buy.
So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. (Amazon also announced new versions of these Kindles today, along with the rest of its lineup, so it's up to you whether you want the current on-sale model or to preorder the new one!) If you're looking for a Paperwhite and Scribe, they aren't on sale yet as of this writing. Neither are Eero routers.
But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).
The Best Early Amazon Device Deals
Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you're set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.
The Best Early Kindle Deals
If you're shopping for a Kindle, this is the best time to buy since most were hit with price increases. You won't get as good a deal anymore, but it's much better to buy it at a discount on the new price than the full, higher price for the same product. There's also new Kindles that were just announced, so it's up to you if you want to grab an older on-sale model (which all work great!) or wait for the new one.
As of this writing, only Kindle Kids models are on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days, but only one is a good deal after taking the price changes into account.
Other On-Sale Amazon Devices We’ve Tested
Looking for a different device during Amazon's sale event? We've tested several other Amazon Echo and Fire TV devices that are also on sale right now. Here's what else you can consider, and what the discount looks like.
- Amazon Echo Dot Max for $80 ($40 Off): If you're looking for a small speaker with bigger sound than the older Echo Dot, the Echo Dot Max has impressive sound for its size, plus a built-in smart home hub. Its price did increase $20, though, so it feels like it's just $20 off even if it looks like $40.
- Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $125 ($75 Off): While this model is on sale, I prefer the older Echo Show 8 (though it seems rarely available anymore) and the Echo Show 11 since both have better sound. It's a good discount, even off the original $180 price tag, but I'd just spend $25 more and get the better Echo Show 11 if you're set on a new Amazon Alexa-powered smart display.
- Amazon Echo Show 15 for $250 ($100 Off): The Echo Show 15 and Echo Show 21 are on sale and both double as a Fire TV device, with a massive screen, a flat back for mounting, and an included Alexa Voice Remote. I don't love the TV experience, but it works, and the homepage fits a ton of widgets if you want to see multiple at once. Both sizes are discounted, but both models also cost more now, so it's not as good as you'd think for the same device.
- Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max for $45 ($40 Off): If you love Amazon Prime as your streaming service, this is the favorite we've tested of Amazon's Fire TV streaming devices. It's not a crazy discount since it went up $25 in August, but it's still a really affordable streaming stick during this same event.
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Kids for $170 ($60 Off): The Paperwhite Kids has everything we like about a Kindle Paperwhite, but adds a cover to protect it from any drops by your kiddo's hands and comes with six months of Kids+ content, which is like Kindle Unlimited but designed for kids. It's a good device, but the discount isn't as good as before; it used to retail for $180, so it's really only $10 off what it used to cost. But you won't find it new for cheaper.
- Amazon Kindle Kids for $123 ($57 Off): This is the cheapest Kindle Kids device, with a 6-inch screen similar to the cheapest Kindle, and it still comes with a colorful cover and six months of Kids+ content like the Paperwhite Kids above. It has the smallest discount out of the Kids devices, and it used to retail for $130, so it's only $7 off the original price. The other Kids models are a better buy.
Which Amazon Device Prices Went Up?
Amazon raised prices across several of its device categories at the end of August. It's not a shocking move, but it hit many affordable products and makes for a worse sale season since we're getting discounts on a higher price tag for no other improvements. Here's a quick breakdown of most of the price changes to help you navigate what sales are good and which are really just bringing you back to the old price.
Either way, I'd only buy an Amazon device on sale now, but it is unfortunate the sales just won't be as good anymore on these existing devices. I expect most, if not all, of these devices to go on sale at some point during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

Mysterious 'whiskers' on Russian drones turned out to be mechanical detonators – 'Flash'

Mysterious 'whiskers' on Russian drones turned out to be mechanical detonators – 'Flash'
photos
        
        Ukrinform
    The mysterious "whiskers" that have begun appearing on Russian Geran drones have turned out to be mechanical detonators.
    Serhii Beskrestnov (call sign "Flash"), a freelance presidential advisor on technology and a technology expert, announced this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
"The 'whiskers' on the Geran have been figured out. It's an ordinary mechanical detonator," he wrote.
Beskrestnov explained that the device contains a metal tube and a metal rod that make contact when they touch something, triggering a command for the explosion.
On September 30, Russian forces used for the first time a warhead on a jet-powered drone specifically designed to destroy high-voltage power lines and steel bridge structures.

No relief at the pump: EU diesel hits new record of €2.24 a litre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:55:56 UTC
21:55:56 KST

Twelve EU countries recorded new diesel price highs as supply disruptions pushed the bloc’s average pump price to €2.24 a litre.
The average price of diesel at the pump across the EU has hit a record of €2.24 per litre, compared with €1.59 before the war erupted in the Middle East, according to European Commission data published on Thursday.
Twelve EU member states recorded fresh all-time highs, including Belgium, Italy, Romania and Poland, according to AFP. The increases are putting further pressure on household budgets. A new Euronews analysis found that filling a 50-litre tank with diesel now costs the equivalent of more than 15% of the gross monthly minimum wage in Bulgaria.
The latest Commission figures show that the price of diesel, the main fuel used by road freight transport and farming machinery, exceeded €2.50 per litre in Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland, and reached €2.44 in Germany.
In Belgium, where prices hit a record, diesel averaged €2.43 per litre on Monday, compared with €2.39 the previous week.
In Italy, the price rose by seven cents to €2.35 per litre. French filling stations, excluding overseas territories and Corsica, were charging an average of €2.37 per litre, a very slight decline.
Across the EU, prices rose by an average of one cent per litre over the past week.
The figures from the European Commission's Weekly Oil Bulletin include taxes, which vary between countries and account for an average of 40% of the price paid at the pump across the bloc.
However, they do not take into account targeted subsidies, such as assistance for high-mileage drivers in France.
The EU average is weighted according to each country's fuel consumption in 2024. It stood at €1.59 per litre in February, before the US-Israeli strikes on Iran sparked the war in the Middle East.
Fuel prices have been driven higher since February by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for fossil fuels from the Gulf, followed by a Houthi blockade of Saudi exports in the Red Sea and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
Supply disruptions are only one factor pushing up pump prices. European refining margins — the difference between the cost of crude oil and the wholesale value of the fuels produced from it — have also remained high. ECB experts told Euronews in September that diesel margins were expected to peak in October, based on futures prices at the time.

No porn, no doomscrolling, no processed foods: Meet Israel's spermmaxxers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:55:39 UTC
21:55:39 KST

"I want my sperm to be high-quality, strong and healthy," says Itamar, a 37-year-old car mechanic from Mishmar Ayalon in central Israel. He recently changed his diet and started exercising, partly with that goal in mind.
"I make sure to eat a lot of meat," he says, "lift weights, rarely turn on the Wi-Fi at home and don't carry my cellphone in my pocket. I mostly wear cotton clothes, buy shampoo and cleaning products only from health food stores, and don't use sunscreen or perfume – except for important events – to avoid hormone-disrupters."
Itamar got most of his information from health-related YouTube content, and podcasts, and a year ago, he participated in Israeli bio-hacker Ram Shechter's "Testosterone Challenge," which teaches participants how to raise their testosterone levels through lifestyle changes.
Itamar is currently in a relationship and hopes to start a family soon, but his interest in fertility began a few years ago, while he was still single. "I've known for a long time that I want to be a father, and it's important to me to rise to the occasion in the best and most fertile physical condition I can," he explains.
Tal Levi, a school caretaker and multidisciplinary artist, has also adopted new habits in recent months in an effort to boost his fertility. The 30-year-old Tel Aviv resident concocts his own hygiene products and creams out of natural ingredients, and avoids passing through metal detectors or placing his laptop on his body. Levy is single, but in his view, the issue can't wait. "Modern life is harming our health and, as a result, our fertility. If I want children in the future, I have to take active steps to increase the chances of that actually happening."
Up until recently, only women were expected to prepare their bodies for pregnancy and support fertility through lifestyle changes such as taking supplements, quitting smoking and looking after their general health. But as of late, signs of change have been budding in Israel, with men adopting new lifestyle habits to support fertility.
Overseas, this phenomenon already has a name: "spermmaxxing" – a wellness trend in which men try to optimize their sperm. Health influencers teach their followers how to boost fertility by "detoxing" metals from the body, avoiding processed foods and regulating dopamine levels by abstaining from pornography and late-night doomcrolling on social media. Thousands of men swap tips in online forums, some of which are backed by research and some less so – from testicle icing with ice cubes and replacing espresso with decaf to taking supplements such as ashwagandha, zinc, selenium and copper.
"Men should have to spend nine months getting into the best physical shape of their lives before having a baby," says one TikTok creator in a video that received 2.5 million likes. He claims that "50 to 60 percent of the baby's epigenetic makeup is because of the man." Another creator shared his fertility-boosting routine – which includes squats, ice baths and protein-rich meals – under the caption: "Just a regular 33-year-old improving his health and fertility one day at a time."
The wellness industry has also started promoting sperm health as part of a general health routine. In recent years, the male fertility market, which generates millions annually, has become saturated with products, supplements and apps designed to help users optimize their reproductive health. The subject has also become increasingly popular in cultural discourse through podcasts, documentaries and television shows. Last year, longevity guru Bryan Johnson proudly boasted his sperm metrics to his two million followers on X, discussing the correlation between sperm health, testosterone levels and life expectancy.
Optimization as compensation
To some extent, the current obsession with the topic is a response to the growing alarm over the male fertility crisis. Israeli epidemiologist Hagai Levine led a major 2017 study that found sperm counts among Western countries had fallen by about 50 percent between 1973 and 2011, and that one in 20 men are currently facing reduced fertility – a statistic that received media resonance and was even dubbed "spermaggedon." A subsequent study published in 2022 found that the decline extended globally.
The studies did not examine the causes of the crisis, but research literature links poor sperm metrics to poor diet, low physical fitness, smoking, alcohol, use of radiation-emitting devices (though evidence on their effects remains mixed), exposure to toxins like phthalates, obesity, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and metabolic syndrome.
Last year, the World Health Organization published its first global guideline on infertility, noting that male infertility can be caused by unhealthy habits, and in 2024, the U.S. National Library of Medicine published a review examining the effects of lifestyle factors on sperm quality. The Israeli Ministry of Health has not published specific guidelines regarding sperm health, but local fertility clinics provide recommendations on their websites for improving sperm count through lifestyle changes.
There is also growing body of evidence that a father's health affects not only sperm quality, but also pregnancy outcomes and the health of his offspring. For example, cigarette smoking during the pre-conception period increases the risk factor for pregnancy loss, while experiments in mice have shown that paternal alcohol consumption affects normal placental development, can alter the baby's facial symmetry and increases the risk of liver cancer during its lifetime.
Despite the new focus on sperm quality, male involvement in fertility treatments remains ambivalent. Prof. Itai Gat, director of Assuta Superm, one of the largest specialized sperm banks in Israel, says that while he has noticed a certain change, it's partial. "We see more men coming for fertility counseling than before, showing more willingness to undergo testing or openness to discussing the issue, but it's not widespread and depends on the population.
"There is also a difference in the role a man assumes in the process based on his sperm test results. Sometimes a man who discovers his sperm is normal deduces that that he is not responsible for his and his partner's difficulties and becomes a kind of support person in the process, rather than an active participant."
Roni Baltuch, a social worker who accompanies fertility patients at Assuta Ramat Hahayal Hospital, says that "in contrast to women, men show a disconnect when it comes to reproductive system issues and their potential implications for fertility and fatherhood. Medicine socializes women for reproduction by treating gynecological checkups as an integral part of general health, while for most men, the first examination they have is during their military draft intake – and often, the only one they'll ever have.
"Even if a finding comes up that requires further medical investigation, men usually won't connect it with the need to protect their fertility later on. They arrive for fertility treatments years later and are surprised to discover they have a fertility problem."
This year, Israel decided to eliminate the testicular examination during the first military draft order appearance, on the grounds that its results rarely affect a recruit's medical profile – which could push the issue even further aside.
Baltuch attributes men's detachment to another factor. "Fertility treatments focus on women, because even when the problem is with the sperm, medical interventions for men are specific and performed in the beginning of the process – while the rest of the interventions are performed on the woman's body."
According to Gat, male fertility problems are primarily treated by diagnosing their source. "A sperm disorder can stem from a variety of causes, each with a targeted treatment. For example, there may be a hormonal disorder requiring hormonal treatment; abnormal dilation of the veins in the scrotum, known as varicocele, which can be corrected through surgery or catheterization; or a genetic disorder requiring genetic testing of the embryo during in vitro fertilization. There are also cases where the source of the problem is unknown, and then we recommend lifestyle changes to prevent deterioration. But usually, treatment for men is specific."
What is the connection between testosterone levels, sperm quality and the ability to conceive?
"The testicles have a dual role: one is sperm cell production, and the other role is testosterone production. Testosterone is essential for a man's general health, and there is an interplay between it and sperm. Men with functioning testicles will have normal sperm production and testosterone production. Men with impaired sperm production will have a higher risk of testosterone disorder. These factors ultimately affect the ability to impregnate a woman; a healthy man with normal testicular function will have a higher ability to impregnate a woman than someone with impaired function."
So, which habits can improve sperm?
Gat explains that "healthy habits such as a good diet, physical activity, quitting smoking and maintaining a healthy weight have been scientifically proven to improve both general health and fertility. However, adopting a healthy lifestyle will not turn a man with a severe fertility disorder into a sperm donor. It can, however, prevent an existing condition from getting worse and can also lead to improvement.
"As for trends like ice baths and so on, there is currently insufficient scientific evidence that they work. Regarding avoiding radiation – the global decline in sperm quality began in the 1970s, before we all had cellphones in our pockets. The decline has also been recorded in different countries around the world, so it goes beyond technology."
As for supplements, he adds, "It's difficult to say scientifically how much they help, because each company produces supplements in different concentrations and combinations, and there can even be variation between capsules. Supplements like zinc and Coenzyme Q10 can certainly benefit a man with a fertility disorder, and we do recommend them. But should healthy men take them? I doubt it would make a difference."
Baltuch notes that "until five years ago, it felt like men weren't part of the equation, and some doctors wouldn't even send them for testing, even though statistically, male factor issues contribute to roughly 40 percent of all couple infertility cases. This has recently changed, and now usually both partners are now sent for testing. In some cases, there is also a greater willingness on the man's part to be involved in the treatment. But I still hear from many women that when they ask their partner to cooperate – for example, by taking vitamins, quitting smoking or giving up a harmful habit – they are met with resistance."
Another factor is gender roles in Israeli society. "Gender roles in the context of reproduction are based on models that could be called prehistoric, or survivalist," says Baltuch. "The man's role is to impregnate and the woman's role is to conceive. While difficulty having children can create a sense of failure in both sexes, for men it's not necessarily linked to the idea of starting a family, but primarily to their masculinity and their perception of themselves as men."
She continues: "For male patients who discover that the fertility problem stems from them, it can feel like a subject too painful to touch, like we have to walk on eggshells. Men also feel they have no right to complain about the emotional difficulty, because their partners are usually the ones who have to undergo the grueling physical treatments. In many cases, men express their difficulty through a desire to ease their partner's burden as much as possible, as a kind of compensation."
Sharing the burden
Nadav (not his real name), a 33-year-old software developer from Tel Aviv, has in recent months begun preparing his body for fatherhood – out of a desire to support his partner. "Until recently, I would smoke a small joint at the end of the day," he says, "but I read studies linking cannabis use to poorer sperm quality, so I stopped. I also discovered that saunas and hot baths – something I really love to do – can harm fertility, so I'm avoiding them now."
Nadav learned about the subject through conversations with his friends who are parents and even consulted ChatGPT about it. He says he is only at the beginning of his journey and wants to educate himself and change other habits that could support fertility. He even intends to make additional sacrifices during his partner's pregnancy, such as abstaining from alcohol – so that the burden is more equal. "I'm doing it out of solidarity with my partner, because she will have to sacrifice quite a lot for the pregnancy and for building our family, so why shouldn't I do everything I can on my end to contribute to the effort?"
"In our society, which is also a militaristic society, gender roles steer men to go to battle and women to stay behind in supporting roles," Baltuch says. "In this context, pregnancy creates a role reversal: Women are on the frontlines, the action is happening to them, while men are in supporting roles. For many couples I meet, this reversal creates emotional distress in men who feel they need to do everything they can to be part of the 'battle.' So changing habits can stem not necessarily from concern about fertility, but from a desire to be involved. In other cases, the male desire to take action over fertility can align with perfectionism. Statements such as 'I want strong sperm' express a desire to excel at masculinity."
Sharon Carmi, a 35-year-old physiotherapist from Beit Herut and the father of a 14-month-old daughter, has also decided to devote the coming year to improving his fertility for his future children. "Before the first pregnancy, I stopped smoking cannabis on my wife's advice," he says. "But now I want to get into the best shape I've ever been in, because I know it's important that the children be conceived with strong, high-quality sperm."
Carmi adheres to an organic diet, has stopped smoking cigarettes, makes a point of wearing natural fabrics such as cotton and linen and uses natural hygiene and cleaning products to avoid chemicals. "I also want to run a marathon," he adds, "because I want to be at my peak. I think it can help us conceive more easily, and I also want to be a healthy and strong father, so I can support my wife and children. It's great motivation to make positive changes in my life."
Prof. Danny Kaplan, head of the Gender Studies program and founder of the Masculinity Studies track at Bar-Ilan University, says that "the body is a central element in the traditional perception of masculinity, a tool meant to achieve and perform. In the post-industrial era, where there is almost no physical difference between men and women in the worlds of work, military or sports, and now in the digital age, where there is almost no need for the body, this poses a threat to what it means to be a man."
According to Kaplan, there is a perception that masculinity today must be proven through a continuous series of tests. "The idea is that in the modern era, masculinity is something that needs to be proven. Physical optimization, longevity and the 'maxxing' trend fit this approach, because the potential for improvement is infinite. There is also a competitive dimension here – whether against others or against yourself. The only place where the male body is almost irreplaceable is reproduction – and now even that is being challenged by technologies such as IVF, sperm donation and so on. This brings the desire to excel and maximize the body down to ever smaller dimensions of medical metrics. Sperm seemingly becomes the ultimate test of masculinity."
The pressure on "sperm value" that Kaplan describes is also reflected in the new sport of sperm racing, in which fresh ejaculate is analyzed under a microscope to see which sperm cell crosses the finish line first. A few months ago, the "Sperm Racing World Cup 2026" was announced, with organizers announcing that "athletes" from 128 countries will compete for a $100,000 prize.
Gat notes that studies have shown that male fertility disorders are associated with an increased risk of long-term morbidity such as testicular cancer and cardiovascular diseases at an earlier age than in the general population. "Today we understand that fertility is a kind of window into general health, and sperm metrics can be seen as a biomarker that predicts future health," he says.
"We need to look at things from a broad perspective: The goal isn't just to impregnate, but to build a family – usually with more than one child. Awareness of the link between lifestyle and fertility and men's willingness to support fertility are extremely important because of their impact on several critical areas – quality of life, the success of their partner's pregnancy and the health of future generations."
Men need to be part of the fertility conversation. But the path there does not necessarily lie in an obsession with metrics. It begins with a medical examination when needed, a healthy lifestyle, giving up smoking and excessive alcohol consumption, and especially in understanding that fertility is a matter for couples and families, not another masculinity test.

Botswana at 60 challenges the story of postcolonial African failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:54:28 UTC
21:54:28 KST

Botswana at 60 challenges the story of postcolonial African failure
From one of the world’s poorest countries at independence, Botswana used diamond revenues to build public services, infrastructure and a stable democracy.
This week, Botswana is marking 60 years of independence from Britain with Diamond Jubilee celebrations across the country. The anniversary underscores the scale of the country’s transformation. In 1966, the former Bechuanaland Protectorate was among the world’s poorest countries, with barely 12 kilometres of paved road, just 22 university graduates and about 100 secondary-school graduates.
Six decades later, Botswana is an upper-middle-income country with one of postcolonial Africa’s most striking development records. Between 1965 and 1980, Botswana’s economy grew by an average of 13.9 percent a year. By 2025, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita had reached about $7,800, higher than South Africa’s roughly $6,600, a striking reversal given South Africa’s position as one of the continent’s largest and most diversified economies. But the significance of Botswana’s growth lies not only in its scale, but in what the country did with it.
In 1994, it became the first country ever to graduate from the United Nations’ least-developed country category. The World Bank now classifies Botswana as an upper-middle-income economy, and the change is visible across the country. By 2024, its road network stretched almost 35,000 kilometres, 80.2 percent of the population had access to electricity and, according to the 2022 census, 66.5 percent of Batswana lived in urban areas, compared with just 9.1 percent in 1971.
Public investment also dramatically expanded access to education. By 2022, Botswana had 192,151 secondary-school pupils, while by 2024 some 60,287 students were enrolled in tertiary institutions. A country that entered independence with only 22 university graduates now educates tens of thousands of students at tertiary level.
The gains extended beyond education. Botswana’s national poverty rate fell from 30.6 percent in 2002/03 to an estimated 14.5 percent by 2022. Public healthcare expanded alongside this transformation. Today, 85 percent of Batswana live within five kilometres of a health facility and almost all births occur in health facilities.
Botswana’s response to HIV is more remarkable still. In 2002, Botswana launched Africa’s first national free comprehensive HIV treatment programme. Twenty-three years later, the World Health Organization recognised it as the first high-HIV-burden country in the world to achieve Gold Tier status on the path towards eliminating mother-to-child transmission. Ninety-eight percent of pregnant women living with HIV receive treatment, transmission to children has fallen to about 1.2 percent and life expectancy now stands at 69 years.
Political stability has also endured through democratic change. In 2024, after 58 years of Botswana Democratic Party rule, voters elected the opposition Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC) and the outgoing government relinquished office peacefully.
Botswana’s achievements are increasingly visible beyond politics and economics, too. Letsile Tebogo won the country’s first Olympic gold medal in Paris in 2024. A year later, Collen Kebinatshipi became world 400m champion. In May 2026, Botswana hosted the World Athletics Relays in Gaborone, a first for Africa, and ended the competition by winning the men’s 4x400m title before its home crowd.
Behind much of Botswana’s economic and social progress lies the way it has managed its diamond wealth.
Today, Botswana owns 50 percent of Debswana, the diamond-mining joint venture it shares with De Beers, while the Pula Fund, its sovereign wealth fund, preserves part of the country’s wealth for future generations and helps cushion the economy against mineral-related macroeconomic shocks. Foreign reserves equivalent to 7.5 months of imports provide an additional layer of financial protection. The state continues to use mineral revenues to finance public services, infrastructure and economic development rather than treating diamonds simply as an export windfall.
Yet for all that Botswana has achieved, it remains vulnerable to the commodity that financed much of this progress. Diamonds have accounted for almost 90 percent of goods exports over the past decade and still generate about a third of national revenue and three-quarters of foreign-exchange earnings.
Natural diamonds have faced softer luxury demand and growing competition from laboratory-grown stones that sell for a fraction of the price. As global demand weakened, Botswana felt the consequences immediately. The economy contracted by 2.8 percent in 2024 and another 0.7 percent in 2025.
The downturn deepens Botswana’s already serious employment challenge. Its latest household survey puts unemployment at 21 percent, rising to 28.9 percent among people aged 15 to 35.
Botswana largely avoided the resource curse, yet it never overcame its heavy reliance on diamonds. The challenge at 60 is no longer how to turn diamonds into development, but how to create prosperity that can survive without them.
That requires looking beyond diamonds. Botswana’s 2025 agreement with De Beers gives the state-owned Okavango Diamond Company 30 percent of Debswana production, rising to 40 percent after 2030 and potentially 50 percent thereafter. It also provides for jewellery manufacturing, diamond grading and vocational training. Botswana should capture as much value as possible from every stone it mines. But processing, polishing and marketing diamonds will not end its dependence on diamonds.
Botswana now needs a broader, more resilient economy, and some of the foundations are already in place. In 2024, 68.9 percent of households had internet access, up from 40.6 percent a decade earlier. That connectivity has yet to translate into many jobs: information and communications technology accounted for only 2 percent of employment in 2025. Botswana must invest in the skills needed to turn connectivity into software, fintech, digital services and technology businesses that employ Batswana and sell beyond its borders.
Tourism is another existing strength, already providing about 50,500 jobs, or 6.7 percent of total employment, and accounting for more than 60 percent of services exports. A conservation model that places roughly 40 percent of the country’s land under protected status gives Botswana an asset it can build on.
Economic diversification will require abundant power. A 500MW solar plant with 500MWh of battery storage is being built at Maun. Cheap, reliable renewable energy could support manufacturing, data centres and new industries rather than simply light homes.
Botswana must also help more businesses compete regionally and globally. More than 95 percent of private-sector sales remain domestic and only 9 percent of surveyed firms export at all. More Batswana need access to finance and training so they can start, own and expand businesses and benefit from the next economy.
The institutions that turned diamonds into roads, schools and healthcare must now use six decades of accumulated skills, infrastructure and capital to create a new economy built on technology, energy, manufacturing and exports.
Botswana matters beyond its borders because its record contrasts sharply with other resource-rich African states. According to the World Bank’s latest available data, copper dominates Zambia’s exports, while 71.7 percent of Zambians live on less than $3 a day. The Democratic Republic of the Congo is rich in copper and cobalt, but 85.3 percent of its people remain below the same threshold. In oil-rich Nigeria, Africa’s largest petroleum producer, 41.8 percent of the population lives on less than $3 a day.
Botswana demonstrates that a decisive question is not whether a country has mineral wealth, but who controls it, how its revenues are protected and whether the state converts them into better housing, stronger infrastructure, reliable public services and greater economic security.
That lesson is especially important as African countries seek greater control over critical minerals. Mineral wealth does not inevitably produce corruption, conflict or poverty. Success must ultimately be measured by whether those resources foster more productive economies, widen opportunity and materially improve people’s lives.
That is the larger meaning of Botswana at 60: in the right hands, postcolonial power can serve the many rather than the few.
There is an old Setswana saying: “Moenyane o pele lebone la waabo” — the one who goes ahead becomes a light for those who come after.
May Botswana light the way for Africa.

Iran War Highlights 2 Challenges for Japan in a Taiwan Contingency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

On February 28, the Iran-U.S. war began. Despite ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran at the time, Israel and the U.S. launched a barrage of attacks, and Iran retaliated across a wide area, including Israel and the Gulf region. In the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on commercial vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, traffic control measures, and a U.S. maritime blockade of Iran combined to impose severe constraints on shipping routes that are vital to global energy transportation. Even in late September, traffic through the strait had not returned to prewar levels, and the crisis had yet to be fully resolved.
Against this backdrop, Japan can use the Iran war to reexamine its security framework, with particular attention to preparations for a contingency involving Taiwan. The Iran war has raised many issues, but two are especially important for Japan. The first is how to evacuate Japanese nationals and travelers when a crisis begins sooner than expected and civilian transportation networks suddenly cease to function. The second is how Japan can help ensure the safety of maritime traffic while avoiding becoming a direct party to the conflict. Both expose gaps in the institutional arrangements Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.
Evacuating People from a Sudden Crisis
The first lesson of the Iran war is that the traditional approach of waiting until a crisis escalates before evacuating people is no longer sufficient. Even before the outbreak of hostilities, the Japanese government had warned of the deteriorating situation in Iran and encouraged Japanese nationals to leave early. Once the fighting began, however, it became necessary to confirm the safety of Japanese nationals and assist with their departure not only in Iran but also across neighboring areas, including Israel, Qatar, Bahrain, and the United Arab Emirates.
In March, the Japanese government supported multiple overland evacuations from Tehran to Azerbaijan and also assisted Japanese nationals in Gulf countries with their return home. Importantly, these evacuations were not carried out solely by Self-Defense Forces aircraft or charter flights; they relied on a combination of overland routes, commercial aviation, and transit through third countries.
An even larger problem was the temporary degradation of airports and airspace across the Gulf, including major hubs such as Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Doha. Dubai is not simply one airport in the Middle East; it is one of the world’s leading aviation hubs linking Asia with Europe and Africa. Disruption there complicated movement not only for people evacuating Iran and Israel but also for travelers and foreign residents throughout the Gulf. The experience demonstrated once again that a crisis may not remain confined within the borders of one country and can quickly engulf regional transportation hubs.
This lesson applies directly to a Taiwan contingency. In peacetime, large numbers of Japanese nationals are in Taiwan for tourism, business, study, and long-term assignments. Once hostilities begin, not only Taiwan’s airports and ports but also the surrounding airspace and waters could become dangerous. Transportation in Hong Kong, coastal China, Okinawa, and the Sakishima Islands could also be affected. In other words, a plan designed only to move Japanese nationals out of Taiwan would be insufficient. Japan must prepare for a scenario in which multiple transportation nodes across East Asia become unavailable at the same time.
Within Japan, civil protection plans to evacuate residents and tourists from the Sakishima Islands to Kyushu and Yamaguchi have become increasingly concrete, with field exercises scheduled for fiscal year 2026. This is an important development. Yet civil protection planning primarily concerns the evacuation of people inside Japan. By contrast, the evacuation of Japanese nationals from Taiwan, Hong Kong, coastal China, and other overseas locations spans several frameworks, including consular assistance by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, transportation under the Self-Defense Forces Act, and the securing of civilian transportation. If domestic evacuation and overseas evacuation occur simultaneously, Japan would still face the unresolved question of how to allocate aircraft, ships, airports, and ports between the two missions.
The lesson from the Iran War is not simply that Japan should increase the transport capacity of the Self-Defense Forces. Moving tens of thousands of people within a short period ultimately depends on cooperation with commercial airlines, shipping companies, airports and ports, and third countries. Japan therefore needs, in peacetime, to identify which civilian services could be maintained during a crisis, which third countries could serve as evacuation hubs, and which ports could be used if air routes were closed.
Plans must also address how to provide shelter, food, communications, and medical care for those who cannot be evacuated immediately. An evacuation plan cannot consist only of a plan for getting people out; it must also include a plan for keeping them safe until evacuation becomes possible.
Ensuring Safe Navigation Without Becoming a Party to the Conflict
The second challenge is how to ensure the safety of maritime traffic. During the Iran War, the Strait of Hormuz was not completely closed, but normal commercial navigation became extremely difficult because of the risk of attacks on and seizures of merchant vessels, heightened vigilance against mines and drones, Iranian traffic control measures, and the U.S. blockade of Iran.
In June, the United States and Iran reached a memorandum of understanding that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the Japanese government also called for the early restoration of free and safe navigation. Yet even in late September, traffic through the strait remained well below prewar levels.
On September 22, Iran indicated that it was prepared to reopen the strait quickly if the United States eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports. This, in turn, shows that as of late September, the restoration of safe navigation remained a matter of diplomatic and military negotiation.
This raised a further question: who should be responsible for ensuring safe navigation? If the United States, as a party to the conflict, leads convoy escorts or other maritime operations, participating states are more likely to be perceived as having been militarily incorporated into the U.S. side. Yet civilian shipping cannot simply be left exposed in dangerous waters.
European states have therefore sought arrangements that would protect freedom of navigation while maintaining a degree of distance from U.S.-led operations. In September, France was reported to be considering a United Nations Security Council resolution for an international mission to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Such an approach can be understood as an attempt to distinguish, as far as possible, alliance military operations from the protection of maritime traffic as an international public good.
A similar dilemma would arise in a Taiwan contingency. If the Taiwan Strait and surrounding waters became dangerous, maintaining maritime traffic would be a major economic and security concern for Japan. Yet the threshold for participation would be extremely high if measures to protect shipping could immediately lead to armed conflict with China. What is needed is an institutional distinction, to the greatest extent possible, between joining combat operations and supporting the safe navigation of civilian vessels. Japan should therefore clarify in advance options that are not integrated into the use of force, including post-ceasefire mine clearance, information sharing, sea-lane monitoring, rescue of vessels in distress, and cooperation with escort frameworks led by third countries.
This issue is also related to the limits of Japan’s 2015 Legislation for Peace and Security. The legislation permits the minimum necessary use of force only when the so-called three new conditions are satisfied, including cases in which an armed attack on a foreign country that is in a close relationship with Japan poses a clear threat to Japan’s survival and to the fundamental rights of its people. It is important to note that, as a matter of law, U.S. participation in a conflict is not itself a requirement for recognizing a situation that threatens Japan’s survival. The Japanese government has also stated with regard to a Taiwan contingency that whether a particular situation constitutes such a threat must be determined comprehensively in light of the specific circumstances actually arising. It is therefore inaccurate to frame the issue as one in which Japan can do nothing unless the United States participates.
However, what is legally possible and what can actually be recognized in practice are different questions. A situation threatening Japan’s survival can be recognized only when there is a clear danger to Japan’s existence and to the rights of its people, and when no other appropriate means are available. Disruption to maritime traffic or higher resource prices alone would not automatically meet that threshold.
Moreover, when Japan seeks to secure safe navigation in a manner that is not directly connected to combat with the opposing state, the framework of a situation threatening Japan’s survival may in some cases be too weighty. In March 2026, views were expressed within the Japanese government that minesweeping in the Strait of Hormuz after a ceasefire could be considered as one option. This is one example of the importance of maritime security measures that are institutionally separated from direct participation in combat.
The same perspective should guide discussion of a Taiwan contingency. The debate should not be reduced to a binary question of whether Japan would exercise the right of collective self-defense. Japan instead needs to strengthen the legal and institutional arrangements that apply before that threshold is reached and in adjacent areas. Specifically, it should clarify the legal basis and timing for measures such as the evacuation of Japanese nationals, maritime security, mine clearance, information sharing, warnings to civilian vessels, coordination with third countries and international organizations, and the alternative use of ports and airports. A U.N. resolution or an international framework led by third countries could be one option. Yet because China is a permanent member of the Security Council and possesses a veto, it would be unrealistic to rely solely on a U.N. resolution. Japan therefore needs multiple legal and diplomatic pathways.
What Should Japan Learn From the Iran War?
The Iran-U.S. war became a major crisis that simultaneously challenged the protection of Japanese nationals and the security of maritime transportation. It demonstrated that preparing for contingencies cannot be reduced to the question of how far the Self-Defense Forces can be used. In the initial phase of a crisis, airport closures and airspace restrictions may halt civilian transportation, while the population requiring evacuation may rapidly expand from the belligerent state to neighboring countries. At sea, Japan may be called upon to help ensure safe navigation even without participating in hostilities, while still facing the risk that such activity could be interpreted as support for one of the parties to the conflict.
The same problems could arise in a Taiwan contingency. The central issue is not to reduce a Taiwan crisis immediately to the questions of a situation threatening Japan’s survival or the exercise of collective self-defense. Rather, Japan needs to institutionalize and operationalize the measures that would become necessary before such a determination: the evacuation of Japanese nationals, the evacuation of residents, the maintenance of air and maritime transportation, protection of sea lanes, and cooperation with third countries. The Iran war has revealed a new “intermediate domain” within the legal and institutional framework Japan has developed with a Taiwan contingency in mind.
Diplomatic efforts to prevent a Taiwan contingency must of course continue. Yet considering what should be done if deterrence fails is also part of security policy. The most important lesson Japan should draw from the Iran War is that the issue should not be framed as a binary choice between participation and non-participation in war. Instead, the many practical tasks that lie between those two poles must be institutionalized in advance.

Rincell unveils high-power drone battery cell
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:51:05 BST
21:51:05 KST

US battery manufacturer Rincell has introduced a new high-discharge 21700 lithium-ion cell aimed at drones and other power-intensive applications, with the company saying the RC50T is already in production and shipping to customers, according to the company.
The California-based firm announced the RC50T ahead of its first European public appearance at DroneX at ExCeL London, where the cell was due to be shown alongside Rincell’s existing RC50 battery.
Built around the widely used 21700 cylindrical form factor, the new cell has a nominal capacity of 5.2Ah and voltage of 3.6V. Rincell states that it can deliver a continuous discharge current of 100A and a pulse discharge of up to 150A, with an energy density above 265Wh/kg.
The company is pitching the RC50T primarily at unmanned aircraft applications where high power demand can occur during take-off, climbing, payload lift and rapid manoeuvring. According to Rincell, its tabless internal design reduces resistance to around 3mΩ nominally, with a maximum figure of 4mΩ, while charging current can reach 15A. Those characteristics are intended to reduce electrical losses and heat generation in battery packs while allowing greater power to be drawn from each cell.
Jignesh Parikh, co-founder and chief executive of Rincell, said in the press release: “In an industry often driven by future promises, we chose to focus on proven results. For three years we have kept our heads down, taken our cells from the lab into volume production and shipped them to customers. DroneX is the first time we have told that story. Everything visitors will see on our stand is a product they can order and fly today. That includes the RC50T, our highest power 21700 cell, and it is already in the air.”
The RC50T is NDAA compliant, according to the company, and is being supplied to drone manufacturers as well as customers working in other high-power applications.
Shashank Sripad, co-founder and chief technology officer of PROPEL AERO, was also quoted in the press release as saying: “The RC50T gives us power headroom, without any loss in energy, that we have not had from a 21700 cell before. With internal resistance this low we can build lighter, cooler packs and let the aircraft use more of the energy it is carrying.”
Rincell was founded in 2023 and develops silicon-graphite lithium-ion and sodium-ion battery cells for defence and commercial markets. Its stated customer base includes the drone, aerospace, communications, medical, industrial and data centre sectors. Research and development takes place in the United States, where the company operates a 6,500 sq ft pilot production line in Fremont, California. Rincell says its higher-volume manufacturing is currently centred in India, while a US production facility is planned to begin operations in late 2027.
The company says it has shipped hundreds of thousands of cells during 2026.

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright attends an announcement made by President Donald Trump at the White House in Washington on Sept. 28, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
BERLIN — The Trump administration has circulated a proposal to European governments asking them to release a large portion of the bloc’s strategic diesel reserves to ease soaring fuel costs, according to four officials in European and U.S. governments.
The plan, put forward by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, was pitched as an alternative to President Donald Trump's threat of a blanket ban on diesel exports from the U.S.
Under the proposal, EU governments would release 120 million barrels of diesel from their national strategic reserves over 180 days, a government official from a European country told POLITICO. The official, like others in this story, was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the proposal's details publicly.
Advertisement
That would account for well over a third of the approximately 315 million barrels of diesel EU countries held in reserve as of June this year, according to Eurostat figures. Among EU countries, Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland hold the largest reserves of the essential transport fuel.
POLITICO reported Tuesday that the White House was floating the idea of asking the EU to use its diesel reserves to bolster global supply and thus lower prices. A German government official on Thursday confirmed that the United States had contacted Berlin in the matter.
Multiple countries in Europe were approached for a coordinated release, according to a person familiar with the Trump administration's plans. One major EU member was approached bilaterally in the U.S. last week, according to a senior European energy official.
"It was very hypothetical: ‘What do you think about Europe releasing some of the reserves in order to decrease prices, put pressure on supplies?'" the official said. "'It could also help our government not to continue the discussion on the export ban.'"
Wright, along with the U.S. oil and gas industry, opposes an export ban on one of the world's most in-demand petroleum products, and the proposal is seen as an attempt to find an alternative to such a drastic measure.
At a press conference Thursday, Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen wouldn’t confirm whether the EU had received Wright’s request but said that any stock releases would only be agreed through the International Energy Agency, a Paris-based institution which coordinates energy policy among rich countries and oversaw an earlier stock release this year. She added that the Commission was in close contact with EU member countries and Washington.
Advertisement
Meanwhile, President Trump on Wednesday confirmed that a diesel export ban by his administration was still on the table. “I’m thinking about it,” Trump said of the export ban at an Oval Office event. “I speak to [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it a lot — they sort of think it’ll help diesel, but it might raise the price of other things.”
Trump declined to rule out restricting diesel shipments. “It’s something that we think about and we talk about every day,” he said. “But it just seems that it would have a negative impact on gasoline, so that would go up a little bit, and diesel would come down a little bit.”
Wright, who was with Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said the administration would soon announce measures aimed at bringing down diesel prices. Europe would also be announcing moves to add supply to the market, he said.
“You will hear announcements from our friends in Europe about new diesel supplies that’ll come to the market that’ll meaningfully push diesel prices down,” Wright said.
Ben Lefebvre and James Bikales contributed reporting.

Central Asia’s Diplomatic Balancing Act on Display from Bishkek to New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

The general debate of the 81st U.N. General Assembly closed this week, and the Central Asian speeches put the region’s balancing act on full display. As the world moves toward multipolarity, the five Central Asian states find themselves in a tight spot. They must manage relations with the two leading global powers, the United States and China, while preserving their ties with Russia, with which they share deep historical, economic, and political bonds.
Three weeks before the debate opened, Kyrgyzstan hosted the Shanghai Cooperation Organization’s (SCO) 25th-anniversary summit on August 31 and September 1. Four of the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan – are SCO members, while neutral Turkmenistan remains formally out, although it occasionally participates as a guest. The SCO is widely seen as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to limit Washington’s footprint in Eurasia, and the 2026 summit’s Bishkek Declaration gave the United States plenty to dislike, from a firm condemnation of military strikes on Iran to opposition to “unilateral coercive measures.”
Taken together, the two gatherings reveal a clear division of labor in Central Asian diplomacy. The region’s governments echo Beijing’s and Moscow’s grievances in regional group settings like the SCO, court Washington with concrete deals via bilateral channels, and use the U.N. General Assembly (UNGA) podium to say as little as possible that might offend any of the three.
The balancing starts with who showed up. Presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Emomali Rahmon, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, and Sadyr Japarov all attended the SCO summit in person, alongside China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and India’s Narendra Modi. Three weeks later, only Japarov traveled to New York, after making a stop in the U.S. state of Utah. All five Central Asian countries had sent their heads of state last year for the U.N.’s 80th anniversary. Xi and Modi also skipped this year’s session, though Xi was in Washington on a state visit around the same time.
This does not mean, however, that Central Asia has abandoned Washington for its rivals. Kazakhstan, for one, backed Security Council Resolution 2803, the November 2025 measure endorsing Trump’s Gaza peace plan and his Board of Peace, even though Russia and China abstained. Tokayev sits on that board. Kazakhstan, which announced it would join the Abraham Accords last November, also took part in its first accords meeting in New York on September 24. Japarov, for his part, carried the SCO’s complaint about Western sanctions to the UNGA podium, yet he also thanked Trump for cutting U.S. funding to foreign NGOs.
These are low-cost gestures aimed at a transactional White House, and they come bundled with commerce. In mid-October, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will lead a delegation of more than 100 American companies to Samarkand for a C5+1 ministerial meeting, his first trip to the region. With the United States and China racing to secure critical minerals, Central Asian capitals have something Washington wants.
Beijing, meanwhile, offers trade on a scale Washington cannot match. Xi paired the Bishkek summit with a state visit to Kyrgyzstan and pledged an SCO center for AI cooperation and 100 joint technology projects over three years. He arrived as the region’s largest trading partner, after China-Central Asia goods trade hit a record $106 billion last year. In Bishkek, all four Central Asian members also reaffirmed their support for China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Competition between the two powers lets Central Asian capitals bargain with both.
Central Asia is also building influence inside the U.N. system, and the great power scramble for its mineral wealth may give it more leverage to raise its global profile. Kyrgyzstan joins the Security Council in January, having been elected with 142 votes in June. Tajikistan used its UNGA address to announce its first-ever U.N. Security Council bid, for 2028-2029. Uzbekistan declared its candidacy for 2035-2036 and will chair the Non-Aligned Movement next year, while Turkmenistan will chair the group of landlocked developing countries.
Uzbekistan’s statement, delivered by the president’s daughter and head of the presidential administration Saida Mirziyoyeva, captured the balancing act neatly. Observing that countries are being asked which side they choose, Mirziyoyeva answered with “human dignity” rather than a camp, echoing the Bishkek Declaration’s own rejection of “bloc-based and confrontational” approaches. Uzbek President Mirziyoyev sat beside Xi and Putin in Bishkek; next month, Samarkand hosts Rubio.
Central Asia’s multivector strategy has not disappeared, but it has changed form. The region now aligns rhetorically with Beijing and Moscow in regional group settings, materially with Washington in bilateral deals, and with no one in particular at the United Nations. As great power rivalry intensifies, the open questions are how long Central Asian governments can hold this position and how much they can gain from it.
