Bedford rail crash: train sped up after red light warning, say investigators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:21:21 UTC
21:21:21 KST

The train that ran into the back of another in the Bedford rail crash sped up after the driver received a warning he had passed a red light, rail investigators have reported.
The driver of the East Midlands train, who died in the crash in June, acknowledged the automatic warning but did not appear to act after passing a danger signal that was rarely ever red.
According to an updated report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch, the train continued to accelerate before the driver applied the emergency brakes when the stationary train in front came into view.
The train, a southbound Luton airport express from Corby, could not stop in time, and the collision killed the driver, 60-year-old Shaun Burton, who was described by his employers as a “dedicated railway professional”.
Investigators had been seeking to establish if the automatic warning system (AWS) had worked properly, after an initial report found the train had passed a red signal.
The latest interim report published on Thursday concluded that the driver had acknowledged the warning, which had not previously displayed a red light during all of 2026, but continued to accelerate to 76mph. After braking, the train slowed to 49mph before it collided with a stationary Nottingham-London train on the same track.
The first train had stopped after braking when an AWS warning incorrectly sounded after passing a green signal. The train was a new Aurora class 810 model built by Hitachi, brought into service within the past six months on East Midlands Railway.
In a cab with an unfamiliar layout, when no warning signal was expected, the RAIB report said that “neither the driver nor driving instructor recognised this sound as being an AWS warning indication”. Without an acknowledgment in 2.7 seconds, the system applies an emergency brake.
The accident inspectors reported that in the weeks after the crash, another class 810 train had also incorrectly received an AWS warning indication at the same signal on green.
The RAIB said it would continue to seek to understand why the Corby train had passed a red light, and whether its safety systems had been functioning correctly, as well as the reason why the first Nottingham train had come to a halt.
The report said 160 people had also been injured in the crash, which happened at about 5.13pm on 19 June. It was the fourth involving passenger trains on the UK railway since 2020, after more than a decade without any similar serious incident.

Swiss glaciers lose over 5% of ice volume in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:16:56 UTC
21:16:56 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Swiss glaciers lost more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 as intense heat waves and a winter with little snow drove another year of extreme melting, according to new data released Thursday.
The Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation of the Swiss Academy of Sciences said the average thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 and 4 meters (8.2 and 13.1 feet), while some glacier tongues lost as much as 10 meters (nearly 33 ft) over the summer.
In the past five years alone, Switzerland's total glacier volume has declined by almost 20%, according to the study.
Winter 2025-26 ranked "among the 10 least snowy" since measurements began, while every month from May through September brought dry conditions and at least one heat wave.
The freezing level remained above 4,000 meters on a record 76 days, more than twice the average. The study stressed that by September, no snow had remained, even at elevations of 3,500 meters (11,483 ft).
Several small glaciers have already disappeared during the heat wave in June, including the Bella Tola Glacier and Griessfiren/Plattalvafirn.
Between July and September, glaciers lost around 2.2 trillion liters of water, more than four times the annual drinking water consumption of all Swiss households.
Researchers said meltwater is still easing summer water shortages, but that contribution is diminishing as Switzerland's ice-covered area continues to shrink.

He failed to close the skies and missed the procurement of missiles for Patriot, but showed an AI video about robots — Magda criticized Fedorov for empty presentations

Political analyst Yevhen Mahda called "Closed Skies" an unfulfilled promise. He criticized the AI videos about the "Army of Robots" and procurement problems.
The “Closed Sky” initiative announced by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, which promised to shoot down 95% of drones, turned out to be a marketing ploy that failed to deliver the promised results. It has now been replaced by AI videos about an “Army of Robots,” further deepening public disappointment amid Fedorov’s failure to secure the purchase of missiles for Patriot systems and the defense budget funds spent ahead of schedule. Political analyst Yevhen Mahda wrote about this, reports UNN.
"While serving as minister, Fedorov assured people that his developments would help intercept at least 95% of missiles and drones." In the end, the pompously presented “Closed Sky” turned out to be nothing more than words,” the political analyst wrote.
Against this backdrop, Fedorov presented the “Army of Robots.” However, instead of offering new hope, the AI videos may cause even greater disappointment, Mahda believes.
"By showing a nice AI video in which robots are fighting, they are giving us yet another false hope. When there is nothing besides videos, it is demoralizing. Because selling hope in this form to a society seeking salvation in anything it can find is immoral," he said.
The political analyst illustrated the gap between presentations and results with data from Ukrainska Pravda, according to which Fedorov’s team missed the opportunity to purchase missiles for Patriot systems and began other defense procurements with a critical delay.
"While handling the distribution of funds, Fedorov’s team missed the signing of an agreement to purchase missiles for Patriot systems. "This is precisely what is frightening. A bubble of attractive presentations—and that is all. The purchase of Patriot missiles was missed because they were busy disbursing the funds; payments to service members were depleted in advance; the “Contract 18–24” program was never properly launched; the pompously presented “Closed Sky” turned out to be nothing more than words. And against this backdrop, we once again see a Hollywood-style AI video. The “Army of Robots,”" Mahda concluded.
He emphasized that during wartime, society expects such projects to protect civilians and military personnel, without noticing signs that they are fake and merely advertisements.
"When Fedorov talks about intercepting 95%, people hear that they will be protected. When he talks about new contracts, service members hear that their terms of service will change. When he shows robots, a soldier on the front line hopes that a machine will go there instead of him. When this turns out to be a lie, a kind of “marketing ploy,” it leads to complete disappointment. Therefore, the responsibility for such statements is much greater than the responsibility for yet another startup presentation," the political analyst summed up.

UK 30-year bond yield hits highest since 1998 amid global sell-off

Unknown Publisher

Mucahithan Avcioglu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
The yield on Britain’s 30-year government bond reached 6% on Thursday, its highest level since 1998, as a global bond sell-off drove up borrowing costs amid concerns over inflation and elevated energy prices.
The yield climbed to 6%, according to London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) data. Bond yields rise as prices fall.
The increase came as higher oil prices and uncertainty surrounding the conflict in the Middle East weighed on government debt markets. Brokerage XTB said Britain’s 30-year yield had crossed 6% for the first time since 1998, with Brent crude trading around $100 per barrel.
The Bank of England warned Wednesday that the financial stability risk outlook had deteriorated since July, citing renewed tensions in the Middle East and growing financial exposures linked to artificial intelligence.
In the record of its Financial Policy Committee’s Sept. 25 meeting, the UK central bank said rising oil, gas and refined petroleum product prices were prolonging the negative supply shock to the global economy and increasing uncertainty over growth and interest rates.
Persistently higher government bond yields could tighten financing conditions for households and businesses, increase market volatility and limit governments’ ability to respond to future shocks, the bank warned.
The committee said the financial system had remained resilient, with market adjustments mostly gradual. However, elevated hedge fund leverage in the gilt market and increasingly interconnected vulnerabilities meant the risk of a sharp adjustment persisted.

WhatsApp introduces optional parental controls for teenagers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:15:18 UTC
21:15:18 KST

Dilara Hamit
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
WhatsApp announced Wednesday that it is introducing optional parental controls for teenage users, giving parents greater oversight of privacy settings and online interactions without allowing them to read their children’s conversations.
The messaging service said parents would be able to decide who can see a teenager’s profile photograph, who can add them to groups and how they use features including Channels and Status.
Parents will receive notifications when their teenager joins or leaves a group, as well as when a group involving their child grows significantly in size.
The controls will be protected by a PIN set up by the parent. Teenagers who want to loosen restricted privacy settings will require parental approval through the PIN.
Parents will also be able to select how their child uses Meta AI, WhatsApp’s optional artificial intelligence assistant. They can choose between the default setting intended for users aged 13 and older or a stricter option labled Limited Content.
Despite the additional controls, parents will not be able to see or listen to their teenager’s private messages and calls.
“Even with controls turned on, your teen’s personal messages and calls stay private and protected by end-to-end encryption,” WhatsApp said in its announcement.
The company said the tools were intended to encourage conversations between parents and teenagers about their use of the platform while maintaining the privacy of personal communications.
Parents will be able to adjust or disable the controls at any time. WhatsApp said participation would be entirely voluntary because different families required varying levels of supervision.
The optional nature of the system, however, has prompted questions about how widely it will be adopted.
The announcement comes as technology companies face growing pressure from governments and regulators to make their services safer and more age-appropriate for children.
The proposed ban is expected to cover services including Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube and X, along with stronger age-assurance requirements.

====================================================================================================

2 Driverless Cars Crashed Going 155 mph. That Could Be a Good Thing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:15:00 UTC
21:15:00 KST

The grandstands erupted with shock as engineers clutched their heads in the paddock. One driverless race car, produced by the company PoliMove, slammed into Unimore’s slowing vehicle in an event held by the Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL).
At the famous racing track in Imola, Italy, Autodromo Internazionale Enzo e Dino Ferrari, both cars crashed in an area called Rivazza. This is the circuit’s final sequence, made up of corners that are notoriously difficult to navigate. Formula 1 champions have met a similar fate here. But this time, the impact posed no danger to the drivers because there weren’t any.
Launched in 2024, A2RL sought to introduce self-driving cars to the motorsport to test the boundaries of their current capabilities. And this year’s race at Imola revealed those edges, demonstrating of the gap between the computational abilities of autonomous vehicles and their capacity to respond when something goes wrong.
Only two of the five cars in the final completed the race. The UAE’s Kinetiz finished first, followed by Germany’s Constructor Racing. PoliMove clocked in at third place, though its battered entrant had to be replaced for the podium ceremony. Two-time winner TUM withdrew its car after it developed a brake problem during the formation lap.
Participating teams had just nine days of physical testing before the race, in conditions that included rain and hail. This also happened to be the league’s first international competition away from its usual testing ground at Abu Dhabi’s Yas Marina Circuit.
So why choose one of motorsport’s most unforgiving tracks?
“Because everybody can do ‘easy’, right?” says Nicola Palarchi, engineering director at Aspire, the company that founded A2RL. “We have to show we go where it matters.”
Palarchi made it abundantly clear that autonomous racing did not intend to compete with human racing, but rather stay its own motorsport. It could even support the latter.
Because autonomous racing is pitched as more than spectacle: It’s a laboratory with guardrails. Its proponents describe it as a way to test perception, prediction, and vehicle control at extreme speeds without endangering a human driver. These are all factors in the safety of driverless cars in the real world, and so measuring the limits at which these vehicles succeed—or perhaps more importantly fail—can inform future improvements in the technology.
The first hurdle is perception. The vehicle’s sensors identify its location and surroundings, informing planning software that then chooses a trajectory. Finally, the control system translates that decision into steering, acceleration, and braking. Racing makes each of these stages more challenging, since at high speeds, vehicles have less time to interpret incomplete information, predict another car’s movements and execute an evasive maneuver.
“The car will be blind for a certain point because the track drops off,” Alexander Winkler, A2RL’s head of sporting, had said before the final. If one vehicle stopped beyond that drop, he explained, the car behind could have less than a second to react.
That warning proved prescient.
Unimore said its car, Gianna, initiated a safety stop after losing all data from its lidar and radar sensors. GPS alone could not locate the car accurately enough to continue racing at speed. The team said future systems could use cameras and an inertial measurement unit to continue at a slower pace until precise localization returned. In other words, the car stopped because it lacked a reliable fallback.
PoliMove’s vehicle, Eva, detected Gianna ahead, according to the team, but could not avoid hitting it. Gianna had braked with a force of approximately 1 g with Eva just 1.5 seconds behind it.
PoliMove said its system identified the danger and began an evasive maneuver. But perception, decision-making, trajectory replanning, actuator response, and vehicle dynamics all introduce delays. Once Gianna braked that severely mid-corner, the team said, a collision was physically impossible to avoid.
Even F1 legends like Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz have crashed at this part of the track. However, the A2RL teams’ explanation exposes a problem that faster processors alone cannot solve: An autonomous vehicle may recognize a hazard and still be unable to respond before physics takes over.
TUM’s failure was less algorithmic but equally instructive. The team said its car, Hailey, retired after the rear-left brake became stuck at low-to-medium pressure during the formation lap. Even sophisticated autonomous software cannot compensate for mechanical faults.
Kinetiz’s car, Sparkz, took the lead all the way to a first-place podium finish with Constructor AI’s vehicle as the runner-up. But almost any result can be considered progress, when the failures produced useful edge cases: sensor loss, compromised localization, sudden braking, limited visibility, and interaction between autonomous systems making separate decisions.
Beyond crash data, Palarchi says these motorsport environments provide the opportunity to develop more resilient hardware. Temperatures in cockpits can get near 170 degrees F, and—while hopefully your robotaxi is not that hot—radars and lidars that can withstand high heat can be useful in our warming cities.
Chee Kiong Ong, deputy team principal at Kinetiz, also observes that predictive algorithms developed on the track could eventually help civilian vehicles respond to emergencies. “You could probably apply it to make the car stop itself in a safer manner or control it at the limits so that you can save lives,” he says.
One caveat is that unlike other lab testing, the companies aren’t required to share the precise data collected from their vehicles. The data from A2RL’s EAV 25, the racing car developed by the league based on modified Dallara SF23 cars, currently stays within the competition.
The next A2RL race returns to Yas Marina, where teams have spent years developing their software. Organizers are already considering making the competition harder by shortening testing periods, increasing the grid to eight cars, or restricting access to GPS.
Those changes could reveal whether the systems are becoming more adaptable. In the meantime, we’ll wait to see how this information transfers into real-life scenarios.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:09:34 UTC
21:09:34 KST

Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices.
Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region.
Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday.
Diesel prices in the US have risen to record highs in recent weeks, adding to cost of living pressures that have helped push Trump’s approval ratings to a career low before next month’s crucial midterm elections.
Energy analysts, however, have pointed to the war in Iran and wider disruption to global oil markets as the leading drivers of the price increases.
Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have nevertheless emerged as an additional headache for Trump, with the attacks also contributing to tighter diesel supplies at a politically sensitive moment for the US president.
Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations.
Earlier this week, Russia – traditionally the world’s second-largest diesel exporter – extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, adding further pressure to a global supply crunch.
Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies, said it was unlikely Kyiv would stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure as long as Moscow continued its daily attacks on Ukraine. “There is no rationale for Ukraine to continue exercising restraint while it is being bombarded and major urban areas are under constant attack,” he said.
“We need to deprive Russia of revenue,” he added.
Zelenskyy has been pushing for a US-brokered energy ceasefire with Russia, but Putin has shown little interest in the proposal, instead vowing to intensify strikes on Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Russia has continued its deadly missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, targeting energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and other businesses in an apparent effort to cripple the country’s economy and render Kyiv increasingly uninhabitable.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday morning, but no one was injured because the children were sheltering in the basement, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
A key bridge in the Ukrainian capital was also hit, forcing authorities to suspend metro services and other public transport.
Kyiv has experienced near round-the-clock Russian attacks in recent weeks, at times increasingly resembling a frontline city in what many see as the most challenging period for the capital since the early days of the full-scale invasion.
Russia’s newer jet-powered drones have proved particularly difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, with success rates significantly lower than for the slower Shahed-type drones.
The sustained attacks have revived fears of another winter with prolonged power and heating outages, after similar strikes last year left parts of Ukraine without electricity during temperatures that fell as low as -20C.

Who will teach the next generation?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:04:01 UTC
21:04:01 KST

On October 12, Jerusalem will be the site of a landmark event in the history of Jewish education – the Global Jewish Educators Summit. Organized by the Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Ministry, the four-day conference will bring hundreds of Jewish educators from around the world together to share ideas and shape the future of Jewish education. The conference, originally scheduled for March, was postponed to October due to Operation Roaring Lion.
Over 200 Jewish teachers, principals, and Jewish educational leaders from around the world, along with 100 Israeli teachers, will gather at Jerusalem’s Ramada Hotel to network, learn about the latest educational tools and methodologies, and build connections that will last long after the conference.
UnitEd, the educational organization that empowers Jewish day schools worldwide, will facilitate the event. Rachel Fink, director of education for UnitEd, explained the significance of the conference, saying, “The future of Jewish education will not be shaped by programs or curricula alone. It will be shaped by the people standing in front of Jewish children every day. “The Global Jewish Educators Summit is about recognizing that responsibility, learning from the extraordinary educators working around the world, and strengthening the connections between them and Israel. We want every educator who comes to Jerusalem to leave knowing that the work they do matters and that UnitEd is with them every step of the way.”
The Global Jewish Educators Summit puts Jewish educators at center stage, recognizing their role in shaping the future of Jewish life in the Diaspora and expressing deep appreciation for their work and dedication. At the event, eight outstanding educators will be presented with the Jewish Teachers Award, recognizing extraordinary Jewish educators and celebrating the transformative role they play in shaping the Jewish future.
Personal, communal, educational
The summit will explore three themes: the educator’s personal identity and mission; the relationship between Israel and Jewish communities worldwide; and the responsibility to pass on Jewish knowledge, values, and belonging. Together, these themes connect the personal, communal, and educational dimensions of Jewish life and invite educators to reflect on their role in shaping the Jewish future.
One of the primary goals of the summit will be to give educators new ideas, strategies, and contacts, so that they may return to their communities with a new network of colleagues from around the world, a professional toolbox of ideas and concepts, and a renewed sense of mission – knowing that they are part of a global Jewish educational community, and that their work is recognized and appreciated.
The summit will also reflect the State of Israel’s commitment to supporting Jewish educators worldwide, strengthening their professional and educational leadership, and deepening the partnership between Israel, Jewish communities across the globe, and the educators who help shape our shared future.
Jewish educators from across the full spectrum of Jewish education, representing diverse educational settings, approaches, and communities from around the world, will participate in the summit. Participants will come from a wide range of Jewish schools and countries, creating an opportunity for meaningful cross-cultural learning, exchange, and connection.
Rabbi Levi Milecki, head of primary at Kesser Torah College in Sydney, Australia, who will be attending the summit, says that the major challenges confronting Jewish education in Australia include assimilation, the high cost of living, and antisemitism, as reflected in the Hanukkah shootings on Bondi Beach in Sydney on December 14, 2025, in which 15 people were killed and 40 people were wounded.
“People always used to think Australia was the safest place to live in the world, and we’ve learned the hard way that that’s not the case,” said Milecki.
Over 90 students from Kesser Torah were on Bondi Beach during the attack, and the school has devoted a great deal of attention to the aftereffects of the tragedy. “The effect on our school was quite significant,” he added. Milecki said that the community is grateful for the assistance it received from Sheba Medical Center, Hatzalah, and One Family after the shootings.
“That really shows that even though we are far, and Australia is very far – on the other side of the world – we are really one family. And no matter what life throws at us, whatever antisemitism throws at us, whatever the world throws at us, when we reach across the world, and we can connect with each other across the world, we really can help each other get through this. Things will be brighter. But it really is up to us to be able to make that happen, and Jewish educators play the most important role because we are raising the next generation.”
Milecki shared that he is looking forward to his trip to Jerusalem for the summit and hopes to gain a different perspective and hear how other educators inspire their students and schools to have a strong Jewish identity and maintain their Jewish pride.
Rabbi Sam Thurgood, head of Jewish life and learning at the United Herzlia Schools, in Cape Town, South Africa, says that while the events of October 7 have highlighted the vulnerabilities of Jewish people around the world, including those in South Africa, they also brought a sense of the responsibilities of Jews toward each other. For Thurgood, responding to antisemitism begins with a clear understanding of Jewish identity and values. “It’s only from that sense of clarity and inspiration within our own Jewish identity and values that it makes sense to respond to antisemitism. We’re not here to defy the antisemites. We’re here because this is who we are. And if we strongly believe in that, we can then formulate the answers to the questions and challenges that come in.”
He shared that one of the great strengths of Jewish education in South Africa is the fact that between 75% and 85% of Jewish children in the country attend a Jewish day school. “What that means is that our day schools are really at the center of our communities, and the values of our communities and what we achieve within the community,” he said.
The large numbers of Jewish children who attend day school also present a unique challenge, he noted. “Because there is such a broad section of the community attending Jewish schools, there is some level of pressure to try to be all things to all people.”
Thurgood said most young South African Jews today have a strong, positive connection to the State of Israel and feel deeply connected to Israel and Israelis. He is looking forward to attending the summit and learning new things. “What I’ve always found with conferences of this type is the exposure to high-caliber educators on the cutting edge of Jewish education, both from those presenting at the conference and those that you meet within the conference, as well as a chance for us to be present in and experience Israel.”
The Global Jewish Educators Summit will bring together learning, inspiration, connection, and belonging; strengthen participants’ sense of purpose and shared responsibility; and recognize the profound contribution educators make to Jewish life.
Written in collaboration with Israel’s Ministry for Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism, UnitEd, Herzog College and the World Zionist Organization’s Department of Education.

EU watchdogs question Binance over unlicensed European operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:03:21 UTC
21:03:21 KST

European regulators are questioning Binance over its use of a narrow legal exemption to keep serving EU customers without a licence, the Financial Times reported. Binance told Euronews it is working towards authorisation, while ESMA said enforcement is a matter for national authorities.
The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange is under scrutiny from EU watchdogs for continuing to serve clients in the bloc, months after it was told to wind down its European business, according to a report by the Financial Times on Thursday.
Binance failed to secure a licence this summer under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), the EU's rulebook for the sector. Unlicensed companies were expected to take "immediate steps" to wind down their EU operations from 1 July and to serve customers only to help them transfer or sell their crypto holdings.
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU's markets watchdog, and national regulators in countries including France, Germany and Greece are now examining how Binance uses "reverse solicitation", the FT reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The legal exemption allows companies based outside the EU to serve customers in the bloc as long as those customers seek out the service entirely on their own initiative.
Some regulators have asked Binance for information and could take enforcement action, including fines, if they are not satisfied with its answers, according to the report, which added that regulators are also looking at smaller crypto firms.
A "very narrowly framed" exception
"The reverse solicitation exemption should be understood as very narrowly framed. It should be regarded as the exception and not be used to circumvent MiCA requirements," ESMA told the FT.
The Dutch market watchdog AFM went further.
"Crypto asset service providers cannot simply claim reverse solicitation: there are clear requirements and guidelines that must be met," it told the newspaper.
Binance's local licences in countries such as France, Spain and Poland lapsed under MiCA, while customers in other EU countries are served by its entity in Abu Dhabi, where it has been regulated since December 2025.
However, the experience for European users on the platform has not changed since the MiCA deadline on 1 July.
In countries where it held no local licence, Binance operates "under reverse solicitation" and is "seeing customers wanting to onboard" of their own accord, one person familiar with the matter told the FT, adding that the company did not want to grow its business that way in the long term.
What Binance and ESMA told Euronews
Asked by Euronews about the regulators' questions, Binance declined to address the situation and instead simply replied that it "complies with applicable regulatory requirements in the jurisdictions in which it operates."
"In Europe, Binance remains committed to operating on a long-term, compliant basis under the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation. We are actively working toward becoming MiCA-authorised," a spokesperson said.
ESMA told Euronews it "does not comment on specific cases".
It stressed, however, that under MiCA, "the supervision, investigation, and enforcement are national competences", while its own role is to promote consistent supervision across the bloc by encouraging cooperation and information-sharing between authorities and issuing guidance.
Any penalties against Binance would have to come from national authorities rather than from Paris-based ESMA itself.
The scrutiny adds to years of regulatory trouble for Binance, which agreed to pay $4.3bn (€3.8bn) in penalties in the US in 2023 and pleaded guilty to criminal charges related to money laundering and breaching US sanctions.
Whether it can hold on to its European users now depends on how regulators judge its reading of the exemption, and whether and how quickly it secures the licence it says it is pursuing.

US datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:51 UTC
21:00:51 KST

DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1m fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.
The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.
Floodlight sent technical data about the generators – obtained through public records requests – to a Rutgers professor and a former EPA air division chief.
“Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers department of environmental sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data.
NOx are a dangerous group of smog-producing gases linked to asthma, heart attacks and even premature death. It was “the most important air pollutant in the US that affects most people”, Jin said.
Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounded like an airplane in the back of her house.
“What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said.
The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit – a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit.
Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution” and the fleet’s potential emissions are “well over the regulatory threshold for a new major source”, said Buckheit.
New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source”. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods – all before construction can even begin.
That didn’t happen at DataOne, despite the operation being capable of emitting more than half the NOx put out by New Jersey’s entire power sector.
“That is basically offsetting some of the air quality improvements [regulators] have achieved for decades,” Jin said.
DataOne did not respond to Floodlight’s emissions analysis. Instead, its spokesperson sent the same statement as they did in response to NJDEP’s decision to fine them, saying the company was “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site’s permanent power solution and have the necessary approvals in place for this solution”.
The company disagrees with NJDEP’s determination and had argued the generators did not require permits – but plans to apply for them now.
A Microsoft spokesperson wrote that “we expect our suppliers and partners to meet all applicable legal and regulatory obligations” and the company was working with DataOne “to support their completion of the facility’s transition to its permanent long-term power solution”.
In press releases, New Jersey regulators said the tractor-trailer-sized generators were detected during a 29 July 2026, site inspection but not during an earlier visit in December. However, the fleet was there to find, according to a letter DataOne later sent NJDEP.
The letter, obtained by Floodlight through a public records request, notes the generators first began to arrive in July 2025. Sixteen generators started operating in October 2025, with another 16 brought online in early February. By June, all 62 had been fired up.
By the time state inspectors noticed them, the unpermitted fleet had collectively run for more than 46,000 hours in total, according to the letter.
“How did 62 generators get installed and operated and nobody did anything until now? That blows me away,” Leone-Vespa said. “Clearly somebody wasn’t doing their job.”
A spokesperson for NJDEP declined to comment.
For many Vineland residents, confirmation that DataOne’s generators have been running for nearly a year is a bittersweet vindication. Locals have reported strange noises emanating from the facility for months, with more than 100 noise complaints submitted to the Cumberland county department of health since March, according to records obtained by Floodlight. Many of the complaints list generators as the suspected source.
“They’re just running these monster generators. And they think, by right, they have every ability to do so at the expense of anyone else,” said local flower farmer Michael Atkinson.
Atkinson’s family has been farming a patch of land beside the datacenter for more than 70 years. He said DataOne was “one of the richest and worst neighbors that I have ever had to deal with in my entire life”.
During a Vineland town hall meeting in late January, DataOne’s chief executive, Charles Beyney, told residents that his datacenter would be “polluting less than a farm”.
“I’m too French to just kill my lungs, the lungs of your kids and all the community around us,” he told the crowd.
Beyney confirmed during that speech that DataOne was running generators, and he said NJDEP was aware – the agency had been at the site that same morning and was “on us big time”.
While the generators may have evaded state regulators for almost a year, local officials knew about them for much longer.
A City of Vineland inspection activity report noted that “phase 1 generators are online” in early February. And in May, a Cumberland county health department inspector responding to a noise complaint visited the site and reported that the source of the noise appeared to be two generators, “possibly more”.
The inspector noted that the noise “exceeded night-time violation”.
As part of the record fine levied against DataOne, the state is mandating the company apply for and obtain the required permits or cease operations, but is allowing them 45 days to do so, according to a NJDEP spokesperson.
During that time, regulators are allowing the facility to continue running the generators – which are capable of emitting more than four tons of NOx in nearby neighborhoods each day.
“I just don’t understand how this is being allowed,” Leone-Vespa said. She hopes independent air monitoring can help protect her community in the future. Until then, she has little faith in New Jersey regulators to watch out for them.
“It’s like they don’t care about the residents.

‘Page one of repressive playbook’: critics warn of Trump’s conspiratorial attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

Since the start of his second presidency, Donald Trump has often launched outlandish conspiratorial attacks on critics and foes that mock them and label their views as hoaxes, prompting scholars and legal experts to say Trump’s attacks endanger US freedoms, public health and science.
Trump’s extensive use of conspiracy theories is the hallmark of an authoritarian leader that has weakened trust in the coming midterm elections, dangerously ignored scientific evidence, and often pushed for prosecutions of his political enemies in ways that seriously erode civil liberties, say critics.
Trump’s conspiratorial and authoritarian-style tactics are palpable say critics, in his false claim that the US faces a “crisis of election security” to bolster his radical push for new curbs on voting rights, and his labeling of climate change as a “hoax” despite extensive scientific evidence that it’s a reality.
To some scholars, Trump-backed conspiratorial claims have had a damaging impact on all levels of US society and democracy and are emblematic of how authoritarian leaders use conspiracies to justify repression.
Steven Levitsky, the Harvard professor of government and the co-author of How Democracies Die, said: “Conspiracies are page one of the repressive playbook,” noting that Mao, Stalin, Putin and other authoritarian leaders have historically launched attacks on enemies by floating conspiracies.
“They’re almost always used to justify repression,” Levitsky added noting that authoritarian leaders can simply allege conspiracies without providing any or only minimal “evidence”.
In a notable twist, Trump charged in mid-September that some AI leaders and experts were engaging in a big “conspiracy” and perpetrating a “HOAX”, by urging strong safeguards to protect against potential extinction-level threats to humanity from this powerful new technology.
Similarly, Trump without evidence disparaged critics of datacenters as people who “want to end up being backwards and poor”, and asserted he was the best “guardrail” to protect society from threats that unregulated AI pose.
Scholars and former federal officials say that Trump’s tarring foes in conspiratorial attacks endangers democracy and recall the tactics of the infamous rightwing lawyer Roy Cohn, a key promoter of the “red scare” in the 1950s who Trump had close ties with in the 1980s during his early New York real estate career.
“Trump, mentored by Roy Cohn, learned that baseless allegations about shady forces working against him could serve to mobilize and lead the public to see him as a victim rather than a wrongdoer,” said the Princeton historian Julian Zelizer. “Whenever faced with criticism, such as from the media or about his AI policies, his instinct is to throw out charges of a vast conspiracy that is out to get him.”
Zelizer stressed: “Trump’s frequent use of conspiracies to attack critics has a damaging impact on all levels of society and democracy, from weakening confidence in elections to hurting our ability to deal with serious problems involving the AI industry.”
Trump’s penchant to paint critics in conspiratorial tones as dangerous enemies was palpable in his attacks last week on three news outlets – CNN, Politico and MS Now – barring them from White House access which prompted them to jointly file a lawsuit on 21 September challenging his moves on First Amendment and due process grounds.
In a Truth Social post on 21 September, Trump boasted that the White House “is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
A federal judge in DC ruled on 23 September that the administration should immediately return the press passes to the three outlets and its punitive action against them was probably unconstitutional.
Former federal prosecutor Ty Cobb who was a special counsel in the White House during Trump’s first term, warned that “Trump denies, denigrates and demeans his foes by painting them as part of a conspiracy … He resorts to abject fabrications in response to any criticism or resistance.”
This year Trump and his justice department have devoted sizable resources to bolster his conspiratorial claims that his 2020 loss to Joe Biden was due to fraud, and that the current voting system is riddled with fraud, notwithstanding overwhelming evidence to the contrary.
Trump has repeatedly pushed bogus claims laced with conspiracies as he did in a nationally televised speech on 16 July, when he urged tough new measures to curb voting by mail and investigate non-citizen voting ostensibly to make elections more secure.
In the TV speech, Trump made the factually inaccurate claim that non-citizen voting, which is illegal and historically negligible, poses a “crisis of election security”.
Trump’s obsession with painting non-citizen voting as a crisis is badly undercut by data from the conservative Heritage Foundation that cites just 100 cases over a 25-year period.
Critics see these moves by Trump to raise bogus fears about election safety and dark forces bent on voter fraud as a tool to “undermine public confidence” in the elections.
“It seems that the Trump administration is grooming the electorate to believe that the fall election will abound with fraud,” said Barbara McQuade, a former US attorney who teaches law at the University of Michigan.
“It is difficult to know if this effort is a pretext for seizing voting equipment, a strategy to intimidate some likely Democratic voters from showing up at the polls, or a campaign to undermine public confidence in the outcome, but all of it is harmful to democracy.”
On another front, Trump’s justice department has struggled for almost a year to find evidence to bring charges in an investigation looking at a “grand conspiracy” against Trump involving the so called “deep state” going back to President Barack Obama and inquiries into Russia’s efforts to influence the 2016 election. The investigation, which Trump has cheered on, has issued subpoenas to several former national security and law enforcement officials including ex-CIA director John Brennan and ex-FBI director James Comey.
This sprawling inquiry has tapped some key Trump-allied election denialists for top posts. Notably, Trump recruited 81-year-old Joe diGenova, a former prosecutor who led the effort until he abruptly announced his departure on 10 September, and ex-White House lawyer Kurt Olsen. Both lawyers had worked to discredit the 2020 election results and Joe Biden’s win.
The sudden move by diGenova to resign – after only five months on the job – raised questions about its direction and credibility. DiGenova’s departure followed that of another top prosecutor who was heading the investigation; Maria Medetis Long, a veteran national security prosecutor, resigned in April after reportedly voicing concerns about its direction.
“The so-called Grand Conspiracy investigation turns prosecutorial practice on its head,” said ex-justice department inspector general Michael Bromwich who has represented ex-FBI deputy director Andrew McCabe in the inquiry.
“It starts with designated targets, the president’s perceived enemies, and then searches for facts and bends the law to support the theory. Joe diGenova found that it was easier to be an outside propagandist cheering the theory from the sidelines than have the responsibility to build such a case with actual facts.”
In other energy and environmental matters, Trump and his top officials have deployed bogus conspiracies and specious information to counter growing evidence of the risks posed by climate change from rising temperatures to dangerous storms worldwide.
The Trump administration has moved hard to kill energy and environmental regulations aimed at fighting climate change, and simultaneously have promoted greater usage of coal, which Trump has lauded erroneously as “clean and beautiful”, and other fossil fuels that worsen climate change.
Late last year, Trump energy officials issued emergency orders to keep open five ageing coal plants in Michigan and four other states that were scheduled to shut down, spurring some states to challenge the costly moves.
In mid-September, a federal judge ruled that the energy department had exceeded its authority by ordering the Michigan plant to stay open past its retirement.
Further, after years of conspiratorial attacks on wind energy by Trump, his administration in December announced it was pausing leases on five offshore wind projects on the east coast in a big blow to the industry.
The five windfarms were slated to power over 2.5m homes and create 10,000 jobs. A federal judge in February issued a preliminary injunction allowing one of the five to stay open.
“Trump’s decisions make no sense from either the perspective of environmental protection or the cost of energy,” Naomi Oreskes, a Harvard University science historian and professor of earth and planetary sciences, told the Guardian earlier this year.
Oreskes added that “by blocking wind projects that [were] just about ready to go on line, and reviving dangerous and uneconomic coal-powered plants, this administration is raising both the direct costs of energy for the American people, and the indirect costs we suffer through polluted air and climate damage.”
Significantly, the Trump administration in February revoked a major scientific finding that climate change endangers public health, an idea that Trump has derided as “a scam”, despite numerous scientific studies saying it’s a well quantifiable harm.
Dr Howard Frumkin, a professor emeritus of public health at the University of Washington told PBS: “It boggles the mind that the administration is rescinding the endangerment finding; it’s akin to insisting that the world is flat or denying that gravity is a thing.”
In healthcare too, Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services (HHS) who has a long history of making factually erroneous claims about vaccine safety, have indulged in flawed and conspiratorial claims about vaccines.
Trump declared flatly in August that the combined MMR vaccine for children could be “quite lethal”, but failed to offer scientific evidence to back his claim. Trump too has advocated breaking up longstanding immunizations into three separate shots that currently are not available in the United States.
Even as the death toll from the worst outbreak of measles in decades rises, Kennedy on 16 September starred at a Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he spearheaded for almost two decades.
“Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy told the gathering in an almost 90-minute talk. “You have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time.”
According to recent polls about one-quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines in the wake of multi-year campaigns against immunizations by groups that once were fringe figures.
From a historical perspective, Zelizer noted that conspiracy theories in American politics have a long history, but that before Trump “the role of presidents and other high-level elected officials had been to push back against this part of politics, rather than to amplify these ideas.”

‘Water yes, mining no!’: the 87-year-old farmer who became a nature hero in Colombia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

In the rural hamlet of Palo Cabildo in Colombia’s western Andes, 87-year-old farmer Porfirio Garcés tends to his anthuriums in the garden of his small house. He talks with passion about his vinyl record collection, which ranges from classical to pop music, but his main interest now lies elsewhere: his homeland, to which he feels a deep connection – and his desire to protect it.
Numerous water sources originate in the area, supplying not only Jericó, where Garcés lives, but also several neighbouring towns in the Antioquia region. A sign with a clear message hangs on the main porch of his property: “Yes to water.”
“We don’t want to wake to the roar of machinery drilling into and destroying our land, destroying the poetry of the landscape,” says Garcés. “We must defend our water sources. Without water, we will die of thirst.”
Since last year, Garcés and 10 other local farmers have faced formal charges for opposing the Quebradona copper mining project, promoted by the multinational AngloGold Ashanti through its subsidiary Minera de Cobre Quebradona. He has since become a symbol of the resistance movement against Quebradona in Jericó.
Social protests in support of the “Jericó 11” gained strength in August as the nature defenders awaited new court hearings. “Water yes, mining no! Water yes, mining no!” the crowd chanted before the hearings, which postponed sentence until March 2027.
The charges against the 11 farmers are “simple” kidnapping (the moving of someone against their will, without factors such as ransom or serious bodily harm), aggravated theft and assault. Although the judge at the initial hearings on 13 May 2025 rejected the prosecutors’ request to keep the 11 farmers under house arrest, they are still awaiting trial.
AngloGold Ashanti arrived in the region 15 years ago to extract copper in an area traditionally known for agriculture, where crops such as coffee, plantains, cassava, beans and corn are cultivated. Its first exploration licence was granted in 2007, covering nearly 8,000 hectares (about 19,800 acres).
This initial stage was extended for 11 years – the maximum permitted by Colombia’s mining code – after which the company consolidated the properties to apply for an exploitation licence to start extraction. However, in 2019, the National Environmental Licensing Authority archived the application due to lack of technical information, requiring the company to conduct new studies before it could begin mining.
In August, Colombia’s National Mining Agency approved an extension of the exploration phase at Quebradona until 8 December 2027. Mining has not yet begun, as the company still needs to address social and environmental concerns and complete additional studies, but Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s far-right president since August, has aggressively prioritised expanding oil, gas and mineral extraction, including fracking, as a core part of his economic platform.
Last month, 281 local organisations signed an open letter declaring AngloGold Ashanti and Minera de Cobre Quebradona unwelcome entities (“entidad no grata”), and arguing that the project endangers the environment, water sources and Jericó’s local agricultural economy. Many campaigners feel AngloGold Ashanti is using the lawsuit as an attempt to suppress dissent over the Quebradona project.
The kidnapping charge arose in 2023 on public land owned by the municipality of Jericó, which is designated for safeguarding underground water sources. According to the community, mining employees entered the land without authorisation to carry out excavations. In response, the farmers say they went to the site to halt the works and alerted the police, the ombudsperson’s office and the mayor’s office to request the workers’ removal. After this, the employees filed complaints alleging they were held against their will.
Gustavo Arboleda, 62, another of the farmers facing charges, says the community became concerned about the direct impact on their water resources after the company installed an exploration drilling platform on the La Fea stream, which provides water to the area. That event, he says, sparked their resistance campaign.
The rural village of La Soledad sits on the mountain where mining is planned and where most of the accused live. Gustavo says its name honours the Piaya cayana bird, locally known as soledad. From the village, you can see the Cauca River basin, one of the nation’s major waterways.
“Since the mine had not completed its studies to obtain exploitation permits, it started bringing in machinery at night and paid some farmers to rent land. We noticed and did not let the machinery in; that was when we received further charges,” Arboleda says.
Rodolfo Tobón, 44, also facing charges, lives in La Soledad with his family on a farm where he grows cassava, bananas, plantains, coffee and beans, crops that ensure subsistence for his household and the wider region. “This land is very fertile; whatever is planted grows,” he says. “This is life – not just for us, but for many more people.”
Tobón, who is president of the village’s community action board, questions how the company has engaged with them since it arrived. He says local people do not want to see Jericó turned into a mining town, “because mining has never existed here”.
“When the mine arrived, they didn’t say they were a mining company. They used other methods, saying they would conduct soil studies to see what could be produced in Jericó,” he says. “Later on, we realised it was for large-scale mining. The company acted wrongly; they didn’t arrive stating exactly what they were going to do.”
AngloGold Ashanti has publicly said its Quebradona project fully complies with Colombian law and does not encroach on restricted zones. In a three-page statement to the Guardian, the company says its activities pose no threat to local water sources, citing environmental studies by Colombian authorities showing no impact on groundwater or surface water.
It also says protests and actions by the activists are illegal and disruptive, prompting it to file criminal complaints for kidnapping, theft and personal injury, and highlights its commitment to dialogue and transparency with local communities.
“We believe in frank, open dialogue, free from clandestine or malicious methods, and regret narratives that unfairly affect our reputation and that of our employees,” says AngloGold Ashanti.
In 2025, the company also announced the Quebradona Biodiversity Initiative, aiming to regenerate more than 2,500 hectares (6,000 acres) of Indigenous tropical dry forest and high-mountain forest in Antioquia and to restore ecosystems affected by land use.
Although water still flows abundantly through Antioquia’s mountains, the Jerico 11 believe that only collective action can prevent drastic changes to their environment. Argiro Tobón, another of the accused farmers, says they are trying to preserve their way of life and landscape by keeping their region focused on food production.
“We take care of the forests, we take care of nature, and we take care of the water,” he says.

A perry respectable alternative to wine – in praise of pear cider
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:50 UTC
21:00:50 KST

“They’re gorgeous little beasts,” Eddie Izzard said on the subject of pears in her mid-1990s show Definite Article, “but they’re ripe for half an hour and you’re never there!” Little did she know that she was touching on one of the difficulties of making perry – the fermented juice of perry pears – a drink that remains, in comparison with cider, a relative cottage industry.
There are some notable exceptions to that rule (anyone familiar with Babycham and Lambrini will have tried a commercial perry, albeit an industrially made one), but the perry I’m interested in is made from specific perry pears grown on vast trees in ancient, biodiverse orchards in the British West Country and northern France; it is made in small batches, because, as Izzard points out, pears are ripe for a notoriously short time; additionally, they begin to rot from the inside out and, such is the height of those gnarly branches, they can be difficult to pick, too. “Perry-making is hard to do well,” says Felix Nash of the Fine Cider Company, a retailer that specialises in craft drinks made from apples and pears.
Nash holds that “fine perry”, a term he uses to distinguish his perries from the industrial kind, is a blank slate; unlike cider, it has no mass-market presence beyond the likes of Babycham, which is largely seen as a kitsch anachronism. The fine perries that Nash sells run the gamut from medium-dry and sparkling to sweet and still; aperitifs to pudding accompaniments. He lists vintage perries, single-varietals and blends of pears with names that make me want to take up wassailing: hendre huffcap, butt, green horse, thorn, gin … Perry-making dates back centuries in Gloucestershire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, and is said to have been one of Elizabeth I’s favoured tipples.
Historic perry may be, but, as we head into 2026’s harvest season, it occurs to me that there is much to love about it for the modern drinker. It has a naturally low ABV (usually 5-6%) and pears contain sorbitol, a non-fermentable sugar alcohol that can leave even a technically dry perry with an impression of sweetness. It’s also surprisingly food-friendly; Nash cites the classic pairing with oysters or cheese, while I enjoyed a bottle of Tom Oliver’s sparkling medium-dry We Aren’t Stopping Now with chilli paneer; it would also be a doozy with most oily fish.
Then there’s the price. The production of fine perry has all the elements of fine wine, Nash says, reflecting fruit varietal, terroir, vintage and skill (some of his perries are made using the champagne method, others have tannins with the grip of red wine): “It’s largely the little known nature of great perry that has helped keep the cost where it currently is.” Without wine’s prestige, and with relatively minimal transport costs and, at those ABVs, considerably lower UK alcohol duty than wine, some of the bottles in today’s picks are nothing short of a giveaway.
Six perries - and what to pair with them
Oliver’s Fine Perry Wild Ferment Rolling Blend £3.50 (330ml) Secret Bottle Shop, 6.5% A great introduction to fine perry, this has notes of elderflower and is happy with everything from butter to spice.
Ross On Wye Cider & Perry Company Red Longdon Perry 2025 £12 (750ml) Fine Cider, 5.8%. Dry enough for an aperitif, grippy enough for a roast or a cheeseboard – extraordinary and moreish.
Little Pomona Fausset Pét Nat Perry 2023 £15 (750ml) Little Pomona, 6%. Juicy, aromatic and sparkling single-varietal perry. I drank it with mapo tofu.
Wilding Cider Moorcroft 2022 £25 (750ml) Fine Cider, 10.1%. Acid, structure, tannin and an unusually high ABV make this single-varietal perry an excellent stand-in for pudding wine.
Eric Bordelet Poiré Authentique £16.50 (750ml) Gnarly Vines, 5%. A Norman perry made by a one-time sommelier, this is off-dry, biodynamic and bloody lovely.
Oliver’s We Aren’t Stopping Now 2024 £14 (750ml) Fine Cider, 5.5%. Struggling to find a wine pairing for your curry night? Look no further than this elegant, medium-dry perry made by a titan in British cider- and perry-making.

====================================================================================================

Kindness isn’t always what it seems: The psychology of women’s competitive altruism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:37 UTC
21:00:37 KST

New research suggests that some women report using kindness and generosity strategically to gain an edge over rivals, a tendency linked to manipulative personality traits and lower agreeableness. These findings, published in Frontiers in Psychology, provide evidence that cooperation can sometimes serve as a subtle tool for interpersonal competition.
The research, led by Maryanne Fisher, a Santamarian Research Chair in the Faculty of Science at Saint Mary’s University’s Department of Psychology, builds on the concept of competitive altruism. The study grew out of a Faculty Mobility for Partnership Building Program grant from the Government of Canada, which allowed Fisher to spend a month at the Universidad del Desarrollo in Santiago, Chile, with additional funding from Chile’s ANID Fondecyt program. “I relocated there for a month and it was amazing,” Fisher told PsyPost.
In evolutionary psychology, competitive altruism refers to the idea that people give away resources or help others in ways that boost their own reputation and social standing. A 2006 experiment showed that people can gain higher status and social influence by making showy, generous sacrifices, as observers tend to prefer these cooperative individuals as future partners.
Initially, scientists viewed competitive altruism as a predominantly male tactic for winning status and attracting mates. For example, a 2012 experiment indicated that men eagerly competed to endure pain and inconvenience to secure status within a group, while women held back from this overt display. Because of findings like this, visible generosity was often treated as a public broadcast of quality aimed at a large audience.
“There was absolutely a research gap we tried to address,” Fisher said. “Most research on competitive altruism (the idea that people compete to be seen as the most generous or kind) has focused on men. It also often centered around men’s conspicuous public displays, such as men becoming more generous in the presence of a potential mate.”
However, research into female social dynamics provides a different perspective. A 2020 review highlighted that women tend to seek social status through subtle, low-risk strategies rather than the overt, public contests that men often favor.
“Past studies that included women produced highly mixed results, and we thought it might be because researchers were looking in the wrong place,” Fisher explained. “A long line of work shows that women’s rivalry tends to involve minimal risk and rely on indirect means, for example, carried out through gossip, exclusion, and the management of reputation rather than open confrontation.”
This pattern of indirect competition raised the question of whether women might weaponize kindness and giving as a subtle way to outcompete others. Fisher and her colleagues suspected that some women use generosity not as a flashy public contest, but as a quiet, low-risk way to win allies and reputation while remaining deniable as competition.
“Given this is how women often compete, kindness seemed like an ideal competitive tool because it wins allies and social standing while being very difficult to call out as competition,” Fisher noted. “The everyday expression ‘kill them with kindness’ captures that thought. We went one step further, though, and tried to actually measure its occurrence, which meant we had to create the Competitive Altruism Survey.”
To investigate this, the scientists developed the survey and recruited 103 heterosexual cisgender women, aged 18 to 45, primarily from the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada, through an online research platform. The participants rated 15 statements describing the strategic use of kindness, such as offering help to gain an advantage or behaving generously to look better than a rival.
Participants rated these statements twice: once based on how they behave toward other women, and once based on how they behave toward men. They also completed several established psychological questionnaires. These included a measure of Machiavellianism, which is a personality trait characterized by treating social life as something to be manipulated for personal gain. Other questionnaires measured general personality traits, such as agreeableness, as well as the participants’ tendencies to give socially desirable answers or claim implausibly virtuous behaviors.
The results indicated a strong positive association between competitive altruism and Machiavellianism. Women who reported higher levels of strategic kindness were also more likely to possess a manipulative, self-interested approach to social interactions. In contrast, competitive altruism was negatively associated with agreeableness, which is the personality trait linked to genuine warmth, trust, and cooperative sincerity.
Some predictions were not borne out: competitive altruism was unrelated to extraversion and conscientiousness. As expected, neuroticism was linked not to strategic kindness itself but to the anxiety and frustration that can accompany it, such as worrying that one’s kindness will seem insincere or feeling upset when it goes unnoticed.
“The biggest finding is that kindness and competition are not opposites, because some prosocial behavior can serve a competitive purpose,” Fisher told PsyPost. “This is not to say we are totally aware that our kindness or generosity might have this motive attached to it, or that all ‘nice’ acts are for competition, but to say they are opposite is incorrect.”
“The real point to consider though is that the average score on the survey was below the neutral midpoint of the scale, meaning that, on average, women leaned towards disagreeing with the strategic statements,” she added. “The study tells us which women report the behavior and how it relates to personality. It does not tell us how common strategic kindness is in women’s daily life, or whether it works. Those need follow up studies.”
The overall average competitive altruism score was 2.51 on a scale of 1 to 5. The audience of the behavior mattered. The participants reported slightly but reliably higher levels of competitive altruism directed toward other women (an average score of 2.58) than toward men (2.43). This aligns with the idea that women’s reputational management and social rivalry frequently occur within female peer groups.
Unexpectedly, the study found a negative relationship between competitive altruism and impression management. The researchers had anticipated that women who use kindness strategically might also try to present themselves as perfectly virtuous on the survey. Instead, women who endorsed strategic kindness appeared relatively open about their manipulative intent and tended to score lower on a measure of the need for social approval.
“What was really unexpected was that women were so open,” Fisher said. “We expected women who use kindness strategically to be the most concerned with presenting themselves favorably but the opposite emerged.”
“It might be that women who endorse strategic kindness are simply more candid about it and less invested in being liked by everyone; this is a very real possibility,” she explained.
When asked to rate their own traits compared to peers, these women described themselves as more manipulative, deceptive, and fake, less honest, and more popular than other women their age, but not as kinder or more generous.
At the end of the survey, 101 participants provided open-ended descriptions of times they had witnessed other women using kindness strategically. The most common themes included offering gifts or favors to create a sense of obligation, performing warmth in public that contradicted private unkindness, and directing exaggerated helpfulness toward superiors or men in romantic contexts.
These findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which investigated concern-framed gossip rather than self-reported generosity. That study similarly found that women use seemingly benevolent behaviors to gain social advantages in competition, successfully knocking down rivals while appearing trustworthy to observers.
“This research offers a new way to think about how people, in this case women, can use kindness in a strategic way and how this relates to other similar measures,” said Daniel Farrelly, a principal lecturer in psychology at the University of Worcester who was not involved in the research. “The authors have found that their newly-created measure of competitive altruism (which is altruistic acts that aim to improve the actor’s reputation compared to others) correlates with some existing personality measures, and that when asked about it women often describe how and when they see such acts being used.”
“There is good evidence that women do compete with one another, but unlike men this competition often involves indirect acts (such as gossip, reputation challenges etc),” Farrelly told PsyPost. “This study further supports the indirect nature of women’s competition, showing that competing to be seen to be cooperative is just another example of this.”
There are a few details to keep in mind when interpreting the current study. Because the data relies entirely on self-reporting, it might underestimate how often this behavior occurs. Women who are deeply invested in maintaining a kind reputation might be unwilling to admit their manipulative motives on a survey, meaning the results only capture the behavior of women willing to be honest about their deception.
Fisher noted another possibility: “women who are strategically kind but unwilling to admit it would score low, which means a self-report survey probably underestimates the behavior among the women most invested in appearing kind.”
“It’s important to note, as the authors rightly do as well, that competitive altruism doesn’t cover all types of altruism,” Farrelly noted. “In this case it is only a very strategic display that is used in particular circumstances, and how much an individual uses competitive altruism is unlikely to have a clear relationship with how kind/altruistic they are overall.”
“We do not want readers to walk away thinking that all kindness is fake,” Fisher emphasized. “We also have not compared how it occurs relative to men, and our findings are really preliminary.”
“There are some clear findings here, but not all hypotheses are supported so as the authors state there is more to find out about this potential effect,” Farrelly said. “One thing I did feel was missing was a comparison with men’s competitive altruism. As this study only used female participants we don’t yet know if the same effects might occur in men’s behavior.”
It is also unknown whether this strategy actually works in practice. The survey measures the intent and the self-reported behavior, but it does not test whether the targets of this strategic kindness actually extend greater cooperation, status, or alliances in return. Future research using observational methods could help determine if competitive altruism successfully tricks observers into granting social rewards.
“The most important question is whether strategic kindness works,” Fisher told PsyPost. “We have a qualitative study underway to start to address this question. We would like to use designs that observe both the person being kind and the people receiving that kindness, such as economic games in which generosity is made more or less visible, partner-choice tasks, and observation of real groups, with the sex of the audience varied.”
“It would be good to see examples of competitive altruism being used in women’s intrasexual competition, this is something that could be explored in future experiments,” Farrelly added. “I would also like to see this study replicated in male participants so we can see if/how the behaviors the authors describe in this study are unique to women.”
Finally, the sample was modest in size and consisted of heterosexual cisgender women from predominantly Western, English-speaking countries. Because cultural norms dictate how competition and self-presentation are expressed, the findings might not apply to populations with different social expectations.
The study, “Kill them with kindness: preliminary evidence for women’s competitive altruism,” was authored by Maryanne L. Fisher, Oriana Figueroa, Nohelia Valenzuela, Ferity Thorne, Pablo Polo, José Antonio Muñoz-Reyes, Nerea Aldunate, and Simón Ramirez.

A video of a humpback whale and her dead calf reveals the animals’ bond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Scientists had a rare view of what could be humpback whale mourning when they spotted a female attending the body of a dead calf.
The sighting suggests that baleen whales may experience grief, marine biologist Olaf Meynecke and rescue boat captain Andrew Mulville report September 16 in Discover Animals.
Some toothed whales, such as orcas, have been seen spending long periods with dead calves, occasionally carrying them at the surface for days. Such demonstrations of apparent grief are rarely seen in baleen whales. This may be because newborn baleen whales are born without the fat stores that would cause a whale corpse to float. If mothers spend time with dead calves on the seafloor, there’s a very low chance humans would see the interaction. The authors believe this is the first detailed documentation of a humpback attending to a calf after its death.
In July 2025, Mulville, who works for the Australian marine animal rescue group Sea World Foundation, saw two adult humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) in the water off Palm Beach in Queensland, Australia, and went to check on them. As he approached, he saw some tissue floating on the surface that looked like amniotic membrane — the placental lining that whales shed into the water at birth.
On the seafloor, he could see a small newborn calf, less than four meters long. The female “ended up diving down, making eye contact and actually putting her pectoral fin — her arm — over the stillborn and resting next to it,” says Meynecke, from Griffith University in Brisbane, Australia.
Two adult whales, which the researchers believe were the calf’s mother and her male escort, were seen in the same area for two more days. “We can’t prove it, but I’m very certain they were the same whales, which also suggests that this is a prolonged change of behavior … something that we might call mourning or a form of grieving,” he says.
“It was pretty emotional to observe,” says Meynecke, but he warns against anthropomorphizing and drawing parallels to humans. Remember that “the whale is experiencing their world in a completely different form and shape,” he says. “They have different ways of understanding their environment.”
