Russia Is Racing to Make Geran-5 Too Fast for Ukraine’s Drone Interceptors—But There’s a Catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:43:15 UTC
20:43:15 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Russia Is Racing to Make Geran-5 Too Fast for Ukraine’s Drone Interceptors—But There’s a Catch
Russia appears to be redesigning its Geran-5 jet-powered drone in an attempt to push it beyond 600–700 kilometers per hour and out of reach of Ukraine’s increasingly effective low-cost interceptors, according to Ukrainian aviation expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, cited by RBC-Ukraine on October 1.
Recent imagery of newer Geran-5 variants shows a major change: the small turbojet engine, previously mounted openly on a pylon above the fuselage, is being moved inside the rear of the aircraft.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
It may look like a relatively simple redesign, but Khrapchynskyi argues the change reveals a much bigger objective: speed.
Earlier versions used a small Chinese Telefly turbojet mounted above the airframe. That configuration was workable at roughly 350–400 kilometers per hour, but trying to push significantly faster created serious aerodynamic penalties.
An exposed engine and pylon effectively become an aerodynamic brake as speed increases. The high-mounted engine also places the thrust line above the drone’s center of mass, continually pitching the nose downward and forcing the flight-control system to compensate.
That means the drone effectively creates additional drag just by keeping itself level.
Moving the engine into the fuselage addresses both problems. The thrust line can be brought closer to the aircraft’s centerline, the external pylon disappears, and the control surfaces no longer have to work as hard to maintain stable flight.
The payoff could be a significantly faster Geran-5. But speed comes at a cost.
An internal engine bay, air ducts and thermal protection all consume space that could otherwise hold fuel. For a thirsty turbojet, that means potentially sacrificing a substantial amount of range.
Heat creates another engineering problem. Exhaust temperatures can approach 700 degrees Celsius, requiring metal shielding, insulation and airflow systems to prevent the composite fuselage from being damaged.
All of that makes the aircraft heavier, more expensive and harder to manufacture. And Ukraine’s interceptors may be the reason Russia is accepting those compromises.
Khrapchynskyi pointed to footage showing Ukrainian high-speed quadcopter interceptors from Wild Hornets pursuing jet-powered Russian drones from the rear.
Early combat results, he said, have demonstrated that targets traveling around 400–450 kilometers per hour can already be successfully hunted by this class of relatively inexpensive interceptor.
That threatens to undermine one of Russia’s key advantages with jet-powered drones.
Ukraine is not yet destroying them systematically at scale, and interceptor production is still expanding. But if inexpensive drones can reliably destroy Russian jet-powered targets traveling below 500 kilometers per hour, Moscow faces the prospect of losing costly weapons to a much cheaper defensive layer.
Khrapchynskyi believes Russia is therefore trying to push Geran-5 into the 700–800 km/h range before Ukrainian interceptors become widespread.
An interceptor attempting a pursuit could need speeds approaching or exceeding 900 kilometers per hour, requiring completely different aerodynamics, more powerful—and more expensive—jet engines, and extremely fast optical guidance capable of processing and reacting within milliseconds.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russian forces have reportedly begun using a new version of the Geran-5 attack drone equipped with an optical navigation system that allows it to navigate using reference images of terrain.

Ukraine Plans 840 Mobile Shelters Along School Routes in 6 Frontline Regions
Ukraine plans to install 840 mobile shelters along school bus routes in six frontline regions, the Ministry of Communities, Territories, and Internally Displaced Persons reported on October 1.
The project covers Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Kharkiv, Kherson, and Chernihiv regions. The ministry presented the initiative during a meeting of the Shelter Coalition for Ukraine, which brings together international partners and financial institutions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s attacks have repeatedly damaged and destroyed Ukrainian schools and other educational facilities, forcing students into shelters, remote learning, or relocated classrooms. As of September 1, Russian strikes had affected 4,650 educational institutions across Ukraine, with 423 completely destroyed, according to figures cited by UNITED24 Media.
“For us, it is fundamentally important that children are protected not only in schools, but also on the way there,” Ukraine’s Deputy Minister for European Integration Artem Husak stated.
He added that Ukrainian donor regions had already joined the project, but additional international financing was needed to cover all requirements. The ministry presented partners with region-specific needs and a targeted breakdown of how funding would be used.
The European Union announced $11.7 million in funding for shelters across Ukraine during the meeting. Other members of the coalition are also considering possible financial contributions, the ministry noted.
Ukraine plans to continue consultations with Finland, which co-chairs the Shelter Coalition alongside Ukraine, to coordinate further steps and possible support mechanisms.
The ministry described the 840-shelter project as a way to improve safety for children in frontline communities and preserve access to education despite continued Russian attacks.
The Shelter Coalition was launched in May 2025 through a joint declaration by the governments of Ukraine and Finland. The EU, Lithuania, Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Switzerland, and the European Investment Bank later joined the initiative.
Its work focuses on attracting international financing, modernizing existing shelters, and building new protective infrastructure.
Recently, Ukraine opened its first underground kindergarten in the Kharkiv region, allowing up to 260 children to attend preschool in person during air raid alerts. Similar protected preschool facilities are now being developed in nine regions, with priority given to frontline communities.

Jewish human rights barrister, 94, arrested for supporting Palestine Action

Jewish human rights barrister, 94, arrested for supporting Palestine Action
Margaret Owen OBE, a celebrated human rights lawyer and a friend Ed Miliband’s late mother, talks to Al Jazeera.
London, United Kingdom – Margaret Owen, a 94-year-old Jewish human rights barrister, has been trying to get arrested for months.
She has attended about a dozen protests wearing a sign reading “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action” in London and has had a placard with those words attached to a window at her home since the group was proscribed under the Terrorism Act in the UK in July 2025.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4UK charities, protest groups: Israeli ban threat ‘will not intimidate us’
- list 2 of 4Palestine Action protesters arrested in Liverpool
- list 3 of 4UK Foreign Secretary confronted by activists over Palestine Action ban
- list 4 of 4UK pledges tougher stance on Israeli actions in Gaza, West Bank
But unlike thousands of others who have been detained for showing support for Palestine Action, officers had not – until Sunday – hauled her into a police van.
“I’ve been trying to get arrested for quite some time,” she told Al Jazeera. “I’m rather proud and glad to have finally joined the club.”
In her pursuit, Owen had also written to the Metropolitan Police, sharing photos and confessing, but “they’ve never done anything about it”.
“I think they never wanted to arrest me because that would be quite a story for the media, this ancient veteran human rights lawyer, aged 94, you know, it’s too much of a story.”
In Liverpool, during a rally held outside the Labour conference, she was finally detained.
“I was the oldest there … Maybe they’d never heard of me, the police up in Liverpool,” said Owen, who in 2013 received an OBE for her contribution to advancing women’s human rights, especially widows’.
Merseyside Police said 82 people were arrested in the same protest “on suspicion of wearing/carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation” and have since been released on bail.
The Metropolitan Police did not comment on Owen specifically, but told Al Jazeera that, in London, “officers may not have witnessed an offence being committed, or the circumstances may not have met the necessary legal threshold for an arrest at that time”.
Owen said she wanted to be detained because the involvement of legal professionals lends a growing civil disobedience campaign “some sort of authority”.
The rallies have been organised by Defend Our Juries, a UK-based activist group demanding the UK lifts the ban on Palestine Action.
Founded in 2020, Palestine Action’s stated objective has been to counter Israeli war crimes – and what it says is British complicity in them – by targeting weapons manufacturers and associated companies. Its main target is Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms company, which has several facilities in the UK.
Several people who participated in raids claimed by Palestine Action are in jail, some having been sentenced as “terrorists”.
‘I admire Ed Miliband’
Many of those who have been arrested for showing support are pensioners, overwhelmingly for holding signs with the same seven words as the ones on Owen’s placard.
Doctors, teachers, lawyers, vicars, magistrates (many of them retired), a former adviser to King Charles and a Massive Attack singer are also among the diverse group, as is Tim Crossland, a coleader of Defend Our Juries and former government lawyer.
“I believe in the right to peaceful protest,” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband recently told LBC radio. “I don’t think it was anyone’s intent to have those people criminalised,” he added, referring to the elderly and Christian leaders who have been detained.
As with the sanctions he announced against illegal Israeli settlements, his comments marked a departure from his predecessors.
Before Labour’s change of guard, few lawmakers under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer criticised Israel’s conduct or the ban on Palestine Action. Just 10 voted against it in the House of Commons, compared with 276 for.
Then-Home Secretary Yvette Cooper ignored warnings from campaign groups, the United Nations human rights chief and leading politicians and peers that the move misused counterterrorism legislation.
“On the specific issue of Palestine Action, there’s a case coming before the Supreme Court, and so I’ll let that case play out, because I think it’s important that that court process takes its course,” Miliband told LBC.
He was referring to another case expected this year; Palestine Action’s cofounder Huda Ammori has been given permission to challenge the ban at the UK’s highest court.
Miliband, who is Jewish, has credited his late mother’s influence when explaining the UK’s new policies sanctioning Israel as it continues a genocidal campaign in Gaza.
“I admire and love Ed Miliband,” said Owen, who has a personal connection to the foreign secretary. She was “great friends” with Marion Kozak, his mother, a Holocaust survivor whose funeral she attended in July.
Kozak had “always been for the Palestinian people; she recognised the terrible Nakba of 1948”, said Owen, adding Miliband’s mother was moved by the plight “before many of us”.
‘I began to see how authoritarian Israel was’
Owen was born in 1932 to a family that also shouldered a painful history.
Her two great aunts and other relatives were killed in the Holocaust, “murdered in the forests of Paneriai in 1941 outside Vilnius”.
Her father was a lawyer and her mother, a doctor.
They were “very good parents”, she said. “I’m sure my mother would have been protesting like mad as well.”
Having studied law at the University of Cambridge, she qualified as a barrister at a time when the education system and legal profession were “very anti-women”. There were just two women studying law in her year, she said.
She later travelled to Israel for nine months, but after just three, “I began to see how authoritarian it was.”
“I began to see that whole indoctrination.”
She also remembered “how discriminate it was to all sorts of people, particularly the Black Jews, they called them, coming from Northern Africa”.
Along with her brother, who travelled with her, “we were questioning the Balfour Declaration”.
“[The experience] made me very, very critical of Israel even from 1956 onwards.”
Throughout her career, she has worked on legal cases across the world.
In late December, Owen will learn more about her own case, whether she will be charged over her show of solidarity for Palestine Action.
“I’m afraid I’m not the terrorist,” she said. “But Israel is a terrorist state, and we are complicit in supporting a terrorist state.”

TEKNOFEST Southeast links 12,000 years of history to Türkiye's technological future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:40:43 UTC
20:40:43 KST

From the 12,000-year-old story of Gobeklitepe to Türkiye’s latest unmanned aircraft, TEKNOFEST Southeast continued on Thursday in Sanliurfa, offering visitors a journey through the past, present and future of technology.
The world’s largest aviation, space and technology festival entered its second day at Sanliurfa GAP Airport with aerial demonstrations, scientific workshops, immersive exhibitions and activities designed especially to inspire young visitors.
The festival is organised under the leadership of Türkiye’s Industry and Technology Ministry and the Turkish Technology Team Foundation, or T3 Foundation, with the involvement of defence company STM.
Among the most distinctive attractions is the Gobeklitepe Experience Area, where visitors get to travel across roughly 12 millennia in just three minutes.
Using 360-degree screens and a replica standing stone, the installation explores the question “Where did everything begin?” while connecting technologies developed by ancient civilisations with Türkiye’s contemporary advancement.
The experience presents Gobeklitepe, often described as the “zero point of history,” not merely as an archaeological site but as the starting point of a continuing story of human invention.
“We have a screen extending from the past into the future, with one of the TEKNOFEST aircraft at its centre,” coordinator Alper Aslan said. “We begin in the past and explain the development of defence technologies up to the present.”
Visitor Elanur Yasar said the presentation allowed her to see the ancient site from a different perspective.
“At Gobeklitepe itself, we experience history in its original setting. Here, we saw Gobeklitepe combined with technology and civilisation,” she said.
Beyond the installation, children from Sanliurfa and surrounding provinces crowded around domestically produced aircraft, including the KIZILELMA unmanned fighter jet, KAAN combat aircraft and AKINCI drone.
For some, it was their first opportunity to see such aircraft at close range.
“I was very excited. This is my first time coming to a place like this, and I was very happy to see an aircraft up close,” said young visitor Amine Abdulvahab. “Hopefully, when I grow up, I can work in something like this.”
Ebubekir Selale said seeing aircraft both on the ground and in the sky deepened his interest in aviation, while Elif Yildirim thanked those who brought the festival to the city.
Japanese Ambassador to Türkiye Masami Tamura, who toured the festival grounds, praised both Türkiye’s defence technology drive and TEKNOFEST’s educational role.
“I find Türkiye’s advances in defence technologies very impressive. I am also greatly surprised by such an excellent event,” Tamura told Anadolu, adding that Japan does not host a comparable event on the same scale.
He said introducing children to science and defence technology through entertaining activities was particularly valuable and predicted deeper Turkish-Japanese cooperation.
“Türkiye and Japan’s cooperation is also important for world peace,” he said. “Japanese people love Türkiye, and I particularly want to emphasise that here.”
Thursday’s programme also includes another performance by the Turkish Stars aerobatic team, alongside displays featuring ATAK helicopters, HURKUS, CEZERI, ANKA, Bayraktar TB2 and TB3 drones and AKINCI.
Visitors can also explore simulators, a planetarium, science shows, educational workshops and national air, land and maritime vehicles. The day will conclude with a concert by Turkish singer Semicenk.
TEKNOFEST Southeast will remain open through October 4.

Turkish Defense Ministry building (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s Defense Ministry has announced a phased handover of the Bashika-Zilkan military base to Iraq following an agreement between Ankara and Baghdad.
“[The compound] will be gradually handed over to Iraqi authorities in accordance with an agreed mechanism and timeline, within the framework of the progress achieved by the central Iraqi government’s security implementations in Sinjar,” local media quoted ministry officials as saying during a weekly briefing on Oct. 1.
The decision was taken during a meeting between President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly meetings. Iraq had announced that all banned armed groups, including PKK, will be expelled from Sinjar, as part of Baghdad’s efforts to establish security across the country.
Türkiye has been using the Bashika-Zilkan base since 2015 within the scope of the fight against ISIL upon the request of the Iraqi authorities.
“We welcome the recent steps taken by the central Iraqi government to establish state authority in Sinjar. We evaluate that these steps will contribute to the normalization of the region, as well as to the creation of an environment of safety, stability and a terror-free region,” the defense officials said.
Türkiye will continue to stand with Iraq in its efforts to establish security and peace, they said, informing that the two countries are planned to take further steps for deepening security cooperation.
“Within the framework of bilateral agreements, we will continue to provide support to the Iraqi Armed Forces in the areas of increasing military capacity, sharing experience and expertise in countering terrorism, military training and defense industry cooperation,” they stated.
Greece’s plan to lay cable under sea
The ministry also commented on Greece and Greek Cyprus’ plans to lay electricity cable under the Mediterranean Sea.
“In accordance with international law, any cable or pipe-laying activities, as well as scientific research activities to be conducted within our continental shelf, must be coordinated in advance with our country as the coastal state,” the ministry said.
It also reiterated that Türkiye will not allow any unauthorized activities within the Turkish continental shelf, which was shaped through a maritime delimitation agreement between Türkiye and Libya in 2019.
The ministry also urged Greece and Greek Cyprus to avoid provocation actions that would undermine security conditions in the island.
Türkiye to supply cargo planes from UK
The ministry also announced that Ankara and London have signed an agreement for the former’s supply of 12 C-130 cargo planes.
“In line with the agreed timetable, it is aimed to gradually bring the aircraft to our country following the ongoing maintenance activities in the United Kingdom. Within this scope, the delivery of the first two aircraft is planned for December,” the officials announced.

Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:37:46 BST
20:37:46 KST

Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
- Published
Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.
The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.
Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.
She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.
Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.
"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."
Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.
Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.
She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.
One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.
For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.
Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.
He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.

How Netanyahu is using the Flydubai incident for electoral gain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:37:24 UTC
20:37:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu exploits Flydubai incident as Israel pushes 'terror' narrative despite conflicting accounts
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has seized on the Flydubai incident ahead of Israel's general election, comparing it to the 11 September attacks and suggesting Iran could be involved, even though investigators have yet to establish whether it was an act of terrorism.
The Israeli leader's remarks follow Wednesday's emergency landing of a Flydubai aircraft carrying 174 passengers, most of them Israelis, in Saudi Arabia after a violent confrontation between its two pilots.
While Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz quickly described the incident as a "terrorist" attack, the circumstances remain unclear, with conflicting accounts emerging from Israeli media and investigations still under way in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
The incident has given Netanyahu an opportunity to promote his security message ahead of the 27 October election, with opposition leader Yair Lapid accusing him of exploiting the passengers' ordeal for political gain.
Netanyahu invokes 9/11 and raises Iran claims
In interviews with CNN and Fox News late on Wednesday, Netanyahu compared the incident to the 11 September attacks in the United States, claiming that the aircraft's Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, and Israeli passengers had prevented a catastrophe on a similar scale.
He claimed that the co-pilot, identified as an Omani national, had intended to crash the aircraft and kill everyone on board, although investigators have yet to establish his motive.
"What distinguishes this incident from the other tragic attacks is that this time the good guys won," Netanyahu told Fox News.
He also told CNN that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump about the incident and its potential implications for global aviation. Trump separately confirmed that the two had discussed the emergency at length.
Netanyahu went on to suggest that Iran could have been involved, despite acknowledging that Israel had received no specific intelligence warning about the flight and that investigators had found no evidence linking Tehran to the incident.
"We'll get to the bottom of this attacker, and we'll find out whether he had accomplices and whether Iran was behind him," Netanyahu said. "I think we'll discover that very soon. It's too early to say."
Katz also described the incident as a "jihadist attack", claiming that preliminary information indicated the co-pilot had intended to kill everyone on board.
Both men linked the incident to security warnings they had issued the previous day, prompting criticism that they were using the emergency to justify their earlier statements.
Netanyahu also turned the passengers' return into a public appearance, welcoming them at Ben-Gurion Airport on Wednesday evening and meeting Yaniv Hayoun, one of the Israelis who reportedly helped restrain the co-pilot.
"You are a hero. You deserve a global medal of honor," Netanyahu told Hayoun.
In his interview with Fox News, Netanyahu also praised Hayoun's actions, telling viewers: "If your plane is hijacked next time, make sure you have an Israeli sitting next to you."
What happened aboard the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai flight FZ1073 departed Dubai for Tel Aviv at 6:05am local time on Wednesday, carrying 174 passengers, including 30 under the age of 18.
Around two and a half hours into the journey, while flying through Jordanian airspace, the aircraft plunged more than 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds.
The crew transmitted a general emergency signal, followed by an alert indicating unlawful interference or a possible hijacking. Israeli fighter jets were dispatched after air traffic controllers lost contact with the aircraft.
According to Israeli officials, the Omani co-pilot stabbed Machchhar and attempted to crash the aircraft. Despite his injuries, the captain reportedly managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to intervene and restrain the co-pilot.
Two off-duty Flydubai pilots travelling on board then took control of the aircraft and landed it safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
Footage filmed inside the aircraft appeared to show the injured captain lying on the cabin floor. Passengers described scenes of panic, with one telling Israeli broadcaster i24NEWS that the cockpit was covered in blood and that those on board feared they would die.
Both pilots were taken to hospital in Saudi Arabia, and India's embassy later confirmed that Machchhar was receiving treatment and was in a stable condition.
The passengers spent several hours at Tabuk Airport before returning to Israel on Wednesday evening.
Images and footage showed Saudi medical teams treating Israeli passengers, an unusual sight given the absence of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
The footage could also become part of Israel's wider push for normalisation with Saudi Arabia, which has resisted establishing diplomatic ties without the creation of a Palestinian state.
Conflicting accounts
Despite Netanyahu's repeated descriptions of the incident as "terrorism", the circumstances and motives behind it remain unclear.
Early Israeli media reports suggested that the co-pilot may have attempted suicide or that a personal dispute had broken out in the cockpit.
Israel's Channel 12 reported on Thursday that the Saudi investigation had found no indication of terrorism at that stage.
Israeli army radio said Israel was not directly questioning the suspect, who remained in Saudi custody, but was seeking information from the investigation.
The UAE's Attorney General, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, ordered a separate investigation on Thursday to establish what happened, including whether the incident involved terrorism, prior planning or outside involvement.
Netanyahu also spoke to UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan following the incident and claimed that the two had agreed Israel would participate in questioning the suspect.
The conversation came just days after Netanyahu's visited Abu Dhabi amid Israeli media reports that he had sought to persuade Mohammed bin Zayed to publicly deny claims that he had warned Netanyahu of an impending Hamas attack before 7 October 2023.
According to those reports, Netanyahu's office had pressed for the meeting as the Israeli leader faced renewed scrutiny over the intelligence and security failures preceding the attacks, an issue that could damage his electoral prospects.
Netanyahu turning incident into 'election propaganda'
Netanyahu's attempts to link the Flydubai incident to his earlier security warnings have drawn criticism from Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid, who accused the prime minister and his allies of turning the emergency into election propaganda.
Lapid, who received a security briefing from Netanyahu on Tuesday, said the prime minister had made no mention of any threat resembling the Flydubai incident.
"Nothing even remotely resembling the plane incident came up in the security briefing," Lapid said.
He said Netanyahu was trying to take political credit for the actions of the passengers and crew, despite having had no advance warning of the emergency.
"The Prime Minister's Office has become such a deranged and out-of-touch place that it is trying to exploit the aircraft incident for political gain, blame the opposition for what happened and claim that Netanyahu deserves the credit for preventing it," Lapid wrote on X.
Flydubai warns against speculation
Flydubai has maintained that the emergency landing followed an altercation in the cockpit, without attributing a motive to either pilot.
"The situation was successfully brought under control by the Flydubai crew on board the flight, who diverted the aircraft and landed safely at Tabuk Airport," the airline said in a statement.
It confirmed that all passengers and crew were safe and that replacement aircraft had been dispatched to Saudi Arabia.
"At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation," Flydubai added. "We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts."

“Every attempt to pressure our positions results in disproportionate casualty losses – both wounded and killed – for the enemy,” the General Staff said.

ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 30, 2026
More than 140,000 people were drafted for mandatory military service between April and July 2026, Burdinsky said.
Russia has operated under a system of year-round conscription since 2026, with recruits drafted throughout the year and sent to their duty stations during the spring and autumn campaigns.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia is intensifying military recruitment and expanding efforts to bring foreign fighters into its armed forces as Moscow struggles to offset heavy battlefield losses.
In a Sept. 28 evening address, Zelensky said Russian authorities had begun a new recruitment drive and were seeking to increase the number of foreigners serving in the Russian military.
He added that more than 8,000 North Korean soldiers are currently in Russia supporting operations against Ukraine, while another 10,000 are being trained for deployment.
“Russia is paying for all of this by various illicit means, and in return, for this help, for the technical assistance by Russia on North Korean territory, there has been set up a production line for Shahed-type strike drones,” Zelensky said.
His comments followed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s order to increase the size of Russia’s armed forces by 15,500 personnel, bringing the total authorized strength to 2,441,630, including 1,550,500 military personnel. The order marked the fourth increase in Russia’s military personnel authorized by Putin in 2026.
The decree did not mention a new mobilization of reservists. Putin has repeatedly denied that Russia is preparing one, calling reports of a planned mobilization “чушь собачья” (“utter nonsense”) earlier in September.
Meanwhile, Russian forces continue to suffer heavy losses in Ukraine. Researcher Ragnar Gudmundsson estimated that Russian forces lost 2,090 personnel on Sept. 28 and 1,960 on Sept. 17 – among the highest daily losses recorded during the war.
Gudmundsson estimates that Russia has suffered more than 405,000 combat deaths since February 2022, while total Russian casualties could exceed 1.6 million by mid-November.

Releasing prisoners won’t solve the crisis in English and Welsh jails. Here’s what will | Enver Solomon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:32:41 UTC
20:32:41 KST

The flipchart in the corner of the staff meeting room, deep inside a prison in the south-east of England, tells its own story about what our overcrowded jails are having to deal with, day in day out. Under the heading “Challenges”, it lists gangs, the destruction of cells, prisoners exploiting each other and complex behaviours.
Committed, hard-working staff talk about the high levels of psychosis, often combined with drug abuse. They provide examples of people actually committing crimes to go back into jail to get some respite from their chaotic, dysfunctional lives.
To tackle the current prisons crisis in England and Wales, planned changes to sentencing will see almost 2,000 people released early from Thursday and over the following month. It is the first tranche of the estimated 5,000 releases that will take place in phases over the coming year.
This will address the immediate crisis, but by the government’s own admission it is not a permanent fix. If it wants to ensure that the new approach to early releases does not need to be further accelerated, wider reforms will be needed across the system.
- 
  As a first step, we need to address the staggering increase in people recalled to prison. The power that probation officers have to send someone back behind bars plays an important role in protecting the public, but with recall now accounting for one in seven of the prison population compared with one in 13 a decade ago, it is neither sustainable nor effective. Cases of people being recalled for missing probation appointments because transport was delayed or for moving out of their accommodation to get away from drug dealers and gangs, are too often punished with a return to custody. A justice secretary under the last Labour government tells me it’s a ludicrous approach that must change if prisons aren’t going to stagger from crisis to crisis.
- 
  Second, we need to focus on the probation service. It is critical to fixing prisons and too often undervalued. Today it is a long way from its original social-work ethos to advise, assist and befriend those once described as clients but now always labelled offenders. The focus is much more on surveillance and compliance. Consecutive reports by the Chief Inspector of Prisons during the last two weeks reveal how, after years of being run down, the service is struggling to get the basics right. Electronic tags are a critical and expanding part of supervision on release from custody, but the inspector found the “systems, processes and frontline practice needed to make it effective have not kept pace”. The standard of probation work is not consistently what it should be, with staff shortages, poor information sharing and gaps in the capability of probation officers to keep people safe. 
The government is committed to recruiting thousands more probation staff and to improving practice but, faced with people who have a complex mix of needs and behaviours, a more person-centred approach closer to the profession’s social-work roots is needed. Those coming out of custody whom we work with say they want probation officers to get alongside them and build trusting relationships so they can get their lives back on track.
- 
  We need to be more open with the public. Prisons and probation are there to keep the public safe, but to do that, ministers need to be much more transparent about the importance of rehabilitation as well as punishment. The justice secretary’s speech to Labour conference this week started this, but far too many are still leaving prison to commit further offences because the system does not provide the drug treatment, access to employment, training and education – and then stable accommodation on release – that will help turn them away from crime. The fact that half of those rough sleeping in England and Wales have spent time in prison is a stark reminder of what’s not working.
- 
  The services need connecting. Fixing this cannot be achieved by the justice system alone. Public bodies from the NHS to local councils have a role to play in giving people the support they need to stay out of prison. Beyond those, community providers can step in where state agencies are not best placed to reach people.
In his party conference speech, Andy Burnham spoke of the importance of being honest with the country. To be honest about our prisons would be to recognise that continuing to lock up more and more people on longer sentences in overcrowded jails will not deliver rehabilitation, nor will it protect communities. This means levelling with the public about what current sentences look like, who needs to be locked up and for how long.
There is a precedent that shows it can be done. When Labour was last in government, in 2010, there were more than 2,000 children behind bars in England and Wales. Today there are fewer than 500. Where there is a will …
- 
  Enver Solomon is chief executive of Nacro, the criminal justice charity

Ukraine-Türkiye free trade agreement takes effect
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:31:26 EEST
20:31:26 KST

The Free Trade Agreement between the Government of Ukraine and the Government of the Republic of Türkiye, which provides for exemption from duties or the application of reduced rates, entered into force on October 1, the State Customs Service (SCS) said on its Telegram channel.
The SCS recalled that the agreement was signed in Kyiv on February 3, 2022, and ratified by a Ukrainian law dated July 14, 2026.
The State Customs Service draws attention to the fact that the tariff preferences provided for by the agreement will begin to apply at different times: for Ukrainian exports to Türkiye from October 1, 2026, and for imports of goods of Turkish origin into Ukraine from January 1, 2027.
"Accordingly, for exports of goods from Ukraine to Türkiye, tariff preference codes 429, cancellation of the export duty, and 430, an export tariff quota, will apply from October 1, 2026. At the same time, for imports of goods of Turkish origin, tariff preference codes 429 and 430 will apply from January 1, 2027," the statement said.
According to the statement, confirmation of the origin of the goods is important for obtaining preferential treatment, and proof of origin may be provided by a EUR.1 movement certificate or a declaration of origin.
According to the departmental customs classifier, the following document codes will be used to confirm the preferential origin of goods: 0954 for a EUR.1 movement certificate; 7012 for a declaration of origin made out by an approved exporter in accordance with the provisions of Article 22 of Appendix I to the Regional Convention on Pan-Euro-Mediterranean Preferential Rules of Origin.
For a declaration of origin made out by an exporter for any consignment of goods consisting of one or more packages originating from a particular country, the total value of which does not exceed EUR 6,000, code 7016 will be used.
As reported, following parliament's ratification in July of the Free Trade Agreement between Ukraine and Türkiye, then-Economy Minister Oleksiy Sobolev specified that for Ukrainian goods the agreement provides for full liberalization for 84% of product groups and tariff quotas for 6% of product groups, within which a zero or reduced duty rate applies up to the quota limit.

Zelenskyy, Zaluzhnyi top presidential ratings, Zaluzhnyi leads trust rating – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:30:49 EEST
20:30:49 KST

Current and former representatives of the security and defense sector are leading in the trust ratings among state, military, and political figures among Ukrainian citizens, according to the results of a sociological survey conducted by the Future Research Foundation and presented during a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Thursday.
The trust rating is headed by Ukraine's Ambassador to the United Kingdom and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), Valeriy Zaluzhny, whom 53.9% of respondents trust and 37.7% distrust. In second place is Head of the Presidential Office and former Chief of the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine (2020–2026), Kyrylo Budanov, with 49.3% trust and 42.8% distrust, followed in third place by current Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapaty, who is trusted by 48.6% and distrusted by 31.3%.
Incumbent President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky ranks fourth with 39.4% trust and 53.6% distrust. The highest levels of distrust were expressed toward Batkivshchyna All-Ukrainian Union leader and former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko (85.3%) and European Solidarity party leader and fifth President of Ukraine Petro Poroshenko (78%).
At the same time, Zelensky leads the presidential rating. To the question "If presidential elections were held next Sunday, who would you vote for?", among those who have decided and intend to vote, 23.6% would vote for him (17.2% among all respondents), and 22.7% for Zaluzhny (16.6% overall).
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov would take third place with 8.5% of decided respondents (6.2% overall), followed by Budanov with 8.4% (6.1%), and Poroshenko with 7.3% (5.3%).
In the event of parliamentary elections in the near future, Zaluzhny's political project would receive the greatest support (19%). High support would also go to Zelensky's party (13.6%), Fedorov's party (10.1%), Budanov's party (9.1%), and European Solidarity (7.7%). Additionally, political projects led by Kharkiv Mayor and Head of the Association of Frontline Cities of Ukraine Ihor Terekhov (7.2%) and the 3rd Assault Brigade party (5.6%) could enter parliament, while Reasonable Politics party is balancing on the verge of the 5% threshold (4.9%). Several other parties poll at 1% or higher, thus failing to clear the 5% electoral threshold.
"This may indicate a significant potential for the reformatting of citizens' political preferences in the future. Even those forces that currently have one percent could reach the passing five percent," noted Svitlana Kushnir, project manager at the Future Research Foundation.
There is a high proportion of undecided voters (16.4% among all respondents) or those who do not plan to participate in voting (8.6%).
"Against the background of transforming public demands, Ukrainians' electoral sentiments demonstrate high dynamics and at the same time significant uncertainty. Currently, the electoral field remains ultimately unformed. And the level of support for key players and new initiatives indicates that while the electoral field is unformed, both veterans and new political projects have a chance," political strategist and Candidate of Historical Sciences Oleh Posternak said during the discussion of the survey results.
The survey was conducted from September 19 to 22 using the CATI (computer-assisted telephone interviewing) method with a random sample of mobile numbers among 1,203 respondents aged 18 and older across all government-controlled territories of Ukraine. The marginal maximum theoretical sampling error does not exceed 2.9% with a 95% confidence probability.

PARIS — France will increase its defense budget next year despite increasingly strained public finances, according to a document obtained by POLITICO.

That's in line with increases foreseen by the military planning law adopted over the summer.
Advertisement
"To ensure our sovereignty, the government plans to strengthen our military capabilities through additional orders for major equipment (surface-to-air defense systems, anti-drone systems, and artificial intelligence)," the document reads.

The defense ministry is one of the very few to benefit from a budget increase in 2027. The government has announced a deficit target of 5% of GDP for next year, and the freeze on most other ministerial budgets at their 2026 levels has been confirmed.

The Real Threat to the Midterms Is Regular Americans Thinking Violence Is the Answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

The attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, was not conducted mainly by extremists or fringe militia groups. It was, according to the data, the work of normal Americans.
That is the conclusion Robert A. Pape lays out in his new book, Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism, citing data about those who were arrested and charged following the attack.
While Proud Boys and Oath Keepers gained most of the headlines, data collected by Pape as part of his work as founding director of the Chicago Project on Security and Threats (CPOST) found that the vast majority (90 percent) of those charged with crimes arising from the attack held no affiliation with militias or militant organizations.
Pape’s analysis found that 22 percent were business owners, and almost 30 percent held a college degree. Among the defendants were doctors, engineers, CEOs, and government employees. Nearly 40 percent held white-collar jobs, while just 8 percent of participants were unemployed.
The findings are key to understanding the warning that is central to Pape’s book: Americans do not understand that the threat of political violence is coming not from the fringes, but from the mainstream.
“As the 2026 midterms approach, US elections are entering a danger zone in which state power, protest, and political legitimacy increasingly collide,” Pape writes in the book. “For most Americans, political violence is still understood as episodic—shocking when it erupts but destined to fade. That assumption is reassuring. It is also increasingly dangerous.”
WIRED spoke to Pape about his book, his concerns about violence in the midterms, why it is so important to understand the attack on the Capitol, and what, if anything, gives him hope that democracy will win out.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
DAVID GILBERT: Your book is centered on the idea of violent populism. What is it, and why is it on the rise in 2026?
ROBERT A. PAPE: Violent populism is a dangerous political climate where substantial segments of the public increasingly accept physical force as a legitimate tool to gain, preserve, or defend political power. It is on the rise due to a profound cultural clash over the nature of American identity and citizenship, exacerbated by elite rhetoric that frames politics as an existential struggle between enemies. This structural dynamic transforms ordinary, mainstream citizens into active participants in political aggression.
You call the midterms “a stress test of whether American competition can remain bounded by nonviolence.” Are you concerned about the political violence around this election?
Yes, the level of concern for this election cycle is at an unprecedented high, surpassing anything seen since the deep social upheavals of the 1960s. With national anxieties amplified by a highly combustible domestic climate and global instability like the ongoing war with Iran, elections have increasingly become dangerous potential flashpoints. This dynamic represents a direct, critical test of whether our foundational institutions can still successfully enforce peaceful political transitions.
Heading into the midterms, a lot of people are focusing on possible action from extremist groups, such as militias. Is this the wrong thing to be worried about?
Focusing exclusively on fringe militias misdiagnoses the primary danger facing American democracy today. The real threat is that political radicalization has broken out of the fringes and fully migrated into the mainstream electorate. Our primary worry should be the tens of millions of ordinary Americans who now passively accept or actively endorse violence to achieve their political goals.
You write that Americans are misreading the warning signs of political violence, again. What are those warning signs?
The primary warning sign is the broad public normalization and passive acceptance of aggressive political acts as standard features of daily political life. This is signaled by an explosion of violent symbolism across the entire media spectrum and elite rhetoric that strips legitimacy away from opposing factions. When ordinary citizens begin to view political opposition as an existential, hostile force, the ground is fully prepared for real-world conflict.
You write in the book that the January 6th attack on the Capitol was a rubicon crossed between "routine political conflict and civil war." Why was it such an important turning point?
The January 6th attack shattered the all-important democratic norm that power changes hands through ballots rather than raw displays of physical coercion. It demonstrated that an electoral outcome could be violently challenged not by foreign adversaries, but by a massive crowd of American citizens targeting their own legislative body. This crossed line signaled that internal political disputes were no longer reliably bounded by a shared commitment to nonviolence.
The narrative around the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol is that it was driven by extremist groups on the fringes of American society. But that's not what the data shows, right?
CPOST data completely disproves the fringe narrative by showing the remarkable mainstream geography of those involved in the insurrection. The vast majority of the actors were not isolated radicals or card-carrying militia members, but “normal” political activists with stable homes, jobs, and 401(k)s. Only 1 in 10 were militia members. Nearly half were doctors, lawyers, CEOs, business owners, US State Department appointees—and some even attended the White House Christmas party the year before. Most represented a cross-section of middle-class America acting on a shared, mainstream belief that democratic institutions were no longer legitimate.
Why do you think the prevailing narrative around the January 6 attack on the Capitol has been so wrong for so many years?
The narrative has been wrong because public institutions and media outlets initially relied heavily on imperfect law enforcement databases that naturally isolated the most prominent, organized fringe actors. And they did not update their readers and viewers as the bulk of the data came in. This approach ignored the underlying, broader structural dynamics of public opinion and extensive survey research. By focusing strictly on the visible, oddball characters, analysts missed the massive wave of passive, mainstream support that actually fueled the event.
My reading of this book is that most people have a fundamental misunderstanding of political violence in America in 2026. Is that accurate?
That is completely accurate and is the central, urgent argument of the entire book. The greatest threat to the United States is not an out-of-control group of radical extremists, but the reality that millions of otherwise ordinary citizens now accept violence as a regular political tool. Once political violence is normalized by the mainstream, old institutional solutions cease to function effectively.
You compare the current embrace of violent populism by middle-class white America to the expansion of the second Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s. Do you think people will be shocked by that comparison?
Many readers will likely be shocked, because the modern imagination associates the Klan strictly with regional, low-income hate groups rather than a massive social movement. However, the historical data shows that the second KKK of the 1920s was a highly mainstream, middle-class organization driven by a cultural clash over American identity. Drawing this explicit parallel highlights how easily normal, institutionalized communities can slide into systemic intolerance when they feel their cultural dominance is threatened.
Do you think readers of the book will be surprised that defense of political violence is not solely the preserve of the right, but that people on the left also reinforce your thesis of violent populism?
Yes, readers who expect a one-sided partisan critique will be surprised to see that the call for political violence comes from both sides of the aisle. [Confessed health care CEO assassin Luigi] Mangione and the recent [accused] Trump assassin at the April White House Correspondents’ Dinner reflect political violence from the left, and they are far from alone. Original CPOST surveys reveal that violent style, aggressive symbolism, and the demonization of political opponents are heavily utilized by figures across the entire political spectrum. This multisided reality proves that violent populism is a systemic, societal failure rather than an isolated partisan phenomenon.
You say that it is not yet determined if the current transitional phase of American politics will “culminate in democratic renewal or deeper political breakdown.” Do you have a sense of when we might have an answer to this question?
We need to lean into the “good news” in my book: that 70 percent of Americans abhor political violence. This is the large, untapped resource that we need to lean into. My book is essentially for the 70 percent and a call to action for what they can do—beyond voting. The 70 percent are the heart of our democracy. Leaning into them is how we save our democracy and avoid a much deeper, systemic breakdown of American governance.
What, if anything, gives you hope that violent populism can be overcome?
Hope lies in the data that can give new active optimism to vast majorities of ordinary Americans on both the left and right that still share a fundamental desire for stability and governance. By recognizing that our enemies are not really each other, but the normalization of violence itself, we can deliberately choose strategies of restraint to rebuild our vital democratic norms—and find productive new solutions.

The Israeli army on Thursday rejected the portrayal of its operations in the film NAZA, which documents Israeli massacres in Gaza, and sought to distance itself from the genocide against Palestinians.
The comments marked the army’s first response to the film, directed by Israeli Oscar-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.

It said the film’s “narrative is based on fundamental factual errors” resulting from a “distorted and manipulative presentation.”
“Artificial intelligence has never independently selected targets to strike. Target identification is carried out exclusively by qualified and authorised intelligence officers, while operational commanders make decisions on striking targets,” the army said.
The army also claimed that “the people interviewed, having served in the army’s intelligence corps, mostly refer to limited and preliminary stages of intelligence work, rather than the much broader process of planning and approving strikes.”
The film, produced by The Guardian, received widespread acclaim at the Venice Film Festival, drawing a 25-minute standing ovation before being awarded the Special Jury Prize.
Abraham and Szor took the stage to accept the award, with Abraham speaking about a smear campaign against their film in Israel and efforts to prevent the facts presented in it from being seen.
The film’s title, NAZA, is an abbreviation used by Israel’s military intelligence directorate, Aman, to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an air strike.
The film was secretly shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv over three years, with the identities, voices and facial features of participants digitally altered to protect their safety.
Participants in the film detailed surveillance systems used in Israeli attacks and long-range bombardment operations.
According to the film, some of those interviewed worked in a secret intelligence unit that reported directly to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity against Palestinians during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.

US removes Syria from arms export ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:25:21 UTC
20:25:21 KST

Syria’s President Ahmed al-Sharaa speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (AP Photo)
The Trump administration is removing Syria from a list of countries that are not allowed to purchase or import U.S. weaponry, a step that is part of a monthslong process of easing sanctions on the new government in Damascus and its leaders.
In a notice published on Sept. 30 in the Federal Register, the State Department said it was amending its International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR, so that Syria no longer was among the nations subject to a policy of denial for licenses and other approvals needed for the sale of U.S. weapons and munitions.
The change effective on Oct. 1 means that arms sales requests from Syria will now be considered on a case-by-case basis.
President Donald Trump acted last year to ease economic sanctions on Syria that had been in place for decades during now-ousted President Bashar al-Assad’s rule.
In August, Secretary of State Marco Rubio rescinded Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism, helping paving the way for the latest step in drawing closer to the current government.
The State Department has also announced plans to reopen the U.S. Embassy in Damascus. It has been closed for 14 years.
With Syria’s removal from the ITAR blacklist, only seven countries remain subject to the policy of denial for licenses for U.S. arms exports: Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, North Korea and Venezuela.

Based in Geneva, UREPH (or Research Unit) aims to improve the way MSF projects are implemented in the field and to participate in critical thinking on humanitarian and medical action.

BRAMU specialises in neglected tropical diseases, such as dengue and Chagas, and other infectious diseases. This medical unit is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Our medical guidelines are based on scientific data collected from MSF’s experiences, the World Health Organization (WHO), other renowned international medical institutions, and medical and scientific journals.
Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care.

MSF staff member tests positive for Ebola disease and is medically evacuated
Share
Statement1 October 2026
Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) confirms that one of our staff members who had been working on the Ebola response in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has tested positive for Bundibugyo virus disease. This person is being safely evacuated under a strict medical protocol in close coordination with the relevant health authorities in the DRC and the Netherlands, where the patient will be received by a designated hospital.
MSF cannot share specific details regarding individual medical evacuations in order to respect medical confidentiality and protect the privacy of our colleague.
The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country. Since May, more than 8,000 confirmed cases and 4,000 deaths have been reported, with the true toll likely higher due to gaps in surveillance and case detection. Healthcare workers are among those at greatest risk. Despite providing its staff with training and the highest possible levels of protection, MSF recognises that the risk of exposure can never be completely eliminated.
MSF stands in solidarity with all those working on the frontlines of the Ebola response. Their courage, commitment and determination are essential to protecting communities and saving lives.
MSF is currently responding to the Ebola disease outbreak across Ituri, North Kivu, Tshopo, and Haut-Uélé provinces. We remain committed to working alongside the Congolese health authorities and with affected communities to try and bring the outbreak under control.

IRGC hails US withdrawal 'victory,' Iraq sets new deadline to disarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards hailed Thursday the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq as a "historic victory" and called for American troops to leave the Middle East entirely.
In a statement carried by their official media, the Revolutionary Guards congratulated "the proud nation of Iraq, the united front of the Islamic Resistance and the revolutionary fighters of the Islamic world on this historic victory."
On Wednesday, the U.S.-led coalition that deployed to Iraq and Syria in 2014 to fight the Daesh terrorist group formally concluded its mission and withdrew.
Daesh, which seized large areas of both countries and committed massacres and atrocities, was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, but coalition forces stayed on to battle the group's remnants.
"The U.S. must leave the region and entrust the management of security to the nations themselves," said the statement by the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran's military.
"Two decades of occupation demonstrated that the U.S. presence brought no security; rather, it was the very source of insecurity, terrorism, and instability in the Middle East," it added.
Baghdad and Washington had recently agreed to wind down the coalition's mission and its troops withdrew gradually from bases across the country, restricting their presence to the semi-autonomous northern region.
The Iraqi government says the coalition's withdrawal removes the excuse powerful Iran-backed militant factions have used to retain their weapons.
On Thursday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced June 30, 2027, as a new deadline for armed factions to turn over their weapons to the state.
"Oct. 1 is considered a serious beginning to address the issue of weapons outside state control ... according to a clear roadmap and agreed timelines extending no later than June 30, 2027," Zaidi said in a statement, after backing away from an original Sept. 30 deadline.
"Based on the constitutional principle, the decision of war and peace should be left to the constitutional authorities, banning all military action to the contrary," Zaidi said Thursday.
While some factions have already handed over their weapons to the state, others have refused to disarm. Many fear that the U.S. pullout might boost Iran-backed factions and draw the country deeper into the Middle East war.
Earlier Wednesday, Iraqi armed factions backed by Tehran said that they were "not bound by any timeline or agreement" to surrender their weapons to the state.
Jaafar al-Husseini, a military spokesman for Kataeb Hezbollah, said at an event celebrating the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces that the factions had been in talks on "regulating" their weapons but had not yet received a response from the Iraqi government.
"Based on this," he said, "the Islamic Resistance declares that it is not bound by any timetable or agreement that any governmental or political party has spoken of or may speak of."
Kataeb Hezbollah has called the withdrawal of "the occupation forces ... a start toward achieving full sovereignty."
But the group also threatened Zaidi's government.
"'A government that does not work for the good of its people will be brought down by all possible means," it said.

As diplomacy reels, Iran readies stronger military response to US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

Iran is preparing a stronger military response if the U.S. resumes large-scale attacks while continuing a diplomatic push Iranian officials privately view as unlikely to succeed, sources said.
The planning reflects a conviction within Iran's leadership that any renewed U.S. campaign must be met with a stronger response than before, even as Tehran seeks to avert escalation through talks.
Senior commanders are reviewing plans to expand potential targets beyond U.S.-linked assets to countries that support U.S. military operations and possibly to locations outside the Middle East, according to three senior Iranian officials and an insider familiar with the discussions.
Since President Masoud Pezeshkian returned from New York last week, commanders and senior officials have focused on the scope and timing of any response if Washington strikes again.
No final decision has been made, but planning has intensified as neither side shows signs of willingness to compromise.
The deliberations follow seven months of conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. Although an April 8 cease-fire ended the 40-day war, hostilities have continued sporadically since then.
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said Tehran remained uncertain whether U.S. President Donald Trump would launch another major campaign or opt for more limited attacks, such as strikes on nuclear facilities.
"But they seem determined not to respond symbolically to a symbolic move and instead to escalate in the hope of reestablishing deterrence," Azizi said.
Tehran is also weighing the political risks for U.S. President Donald Trump of a prolonged conflict. Polls show the war has been unpopular with Americans, while higher fuel prices remain a concern ahead of the midterm elections.
Two of the officials said Tehran had instructed allied groups in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq to be ready to support Iran in the event of a renewed large-scale U.S. attack.
The guidance, they said, was to prepare for a coordinated response stretching "from the Strait of Hormuz to U.S. interests in the region and outside the Middle East."
Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
However, Tehran is still keeping open a channel for negotiations even as it readies for a wider war.
Iran will never shy away from dialogue with the US, Pezeshkian said Thursday, as Tehran weighs a U.S. response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed deal.
"We have never shied away from talks, and we never will, although the United States has targeted our country three times despite having signed an agreement," the semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted him as saying.
Underlying Iran's calculations is a second concern: whether its economy can withstand a prolonged confrontation under a U.S. blockade that has cut off oil exports, a critical source of revenue.
Years of sanctions and mounting economic hardship have already placed growing pressure on ordinary Iranians.
At last week's United Nations General Assembly in New York, Tehran submitted a proposal to Washington through Qatari mediators that, if accepted, could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt hostilities across the region within seven days.
Iranian authorities say the proposal calls for an end to fighting, the lifting of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, the release of at least $12 billion in frozen Iranian funds and a waiver of oil sanctions.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday he had rejected the proposal. Iranian state media reported, however, that a U.S. response was delivered to Tehran through Qatar Tuesday and is now under review.
Iranian sources said Washington wants Iran's disputed nuclear program included in negotiations, but Tehran insists that the nuclear talks can only begin after its seven conditions are met, not before.
"Even if Iran does not reject the U.S. response outright and indirect talks continue, it is very unlikely that the two sides will reach an agreement," said one of the officials.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said prospects for diplomacy remained limited.
"Iran cannot afford continuation of U.S. blockades that could be a major game changer, essentially taking the oxygen out of the lungs of the regime. Escalation at this point is conceivable," Vatanka said.
Since hostilities began, the conflict has alternated between lulls and renewed strikes, killing thousands of civilians, degrading Iran's military capabilities and damaging an already fragile economy.
For the U.S., the war has failed to achieve U.S. President Donald Trump's shifting goals while depleting the Pentagon's missile stockpiles.
Iran and its allies have sought to raise the cost for Washington by widening the conflict across the region, disrupting oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and increasing risks to global energy markets.
Iran has launched drone and missile attacks against U.S. allies in the Gulf, while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests.
The Houthis' advance toward Bab el-Mandeb has opened a second pressure point on global energy routes, giving the Iran-aligned group leverage over the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
An insider close to the decision-making process said the combination of military pressure and economic restrictions was becoming increasingly difficult for the clerical rulers to sustain.
That strain is also fueling concerns within the leadership about domestic stability.
A former senior reformist Iranian official said the leadership fears a repeat of the nationwide protests that erupted in January, when worsening economic conditions triggered unrest across the country.
Authorities ultimately crushed the demonstrations, killing thousands of protesters.
"Facing unrest at home while the system is under U.S. pressure and bombs could pose a very serious challenge to the legitimacy of the ruling establishment," he said.
As the anniversary of January's unrest approaches, the authorities have tightened controls while attempting to maintain public mobilization, encouraging loyalists to return to nightly gatherings.
Rights groups say the government has intensified its crackdown on dissent during the war.
Amnesty International said in May that more than 6,000 people had been arrested since hostilities began, while a September report by U.N. investigators cited mass arrests, torture and increased use of the death penalty.

Ukraine is downing Russia’s fastest drones—just not often enough, and scaling up comes down to money
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:20:55 UTC
20:20:55 KST

Ukraine is stitching together a layered answer to Russia's faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, leaning on electronic jamming, fighter jets, and a new class of homegrown interceptors, RBC-Ukraine reported. Each tool has limits, and the new interceptors still bring down only the occasional jet drone. The bottleneck now is money and factory output, not ideas.
Russia is pouring faster jet-powered drones into the air war as winter nears, a campaign Western analysts say is meant to wear Ukraine's defenses down—and holding those skies now turns on which side can keep out-producing the other's cheap weapons.
Fighter jets help, but they run on imported rounds
Electronic jamming can work against some of the drones, and Ukraine is also sending combat aircraft up after them. But aviation has a catch: the jets need air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds, and for the F-16 and Mirage those are imported and not always in stock. Flying over Kyiv adds danger to the civilians below and to the pilots, so Ukraine would rather catch the drones out on the approaches.
New interceptors are landing hits—just not enough
The newest piece is a wave of Ukrainian interceptor drones built to chase the jet versions, which fly three times faster than the propeller Shaheds. Ukrainian crews have been downing the jet Gerans in a recent run: on 19 September, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, confirmed one Geran-5 shot down, and in late September, operators of the National Guard's Separate Artillery Brigade brought down a Geran-4 with the Bullet interceptor made by General Cherry, the first Geran-4 that drone has downed, Ukraine's National Association of Defense Industries said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said several prototypes have proven themselves in combat.
Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest
Across all methods, Ukraine now intercepts about 57% of the jet drones Russia launches, Zelenskyy said on 28 September—a rate that has climbed but still trails the 90%-plus it manages against slower Shaheds. Kills by the new interceptors specifically remain isolated. In August, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said jet drones can make up as much as two-thirds of the drones in some raids—though not every time. One promising route is reworking Ukraine's own long-range strike drones into interceptors. Kyiv is in talks with partners over the money; on 28 September, Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara asked the EU to help finance the interceptors so enough reach the front quickly.
Hitting the launch sites and jamming the controls
Ukrainian forces strike the Russian airfields the jet drones launch from, RBC-Ukraine's sources said, though the raids have not forced Russia to abandon the attacks. On 20 August, military intelligence hit drone storage and launch sites at Primorsko-Akhtarsk, one of the launch bases RBC names, and at occupied Donetsk airfield. Ukraine also keeps going after the Belarusian relay towers Russia strings into a mesh network to steer the drones in, RBC's sources said.

Unknown Publisher

Russian drone attacks Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv
According to Ukrinform, the State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine reported this on its website.
According to the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, at 18:18 Kyiv time on September 30, 2026, a Russian UAV struck the institute's premises, where the Kyiv research reactor (VVR-M) is located. A fire caused by the attack was quickly extinguished.
The inspectorate emphasized that the reactor and safety-critical systems were not damaged. No changes in radiation levels were detected. Radiation levels remained within the natural background range of 0.16–0.20 μSv/h and did not change.
In addition, to reduce risks, the reactor has remained shut down since February 2022, with its entire core unloaded. Its operation is limited to scheduled maintenance of safety-critical systems.
"The VVR-M reactor is used as a source of neutrons for fundamental and applied research in nuclear physics. Therefore, the UAV strike on the premises of the Institute for Nuclear Research is an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility that performs exclusively scientific and research functions. It is yet another cynical disregard by Russia for internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety and constitutes a war crime," the State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate said.
As previously reported, two drone strikes were recorded near a support structure of Kyiv's Southern Bridge, and traffic across the bridge has been suspended.

The motive of the Omani copilot who stabbed his captain on a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously and forcing it to land in Saudi Arabia, remained unknown on Oct. 1, as investigators across the region raced to learn more.
Israeli passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft carrying 174 people from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the copilot and stabilized a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away.

He said the UAE, the United States and Oman also were involved. The official did not describe the extent of Israeli involvement.
“All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the probe.
Israeli intelligence and security officials were investigating the copilot in Saudi Arabia, according to another regional official who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
Video shot inside the plane by Shota Musayev, a dentist who treated the captain, shows the copilot on his knees, with his hands tied behind his back. The copilot’s name still has not been released.
The UAE government said its investigation team had begun its work into the motive and “whether it was linked to any terrorist purpose.”
Capt. Smit Machchhar, widely praised as one of the heroes of the flight, was reportedly in stable condition. The condition of the copilot was not clear.
Asked if there is any indication of Iranian involvement, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News “it’s too early to say.” The prime minister told CNN that Israel had received no specific warning.

Morocco's Mansouri-led gov't faces major challenges ahead
