Breadcrumb
Major challenges ahead for Morocco's Fatima El Mansouri-led government
The government under Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri in Morocco, expected to form soon, faces major internal and external challenges, putting it to a real test over its ability to manage complex political, social and economic issues that remained unresolved under previous governments.
The new government, which is expected to be announced in the coming days, will not face an easy road ahead. From its first day, it will face many pending and pressing issues that require solutions, at a time when the Moroccan public hopes it will meet their aspirations and address issues affecting their daily lives.
Mansouri appeared keen, moments after her royal appointment and being tasked with forming the government, to send messages to those concerned, stressing that she would work to "propose a government that meets the expectations of His Majesty the King and all Moroccan citizens, particularly young people".
"We will come with a programme that proposes real and realistic solutions," she added.
A question of confidence
As the formation of Morocco's new government occurs amid domestic and international anticipation, Abdelhafid Younsi, professor of constitutional law and political science at Hassan I University in Settat, argued that the first challenge for the Mansouri government remains political and concerns the question of confidence after a low voter turnout in the elections (38%) and some practices that harmed the electoral process by members of the party that will lead the government, namely the Authenticity and Modernity Party.
Younsi told The New Arab that, whatever the circumstances, the legitimacy of this government needs to be strengthened through achievements on the ground and their impact on citizens.
He also argued that state and society resources must be kept away from the exploitation of public office to accumulate wealth, or what is known as conflicts of interest.
According to the professor, the social challenge remains at a priority too, particularly improving purchasing power and making progress on health and education, which requires not only funding but primarily how public services are delivered, including citizens' dignity in Morocco and their sense of citizenship when accessing these services.
Younsi further said the growing proportion of young people in the population pyramid requires sustained and stable economic growth exceeding 5%.
"This is the third challenge, namely the economic dimension, which requires genuine competitiveness, moving away from monopolies and restoring vitality to national enterprises, all within the challenge of an unstable regional and international environment where uncertainty prevails," he added.
Rachid Lazraq, head of the North Africa Centre for Studies, Research and Public Policy Evaluation, said the Mansouri government will likely find itself facing the challenge of turning investment and growth dynamics in Morocco into employment opportunities and a tangible improvement in citizens' living standards.
The strength of public investment alone is not enough to address unemployment and low participation in the labour market, particularly among young people and women, he argued.
Moreover, Lazraq noted there is a need to maintain fiscal balances amid rising financing needs for major projects and infrastructure linked to the 2030 horizon, which includes completing reform of the social protection system, improving the business climate and increasing economic productivity, as well as addressing the cost of water stress and climate change on agriculture, food security and prices.
Morocco's social challenge
According to Lazraq, the main social challenge will be narrowing the gap between economic indicators and Moroccan families' daily perception of their standard of living and the quality of public services.
He told The New Arab that the government will be required to address unemployment, the high cost of living and difficulties accessing housing, and must also improve the quality of education and healthcare and reduce disparities between cities and rural areas and between regions, while ensuring the sustainability of the social protection programme and targeting vulnerable groups more effectively.
Lazraq argued that this issue will be highly sensitive because the success of social policies will not be measured only by the scale of public spending, but also by the extent to which spending directly affects household incomes, the quality of schools and hospitals, and young people's ability to obtain stable jobs and opportunities for social advancement.
Politically, the biggest challenge facing Mansouri, according to Lazraq, will be to build a coherent government majority capable of producing decisions and collectively taking responsibility for them, rather than merely assembling a numerical majority in parliament.
He explained that the next government in Morocco will need clear mechanisms for coordination among its parties, and need to link the government programme to measurable targets in employment, investment, public services and social protection, while managing high public expectations regarding the results of public policies.
For his part, Nabil Al-Andaloussi, head of the Maghreb Centre for Strategic Research and Studies, said the biggest test for the Mansouri government, if she succeeds in forming it, will not be the number of projects it announces but rather its ability to turn growth, investment and reforms into a tangible improvement in citizens' lives and to safeguard their dignity and rights.
Regarding the main challenges facing the expected government, Al-Andaloussi told The New Arab that they are concerned about its ability to restore trust between citizens and institutions, particularly after the elections and the debate surrounding their integrity and turnout.
He said the government must move from day-to-day management to a government with a clear political vision and defined priorities, capable of dealing with internal and external challenges.
He said the government faces a social challenge in how it deals with major issues such as employment, healthcare, raising living standards and addressing inflation, as well as reduce social and regional disparities, particularly between cities and rural and mountainous areas, in addition to the challenge of addressing rising living costs and protecting the purchasing power of the middle class and vulnerable groups.
Andaloussi also noted that the economic challenges require achieving economic growth that creates more jobs.
The government also faces a regional development challenge, according to him, through reducing disparities between regions and provinces, including meaningful substance to advanced regionalisation (granting broad powers to local regions), linking responsibility to accountability, and finding a fundamental solution to the problem of conflicts of interest, which had been a defining feature of the previous government's failure.
On the other hand, Al-Andaloussi said the government faces an external and diplomatic challenge through continuing to defend territorial integrity and Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara and strengthening diplomatic gains in this context.
He stressed the importance of managing relations with the European Union, the United States, Spain and France, while maintaining the independence of Moroccan decision-making, and also dealing with geopolitical changes in the Sahel, Mediterranean and North Africa, as well as maintaining balanced relations with international partners in a world that has become more competitive and tense.
For his part, political analyst Rachid Lamsalem said that, with Mansouri tasked with forming the government, her first major challenge will be the search for parties that share its main priorities for the electoral programme put forward by the Authenticity and Modernity Party, which focused on major economic and social reforms affecting broad sections of Moroccan society.
Lamsalem remarked to TNA that the incoming Mansouri government will face the challenge of approving social projects related to reforming the healthcare system, which is experiencing a shortage of medical staff and poor services, and the employment crisis, which is considered one of the major issues facing the government, as the unemployment rate is rising significantly, both among degree holders and those who have lost their jobs.
Lamsalem further said the incoming government will have to deal with choosing highly qualified ministers to address the most pressing issues, "since ministers in the previous government demonstrated weakness and an inability to produce public policies that respond to the needs of Moroccan citizens".

Latvia orders new howitzers and rocket launchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:16:25 UTC
20:16:25 KST

- Latvia, Slovakia and Czech firm Tatra Defence Systems signed a contract on Sept. 30 for Morana 155 mm wheeled howitzers and rocket artillery systems.
- Latvia plans to fund the purchase through the EU's SAFE loans, with part of the equipment produced and assembled in Latvia.
Latvia has signed a contract to buy Czech-made Morana 155 mm wheeled howitzers and rocket artillery systems for its armed forces, in a three-way deal with the Slovak government and Czech manufacturer Tatra Defence Systems, the Latvian Defense Ministry said.
The ministry, the Slovak government and Tatra Defence Systems signed the contract on Sept. 30. Neither Latvia nor its partners disclosed how many howitzers or rocket launchers the deal covers, which rocket artillery system Latvia is buying, what the contract is worth or when deliveries will begin.
Both the howitzers and the rocket launchers will be built on Tatra truck chassis. The ministry said using a common vehicle platform will make logistics, maintenance, training and long-term support easier for the National Armed Forces, since crews and mechanics will work on the same trucks across both systems.
Latvia plans to pay for the purchase through Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, a European Union program that offers member states low-cost loans of up to €150 billion ($169 billion) in total for joint defense purchases. The contract also requires a gradual move of production to Latvia, with part of the equipment to be built and assembled in the country with support from Czech and Slovak companies.
“Our goal is not only to acquire modern military equipment, but also to develop local production, service and technological capabilities that will strengthen Latvia’s long-term resilience and security,” said Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis.
Slovakia’s role centers on its defense industry, which will supply what its defense minister described as technologically important components for the systems.
“Slovakia’s defense industry will play a significant role in this project, providing technologically important components for the systems,” said Robert Kaliňák, Slovakia’s deputy prime minister and defense minister.
The contract follows a Latvian cabinet decision on Sept. 15 to buy the Morana, built by Czech company Excalibur Army, over Sweden’s Archer howitzer. Latvia had signed a letter of intent with Sweden in June 2025 to negotiate an Archer purchase, but the Defense Ministry concluded that the Swedish system would cost more than the defense budget allows and take longer to deliver, The Defence Blog reported.
The Morana mounts a 155 mm, 52-caliber gun on a Tatra Force 8×8 truck and replaces the Czechoslovak-era DANA family of wheeled howitzers. Excalibur Army says its automated loader can fire six rounds in the first minute and five rounds per minute after that, with a maximum range of about 41.5 km (26 miles) using extended-range ammunition. Its crew of three or four rides in an armored cab and the vehicle carries a 12.7 mm remote weapon station for self-defense.
Latvia, which borders Russia and Belarus, has been rapidly building up its artillery. The new howitzers and rocket launchers will expand the National Armed Forces’ indirect fire units, the ministry said.

This photo shows Turkish seismic research vessel Oruç Reis. (AA Photo)
Türkiye has issued a new navigational warning covering parts of the Eastern Mediterranean, as its research vessel Oruç Reis prepares to conduct surveys related to a planned undersea natural gas pipeline linking southern Türkiye with Turkish Cyprus.
NAVTEX 0953/26, issued by the Antalya hydrographic station, covers waters extending from Türkiye’s southern coastline toward Turkish Cyprus and will remain in force from Oct. 1 through Oct. 25.
Oruç Reis is expected to carry out preparatory survey work for the pipeline project, accompanied by the vessels Denar Pathfinder, Denar Echo and Kırıcı.
The research vessel was also deployed last year as part of Türkiye’s offshore drilling operations in Somalia. Ahead of the latest survey, Oruç Reis docked at Taşucu Port in the southern province of Mersin on July 19 for final preparations.
The planned pipeline will span 101 kilometers, including 97 kilometers of subsea infrastructure and a four-kilometer section on land.
It will link Anamur in Mersin province with Teknecik, located east of Kyrenia in Turkish Cyprus, and will be capable of transporting natural gas in both directions.
The project is scheduled to become operational in 2028, with construction-related activities already underway.
Türkiye and Turkish Cyprus signed a memorandum of understanding on July 10 to launch the pipeline project, describing a major step toward bolstering the Turkish Cypriot administration’s long-term energy security.

Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:14:24 UTC
20:14:24 KST

Whale sinks yacht in South Pacific, sailors rescued alive 18 hours later
A sperm whale cracked the hull of a yacht sailing in the remote South Pacific, forcing four sailors into a day-and-night fight for survival on the high seas.
Crew members on the 52-foot Tai Tam told AFP on Thursday of their weekend encounter with a pod of sperm whales 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island.
"There was sort of a loud thud. The whole boat was pushed sideways," said Australian Jemma Cooper, who was thrown from the steering wheel by the force of the blow.
Not knowing at first what had happened, she noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a sperm whale.
"We looked out to our port side, and there were six to eight, a pod, of whales there. So then it became clear that that's what it was," she told AFP.
Her husband Jeremy Cooper said he was sleeping below deck when the impact woke him.
"It was pretty immediately evident it was very serious," he said.
"All the steering gear was smashed on the starboard side, and there was a significant amount of water coming in," Jeremy told AFP.
At 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday — about 30 minutes after the whale collision — they activated an emergency beacon.
 "We declared a full mayday," said New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington, adding they spent the next few hours bailing out as much water as they could.
 
"Terrible ending"
The Royal New Zealand Air Force flew a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to the area to establish radio communications and coordinate the rescue, the military said in a news release, which included images of the rescue.
French crew member Martin Jaffre said the whale collision left several gashes in the hull and cracked the fiberglass structure, as well as breaking the steering.
"We could no longer steer the boat, and a boat with no steering quickly becomes a problem," he told AFP.
Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water with anything to hand, including expansion foam, and swam below the boat to inspect the hull, his crewmates said.
The sailors tried to stay aboard as long as possible, struggling to stop the engine getting clogged and bailing by hand.
Late at night, they abandoned the boat and transferred to a life raft in calm seas and under a full moon.
In the early hours of Sunday morning, they cut the tether to the yacht, fearing it might drag them down. Soon after, it slipped beneath the waves.
A 470-foot container ship, the MV Sofrana Surville, rescued the sailors at 6 a.m. on Sunday, the New Zealand military said — about 18 hours after their encounter with the sperm whale.
Even the rescue was scary as the giant ship approached their tiny life raft, recalled Jeremy Cooper.
But within half an hour they had scaled a ladder to join their rescuers, have a cup of coffee and chat with the captain, he said, ruing the end of their Pacific holiday voyage.
"It was wonderful, wonderful, and just a terrible, terrible ending — but luckily no loss of life."
Rescue Coordination Centre Operations Manager Mike Clulow praised the efforts of the rescue team and the yacht's crew.
"This was a well-coordinated and executed rescue," Clulow said. "The crew of the yacht did all the right things, and it was unfortunate to have struck a whale in open water. They were well prepared and the early activation of their EPIRB (Emergency Position-Indicating Radio Beacon) was key to helping get them to safety. It is an excellent reminder that being prepared when going to sea can save your life."
Adult male sperm whales measure between 50 and 60 feet. They are considered a "vulnerable" species by the nonprofit International Union for Conservation of Nature. Sperm whales reproduce once every five to seven years and have experienced significant population decline. The species is under threat from noise pollution, plastic consumption and ship strikes.
The incident in New Zealand marks at least the second time in less than two months that a whale has sunk a boat. In July, a whale that surfaced for air slammed into a New Jersey fire department's boat, sinking the ship with firefighters on board. Someone on a personal watercraft nearby and a boater helped rescue the firefighters from the water.

Ghost Song: Fatih Akin's haunting tale of love beyond death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

20:13:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Ghost Song: Fatih Akin's haunting meditation on love, grief and what comes after death
Is there anything more potent than young love? The fireworks of desire fuelled by adolescent hormones that make the promise of everlasting romance feel like life or death if you can’t be with the one person who has captured your heart?
German-Turkish film director and screenwriter Fatih Akin distils the palpable expression of first love in his latest drama, Ghost Song.
Opening the San Sebastian International Film Festival, it follows two star-crossed teenagers in Germany, forever tied together by the tragic circumstances of their meeting.
Farah, or Farasha to her friends, a name that means ‘butterfly’ in Arabic, is the eldest of five sisters and is mourning her father’s death at his grave on the same day that she passes her high school exams. That evening, she attends a graduation party for students from across the city, where she meets Faris.
At first, their eyes linger as she dances to Arab trap and he glides past. Later, they both find themselves at the bar trying to order some water.
She is a hijabi Muslim and a Syrian refugee; he is of mixed German-Turkish heritage and the designated driver for the night.
The film might be in luscious black and white, but Mariam Dawoud and Eren M. Güvercin exude the stirrings of adoration with such blushing delight that it radiates off the screen.
One might assume that coming from different walks of life, amid the historical friction between Turks and Arabs, will be the root of the film’s conflict.
Farasha’s othering is felt early on, when the bartender ignores her pleas to be served and instead answers Faris. His best friend Max (Gabriel-Winner Amorim) calls her a 'jihadi ninja' as he questions why they are offering a lift home to Farasha and her inebriated best friend, Una (Carlotta von Falkenhayn).
But as a thunderous bolt of lightning crackles across the night sky, their romantic future is extinguished, at least in the corporeal world.
Here, Akin and Ruth Toma’s script takes a turn into the supernatural, with Faris waking up in a hospital bed and slowly, heartbreakingly, realising that he took a wrong turn and crashed his car into a river.
Everyone survived, apart from Farasha.
A love that lingers
Güvercin carries the profound grief and guilt of her death in every wide-eyed stare, the tension in his body and his inability to truly process her loss.
But Farasha has not passed on. She remains in the spiritual world, watching Faris mourn at the crash site, her sisters prepare her body for its final rest, and her tearful loved ones throw dirt onto her grave at her funeral.
She doesn’t need to fade away into memory just yet. The film’s conceit is that she can pierce the veil between life and death by visiting those who remember her in their dreams for 40 days.
Despite a warning from her ghostly father, Farasha begins nightly excursions into Faris’ mind, and their courtship continues with the same rigorous passion, even if it is always tinged with the melancholic notes of Malakoff Kowalski’s score.
For this is a doomed romance, akin to Orpheus and Eurydice, and no matter how much they laugh, dance and love in the darkness of their dreams, the sunrise will always pull them apart. For both of them, that separation proves untenable.
As their love deepens, the journey gets darker, with depression and suicide entering the devastating equation.
Some scenes are truly harrowing, but never overwrought with melodramatic displays.
Even at its most discomforting, Dawoud and Güvercin earn your empathy through their sensitive portrayal of two teenagers desperately in love who cannot let go, even when the consequences become all the more unbearable for those left behind.
Lama Alhalabi and Anna Bederke, as Farasha and Faris’ mothers respectively, showcase the poignant motherly devotion and pain of losing a child, whether physically or psychologically.
Yet flashbacks to that fateful night, captured breathtakingly by cinematographer Frank Griebe in the inky black depths of the water, reveal the courageous truth of Farasha’s demise.
Akin ends the film with a life vest for the lovers to cling to, offering hope, acceptance and spiritual ease in the sea of sorrow that is their love story.

Follow her on Instagram: @hannainesflint

UNICEF warns of severe child deprivation in Lebanon as displacement, economic tolls mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:11:31 UTC
20:11:31 KST

The economic toll of the war with Israel and its related displacement in southern Lebanon has left 22% of Lebanese children going to bed hungry, while 20% have been out of school for a year, according to a new UNICEF rapid assessment published on Wednesday.
Hezbollah’s decision to restart hostilities with Israel on March 2 in response to the targeted elimination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Iran led to 1.2 million people being displaced in Lebanon at the height of the conflict, with roughly 340,000 still unable to return to their homes there, according to UN figures. One third of those unable to return are children.
According to UNICEF, the last six months of war have seen an average of seven children killed or wounded per day. An estimated 12% of injured children now live with a disability as a result of the conflict.
Having fled their communities and jobs for safety, 71% of families were found to be struggling to meet their children’s medical needs, triple the figure from six months ago. Approximately 38% said they did not have access to medicine their children needed, while 31% said their children had not received the health care they needed, largely due to the cost of treatment.
Around 6% of surveyed households also reported that their children had become sick or injured due to the war, and 34% of those children did not receive the care they needed. A recent assessment also estimated that more than 700,000 people, including 238,000 children, were affected by disruptions to water systems, increasing the risk of preventable infectious diseases spreading.
Children go to bed hungry, child labor rates increase
More than four in five households (82%) said they were also struggling to afford more necessities compared to three months ago, and 22% said that their children went to bed hungry in the two weeks prior to the survey. More than half, 55%, said they were unable to provide their children with three meals a day and only 10% of households with children under age five said they were able to provide a sufficiently varied diet;
Additionally, 14% of families said that at least one of their children had been forced to take up a job, a figure that had grown from only 6% in January 2025.
Beyond the immediate deprivation, UNICEF warned that the impact on academic infrastructure was likely to carry long-term consequences. At the height of the conflict, 433 public education institutions, around a third of Lebanon’s public-school network, were repurposed as shelters, leading to around 100,000 children potentially losing access to their classrooms. Additionally, 436 schools were damaged over the course of the war, and 37 were destroyed.
Learning institutions lacking, families can't meet needs
76% of families said they had more trouble meeting their children’s educational needs compared to three months ago, 46% said they had to reduce expenses related to education, and 17% said they had to stop their children’s education altogether due an inability to find available schooling.
One in five households reported that their children did not attend school last year at all, and of those who did attend, 29% were said to have been unable to learn fully, often because of difficulty focusing and emotional distress.
“Without urgent and sustained action, an entire generation of children [in Lebanon] and young people risks carrying the scars of this crisis into adulthood,” said UNICEF Lebanon Representative Marcoluigi Corsi.

CENTEF report reveals Hezbollah acquired $157m of weapons in 2024, majority provided freely by Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:11:02 UTC
20:11:02 KST

Hezbollah acquired an estimated $157 million worth of weaponry in 2024, despite its war with Israel, with the vast majority of it donated by the Islamic Republic of Iran at no cost to the terror group, according to the Israeli Center for Research of Terror Financing’s new research published on Thursday.
The report, “Hezbollah Financial Statements,” is the first installment in a series set to expose Hezbollah’s media spending, payments to wounded fighters and spending on its military infrastructure.
Based on open-source information and valuations of known Hezbollah military assets, CENTEF estimates that Iran provided roughly $129 million worth of weapons and military equipment as an in-kind grant while Hezbollah itself spent approximately $28 million in cash on its acquisitions.
Seeking to understand Hezbollah’s expenses as a business entity, to better assess the terror group’s financial health and identify ways to weaken it, while avoiding the costly airstrikes that can have significant consequences for Lebanese civilians, the researchers examined the group’s weapons procurement and manufacturing costs, as well as its ability to sustain its arsenal if the Islamic Republic’s capacity to supply it were reduced.
Explaining the rationale behind the analysis, CENTEF CEO Sharon Gal told The Jerusalem Post that breaking down Hezbollah’s finances could help legislators and operators efficiently identify and prioritize key supply chains to disrupt, creating pressure points for the Iranian-backed terror group.
Researchers aim for interactive tool on Hezbollah finances
Expanding those efforts, researcher Marc Cohen told the Post that they plan to release an interactive tool to help civilians understand Hezbollah’s financial statements, with the hope that it can raise awareness of Hezbollah’s negative impact on the Lebanese economy and the scale of its operations.
The researchers looked at the different types of military equipment Hezbollah is estimated to have acquired in 2024, including rockets, missiles, drones, ATGMs, air-defense systems, ammunition, launchers, naval equipment, and IED-related assets.
Hezbollah’s own investment in its weapons is limited to small arms, ammunition, drone components, dual-use equipment, and equipment obtained through its international procurement networks.
Because Hezbollah’s weapons acquisitions are clandestine, the researchers had to estimate how many weapons the group acquired in 2024 rather than rely on procurement records. They used three methods: Analyzing Hezbollah’s historical rate of replenishing its arsenal, assessing Iran’s capacity to manufacture and deliver weapons, and comparing global benchmarks for the costs of equipping, training, and mobilizing military forces.
The first method was based on Hezbollah’s growth over the past two decades. According to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Hezbollah had approximately 15,000 rockets in 2006 and had expanded its arsenal to roughly 150,000 by 2024, amounting to an average increase of about 7,500 rockets per year over 18 years of Iranian resupply.
Acknowledging that Hezbollah’s replenishment likely varied year-to-year, it estimated that the disruption to Hezbollah’s supply chain and manufacturing abilities during the 2024 fighting resulted in them acquiring approximately 4,500 to 6,500 rockets and missiles during the year.
The second method considered was Iran’s ability to directly supply Hezbollah. The researchers noted that Iran can only manufacture and physically deliver a limited number of sophisticated weapons, and those weapons must be distributed among Iran’s own forces and multiple proxies.
Iran is estimated to produce approximately 50 to 240 ballistic missiles per month and 1,800 to 3,000 attack drones per year total. This places a ceiling on how many guided missiles and drones Hezbollah could realistically have acquired in 2024. With that in mind, researchers analyzed the value of weapons in Hezbollah’s arsenal to understand exactly what Iranian support was worth and confirm that Hezbollah would be unable to afford such advanced weaponry without Tehran’s patronage.
Hezbollah arsenal includes heavy Iranian Falaq rockets, Katyushas
A staple of Hezbollah’s arsenal is the Katyusha rocket, alongside Iran’s heavier Falaq-1 and Falaq-2 rockets, which have 240mm and 333mm warheads respectively, and the crude, large-warhead Burkan rocket. The 122mm Katyusha is one of the few systems for which there is a publicly available price, at approximately $300 per round, while the Burkan is estimated to cost around $400 per rocket. Based on OSINT, the researchers estimate that Hezbollah acquired approximately 4,000 of the short-range rockets, 400 Falaq rockets, and 120 Burkan rockets in 2024.
Hezbollah’s inventory also includes Iran’s Fajr series and Syrian-origin heavy rockets. The Fajr-3 is a 240mm artillery rocket armed with a 45-kilogram warhead, while the Fajr-5 is a 333 mm rocket with a GPS-guided Fajr-5C variant. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah acquired approximately 600 rockets across this class in 2024, at an estimated cost of $2,000 to $10,000 per unit.
The inventory also includes the unguided Zelzal-2, which costs an estimated $25,000 per rocket, and the GPS-guided Fateh-110/M-600, a high-priority transfer estimated by JINSA to cost $110,000. The transfer can also be fitted with a $5,000 to $10,000 GPS guidance kit to turn them into a guided weapon.
With Iran’s missile production shared among several recipients and the supply corridor repeatedly disrupted during 2024, Hezbollah’s acquisition of these systems was thought to have been tightly constrained, and it is understood the group acquired only 60 Zelzal rockets, 40 Fateh-110/M-600 missiles, and 150 guidance kits.
The inventory also includes Iran’s Paveh land-attack cruise missile, which has a range of approximately 700 to 2,000 kilometers. Given its high unit value, CENTEF estimates that only about 12 were acquired in 2024.
Anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs) accounted for about 20% of Hezbollah’s attacks on Israel during its attacks after October 8, 2023, and were likely its largest-value weapons category, according to the researchers.
The Russian-made Kornet, supplied via Syria, costs approximately $26,000 per round, while Iran’s reverse-engineered Dehlavieh costs an estimated $12,000 to $15,000. Hezbollah also uses the Iranian Almas, older Konkurs and Metis systems, and the RPG-29. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah received approximately 700 Kornet and 500 Dehlavieh rounds, 500 Almas missiles and 400 Konkurs/Metis missiles, along with 30 launchers in 2024.
The RPG-7, a standard squad-level anti-armor weapon with reusable launchers, costs about $350, and rounds cost $100 to $500; CENTEF estimated that Hezbollah acquired approximately 800 RPG launchers and 15,000 rounds in 2024, with some rounds procured on the black market.
Hezbollah also acquired drones and unmanned aerial vehicles, including the Iranian Mirsad-1 and Ababil-T and small Shahed-101-class loitering munitions. Loitering munitions cost an estimated $20,000 to $40,000, while commercial and FPV quadcopters range from $1,000 to $15,000. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah acquired approximately 300 Mirsad and Ababil drones combined, 200 loitering munitions, 400 commercial and FPV drones, and several reconnaissance UAVs in 2024.
Hezbollah’s air-defense inventory includes MANPADS costing roughly $5,000 to $100,000 each depending on the model, and it is thought to have also received 358 of Iran’s loitering surface-to-air missiles.
Small arms, IEDs relatively cheap for Hezbollah
Small arms are comparatively inexpensive. Hezbollah uses AKM and AK-103 assault rifles, along with PKM and DShK machine guns and SVD sniper rifles. CENTEF estimates that it acquired about 5,000 rifles, 900 crew-served weapons, 80 mortar tubes, 15,000 mortar rounds, and 8 million rounds of ammunition in 2024.
Given that IEDs are relatively cheap to manufacture and can be produced in Lebanon, the researchers estimated the group invested in 2,000.
CENTEF is also gathering data on how Hezbollah spends money on its civilian arm, including through charities that assist residents of Lebanon’s south displaced through the group’s wars. While still analyzing the cost of Hezbollah’s media landscape, it has already estimated that Hezbollah spent $26 million to $28 million on media in 2024, with Al-Manar alone accounting for $16.5 million to $17.2 million.
The researchers said understanding these expenses, alongside Hezbollah’s military spending and Iran’s support, could provide a fuller picture of the group’s financial dependencies and generate more choke points to pressure it.

====================================================================================================

Ethiopian-Eritrean conflict could intersect with increased Houthi escalation in Yemen, experts fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:10:52 UTC
20:10:52 KST

Renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia and worsening tensions between Addis Ababa and Asmara are reopening one of the Horn of Africa’s most dangerous fault lines at a moment when the Red Sea itself is under growing pressure.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The latest fighting in Ethiopia has already shaken the 2022 Pretoria agreement that ended the previous Tigray war. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive last week, seizing airports and advancing into neighboring areas before Ethiopian federal forces and allied militias began counterattacks. On Monday, pro-government forces claimed to have recaptured the strategic town of Alamata, south of Mekelle.
But the concern now extends beyond another internal Ethiopian conflict.
Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, has publicly accused Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt of supporting forces fighting the federal government, adding a regional dimension to an already volatile confrontation. All three countries have denied involvement, while Sudan has in turn accused Ethiopia of supporting forces hostile to Khartoum - allegations Addis Ababa denies.
At the same time, just across the Red Sea, the Houthis have dramatically expanded their position along Yemen’s western coast, taking Mokha and strategic islands near Bab el-Mandeb in September. The advance has increased pressure on one of the world’s most important maritime passages and renewed fears that conflicts on the two shores of the Red Sea could increasingly intersect.
Ethiopia–Eritrea conflict is serious, expert says
For Dr. Gashaw Ayferam Endaylalu, Senior Researcher of Hydropolitics and Geopolitics in the Horn of Africa and Director General for African Affairs at the Institute of Foreign Affairs, the current Ethiopia–Eritrea tensions cannot be reduced to another temporary deterioration in bilateral relations.
“It is serious, and it would be a mistake to treat it as a passing spike in tension,” Endaylalu told The Media Line. “The current escalation has several layers. On the surface, there is renewed fighting between the federal forces and TPLF [Tigray People’s Liberation Front]-affiliated elements in the north. Beneath that is a wider effort to build an anti-Ethiopia alignment, the so-called ‘Tsimdo’ alliance, in which Eritrea is a key organizer and driver.”
“In my assessment, Asmara pushed for the early resumption of hostilities and provides political and logistical backing,” he further noted.
Those claims reflect an Ethiopian assessment of Eritrea’s role and remain contested. Asmara has denied Ethiopian accusations of destabilization, while the precise extent of external support for the various armed groups remains difficult to establish independently.
The deterioration is particularly striking because Ethiopia and Eritrea were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war. Their relationship worsened after the Pretoria peace agreement, from which Eritrea was excluded despite the participation of Eritrean forces in the conflict. Red Sea access has since emerged as another point of friction, with Addis Ababa repeatedly stressing the economic and strategic importance of obtaining reliable maritime access.
Endaylalu, however, argued that the port question should not be viewed as the main cause of the present confrontation.
“Ethiopia sees access to the sea as an existential and economic necessity,” he said. “A country of more than 120 million people cannot indefinitely depend on a single corridor, given that over 97 percent of its trade passes through Djibouti,” he added.
But, he continued, “I would not describe the sea-access question as the likeliest cause of war. If confrontation comes, sea access will be a secondary cause, not the primary one.”
Main disagreement stems from Horn of Africa political order, expert says
For Endaylalu, the deeper disagreement concerns the political architecture of the Horn itself.
“The primary driver is a deeper disagreement between Addis Ababa and Asmara over the regional order in the Horn of Africa,” he said. “Ethiopia envisions a Horn based on interdependence and shared economic opportunity, while Asmara’s approach depends on an Ethiopia that stays inward-looking and divided.”
He pointed to the earlier Ethiopia–Eritrea war as evidence that bilateral hostility predates the latest debate over Assab and Red Sea access.
“Look at Asmara’s conduct during the EPRDF [Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front] era, from 1991 to 2018. That government did not press any claim on Assab, and yet relations still deteriorated into a devastating war and years of hostility,” he said.
“The risk is real, but it is not inevitable,” he added.
The danger becomes more complicated when Ethiopia and Eritrea are placed within a much wider regional map.
Mowlid Ali, a security intelligence analyst on the Red Sea at INGO Advisory, said the Horn can no longer be analyzed separately from the competition among regional and international actors for ports, military access and influence.
“The situation in the Horn of Africa is deteriorating because of the dominance of powers trying to come to Africa and occupy the ports,” Ali told The Media Line. “They are all in competition. So the violence in the Horn of Africa is going to get worse,” he added.
That competition now overlaps with instability from Sudan to Yemen.
Sudan has been at war since 2023, while Ethiopia and Sudan still have unresolved tensions along their border. At the same time, both governments have traded accusations of assisting hostile armed actors. Reuters reported this month that diplomats increasingly fear a renewed Ethiopian conflict would unfold not in isolation but alongside Sudan’s civil war, Nile tensions, and the spillover of Middle Eastern rivalries into the Horn.
Endaylalu called the Ethiopia-Sudan-Eritrea border area one of the most vulnerable points in that landscape.
“The border triangle is the region’s most delicate fault line,” he said, citing “unresolved border issues between Ethiopia and Sudan” and “the convergence of three states at a single point, with overlapping security interests.”
“Any confrontation in this area would very likely make the conflict regional,” he further noted.
He also alleged that Port Sudan and Eritrea are facilitating forces hostile to Addis Ababa. Such claims have not been independently established, and Sudan’s military has called Ethiopian accusations that it supports armed opposition groups “baseless.”
Egypt-Ethiopia-Eritrea dynamics add layer of diplomatic complexity
Egypt adds another layer.
Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa have for years been strained by the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and disagreements over the Nile. Eritrea, meanwhile, has developed closer relations with both Sudan and Egypt, creating a diplomatic geometry that Ethiopian officials increasingly view with suspicion.
Endaylalu described Cairo as a major actor in the current regional competition.
“Egypt is already deeply engaged. Cairo’s policy in the Horn is one of encirclement, aimed at limiting Ethiopia’s strategic reach and thereby sustaining its own dominance over the Nile and the Red Sea,” he said.
“We see Egypt trying to assemble an anti-Ethiopia axis - Cairo, Port Sudan, Asmara, and others - to pressure Ethiopia into accepting a Nile arrangement that reflects colonial-era assumptions,” he added.
That is Endaylalu’s assessment, rather than an established description of Egyptian policy. Egypt on Tuesday rejected allegations that it was supporting Ethiopian opposition forces and said its foreign policy is based on respect for sovereignty and non-interference in other states’ internal affairs.
For Cairo, however, developments farther north in the Red Sea create an additional security concern. Egypt and Saudi Arabia have already stressed the need to guarantee freedom of navigation through Bab el-Mandeb and the Red Sea as Yemen’s conflict intensifies.
That is where the Horn’s internal tensions risk intersecting with a second crisis.
The Houthi advance through western Yemen has brought the group to strategically important territory overlooking Bab el-Mandeb. Although commercial shipping has not been completely halted, the military shift has increased the Houthis’ capacity to threaten or influence navigation through the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Ali said the implications go far beyond Yemen.
“If they get hold of Bab el-Mandeb, it is going to become a chokehold for humanitarian access and for the shipping lines,” he said.
He warned that deteriorating security on both shores of the waterway could turn separate crises into an interconnected regional security problem.
“You have the situation in Somalia to the east, piracy, and you have the Houthis on the other side of the Red Sea attacking ships and cargo vessels,” Ali said. “There is also a humanitarian catastrophe in Sudan,” he added.
“We have to keep an eye on the escalating security situation in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” he further noted.
Horn of Africa-Red Sea intersection makes conflicts hard to contain
For both analysts, that intersection is what makes the present moment particularly difficult to contain.
Endaylalu warned that the Horn already contains “overlapping alliances, including Gulf, Turkish, Egyptian, and Israeli engagement,” and said that if Ethiopia’s internal conflict develops into “a proxy arena for these competing alignments, the consequences could extend well beyond Ethiopia’s borders.”
Ali reached the same broader concern from the maritime-security side.
“If Iran blocks the Strait of Hormuz and then you have the Houthis in Yemen blocking Bab el-Mandeb entirely,” he said, “it is going to be catastrophic.”, he concluded.
Neither an Ethiopia–Eritrea war nor a wider regional confrontation is inevitable. But the number of unresolved disputes is increasing at the same time: renewed war in northern Ethiopia, tensions with Eritrea, Sudan’s continuing conflict, the Nile dispute with Egypt, and a rapidly changing military balance across the Red Sea in Yemen.
The risk is therefore no longer limited to one border or one conflict. It lies in the possibility that crises that have so far remained partly separate begin to converge around the same strategic space - the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea.

Why the US Air Force Needs to Invest in Electronic Warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

United States air forces are engaged in combat operations today, and not all the aircraft are modern stealthy platforms like the B-2, F-22, or F-35. The venerable Lockheed Martin F-16 Fighting Falcon remains the backbone of the U.S. Air Force fighter fleet and will be in service for two more decades, yet combat operations in Operation Urgent Fury prove it needs electromagnetic warfare (EW) upgrades to survive in modern threat environments.
Our knowledge of the frequencies and waveform characteristics across the Electromagnetic Spectrum (EMS) and our ability to manipulate them with hardware and software have grown tremendously. We harness our knowledge and capabilities continuously for tracking, intelligence, communication, jamming, radar, and many other applications. Unfortunately, so do our adversaries.
To survive and accomplish combat missions, F-16 pilots need to first detect enemy threat systems, like surface-to-air missiles or air-to-air radars, via a Radar Warning Receiver (RWR) and then counter the threat with Electronic Countermeasures (ECM) that manipulate radio signals to jam guidance systems outright or deceive them in such a way that makes them ineffective. If it were only that easy.
In 2023, Commander-in-Chief of the Ukraine Armed Forces, General Valerii Zaluzhnyi, wrote a paper listing five reasons why the war with Russia had ground into static trench warfare. He cited the critical importance and rapid adaptation of electromagnetic warfare along with air superiority, counter artillery battery fires, minefield clearing, and reserve forces.
The electromagnetic spectrum is the tissue that continuously connects all our systems together and allows us to coordinate our actions, detect adversaries, deceive threats, survive, and win. Acknowledging the EMS’s asymmetric impact, both Russia and China created separate branches of service and senior commands specifically focused on electromagnetic warfare.
While superiority in the EMS is critical across all warfighting domains: land, sea, space, and cyber, it is particularly important in air operations.
While the U.S. Air Force has re-prioritized EMS for a portion of the F-16 fleet, approximately 50% of the remaining F-16 aircraft fleet across the active duty, Air National Guard, and Reserves will not have EW protection with no clear plan going forward.
International partners have invested over $1B in procuring Viper Shield systems for their F-16s over the past seven years. The Air Force could add EW pods and leverage foreign investment to save taxpayer money. This foreign investment is funding development, lab testing, flight testing, and current production of operational Viper Shield systems, which presents the U.S. Air Force with a massive savings opportunity to avoid those upfront costs.
As the Air Force considers options to resolve the F-16 EW capability gap, a modest number of advanced EW pods would be a reasonable expense for near-term capability to mitigate against potential program delays, maximize flexibility across the F-16 fleet, and reduce invasive internal modifications.
Furthermore, the pod version of Viper Shield offers maximum flexibility to rotate systems across deploying squadrons, share them among operational units during training periods, and maintain them without taking an aircraft off the flying schedule.
F-16 pilots today – and for the next 20+ years – deserve the capability an EW pod like Viper Shield brings to the fight.
Lt. Gen. Lance Landrum, USAF (Ret.), served over 30 years as an F-16 Weapons Instructor and operational fighter pilot in several deployed locations developing firsthand combat experience on the importance of Electromagnetic Warfare. During his role as the Joint Staff J8 Deputy Director for Requirements and Capability Development, he stood up and led the interagency Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations Cross Functional Team that developed the current U.S. EMS Superiority Strategy and subsequent implementation plan. His insights are based on that experience and from his efforts to champion EMS capabilities as the U.S. European Command J3 and Deputy Chair of the NATO Military Committee.

- Turkish defense manufacturer Otokar signed a $1.47 billion export contract for wheeled armored vehicles and integrated logistics support with an undisclosed customer.
- The contract takes effect after official approvals and an advance payment, with deliveries planned from 2027 in batches over three years.
Turkish defense manufacturer Otokar has signed a $1.47 billion contract to export wheeled armored vehicles and logistics support to a customer it has not named, though the deal will not take effect until government approvals are in place and the buyer pays an advance.
The contract, worth exactly $1,472,080,360, covers the supply of several types of wheeled armored vehicles and integrated logistics support services for them, Otokar said in a disclosure filed on Oct. 1 with Türkiye’s Public Disclosure Platform, the country’s stock market disclosure system. The filing did not identify the buyer, the vehicle models or the number of vehicles.
The contract will enter into force once the required approvals from official authorities are obtained, the letters of guarantee are completed and the customer makes an advance payment, according to the filing. Otokar will provide the customer with letters of guarantee totaling $441,624,108 to cover its obligations under the deal and the advance it will receive.
Once the contract is in force, vehicle deliveries are planned to start in 2027 and be completed in batches over three years. The contract will remain in effect for seven years, which leaves time for logistics support after the last vehicles are handed over.
The deal is larger than Otokar’s previous headline export, a 2024 contract with Romania for 1,059 Cobra II 4×4 armored vehicles worth roughly $1 billion. Under that contract, the first 278 vehicles are being built at Otokar’s plant in Sakarya, in northwest Türkiye, and the rest in Romania through a joint venture, with the first vehicles delivered in June 2025.
The filing’s reference to “wheeled armored vehicles” narrows the possible models. Otokar’s wheeled range includes the Cobra and Cobra II 4×4 tactical vehicles, the Arma 6×6 and 8×8 armored personnel carriers and infantry fighting vehicles, and armored internal security vehicles, while its Tulpar tracked infantry fighting vehicle falls outside that description.
Otokar, part of Türkiye’s Koç Group, sells military vehicles to customers in Europe, Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. Estonia ordered about 230 armored personnel carriers, roughly half of them Arma 6x6s, in 2023, and Cobra vehicles serve with armies including those of Nigeria, Ghana and Rwanda. Kazakhstan has been reported to be buying Arma 8x8s, though that order has never been officially confirmed.

Kyiv • UNN
London has added 23 individuals and organizations and 8 vessels to the sanctions list. The restrictions target the financing of aggression, disinformation, and repression.
The United Kingdom has announced a new package of 31 sanctions measures against Russia, targeting sources of funding for Putin’s war, including vessels from the so-called LNG “shadow fleet,” propagandists, and individuals involved in the torture of civilians and the forced ideological indoctrination of children. This was reported by the British Foreign Office on October 1, UNN writes.
Details
London said the new sanctions package is intended to restrict funding for Russian aggression against Ukraine, undermine disinformation networks, and hold accountable those responsible for torturing Ukrainian civilians and deporting Ukrainian children.
“Following the sham elections held earlier this month in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, the United Kingdom is taking decisive action against individuals and organizations that undermined Ukraine’s territorial integrity and were involved in human rights abuses,” the statement said.
Who has been sanctioned
According to reports, those sanctioned include:
-  eight individuals involved in the arbitrary detention, torture, and cruel treatment of Ukrainian civilians. These crimes are part of a broader system of repression in the territories occupied by Russia, where Ukrainian civilians are also subjected to enforced disappearances and denied access to justice; 
-  seven more people have been added to the sanctions list for their involvement in the ideological indoctrination and militarization of Ukrainian children, including those deported by the Russian authorities. An estimated 6,000 Ukrainian children have been forcibly transferred to a network of infamous so-called “re-education” camps. Millions of Ukrainian children living in territories under Russian occupation are exposed to Kremlin propaganda programs; 
-  in addition, the Russian authorities are attempting to create a new dangerous “shadow fleet” to circumvent sanctions and preserve revenues from gas exports. Several vessels acquired to support these efforts are subject to today’s sanctions, including vessels commissioned only in July this year. By imposing sanctions on these vessels, the United Kingdom is increasing pressure on a sector that the Russian authorities regard as one of the key sources of future revenues; 
-  today’s sanctions package affects seven individuals, including four Georgian citizens involved in spreading disinformation from the Russian regime, ranging from attempts to legitimize Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territories to working in Russian-appointed authorities in the occupied territory of South Ossetia. 
Overall, the sanctions package includes 23 individuals and legal entities, as well as eight vessels.
Sanctions involving asset freezes, restrictions on the provision of trust services, and bans on serving as company directors are being imposed on the 23 individuals and legal entities. Individuals will also be banned from entering the United Kingdom. Shipping and trade restrictions are being imposed on the eight vessels. The sanctions apply to three “shadow fleet” vessels, two vessels that provided them with bunkering services, and three Russian ice-class vessels.

Almost three-quarters of Ukrainians favor peace talks with Russia, but even larger majority opposes concessions on Armed Forces – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
14:05:15 EEST
20:05:15 KST

An absolute majority (72%) of Ukrainians support holding peace talks with Russia, but about half of citizens are willing to accept territorial compromises to end the war, while an absolute majority considers any reduction or limitation of the Armed Forces of Ukraine unacceptable, according to the results of a sociological survey conducted by the Future Research Foundation and presented during a press conference at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Thursday.
"The dynamics of public sentiment demonstrate a high demand for finding diplomatic ways to end the fire. In particular, 72.2% of respondents rather support holding peace talks with Russia. Opponents account for 20.8% of those surveyed," said Svitlana Kushnir, project manager at the Future Research Foundation, during the presentation of the survey results.
Among possible formats for ending the war, 48.5% choose compromises and truce negotiations, even with territorial or political concessions; 24.6% support a temporary "freeze" along the frontline without official recognition of lost territories; while 18.6% of respondents favor continuing the war to the 1991 borders without compromises.
At the same time, territorial compromises to end the war are accepted by 51.7% of citizens (29.4% – "yes, if it leads to the end of the war," 22.3% – "rather yes"), while 41.3% of respondents oppose territorial compromises (20.4% – "no, under no circumstances," 20.9% – "rather no").
"This negotiation track is closely tied to red security lines, which society considers unacceptable to cross. In particular, 76.3% of respondents consider reducing or limiting the size of the Armed Forces at the demand of the other side unacceptable even under security guarantees (for 55.2% of respondents, this is categorically unacceptable)," Kushnir reported.
According to her, 58.7% of respondents believe the situation in Ukraine is moving in the wrong direction (30.9% definitely, 27.8% rather). Meanwhile, 32.5% of respondents assess the direction of development as correct (8.6% definitely, 23.9% rather), and 8.8% hesitated to answer.
At the same time, readiness for compromise is pressured by acute socio-economic problems, notably bribery and corruption in government (51%) and rising food prices (39.6%). In addition, there is anxiety regarding the winter period: 56.1% of families are fully or partially prepared for possible prolonged power and heat outages, while 43.2% assess their readiness as insufficient.
According to the poll, 84.5% of respondents consider the current mobilization process unfair, with 59.6% considering it completely unfair.
Political expert, former Minister of Youth and Sports of Ukraine (2014–2019), and head of the "Information Defense" project of Open Policy Foundation, Ihor Zhdanov, noted that such survey results indicate that Ukraine and its politicians are ready for negotiations, but "want negotiations with specific substance, rather than just talks about capitulation."
"Obviously, there is no talk whatsoever about any capitulation in Ukrainian society. Rather, the point is to hold negotiations, find some compromise, and society is ready for a compromise. Why isn't peace being achieved? Why aren't substantive peace consultations and negotiations taking place, or truces being announced for this? And the Russian dictator Putin is not ready to hold peace talks; he does not want this. Because conditions that would force or push him toward peace have not matured in Russia," he noted during the press conference.
Commenting on the fact that 76% of Ukrainian citizens consider limiting the size of the Armed Forces unacceptable, the expert noted that this indicates Ukrainian society relies solely on itself and its own Armed Forces. "We rely on ourselves and our Armed Forces. We also need to develop our own defense-industrial complex to ensure a predictable situation and equal conditions for Ukrainian and international companies," Zhdanov said.
He also drew attention to the fact that more than half of Ukrainians name government corruption as an especially pressing problem, even surpassing rising prices and low wages.
"Bribery and corruption in government are not just a public perception, but also a problem tied to receiving funds from the European Union. We were told clearly: you must carry out judicial reform, there is the Kakhovka-Koz plan [EU reform agenda] related to anti-corruption activities, such as adopting an anti-corruption strategy, competitive selection of prosecutors, and carrying out judicial reform. Unfortunately, out of 10 points, zero have been fulfilled. All these bills would benefit the country. There are none among them that cause ambiguous attitudes like socio-economic bills. They need to be passed, but for some reason they are not, and this simply leads to us not receiving the corresponding funds from the EU," Zhdanov noted.
The survey was conducted from September 19 to 22 using the CATI (computer-assisted telephone interviewing) method with a random sample of mobile numbers among 1,203 respondents aged 18 and older across all government-controlled territories of Ukraine. The marginal maximum theoretical sampling error does not exceed 2.9% with a 95% confidence probability.

How climate change is altering petrichor, the glorious smell after it rains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:03:20 UTC
20:03:20 KST

The distinct, earthy smell that fills the air after rain following a long dry spell can trigger some serious nostalgia. This scent, petrichor, goes right to our brain’s memory and emotional centers for reasons that may be to do with our very evolution. But as climate change alters Earth’s weather and environment, petrichor is going to transform, too.
First, it helps to know why petrichor even happens. During dry periods, soil-dwelling bacteria produce a compound called geosmin that deters insects such as fruit flies. The chemical signals to the flies that the plant material the bacteria grow on isn’t appetizing and that it might be toxic. Geosmin also attracts spore-spreading animals, such as springtails, which help disperse the compound even more widely.
“Humans are extremely sensitive to geosmin,” says Johan Lundström, a psychologist specializing in olfactory perception at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden. “If there was one drop of geosmin stirred up into an Olympic-sized swimming pool, we’d still smell it.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
READ MORE: Weird Weather: How to Tell a Williwaw from a Haboob
While bacteria in soil produce geosmin, plants discharge aromatic oils during a drought to create a shield to protect against harsh heat and minimize water loss. When raindrops hit dry ground and plants, the impact creates microscopic bubbles filled with geosmin and oils that rise into the air, pop and scatter into tiny particles that can then fill human nostrils.
Exactly how petrichor changes will depend on where you are as the effects of rising global temperatures on weather and climate patterns will vary from place to place and year to year. Overall, parts of the world that get more rainfall will experience less petrichor, whereas areas that have droughts will experience more, says Jeppe Lund Nielsen, a professor of microbial physiology at Aalborg University in Denmark.
Droughts cause geosmin to build up, and when they occur with hotter temperatures, bacteria produce even more geosmin as heat speeds up chemical reactions inside the microbes. “If you get a higher temperature, you also get a higher production of the compounds,” Nielsen says. So when it finally does rain, more geosmin is released. But if soils get too dry, “the geosmin will dry up and not be released,” Lundström says.
Where rain falls more frequently, there will be less petrichor because the aromatic compounds won’t have enough time to accumulate. And heavy downpours—which are increasing as the planet warms—are too forceful to trap the tiny air bubbles required to launch the scent into the air. Instead the compounds are diluted, pushed underground or mixed in surface floodwaters.
Soil degradation—which has also increased as a result of higher temperatures and heavier downpours—plays a role, too, because it means fewer geosmin-producing bacteria can grow.
Any changes to geosmin won’t stop at what humans smell. Insects that react to petrichor will also have to adjust their behavior, Nielsen says. For example, areas with large amounts of petrichor will likely see an increase in mosquitoes, because the smell indicates to these insects that the dry ground is now a moist fertile environment in which to lay their eggs.

Tractive Cat 6 Mini Review: A Fitbit for Your Cat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:03:00 UTC
20:03:00 KST

Cats are finally getting the dog treatment. This smart cat collar features GPS location, activity, and sleep tracking, plus all-new heart and respiratory rate monitoring.
Advanced health monitoring with heart and respiratory rates. Weekly AI-powered health summaries. New visual health history timeline.
TIRED
Battery dies in about four days. Collar clasp and adjustments are tricky. Proprietary charger. Location data isn’t very granular. Needs a subscription to use.
As the pet tech industry expands rapidly, pet owners are more eager to adopt technology that tracks health metrics, similar to human wearable devices like smart rings, smartwatches, and fitness trackers.
I've been testing smart collars for the better part of the year, previously testing the Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker on my cat Basil, which monitored his location, movement, and sleep.
The Tractive Cat 6 Mini was released this spring, and I tested it on Basil for a month, comparing how this new-and-improved smart collar made specifically for cats with improved health features, like heart and respiratory rate, stacked up against other models.
This new model had surprisingly accurate health and activity stats that helped me understand Basil's routine and baseline a bit more than the previous models I've tested. I think these new health features would be especially helpful for people with aging cats or cats in poor health. (If you have an outdoor cat that roams, I'd go with the Fi Mini because it's more compact with a longer battery life.)
I valued the Cat 6 Mini's new AI-powered weekly reports and comparisons to similar cats to know if Basil is healthy. However, the collar itself died quickly, was a pain to charge, and GPS location accuracy could be hit-or-miss. Whether this smart cat collar is the right fit for you largely depends on your and your cat's needs.
Photograph: Molly Higgins
Feline Features
The Tractive Cat 6 Mini cat tracker is available in three colors: black, brown, and lavender. Unlike the previous Fi Mini and Tractive Smart Cat Tracker models I tested, which used an attachment that fits on the cat's existing collar, this device is the collar itself, and the entire thing needs to be taken off the cat to charge on its proprietary magnetic charger. (It takes about three hours to fully charge.) To set it up, all you need to do is download the Tractive app, choose a subscription plan, and set up your pet's profile.
For the 6 Mini model, there is one plan, but you can choose between one-, two-, and five-year contracts. One year is $10 per month, or $120 annually; two years is $7 per month, or $168 annually; and five years is $5 per month, or $300 every five years. The smart collar also has a two-year manufacturer's warranty. All plans include a 30-day money-back guarantee as well as family sharing, LTE cellular coverage, 365-day location history, and GPS data export.
The tracker weighs only 1.1 ounces and is suitable for cats weighing 6.6 to 17.6 pounds, to ensure the breakaway collar opens when it should. Basil is 17 pounds, and the Cat 6 Mini fits him well with room to spare. This smart collar fits necks between 7.5 and 9 inches, whereas the previous Tracker Mini model could fit virtually any neck size because it attached to your existing collar.
Tractive claims the collar's charge lasts up to seven days for indoor cats and that it needs to be charged nearly daily if your pet roams outside. When I tested the smart collar on my indoor-only cat Basil, the battery needed to be charged by the fourth day of use.
Because the device itself is the entire collar, I felt like I was taking Basil's collar off more often than I'd like in order to charge—I didn't like that he was collarless while it charged. My anxiety told me that in this brief moment of his nakedness, he would escape. Also, because charge time took several hours, there were a few times I forgot to put it back on him until the next day.
Another gripe I had was that it was very difficult for me to remove the collar and adjust its diameter. I'm physically disabled and have reduced grip strength and fine-motor function. The collar has a simple looped clasp, but the thick material was difficult to slide under the plastic buckle; it often fell too long or too short, and I couldn't take off the collar without pulling it to trigger the breakaway feature, which was stressful for Basil—especially since the collar needed to be charged every four days.
I would've preferred the clasp to open by easily squeezing the top and bottom to release. Again, this would probably not be as big of an issue if I were able-bodied, but it is a potential issue for other pet owners who may have reduced motor function.
Photograph: Molly Higgins
Once you've picked a coverage plan, you'll create your pet's profile, set your home's location so the device enters power-saving mode when at home, and set up a virtual fence so you'll be alerted if the pet leaves the safe area. Using the stats I provided, Tractive compared Basil to cats of similar age and weight to set a personalized daily activity goal and compared his health stats to those of similar cats.
Putting It to the Test
The Tractive app lets you track activity daily (by the hour) and over time, recording minutes to compare your cat's activity and sleep patterns. Each week, the app provides an AI summary of the previous week's activity and health stats. This pretty much always said Basil slept and relaxed a lot, but noted that he is more active than cats of similar age and breed. There's also average activity per day, which was around four hours for Basil, and average calories burned per day, which was helpful for knowing how much Basil should be eating.
Tractive estimates the cat’s daily calories burned by factoring in your pet's biometric info like weight, size, age, and spay/neuter status to create a baseline. The device contains a three-axis accelerometer that “continuously records the orientation and intensity of your cat’s physical movements,” while algorithms filter out minor movements like stretching to try to prevent false stat inflation. When the sensor detects physical acceleration, like running or playing, it logs these as the “active” minutes and converts them into daily activity time.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
Sleep metrics break down the data by day and week and classify sleep into night sleep, day sleep, and “calm” time (when a cat is awake but not active). Each day's stats are compared to the average, which helped me track Basil's habits throughout the week. Similarly to how the device tracks activity, the built-in accelerometer motion sensor tracks when the cat is still and translates that into sleep and calm time, respectively, based on micro-movements.
You can opt out of Tractive using your cat's data for their anonymized global database and leaderboard comparison features. The device continuously syncs health metrics to the app via cellular networks, but you can request a full copy of what data has been gathered or request the permanent erasure of your data.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
This model's new health metrics for cats include heart and respiratory rates. Basil's resting heart rate was consistently lower than that of cats of similar age and weight. On one day, it was 92 bpm, compared with the normal range of 105 to 168, according to the app. This was a bit alarming to me, and I plan to bring this data up the next time we visit the vet. The app also listed “potential reasons” for the low heart rate, including “fitness and conditioning” and “cold temperatures."
As with the heart rate, the app tracked respiratory rate over time by day and compared it with Basil's historical stats and those of similar cats. His daily average was 20 breaths per minute, which was within the normal range of 15 to 30. This number closely aligned with my personal tests using visual evidence and a timer on my phone.
Screenshot courtesy of Molly Higgins
Live and historical location services weren't as useful for Basil since he's indoor-only. Like the earlier Tractive model, the 6 Mini features a built-in SIM card, similar to what’s on your phone, which uses nearby mobile networks for location updates. You can set up to five virtual fences through the app, which will notify you when your pet enters or leaves these zones. However, similar to the previous model, the default virtual fence was too small around my apartment, so I had to expand it to cover my entire complex. This is concerning because if Basil escapes but stays near my building, I wouldn't receive an alert.
Since my cat is indoor-only, I ran some experiments to track location accuracy. I had my roommates take the collar with them when they left to run errands, and I timed how long it took to receive an alert that Basil had left the “safe zone." I also took the tracker with me along with my phone, and tracked how long it took to receive a notification via Bluetooth.
When I took the tracker outside the safe zone with my phone, I was alerted via a notification on my home screen that Basil had left the “safe zone” almost immediately after exiting it. It provides an approximate location rather than pinpointing the exact spot on the street where he'd be, but it is still more helpful than randomly searching in the event he did get out. If I were to engage it in lost mode, the battery usually dies within four hours, so there is also a bit of a time limit in the event he did escape.
The alerts when the tracker was away from my phone were less precise. I tested it three times—once I was notified within a minute, the next time took about eight minutes, and the last time it took about five and a half minutes to alert after exiting the allotted safe zone. I should note that I get very poor cell phone service near my home, which could affect tracking and notification timing. Tractive also falsely alerted me that Basil had left the “safe zone” about once a week (during one week of testing, it alerted me four times). Each time, he was sitting in my home with the smart collar still on. I noticed it tended to send me false notifications more often when the battery was low or while it was on the charging dock.

I just wish the battery didn't die so damn fast and that the collar had a universal design that was more accessible.

Children across Ukraine now start the school year in bomb shelters, as Russian drones, missiles, and glide bombs keep hitting schools, homes, and hospitals far from the front—part of a civilian toll the UN says has already outrun all of last year's.
A school full of children, all in the shelter
A Russian drone hit a school in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district on the morning of 1 October and started a fire, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, adding that the children were in the shelter. More than 100 students and about 60 staff were sheltering inside, and none were hurt, police said. The jet-powered drone damaged the building's facade at third-floor level, RBC-Ukraine reported.
A café and warehouses among the sites hit
On the evening of 30 September, a Russian strike started a fire at a café on the ground floor of a residential building in Solomianskyi, while warehouse buildings burned in the northern Obolonskyi district. One person was injured in the warehouse fire and handed to medics, RBC-Ukraine reported.
42 sites damaged across Kyiv Oblast
Across Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks over the previous 24 hours damaged 42 sites and injured six people, regional authorities reported.
Kyiv is now under Russian air attack daily. On 28 September, Russian drones hit the city center in daylight, including the National Academy of Sciences, and earlier waves struck filling stations and other everyday sites across the capital.
