Fact-Checking What Donald Trump Said in His Latest Interview With TIME
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

On Sept. 28, about five weeks before Election Day, President Donald Trump sat down for an interview with TIME in the White House.
TIME has published the transcript of that conversation. Below is a review of some of Trump’s statements from the interview.
What Trump Said: “I won all seven swing states. They said if you won three swing states, I won all seven. I won the counties. It's very important, 86% popular vote.”
The Facts: Trump did win the popular vote in the 2024 presidential election, and he did win all seven swing states, but he’s conflating two figures. He won the popular vote by receiving 49.8% of the vote to Kamala Harris' 48.3%. He won the electoral college by 86 votes, 312 to Harris’s 226. He did not win all of the counties in the seven swing states, but he surprised many pundits by winning counties in the Detroit, Milwaukee and Philadelphia metro areas.
What Trump Said: “Their economy is gone. Their inflation is at 300% or something like that.”
The Facts: At the end of August, Iran’s Central Bank reported inflation at 84%, according to The New York Times. The price of food in the country has skyrocketed, and Iran’s currency hit a record low, tumbling to 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar. At the end of 2025, the exchange rate was 1.2 million rials to the dollar.
What Trump Said: “I think the press fed it to them.”
The Facts: Trump was responding to being asked why many thought the war in Iran would be over in four to six weeks. Operation Epic Fury launched Feb. 28. In early March interviews, the President said the action would last four to five weeks.
What Trump Said: “We had more barrels of oil come through last night than at any time in the history of the Strait.”
The Facts: Various reports show about 20 million barrels of oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz daily before the war. On Sept. 26, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Fox News that there was a day last week “where over 20 million barrels of oil, more than pre-conflict levels, flowed out of the straits. The running average today is almost 13 million barrels a day.”
According to Oil & Gas Mideast, oil is flowing at about 13 million barrels per day, about 77% of pre-war levels.
What Trump Said: “They killed 75,000 people in the last number of months. Protesters…”
The Facts: Trump is referring to the killing of civilians by the Iranian regime during protests that began at the end of December 2025 and lasted until mid-January.
The protests began in Tehran after the country’s currency collapsed, and morphed into a widespread anti-regime movement that expanded across the country—until reaching its deadliest peak on Jan 8th and 9th. Iranian authorities responded to the protests by cutting off the internet and embarking on what is now considered the deadliest government crackdown by the Government of Iran since the 1979 Revolution.
The death toll was likely lower than Trump alleges—and the crackdown is believed to have reached its deadliest point earlier this year. Iran’s state run media has put the death toll at 3,117, while human rights organizations estimate it to be in the tens of thousands. At the end of January, two senior officials from Iran’s Ministry of Health told TIME that as many as 30,000 protesters could have been killed on Jan. 8th and 9th alone.
What Trump Said: “We're popular [in Israel], like 99%”
The Facts: A poll showing a 99% approval rating for Trump among Israelis does not exist, but he has polled well in Israel in the past. A 2026 Pew Research Center survey found “66% have confidence in Trump, while only a third or fewer have confidence in the other leaders.” A 2026 survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute found 73% of Israelis think of Trump as a better-than-average U.S. president for Israel’s interests, and 49% described him as one of the best U.S. presidents for Israel. However, the poll was sharply divided on party lines, with 92% of the Israeli right calling Trump an above-average president, but only 34% of the Israeli left had a positive view of Trump.
What Trump Said: “He [Biden] allowed 25 million people that shouldn't have been here.”
The Facts: There is no U.S. Customs and Border Protection data to back up this 25 million number, and there is a lack of definitive data on unauthorized immigrant numbers. The agency tracks encounters at ports of entry, instances of people being detained for trying to enter illegally or who were seeking legal entry but deemed ineligible. Between the start of the 2021 fiscal year through late 2024, the agency reported 10.8 million of these encounters. Pew Research Center has been publishing its own estimates of unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. for the last two decades and reported in 2025 that there were 14 million unauthorized immigrants in the U.S. in 2023—an all-time high.
What Trump said: “Look at the poverty numbers. The lowest we've had in…ever.”
The Facts: This is correct. According to the Census Bureau’s annual poverty report, the official poverty rate fell to 10.2%—the lowest on record since the agency began tracking in 1959. However, the bureau also publishes a supplementary poverty measure (SPM), created in 2009, which accounts for government benefits, like food stamps and housing subsidies, and has a more expansive view of poverty that considers whether a household has the resources for basic needs—like food, housing, clothes, and utilities. The SPM was at 13.1% in 2025, several percentage points above its all-time low of 7.7% in 2021.The Census Bureau’s report also relies on data from a survey conducted in March 2025—just three months into Trump’s presidency.
What Trump Said: “When I took over, I inherited the greatest inflation in history.”
The Facts: The Federal Reserve’s official inflation target for the U.S. economy is 2%. Towards the end of Trump’s first term, in Jan. 2020, the inflation rate was 2.5%. By the time his term ended that Dec., it was at 1.4%. Under Joe Biden, inflation reached a peak of 8% in 2022, the highest inflation the country had seen since 1980, when it hit 13.5%. However, by the end of Biden’s term, inflation dropped to 2.9%.
What Trump Said: “Look, we're building more automobile plants in the United States, and bigger ones, than we've ever built before.”
The Facts: Instead of building new factories, automakers appear to be largely adapting current ones.
General Motors has also announced plans to convert a number of internal combustion engine plants—located in Michigan, Tennessee, Ohio, and Kansas— to EV production as it moves to end the sale of gas-powered vehicles by 2035.
Hyundai announced that it will invest $5.8 billion in a steel plant in Louisiana to produce steel that will be used by Hyundai’s two existing U.S. auto plants.
Nissan has a target to reduce imports from Japan, aiming to produce 80% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. domestically by 2030. However, the company has no plans to open a new plant.
What Trump Said: “We did a convention that had 107 million views, and it stupidly was put opposite the NFL opening, and we got more views, they got 25 million, we got 107 [million].”
The Facts: The ratings tell a different story. Nielsen data showed that Trump’s approximately two-hour speech at the GOP midterm convention on Sep. 9 in Dallas averaged 2.5 million viewers on Fox News, the only major cable network to carry the speech in full. NBC said the Patriots-Seahawks NFL kickoff game averaged 25.1 million views.
What Trump Said: “We got more manufacturing jobs coming online than at any time in the history of our country.”
Manufacturing employment peaked in 1979 with 19.6 million jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. While 16,000 manufacturing jobs were added in August, the total number is 12.6 million, well below the 1979 peak.

Gaza documentary ‘NAZA’ beating ‘Avengers Endgame: Encore’ at box office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:58:22 UTC
19:58:22 KST

'NAZA', the award-winning documentary which examines "the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians", is currently beating the recently re-released Marvel film ‘Avengers Endgame: Encore’ at the Italian box office. The documentary is set to be released globally this month.
NAZA, the Venice-winning documentary about the Israeli attacks on Gaza, is currently beating Marvel’s Avengers Endgame: Encore at the Italian box office.
Directed by Oscar-winners Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Israeli filmmakers behind No Other Land, NAZA shows “in detail the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to its official synopsis.
Shot in secrecy at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv during the ongoing Gaza war, it features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers, soldiers and whistleblowers. They describe how Palestinians are targeted and how strikes are carried out using AI and automated surveillance in military targeting systems - despite Israel being aware that civilians are present in targeted areas. The participants' faces and voices were digitally altered to protect their identities.
The 80-minute hot-button doc builds on reporting between 2023 and 2025 published by the Israeli-Palestinian +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call, and The Guardian. It left this year's Venice Film Festival with the Special Jury Prize and received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at the festival.
NAZA premiered in Italian cinemas on Monday (28 September) and by Tuesday, had taken a reported €1.1 million at the box office. By comparison, Avengers Endgame: Encore - a rerelease of the 2019 blockbuster featuring new scenes that tie the film to the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, made €356,000 over the same period (via The Guardian).
NAZA was originally booked for a three-day theatrical run but that’s now been extended due to sold-out screenings. More than 150 other cinemas in Italy are expected to extend programming.
“As long as theatres want to show it, NAZA will continue to be screened,” Andrea Romeo, founder of I Wonder Pictures, the film’s distributor in Italy, told La Repubblica.
“We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible,” explained Abraham and Szor.
“While filming over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanisation of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like?”
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hasattacked the makers of NAZA, accusing the film of contributing to “global antisemitic incitement”.
“It’s shocking. We are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram. “And now two Israeli directors portraying the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”
Netanyahu's comments followed those of Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar, who directly equated criticism of Israel's actions to antisemitism and announced that he would “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship” of the Israeli directing duo Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.
NAZA will be released in more than 50 territories in the coming weeks before being made free-to-watch on The Guardian’s website in November.

Pentagon wants a hypersonic cruise missile for jets, ships and bombers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:56:30 UTC
19:56:30 KST

- DARPA issued a request for information on Sept. 30 for a Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile demonstrator, with responses now due Nov. 6.
- The agency wants an air-breathing missile that leaps ahead in range, speed or altitude and can be built affordably at high rates.
The Pentagon’s research agency DARPA is asking industry how to build a new hypersonic cruise missile that would fly much farther, faster or higher than current designs and could still be produced cheaply in large numbers.
DARPA’s Tactical Technology Office posted a request for information for the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile on Sept. 30 and later pushed the response deadline back a month, from Oct. 6 to Nov. 6. The agency says the answers will shape the requirements and acquisition plan for a possible competitive program whose goal is to design, build and flight-test a complete hypersonic cruise missile demonstrator. The notice is not a solicitation, and DARPA has not said how much the program could cost or when a first flight might take place.
A hypersonic cruise missile flies at more than five times the speed of sound using an air-breathing engine, usually a scramjet, that draws oxygen from the atmosphere instead of carrying it on board. DARPA says earlier demonstration programs have already proven that scramjet-powered flight works, but that existing concepts deliver only incremental gains and that legacy manufacturing makes them too expensive and complex to build at the scale a war with a major power would demand.
The agency wants a “revolutionary leap” in at least one of three areas, range, cruise speed or altitude, so the missile can strike targets defended by advanced air defense networks. It also wants the design built for easy manufacturing and assembly from the start, with a realistic path from a demonstrator to affordable, high-rate production.
DARPA is open to very different sizes of missile. The notice lists four broad classes: a weapon carried inside or under a fighter jet for quick response, one sized for a bomber’s internal bay, cargo-aircraft pallets or a ship’s vertical launch tubes, a larger missile carried under a heavy bomber, and a large ground-launched version for strategic missions that would make the most of an air-breathing engine’s range at bigger scales.
The request covers three areas for industry. One asks for overall missile concepts and a fast plan for reaching a first flight. Another seeks high-risk technologies such as new engines, high-energy fuels, boosters, heat-resistant materials and cooling systems, and DARPA says it is not interested in modernization or incremental improvements. A third asks for new ways to test hypersonic weapons, which is one of the slowest and most expensive parts of any program. DARPA is running its own studies on the missile’s operational use in parallel.
The testing section stands out. DARPA wants flight test methods that can cover distances of 250 to 2,000 nautical miles (460 to 3,700 km), reduce reliance on traditional test ranges so programs can test on demand, and give off fewer signs that a test is about to happen. It asks for autonomous telemetry, tracking and data systems that could be based on the surface, underwater, in the air or in space.
DARPA is encouraging companies outside the traditional defense industry to respond, particularly on the technology and testing questions, and to form teams with established contractors. The agency’s earlier Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept program flight-tested scramjet-powered designs from Raytheon, Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin and fed into the U.S. Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile program.

The left-wing Die Linke party, which won Berlin’s election about two weeks ago, is facing growing scrutiny over its ties to figures linked to Arab crime families in the German capital, as well as antisemitic and anti-Israel activists. Now, questions are also being raised about Elif Eralp, the party’s candidate for mayor, and her involvement in a group that Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has described as one of the country’s most important far-left organizations.
Warning signs emerged on election night, when Issa Remmo, head of Berlin’s largest crime clan, attended the party’s victory celebration in the immigrant-heavy district of Neukölln. Remmo said the party had finally given him a sense of political belonging. Ibrahim Ibrahim, a representative of an umbrella organization linked to Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine in Germany, was also present.
The party sought to distance itself from the two men, but the Remmo clan later publicly released messages between its members and Die Linke lawmakers who had asked the family to distribute campaign material on their behalf.
It has now emerged that until a year ago, Eralp was a member of the organization Red Aid, whose motto is “the end justifies the means.” The group provides legal and financial support to offenders as long as their crimes were committed in pursuit of left-wing political causes.
Many Germans had already raised concerns over the party’s ties to crime clans and its calls to reduce police funding and presence. Some voters are now questioning whether Eralp’s past in an organization seen as supporting violence, or turning a blind eye to violations of the law in pursuit of its goals, could undermine her ability to serve as Berlin’s democratic, law-abiding leader.
While a left-wing coalition involving the Greens, Die Linke and the Social Democrats is beginning to take shape in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a similar coalition in Berlin, though mathematically possible, appears increasingly remote. Many Social Democrats and Greens have warned against opening coalition talks with Die Linke.
Once again, the party is giving potential coalition partners reasons to keep their distance.
It was revealed this week that representatives of the Barbak clan were also present at Die Linke’s victory party in Neukölln, where the party won 31% of the vote, compared with 25.7% citywide.
The clan arrived in Berlin from Khan Younis in recent years and now numbers more than 130 family members, most of them living in Neukölln.
Unlike the Remmo clan, the Barbak family is not considered heavily involved in conventional criminal activity. Its members are primarily involved in organizing anti-Israel demonstrations, supporting Hamas and its military wing, the Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades, disseminating inflammatory messages, spray-painting red triangles associated with Hamas on walls across the city and sharing extremist Islamist content on social media.
According to police, the family’s activities, violence by some of its members against officers, calls for Israel’s destruction and attacks on Jews, as well as efforts directed against Germany’s constitution and democratic order, have led intelligence agencies to place many of its members under surveillance.
Despite this, two representatives of the family not only attended Die Linke’s victory celebration but also interviewed senior party officials and filmed them on video.
“We express full solidarity with the Barbak family,” wrote the Palestine Solidarity group, which is affiliated with the party.
The group also wrote on its Instagram account that “the Palestinian resistance will not stop until Tel Aviv is Palestinian. Solidarity with Palestine is not a crime.”
Meanwhile, Jewish and Israeli activists in Germany are continuing efforts to provide Eralp with a degree of public legitimacy in response to warnings from numerous Jewish institutions and public figures against including her in a coalition because of manifestations of antisemitism within the party.
After 150 Israeli and Jewish artists and cultural figures signed a letter supporting the party, Eralp visited a solidarity sukkah organized by the group Israelis for Peace on Monday.
She delivered remarks there with sukkah decorations behind her bearing slogans including “Israelis against genocide” and “Germany, impose sanctions on Israel now.”

The US considers a Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year unlikely - Reuters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
13:54:21 EEST
19:54:21 KST

The US considers a Chinese invasion of Taiwan next year unlikely - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
US officials consider a Chinese invasion of Taiwan by 2028 increasingly unlikely. Beijing is waiting for the 2028 elections.
U.S. officials believe that a Chinese invasion of Taiwan by 2028 is becoming increasingly unlikely, despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s instructions to the Chinese military to be ready by 2027 to seize the democratically governed island by force if necessary, people familiar with the U.S. assessment said. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The main reasons are delays in preparing the military amid the Chinese Communist Party’s anti-corruption campaign, as well as Beijing’s desire to see the results of Taiwan’s 2028 elections. Some Chinese officials hope they could bring to power a government more favorable to bringing the island under China’s control.
Beijing may increasingly consider using force in 2028 and beyond if the Democratic Progressive Party wins a fourth consecutive term in Taiwan’s elections, especially if incumbent President Lai Ching-te is re-elected, the sources added.
If that happens, then I think 2028 will be quite tense
Lai, who took office two years ago, and his ruling Democratic Progressive Party advocate a separate Taiwanese identity from China — a position that often irritates Beijing. China considers the island an inalienable part of its territory. Taiwan categorically rejects China’s claims and says that only its people can determine their own future.
The assessment, which has not previously been reported, is a significant update to the longstanding view among U.S. officials that Xi wanted his military to be ready to potentially seize Taiwan by force in 2027 — the centenary of the founding of China’s People’s Liberation Army. China has never ruled out using force to establish control over Taiwan, but it has never publicly confirmed an order to be ready by 2027.
The 2027 benchmark, which analysts say concerns the readiness of the Chinese military rather than a set deadline for an invasion, has for many years created a sense of urgency in several U.S. administrations regarding countering China in the Asia-Pacific region.
The United States is Taiwan’s most important international partner and arms supplier, despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations. U.S. officials differ in their assessments of how seriously China may view the 2028 U.S. presidential election as a factor in deciding whether to take military action.
Three people familiar with the situation said Beijing may also want to assess the results of the U.S. elections, particularly in light of growing opposition among American voters to U.S. involvement in military operations abroad. At the same time, the first U.S. official said Beijing views both Democrats and Republicans as largely united on the Taiwan issue.

Christa Pike execution fails: What next when a lethal injection is botched?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:52:42 UTC
19:52:42 KST

Christa Pike execution fails: What next when a lethal injection is botched?
The only woman on Tennessee ‘death row’ is in hospital after two injections failed to kill her.
Two doses of a lethal injection drug have failed to kill Christa Gail Pike, a 50-year-old woman who was due to be executed on Wednesday. Pike was taken to hospital after it was found that her heart was still beating following the procedure.
Pike would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be put to death in Tennessee and was the only woman on the state’s death row. Her attempted execution with doses of the sedative pentobarbital went ahead despite a last-minute stay by a federal appeals court on Wednesday, which was overturned just an hour before her execution by the Supreme Court.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US appeals court halts Tennessee execution of Christa Pike
- list 2 of 3Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike survives lethal injections
- list 3 of 3Execution of US woman Christa Pike fails after botched lethal injection
Human rights experts said the botched execution illustrates why the death penalty is inhumane and should be abolished.
Clive Stafford Smith, a human rights lawyer who has represented many American death row inmates as well as detainees held at the notorious Guantanamo Bay detention centre, told Al Jazeera: “I’ve been in the execution chamber with six of my clients and it’s never the clinical process they’d have you believe. And it’s always a desperate midnight struggle to stop it.”
He added: “In the end, you have to question whether this makes the world a better, more civilised place. Why, indeed, do we kill people to prove that killing people is wrong?”
Ahead of the planned execution, Morris Tidball-Binz, the UN special rapporteur on arbitrary executions, told the UK’s Times newspaper: “If executed, Christa Pike would be a victim of torture to death. This will be a gross violation of human rights.”
Here’s what we know about what happens when an execution goes wrong.
What is the case against Pike?
Pike was found guilty of the murder of another young woman she had viewed as a romantic rival, when she was aged 18, more than 30 years ago.
In January 1995, Pike, her 17-year-old boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson lured Colleen Slemmer, 19, into a wooded area and tortured and killed her. All four were students at a Job Corps vocational centre in Knoxville.
The case attracted huge public interest, especially after it was revealed that the attackers had carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest, which Shipp later admitted to doing. Pike, who delivered the killing blow to the victim’s head, smashing her skull, kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull afterwards.
Pike and Shipp confessed and were convicted of first-degree murder in 1996. Pike was sentenced to death; Shipp, who was 17 at the time and therefore ineligible for the death penalty, received life with the possibility of parole.
Her case is highly unusual in that she is a woman and was a teenager when she carried out the murder. Other death row inmates who were convicted at the age of 18 – all men – have had their sentences commuted to life in prison without parole.
“Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions,” her lawyers wrote. They also argued that Pike had been the victim of appalling childhood abuse – including two rapes when she was aged 11 and 17.
Stafford Smith told Al Jazeera: “Very few women are executed, but fewer still in Tennessee – it has been 200 years. So, this is a step back to about 1820. Christa was just a teenager, and had undergone horrendous abuse as a child. Now she is 50, a totally different person. It is so pointless – will this really make the world a more civilised place?”
Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, however, has spoken out in support of the execution.
On Wednesday, a federal court temporarily put the planned execution on hold, on legal and technical grounds. But an hour before the midnight deadline for her execution was to expire, the US Supreme Court overruled the stay on her execution, paving the way for jail authorities to proceed.
Pike had asked to be shot by an all-female firing squad instead of by lethal injection, which she said she feared would be too painful.
Her lawyers had also argued that the injection would be torturous for her as she has “small veins”. This request was denied, however.
How did the execution go wrong?
Following the Supreme Court’s order to go ahead with the execution, Pike was administered two doses of the sedative pentobarbital at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, on Wednesday evening, according to media witnesses.
From outside the prison, The Associated Press journalist Kim Chandler reported that, initially, when the injections were administered, Pike appeared noticeably awake.
“The blinds were closed for the first time to the execution chamber at 7:46pm (23:46 GMT), they opened again at 7:49pm (23:49 GMT),” Chandler said.
“Her mouth fell open a few times, and she began to loudly snore. She gasped a few times,” she noted.
“The curtain to the execution chamber closed for the final time at 8:06pm (00:06 GMT), and she could be heard loudly snoring, clearly very alive, in the chamber until media witnesses were told to leave the area at about 8:53pm (00:53 GMT),” Chandler added.
The Tennessee Department of Correction did not immediately explain why the execution had not been completed.
According to NBC News, late on Wednesday, Pike’s lawyers had filed a federal court motion during the process seeking again to halt her execution, citing witnesses’ accounts that “executioners had injected both syringes of lethal injection chemicals and Pike is still alive and snoring”.
“Ms Pike has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring,” they said, according to the court documents seen by the media.
Her lawyers also told US media that while she was being treated at a hospital, she needed “immediate medical care”.
Why didn’t the execution work?
Tennessee authorities have not explained this yet.
However, Stafford Smith, who has attended several executions in support of clients in the past, told Al Jazeera that there are two probable reasons why the injection failed to kill Pike.
“The first is that the drugs were probably out of date. Something that we’ve been observing a lot for the last 10 years is that they administer drugs that are no longer valid,” he said.
Stafford Smith noted that there is, however, a valid reason for this, which is that drug companies make sedatives like pentobarbital to help people and save lives and are often opposed to their drugs being used to execute people.
“So the states have a real problem getting drugs to kill people and they’ve gone to extraordinary extents with very unreliable providers. So you can suspect that they just had an invalid batch of drugs in Pike’s case,” Smith explained.
“The other thing about Pike is that, as is very common with people who end up in her situation, they’ve been through a lot of abuse and drug abuse. So it might have been very hard to find her veins and get a needle into it. Moreover, doctors are also not allowed to take part in this process in the US. So they have incompetent people administering such drugs, which could have resulted in the injection failing,” he added.
Defending its handling of the case, the Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement late on Wednesday that the agency had “followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office”.
“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility,” the statement concluded.
What happens to Pike next?
At the moment, it is unclear, as Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has paused all remaining 2026 executions in the state following Wednesday’s incident with Pike and has called for a comprehensive, third-party review. She is currently in hospital. She may return to death row, but Stafford Smith said this is uncertain.
Has this happened before?
Yes. Botched executions do happen but the frequency varies substantially by method, according to data compiled by legal scholar Austin Sarat and the Death Penalty Information Center.
In his 2014 book, Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death Penalty, Sarat noted that from 1890 to 2010, 8,776 people were executed in the US and 276 of those executions (3.15 percent) went wrong in some way. Sarat also noted that lethal injection was the method that had the highest rate of botched executions at 7.2 percent in this period.
Previous botched lethal injection cases include the case of murderer Alva Campbell in November 2017 in Ohio. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, “the execution team first worked on both of Alva Campbell’s arms for about 30 minutes.. while he was on a gurney in the state’s death chamber and then tried to find a vein in his right leg below the knee. … About 80 minutes after the execution was scheduled to begin, the 69-year-old Campbell shook hands with two guards after it appeared the insertion was successful.”
“About two minutes later … Gary Mohr, head of the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction … called off the execution after talking with the medical team, [saying] ‘It was my decision that it was not likely that we’re going to access veins.’” But a few months later, in March, 2018, Campbell died on death row due to terminal medical conditions.
“Botched executions have happened many times. I’ve had six of my clients executed over the years. Two were with the gas chamber, two with the electric chair and two with lethal injection, and there’s almost always some form of botching,” Stafford Smith said.
“But it’s just an uncivilised process carried out by people who are pretty uncivilised,” he added.

Poland implements new response rules for air defence amid Russian attacks on Ukraine
Poland enacts simplified procedures for detecting and shooting down foreign aerial assets starting 1 October. The rules are being changed to protect Polish airspace during Russian attacks on Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda, citing Polish media outlet Gazeta Prawna
Details: Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the full readiness of the new, simplified rules for detecting and shooting down foreign objects in Polish airspace, which take effect on 1 October.
"First of October is always a good time to implement these procedures," Kosiniak-Kamysz noted.
On 28 September, Cezary Tomczyk, Deputy Minister of National Defence, spoke about the planned changes to the rules for Polish pilots participating in missions to protect Polish airspace during Russian airstrikes in Ukraine.
Tomczyk explained that these changes primarily concern modifying the rules for identifying foreign aerial assets. Peacetime procedures requiring visual identification of a target before shooting it down are to be replaced by dynamic sensor-based identification.
Following the procedural changes, a pilot or their commander will be able to make the decision to shoot down an unidentified object based on information gathered by radars and other systems or on information provided by the Ukrainian side, which regularly faces attacks from Russian drones and missiles.
Background:
- On 28 September Cezary Tomczyk reported that Poland would change the rules for shooting down aerial assets that violate its airspace.
- Earlier, it was reported that starting Friday 25 September, the Polish government will begin to distribute guidance on how to respond to air attacks which explains the basic rules for finding a safe place – indoor or outdoor – in the event of threats from the air.

House prices in Portugal hit new record high in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:49:25 UTC
19:49:25 KST

Eurostat data shows Portugal recorded the EU's sharpest rise in house prices in Q2 2026 versus a year earlier. In September, national housing costs hit a fresh record high.
House prices are once again on the rise in Portugal, reaching a new all-time high in September.
According to the Idealista price index, prices rose by 7.9% in September compared with the same month last year. On a monthly basis, they also rose by 0.6% nationwide.
Data from the property sales and rental portal show that the median asking price for a home was €3,228 per square metre last month.
Vila Real (17.8%), Leiria (17.6%), Beja (14.4%), Faro (14.3%) and Guarda (14%) posted the steepest annual increases among the cities surveyed, with the Centro region leading the way in terms of regional price growth.
Aveiro (9.3%), Setúbal (9.1%), Porto (9%), Castelo Branco (9%), Ponta Delgada (7.1%), Funchal (5.3%) and Lisbon (4.4%) were the areas where prices rose the least.
Lisbon remains the country’s most expensive city in which to buy a home. The Portuguese capital has a median asking price of €6,256 per square metre. The wider Lisbon region is also the priciest area in which to buy a home, with a median asking price of €4,501 per square metre.
Portugal posts the sharpest house price rise in the EU
Portugal also recorded the EU’s fastest annual house price growth in the second quarter.
According to the latest Eurostat figures, the country recorded the biggest increase in the European Union in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier.
"The largest increase was recorded in Portugal (+16.5%), followed by Bulgaria (+15.5%) and Lithuania (+14.3%)", the statement says, adding that Finland (-2.7%), Luxembourg (-2.2%) and France (-0.8%) were the only countries where prices fell.
Overall, in the second quarter of 2026, house prices rose by 4% in the eurozone and 4.7% in the EU compared with the same quarter of the previous year.
Compared with the first quarter of 2026, house prices increased by 1.1% in the eurozone and 1.2% in the EU in the second quarter.

Portugal posts the sharpest house price rise in the EU

According to the latest Eurostat figures, the country recorded the biggest increase in the European Union in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier.
"The largest increase was recorded in Portugal (+16.5%), followed by Bulgaria (+15.5%) and Lithuania (+14.3%)", the statement says, adding that Finland (-2.7%), Luxembourg (-2.2%) and France (-0.8%) were the only countries where prices fell.
Overall, in the second quarter of 2026, house prices rose by 4% in the eurozone and 4.7% in the EU compared with the same quarter of the previous year.
Compared with the first quarter of 2026, house prices increased by 1.1% in the eurozone and 1.2% in the EU in the second quarter.

That is why the safety of everyone involved in the education process remains the top priority. When an air-raid warning is in effect, shelters are the only option for every child and every adult. The education process must be organised in accordance with the safety situation in each hromada."

Russia Has 10,000 Attack Drones Stockpiled—and Is Building 2,000 Jet-Powered Gerans a Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:47:35 UTC
19:47:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Has 10,000 Attack Drones Stockpiled—and Is Building 2,000 Jet-Powered Gerans a Month
Russia is currently producing around 2,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones per month while maintaining a stockpile of approximately 10,000 conventional piston-engine strike drones, RBC-Ukraine reported on October 1, citing sources within Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the outlet, Russia has been able to increase production of the newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 variants after discontinuing the earlier jet-powered Geran-3 and redirecting some of its components toward the newer models.
Further expansion of production, however, remains uncertain because of Russia’s dependence on turbojet engines. According to the report, most of these engines are supplied by China, while Russia is also attempting to establish domestic production.
At the same time, Russia has accumulated substantial reserves of conventional strike drones powered by piston engines. A source told RBC-Ukraine that the stockpile could have reached around 10,000 units as of last week.
During aerial attacks, Russian forces combine jet-powered and conventional gasoline-powered Shahed-type drones, launching them in small groups and successive waves. These formations typically consist of two or three drones, and occasionally four or five, with both types potentially used in the same group.
According to the report, the groups are launched one after another, extending attacks over several hours and forcing Ukrainian air defenses to repeatedly respond to new aerial targets.
One of the goals of this tactic is to maintain a prolonged aerial threat, exhaust Ukrainian air defenses, and force them to constantly respond to new targets, RBC-Ukraine reported.
The reported increase in drone production comes as Russia continues to expand infrastructure used to support its unmanned aerial operations. Over the past four weeks, the Tsymbulova drone base in the Oryol region has undergone further expansion, with new launch infrastructure, shelters, and storage facilities under construction, OSINT channel Strategic Aviation reported.
Satellite imagery reportedly shows a newly developed area southeast of the existing launch sites, featuring eight dome-shaped shelters intended for jet-powered drones and an additional launcher. According to Strategic Aviation, paved sites have also been prepared for eight more shelters and two additional launchers.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has been developing interceptor drones to counter the emerging threat from Russia’s jet-powered UAVs. On September 30, Ukrainian manufacturer SkyFall told Ukrinform that its domestically produced P1-SUN JetKiller interceptor had shot down a Russian Geran-5.
The Geran-5 was downed by operators from Lasar’s Group, a Ukrainian National Guard unit specializing in unmanned systems, according to the outlet.

Ukraine Hunts Russian Missile Launchers So Hard Moscow Pulls Them 100 Km Back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:47:19 UTC
19:47:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hunts Russian Missile Launchers So Hard Moscow Pulls Them 100 Km Back
Ukraine’s intensified hunt for Russian missile systems has reportedly forced Moscow to move some launchers roughly twice as far from the Ukrainian border, creating new range problems for shorter-range weapons, RBC-Ukraine reported on October 1.
According to RBC-Ukraine sources, Russian forces had previously launched ballistic missiles from positions around 100 kilometers, or 62 miles, from Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the past several weeks, however, Ukrainian forces have stepped up efforts to locate and strike the launchers themselves.
That pressure has reportedly pushed some Russian systems back to positions roughly 200 kilometers, or 124 miles, from the border.
The withdrawal does more than make the launchers harder for Ukraine to reach. It can also reduce which Ukrainian targets some Russian missiles are capable of hitting.
One source specifically pointed to the RM-48U, a surface-to-surface weapon adapted for Russia’s S-300 and S-400 systems.
The missile’s range is reported to be no more than about 250 kilometers, or 155 miles.
If launchers carrying such weapons are positioned approximately 200 kilometers from Ukraine’s border, their remaining reach inside Ukrainian territory becomes significantly more limited.
Previously, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Iskander ballistic missile launcher near the border in a rare and potentially significant operation aimed at destroying Moscow’s missile systems before they can fire.
“We hit an Iskander launcher near our borders. I’m grateful to our soldiers who carry this out. This is our operation of hunting their systems that are positioned nearby,” the President said.

Türkiye vows continued co-op with Iraq after troop withdrawal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Bashiqa-Zilkan, a key Turkish base in Iraq, will soon be handed over to Iraqi authorities while Turkish troops are expected to withdraw from the country. The development, which comes amid the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the country, which remained there as part of an anti-Daesh coalition, signals the start of a new era for Iraq and Türkiye. The Ministry of National Defense said in a statement on Thursday that the handover of the base did not mean an end to cooperation with Iraq and, on the contrary, Türkiye would continue supporting Iraq’s security and stability.
Türkiye and Iraq agreed earlier this month to deepen security cooperation, restore full Iraqi state authority in Sinjar and begin the gradual handover of the Bashiqa-Zilkan military base to Baghdad under an agreed timetable.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi announced the steps in a joint statement following talks in New York on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.
The ministry said Türkiye welcomed steps to ensure state authority in Sinjar. The base was set up in 2015 to help Iraq fight against Daesh and later maintained its presence when the terrorist group PKK sought to replace Daesh following the liberation of Sinjar.
“These steps will contribute to normalization of the region, establishing an environment of security and stability and a terror-free region,” the ministry said, using an expression referring to Ankara’s “terror-free Türkiye” initiative, which aims to disarm the PKK.
The statement also said it was decided to gradually hand over the compound to the central government in Baghdad, “based on improvement of security in Sinjar.”
“Our country, as it did in the past, stands with our neighbor Iraq in terms of maintaining an environment of security and stability. Throughout future contacts, we are planning to take steps that will further advance military and security cooperation. We will continue supporting Iraq’s armed forces in increasing military capacity, sharing know-how in counterterrorism and in the fields of military training and defense industry cooperation, based on bilateral agreements,” the ministry stated.
Ayhan Sarı, an assistant professor at the Turkish-German University and a security and foreign policy expert at the Turkish Research Foundation (TAV), noted that Türkiye’s withdrawal was linked to ending the PKK’s presence in Sinjar and the re-establishment of Baghdad’s authority there.
Sarı told Daily Sabah that Türkiye has been in Iraq as an exercise of its right to self-defense under international law, particularly Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, which recognizes the right to individual and collective self-defense against armed attacks. “Türkiye’s presence in Iraq has been due to the PKK threat in the north. (The dissolution) of the PKK will remove the need to remain in Iraq,” Sarı said.
He noted that the PKK and other terrorist groups had, for years, filled the power vacuum that emerged in Iraq’s northern region following the beginning of the Iraq War.
“Iraq’s central government claims it can find a solution to this vacuum through recent steps and establish full authority within its borders after the U.S. withdrawal,” Sarı said.
A U.S.-led coalition deployed in Iraq more than a decade ago against Daesh formally concluded its mission on Wednesday. Daesh was largely expelled from Iraq and Syria, also thanks to Türkiye’s cross-border operations in Assad-era Syria, but U.S. forces remained. Washington and Baghdad reached an agreement two years ago to wind down the mission.
Sarı said it was only natural that Türkiye was supportive of Iraq’s steps to ensure security on its own, since Ankara was committed to developing good relations with its neighbors and centered its foreign policy on peace and stability.
“As it did in Syria, Türkiye sides with central authority, stability and security in Iraq. Türkiye will support this move and will do whatever it can to ensure that this mission succeeds in maintaining stability and security, based on its neighborly relations,” he said.
Sarı added that Iraq’s efforts were compatible with Türkiye’s foreign policy and plans. “Iraq’s success will also mean the complete expulsion of the PKK from that country. This expulsion, removal of this malignant tumor between Türkiye and Iraq, will certainly add momentum to Turkish-Iraqi relations,” he also stated.

Barcelona-El Prat airport runs Europe's most stressful route for fearful flyers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:42:23 UTC
19:42:23 KST

The route between Barcelona El Prat and Amsterdam Schiphol tops a ranking that also lists Madrid-London Heathrow in 10th place, according to AirAdvisor.
The route between Amsterdam Schiphol and Barcelona El Prat is Europe's most stressful air route for passengers who are afraid of flying, according to an analysis by AirAdvisor, which also places the Madrid Barajas–London Heathrow connection among the top ten in the ranking.
The study takes into account factors such as delays, cancellations, weather conditions and flight duration, but does not assess air safety.
"Fear of flying rarely depends on a single factor," said AirAdvisor chief executive Anton Radchenko, quoted in a statement. "Long waits at the boarding gate, unexpected last-minute cancellations and tricky weather conditions can significantly increase a passenger's anxiety."
The Amsterdam–Barcelona connection scores 75.1 points out of 100, the highest rating of the 26 European routes analysed. Between September 2025 and August 2026, 7.02% of its flights were delayed by more than an hour, 0.83% were delayed by over three hours and 2.93% were cancelled. On top of this comes exposure to adverse weather conditions at the Dutch airport.
The second most stressful route, according to the study, is London Heathrow–Amsterdam, which has the highest cancellation rate, at 3.69%. This route, linking two of the world's busiest airports, scores 63.8 points.
The route between Madrid Barajas and London Heathrow ranks tenth, with 40.8 points. 3.38% of its flights recorded delays of more than an hour, while 0.17% were delayed by over three hours and 1.15% were cancelled.
Other Spanish connections also appear in the ranking. Barcelona El Prat and Rome Fiumicino occupy seventh place, with 45.2 points, while the route between Barcelona and Palma de Mallorca comes thirteenth. The latter stands out for its delays, which affected 6.89% of flights.
The index, which weights cancellations, delays, weather and journey duration, measures the predictability of flights, not their safety. According to Radchenko, knowing what incidents have been recorded can help passengers who are afraid of flying to prepare better for their journeys.
The 10 most stressful routes in Europe
- Amsterdam–Barcelona - 75.1
- London Heathrow–Amsterdam - 63.8
- Manchester–Dublin - 63.4
- Lisbon–Madeira - 61.4
- Paris Charles de Gaulle–Nice - 60.8
- Oslo–Stavanger - 46.8
- Barcelona–Rome Fiumicino - 45.2
- London Heathrow–Frankfurt - 44.2
- Oslo–Trondheim - 42.4
- Madrid–London Heathrow - 40.8

Russian glide bombs scarred a statue of Christ and damaged a 19th-century church in Sumy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:39:20 UTC
19:39:20 KST

Russian glide bombs that struck central Sumy on 29 September damaged a 19th-century church, the city cemetery around it, and a bronze statue of Christ, NV reported, citing the diocesan outlet Pravoslavna Sumshchyna. The same strike hit a school and nearby homes. Russia kept up its attacks across Ukraine over the following night and day.
Russia continues its terror campaign against Ukrainian civilians, and churches are among its routine targets, from a church its incendiary drone burned to the ground in Donetsk Oblast to one its drone damaged in western Ukraine's Lviv. Its strikes keep landing in city centers where people live, study, and pray, as when a drone hit Kyiv's Academy of Sciences in broad daylight.
The church near the epicenter
Russia struck Sumy with four guided aerial bombs. The blast damaged the Church of Saints Peter and Paul, a national-level architectural monument that stood near the epicenter. The church belongs to the Sumy Diocese of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church (Moscow Patriarchate).
Almost the entire building was damaged, said the rector, Archpriest Mykola Holyk. The blast wave knocked out windows and broke nearly every pane.
Plaster fell and the ceiling collapsed in several places. It tore out doors and wooden fittings, knocked some icons from their places, and holed the roof in many spots. Large and small fragments of the bomb pitted the walls.
Local patrons paid to build the church between 1843 and 1851, in the late classicist style.
A cut across Christ's chest
In front of the church stands a bronze statue of Christ, placed in the late 19th century on the grave of Dmytro Sukhanov, a merchant and former mayor of Sumy. Bomb fragments left a cut across the statue's chest. The statue is a local landmark of monumental art, the outlet Tsukr noted. The strike also damaged about 50 graves in the Central City Cemetery beside the church.
"The godless enemy continues to kill civilians, endanger children, and destroy schools, homes, hospitals, churches, and cemeteries," the diocese said.
The same attack hit a school where students were sheltering, and a residential area where two people were killed and six injured, three of them children. In September, Russian strikes on Kyiv also damaged two churches belonging to the same Moscow-linked church, the Exaltation of the Cross on Podil and the Pokrova Church on Priorka.
Another day of Russian strikes
Overnight on 1 October, Russia launched 107 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine, 63 of them jet-powered, the Air Force said. Air defenses downed or suppressed 87, and drones hit 11 locations. In Sumy, a guided bomb hit private homes, injuring two women and damaging about six houses, city military administration head Serhii Kryvosheienko reported. On the morning of 30 September, a Russian strike set a shopping center in Sumy Oblast's Romny district on fire, and crews fought the blaze until late that night, the State Emergency Service said. In Kyiv on the morning of 1 October, a drone hit a school in the Solomianskyi district while children sheltered inside, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. More than 100 students and about 60 staff were in the shelter, and no one was hurt, police said. A warehouse fire in Kyiv's Obolon district injured one person.
Kyiv’s supermarkets are the new front line as Russia hunts civilian life before winter
Over the past 24 hours, Russian mortar fire killed two men in Sumy Oblast's Seredyna-Buda hromada, and 15 people were injured across the oblast, the regional administration reported. A morning drone attack killed a 50-year-old man in Mykolaiv Oblast, and drones killed a 44-year-old man in Nikopol district, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured four. Eight people were hurt in Kharkiv Oblast, six in Kyiv Oblast, five in Donetsk Oblast, and three in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, according to regional authorities.

Israel’s Supreme Court on Thursday began hearing appeals against the disqualification of Arab electoral lists and candidates from the upcoming Israeli parliamentary elections.
According to an Anadolu correspondent, the Supreme Court in West Jerusalem convened a nine-judge panel to hear cases involving the disqualification of Arab candidates and electoral lists.
Arab lawmakers and their supporters held a protest outside the court before the hearings began, the correspondent reported.
At the same time, Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir arrived at the court and made remarks against the protesters.
Ben-Gvir was accompanied by a group of far-right Israelis who chanted against Arab participation in the elections.
Meanwhile, Knesset member Ofer Cassif told supporters gathered outside the court: “We will fight fascism, achieve justice, peace and a bright future for all our children, Palestinians and Israelis, Jews and Arabs.”

Palestinians make up about 21 percent of Israel’s total population of more than 10 million.
Opinion polls project Arab lawmakers to win 12 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, with elections scheduled for October 27.
Under Israeli electoral rules, the disqualification of an individual candidate requires Supreme Court approval before it can take effect.
The Supreme Court has previously overturned decisions by Israel’s Central Elections Committee to disqualify Arab lists and lawmakers in past years.

Details: The report notes that the reactor itself and safety-important systems were not damaged. No changes in the background radiation level were recorded. Its readings remain within natural background levels (0.16–0.20 µSv/h) and have not changed.
Scientists note that in order to reduce radiation risks, the reactor has been in a shutdown state since February 2022, with a full core discharge. Its operation is limited to routine maintenance of safety-critical systems.
As is known, the VVR-M reactor is used as a neutron source for fundamental and applied research in nuclear physics.

Surviving the execution chamber: Five US cases before Christa Pike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:33:11 UTC
19:33:11 KST

Christa Pike, the only woman on Tennessee’s death row, has survived an execution attempt after receiving two injections of a lethal drug.
Her lawyers said on Thursday that she was being treated in hospital, while Governor Bill Lee suspended executions for the rest of the year and ordered an independent review.
Pike’s case is not the first in which a prisoner has left the execution chamber alive in the United States. Previous failed attempts have ended with prisoners later executed, sometimes using a different method, or dying in custody before another attempt.
Surviving an execution attempt does not automatically overturn a death sentence. US courts have permitted authorities to try again, including in a 2016 Ohio Supreme Court ruling that a second attempt was not inherently barred by the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
Here are five earlier cases and what followed.
Tony Carruthers: Two failed executions, one doctor
Tennessee halted its attempt to execute Tony Carruthers on May 21 2026, after staff were unable to establish the intravenous access required by the state’s lethal injection protocol.
The physician involved was Dr Mark Fowler, who was later selected to oversee Pike’s execution and administer her lethal injection, according to NPR. Tennessee-based broadcaster WVLT subsequently reported that the same doctor administered the injection that Pike survived.
In Carruthers’ case, officials said medical personnel secured a primary IV line but could not establish a backup. An attempt to insert a central line also failed.
Carruthers, sentenced to death for the kidnapping and murder of three people in 1994, was returned to his cell after officials spent more than an hour attempting the procedure, according to Reuters report.
Governor Bill Lee then granted him a one-year reprieve, postponing his execution without commuting his death sentence.
Kenneth Eugene Smith: Executed with nitrogen after surviving lethal injection
Alabama’s first attempt to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith in 2022 was abandoned after officials were unable to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
Smith spent about four hours strapped to a gurney as legal challenges played out and staff repeatedly tried to access his veins, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
His lawyers later argued that a second execution attempt would violate the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment, but the US Supreme Court declined to stop it.
On January 25 2024, Alabama executed Smith, this time using nitrogen gas. Smith, 58, became the first person executed using the method, breathing pure nitrogen through a mask that deprived him of oxygen.
The execution lasted about 22 minutes, and Smith appeared to remain conscious for several minutes.
Alan Eugene Miller: A second attempt using a different method
Alabama’s attempt to execute Alan Eugene Miller by lethal injection in September 2022 failed after difficulties accessing his veins. A federal judge subsequently ordered the state to preserve evidence relating to the aborted procedure.
On September 26 2024, Alabama executed him using nitrogen gas, making him the second person put to death by that method.
Witnesses reported that he shook, pulled against his restraints and gasped for several minutes. Alabama’s corrections commissioner said the movements were involuntary and that the execution had proceeded as planned.
Miller had been sentenced to death for killing three men in workplace shootings in 1999.
Doyle Lee Hamm: A bloodied execution chamber and a deal preventing another attempt
Alabama abandoned its attempt to execute Doyle Lee Hamm in February 2018, after about two and a half hours of unsuccessful efforts to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
The procedure left Hamm, then 61, with at least 12 puncture wounds and the execution chamber bloodied, his lawyer, Columbia Law School professor Bernard Harcourt, said, according to a 2018 Reuters report. Medical personnel had tried to access veins in his groin and lower legs.
His lawyers had warned that terminal cancer and a history of intravenous drug use had severely compromised his veins. Alabama maintained that it could carry out the procedure, but stopped when officials determined the difficulties could not be resolved before the death warrant expired at midnight.
A federal judge subsequently ordered the state to preserve evidence, including Hamm’s clothing.
In March 2018, Hamm and Alabama reached a confidential settlement preventing further execution attempts, according to Harcourt.
Hamm remained on death row and died in November 2021 after suffering from cancer. It was the agreement, rather than an automatic legal exemption for surviving the first attempt, that prevented another execution attempt.
Romell Broom: Courts allowed another attempt, but he died before it could take place
Ohio stopped Romell Broom’s execution on September 15 2009, after staff spent about two hours trying unsuccessfully to access a vein to administer the lethal drugs.
Broom challenged the state’s right to try again, arguing that another attempt would violate constitutional protections against being punished twice for the same crime and against cruel and unusual punishment.
In 2016, the Ohio Supreme Court rejected his challenge in a 4–3 decision, noting that no lethal drugs had been administered during the first attempt.
His execution was eventually rescheduled for March 2022 after a shortage of execution drugs forced another postponement.
But Broom died in custody on December 28 2020, aged 64, before another attempt could take place. Prison authorities said he was suspected to have died from complications of COVID-19, pending confirmation.

Russian troop losses rose 46% since January, hit 2026 high in September, Ukraine says

Unknown Publisher

Russian troop losses soared 46% since January, hit 2026 high in September, Ukraine says
Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1.
The September figure surpassed previous summer highs of 42,860 in July and 42,020 in August. According to the General Staff, Russian personnel losses have risen from 31,710 in January to 46,230 in September — an increase of nearly 46%.
"This dynamic demonstrates the complete inability of the occupying forces' military leadership to achieve its objectives, as well as the growing accuracy and effectiveness of Ukrainian units' strikes," the General Staff said on Telegram.
Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to "kill 50,000 Russians per month," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
The September figure brings Russia's estimated monthly losses closer to that target than at any previous point this year.
The increase also comes as Russia faces growing pressure to replace troops while sustaining offensive operations along the front.
December 2025 marked the first month in which Russian personnel losses exceeded the number of troops Moscow managed to recruit, according to the General Staff. Since then, the manpower balance has remained an increasingly important issue as the Kremlin seeks to sustain the war without announcing a new wave of mobilization.
Russia continues to rely heavily on contract recruitment and financial incentives, but recruitment has slowed.
Janis Kluge, a research fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said, citing regional budget data, that 234,000 new military contracts were signed in the first eight months of this year, compared with 260,000 in the same period in 2025.
Ukrainian intelligence has also said Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 people in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027 if needed.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Russia has lost more than 1.5 million troops killed or wounded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The figures cannot be independently verified, and Moscow does not publish comprehensive casualty data.

Bolivia arrests attorney general accused by U.S. of drug cartel ties

Bolivian attorney general blacklisted by U.S. is arrested for alleged money laundering and drug trafficking
Bolivia's attorney general arrested for alleged money laundering and drug trafficking
U.S.-sanctioned Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca has been arrested on suspicion of money laundering and drug trafficking, with police finding bundles of cash smuggled out of his house, the government said Thursday.
Mariaca was arrested on Wednesday night in the eastern city of Santa Cruz, two days after the United States revoked his visa due to his alleged links to drug trafficking.
"A criminal organization entrenched in the justice system has been dismantled," Interior Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo told a press conference.
Oviedo said that in the early hours of Thursday, four people were caught trying to remove bundles of cash from Mariaca's house aboard an ambulance.
A video released by the interior ministry showed police removing wads of cash from the ambulance's panels.
Oviedo said that the Attorney General's Office, "headed by Roger Mariaca, became a criminal organization dedicated to protecting, encouraging, and safeguarding narco-terrorism."
According to the Reuters news agency, a prosecutor's office official reported the "abduction" of Mariaca during a live broadcast. Local media said Mariaca had been detained at Viru Viru International Airport, Reuters reported.
The U.S. State Department said Monday that Mariaca received "bribes to facilitate drug trafficking and help violent criminals evade justice." Mariaca has denied the allegations.
Oviedo said that Mariaca's arrest took place with the "cooperation of the U.S. government" as part of the "fight against terrorism."
In total, four prosecutors, six employees of the public prosecutor's office and the four people found aboard the ambulance were arrested.
The raids come as Bolivia's center-right President Rodrigo Paz, who took office in November 2025, seeks to strengthen ties with the United States after two decades of socialist rule marked by mutual enmity.
On Monday, the U.S. revoked the visas of 12 Bolivian officials and nine other Bolivian nationals who do not currently have visas were rendered ineligible to receive them.
 In March, Paz took Bolivia into the "Shield of the Americas," a U.S.-led alliance of right-wing Latin American governments to combat transnational organized crime.
 
"Mariaca is my friend"
Mariaca was appointed attorney general in October 2024.
The Attorney General's Office stated in a press release that, given Mariaca's "definitive absence," the next most senior public prosecutor, Luis Montano Morales, would replace him on an interim basis.
Mariaca's lawyer Romel Ipamo told local media that his client would "cooperate fully" with the investigation.
During Mariaca's tenure, Bolivian police captured Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastian Marset earlier this year. Marset, who was on the U.S.' most-wanted fugitives list, was passed to agents of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration at the Santa Cruz airport, then put on a U.S. airplane, state TV showed. In March, he made his first appearance in a federal court in Virginia.
Local media on Wednesday broadcast a video purporting to show Marset on the day of his arrest declaring: "Mariaca is my friend."
AFP has been unable to verify the authenticity of the video.
Police also raided the headquarters of the public prosecutor's office in the southern city of Sucre, according to footage shared by the police on social media.
Surrounded by hooded police officers, Claudia Pardo, head of communications for the prosecutor's office, denounced the raid as "illegal."
She told AFP later that she was under arrest.
 The public prosecutor's offices in Santa Cruz and La Paz were also targeted in the nationwide raids, according to images broadcast by local media.

'We didn’t think for even a second about our own lives': Flydubai heroes adjust to new reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:31:42 UTC
19:31:42 KST

Dr. Shota Musaev, the dentist who treated the wounded Indian captain aboard the Flydubai flight targeted in an attempted hijacking, said Thursday that his medical instincts — and the example set by his late parents — guided him as passengers fought to save the aircraft.
“I come from a family of doctors. My late father was a cardiologist and my late mother was a biologist, so I knew what to do when I was faced with the injured pilot,” Musaev, 47, said at his home in Rishon Lezion, south of Tel Aviv.
Musaev was among a group of Israeli passengers who intervened during Wednesday’s dramatic flight to Tel Aviv after the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to crash the aircraft. He said he saw three Israelis — Yaniv Hayun, Zvika Manes and Assaf Rajuan — rush the co-pilot and realized he had to help.
“My wife initially tried to stop me, but I saw there were heroes there and I joined them,” Musaev said. “At that moment, we didn’t think for even a second about our own lives or what might happen to us. We thought about how to save the entire plane.”
Musaev, who owns a dental clinic in Holon and was born in Georgia, helped restrain the suspected attacker before turning his attention to the wounded captain, Smit Machchhar.
“The captain told me he wanted to live and didn’t want to die there,” Musaev said. “There were moments when I thought we wouldn’t manage to land in time because he was bleeding heavily, but after we stopped the bleeding, his condition stabilized.”
Musaev said a series of chance events played a role in preventing a disaster, including a child going to the bathroom at a critical moment, the passengers who rushed the cockpit and additional pilots who happened to be aboard.
He said he now considers Hayun, Manes and Rajuan members of his family.
“I wrote in the WhatsApp group we created after the incident that all of us were born again yesterday,” he said. “We went through a historic event and even landed in Saudi Arabia.”
Passengers praise treatment in Saudi Arabia
The aircraft made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where Musaev said passengers were treated well.
“There was some chaos after landing because the children were under a lot of stress,” he said. “Even very senior officials came and spoke with us, and they assigned doctors to us who made sure everything was OK.”
The Israeli passengers then faced another difficult decision: whether to board another Flydubai aircraft for the trip home to Ben Gurion Airport.
Musaev favored returning on the airline despite what had happened.
“I spoke with a very senior official and with the manager of the local airport,” he said. “I was on the side that said we should get on the flight, mainly because you can’t fly only on Israeli airlines. Despite the serious incident we experienced with Flydubai, you can’t simply rule them out.”
He said passengers ultimately made the decision together after learning that an Israeli aircraft would not be allowed to land there.
“I told everyone we needed to get on,” he said. “We told the parents with children that they would decide what we did, and in the end, when they said they wouldn’t allow an Israeli plane to land there, we made the decision together and boarded.”
Musaev said he took several girls into the cockpit to meet the pilots before the flight home.
Back with his wife and children Thursday, he said the enormity of what happened was only beginning to sink in.
“We’re emotional to be with them again and are starting to understand more deeply that we’re alive,” he said.
Musaev stressed that saving the plane had been a collective effort.
“The act of heroism was something we did together,” he said. “I tied up the terrorist pilot and then treated the other pilot. But the other three were the ones who entered the cockpit and neutralized the terrorist. Others took care of the children on the plane. We did everything together, hand in hand.”
‘I’m an upgraded plumber’
Hayun, 38, of Ness Ziona, helped stabilize the aircraft as the Omani co-pilot allegedly tried to disable the instrument panel.
On Thursday, Hayun responded to remarks by U.S. President Donald Trump, who described him as an Israeli plumber who had never flown a plane and rarely traveled by air but saw what was happening and intervened.
“I’m an upgraded plumber,” Hayun joked. “He wasn’t wrong. I don’t work at NASA and I don’t deal with space. I deal with stinking pipes, and he was right. I wasn’t offended.”
Hayun said he never imagined the U.S. president would talk about him.
“I never dreamed Trump would talk about me and what I did. I actually like his sense of humor,” he said. “It was amusing how he described it. I’m not exactly Bruce Lee. But I did manage to overpower the terrorist with a few other Israelis and pull him backward in a chokehold, and that’s the most important thing.”
Hayun said he had not slept since the ordeal.
“I just want to get back to my routine now, to work, to my truck,” he said. “I’m getting so much love and I thank everyone — everyone who was on that flight, who worked hand in hand and helped us get our lives back because they were hanging by a thread. I hope it doesn’t come back to me in my dreams.”
Herzog recommends civilian bravery awards
President Isaac Herzog spoke with the passengers who intervened and said he would recommend that Musaev, Hayun, Manes and Rajuan receive the Presidential Medal for Civilian Heroism, Israel’s highest civilian bravery award.
“At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness and extraordinary mutual responsibility,” Herzog told them. “You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster.”
“Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society,” he added. “I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”
Herzog said he would bring their actions before the advisory committee responsible for the award and recommend that they receive the honor.
The president also praised the Indian captain, who fought the co-pilot and opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers to intervene.
Herzog later recommended Tali Manes, Zvika Manes’ wife, for the same civilian bravery award after further accounts indicated she played a crucial role in alerting passengers to the danger.
According to the President’s Residence, Manes heard violence and commotion coming from the cockpit and was the first to alert other passengers and call for help, prompting those who ultimately rushed in and subdued the suspected attacker.
After he was restrained, she continued to act, calling pilots who were traveling in the rear of the aircraft to come forward and help restore control of the plane.
“Tali, the more we learn about what happened in those dramatic moments, the clearer it becomes how significant a part you played in saving the lives of the passengers,” Herzog told her.
“You heard that something terrible was happening, immediately understood the scale of the danger, raised the alarm, called for help, and did not stop acting even after the attacker had been subdued,” he said. “The resourcefulness, responsibility, and composure you showed in moments of mortal danger are civilian heroism in the fullest sense of the word. You are a hero, Tali, and I am proud of you and thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”

Russian drone struck the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv; reactor was not damaged, regulator says

The strike caused a fire, but the reactor and safety systems were not damaged. There were no casualties, and the radiation background did not change.
A Russian drone struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv on September 30. The reactor was not damaged. The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine reported this on October 1, UNN writes.
According to the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, on September 30, 2026, at 18:18 (Kyiv time), a Russian UAV struck the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research, where the Kyiv Research Reactor (VVR-M) is located
The fire that broke out as a result of the attack was promptly extinguished, it is noted. There were no casualties. An investigation and assessment of the damage are ongoing.

What is the Institute for Nuclear Research

"The UAV strike on the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research is an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility that performs exclusively scientific and research functions, and is yet another cynical disregard by Russia for the internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety, as well as a war crime," the SNRIU emphasized.
