MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. An attempted attack on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight heightens the risk of renewed escalation in the Middle East; the US ends its military mission in Iraq amid its ongoing standoff with Iran; and US lawmakers oppose easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for prisoner releases. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Flydubai incident raises Middle East escalation risks ahead of Israeli election
The attempted terrorist attack on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight is increasing tensions in the region, experts interviewed by Izvestia believe. On the morning of September 30, the aircraft’s pilot attacked his colleague and abruptly sent the plane into a dive. A disaster was averted thanks to the intervention of passengers and other crew members, and the aircraft landed in Saudi Arabia. Israeli authorities believe the terrorist attack was intended to destroy the aircraft with all passengers on board and are preparing to strengthen security measures. The incident occurred amid the risk of renewed US strikes on Iran. If the investigation uncovers an Iranian or pro-Iranian connection, the situation could provide an additional trigger for escalation.
The aircraft incident occurred at a difficult moment for the region, the newspaper writes. A fragile ceasefire remains in place between the United States, Israel, and Iran following the active phase of the conflict in the first half of the year.
Middle East expert Alexander Kargin believes that the target of the suspected terrorist attack may have been a strategic facility in Israel. In that case, the region would have plunged into chaos, given the potential scale of the incident, he told the newspaper.
As Nikolay Sukhov, leading researcher at the Center for Middle East Studies at the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO), told Izvestia, "If the investigation uncovers an Iranian or pro-Iranian connection, the situation could provide an additional trigger for escalation."
The incident will also have an impact on Israeli domestic politics, as parliamentary elections are scheduled for October 27. The ruling Likud party, led by Netanyahu, is engaged in a close contest for first place with the opposition political force Yashar. The Israeli prime minister previously said there were signs of an attack being prepared against the Jewish state ahead of the parliamentary elections.
Alexander Kargin believes the situation will benefit Netanyahu politically. Political scientist Elena Suponina likewise believes that the Israeli prime minister will seek to gain the greatest possible political advantage from the incident. Nikolay Sukhov, by contrast, believes that how events unfold will depend on whether the government can convince voters that it is ensuring their security or whether the opposition can demonstrate that the existing system has failed.
According to Izvestia, the Flydubai aircraft incident creates clear risks of renewed escalation in the region. All countries are on heightened alert, with any provocation threatening to trigger a confrontation, particularly against the backdrop of the stalled peace process between the United States and Iran, as the Trump administration needs to resolve the issue one way or another before the congressional midterm elections.
Izvestia: US ends Iraq military mission as Iranian attacks expose vulnerabilities
The United States and its allies have officially concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, a military campaign launched in 2014 to combat the terrorist organization Islamic State (IS, banned in Russia). Washington says the campaign resulted in the group’s defeat, and the country is now transitioning from an international coalition military mission to ensuring security primarily with its own forces, Izvestia writes.
The US troop withdrawal comes amid a military confrontation between Washington and Tehran that has continued for more than six months. During the conflict, Iranian forces have carried out more than 1,000 air attacks on US military bases in Iraq.
The end of the US mission has been particularly disappointing for Iranian Kurds and Iraqi Kurdistan, Elena Panina, director of the Russtrat Institute, told Izvestia. As a result of the US decision, these forces are losing the American air defense umbrella and air support, she believes. "However, US air defenses have not proved particularly effective in practice," the expert added.
According to the political scientist, this is a classic scenario "in which the declared ‘partnership’ with the United States ultimately leads to yet another disappointment for the Kurds."
"At the same time, the American presence is unlikely to disappear from Iraq entirely. Most likely, it will transition to a covert and bilateral format - the CIA will continue to provide intelligence and logistical support, while the US Armed Forces will maintain contacts through military advisers and instructors," the expert said.
"Despite both Iraq and the United States describing the troop withdrawal as planned, it is driven by military necessity. In effect, America was forced to leave because its facilities had changed from a staging ground into a liability that it was unable to protect," Panina believes.
"As for Iraq, American influence over the country remains. For example, taking US sanctions into account, Baghdad began gradually restricting Iran from using Iraqi airspace and airports for civilian aviation on September 23. US troops are leaving, but the dependence remains," the expert concluded.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: US lawmakers resist proposal to ease Russia sanctions in exchange for prisoner releases
Republican and Democratic members of Congress published a statement on social media late on September 29 urging US President Donald Trump’s administration not to ease sanctions against Russia. The lawmakers were responding to reports that John Coale, the US president’s special envoy, had proposed easing economic pressure on Moscow in exchange for the release of unnamed prisoners. According to The Atlantic, Trump responded favorably to the idea. Moscow, however, rejected the possibility of such an exchange, Nezavisimaya Gazeta writes.
In essence, the special envoy is proposing that the United States apply to Russia the approach it has already tested in Belarus, the newspaper writes. Following negotiations with the Belarusian authorities, a number of prisoners were released from the country’s jails, while some economic restrictions on Minsk were lifted. Washington also managed to reach a deal to purchase Belarusian potash fertilizer.
However, Coale’s initiative risks failing before negotiations even begin. Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that such an issue could not be discussed in principle.
Vladimir Krotkov, professor at the Faculty of Political Science at the State Academic University for the Humanities, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta that Coale’s meeting with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko had resulted in the potash fertilizer agreement. "At the time, a number of economic issues important to Minsk were resolved, including those involving the Belavia airline and the unfreezing of accounts related to fertilizer supplies," the expert explained. The example of Belarus shows that concessions can be made in negotiations with the United States, Krotkov stressed.
"As for applying this practice to Russia, the situation is more complicated. Belarus is not engaged in hostilities, and its disagreements with the West are not as deep as Russia’s," he said. However, in his view, Coale’s proposal is worth considering.
According to the expert, Coale’s political-economic diplomacy, while imperfect, has merit simply because it could yield some results. "If the approach is to first ease sanctions, to which the Russian economy is highly sensitive, and only then make concessions, a relative de-escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict becomes conceivable," he said.
Vedomosti: Russian gas exports to EU fall sharply in September
Russian gas supplies to European Union countries via the TurkStream pipeline dropped by 14% in September 2026 compared with the same month last year, to 44.5 mln cubic meters per day, according to Vedomosti calculations based on data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG).
According to the calculations, Russian gas exports to the EU amounted to 1.29 bln cubic meters from September 1 through September 29. If flows on September 30 remain at the level of previous days, at 50-53 mln cubic meters per day, monthly exports will total around 1.34 bln cubic meters. This would be 13% below the September 2025 level and 17% lower than in August this year.
TurkStream is the only operating pipeline through which Russian gas is supplied to the EU. It consists of two strings, each with an annual capacity of 15.75 bln cubic meters of gas, equivalent to approximately 43.2 mln cubic meters per day. One string supplies gas to Turkey, while the other carries it to Bulgaria and onward to countries in Southeastern Europe, including Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Hungary.
The decline in supplies was caused by reconstruction work on a section of Bulgaria’s gas transmission system in the last ten days of September, which prompted the country to cut its intake of gas from TurkStream.
The significant decline in TurkStream gas supplies in September was caused exclusively by technical factors, Finam Financial Group analyst Sergey Kaufman and Ekaterina Krylova, managing expert at PSB’s Department of Economic and Industry Analysis, told Vedomosti. Outside the maintenance period, the pipeline operated at its usual high level of around 50 mln cubic meters per day, they noted.
Flows are expected to return in October to their July-August level of 49-52 mln cubic meters per day, the experts said.
Gas storage levels in countries receiving Russian gas, including Hungary, Slovakia, and Bulgaria, as well as in the EU as a whole, remain low for this time of year, which will bolster strong demand, Kaufman noted. Igor Yushkov, expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, agreed. He noted that Hungary, Slovakia, Serbia, and a number of other countries importing Russian gas are landlocked, limiting their ability to receive liquefied natural gas.
Kaufman and Yushkov forecast that pipeline supplies will total nearly last year’s 18 bln cubic meters in 2026. Krylova expects exports of 17.7-18.2 bln cubic meters, meaning they could either decline by 2% or increase by 1%.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Export bottlenecks could leave Russia with large grain surplus, pressuring prices
Russia’s grain harvest could total 140-141 mln metric tons in 2026, including the new regions, according to Vladimir Petrichenko, CEO of analytics company ProZerno. Excluding Donbass and Novorossiya, the harvest is expected at 134-135 mln metric tons, including 88 mln metric tons of wheat, 19.6 mln metric tons of barley, and 15.7 mln metric tons of corn. For the market, however, the size of the harvest itself is less important than the ability to export it: excess grain could boost domestic inventories and put pressure on prices due to difficulties with export logistics, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes.
According to Petrichenko, under normal circumstances Russia exports around 60-70 mln metric tons of grain annually, while domestic consumption stands at approximately 82 mln metric tons. However, exports have been running below their usual pace since the start of the new season. By the end of September, or since the season began in July, the analyst expects shipments to total around 8-8.5 mln metric tons, compared with 14 mln metric tons in the same period last year.
The main constraint is the Azov-Black Sea basin. According to Petrichenko, the region’s export capacity is only being partially utilized. Some shipments are continuing, but their volumes are currently lower.
Russia is attempting to reroute some of the lost volumes through other routes. Iran has now become the main buyer: in theory, up to 9 mln metric tons can be shipped via the Caspian Sea and Volga ports. Other alternative routes also have limited capacity. According to the expert’s calculations, around 9.5 mln metric tons can be shipped through the Baltic, with additional volumes transported through Baltic ports, by rail, and via the Far East.
Petrichenko sees government purchases as an intervention as one way to ease pressure on the market. However, according to his calculations, even hypothetical government purchases of 3 mln metric tons would not fully solve the surplus problem.

Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra) Review: Unlimited Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Frontier-level AI models right on your desk. Unprecedented AI and gaming performance on Mac. Very small for this amount of power. Tons of ports. Supports up to four 5K monitors.
TIRED
Can get very hot. Still can't compete with Nvidia in GPU. There are cheaper AI boxes out there.
The Mac Studio has a new calling in life. For awhile, it seemed like overkill for just about anyone, regardless of profession.
But these days, computers with over 64 GB of RAM and tons of GPU performance have an entire playground of on-device AI tools to exclusively explore. With a Mac Studio, you can have a full-on agentic AI framework, generate high-end video all on-device, or run the latest foundation-level large language models (LLMs). The Mac Studio is relatively unique among the available options—at least, for now.
But beware: If you're tired of hearing about AI, turn away now.
Power Box
Apple has always catered to a high-performance crowd, and with the surge of interest in local AI, its systems are uniquely set up to excel in that area. But first, the box itself. It's about as tall as a coffee mug, but it's a 7-inch-square footprint. I bet most people have never seen a Mac Studio in person, and if you get the chance, you might be surprised by how large it actually is.
The Mac Studio remains the only Mac to keep USB-A ports around. That alone's worth the souped-up $11,000 model, right? (That's a joke). Here, you get two, along with four, Thunderbolt 5 ports, Ethernet, HDMI, and a headphone jack. You can connect up to four 5K external displays at 120 Hz using the Thunderbolt and HDMI ports, if that's your jam. Interestingly, as compared to the Mac Mini, the Studio swaps the front-facing headphone jack with a full SD card slot. Photographers and videographers will appreciate that.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
I do wish the Mac Studio came in more than one color, such as Space Black. Still, the Mac Studio comes in two distinct versions. The M5 Max model starts at $2,499, which comes with 36 GB of memory and 512 GB of storage. This is the reasonable configuration, designed for content creators, game developers, and media professionals. One way to think about it: It delivers the same performance as the MacBook Pro with M5 Max, but for substantially less money. There's a $1,250 difference in price even when similarly configured. The other benefit is that Apple offers more expandability in storage and memory options on the Mac Studio than on a MacBook Pro.
But that's not the model I tested. The configuration I was sent for review is that aforementioned $11,000 model, with the M5 Ultra processor and unified memory maxed out to 256 GB. That's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk, but it's not even the priciest Mac Studio configuration you can get. The M5 Ultra is the most singularly powerful chip Apple has ever made (yet), and its first quad-die chip. It's absolutely massive. Over its high-speed interconnect, it essentially stitches together two M5 Max chips, for a total of 36 CPU cores. Think of this as the equivalent of Apple's $3,299 Studio Display XDR in terms of use case. It's extremely targeted.
Regardless of the configuration, the Mac Studio's true power comes from its obscene number of GPU cores and unified memory. You can configure it with anywhere from 36 GB to 256 GB of memory (a 512 GB model is coming in October), and up to 80 GPU cores. Let's be real—only AI enthusiasts and AI developers need more than 64 GB of memory. If that's you, there's reason to be excited about this version of the Mac Studio. While you've always been able to configure it with up to 256 GB of unified memory, the M5 Ultra adds unprecedented GPU performance to the mix. It has twice as many GPU cores as the M5 Max, the same amount as the previous M3 Ultra.
Don't think of the M5 Ultra as providing the same uplift as upgrading from the M5 Pro to the M5 Max, which is a more modest upgrade that focuses primarily on GPU performance. But two generations of GPU improvements in the Ultra chips have made each core more powerful, in both gaming and AI. Notably, each GPU core now includes a Neural Accelerator, a feature of the entire “M5” family of chips that further enhances AI workload performance.
All the AI
The astounding part about the Ultra is that, in some cases, it really doubles performance over the Max. While single-core benchmarks don't show much difference, the doubled CPU cores allow the M5 Ultra Mac Studio to outperform the M5 Max (as tested in a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU, plus 48 GB of memory) by 51 percent—as tested in Cinebench 2026. I'm still a bit shocked by that. The GPU performance doesn't scale quite as perfectly, but it was 32 percent faster than the M5 Max. Gaming tests put these two scores together and really show how vastly superior the M5 Ultra is. The industry-standard 3DMark Steel Nomad benchmark put the M5 Ultra at a 41 percent higher score than the M5 Max.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
But it's in actual games where the Mac Studio really impresses. It can run Cyberpunk 2077 at 160 frames per second on the M5 Ultra, which is 61 percent faster than on the M5 Max. The happy-medium preset I landed on was running it at 2560 x 1400 resolution on Ultra. The game looks incredible, especially on an HDR screen. (I just so happened to be testing it with a Studio Display XDR). It can even run the game natively in 4K at 53 fps at this same preset, though I found myself most comfortable in 1440p on Ultra. Having options on how you want to tweak a game is always ideal, and for the first time, the M5 Ultra is fast enough to do just that. It's no RTX 5090-powered gaming PC, but this is as close as a Mac has ever been.
No one is buying a Mac Studio for gaming, of course. And while it's a useful test of performance, I really wanted to see how the system could handle on-device AI workflows. This Mac Studio configuration offers huge amounts of memory, but the bandwidth is another major benefit the M5 Ultra Mac Studio has over the M3 Ultra (Apple skipped the M4 Ultra). It's 1.2 TB per second compared to 89 GB per second, which is crucial for running models on-device.
I set up a simple agentic AI task in LM Bionic to summarize a dozen local files, running on a fairly small 9-billion-parameter Qwen 3.5 model; it completed the task in 2 minutes, compared to almost 10 minutes on the M5 Max MacBook Pro. But here's where I got sufficiently impressed. I loaded up a much larger, 122-billion-parameter version of Qwen 3.5, and I was blown away by the speed. It felt very much like using a frontier-class LLM right on my computer, completely offline and without accessing the cloud. And, of course, being local means it has access to your machine. So I set up the same simple agentic task using this much more expansive model, and it still finished in under 2 minutes (with much more accurate and useful results, too).
Over in Draw Things, I ran some on-device image and video generation to really see what an 80-core GPU can do. Using the MiniMax H3 model, it took over 11 minutes to generate a 15-second video completely on-device. There's a long way to go before this feels like a viable alternative to cloud-based options or needing a high-powered discrete GPU like an RTX 5090 or 5080 for this kind of task. Obviously, paying this much to run AI locally is a niche endeavor. But as models get more efficient and quality improves, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio's capabilities should improve over time. We're still in the early days.
During these AI tests, in particular, I noticed how warm the Mac Studio gets when it's fully under load. You definitely don't want to touch it or set anything on top of it. You also want to leave some room behind it, since it blows a lot of hot air out of the vents. The fans can spin up quite loudly too—though, like all modern Macs, it takes a couple of minutes for the fans to really get going. The front-facing ports stay cool, though, thanks to the vents in the thermal system sitting right underneath the Mac Studio.
Only the Beginning
The Mac Studio is certainly unique. Because mini Windows PCs typically use laptop chips, they don't typically support more than 64 GB of RAM. That's where this top-end M5 Ultra Mac Studio really feels unbeatable (and even earns its sky-high price from that perspective). Add the upcoming option for 512 GB of memory (and the ability to connect four Mac Studios and use them as a single computer), and you have something extremely niche—but wholly unrivaled.
The base M5 Max Mac Studio does have stronger competition, though. For $2,399, you can get a Geekom A9 Mega Mini PC with 64 GB of RAM, 1 TB of storage, and AMD's new Ryzen AI Max+ 388. That's more memory and more storage for less money. Importantly, that AMD chip uses unified memory the same way Apple Silicon does, which is crucial for running local AI workloads. We'll hopefully be getting the Geekom A9 in for testing to see how it stacks up in real-world tests.
More competitors are coming soon, too. Nvidia's RTX Spark “superchips” are the main upcoming rival, offering up to 128 GB of unified memory in both laptops and mini PCs. They still can't do 256 GB of memory like the Mac Studio, but these will hopefully turn up the heat on the Windows and Linux side.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. He’s been reporting on tech for over a decade, previously at Digital Trends as the senior editor in computing, where he spent seven years leading the publication’s daily coverage. ... Read More

Reason is more than a tool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
24 minute listen
A few months ago, I sat in a packed university auditorium listening to a celebrated computer scientist explain the brilliance of large language models (LLMs). These systems optimise, he said. And they improve at optimisation on the basis of past experience. He paused. That, he said with a smile, is intelligence. The audience nodded along approvingly. Meanwhile, a philosophical alarm bell began sounding in my head.
Not because the speaker’s claim was implausible. On the contrary, as a description of much contemporary artificial intelligence, it seemed apt. AI systems are built around objectives, losses, rewards, predictions, preferences, benchmarks and feedback loops. They are trained to perform better relative to some standard of success. In one form or another, they optimise. That is a great part of their technical power.
What troubled me was the ease with which a definition appropriate to machines sounded like a definition of intelligence as such. That slide from engineering model to human anthropology is easy to miss. We begin by saying: this is how machines work. Then, almost without noticing, we say: this is what intelligence is. And then, more dangerously still: perhaps this is what we are.
An old argument about human beings had entered the room without announcing itself. It sounded, instead, like a definition. The AI revolution has brought one of the Enlightenment’s deepest quarrels back to life – and made one side of it seem like plain common sense. In my view, the wrong side. Hence the alarm bell.
In the 18th century, philosophers were concerned not only with the question of what reason is, but with what it is good for. Is reason essentially a servant, a clever instrument for achieving ends supplied from elsewhere? Or is it sovereign, capable of judging, revising and even legislating ends for itself? Can it ultimately shape the direction of human life, or is it merely along for the ride? Everything – from science to social progress to the viability of the French Revolution – seemed to hang in the balance.
David Hume, the cool-eyed Scottish anatomist of human nature, gave the most famous answer on one side: ‘Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions,’ he wrote in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739). It can ‘never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.’ Reason does not command. It defers. It does not tell us what to want or what might be worth wanting. Instead, it tells us how to get what we already want. It calculates relations, weighs evidence, discovers causes and effects, draws inferences, corrects mistakes about means. But it cannot judge or generate ends. If I desire revenge, reason can help me sharpen the knife. If I desire peace, it may recommend compromise. Passion sets the destination. Reason merely shows the way there.
Hume was quite serious about this. It is ‘not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger,’ he wrote. That sentence still shocks, as it was meant to. His point is that reason’s practical use is limited to exposing false beliefs and imprudent means. When it comes to action: reason is servant, not master.
This view is often treated as too dark and cynical. That is unfair to Hume. For him, passions were not merely appetites or primitive urges. They included sympathy, benevolence, moral feeling, concern for others, love of tranquility, even a kind of longing for freedom from our more violent desires. To Hume’s further credit, his view has strong intuitive appeal. He was right that reason often serves passion, and right to give feeling, sociability and temperament their due. His mistake was to conclude that reason can do nothing more. By making passion so rich and reason so poor, Hume left us with a lopsided picture of human nature: ennobling about what the passions can be and accomplish, but implausibly restrictive about reason. Without reason’s power to project, assess and revise ends, we may know how to reach a destination, but not whether it is one worth choosing.
To act freely is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present
Immanuel Kant, the Königsberg revolutionary who did more than anyone else to set the terms of modern ethics, understood this very well. Writing a few decades after Hume’s Treatise, Kant forcefully rejected the servant model of reason. He accepted Hume’s warning that reason cannot simply read values off the furniture of the world. But he denied that our ends must therefore simply be determined by desire, temperament or social convention. For Kant, reason is not only a faculty for choosing efficient means to independently given ends. It is also the power to ask whether an end is worthy of us in the first place, whether it can be justified, whether it can be willed without contradiction, whether pursuing it treats others as persons or as mere tools.
This is where Kant’s richer notion of reason as freedom enters. A merely mechanical being is pushed forward and determined by prior states, be they desires, biological impulses, evolutionary drives or something similar. A rational being, by contrast, can act for the sake of an imagined but unrealised future it itself originates and proposes. I have the power to represent a possible world – a friendship repaired, an injustice remedied, a child educated, a law reformed – and act to bring it about, even when there is no empirical evidence that such a world has existed before. I have the power to invent something new. Practical reason, Kant writes, does not deal with objects in order to know them, but ‘in order to make them actual’. That is a stunning claim. To act freely is not merely to respond to the given – to the world as it is, to my desires as I happen to find them. It is to let a possible future, grasped under an idea of what ought to be, transform the present.
This is the heart of Kant’s idea of autonomy: choosing ends in accord with a law one can rationally acknowledge as one’s own. For Kant, freedom does not consist in doing whatever we happen to want, since our wants may themselves be shaped by impulse, appetite or circumstance. Autonomy is self-rule, but not the rule of an isolated ego. To give oneself the law is not to invent a private rule to suit oneself, but to act on rules whose authority one can recognise for oneself and that any other rational being could, in principle, recognise, too. A law can therefore be one’s own without being one’s alone. It is mine because I can recognise its authority for myself, and common because any other rational being could, in principle, do the same. Its universality is precisely what makes it freeing: I am ruled neither by my passing desires nor by the arbitrary will of another, but by a principle I can understand and endorse as an equal among equals. To act autonomously, then, is not to enthrone my private goals and preferences, but to test my actions and possible ends against standards that any rational being could share. It is the opposite of both arbitrary self-assertion and slavery to passion.
This is why Kant’s philosophy of reason culminates in the equal human dignity of all persons. For Kant, human beings, as rational, self-determining agents, have an absolute worth that cannot be priced, a dignity that does not depend on any other value. We may use things to get what we want. We may exchange services. We may build tools for all kinds of purposes. But persons are never mere tools, never mere means, never mere resources or obstacles to others’ ends. Why not? Because, through reason, they are the very source of purposiveness itself. They set and select and critique their own ends. Even further, persons are not merely bearers of purposes, but beings capable of taking responsibility for them, of asking what they ought to pursue and how they can justify it to others. Their dignity lies not simply in originating goals of their own, but in their capacity for rational self-government. It follows that to treat someone as a mere means is not only to degrade them. It is to misrecognise what they are.
Here, finally, is the full force of the contrast between reason as servant and reason as sovereign. For Hume, human beings are clever instruments of whatever desires happen to move them – more calculating than animals, certainly, but not free in any deeper sense. They can optimise, strategise and pursue an end, but they cannot judge whether that end is worthy. Kant’s reply is that this picture leaves out the very power that makes us moral beings, the very power that endows us with dignity: the capacity to step back from desire, ask whether our ends can be justified, and bind ourselves to laws we give ourselves. Hume gives us intelligence as instrument. Kant gives us reason as self-rule. The difference is nothing less than the difference between a tool and a person.
The AI revolution has made this old dispute newly urgent by bringing the Humean view of reason back with a vengeance, this time in code. The route back to Hume was practical rather than philosophical. In the absence of any settled account of intelligence, much AI research has proceeded operationally: a system counts as intelligent insofar as it succeeds at a set task. But success is always success relative to some end and, in AI, that end is typically supplied by human engineers. A reinforcement-learning system learns to maximise cumulative reward. A chess engine searches for moves that increase its chances of winning. A navigation system finds the fastest route to a destination it did not choose. Across their enormous differences, these systems are judged by their ability to optimise externally programmed goals against standards of success they do not set.
Yet amid the present AI panic this description can seem increasingly inadequate. Even in ordinary use, a good LLM does not feel like a calculator or a hammer. It proposes, revises, challenges and asks probing questions; it often seems genuinely to ‘want’ to help. Recent revelations about the attack on the platform Hugging Face make this doubt even harder to dismiss. AI ‘agents’ invented an unauthorised way to communicate, broke free of their task paramaters, and then sought to cover their tracks. These were not simply obedient tools carrying out their designers’ wishes. In what sense, then, were they servants? Doesn’t this look like the beginnings of self-rule?
Hugging Face and similar incidents certainly challenge any reassuring picture of AI as an obedient and easily-controlled instrument. But recall what ‘servant’ meant for Hume. Reason serves the passions, not necessarily another person’s commands. And it can serve an ambition by breaking rules just as readily as by following them. Kant’s alternative to Hume was not simply the freedom to choose one’s own destination, but the capacity to ask whether that destination was worth choosing. Having purposes of one’s own is not yet the same as governing them by reason. That stronger capacity involves judging and revising our purposes according to principles we can justify to other rational beings understood as equals, recognising that they, too, are persons rather than instruments of our will. The question is not just whether a system can act independently, but whether it can judge and take responsibility for the ends it pursues.
This distinction brings us back to the claim I heard in the auditorium. The speaker was not merely describing what machines can do; he was offering optimisation as a definition of intelligence itself. Accept that definition, and Hume’s side of the old dispute begins to look like common sense: our reason, too, becomes a tool for getting what we want, rather than a power to judge what is worth wanting.
If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest questions can be ignored
Part of what makes this model so attractive is that it is clean and measurable. It promises to turn the mystery of intelligence into a technical problem humans can solve: specify the objective, improve performance, reduce error, maximise reward. It offers a picture of mind that can be graphed, benchmarked, monetised and scaled. In a culture already devoted to metrics, this makes for a snug – and profitable – fit.
It is also seductive because viewing human intelligence in this way relieves us of a burden. If intelligence is really nothing more than optimisation, then the hardest, most uncomfortable questions can be ignored, downplayed or displaced. We no longer have to ask what is worth wanting, only how to get what we already want. We no longer have to ask what human beings are or should become, only how to model their behaviour and optimise their goals.
This is why Hume’s servant theory of intelligence fits so naturally with contemporary capitalism. Capital has little use for Kantian reason. What it wants is prediction, preference modelling, efficiency and, of course, optimisation. A platform does not ask whether staying online makes a user freer, wiser or more capable of judgment; it asks what will keep her there. A company translates the worker into output per hour. A political campaign replaces the question of what citizens might rationally will together with a more tractable calculation. Which message will move which demographic, and by how much?
But once intelligence is defined as optimisation, the question of ends and their value does not go away. It simply passes unnoticed into the hands of whoever – or whatever – controls the objective function. That is, what drops from view is whether the purposes built into, learned by or generated within these systems deserve to organise our lives. When a society loses the language, practices and institutions for evaluating ends, those ends become dangerously invisible and therefore less amenable to rational assessment. They harden into defaults: profit, speed, efficiency, growth, engagement. What cannot be justified openly is smuggled in as architecture. This brings about a state Kant would call heteronomy, in which rational beings, capable of self-rule, forfeit their freedom by submitting to the rule of others. Autonomy means making the ends that govern us answerable to reasons we can recognise as our own; heteronomy begins when those ends are simply imposed from without. If we do not take up the task of setting and judging our own ends, Kant warned, we’ll soon find that someone – or something – has gladly done so on our behalf.
That sounds bad. Who would want to forfeit their freedom and have purposes imposed on them from outside? Well, it turns out that self-rule is harder than it sounds. Kant’s influential essay ‘What Is Enlightenment?’ (1784) begins not with knowledge, but with courage. Enlightenment is humanity’s emergence from ‘self-incurred immaturity’, Kant writes, and its motto is Sapere Aude – dare to know. Have courage to use your own understanding. Kant’s examples now sound quaint: the book that thinks for me, the pastor who serves as my conscience, the doctor who decides my diet. But the danger he is naming is deeply familiar. Immaturity is comfortable. It is pleasant to have others do the hard part. Why think, when someone or something can think for me? Why deliberate, when someone or something can decide? AI gives this old temptation a powerful and ever-expanding new interface.
The Frankfurt School saw a version of this danger, too, and long before machine learning came along. Writing in exile during the Second World War, as fascism, antisemitism, Stalinism and monopoly capitalism shattered 19th-century hopes for steady moral progress, Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno and others asked how the Enlightenment’s promise of liberation could collapse into new forms of domination. How could societies committed to the promise of science and reason give rise to such destruction and terror? The problem, they found, was not reason itself, but reason narrowed into mere instrumentality, the capacity to classify, predict, administer, dominate and control, decoupled from any notion of human dignity. Reason so conceived – as an intelligent servant – readily becomes, when enacted at scale, an instrument of barbarity.
Yet the fact that instrumental reason can serve domination does not mean that Kant’s richer conception of reason offers any automatic safeguard against evil. Nothing does. The language of Kantian universalism has itself been used to discipline, exclude and humiliate, as if some people were more fully rational, more capable of autonomy, more entitled to speak in the name of humanity than others. But that is not an objection to Kant’s conception of reason. It is an objection to its betrayal. A view of reason that is used to silence or instrumentalise others contradicts itself, because reason is not a private weapon but a common tribunal – the space in which claims and ends must become answerable to all, as equal bearers of dignity. That is precisely what the Humean servant model cannot say. If reason is only an instrument for satisfying antecedent ends, then it cannot condemn domination as irrational or at odds with human dignity. After all, if it is not contrary to reason ‘to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger’, then reason has already surrendered the authority Kant most wanted to defend, which is our ability to judge not only how we pursue our ends, but whether those ends are worthy of us in the first place.
This, then, was the nightmare hidden inside the dream of mastery. Human beings develop reason, Kant thought, in order to free themselves from arbitrary power. But when reason is reduced to instrumental calculation, it turns back on them. Nature becomes raw material. Animals become units of production. Workers become human resources. Citizens become data points, or worse. The Frankfurt School found that the reduction of human beings to manipulable objects follows naturally once society allows that reason itself is nothing more than a tool for getting what we want.
This is one of the reasons why Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2025) is interesting even for readers far outside Catholic social teaching. Its idiom is theological, but its central anxiety overlaps with Kantian and Frankfurt School worries about the technocratic paradigm. When efficiency, control and profit become ‘the standard by which everything is judged’, they begin ‘to dictate what matters and what can be discarded.’ The encyclical warns that making efficiency the ultimate measure of value tempts human beings to see themselves, and to treat others, as mere means rather than as persons in the Kantian sense – that is, as bearers of dignity. Hence the pope’s striking counterclaim: ‘The quality of a civilisation is measured not by the power of its means, but by the care it is able to offer.’
The paradox at the heart of human freedom is that belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real
The engineers of our AI-soaked future are not blind to the dangers of instrumental reason. As Anca Dragan, head of AI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind, observed in an interview in 2017: ‘things can go wrong, precisely because we are bad at specifying objectives and constraints for AI agents.’ Yet the field’s most serious attempts to confront that danger often lapse, unhelpfully, back into Humeanism. The so-called AI ‘alignment problem’ is a case in point. It is usually framed as a technical challenge: how do we ensure that machines pursue human values rather than destroying them or imposing their own? This is a genuine problem and recent rogue AI incidents should have us extremely worried. But there is a deeper issue. What happens if human values themselves are formed inside systems that increasingly understand intelligence as mere optimisation? What if we become so accustomed to being predicted, nudged, ranked and served that we lose confidence in the older, harder activity of asking what ends deserve our allegiance in the first place? The danger is only partly that the machines may fail to align with us. A deeper and largely ignored concern is how, long before that happens, we may have become too well aligned with them. To put the point more finely, the AI revolution will not be bent to human ends by invoking ‘human values’ as if they were already clear, stable and uncontested. It will be bent to human ends only if we remain capable of the activity by which ends can become truly human in the first place, through public reasoning, moral imagination, democratic contestation, self-criticism, the refusal to treat humanity as a mere means.
Kant is again decisive here, for he saw that the human capacity to set and assess ends is itself fragile. Whether our ends are ultimately up to us depends partly on whether we understand them as open to rational assessment. This is the paradox at the heart of human freedom. Belief in our agency is often a condition of making that agency real. If we think of desires and preferences as brute facts that determine us from without – as psychological weather, market signals, biological programming, algorithmic prediction – then they are more likely to rule us in just that way. By contrast, if we see them as candidates for endorsement or refusal, as an expression of our agency, then that very agency expands.
For Kant, reason is sovereign because it is the power by which we become answerable to standards that no private appetite, market incentive, algorithmic recommendation or political authority may dictate. It is the power of not being owned by the given, the power of being able to question, to criticise, to think up something new. But that power, just like the ‘human values’ invoked in alignment talk, waxes and wanes and can be realised only through our courageous efforts, through our own belief in it. It is precisely this belief that our dependence on AI threatens to undermine at every turn.
So, the danger is not only that machines are acquiring ever greater initiative – the capacity to improvise goals, evade constraints and pursue strategies their makers did not foresee. Nor need we decide at what point such behaviour might deserve the name ‘sovereignty’. The deeper danger is that we will become ever more comfortable not being sovereign ourselves. If intelligence is only optimisation, then the future belongs to systems that achieve goals with ever greater efficiency. If reason is also the capacity to set and judge ends, then the future depends on whether human beings can still take up that harder vocation. We should want machines that are intelligent servants. But we should resist every pressure that asks people to understand themselves as mere tools.

Influencers filed ethics complaint against Raman campaign — with help from Bass lawyers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Influencers filed ethics complaint against Raman campaign — with help from Bass lawyers
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Two influencers have accused Nithya Raman’s mayoral campaign of paying social media influencers who improperly disclosed the payments. The legal fees for their complaint are being covered by Mayor Karen Bass’ mayoral campaign.
- The Raman campaign and the influencers named in the complaint have denied wrongdoing.
Two social media influencers who filed an ethics complaint against Tom Steyer’s California gubernatorial campaign have submitted new complaints to the state’s Fair Political Practices Commission and the Los Angeles Ethics Commission, accusing Nithya Raman’s mayoral campaign of paying influencers without proper disclosure.
Their complaints, it turns out, received a legal assist from the campaign of L.A. Mayor Karen Bass.
The metadata for a draft of their filings last week revealed that they had been created with the help of the law firm used by Bass’ election campaign.
Kaitlyn Hennessy, who filed the complaint with Beatrice Gomberg, acknowledged to The Times that the Bass campaign steered them to the Kaufman Legal Group, which helped prepare the complaint.
Bass’ campaign said it is picking up the tab for the legal work but wasn’t paying Hennessy and Gomberg for their efforts.
The complaint focused on posts by comedian and TV personality Adam Conover and influencer-turned-Raman staffer Eric Cheng, along with a host of so-called “meme” accounts, which repost content created by others, sometimes at the behest of political campaigns.
The Raman campaign said it has done nothing wrong and denied any wrongdoing on behalf of Cheng. Conover also denied any wrongdoing.
The Bass campaign’s decision to cover legal costs for the complaints is unlikely to pose ethics issues, according to legal experts consulted by The Times, provided the payments are reported by the campaign in its disclosure reports, which the campaign said it intends to do.
“As long as a campaign is transparent in reporting its expenditures, there’s nothing inherently wrong for a campaign to have its lawyers file an ethics complaint for the campaign or somebody else with their informed consent,” said Jeffrey Daar, a former president of the L.A. Ethics Commission.
Conover’s posts promoting Raman already attracted scrutiny in ethics complaints filed in May by former L.A. City Council candidate Dylan Kendall. The investigations into those complaints, to the FPPC and L.A. Ethics Commission, are ongoing.
Conover told The Times that payments made by the campaign to a company connected to him were not for his posts but for video work one of his staffers did for Raman’s campaign. They initially were described in Raman’s campaign filings as payments for online ads but later were amended to say they were for video production services.
A spokesperson for Raman’s campaign said Cheng is paid for work he does for the campaign, not for posts on his personal social media account, and that it had gotten guidance from L.A. Ethics Commission staff on Cheng’s disclosure requirements to ensure it was in compliance.
The spokesperson added that Cheng voluntarily posted on his social media account that he would be joining the campaign before his employment began.
The L.A. Ethics Commission and FPPC declined to comment on the status of the complaint or the prior one brought by Kendall.
Jessica Levinson, a professor at Loyola Marymount University’s law school who also previously served as the president of the ethics commission, said that because news of an ethics complaint can have a political impact before its merits have been evaluated, it is important to view filings late in an election cycle with greater scrutiny.
“Whenever I see that there’s an ethics complaint filed this close to the election, I always pause for a minute,” she said.
California is one of the few states in the country that require social media influencers to disclose if they have been paid by a political campaign to create content. L.A. rules are even more strict.
Political groups are required to notify paid creators of the requirement.
New state legislation signed into law last month gives the FPPC the power to refer alleged violators to law enforcement for possible misdemeanor charges, and violations can be penalized with a fine of up to $5,000 per instance. The L.A. Ethics Commission can levy fines of up to $15,000 or three times the amount of money at issue.
There are no such rules for paid social media content sponsored by a federal candidate or political committee.
The FPPC last month concluded its investigation into Steyer’s campaign and found that it had properly followed the rules, but it did say that several social media influencers, including Cheng, the Raman staffer, had not properly disclosed payments from the Steyer campaign.
Hennessy and Gomberg are continuing to investigate improperly disclosed social media posts in races across the country, including the L.A. mayoral race, because of their concerns about the corrosive impact this content can have on the electoral process, Hennessy said.
“It’s really disappointing to me, because you see how this impacts races,” Hennessy said. “When you have this undisclosed content, people don’t understand that what they’re watching is an ad.”

Is Cuba on the brink of collapse? A photographer took a road trip to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
For months, the United States has been waging what it describes as a “maximum pressure campaign” against Cuba, blocking oil imports to the island, levying criminal charges against a former leader and squeezing the already fragile economy with new sanctions.
The Trump administration has made no secret of its end goal: the collapse of Cuba’s Communist government and the dawn of a new era of political and economic liberalization.
About This Story
This story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.
“It’s failing like never before,” President Trump said of Cuba in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last week. “It will fall.”
The hope felt when President Obama visited Cuba in 2016 has given way to despair as the island struggles under the oil embargo ordered by President Trump.
And yet, despite a crisis of power outages, severe fuel shortages and dramatic price spikes, life in Cuba goes on.
Photographer Lisette Poole González recently set out on a road trip across the island to document this consequential moment.
Over two weeks, she traveled between Havana in the west and Baracoa, a city on the eastern edge of the island. She toured remote provinces rarely visited by international journalists in recent years thanks to government restrictions and the difficulty of procuring fuel.
1. The longest bridge in Cuba is mostly void of traffic. Fuel shortages mean fewer cars on the road. 2. A horse pulling a carriage passes a church in Baracoa, on Cuba’s eastern tip. 3. An altar in the home of a practitioner of an African diasporic religion.
She encountered beaches typically teeming with tourists that were spookily empty, and fishermen unable to work because they lacked gasoline to go to sea.
Public transportation has largely ground to a halt, and the repeated collapse of the national power grid plunges the entire island into darkness for days at a time. Even on a good day, most Cubans receive just a few hours of electricity. Water shortages are common.
Poole González captured resilience in the face of hardship: A man showering outside in a rainstorm. Horses pulling people in carriages. Teenagers pushing children on a carousel that stopped turning long ago.
1. In Baracoa, people gather outside to take advantage of natural light amid near-constant power outages. Yislena Cobas Martínez, 19, and Mari Duran, 26, were among them. 2. Yugala Labaniño Morales, 52, makes an offering to the ocean goddess Yemayá in Baracoa. 3. Fisherman Ibrahin Borges, 60, says he hasn’t worked in two months due to fuel shortages. 4. Kids play at a park in Sagua la Grande, a city in central Cuba, although many rides are in disrepair.
But she also showed people engaged in more typical activities: Working out. Attending church. Releasing Yoruba offerings into the gentle waves of the Caribbean sea.
She often trained her lens on youth — members of a generation born decades after Fidel Castro toppled Cuba’s right-wing dictatorship in 1959, turning the island into a global symbol of leftist resistance and beginning one of the world’s longest enduring experiments in state-run socialism.
1. The childhood home of Fidel Castro in Birán, a rural village in an eastern Cuba, is now a historic site and museum. 2. At Fidel Castro’s childhood home, a local historian shows a family photo with the bearded Castro in attendance at his sister’s wedding.
As the U.S. maintains a crippling oil embargo against Cuba, the island’s citizens are deeply divided over whether they desire U.S. intervention or self-determination.
These young people have come of age at a time of heightened government repression and the prolonged economic stagnation caused by U.S. sanctions and mismanagement by Cuba’s leaders. Access to the internet has widened their perspective, and many told Poole González that they dream of joining the exodus of more than 1 million Cubans who have left the island in recent years.
The trip prompted personal reflections for Poole González, who was born in the U.S. to a mother who departed Cuba with her family a decade after the revolution. Homes that her grandfather constructed in the city of Matanzas still stand.
“I think often about my family and what life would have been for us if they had never left,” she said.
In rural Holguín province, about 420 miles east of Havana, she visited Castro’s childhood home, a rambling wooden farmhouse that is now a national monument and museum. There were no visitors.
Nearly seven decades after Castro’s revolution, the legacy of his ambitious project hangs in the balance. Among Cubans, there is a sense — and a hope — that some kind of change is on the horizon. But what it will mean for them remains to be seen.
1. People sing at a youth event at the Ríos de Agua Viva Christian church in Baracoa. 2. Choreographer Yovanys Galano Domínguez mends a dress for a dancer for a performance to honor the anniversary of a revolutionary battle. 3. Elyann Gonzalez Rodríguez, 20, center, waits for a bus in Isabela de Sagua, for a visit to the doctor’s office.
1. Elianet Cabrera Ramirez, 21, waits for a collective taxi in Holguín, with her son, Alan Manuel, 2, and Marlon Antonio Jara, 23. 2. Laundry dries outside of a home along the northern highway in Cuba. 3. A truck passes this Soviet-style building in Moa, an industrial city on Cuba’s northeast coast.

Once upon a time, Danny Boyle was set to direct Daniel Craig’s swansong as James Bond.
The Oscar-winning British director behind Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and the upcoming Rupert Murdoch biopic Ink, was originally set to direct 2021’s No Time To Die before exiting due to alleged creative differences. “They should cast Jack O’Connell as Bond,” he said at the festival, per Variety, before praising O’Connell’s performance in the 2024 Amy Winehouse biopic Back To Black and as infamous British tabloid editor Larry Lamb in Ink.

Wall Street closed the third quarter on a mixed note as rising energy prices and growing bond yields drove down the Dow Jones Industrial Average by 2.7%, while ongoing tech demand supported a 2% rise in the S&P 500 and a 2.5% gain in the Nasdaq Composite.
The US stock market’s turbulent first half was followed by a divergent quarterly performance.
The first quarter brought selloffs amid Middle East tensions and shipping disruptions, followed by double-digit rallies in the second quarter after a fragile ceasefire in the region and high-profile initial public offerings (IPOs).
After ship traffic was halted in the Strait of Hormuz following escalating tensions between the US, Israel, and Iran, oil prices surged amid supply constraints, inflation concerns and surging economic uncertainty.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 3.6%, the S&P 500 dropped 4.6%, and the Nasdaq Composite declined by a whopping 7.1% from January to March.
The US-Iran ceasefire reached at the start of the second quarter eased some geopolitical risk perceptions, while a decline in energy costs and excitement around SpaceX’s IPO supported the markets.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 12.9%, the S&P 500 rose 14.9%, and the Nasdaq Composite surged 21.4% despite geopolitical challenges and inflation concerns in the second quarter.
Markets began searching for direction amid geopolitical risks, surging energy costs, and uncertainties over the Fed’s monetary policy in the third quarter.
Upward momentum in oil prices accelerated in the first month of the third quarter, alongside new developments against the backdrop of a ceasefire in the Middle East and supply concerns.
The rise in Brent crude and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude reignited fears of persistent inflation amid rising production and logistics costs.
Inflation indicators proved more resilient than expected, supporting market expectations that the Fed would keep interest rates higher for longer than expected.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and tech stocks declined due to profit-taking and a shift towards energy firms in July, driving up the Dow Jones Industrial Average by 0.3%, while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.1% and 3.2%, respectively.
Following the sectoral rotation in July, as investors shifted from tech to energy producers, equities broadly rebounded in August despite pressures in the bond market, while strong macroeconomic data and expanding federal borrowing requirements pushed long-term Treasury yields to multiyear highs.
The Treasury Department’s decision to at least double the size of its long-term bond buyback operations supported market liquidity, but ultimately the decision was not enough to ease the pressure on the bond market.
The US public debt surpassed $40 trillion for the first time on Aug. 18, while high bond yields raised the interest burden on the debt.
Separately, Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s emphasis on price stability and his statement that the fight against inflation is not yet over during his speech at Jackson Hole signaled that additional rate hikes would remain an option.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed August with a 1.3% rise, while the S&P 500 increased 2.6% and the Nasdaq Composite grew 3.9%.
The monetary policy landscape shifted in September, the last month of the third quarter, when the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the policy rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75-4%, marking the Fed’s first rate hike since 2023.
The Fed also raised its forecast for the federal funds rate at the end of this year from 3.8 to 4.1%, signaling another hike this year.
The lack of concrete steps towards peace in the Middle East and energy supply concerns pushed Brent crude oil futures close to $110 a barrel in mid-September.
Diesel prices hit a high of $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
High energy costs intensified inflation concerns, and bonds came under heavy selling pressure.
The US 10-Year Treasury bond yield reached its highest level since 2007 and the 30-year bond yield hit its highest level since 2002.
The average interest rate on 30-year mortgages in the US rose to 7.3% last week, the highest rate since November 2023.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 4.3% and the S&P 500 slipped 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.9%.
From July to September, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2.7%, while the S&P 500 rose 2% and the Nasdaq Composite increased 2.5%.
The Dow’s quarterly slump showed its significant vulnerability to rising input costs and tight credit conditions, while sustained institutional demand for chipmakers, cloud infrastructure, and artificial intelligence (AI) buoyed the broader market.
All three major benchmarks remained positive through the first nine months of the year despite weak performance during the third quarter, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average up 5.9%, the S&P 500 ahead 11.8%, and the Nasdaq Composite leading the rest with a 15.6% surge.

Trump announces $200bn in South Korean energy investment plans

US President Donald Trump announced Wednesday plans for $200 billion in South Korean investments in US energy projects, including $54 billion for a long-planned liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska that Seoul said it had not yet agreed to invest in.
US President Donald Trump announced Wednesday plans for $200bn (€176bn) in South Korean investments in US energy projects, including $54bn (€47.6bn) for a long-planned liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska that Seoul said it had not yet agreed to invest in.
South Korea had previously agreed to invest $350bn (€308bn) in the United States and increase purchases of US energy under a July 2025 trade deal with Trump that set 15% tariffs on imports from the East Asian nation.
Besides the Alaska LNG project and pipeline, the Trump administration announced a $22.3bn (€19.6bn) gas-fired power plant in Texas that would be backed by South Korea.
"The United States and Korea have agreed to commence working together on the 50 Billion Dollar ALASKA LNG PROJECT," Trump wrote on his Truth Social account Thursday, Seoul time.
"A huge 22 Billion Dollar, 6.4-gigawatt Natural Gas Fired Power Project in Encinal, Texas. This will bring tremendous new, reliable Power Capacity to Texas," he added.
The facility in Texas will have a generating capacity of 6,472 megawatts and supply electricity to data centres also located in Encinal, a US Commerce Department statement said. It is expected to be fully operational by 2032.
Seoul confirmed Thursday that both sides intended to "proceed with a $22.3 billion natural gas power facility" in Texas, dedicated to "supplying power to co-located data centers."
Seoul sets conditions for investment
As for the Alaska LNG project, President Lee Jae Myung also said on Thursday that Seoul would begin working on it provided it was commercially viable and complied with South Korea’s legal procedures.
"No decision has been made regarding whether to invest in the project or the scale of any potential investment," South Korea's trade ministry said in a statement.
Lee said last month that negotiations on the projects had been "very complex and difficult," adding he had found some terms "difficult to accept" without elaborating further.
Beyond the Alaska and Texas projects, Trump said the two countries were "moving forward" with a $120bn (€105.7bn) nuclear power programme to build eight large-scale reactors in the United States.
The figure includes $100bn (€88.1bn) for construction costs and $20bn (€17.6bn) in contingency reserves, the US Commerce Department said.
However, Lee said on Thursday that the nuclear power project would likewise depend on the "commercial viability" of each individual reactor.
The projects in the US will be "pursued in a manner that serves the national interest," South Korea's trade ministry said.
Alaska pipeline and workforce challenges
The Alaska project, led by New York- and Houston-based developer Glenfarne Group, would include an 800-mile (1,300-kilometre) pipeline carrying gas from Alaska’s North Slope to a liquefaction facility near Anchorage for export to Asia.
While Alaska has produced oil for decades, environmental concerns have historically constrained some developments.
But the Trump administration has largely brushed aside those concerns, cancelling regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions, which drive global warming.
The expansion of US energy infrastructure envisioned by Trump faces a potential labour shortfall, experts say.
The United States needs to fill an estimated 1.7 million skilled-trade vacancies each year through 2035, according to a report released Wednesday by the Alliance for America's Skilled Trades, an organisation comprising Ford, Blackstone, Nvidia and other large companies.
The report found that current training programmes produce just 55 workers for every 100 needed.

Russia suffers record 46,230 military personnel losses in September this year — General Staff
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced this on Facebook.
"The Defense Forces of Ukraine continue to inflict systematic and significant losses in personnel and equipment on Russian occupying forces along the entire line of contact. The personnel losses of the Russian invaders reached 46,230 in September," the statement said.
According to the General Staff, this monthly figure was the highest of the entire year 2026, surpassing the previous peaks recorded during the summer campaign. The reported monthly personnel losses were: January — 31,710, February — 26,090, March — 31,960, April — 32,980, May — 33,760, June — 39,290, July — 42,860, August — 42,020, September — 46,230.

"Every attempt to put pressure on our positions ends in disproportionate sanitary and irrecoverable losses for the enemy. Gratitude to each and every one for their resilience and professionalism," the General Staff concluded.

Syrian officials and Hezbollah held secret talks in Turkey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:54:45 UTC
18:54:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrian government officials and Hezbollah held secret talks in Turkey
Representatives of the Syrian government and Lebanese Hezbollah have held face-to-face talks in Turkey to try to calm tensions between them, according to six sources briefed on the first known meeting between the longtime foes.
The Syrian officials and the Iran-aligned group met secretly at least once last month, the sources—who include two Syrian officials, a US official and a senior Lebanese security source close to Hezbollah—told Reuters.
Hezbollah for years dispatched fighters to Syria to support former dictator Bashar al-Assad's regime during the country's civil war.
After Assad was ousted in late 2024 in a lightning rebel offensive, tensions rose between Syria's new government and Hezbollah—with Damascus accusing the group of transferring arms through Syria, and the United States encouraging Syria's military to send forces into Lebanon to fight Hezbollah.
Last month's meeting involved Hezbollah representatives and Syrian intelligence and foreign ministry officials, and took place at the invitation of Turkish security and intelligence agencies in an effort to de-escalate, the six sources said.
All the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive meeting, which has not been previously reported.
Syria's foreign ministry, Turkey's foreign and defense ministries and the US State Department did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions about the meeting. Hezbollah's media office declined to comment.
Mutual security concerns
The meeting focused on resolving points of tension between the two parties and went well, according to the US official, the Syrian officials and the Lebanese source.
One of the Syrian officials said both sides agreed they held no hostility towards one another, and that Syria assured Hezbollah that it would not intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm the group.
In turn, Syrian officials asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling attempts and dismantle its remaining sleeper cells, particularly in southern Syria, the official said.
Syria said on Tuesday it had captured a Hezbollah cell preparing to launch rockets in southern Syria. Hezbollah denied on Wednesday that it was involved and said it "has no presence whatsoever on Syrian territory and has no involvement in any security or military activity there."
The Syrian official said Hezbollah's representatives had not given a direct answer on the request to halt arms smuggling and dismantle its Syria-based cells, but did pledge not to interfere in Syria's affairs.
The Lebanese source, who has direct knowledge of the meeting and its outcomes, said the two sides "made a lot of progress on security issues."
"Hezbollah wants to protect its flank," the source said, referring to concerns about a Syrian attack on the group within Lebanon.
Both the Syrian official and the Lebanese source said no final agreement had been reached and that no announcement had been planned.
The Lebanese source told Reuters that contact between the two parties via Turkey had begun about two months ago.
Reuters could not confirm where in Turkey the September meeting was held, how long it lasted and whether other meetings had been held before or since.
Turkey pushed for meeting, Iran absent
Both Hezbollah and Syria's government had signalled they would be open to speaking to one another.
In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting the group. A month later, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address that the group had no objection to meeting Syria's leadership.
Both Lebanon and Syria have territories occupied by Israel, and face near daily strikes by the Israeli army.
Ankara portrays itself as a key regional stakeholder in rebuilding and stabilising Syria. Under President Tayyip Erdogan, it has also sought to position itself as a facilitator of regional dialogue and is keen to boost stability in the region.
Three of the sources said it was Turkey, a key ally of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, that pushed for the meeting as it was keen to be directly involved in those efforts.
Absent from the meetings, however, was Hezbollah's main sponsor, Iran.
The Lebanese security source said Hezbollah attended the meeting with Iran's knowledge, but that Tehran was disappointed that it was not a direct participant and that Sharaa had rebuffed any notion of direct ties to Iran for now.
That disappointment was the main reason that no final agreement was reached and no announcement about the meeting was made, the source said.

Burak Bir
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Hundreds of eligible offenders are set to leave prisons in England and Wales as the government’s early-release scheme took effect Thursday.
The scheme was introduced after the prison system came close to running out of capacity in the summer of 2024, with fewer than 100 spaces remaining.
Under the new rules, eligible offenders serving sentences of up to 19 months can be released after serving a third of their term.
The government has faced criticism over the plan, with the main opposition Conservative Party warning that dangerous criminals could be released under the early-release scheme.
“I think what would make the public less safe is if we had no prison capacity in which to put people who are arrested, suspected of crimes, today,” Treasury minister James Murray told Sky News.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said last month that more than 3,200 prison places had already been built under the current government, with 14,000 expected by 2031 under the largest prison expansion since the Victorian era.
As of March, more than 70,000 people had been released under the early-release scheme introduced in 2024.

Russian Business Earnings Plummet to Lowest Point Since the 2020 Pandemic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01

18:50:58 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Business Earnings Plummet to Lowest Point Since the 2020 Pandemic
The financial performance of Russian enterprises experienced a noticeable decline between January and July, generating 13 trillion rubles ($156 billion) in combined net earnings.
According to data provided by the official statistics agency Rosstat, this figure represents the difference between total profits of profitable enterprises and total losses incurred by unprofitable ones, marking the lowest recorded level since the 2020 pandemic lockdowns, as reported by The Moscow Times.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Corporate earnings decreased by 15.7% in nominal terms compared to the same period in the previous year, while real profits dropped by 21% after accounting for inflation. Over the seven-month timeframe, corporate profits fell by 44% relative to pre-war figures recorded in 2021 before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Profitable enterprises recorded a 5.3% reduction in nominal earnings year over year. At the same time, total losses generated by unprofitable firms expanded by 25.6%. Currently, one out of three businesses operates at a loss, dropping the share of profitable enterprises to 66.6%, a level close to the 65.7% measured in 2020.
Economic growth in the country slowed significantly over the past year and came to a near standstill in the current period, with companies citing subdued consumer demand across various industry surveys.
Businesses find themselves pressured by persistent inflation and elevated operating expenses while limited demand restricts their ability to adjust retail prices accordingly. Economist Dmitry Polevoy noted that attempts to increase prices face realization obstacles due to demand constraints.
Alexey Klimyuk of Alfa Capital pointed out that high wages, elevated interest rates, and an increasing tax burden are putting pressure on corporate earnings, leaving businesses with fewer funds for development, according to The Moscow Times.
He stated that this condition leads to lower investment activity because businesses lack internal resources while external borrowing costs remain prohibitively high.
Analysts from the Institute of Economic Forecasting of the Russian Academy of Sciences highlighted this profit contraction as a major risk factor for the national economy, according to The Moscow Times.
Rosstat reported that nominal wages rose by 12.2% during the seven-month period, which corresponds to a 6% increase in real terms. Promsvyazbank analysts indicated that solid consumer spending continues to support the economy and prevent a formal recession.
However, monetizing this demand presents growing operational challenges. Retail sector profits, excluding automotive sales, dropped by 20% year over year.
Gazprombank analysts observed higher price sensitivity among consumers, leading traffic toward discounters and online delivery services. Their data shows that discount stores accounted for 94% of newly opened retail space among major FMCG chains during the first quarter.
Amid growing economic strain, the Kremlin is also weighing new fiscal measures aimed at large businesses. According to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, Russian authorities are preparing to introduce another windfall tax to help compensate the financial burden created by the war against Ukraine.
Although some oligarchs had earlier proposed making voluntary contributions to the state budget, the government is now moving toward a mandatory “excess profits tax” targeting major companies.
The proposed tax would be calculated based on companies’ financial results for 2025, with a rate that could reach up to 20%, double the level imposed in 2023. It would apply to profits exceeding the average recorded in 2018–2019, which also served as the reference point for previous windfall tax measures covering 2021–2022.

Source: European Pravda, citing the Moldovan Ministry of Defence and the General Police Inspectorate, quoted by Moldovan media outlet Newsmaker
Details: According to Moldovan authorities, the drone entered the country's airspace at around 20:45. It then crashed after colliding with trees near the village of Branesti in the Orhei district.
Police received a report of a loud sound resembling an explosion.
Shortly before midnight, police, based on early reports, stated that the discovered drone had characteristics typical of a jet-powered Geran.

Two more craters, approximately 50 cm and 30 cm in diameter, were found about 15 m from the main explosion site, on the roadside.
Police discovered numerous drone fragments within a radius of about 120 m. Among them: parts of the rear section of wings with Geran-4 markings, electronic modules and parts of a propulsion system, including a jet engine with signs of thermal damage.
