Moscow’s message to European business: your Russian assets are now leverage against your governments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:47:27 UTC
18:47:27 KST

The Kremlin is signaling that it will hold the Russian assets of European companies hostage to pressure Europe into rethinking its sanctions, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) wrote on 30 September. Moscow has already put well-known European retailers and food makers under Russian "temporary management." A senior Russian official has now hinted that European banks could be next.
As Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine, it has long turned hostages and threats into weapons. Its record includes nuclear threats against Europe from its Oreshnik missile launch sites and a fresh warning over Kaliningrad. It has played games with Europe's largest nuclear plant that it occupied in 2022, applied gas and water pressure on its neighbors, and Kyiv accuses it of blackmailing the families of Ukrainian prisoners of war. Europe's companies are now one more lever in that kit.
"Let them be scared"
Russia is taking "asymmetric measures" to make Europe rethink its sanctions, a senior Russian government source with direct knowledge of the seizures claimed, Reuters reported. "Let them think about what measures they are taking and what sanctions they are introducing," the source said.
Asked whether the Russian units of Italy's UniCredit and Austria's Raiffeisen could be placed under temporary management, the source answered: "Let them be scared."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed the decisions were driven by "the increasing level of involvement of these unfriendly countries in direct battlefield hostilities" against Russia. He suggested the moves were "reversible," but added: "For now, we do not see any grounds for a reversal."
EU lawmakers renew push to seize frozen Russian assets as Ukraine faces its toughest winter yet with a €23 billion defense funding gap
Nestlé, Auchan, and Metro under "temporary management"
Putin's decree of 17 September placed 16 companies under the "temporary management" of a firm called L.E.V. Management, with no end date. They include the Russian units of France's Auchan and Lemana PRO, formerly Leroy Merlin, and of Switzerland's Nestlé. A second decree, on 28 September, handed the Russian assets of German wholesaler Metro AG to UK Torg Rus.
Both decrees amend Putin's April 2023 decree No. 302, which lets Moscow take over the property of firms tied to countries it labels "unfriendly." Because the "temporary" management has no expiry date, ISW considers it effectively nationalization. Independent outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe identified L.E.V. Management's director as retired Russian Major General Andrei Krayushkin.
European companies as corporate hostages
The Kremlin likely wants to use the seizures to take European companies as corporate hostages, ISW assessed. It also likely expects a temporary fiscal boost from the revenues of the seized businesses.
The strategy assumes that European firms will judge the benefits of staying in Russia to outweigh the risk of losing their assets, the think tank said. Whether a company is seized depends entirely on Moscow's relations with the country where it is headquartered, ISW added.
Seizing others' property is an old Moscow habit
Since the start of the full-scale war, Russia has introduced temporary administration at 135 foreign-linked firms, mostly from EU countries, according to TASS data cited by Reuters. Earlier targets included French food group Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg.
The method was tested on Ukraine first. Russia's proxies in occupied Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts stole most Ukrainian assets there in 2014 and 2015. In March 2017, after Ukrainian activists blocked rail trade with the occupied areas, they placed the remaining Ukrainian-registered firms under "temporary administrations," a label close to the one Moscow uses today. The published Donetsk list alone ran to 43 assets, from coal mines and ironworks to the Donbas Arena stadium. Much of the coal and steel business later ended up with firms tied to Serhii Kurchenko, a fugitive oligarch from Yanukovych's era.

Major drug smuggling gang at Brussels Airport busted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:44:09 UTC
18:44:09 KST

The international drug network had been smuggling cocaine and cannabis via Brussels Airport for many years. In a major police operation in Belgium and France, 21 suspects were arrested and 27 properties were searched. The gang made use of cheap flight tickets to gain access to the baggage hall.
The investigation began in February 2025. At that time, sports bags containing approximately 30 kilograms of cocaine were found at Brussels Airport. They had arrived on a flight from Cancún in Mexico.
The police subsequently spotted a suspicious man in the baggage hall. He had bought a flight ticket but had not boarded a flight. However, his ticket allowed him to enter the baggage hall. The man is now one of the suspects who have been arrested.
Cheap ticket to collect suitcases
According to investigators, the drug gang had couriers fly to Brussels Airport with suitcases full of drugs. Upon arrival, these couriers did not collect their suitcases from the baggage carousel themselves. This meant they did not have to go through security checks with the drugs.
Other people were tasked with collecting the suitcases. They booked a cheap flight at the last minute, but had no intention of travelling. Their ticket allowed them to enter the baggage hall.
The gang mainly recruited these so-called ‘collectors’ via social media. They took the suitcases to an agreed location near the airport.
Dozens of kilograms of drugs intercepted
In April 2025, the first suspect was caught. Customs officers found around 30 kilograms of cannabis in a suitcase from Canada. A few weeks later, another suspect was intercepted with two suitcases. Together, they contained around 55 kilograms of cocaine.
The investigation also led to France and the Netherlands. Consequently, Belgian police collaborated with investigators in both countries, as well as with Europol, the official law enforcement agency of the European Union, and Eurojust, the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation, coordinating investigations of serious cross-border crime in Europe and beyond.
Airport staff also enlisted
When several suspects were arrested, the gang changed its approach. According to the investigators, they also enlisted the help of airport staff.
These staff members removed the drugs from the suitcases before they reached the baggage carousel. The empty suitcases were then sent to the baggage hall. The drugs were taken out of the airport by other means.
Some suspects also used false identity documents and travelled under different names. This made the investigation more difficult.
21 suspects arrested
A major police operation took place on 30 September. In Belgium, 19 people were arrested and 21 properties were searched. In France, there were 2 arrests and 6 properties were raided.
Investigators seized more than 57,000 euros in cash, digital wallets containing cryptocurrency, 8 vehicles, jewellery and a luxury watch. They also found a banknote counting machine and various weapons.
The investigation is ongoing. Investigators aim to track down all members of the network and also seize the organisation’s money and other assets.

Altruistic Aliyah: A tool for world Jewry to transform Israeli policy from within - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:43:39 UTC
18:43:39 KST

Wanted: Individuals willing to leave behind their homes, communities, native language, and careers built over decades. People prepared to start from scratch in another country and bear a steep personal, familial, and financial cost - all to solve a problem whose ultimate benefits may largely be enjoyed by others.
In plain terms: Israel needs altruists to make Aliyah.
In recent years, an argument has surfaced with increasing frequency: Israeli policy directly affects the safety and standing of diaspora Jewry. Antisemitism, of course, was not invented by any particular Israeli government; it predates the modern Jewish state by centuries.
Yet even if one accepts the premise that Jerusalem’s actions can inflame anti-Israel hostility, which often bleeds into overt antisemitism, an untenable dynamic emerges. A Jew in Los Angeles, Paris, London, Toronto, or New York pays the price for decisions made in Jerusalem, despite having zero say over the leaders making them. They cast no ballot in Israeli elections; they shape no policy.
Yet they possess an extraordinary alternative: they can become voters. They can make Aliyah.
The moment a Jew becomes an Israeli, they cease to be a passive policy bystander
The moment a diaspora Jew becomes an Israeli citizen, they cease to be a passive bystander affected by Israel's policies - they become an active participant in shaping them. And if enough people make that leap, immigration stops being merely a collection of private life choices and becomes a transformative demographic and political force.
This is not a theoretical thought experiment. Israel has already witnessed what happens when Aliyah reaches critical mass. In the 1990s, hundreds of thousands of immigrants arrived from the former Soviet Union. They reshaped Israeli society and rapidly formed a formidable electoral bloc. By the 1992 elections, their collective strength was estimated at eight to nine Knesset seats; by 1996, the immigrant-led party Yisrael BaAliyah won seven seats on its own.
They did not emigrate with the primary goal of reshaping Israeli governance, yet they proved that large-scale Aliyah can do precisely that. This raises a compelling question: What would happen if the next major wave of immigration came from Western Jewish communities?
If Jews in Los Angeles, London, Paris, Toronto, and New York believe that Israel’s trajectory directly impacts their own security abroad, why settle for rallies, petitions, and op-eds? The Law of Return grants them an instrument unavailable to virtually any other diaspora in the world: the power to arrive, receive citizenship, and step straight into the voting booth.
A more liberal Israel as a result
Consider the implications if such an effort succeeded. Tens of thousands of Western Jews make Aliyah, build their lives in Israel, and exert their influence at the ballot box.
The result would be a more liberal Israel. The arrival of hundreds of thousands of Jews - many rooted in Reform and Conservative movements - would bridge Jewish tradition with modern democracy, pluralism, and gender equality. Coming of age in established Western democracies, these immigrants carry an innate commitment to strong civic institutions, civil rights, free speech, and equality before the law. Their presence would fortify Israeli democracy from within.
If this demographic shift were to alter Israeli policy in a way that eases friction with the international community, it might also neutralize one of the pretexts used to justify antisemitism abroad.
Herein lies the paradox.
Should this movement succeed, the Jew walking the streets of Paris may feel safer, and the Jewish student on an American campus may face far less hostility. But the individuals who bore the personal cost to catalyze that change will no longer be there to enjoy it. They will be in Israel. They paid the price; someone else reaped the dividend.
We are accustomed to viewing Aliyah driven by antisemitism as an act of self-defense: things have grown intolerable here, so I must leave. But there is another framing: making Aliyah not to escape, but to lead; not running away from a problem, but stepping forward to solve it. This does not replace traditional Zionism, a sense of belonging, or the desire to build a home in the Jewish homeland - it complements them. It redefines Aliyah as an act of collective Jewish responsibility.
This is the profound paradox of altruistic Aliyah: moving to Israel not merely to transform your own life, but to safeguard the lives of those who choose to stay behind.
Gilad Ramot is the Founder and Chairman of Belong, a social venture dedicated to encouraging Aliyah.

The euro area’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at 6.4% in August, unchanged from July but up from 6.3% a year earlier, Eurostat figures showed Thursday.
The unemployment rate across the European Union also held steady at 6.1%, compared with 6% in August 2025.
Eurostat estimated that 13.6 million people were unemployed in the EU in August, including 11.357 million in the euro area.
Compared with July, the number of unemployed increased by 12,000 in the EU and 26,000 in the euro area. On an annual basis, unemployment rose by 348,000 and 267,000, respectively.
Among EU countries, Finland recorded the highest unemployment rate at 10.3%, followed by Spain at 10% and Sweden at 8.7%.
Czechia had the lowest rate at 3.2%, while Malta, Poland and Slovenia each recorded 3.4%.
Among the bloc’s largest economies, Germany’s unemployment rate remained at 4%, while France’s eased to 8.2% from 8.3% in July. Italy’s rate increased to 6.2% from 6%.
Youth unemployment showed a mixed picture, rising to 15.4% in the EU from 15.3% in July, while falling to 15% in the euro area from 15.1%.
Some 2.973 million people under the age of 25 were unemployed across the EU, including 2.391 million in the euro area.
The unemployment rate for women stood at 6.7% in the euro area, compared with 6.2% for men. Across the EU, the corresponding rates were 6.4% and 5.9%, respectively, all unchanged from July.

Greece urges EU to loosen fiscal rules as energy crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

High energy prices and military escalation at energy facilities in the Middle East prompted Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis to ask Brussels for greater fiscal flexibility. Greece has the largest debt among EU countries and is heading to polls in 2027.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis is calling on the European Commission to "take action" in giving national governments more fiscal room to shield households and businesses from a renewed energy-price shock, according to a letter seen by Euronews.
"We need more breathing room to protect our citizens and businesses (...) We must find the additional necessary flexibility within the Economic Governance Framework to allow Member States to take additional support measures (...) while safeguarding fiscal sustainability," reads the letter dated 30 September.
Addressing Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis, Mitsotakis said that Europe’s latest energy crisis is lasting longer than expected, with increased attacks on energy facilities in the Middle East threatening to turn it into both an economic and political challenge for Athens.
Greece has the largest national debt among the 27 EU member states. While the country’s economy is growing, a wave of generous government subsidies and sweeping tax cuts is making it much harder to chip away at its massive national debt.
To help families cope with rising costs, Athens has been handing out hefty cash aid for energy bills, fuel and farming. At the same time, Mitsotakis has slashed income and property taxes to please voters and jump-start businesses ahead of parliamentary elections slated for 2027.
Artificially lowering energy prices
Several EU countries have already spent billions of euros in tax cuts and subsidies to shield against skyrocketing prices. But governments are reaching a tipping point when "there is no money", as the Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever bluntly put it when he ruled out broad measures to tackle rising energy prices.
The Greek leader pointed to sharp price increases since the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February: EU gasoline prices before tax are up 53%, diesel 66%, while gas has risen from just over €30/MWh to around €70/MWh.
In most EU countries, electricity prices have exceeded €100/MWh over the past month, up from €42/MWh before the Middle East disruption, with some markets approaching or surpassing €200/MWh. Mitsotakis argued that the problem is no longer just energy costs but their knock-on effect on wider inflation and household affordability.
Greece is proposing that temporary national measures to support consumers and companies could, up to a certain limit, be excluded from the EU's net-expenditure indicator, a government spending cap that sets limits on how fast a national government can increase its day-to-day budget.
It also proposes that governments be able to account for additional VAT revenues generated by unexpectedly high inflation linked to energy prices.
If the European Commission considers these measures, it would give governments more fiscal space to subsidise or otherwise support citizens and businesses without the same pressure from EU fiscal rules.
The Greek leader expects the request to be discussed at the gathering of energy ministers in Brussels later in October and at next year's summit of EU heads of state and governments.
"It is not politically acceptable that the main course of action that has been proposed by the Commission so far is just to reduce energy demand. We need to have on the agenda a broader set of ideas that speak to the urgency of the current moment," reads the letter.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also urged President von der Leyen to loosen fiscal rules, the Italian leader said on 30 September, according to local media.
Meloni has previously called for greater fiscal flexibility, as Italy has the second-highest national debt in the EU.

Herzog to honor four Israelis who helped avert Flydubai disaster: ‘You put yourselves at risk to save others’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:38:34 UTC
18:38:34 KST

President Isaac Herzog spoke with the Israelis who showed extraordinary bravery aboard the Flydubai flight and told them he intends to recommend all four for the President’s Award for Civilian Bravery: Yaniv Hayun, Dr. Shota Musaev, Zvika Manes and Assaf Rajuan.
The President’s Residence said the Israelis “acted quickly and decisively,” alongside the Indian pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, who fought the attacker and opened the cockpit door. Herzog also mentioned Tali Manes, Zvika’s wife, who alerted others to the unusual incident.
The statement said the four “overpowered the attacker, placing their own lives in real danger, while Hayoun steadied the aircraft's controls.”
“Once the attacker had been subdued, Dr. Musaev provided lifesaving medical treatment to the seriously wounded flight captain, helping to stabilize his condition until the aircraft made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The swift action of the passengers and crew averted a major disaster.”
In his conversations with them, Herzog expressed appreciation for the resourcefulness, courage and mutual responsibility they showed in moments of extreme danger. He told them he intended to bring the story of their actions before the advisory committee for the President’s Award for Civilian Bravery.
“At a time when the lives of so many people were in danger, you acted without hesitation, with courage, resourcefulness, and extraordinary mutual responsibility,” Herzog told them. “You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster. Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society. I am proud of you, and I thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.
“I intend to bring your story of heroism before the advisory committee for the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism and to recommend that it grant you the award.”
Herzog added: “In addition, I extend my gratitude and deep appreciation, on behalf of the State of Israel, to the Indian pilot, Captain Smit Machchhar, whose determination and actions made it possible to subdue the attacker and saved many lives.”
Herzog later recommended Tali Manes, Zvika Manes’ wife, for the same civilian bravery award after further accounts indicated she played a crucial role in alerting passengers to the danger.
According to the President’s Residence, Manes heard violence and commotion coming from the cockpit and was the first to alert other passengers and call for help, prompting those who ultimately rushed in and subdued the suspected attacker.
After he was restrained, she continued to act, calling pilots who were traveling in the rear of the aircraft to come forward and help restore control of the plane.
“Tali, the more we learn about what happened in those dramatic moments, the clearer it becomes how significant a part you played in saving the lives of the passengers,” Herzog told her.
“You heard that something terrible was happening, immediately understood the scale of the danger, raised the alarm, called for help, and did not stop acting even after the attacker had been subdued,” he said. “The resourcefulness, responsibility, and composure you showed in moments of mortal danger are civilian heroism in the fullest sense of the word. You are a hero, Tali, and I am proud of you and thank you on behalf of the State of Israel.”
The President’s Award for Civilian Bravery was established by Herzog during the war to honor civilians who acted with exceptional bravery while facing a genuine risk to their lives, out of a sense of mutual responsibility and in an effort to save lives.
The award is granted after cases are reviewed and recommended by an advisory committee appointed by the president. In recent years, it has been awarded to exceptional Israeli civilians, including some who distinguished themselves during the October 7 attacks in communities near the Gaza border and in other incidents. It is Israel’s highest civilian bravery award.

"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:38:00 EEST
18:38:00 KST

"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
When the Russian forces began stepping up their use of jet-powered drones, perhaps the most common question among Ukrainians was: "Why haven't we destroyed the launch sites yet?"
Although Ukraine's defence forces regularly attack Russian drone launch sites, the strikes have not produced an effect on the scale of Operation Spider's Web, in which a dozen Tu-95MS and Tu-22M3 bombers were destroyed.
The reason is that, over the past two years, Russia has built an extensive network of specialised drone launch facilities, capable of handling dozens of jet-powered and conventional drones every hour. In Ukrainian and Russian discourse, these facilities are dubbed "droneports" – a catch-all term for dedicated sites used to operate drones.
Ukrainska Pravda and CyberBoroshno, a Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) community, have looked into Russian drone launch sites and attacks on them. Read on to find out where Russian forces launch their UAVs from and why it is highly unlikely that these droneports will ever be destroyed.
Where does Russia launch its Shaheds from?
When the first Iranian-made Shahed loitering munitions arrived in Russia in autumn 2022, little preparation was needed before they could be put to use. The drones could be launched straight out of the box.
The only thing they needed was a site from which they could be launched.
Military airfields were among the first – and perhaps the most obvious – choices for launching the drones. They already had everything needed: secure perimeters, security personnel, ground staff, air defence systems and established logistics for receiving new drones. The airfields were also located away from civilian infrastructure and prying eyes.
Long runways also made it possible to use pick-ups and lorries as mobile launch platforms for Shaheds. Lightweight launchers were also deployed at the airfields. The UAVs took off from these launchers with the help of solid-fuel rocket boosters before switching to their piston engines for the rest of the flight. For the Russians, the existing airfield infrastructure was more than enough.
The first airfields used by Russian forces to launch Shaheds were in occupied Crimea and the border regions of Bryansk and Kursk oblasts. As the number of drones Russia received grew, so did the geographical scope of their deployment. Known launch sites included Cape Chauda, Yeysk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Kursk and Seshcha.
The Russians later began using sites other than airfields to launch Shahed drones, including positions around Balaklava on Crimea's southern coast.
This enabled Russian forces to launch dozens of drones every week. The locations were also far enough from the combat zone to keep the launch sites relatively safe, yet close enough to Ukraine for the drones to reach Ukrainian territory within a few hours.
The droneports
When Russia acquired the technology to produce Shahed loitering munitions, another problem emerged: there was a shortage of existing airfield infrastructure.
Unlike the Shaheds supplied by Iran, Russia's domestically produced versions, known as Geran drones, had to be not only launched but also maintained. They had to be assembled, stored, inspected and prepared for launch somewhere. Although the existing infrastructure could support an increase in the number of launch sites, it was still not enough.
Therefore, as Geran production got underway, the Russians began preparing new launch sites in parallel.
Garages for assembling and storing drones began appearing at airfields already used as launch sites. Russia also built underground storage facilities large enough to accommodate both the drones and their warheads. Launchers were also being installed in revetments – protected bays surrounded by earth banks or blast walls.
Alongside the expansion of existing sites, new ones have begun to appear across Russia. In just a few months, large drone bases capable of launching hundreds of drones a day have sprung up on land that was previously covered by fields or forests.
Perhaps the best-known of these is Tsimbulova in Oryol Oblast, about 180 km from the Ukrainian border. Russian sources describe it as "the world's largest droneport". And with good reason: the site covers 5 sq km.
OSINT analyst Dnipro Osint ⟨Harbuz⟩ told Ukrainska Pravda: "The Alabuga began building the site in August 2024, and by February 2025, the main facilities had been completed. Its construction was directly linked to the expansion of drone production at Alabuga. This droneport has, in essence, become the first facility whose infrastructure was designed entirely for storing, maintaining and launching drones."
Tsimbulova has been equipped with runways and fixed catapult launchers for drones. The site also includes hundreds of garages and dozens of underground shelters.
The base's facilities are spread out across the site, with each one separated from the others and surrounded by earthworks. The droneports were built on the assumption that they would eventually be attacked. The Russians therefore sought to ensure that only a direct bombardment could destroy them.
The drones themselves can be stored not only inside buildings but also outdoors. Satellite imagery shows both Shahed attack drones and Gerbera decoy drones, which are also launched from these droneports.
The sites are supported by the infrastructure needed for day-to-day operations: solar panels, diesel generators, fuel depots and radio and navigation equipment for drone control. Each facility has its own access roads, parking areas and additional exit routes. It is also protected by air defence and electronic warfare systems intended to counter Ukrainian attacks.
Harbuz says: "The droneports were initially built much larger than 'necessary'. By the end of 2024, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine estimated the production rate of Shaheds at 2,000 units per month – roughly 64 UAVs a day – yet the droneport infrastructure at Tsimbulova could store up to 3,000 combat drones and 100 UAVs simultaneously. It was clearly built with capacity to spare."
In 2026, the infrastructure at Tsimbulova has continued to expand. New hangars and warehouses were built at the droneport, alongside larger specialised launchers for Geran-4/5 jet-powered drones. These drones can also be launched from mobile platforms mounted on vehicles.
An analysis of satellite images by Ukrainska Pravda estimates that Tsimbulova has 23 launchers for different types of drones, 387 garages and 26 underground storage facilities. The site is still expanding: the Russians are preparing to build four more launchers for jet-powered drones, plus 83 garages and underground shelters.
Another well-known droneport has been established at the site of the destroyed Donetsk airport (DAP). Despite being 50 km from the front line, the site now has hangars and drone launch pads used to launch drones towards frontline areas and targets in the rear.
Up to 95% of drone launches take place from bases in Russia's Bryansk, Rostov, Smolensk and Oryol oblasts, as well as in Krasnodar Krai and occupied Crimea. There are also research droneports where Russia tests UAVs in flight.
Although these sites are smaller than Tsimbulova, they have much the same basic infrastructure.
Ukrainska Pravda has identified at least 63 launchers at the main droneports, but the total could be higher. The sites can accommodate hundreds of drones and tens of thousands of combat components for them.
Can droneports be destroyed?
Ukraine's defence forces could not ignore the fact that Russians were launching Shaheds across Ukraine. Therefore, they gradually began targeting the drone launch sites, choosing their targets according to the capabilities and resources available to them.
Some of the first known strikes on Shahed launch sites were carried out in 2024. Ukrainian forces hit a Shahed depot near Balaklava and a storage facility for the drones near Yeysk.
After the strike, the area near Balaklava ceased to be used for Shahed launches. Yeysk was the first – and so far the only – case in which the impact of a strike could be seen in the launch figures. For the first time, Russia then went 48 days without launching Shaheds on Ukraine.
Russia's droneports have also been struck whilst under construction. On 26 December 2024, at least three Storm Shadow cruise missiles hit a facility between Tsimbulova and Rudnevo. Russian media outlet Astra said two Russian service members were killed and seven others were taken to hospital as a result of the strike.
A month later, the same complex was once again targeted by Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles. Ukraine's General Staff reported that more than 200 Shaheds had been destroyed. The images show damage to one of the warehouses.
Donetsk airport is another well-known target that has come under repeated attacks by Ukraine's defence forces. In a separate article, Ukrainska Pravda details how Ukraine's drone forces have been destroying Shahed launchers at the airport.
Because the airport is so close to the front line, Ukraine's 1st Separate Centre of the Unmanned Systems Forces has been able to regularly destroy Russian weapons, mobile fire groups defending the airfield and infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used mid-range drones and even FPV drones to strike targets at the airfield.
(12) FP-2 drone strikes on the DAP. Video: Special Operations Forces
DAP itself is a good example of just how difficult droneports are to strike.
Harbuz says: "The Russians have built drone launch sites to make them as costly as possible for Ukraine's defence forces to destroy. Ammunition and fuel depots are concealed beneath concrete and earth. Conventional UAVs cannot penetrate these structures, and even if they do, the explosion is contained inside, preventing debris from reaching other depots and triggering a chain reaction.
If any facilities are destroyed, they can be rebuilt relatively quickly and cheaply. As the example of Donetsk airport shows, the Russians are adapting and expanding the drone launch site even there, despite constant Ukrainian strikes."
Therefore, the main objective of Ukraine's defence forces when striking drone launch sites is to disrupt Russia's ability to launch drones.
Falco, an officer with Ukraine's 1st Separate Drone Centre, tells Ukrainska Pravda: "The primary objective is to disrupt their ability to launch drones, so that they are unable to launch them for an extended period. This also affects the overall coordination of their actions and the cohesion of their units. It also makes it easier for our air defence units to engage aerial assets, because there are generally fewer of them."
There are several ways to disrupt drone launches: striking launchers and storage facilities, or creating an aerial threat over the droneport. The attacks can force launches to be postponed indefinitely, while the destruction of infrastructure can reduce the overall number of drones launched.
According to Falco, launch pads and storage garages are among the easiest targets to strike: they are stationary, and there may not always be personnel nearby. But the value of hitting static targets depends on the circumstances and the overall strategy. If a garage or warehouse is packed with explosives or drones, then it makes sense to strike it.
Over the past two years, Ukraine's defence forces have stepped up attacks on Russian droneports. Alongside DAP and Tsimbulova, they have repeatedly targeted sites at Navlya, Hvardiiske, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and elsewhere. The strikes have hit warehouses, launchers, garages and drones left out in the open.
In the latest attack on Tsimbulova, on 21 September, Ukrainian strikes hit a bunker used to store combat drones. One strike penetrated the bunker, and another caused an explosion on the surface. Separate strikes also hit drones near the launch sites.
The strategy behind the strikes has also evolved. Ukraine is no longer targeting only storage, preparation and launch sites, but has also begun striking relay stations used to control Geran and Gerbera drones. UAV ground control stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trubchevsk, Russia, and in the temporarily occupied settlements of Zaliznyi Port, Skadovsk, Chornomorsk and Olenivka.
These facilities are important too, but Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces have another target in their sights: the drone operators themselves.
"The most difficult target there is also the most valuable one: the operator," Falco says. "They don't stay near the launch sites for very long. So when you take out the people launching the drones, you're taking away a scarce resource. There aren't many operators to begin with, and the enemy then has to spend even more money training new crews."
Military personnel are not the only people involved in launching Russian drones. Staff from Alabuga take part in the process on a daily basis too. In its study of Russian drone launch sites, the Molfar Intelligence Institute released several classified Alabuga documents.
According to the documents, Alabuga employees complained about "unjustified risk" after a Ukrainian attack on a major droneport in Oryol Oblast in December 2024. They said they were expected to continue working even though Russian air defence systems could not prevent strikes on the launch sites. Many employees said they wanted to leave the sites – and Alabuga itself.
Employees were threatened that they would be shot in the knees if they did not come to work, and were forced to turn up. Apart from Alabuga staff, local residents are also enlisted to assemble drones. Staff at droneports, however, complain about the low efficiency of their work.
Meanwhile, keeping droneports out of operation requires constant pressure on Russian positions.
Falco concludes: "If we want to keep the pressure on, we need to increase the scale of our strikes. The more we can hit, the better. As a country, we are constantly moving towards the level we need. But it's not just about strikes. We also have to think about how the enemy may respond and plan our operations accordingly."
Another factor that could significantly disrupt the operation of Russian droneports would be the use of Ukraine's own ballistic missiles. Their speed and penetrating power could allow them to target drone operators during launches – as has already happened at Donetsk airport – and destroy underground depots.

Ukraine business sentiment dips slightly in Sept – National Bank
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:36:37 EEST
18:36:37 KST

The Business Activity Expectations Index (BAEI), which the National Bank calculates monthly on a scale where readings from 0 to 50 are negative and those from 50 to 100 are positive, fell to 48.2 in September 2026 from 48.3 a month earlier and 50.4 a year earlier.
"The further deterioration of the security situation, the destruction of logistics, production and warehouse facilities, rising business costs driven by higher fuel prices, the limited domestic supply of goods and services, a shortage of skilled labor, and a slight worsening of exchange rate expectations constrained businesses’ economic activity," the NBU explained the result on its website.
Positive factors included a stable energy supply situation, a strong harvest and the development of new logistics routes.
Among other things, industrial companies resumed positive assessments of their performance amid an improvement in the situation in manufacturing and stability in the energy sector: the sectoral index in September was 51.0, compared with 47.3 in August this year and 49.1 in September last year. Unlike the previous month, industrial companies expected an increase in the volume of products manufactured and new orders for products, including export orders. An increase in inventories of raw materials and supplies was also expected. At the same time, subdued assessments of the volume of work in progress (unfulfilled orders) and inventories of finished products persisted.
After six months of positive sentiment, construction companies gave a restrained assessment of their current business activity, taking into account the suspension of state funding for road and infrastructure reconstruction, the seasonal nature of construction work and rising expenses: the sectoral index fell to 48.8 in September from 50.7 in August and 50.0 in September 2025. The National Bank said construction companies continued to expect an increase in construction volumes, new orders and purchases of raw materials and supplies, although at a slower pace. Respondents expected growth in purchases of contractors' services to slow amid further increases in their costs. At the same time, subdued assessments regarding the availability of contractors eased.
Retail and wholesale trade companies had the most subdued expectations among the sectors surveyed regarding their current activity due to the continued destruction of warehouse complexes, as well as costly and complicated logistics: the sectoral index fell to 45.9 in September from 47.5 in August this year and 54.0 in September 2025. Trading companies expected further declines in turnover and purchases of goods for sale, as well as inventories/stocks of goods for sale. Respondents expected trading margins to decline further.
Service-sector companies also gave a more subdued assessment of their performance, taking into account further destruction of logistics and warehouse infrastructure, higher fuel prices and a shortage of skilled workers: the sectoral index stood at 47.3 in September, compared with 49.5 in August and 49.4 in September 2025. Respondents assessed the volume of services provided as being at the previous month's level, while, unlike in August, they expected a decline in the volume of new orders and the volume of services in progress.
"Most respondents in all sectors expected growth rates to accelerate for both purchase prices/prices of raw materials and supplies and prices/tariffs for their own products/services, as well as the cost of goods purchased for resale," the NBU added.
The labor market situation remains mixed: only construction companies continued to expect an increase in their total number of employees, while companies in other sectors expected staff reductions, most notably in the services sector.
The monthly business survey was conducted from September 3 to 22, 2026. A total of 588 companies participated. Of the companies surveyed, 43.0% were industrial companies, 25.9% were service-sector companies, 24.7% were trading companies and 6.5% were construction companies; 31.6% of respondents were large companies, 29.1% medium-sized and 39.3% small. Among the companies surveyed, 34.5% conduct both export and import operations, 8.2% conduct only export operations, 18.5% only import operations, and 38.8% do not conduct foreign economic operations.

Global markets are trading on a mixed trend even though US macroeconomic data fueled expectations that the Federal Reserve may postpone its rate hikes.
The US economy grew 2.2% year-on-year in the second quarter, above the preliminary estimates of 1.5%.
The core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, the Fed’s inflation indicator excluding food and energy, rose 0.2% month-on-month and 3% on an annual basis in August, above the 0.3% monthly rise estimates but below the 3.3% annual growth expectations. The index followed a 0.1% month-on-month and 3% annual increase in July.
The US PCE grew above expectations by 0.9% on a monthly basis but rose below estimates by 0.2% year-on-year.
Private sector employment surpassed market expectations by rising 90,000.
The Fed is expected to make a soft landing in its policy given the strong data, while the downward trend in inflation showed the American economy remains resilient and the bank may not be forced to hike rates any time soon, analysts say.
The Fed’s likelihood to raise rates in October fell from 70% to 38% following the data release, according to money market estimates.
Meanwhile, the impact of surging diesel prices in September has yet to be reflected in the data, causing uncertainties to persist over whether inflationary pressures will ease.
Interest rates will remain at high levels despite the lower-than-expected inflation and better-than-expected growth and ADP private-sector employment figures, dampening risk appetite.
The US 10-Year Treasury bond yield hit its highest since 2007 at 5.31%, while the 30-year yield topped 5.65%.
Despite easing rate hike expectations in October, the Fed is still estimated to continue with these hikes at subsequent meetings, driving up Treasury bond yields.
The US dollar rose to 101.7 on Thursday, reaching its highest level since June 24, supported by the rise in yields.
Gold rose 0.7% to $4,184 per ounce and December-delivery Brent crude fell 1.4% to $96.6 a barrel.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump said former Fed chair Jerome Powell should be made to resign from the Board of Governors due to cost overruns in the bank’s building renovation project.
Trump also said South Korea plans to invest up to $200 billion in major US energy projects.
He is also considering a ban on diesel exports but he later acknowledged this would affect gas prices.
At the same time, Fed board member Lisa Cook said inflation remained above target for over five years, pledging to bring inflation back to the target level while preserving the labor market’s strength.
The Fed finalized changes to its annual stress test of large bank finances to increase transparency and public accountability, while reducing volatility in capital requirements linked to these tests.
Stock markets
The New York Stock Exchange closed Wednesday on a mixed trend due to the selling pressure in the bond market despite inflation coming in below estimates.
US chipmaker Micron Technology’s shares rose 0.6% in after-hours trading due to its better-than-expected earnings.
The average interest rate on 30-year mortgages rose 7.3% last week in the US, reaching the highest level since November 2023.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.86% and the S&P 500 dropped 0.25%, while the Nasdaq gained 0.24% on Wednesday. American indexes started Thursday on a positive trend.
Meanwhile, European stock markets traded lower on Wednesday amid rising energy costs fueling inflation concerns and pressuring the bond market.
Germany’s annual inflation rose above expectations to 3.3% in September due to escalating Middle East conflict driving up energy costs.
The European Central Bank (ECB) is more likely to continue its tight monetary policy given this data.
The UK economy grew 0.5% quarter-on-quarter and 1.4% on an annual basis in the second quarter, exceeding expectations.
The Bank of England (BoE) is expected to hike rates with an 85% possibility, money market estimates show.
The UK’s FTSE 100 fell 0.29%, Germany’s DAX 40 declined 0.79%, France’s CAC 40 dropped 0.89%, and Italy’s FTSE MIB 30 was down 0.84% on Wednesday. European indexes opened Thursday on a negative trend.
Near Thursday’s close, Asian equity markets traded higher as Fed rate hike expectations eased and Micron’s better-than-expected earnings positively impacted chipmaker shares in Japan and South Korea.
Japan’s manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) reached 54.1 in September, within estimates.
South Korea’s exports exceeded expectations by rising 83.5% on an annual basis, driven by record levels of semiconductor shipments as global artificial intelligence (AI) investment continues to boost chip demand.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 2.9% and South Korea’s Kospi climbed 1.9% near Thursday’s close, while trading is suspended in Chinese and Hong Kong markets due to a holiday.

Burnham ‘really concerned’ if Man City’s UAE owners sell club after breaking rules

LONDON — U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be “really concerned” should Manchester City’s Emirati owners sell up after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.
An independent commission found the club guilty of a majority of the charges they faced, including arranging “sham contracts” with commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise more than £830 million of secret funding.

Advertisement

Exclusive: Inside Lebanon's 200-page Israeli war crimes dossier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:34:46 UTC
18:34:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Inside Lebanon's 200-page dossier on Israeli war crimes
A report obtained exclusively by The New Arab documents suspected Israeli war crimes and crimes against humanity during the latest war on Lebanon, detailing attacks on civilians, journalists, medical personnel and infrastructure, as well as widespread destruction and forced displacement.
The more than 200-page report, compiled by Lebanon's National Committee for International Humanitarian Law, was handed to Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri on Tuesday by Deputy Prime Minister Tarek Mitri, who heads the committee.
The findings come despite Lebanon agreeing to waive its right to pursue legal action against Israel over war crimes under a framework ceasefire agreement, with Article 13 of the agreement, signed in Washington on 26 June, requiring Lebanon to end "all hostile or harmful actions in international political or legal forums" against Israel.
According to information obtained exclusively by The New Arab, the report focuses on Israeli violations committed after 2 March 2026, placing them within the broader context of the conflict in Lebanon since 8 October 2023.
It examines numerous incidents classified by the committee as war crimes and crimes against humanity, supported by an independent evidence file containing screenshots, original links, statements from official bodies and human rights organisations, published photographs, maps, witness testimonies, press materials and other sources used to assess the incidents in accordance with international standards.
The report also outlines the methodology adopted by the National Committee for International Humanitarian Law to collect information and document and verify violations. It evaluates Israeli accounts of the incidents and provides legal assessments and analysis of the documented violations.
The violations examined include the destruction of infrastructure, bridges and crossings; attacks on cultural property, civilians, civil defence personnel, rescue teams, journalists and media workers; attacks on hospitals, health facilities and medical and humanitarian services; attacks on civilian property; and forced displacement.
The committee faced significant difficulties in compiling the report, particularly because the Lebanese authorities had not opened investigations into the crimes and therefore had no official investigative records. In many cases, the names of those killed were unavailable, with only casualty figures recorded.
The lack of cooperation from relevant ministries, which failed to provide the assistance required to complete the documentation, created further obstacles.
Despite these challenges, the committee intensified its efforts to document the violations and prepare a comprehensive report that could support future legal proceedings against Israel.
Killing of journalist Amal Khalil
Among the cases examined was Israel's killing of Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil during attacks on the southern town of Al-Tayri on 22 April 2026.
Journalist Zeinab Faraj, who was accompanying Khalil, was also wounded in the attack.
The report concluded that the incident constituted a blatant violation of international humanitarian law on several grounds, including the deliberate and direct targeting of Khalil, who was left surrounded at the site for several hours while emergency teams were prevented from reaching her, despite her still being alive.
Several organisations, including Human Rights Watch, described the 22 April attack as a deliberate targeting of civilians that would constitute a war crime.
They also highlighted the Israeli army's obstruction of rescue efforts, including the use of a stun grenade dropped from a drone, which forced Lebanese Red Cross personnel to withdraw temporarily without rescuing Khalil or providing potentially life-saving medical assistance.
Deadly Israeli attacks on 8 April
Another major case examined in the report was Israel's large-scale bombardment of Lebanon on 8 April 2026, which the committee found had involved attacks in the absence of military targets.
Israeli forces launched around 100 attacks within a short period, striking Beirut, its southern suburbs, Mount Lebanon, the Bekaa Valley and southern Lebanon.
The attacks killed more than 303 people and wounded over 1,200 others, including dozens of women and children.
Lebanon subsequently submitted an urgent complaint to the UN Security Council over the 8 April bombardment and Israeli attacks on medical and emergency facilities since 2 March 2026 as a blatant violation of the principles of international law.
UN experts, in a statement published by the UN Human Rights Council, also condemned Israel's bombardment of Lebanon on 8 April, saying it was unlawful aggression and a campaign of indiscriminate bombing.
Systematic destruction and forced displacement
The report also documents the systematic destruction of Lebanese cities and villages, including the destruction of cultural heritage, which it classifies as crimes against humanity and serious violations of international humanitarian law.
Among the examples cited is the extensive bulldozing and destruction of the southern city of Bint Jbeil. Satellite imagery, maps and field reports document the scale of the damage to the city's landmarks, infrastructure and residential areas.
The committee also found that Israel had violated fundamental principles of international humanitarian law through unlawful evacuation orders that triggered unprecedented waves of mass displacement, emptied entire villages of their residents and left them uninhabitable.
According to the report, the available evidence indicates that Israeli attacks were indiscriminate, particularly where their effects extended beyond the intended targets into wider civilian areas or where weapons with wide-ranging effects were deployed in environments in which their impact could not be contained.
The evidence also provides sufficient information for a preliminary assessment of the weapons used, with the documented damage consistent with the use of highly explosive munitions, most of them dropped from aircraft on civilian residential areas.
Geographical analysis identifies three main areas where evidence of the violations is concentrated.
The first is central Beirut, where footage of direct attacks, images recorded in their aftermath and victims' testimonies provide evidence of strikes in densely populated residential neighbourhoods.
The second is Beirut's southern suburbs, where repeated footage of attacks, widespread destruction and testimonies documenting continued bombardment and displacement indicate that civilian areas were subjected to sustained military pressure.
The third is southern Lebanon, where attacks on villages, damage to infrastructure and civilian testimonies reveal a similar pattern of harm inflicted on residents.
The committee concluded that these findings raise serious concerns about violations of the fundamental principles governing the conduct of hostilities, as established by the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law.
The report also examines a series of Israeli attacks on major bridges and crossings over the Litani River and its tributaries, as well as roads leading to them, during March and April 2026.
According to the committee, the evidence indicates that the destruction constituted unlawful attacks on protected civilian infrastructure and crossings vital to the civilian population, violating the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution, as well as obligations concerning the facilitation of humanitarian relief.
Other incidents examined include attacks on medical services in the town of Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district, civil defence personnel in Majdal Zoun in the Tyre district and a residential apartment in the hills of Ain Saadeh on 5 April 2026.
Legal avenues for prosecuting Israel
Separately, the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies in Beirut, headed by former minister Nasser Yassin, has been documenting Israeli violations and assessing the cost of the war on Lebanon, particularly the direct and indirect damage inflicted on the country's vital sectors.
During a discussion hosted by the centre on 27 August under the title "Israeli violations of international humanitarian law", Mitri addressed the legal options available for pursuing accountability for Israeli crimes, including the possibility of bringing cases before the International Criminal Court (ICC).
"Lebanon is not a party to the Rome Statute, which established the International Criminal Court, preventing the Lebanese state from resorting to it to prosecute Israel under the current circumstances," he said.
Mitri nevertheless explained that the ICC could, under specific circumstances and through established legal mechanisms, exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed during a particular period, even if the state concerned had not fully joined the Rome Statute.
"The inability of the Lebanese state at present to turn to the International Criminal Court does not remove the right of Lebanese individuals to pursue Israel before several European courts, such as those in Spain, Belgium and France, where some European judicial systems allow, under specific conditions, the filing of cases related to international crimes or serious violations," he said.
He stressed that some individuals had already begun taking such steps.
Mitri also called on civil society associations, human rights organisations and other bodies that have documented Israeli violations to submit their research and reports to the government.
He said coordinating official and civil society efforts was essential to consolidating the evidence and preparing legal cases to pursue accountability for Israel's actions.

Kyiv said it was Moscow's opening salvo in an expected campaign to try to knock out heating and power as winter approaches.
A recent increase in strikes has prompted fears about another winter with little or no power or heating, after similar attacks last year when temperatures plunged to -20C.
Some emergency power outages were implemented in Kyiv on Wednesday night.
Ukrenergo urged domestic consumers to switch "intensive energy use" to daytime hours and said "economical" use was needed in some areas in the evening.

Russia launched 107 drones at Ukraine overnight into Thursday, including 63 jet-powered drones, Ukraine’s Air Force said in its daily report.

The Air Force said the attack was still ongoing, with more drones in the air.

====================================================================================================

The Secrets of the US Spyware King
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Spyware maker Paragon Solutions has long positioned itself as the good guy in an industry seemingly filled with bad ones, vowing to never sell its mobile spyware to authoritarian regimes or ones with poor human rights records. It also promises to cut off any customer caught misusing its products against journalists, dissidents, or other non-legitimate targets.
Yet weeks after Paragon, then Israeli-owned, was acquired by the US equity firm AE Industrial Partners in December 2024 and merged with REDLattice—an American offensive cyber firm owned by AE that this week announced plans to go public—WhatsApp alleged that Paragon’s Graphite spyware was used to infect the phones of more than 60 individuals in more than 20 countries, including journalists and activists. Most of the targets were not identified, but the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab named two journalists and two activists in Italy.
Italian authorities denied misuse. Paragon and its new US owners, despite their zero-tolerance policy for customer abuse of their software, initially declined to comment on the allegations, and reportedly was exploring potential legal action against WhatsApp after the company sent a cease-and-desist letter to Paragon. Within a week, however, Paragon had canceled the two contracts it had with Italy’s domestic and foreign intelligence agencies.
From the outside, it seemed Paragon must have conducted an investigation and verified the allegations before canceling the contracts. But Paragon and RedLattice’s new CEO, Andrew Boyd, now says in an exclusive and surprisingly candid interview with WIRED that the company simply “fired” Italy because it “just was not worth it, from a risk perspective, to maintain the relationship” following the allegations.
In other words, there was no Paragon investigation and no interest in conducting one to determine if the allegations were true—Italian government investigators concluded they were not. Paragon didn’t even follow up with WhatsApp or Citizen Lab to obtain details about the alleged abuse and determine if any contracts in the other countries named by WhatsApp should be canceled as well. More damning, according to critics, is what Boyd revealed next: Paragon has no technical way to know if customers misuse its software, because it can’t see who customers target or the data they extract from targeted devices. It can only learn about misuse if customers admit to it or third parties uncover it. He says WhatsApp and Citizen Lab did the company a great service when they exposed the alleged misuse last year.
Paragon also doesn’t have a “kill switch” to disable customers when misuse occurs. All they can do is halt customers’ 24-hour support and system “updates.” But Boyd says the updates, the nature of which he won’t specify, are frequent and essential to using the spyware, and without them the system is rendered ineffective in about 12 hours.
“Things start falling apart quite quickly,” he says.
Boyd’s comments mark the first time a Paragon executive has spoken in detail about the secretive company or its handling of the Italian affair. He agreed to speak with WIRED now because he says more public discussion is needed about the offensive cyber industry and what it means for a US company to operate responsibly in this space. Prior to the interview, REDLattice founder John Ayers wrote in an email that they were “not looking for a favorable write-up.”
“If the honest assessment is still damning, that's a conversation we're prepared to have,” he wrote.
But Boyd’s admissions reveal that despite priding itself on being better than competitors, Paragon/RedLattice has less oversight and accountability than its most significant one—NSO Group, the Pegasus spyware maker, which has been excoriated for selling its tool to Saudi Arabia and other countries with poor human rights records. According to NSO’s transparency reports, which the company began publishing in recent years in response to criticism, it sets up infrastructure and portals that customers use to infect targets and, like Paragon, can’t see who customers target or detect misuse. But it claims it does have a kill switch to disable a customer’s access to the spyware if allegations of misuse arise, and NSO says its systems keep “tamper-proof” logs to record user activity. Customers are contractually obligated to provide these to NSO if allegations of misuse occur or else face “immediate suspension.”
By contrast, Boyd says Paragon customers can enable logging on some systems if they opt to, but Paragon has no access to the logs, nor does it want access. Instead, he says, government oversight bodies can use the logs to investigate allegations of misuse among their agencies, as an Italian parliamentary committee did last year in the case of the Citizen Lab allegations. However, this raises the possibility that a government investigator could lie about misuse if they uncover it in logs.
Rather than see Paragon’s lack of access to logs as an accountability problem, however, Boyd describes it as a selling point: No one would buy their products if the company could see a customer’s sensitive targeting information or logs that contain it.
“There's a balancing act between privacy and security and being able to ensure that our customers are using these things correctly,” Boyd says. “And I think we've landed on the best balance.”
That balance is achieved mostly through careful vetting of customers, he says, and rejecting any country that might be prone to abusing the spyware.
John Scott-Railton, senior researcher at Citizen Lab, which has tracked government misuse of commercial spyware for years, calls the revelations astonishing and the lack of mandatory logging “reckless.”
“What Paragon is saying in several substantial ways means [it has] less oversight, less transparency, less contractual protection against abuses than NSO Group,” he says. “It’s exactly the opposite of the picture that Paragon has painted for itself for years. The CEO admitting that his customers won’t tolerate oversight is refreshing honesty: Accountability is bad for business. And it signals to lawmakers and regulators that the spyware industry cannot be trusted to self-regulate."
Scott-Railton also finds it ironic that Paragon relies on Citizen Lab and others to uncover customer misuse when Paragon actively works to hide its spyware on infected devices and prevent discovery—which inherently includes potential misuse.
“We only find a very, very, very small subset [of infections], and the total numbers are always larger,” Scott-Railton says. “These companies spend millions trying to hide from us.”
US senator Ron Wyden tells WIRED that surveillance tools that lack oversight and transparency are “inevitably abused.”
“It’s easy to claim your powerful hacking tool isn’t being misused if you go out of your way to ensure you don’t know how customers use it,” Wyden says. “The fact that Paragon refuses to audit use of its tool, or even attempt to match the work of a small team of researchers at the Citizen Lab is a massive red flag.”
Israeli Intelligence Roots
Paragon was launched in 2019 by Israeli Brigadier General Ehud Schneorson, former commander of the Israeli military’s signals intelligence group, Unit 8200. He cofounded it with three other 8200 veterans and former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak. Two years later, the company reportedly had no customers but was developing Graphite and hoping to conquer the lucrative US market. But then the US government began cracking down on foreign spyware companies after NSO’s Pegasus and Candiru’s DevilsTongue tools were misused by their customers against government workers, journalists, dissidents, activists, and academics.
The US Commerce Department sanctioned both companies in 2021, and the Israeli government drastically cut the number of countries to which Israeli firms could sell spyware—from 102 countries to 37, excluding Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Morocco, and Mexico. Over a year later, the Biden administration and Congress imposed guardrails making it difficult for the US government to purchase foreign-made commercial spyware if it posed a national security risk or could be misused by foreign governments.
By then, Paragon reportedly already had a contract with the Drug Enforcement Agency to combat drug traffickers outside the US, but it otherwise could not “make any substantial headway” in the US, Boyd says. So the company began looking for a US buyer to overcome its foreign-ownership handicap. In December 2024, AE acquired it for $900 million. The result is a company that is now American on paper, but is still effectively Israeli. Paragon is a RedLattice company—though Paragon has no working website, and the RedLattice website currently doesn’t mention Paragon—but, according to Boyd, it retains its name and offices in Israel, where it has more than 600 employees. Any Paragon-built products still require licensing approval from the Israeli government to sell abroad, while RedLattice-made products sold to non-US customers are governed by US International Traffic in Arms Regulations.
Nonetheless, the US acquisition has served as an end-run around foreign-ownership guardrails. Once the AE deal closed, Boyd says, “everybody started talking” to them about Paragon products, and Paragon began looking to hire 150 new workers to handle its expected new business.
Ayers, the REDLattice founder, told WIRED in an email that prior to acquisition, REDLattice and AE spent more than two years in discussion with US and allied governments and “didn't move without their buy-in.” But asked whether the government pushed back on the acquisition, Boyd says there were no objections, and no one imposed conditions or governance requirements on them either.
“The US government in any form [was] never going to formally say … we approve this acquisition,” he says. “But they didn't have any discomfort with it … If the [National Security Council] said, ‘This would be a colossally bad idea,’ we probably wouldn't have gone through with it.”
Less than a year after Paragon merged with REDLattice, NSO Group and Candiru copied their savvy acquisition move. A US investment group acquired controlling ownership of NSO and appointed David Friedman, former US ambassador to Israel under President Donald Trump, as executive chairman. Candiru was acquired by the US-based Integrity Partners. Now all three companies are vying for US contracts.
Boyd, who became CEO of RedLattice and Paragon eight months after the acquisition, gives the companies an edge in the US market. As a former military intelligence officer, State Department diplomat, and director of the CIA’s Center for Cyber Intelligence until retiring in 2023, he has many US government, military, and intelligence community connections to help secure contracts.
During the interview, Boyd was open with many of WIRED’s questions, but also inexplicably opaque with others. He wouldn’t even, for example, confirm that Graphite is the name of a product the company sells or say how many products the combined companies possess. He says only that before the acquisition, Paragon had fewer than five products, and together they now have between five and 10. Some of these do “over-the-horizon” data collection (by hacking devices and systems remotely), while others require physical access to targeted devices. He bristles at calling the tools “spyware,” though. He considers them “defensive” tools since, broadly speaking, they help defend against national security and criminal threats. But in truth, they are designed for surveillance, espionage, and possibly even disruptive cyber operations.
Graphite, the only product ever publicly identified, extracts communications from chat applications, particularly encrypted messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Signal. This contrasts with NSO Group’s Pegasus, which can spy on all aspects of a mobile phone, including surreptitiously activating its microphone and camera to spy on targets. Reportedly, Graphite’s capabilities can be expanded through modules, though its full feature set is not publicly known.
WhatsApp and Citizen Lab have reported that Graphite uses a powerful zero-click zero-day exploit to infect phones without user awareness. Boyd won’t say if the companies hunt for zero-day vulnerabilities and develop their own exploits or purchase them from others, but says both Paragon and RedLattice have “substantial” research and development teams. RedLattice’s website says the company has more than 200 “vulnerability research experts.”
In addition to their products, Paragon and RedLattice build bespoke solutions for some customers, and some contracts provide customers with personnel who possess “appropriate clearances” to do a “variety” of tasks. Boyd won’t elaborate on the tasks but says his company doesn’t do offensive operations for customers; it just provides hardware and software. But after the Trump administration recently announced plans to contract with select private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against cybercriminal groups, he says RedLattice will pursue these contracts.
Customer Vetting
Without the ability to monitor customer activity and detect misuse, Paragon relies on its governance model to prevent abuse. This involves customer vetting and contractual deterrence. Customers, and the countries in which they reside, are vetted by an internal risk committee that Boyd and other board members chair using various criteria to determine if a prospective country or customer might have a negative business or reputational impact on the company.
“We don't want our products to be involved in things that they weren't intended to be used for,” he says.
Boyd wouldn’t provide a full list of the country-assessment criteria but mentioned several during the interview: political and government stability, human rights record, corruption-index ratings, strength of a country’s legal system, and whether a potential customer has a track record of adhering to its national laws. He says they lean more toward rejecting countries than approving them. They currently have between 20 and 30 countries on their approved list, and have more than 100 customers in 23 countries.
“I think there's some people that would argue that we're too conservative [about who we’ll sell to],” he says, but notes that “it's better to take a hit on revenue” than sell to countries that could prove detrimental in the long run. (Boyd says, for example, that canceling Italy’s two contracts cost the company “seven figures” in revenue. He would not specify the exact value, but Israeli media have estimated the contracts were worth “tens of millions of dollars.”) In the year since he became CEO, he says a “handful” of countries have been rejected as potential customers but won’t say which ones.
Paragon sells only to the US and select US allies (whether democratic or not), and only to national entities, not state or local governments and police forces. But being a US ally doesn’t guarantee a sale. They won’t sell to Saudi Arabia, even though it’s an ally. After the Saudi government reportedly used NSO’s Pegasus to spy on the fiancé and close associates of Washington Post opinion writer Jamal Khashoggi, who was murdered by Saudi government agents, the Israeli government reportedly asked Paragon to take over the Saudi Arabia contract from NSO Group, but Paragon reportedly refused. Boyd says they still won’t sell to Saudi Arabia, and also says the company has no commercial relationships with any country in the Middle East.
“I think there's very important national security reasons why [the US] would want a close relationship with the Saudis from a nation-state to nation-state level,” he says. But that “does not translate into … this private-sector company having a business relationship with them … I don't need to get into the why’s, because you probably know the why’s.”
They also won’t sell to Venezuela, even with President Nicolas Maduro gone. “There's too much chaos,” Boyd says, “and it wouldn't fit our risk calculus for other variables.”
Yet the company reportedly signed a lucrative contract in Singapore in 2023 worth tens of millions of dollars. Though an electoral democracy, Singapore imposes significant restrictions on free speech, media independence, and human rights.
The customer vetting, Boyd says, “usually works 99 out of 100 times” to eliminate those who might misuse their tools—the assumption being that if they choose only reputable customers, the customers they choose will act only reputably. For the remaining 1 in 100, the customer contracts and zero-tolerance policy are meant to deter misuse. These prohibit using the tools against journalists, civil society members, opposition politicians, and anyone else who is not the target of a legitimate intelligence or criminal investigation. Also embedded in any system sold to non-US customers is a block that prevents targeting of any person in the US—that is, any number that requires the US +1 country code to dial. US law enforcement agencies who have a warrant can get the block disabled, he says.
What if a US customer let a non-approved country use Graphite to spy on targets? During the first Trump administration, the CIA reportedly purchased NSO Group's Pegasus to give to an East African country to use. Boyd insists they would know if this occurred.
“We know where the system is, because we [help customers] install it and train [them on it] … And so we would know if it was not installed in the place where they intended it to be,” he insists.
Would they also know if a customer used the tool on their own infrastructure but to spy on behalf of another non-approved country? He says they would, because the majority of customers have similar intelligence, military, or law enforcement backgrounds to RedLattice and Paragon employees, and they have robust relationships with customers. They would have a “sixth sense” if something were “fishy” about a customer, he says.
Boyd insists that the fact that there has been only one allegation of misuse so far is evidence that the company’s vetting and governance model is effective. This, however, ignores the fact that the odds of someone uncovering misuse are low, especially because the company takes care to ensure its spyware won’t be easily detected on infected systems.
All of this, of course, leads to questions about US customers. Based on Paragon’s vetting criteria, some might wonder how the current Trump administration would meet them. Given reports of corruption, disregard for the rule of law, and Trump’s unveiled threats to use government power against political opponents, fears of misuse by US agencies are not irrational. Asked what the company would do if there were allegations of misuse by a US customer, Boyd said an inspector general or legislative committee would likely investigate the matter, and if they found concrete evidence of misuse, Congress or the company would likely take action.
A year after the acquisition, however, it’s unclear how much US sales have expanded. Shortly before the 2024 acquisition, Paragon signed a $2 million contract with Homeland Security Investigations, a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, to help dismantle foreign terrorist operations and disrupt fentanyl traffickers. And RedLattice has had long-standing contracts with the US Air Force. But no other government contracts for the companies show up in a search of public databases, though classified contracts likely would not appear. Boyd won’t identify customers but indicates the company is particularly interested in Pentagon and CIA contracts.
“There are offices across the national security enterprise that don't even know they need our product yet,” he says. “And I consider that an unaddressed market.”
