'It's coming for everything': Eddie Perfect on AI and his new satire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Eddie Perfect turns Molière satire Tartuffe into a black comedy about AI
Eddie Perfect doesn't want his teenage daughters talking to AI chatbots.
"We have a rule in our house that no one talks to the machines," he says.
He sees the technology as outsourcing thinking and cognition, which he reckons is particularly harmful to young people.
"Maybe everyone should have access to AI once they turn 25, and that would be perfect," he says.
"I really hate it because I think it's coming for everything."
It's something Perfect has been thinking about a lot as he works on his latest show, a new adaptation of 17th-century French playwright Molière's Tartuffe for Melbourne's Malthouse Theatre.
The original play, otherwise known as The Impostor, or The Hypocrite, is a satire about a charlatan, posing as a religious man, Tartuffe, who manipulates his way into foolish Orgon's home and family.
Perfect's answer to a quasi-religious figure for a modern audience? A hairdressing AI robot.
"I can't write anything but what I know, so what's been really fun is to meet Tartuffe where I am in my life," he says.
"And I love a good sci-fi. I love synthetic humans and the idea of robots and machines and our relationship with them into the future.
"So, it just felt right to make Tartuffe a robot."
Perfect's The Tartuffe, in which he will also star as Orgon, is one of eight plays in Malthouse's 2027 season, the first from artistic director Dean Bryant
The season is notable for being all-Australian, with seven plays making their world premiere, including an adaptation of Charlotte Wood's Booker-shortlisted novel Stone Yard Devotional and the second play from Logie-winning actor Thomas Weatherall.
It reflects Bryant's approach to the top job, which he took over from now-Adelaide Festival director Matthew Lutton in October 2025.
"We want to have new experiences," Bryant says. "We want to see things we haven't seen on stage before."
While it's thrilling for Bryant to have a season made up of new Australian work, it also feels scary.
"New work is the hardest work to make," he says.
"It's dealing with the unknown … But when it comes off, there's nothing like a new play."
Creativity and AI
The announcement of Perfect's The Tartuffe arrives as the federal government considers a proposal to water down copyright protections in an effort to lure AI companies to Australia, angering local artists and creatives.
Perfect is impressed by the ways AI can be used in areas like translation and learning new skills but is frustrated by how it came about — being trained for free on human creativity — and that it is now being deployed to replace that creative process.
"The game of creativity is who can sit in the discomfort of not knowing what to do the longest," he says.
"If you know there's AI there that can give you an answer, any answer, to stop the discomfort of not having anything on the page, then I think you've lost the game.
"You've got to go to the fire for creativity."
For Bryant, there's also something interesting about taking a story about a family trying and failing to connect with each other through technology and putting that into a theatre, a space that can't be replicated by AI.
"[Theatre] is a communal experience where we still voluntarily put our phones away," he says.
"It's such a beautiful kind of metaphor to go, you've all come here to have the human experience of this, and we're telling you a cautionary tale about where not to find connection."
While The Tartuffe may have a serious message, Perfect stresses it's a "front-footed black comedy", which might entice new audiences to the theatre.
"I know that I and people like Dean are always looking for new ways to connect with new audiences and to engender a greater sense of ownership or belonging from people for theatre," he says.
"It's not a big shiny gold edifice with fancy carpets you're always worried about getting dirty.
"It's a place of welcome where you should be able to go and see an Australian take on a classic or a new Australian story and have a conversation about what it is to be Australian and alive right now."
Adaptations that explode expectations
The Tartuffe is one of four adaptations in Malthouse's 2027 season, alongside Stone Yard Devotional; Henry James's The Turn of the Screw; and Gone with the Wind, from theatre collective Bloomshed.
Bryant says the appeal of adaptation is about more than familiarity.
"You get a whiff of a context of the evening, a sense of what you're going to see," he says.
"Our job is to then explode that."
Artist Tamara Dean will collaborate with director Sarah Goodes and adaptor Joanna Murray-Smith on Stone Yard Devotional to help create the visual world of the novel, which follows a woman who leaves her home and marriage in the city to live in an enclosed religious community on the Monaro plains in regional NSW.
It will star Lisa McCune as the unnamed protagonist, alongside Catherine McClements as a celebrity nun who visits the community.
"There's so much about atmosphere and the plains and the way the nunnery feels [in the novel]," Bryant explains.
"[Goodes] wants it to feel like [the show] crosses over with art installation, and for the sound design to be as immersive and important in the dramaturgy as the text … That will give the kind of transcendent feeling of the book."
Meanwhile. The Turn of the Screw has been turned into a one-woman show, starring AACTA winner Tuuli Narkle (ABC TV's Mystery Road: Origin).
Bryant emphasises Narkle will be doing more than playing all the characters in the Victorian gothic novel about a governess looking after two children in a country house.
"She's creating an incredibly chilling atmosphere," he says.
"It's a really big ask to be a solo performer taking us into a world where there may or not be ghosts."
Bryant stresses the technical skill and artistry needed to build a world entirely on your own.
"It's the ultimate challenge for an actor to be given a one-person show," he says.
Building capacity in the sector
The collaboration with Bloomshed is part of Malthouse's commitment to developing the local theatre sector.
"We scour the independent scene for makers that have developed a unique voice, and we are actively putting at least one of those companies in our seasons each year," Bryant says.
"[That's] to either elevate a piece they've put on in an independent venue and scale it up for the main stage, or to build with them a new piece for the main stage."
This year, Bloomshed brought their new take on Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, which took aim at the housing crisis and replaced Mr Bennet with a pot plant, to Malthouse, after it premiered in 2025 as part of Darebin Arts Speakeasy.
Next year, Malthouse will be helping the collective to create from scratch its version of Gone with the Wind, which will look at the relationship between resource ownership and power.
"Melbourne has always had a really interesting independent scene, and they fizzle out if they don't get more of a spotlight on them," Bryant says. "It's our job to give them that lens."
But it's about more than simply shining a light on the talent that already exists in Melbourne.
Instead, it's about building capacity within the sector.
"By moving into a company that's set up to create this kind of work, they upskill really quickly," Bryant explains.
"It elevates their practice as well, which makes them better inclined to have longevity."
Capacity-building at Malthouse in 2027 also means giving opportunities to young writers to debut new work, including Yve Blake (Fangirls) and Thomas Weatherall (Blue).
Blake's play Jackpot is about intergenerational inequality, while Weatherall's play Lucy is an intimate relationship drama.
"They both think very deeply about where we find ourselves and yet write from the age they actually are," Bryant says.
"They understand the generation they're in."

Bristling with steel spikes and guarded by a bomber drone, two Ukrainian tanks charged Russian infiltrators and lived to tell the tale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:29:24 UTC
18:29:24 KST

- The 475th Assault Regiment found a new way to protect its tanks from Russian drones
- It surrounded its up-armored tanks with drones of its own
- During a recent counter-infiltration mission, two 475th Assault Regiment tanks were shepherded into battle by three different drone types
Russian infiltrators have been slipping into villages and towns along Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia, likely aiming to draw Ukrainian troops away from the bigger fights farther south around the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Desperate to clear out the infiltrators without dedicating too many precious infantry to the task, the Ukrainian 475th Assault Regiment formed a unique team: two heavily up-armored tanks plus three different types of drone. The drones scouted ahead of the tanks and protected them as they trundled through Russia's own drone kill zone on their way to a point-blank clash with Russian troops.
In this mission, the blend of mechanized and unmanned forces worked: the tanks accomplished their mission and survived to fight another day. If the tank-drone pairing keeps working, expect it to become more common all along the 1,200-km gray zone as Ukraine struggles with a deepening shortage of manpower.
It's unclear what kinds of tanks the 475th Assault Regiment operates. It is clear how the regiment protects the tanks from ever-present Russian drones. The unit wraps the tanks in metal cages and then welds hundreds of metal spines on the cages. The spines trigger incoming explosive drones at a safe distance from the tank's hull. The cage supports the spines and catches any drones the spines may miss.
We call these kinds of tanks "hedgehog tanks." The Russians developed the hedgehog application but, seeing that it worked, deflecting potentially dozens of drones at a time, the Ukrainians copied it.
Hedgehog helpers
But even the best-protected hedgehog tank might struggle to get through the enemy's kill zone when that kill zone may include bomber and one-way attack drones in the air and loitering ambush drones waiting on the ground as well as mines and other threats.
Sometimes the best defense against a drone is another drone, and the 475th Assault Regiment put that truism into practice. To shepherd those two hedgehog tanks into battle with Russian infiltrators in the village of Vilkhuvatka, in Kharkiv Oblast 9 km from the border with Russia, the regiment deployed a Vampire heavy bomber drone, at least one explosive first-person-view (FPV) quadcopter, and at least one surveillance quadcopter.
Trending Now
The surveillance drones could scout ahead. The bomber drone could blast mines and loitering ambush drones. The FPVs could intercept incoming enemy FPVs. The layered protection was effective. As evident in the 475th Assault Regiment's video depicting the two-tank counter-assault, the tanks took multiple hits from Russian drones and mines, but not enough hits to slow them down.
Both tanks reached an intersection inside Vilkhuvatka, fired their cannons at nearby Russian infiltrators, and then withdrew.
It should come as no surprise that the 475th Assault Regiment is pioneering mixed formations of drones and tanks. The regiment recently partnered with the 1st Assault Regiment to develop new "multi-domain" tactics combining ground, air, and cyber forces. "We came to the conclusion that fighting in only one domain makes no sense," said "Perun," the 1st Assault Regiment commander. "We'd simply lose because the enemy would bring another domain into play."
The key takeaway is that, despite the serious threat that drones and mines pose to tanks in the fifth year of Russia's wider war on Ukraine, tanks can still fight, win, and survive—if they have plenty of support from the same kinds of drones that, in enemy hands, vex them along every kilometer of disputed terrain. The tank isn't dead yet. It just needs a little help.

Türkiye’s capital markets regulator approves interim payments to investors in funds under liquidation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:27:38 UTC
18:27:38 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye’s Capital Markets Board (SPK) has approved interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish liras ($20,394) per eligible investor in funds established by Tera, Pusula, Atlas and Hedef portfolio management companies that are undergoing liquidation.
According to the board’s latest bulletin, the payments will be made to all fund unit holders whose account reconciliation has been completed, as advances against the amounts they will ultimately receive once liquidation is finalized.
Payments will be based on each investor’s net investment amount calculated by the Central Securities Depository (MKK).
Investors with net investments below 1 million liras will receive that amount, while payments to those with net investments of 1 million liras or more will be capped at 1 million liras.
The process will begin with money market funds. Fund units will remain outstanding during the interim payment stage and will be redeemed when final liquidation payments are made.
The board also set liquidation priorities for funds established by A1 Capital, Bulls and Pardus portfolio management companies.
Money market funds will be liquidated first, with other funds processed in descending order of investor numbers.
Once liquidation is completed, funds outside the liquidation process whose trading was suspended under the board’s Sept. 17 decisions may reopen simultaneously across all distribution channels for purchases and/or sales.
The founding portfolio management companies will determine reopening dates and trading conditions, taking into account portfolio composition, liquidity, market conditions and investors’ interests.
The SPK said last month that 131 investment funds set for liquidation hold approximately 826 billion liras across 455,758 investors.
“Our institutions are continuing their efforts regarding the troubled funds in close coordination and with utmost diligence,” Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said in post on X on Nov. 1.
“The necessary steps are being taken to ensure that investors receive payments as quickly as possible and to the greatest extent possible,” he added.
“The strengthened macroeconomic fundamentals and the measures already implemented will help limit the impact of recent developments on the financial system and the real economy. Through the steps we have taken, our capital markets will emerge stronger, healthier, and more resilient,” said Şimşek.
Meanwhile, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said the second meeting of the Fund Coordination Board, established by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, would be held today.
In a statement on social media, Yılmaz said a roadmap had been determined and that all relevant institutions were taking coordinated and concrete steps within their areas of responsibility.
He stressed that every stage of the process would be managed within the framework of the law, adding that the authorities’ main objective was to protect the rights of the public and investors while taking the most effective measures against manipulators and speculators who obtained unfair gains through unlawful transactions.
Yılmaz said Türkiye’s economic fundamentals and the structure of its capital markets remained strong, adding that the country’s capital markets would emerge stronger once problems affecting a limited segment of the fund industry were resolved.
Separately, the SPK announced that “Voluntary Return Accounts” had been opened at Birleşik Fon Bankası on behalf of the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) for individuals willing to voluntarily return excessive profits obtained from share sales conducted before the liquidation decisions affecting investment funds.
The regulator said the amounts deposited into the accounts would be allocated solely to the liquidation assets of the relevant fund and could not be transferred to another fund or account.
The funds will be transferred to state-owned Ziraat Bankası and private lender İşbank, which have been appointed to carry out the liquidation process, and will be used for payments to investors holding participation shares in the affected funds.

Finance Ministry aims to cut record high gas prices by 50 agorot, needs attorney-general's approval
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:27:35 UTC
18:27:35 KST

The Finance Ministry is seeking to cut gasoline prices by another 50 agorot per liter for one month after the price rose overnight Thursday to a record NIS 8.27 per liter, with the move still awaiting approval from the attorney-general.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich intends to introduce the additional reduction, which, if approved and completed, is expected to bring the price of a liter of gasoline down to about NIS 7.77, almost exactly the price motorists paid in September.
The price of self-service 95-octane gasoline rose by 52 agorot from September's NIS 7.75 per liter, following a reduction in the excise tax. Motorists choosing full service will pay an additional 26 agorot per liter, bringing the price to NIS 8.53.
The previous record was NIS 8.25 per liter, set in September 2012. At the beginning of September, the price of gasoline returned to exactly that level, before Smotrich intervened and reduced the excise tax by 50 agorot per liter.
That reduction brought the price down to NIS 7.75, but a sharp rise in global gasoline prices and the strengthening of the US dollar wiped out the entire reduction in less than a month and pushed the price two agorot above the previous record.
Steep increase in gas prices come from international markets, dollar strengthening
According to the Energy Ministry, gasoline prices on international markets rose by approximately 13% during the calculation period, while the dollar strengthened by about 3%. Both figures feed directly into Israel's regulated fuel-price formula and led to the unusually steep increase that took effect at midnight.
However, the new reduction cannot yet take effect. The Finance Ministry's legal advisers have already determined that there is no legal impediment to the finance minister signing another reduction, but the ministry is now waiting for the position of the attorney-general.
Only then will it be possible to publish the wording of the order for public comment, review the comments submitted, and proceed to the minister's signature.
This would be the second excise-tax reduction within a short period and during an election period, making the legal issue particularly sensitive. Legal approval was also required for the excise-tax reduction in September, which was approved as an exceptional measure and lowered the price by half a shekel.
This time, Smotrich is seeking to repeat the same move after the price increase that took effect overnight effectively erased the entire previous discount.
Smotrich may sign reduction in gasoline prices, ministry announces
The Finance Ministry said on Thursday morning that "The position of the Finance Ministry's legal advisers is that there is no impediment to the finance minister signing a reduction in the price of gasoline for the coming month, as he requested. The attorney-general must now provide her position, and accordingly it will be possible to publish the wording of the price-reduction order for public comment."
The ministry further said, "Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich intends to sign a reduction of 50 agorot per liter of gasoline for one month, subject to consideration of the public's comments."
Until the entire process is completed, if it is ultimately approved, motorists will continue to pay the full price of NIS 8.27 per liter for self-service gasoline, the highest price ever paid at Israeli gas stations.

Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added.
The US State Department told Reuters in an email late on Wednesday that it does "not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments," while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said on Wednesday that the details of the agreement were not yet available.

Why Algeria propping up Kais Saied is bad news for North Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:26:42 UTC
18:26:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Algeria propping up Kais Saied is bad news for North Africa
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s televised summer pledge to defend Tunisia from external threats both bolstered bilateral ties and sparked discontent over Algiers’ growing regional influence.
Warning that Algeria treats an attack on Tunisia as a threat to its own sovereignty, Tebboune claimed secret forces are trying to break their ties and isolate its North African neighbour.
Using the Algerian dialect, he also warned: "Whoever brings terrorism to Tunisia or near Tunisia, we will destroy him in his parents' tent". While he did not name a specific hostile force, this has been interpreted as a direct reference to the UAE, which has been accused of trying to destabilise Algeria after years of disagreements over Western Sahara, the Sahel, and other regional conflicts.
Algeria reinforced this by formally severing ties with the UAE earlier this month, citing what it called “provocative and hostile” actions after repeated warnings. The Emirati ambassador was summoned and given 48 hours to leave, and UAE-registered aircraft were restricted.
Ultimately, Tebboune fears rival nations could pull Tunisia into their orbit and sideline Algeria, so his recent actions are seen as an attempt to reinforce alliances with Tunis and counter the growing influence of Gulf countries.
Indeed, Emirati investment in Tunisia has expanded steadily, particularly through economic and diplomatic engagement. In 2025, bilateral non-oil trade reached approximately $414 million, up 27.8% from the previous year, while both countries launched negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement.
Enabling repression
Forged during their shared struggle for independence from French colonialism, a deep-seated solidarity often characterises relations between the leadership and people of Algeria and Tunisia.
Algeria shares a strong historical and cultural bond with its neighbour. Both territories share Arab and Amazigh (Berber) roots, along with a strong Islamic cultural tradition. Families often live on both sides of the border that spans over 1,000 kilometres.
However, Tebboune's comments came at a tense moment for Tunisia’s population. Widespread blackouts have triggered intense public anger towards the government. The energy crisis also unfolded on the fifth anniversary of Tunisian President Kais Saied’s coup, during which he dissolved parliament, ousted the prime minister, and established centralised rule by decree.
Saied's post-2021 power grab has since led to heavy repression and the imprisonment of countless political opponents and dissidents.
Although Algeria initially called for constitutional order in Tunisia, the regime progressively became a staunch ally of Saied, providing vital political and economic support.
When Algeria and Tunisia signed a defence cooperation agreement last October covering border security, intelligence sharing, and military training, Tunisians criticised it for its lack of transparency.
People are also resentful that, with Tunisia on the brink of financial collapse, Algeria has become indispensable to Saied, enabling him to maintain control.
To cushion the impact of stalled IMF negotiations, Algiers heavily subsidised the struggling Tunisian economy between 2021 and 2025. Financial assistance included a $150 million central bank deposit, a $300 million loan in 2021, and a $200 million loan in 2022. Algeria also extended vital resource aid by supplying fuel and gas at discounted rates, including more than 22,000 tons of liquefied gas in 2025.
Consequently, Tunisia's foreign policy has tilted decisively toward Algiers. For example, when Saied hosted a diplomatic reception for Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali, this challenged Tunis’ longstanding policy of neutrality on the Western Sahara dispute between Algeria and Morocco.
Human rights organisations like Amnesty have also condemned aspects of the growing legal cooperation between Algeria and Tunisia, particularly after Algerian authorities extradited Tunisian opposition figure Seif Eddine Makhlouf earlier this year.
Both authorities stand accused of aiding one another in the crackdown on political dissent. One notable case is that of the Algerian social media activist Slimane Bouhafs, who held political refugee status in Tunisia until Algerian security services were allowed to abduct and detain him in 2021.
Two sides of the same coin
In reality, both regimes are cut from the same cloth.
Despite diverging during the 2011 Arab uprisings, Tunisian and Algerian politics have converged once again. Tunisia's slide into authoritarianism in recent years coincides with Algeria’s dismantling of the Hirak movement and its ongoing crackdown on civil society.
A striking parallel exists between Presidents Saied and Tebboune, who both ascended to power in the wake of socio-political movements that shook their security systems, a vulnerability both leaders have since pledged to aggressively prevent from recurring.
Indeed, under Tebboune, Algeria has jailed key Hirak figures and curbed human rights. Meanwhile, in Saied’s Tunisia, many opposition leaders and activists have faced similar repression.
Furthermore, on each side, leaders have stifled democracy by altering constitutions, demonising opposition, and ramping up the criminalisation of critics, as external interference is routinely invoked to justify crackdowns on political opposition.
Over the years, Saied has also mirrored Algeria's judicial tactics to alter his country’s legal system. The framework adopted relies on vague conspiracy charges and exceptional courts to target dissent. And Algeria has effectively insulated Tunisia from international scrutiny, enabling the Tunisian president to dismantle democratic reforms under the guise of protecting national sovereignty.
The paradox of paradoxes is that, despite tensions between Algiers and Abu Dhabi, both North African leaders have pursued political trajectories that overlap with the UAE’s broader counter-revolutionary agenda: curbing the political influence of Islamist movements and resisting a return to the pluralistic politics that emerged after the Arab Spring.
Dr Abd-el-Kader Cheref is a US-based Algerian scholar, freelance journalist, and former Fulbright grantee. He holds a PhD from the UK's University of Exeter and serves as an Assistant Professor of Africana and Multicultural Studies at Southern Illinois University. His research and writing focus heavily on African and MENA politics, democratization processes, postcolonial studies, Islam/Islamism, migration, and political violence.

wood-framed family home in osaka revolves around flexible open sports space
the free space accommodates sports, play, and everyday activities, and can be quickly reconfigured.
Flexible ‘free space’ adapts to sports, play, and family life
Osaka House by SHIOYA DESIGN is a two-generation residence in Japan organized around a large, flexible open space known as the ‘free space.’ Initially conceived as a dedicated judo area, the space developed during the design process into a gymnasium-like room that can accommodate multiple sports, play, and everyday family activities.
Rather than assigning a fixed function, the free space can be adapted to changing needs and interests. Judo, basketball, golf, bouldering, and other activities take place within the generous volume, with ceiling heights calibrated to different sports. A retractable golf net, basketball hoop and court markings, and bouldering wall are integrated into the room. Loose-laid tatami mats can be rearranged, allowing the space to be reconfigured in around 15 minutes.
‘free space’ connects Osaka House’s interior and exterior
The open volume also forms a visual and spatial connection with the surrounding living areas. A shared kitchen and dining space brings the two generations together, while a second-floor living room and rooftop terrace overlook the free space below. Gardens and additional outdoor areas extend the house beyond its enclosed rooms, while planting around the perimeter provides privacy without fully separating the residence from its surroundings.
Completed in 2025, Osaka House by SHIOYA DESIGN Studio is a wood-framed residence of approximately 183 sqm. Its undefined central space provides a flexible framework for movement, exercise, play, and shared activities, allowing the domestic layout to change over time.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, the former Dutch prime minister, said there is no risk of Russia using nuclear weapons against the Baltic States in response to a question about Moscow's warning over Kaliningrad at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit in Brussels on 30 September, according to NATO's transcript of his remarks.
Russia routinely brandishes nuclear threats as a pressure tool against Europe, and its latest one targets the Baltic. In a written warning to NATO, Moscow claimed it was ready to use nuclear weapons if the alliance tried to isolate Kaliningrad, its exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
NATO tells Moscow to stop the nuclear threats
Rutte said NATO had responded to the Russian document by making clear that it is a defensive alliance and telling Moscow to stop its nuclear threats. "This is absolutely not called for and not helpful," he said.
Asked whether "the risk of nuclear weapons being employed against the Baltics is now real?" Rutte said: "No, it's not." He said Russian President Vladimir Putin knows he cannot defeat NATO and said he did not take the threat too seriously.
Rutte added that NATO should remain calm while continuing its work, and that Russian hybrid actions in Europe would bring more support for Ukraine, not less.
"We can allow a bit of calm, but also a bit of making sure we continue with what we are doing," he said.
Moscow warns of strikes on NATO decision-making centers
The Russian document, seen by Reuters, claimed NATO was pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" carrying "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict." It warned that Russia could strike decision-making centers in NATO member states from the start of a conflict.
NATO said none of its exercises or activities pose a threat to Russian territory and called on Moscow to end its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, refrain from increasingly reckless behavior toward NATO members, and cease its "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," according to the alliance's written response seen by Reuters.
Russian embassies take the warning public
Russia's Embassy in Ireland repeated the nuclear warning on 29 September, claiming NATO was preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and that Moscow would be ready to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if NATO countries tried to isolate the exclave from the rest of Russia. The embassy also claimed Russia had no plans to escalate tensions with Europe and accused European politicians of "playing a dangerous game."
The embassy linked its warning to statements by European politicians about an increased Russian "alleged hybrid campaign against European countries." Reuters said Russian embassies in at least three European countries had issued similar statements in the previous three days.

The army also claimed that “the people interviewed, having served in the army’s intelligence corps, mostly refer to limited and preliminary stages of intelligence work, rather than the much broader process of planning and approving strikes.”
The film, produced by The Guardian, received widespread acclaim at the Venice Film Festival, drawing a 25-minute standing ovation before being awarded the Special Jury Prize.
Abraham and Szor took the stage to accept the award, with Abraham speaking about a smear campaign against their film in Israel and efforts to prevent the facts presented in it from being seen.
The film’s title, NAZA, is an abbreviation used by Israel’s military intelligence directorate, Aman, to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
The film was secretly shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv over three years, with the identities, voices and facial features of participants digitally altered to protect their safety.
Participants in the film detailed surveillance systems used in Israeli attacks and long-range bombardment operations.
According to the film, some of those interviewed worked in a secret intelligence unit that reported directly to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity against Palestinians during Israel’s war in the Gaza Strip, which began in October 2023.

PACE calls for compensation to Ukraine under ECHR judgments to be paid from Russian assets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:21:00 UTC
18:21:00 KST

PACE calls for compensation to Ukraine under ECHR judgments to be paid from Russian assets
PACE adopted the relevant resolution and recommendation on September 30, Ukrinform reports.
"The Assembly urges member and observer States of the Council of Europe to adopt without delay the necessary legal and/or practical measures to repurpose assets of the Russian State that are within their jurisdiction so that, when the European Court of Human Rights delivers judgment(s) awarding just satisfaction in inter-State cases brought by Ukraine against the Russian Federation relating to the war of aggression," the document states.
PACE considers that directing Russian state assets toward such payments would constitute a lawful countermeasure under international law. The resolution stresses that Russia must bear the legal consequences of its aggression and compensate Ukraine for the damage it has caused.
The document notes that the ECHR has already established Russia's responsibility for serious human rights violations in two interstate cases brought by Ukraine, although the amount of compensation has not yet been determined. Given the scale of the damage, future payments could amount to "tens of billions, or hundreds of billions of euros," according to the resolution.
In its adopted recommendation, PACE proposes establishing, under the auspices of the Council of Europe, a mechanism to receive Russian state assets designated for compensation payments. Funds transferred to Ukraine would be counted as compensation owed to it by Russia. Such a mechanism could operate independently or become part of a future compensation fund.
PACE also called on countries to ensure the implementation of ECHR judgments on compensation through national legal procedures for as long as Russia refuses to pay.
"Russia has an unconditional legal obligation under Article 46 of the Convention to implement judgments of the Court in respect of violations that occurred up to 16 September 2022. This obligation under international law does not diminish with time and cannot be set aside by Russian domestic law," PACE stressed.
According to PACE, approximately EUR 260 billion in Russian Central Bank assets were frozen following the full-scale invasion, of which around EUR 210 billion are held in the EU.
As Ukrinform reported, the PACE Committee on Legal Affairs and Human Rights had called for the creation, under the auspices of the Council of Europe, of a mechanism that would allow frozen Russian state assets to be used to pay Ukraine compensation awarded under judgments of the European Court of Human Rights.

The French government's deficit reduction plans in its 2027 budget represent a minimum effort in light of the challenge of getting the finances back on track, the country's independent fiscal watchdog said on Thursday.
The High Council for the Public Finances, which is charged by law with determining whether the government's fiscal plans stack up, said the deficit target for this year of 5.4 percent of economic output was "plausible" though it could still be missed.
Plans to reduce the deficit next year to 5 percent of output are "limited", the watchdog said after the government presented its 2027 budget, adding a "significant" effort was needed to stabilise France's debt.
"The High Council firmly reiterates that the deficit reduction target set for 2027 is a minimum given the alarming state of public finances," it said in its review of the budget bill.
It also said that the government's forecast for economic growth of 1 percent next year is "optimistic", especially if concern about the belt-tightening effort grow and weigh on the outlook.

As has become common in France, where the two previous prime ministers were toppled over their austerity plans, the budget bill faces a tough ride in a deeply divided parliament, as political parties position themselves for one of the country’s most consequential elections in modern times.
The vote is due to take place on April 18-May 2, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen far ahead in the polls amid a growing backlash against President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist legacy.
Budget squeeze
According to a plan seen by AFP ahead of the presentation, the government hopes to reduce the country’s ballooning deficit with €43 billion in "recovery measures”.
If voted through, they would bring the “total effort” in 2027 to “€54 billion”, the document said.

In total, net tax revenue in the state budget would increase by €18 billion compared to this year to reach €375 billion, it indicated.
Reuters reported that the budget squeeze would also come from freezing public sector wages and all but the lowest pensions.

Finnish football fans and Finland's national team made clear their opposition to Russia's war in Ukraine, as well as Belarus' political support for the Kremlin, during Tuesday evening's Nations League match in Helsinki.
The decision to host the game in Helsinki sparked controversy even before a ball was kicked, with Ukraine’s ambassador to Finland Mykhailo Vydoinyk saying it "will only play into the hands of Russia".
However, to demonstrate their opposition to the ongoing war in Ukraine, the Finnish players warmed up before the game in blue shirts bearing the yellow text "We stand for peace".
In addition, Finnish fans loudly booed the Belarusian national anthem before kick off, and then unfurled a large tifo — or giant banner — depicting an eagle owl (referring to the nickname of the Finnish national team) clutching in its claws a cockroach with a face resembling Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko.
The tifo also carried a slogan in Finnish, "sun päiväs koittaa", which roughly translates as "your day will come".
Problems for state broadcaster
According to reports by the independent Belarusian media outlets Tribuna and Tšestnok, the protests by the Finnish team and fans caused problems for Belarusian state television.
The match was broadcast in Belarus by the state sports channel Sport TV.
Tribuna reported that Sport TV's broadcast only began moments before the match kicked off, suggesting this prevented the channel having to show the Finnish fans' booing of the national anthem. The broadcaster also made efforts to keep the tifo off-camera by showing pre-prepared crowd shots.
Jaroslav Pisarenko, host of the YouTube channel Tšestnok, meanwhile noted that the state channel's broadcast of the match was difficult to follow because of the random cuts.
Pisarenko further pointed out that the Russian channel Okko Sport's broadcast of the game used similar tactics, for example by using ambient background noise instead of the actual sounds from the stadium.
However, Tribuna also reported that Sport TV failed to filter out the chant by Finnish supporters just before kick off in reference to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Before the opening whistle, Finnish fans started singing [in Russian] 'Putin huylo' [which translates to English as 'Putin is a dickhead']. It could be heard in the broadcast," the outlet wrote.
Fans also vote with feet
Shortly after the draw for the Nations League was made in March, the Football Association of Finland initially said the home match against Belarus would be played at a neutral venue.
This decision was reversed in May, when Helsinki's Olympic Stadium was announced as the venue for the match.
The official attendance for the game on Tuesday was around 7,000 — a notably small turnout for a competitive fixture involving the Finnish men's national team. Aside from during the Covid years, the last time a crowd of fewer than 10,000 people attended a Finland national team game at the Olympic Stadium was in 2015.
Tuesday's match ended in a 0-0 tie.

Can a mobilized employee be dismissed — a lawyer&apos;s clarification
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
12:16:35 EEST
18:16:35 KST

Can a mobilized employee be dismissed — a lawyer's clarification
Kyiv • UNN
A mobilized employee retains their position and workplace throughout their service. Dismissal is possible only in cases specified by law.
Mobilization cannot constitute grounds for dismissing an employee at the employer’s initiative—this guarantee remains in effect throughout the entire period of military service, regardless of its duration. Labor law attorney Yana Syrotenko of LLC "LAW FIRM ‘LOGIC’ told UNN in a comment.
According to her, pursuant to Part Three of Article 119 of the Labor Code of Ukraine, mobilized employees retain their jobs and positions at the enterprise, regardless of its form of ownership or subordination.
Military service cannot constitute grounds for terminating employment relations
The attorney noted that the current version of Article 119 of the Labor Code provides specifically for the retention of the employee’s job and position, whereas the guarantee of retaining average earnings for most mobilized employees was abolished by legislative amendments.
At the same time, according to the attorney, the law provides for a limited list of cases in which an employment contract with a mobilized employee may be terminated—in particular, the liquidation of the enterprise, the employee’s death, or the expiration of a fixed-term employment contract.
In practice, Syrotenko noted, some employers attempt to avoid fulfilling this obligation by formally transferring the employee, removing the position from the staffing table, or changing the organizational structure of the enterprise. However, according to her, such actions do not release the employer from its obligations.
Even in the event of the reorganization of the enterprise or a change in its structure, the employer must ensure that the employee can return to performing their work duties after completing military service
She also pointed out that the length of an employee’s military service cannot constitute grounds for their dismissal.
Attempts by an employer to dismiss an employee because of a prolonged absence from work due to military service constitute a violation of the guarantees established by law and may be challenged in court
The attorney separately warned of risks for the employer after the mobilized employee returns from service.
Preventing an employee from returning to work after completing military service or refusing to restore their employment rights constitutes a violation of statutory guarantees and may be grounds for applying to court with claims for reinstatement, recovery of average earnings for the period of involuntary absence, and protection of other violated rights
She also explained that if another person was temporarily hired to replace a mobilized employee under a fixed-term employment contract, then after the primary employee returns, that fixed-term contract is subject to termination due to the expiration of its term.

Ukraine carries out first logistics mission using an amphibious UGV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:08:41 UTC
18:08:41 KST

Ukrainian service members have completed the country’s first logistics mission using an amphibious unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), according to an announcement from Ukraine's Defense Ministry.
Such platforms are designed to maintain mobility in areas where conventional unmanned ground vehicles cannot operate due to flooding, deep channels, or unstable ground.
According to the ministry, the system traveled more than 40 km. while carrying ammunition and food supplies to frontline positions, moving across terrain that included rivers, canals, and marshland.
The vehicle operated as a wheeled platform on land and switched to swimming mode when encountering water obstacles. The cargo remained onboard throughout the transition, allowing the route to be completed without relying on bridges.
Ukraine’s Brave1 defense innovation cluster said in a statement that operators of the "Alter Ego" unit of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade deployed the robotic system.
While the ministry did not identify the vehicle’s developer, it said that the platform had been developed and refined over several months in cooperation with the military and took into account “real-world missions, operational experience, and the specific characteristics of front-line terrain.”
The Brave1 defense innovation cluster, which recently introduced a dedicated funding track for amphibious unmanned systems, supported the development of the platform through grant funding.
Although the ministry did not specify the model used, there is a growing number of domestically manufactured amphibious UGVs, including platforms such as the UNEX, Triton, Rage Robot, Dodger multi-purpose UGVs.
The UNEX system, which became operational last year, is built on a specialized chassis and can cross water, floodplains, swamps, sand, ice, and other difficult terrain. The ministry claims that the weight distribution across its axles and its wide tires “generates less surface pressure than an infantry soldier’s foot, preventing the activation of mines designed to target automotive equipment and armored vehicles.”
The platform is fully electric, has an autonomous operating time of up to six hours and a payload capacity of up to 1,700 kg. It can be placed in various configurations, tailored for logistics, evacuation, and demining, and can be equipped with a weapons station or electronic warfare system.
Ukrainian forces have expanded their use of unmanned ground vehicles for logistics and evacuation missions over the past year. Ukrainian media have reported that the number of frontline units using UGVs has increased from 67 in late 2025 to 167 by the spring of 2026.
On its website, Brave1 says that UGVs are already carrying out over 7,000 combat missions per month. In April, the country’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said that it aims to have UGVs carry out all front-line logistics operations.
UGVs have become one of the most consequential technologies in modern warfare. Once limited to bomb disposal and remote reconnaissance, UGVs now support frontline combat, logistics, electronic warfare, and casualty evacuation across multiple conflict zones. Their rapid evolution is transforming how militaries fight, supply, and survive on increasingly lethal and electronically contested battlefields.
According to Brave1, troops from the Alter Ego UGV battalion of the 93rd Mechanized Brigade engineered a variation of the Desantnyk UGV along with a precision drop mechanism for heavy drone bombers. The entire process, from initial concept to combat application, took 10 days.
Earlier this month, troops used heavy bomber drones to air-drop those UGVs several miles behind Russian positions in a surprise assault called Operation Vivaldi.
The use of the UGVs, which acted as suicide ground robotic systems, helped Ukraine take back 125 sq.km. from Russian control. Business Insider reported that UGVs completed over 15,700 different missions, delivering around 3,300 tons of cargo during the offensive.

What one flydubai flight revealed about the new India-Israel-Gulf map - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:08:36 UTC
18:08:36 KST

The extraordinary events aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv were, first and foremost, a story of personal courage. Indian Captain Smit Machchhar was seriously wounded during the violent incident in the cockpit.
Despite his injuries, he managed to help others gain access to the cockpit and regain control of the situation, preventing what could have become a far greater tragedy. The aircraft eventually made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, with 174 passengers on board.
His actions were quickly recognized in both India and Israel. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly praised his courage. There is always a danger in turning a dramatic human story into a geopolitical metaphor. Machchhar did not act because his passengers were Israeli, nor because he was Indian. He acted as a professional responsible for the lives of the people aboard his aircraft.
That distinction matters.
Circumstances around flydubai incident tell us about shifting relations
But for those of us who study India-Israel relations, the circumstances surrounding the incident are nevertheless striking. They tell us something not simply about how India-Israel relations have changed, but about how the geography around them is changing as well. For decades, the relationship was viewed primarily through a bilateral lens: Delhi and Jerusalem, with defense cooperation at its center. That picture is no longer sufficient.
India and Israel have expanded their relationship into technology, innovation, agriculture, water, education, and people-to-people ties. In February, during Modi’s state visit to Israel, the two countries formally elevated their ties to a “Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity.”
But the more interesting transformation may be taking place beyond the bilateral relationship itself.
Consider the geography of Flight 1073: an Emirati airline, an Indian captain, Israeli passengers, an Omani co-pilot accused of carrying out the attack, and an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
None of these nationalities should be used to assign collective responsibility. The fact that the alleged attacker is Omani does not explain his actions, and until investigators establish a motive, it would be irresponsible to suggest otherwise. But Oman’s presence adds another layer.
For India, Oman is a longstanding strategic partner and one of its most important defense relationships in the Gulf. Maritime security, military exercises, and defense cooperation have become significant components of the partnership. For Israel, Oman occupies a very different position. The two countries do not have formal diplomatic relations, even though Muscat has at various moments demonstrated a willingness to engage with Israel.
This difference is important because it captures something fundamental about India’s position in West Asia: India can simultaneously maintain close relationships with Israel, Oman, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates without requiring those countries to have equivalent relationships with one another.
This is not an alliance system. It is a network of overlapping relationships between countries that do not necessarily share the same friends, adversaries, or political objectives.
That network has become increasingly visible in recent years. The Abraham Accords opened new possibilities for cooperation between Israel and Gulf states. I2U2 brought India, Israel, the UAE, and the United States into a new economic and technological framework. The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor went further, imagining India, the Gulf, Israel, and Europe as part of a shared connectivity architecture.
For India, West Asia is therefore no longer viewed primarily through the traditional lenses of energy security, diaspora interests, and separate bilateral relationships. It is increasingly part of a wider strategic and economic space connecting India with the Gulf, Israel, the Mediterranean, and ultimately Europe.
Yet the events following the emergency landing also demonstrated the limits of this transformation.
Connectivity moving forward slower than diplomacy
Saudi Arabia allowed the aircraft to make its emergency landing, but Riyadh still has no diplomatic relations with Israel and reportedly rejected an Israeli request to send aircraft to retrieve the passengers. That apparent contradiction is, in fact, the story. Regional integration and political fragmentation are occurring at the same time.
Trade routes, airlines, technology partnerships, and strategic initiatives are creating connections that would have been difficult to imagine two decades ago. But they coexist with unresolved conflicts, the Israeli-Palestinian issue, the absence of Israeli-Saudi diplomatic relations, and very different political calculations across the Gulf.
Connectivity is moving forward, but not always at the same speed as diplomacy.
This is particularly important for understanding India’s role. New Delhi does not need to choose between Israel and the Gulf in the way observers once assumed it might. Its strategy has increasingly been to build parallel and sometimes interconnected relationships across the region while preserving its own strategic autonomy.
Israel, meanwhile, increasingly encounters India not only through the traditional Delhi-Jerusalem relationship but through a wider regional network that passes through Abu Dhabi, Muscat, Riyadh, and beyond.
What happened aboard Flight 1073 does not prove that a new Middle East has arrived. Nor should one extraordinary incident carry more geopolitical meaning than it can bear. Captain Smit Machchhar’s actions deserve recognition for what they were: an extraordinary act of courage under extreme circumstances.
But sometimes geography tells its own story. An Indian captain, an Omani co-pilot, Israeli passengers, an Emirati aircraft, and a Saudi landing site briefly came together on one flight between Dubai and Tel Aviv.
In that unlikely convergence, we caught a glimpse not of a completed new regional order, but of one that is still being built.

Bones of medieval tsar, 48 religious relics to be exchanged under new Greece-Bulgaria heritage MoU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:08:09 UTC
18:08:09 KST

The remains of a medieval Bulgarian tsar and nearly 50 religious Greek relics will be handed over to their respective nations under a newly signed Memorandum of Understanding between Greece and Bulgaria on Tuesday.
The MoU was signed between Greek Culture Minister Lina Mendoni and Bulgarian Culture Minister Evtim Miloshev.
As part of the agreement, Bulgaria will return 48 religious relics from the Holy Monastery of Panagia Eikosiphoinissa, the Holy Monastery of Timios Prodromos of Serres and the Holy Metropolis of Serres and Nigritis to Greece.
The relics were transferred to Sofia during WWI and have since been kept at the National History Museum of Bulgaria.
Following their return, the 48 relics will displayed at the Museum of Byzantine Culture until November 5. Afterwards, they will be returned to their place of origin.
In turn, Greece will hand over the remains of the medieval Bulgarian tsar, Samuel (997-1014), found in the Basilica of Saint Achillios in 1965.
Samuel, or Samuil, reigned from 997 to 1014 during the First Bulgarian Empire and is deemed a national hero by Bulgarians for struggling to preserve his country's independence from the neighboring, Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire.
Alongside Samuel's remains, those found in two other sarcophagi within the basilica will also be returned.
The additional remains are believed to belong to Tsar Gabriel-Radomir, Samuel's son who ruled the First Empire of Bulgaria between October 1014 to August or September 1015, and other members of the Bulgarian royal family.
The remains have recently been kept at the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki.
A 'historic' agreement between Greece, Bulgaria
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described the accord as a "historic agreement" and said the handover of Samuel's remains ended six decades of efforts by Sofia to bring them home after their discovery in Greece.
"We have had the historic honor of achieving this," Radev said in a statement shared by the Bulgarian Culture Ministry. "I would like to express my deepest gratitude to the Prime Minister of friendly Greece, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, for his statesmanlike vision, for his political courage and for the friendship that binds Bulgaria and Greece even more strongly."
Radev emphasized that the memory of the tsar "unites, not divides," the two countries today.
"The joint membership of Bulgaria and Greece in the European Union helps each of the two countries to better understand the sensitivity of the other," he added. “On Saturday, October 3, at 12:30 p.m., I invite all Bulgarians to Battenberg Square in front of the Prince's Palace in Sofia to welcome the mortal remains together and pay homage to the great Bulgarian ruler."
The two sides agreed to continue negotiations regarding the identification and inclusion of historical artifacts of mutual interest that were not covered by the current agreement.
The official handover ceremony will take place on October 3, at the the Museum of Byzantine Culture in Thessaloniki. It will be hosted by Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and attended by Radev.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Germany’s municipalities recorded a €20.1 billion ($22.7 billion) budget deficit in the first half of 2026, matching the highest first-half shortfall since German reunification in 1990, official figures showed Thursday.
The deficit remained at the record level registered in the same period last year, according to preliminary data released by the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis.
The figures cover the core and extra budgets of municipalities and municipal associations, excluding Germany’s city states.
Core municipal budgets accounted for €20 billion of the shortfall, while extra budgets recorded a deficit of €100 million.
Expenditure rose 2.7% from a year earlier to €204.1 billion, while revenue increased 3% to €184 billion. Both grew more slowly than in the first half of 2025, when spending rose 6.9% and revenue increased 6%.
Personnel expenditure climbed 5.2% to €54.7 billion, while social benefit spending increased 3.9% to €46.3 billion. Interest costs rose more sharply, jumping 13.1% to €2.4 billion.
Meanwhile, capital investment fell 4.5% to €21.7 billion, with construction expenditure declining 2.4% to €15.5 billion.
Net municipal tax revenue increased just 0.9% to €57.3 billion. Net trade tax receipts fell 2% to €30.8 billion, with gains in other tax categories offsetting the decline.
Municipal revenue from administrative and user fees rose 5.7% to €26.5 billion.

Lithuania Moves to Block Russian Property Deals Near High-Risk Strategic Sites
The Lithuanian government approved a draft law prohibiting citizens of Russia and Belarus from purchasing real estate in areas located near strategically important assets.
This restriction applies to individuals from both nations even if they hold valid residence permits in the country, according to LRT on September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed legislation also bars Belarusian citizens without a residence permit from purchasing real estate anywhere in Lithuania. A similar ban for Russian citizens without residence permits was already included in a previous legislative draft.

Under the proposed measures, individuals and corporate entities supporting Moscow’s war effort were to be prohibited from conducting public activities in education, culture, sports, and entertainment.
To enter Lithuania, visiting figures were required to sign a public declaration condemning Russian military aggression and supporting Ukrainian sovereignty, with refusal resulting in an automatic denial of entry. ‘Thrilling’: Dutch cattle farmers switch to rice as solution to warmer climate and sinking peatlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:58 UTC
18:00:58 KST

Dutch cattle farming dries out peatland and releases CO2. Is switching to Japanese rice-growing a solution?
The warming climate is allowing Dutch farmers to grow a grain never before harvested in the Netherlands: rice.
For centuries, cows were the country's agricultural staple. But now farmers are experimenting with produce previously unthinkable in such a wet, temperate country.
And researchers behind the scheme hope rice cultivation could help address one of the country's most pressing environmental challenges: peat soils that are sinking as they dry out, pushing parts of the low-lying Netherlands ever lower.
"It's extraordinary," says Philippe Terheggen, chairman of the Land van Ons association that has provided the fields for the rice harvest.
"We would never have thought maybe 20 years ago that we would be able to grow rice in the Netherlands," says the 68-year-old.
"But it's also scary because it tells you what is possible... now the climate has changed," he says.
For now, the project is a pilot scheme, consisting of just 0.6 hectares, with organisers hoping to produce around three tonnes of short-grain rice suitable for sushi or risotto.
The team is working with around 30 different rice cultivars from as far afield as Russia, China, Japan and Uzbekistan, to see which grows best in the Dutch climate.
'I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future'
In a soggy field between Amsterdam and The Hague, farmer Sander Roeleveld ploughs his rice crops with a combine harvester, backdropped by windmills and canals.
Roeleveld, who describes himself as a "pioneer", says he wants to show other farmers that rice could grow in boggy Dutch soil.
"My goal is to show that more things are possible on wetland than just grass," the 53-year-old says.
"Of course, when you have had cows for 600 years, it's really hard to imagine that you want to do something else than having milk from your cow," he laughs.
"I just want to show that things can be changed for the benefit of the future."
How rice farming could cure dried out peatlands
But the project is about much more than crop diversification. Researchers believe it could help tackle one of the Netherlands' most persistent environmental problems.
Roughly one-tenth of the country is peatland, which farmers drain for grass to feed their cattle.
As the peat dries out, it releases millions of tonnes of carbon dioxide while causing the land to subside by up to several centimetres a year in the worst-affected areas.
According to Wageningen University, greenhouse gas emissions from Dutch peat soils account for around two to three per cent of the country's total emissions.
The only way to resolve this vicious cycle is to keep the fields wet – but then farmers would have nothing to grow there... until now.
"Basically it started with just a crazy idea," explains Julian Helfenstein, a researcher from Wageningen University and Research, who is piloting the project along with colleagues from nearby Leiden University.
It is a rare combination of both adapting to climate change and mitigating its effects, says the 36-year-old.
"Rice is an opportunity for this part of the world to adapt to climate change, so to grow something that previously wasn't possible," he says.
"But also to mitigate climate change because it stops this peat from degrading and emitting all the CO2 because you can keep it wet."
The peat issue affects not just the Netherlands, but much of northern Europe, including Germany, Belgium, even the Baltic states, he says.
Helfenstein and his team are closely monitoring the CO2 and methane emissions from cultivating rice compared to maintaining grassland – to ensure the cure is not worse than the illness.
"So far the results are promising," he says.
"As an environmental scientist, you're always pointing to the problems. And it can be a bit depressing, like, 'Oh, here's more climate change, here's more pollution'," says Helfenstein.
"And then here's an opportunity for science to work also towards a solution. So I find that thrilling."
'Chewy, but great': Dutch rice could be used to make sushi and sake
Local restaurants have already voiced an interest in offering premium Dutch-sourced rice, says Guusje van der Vossen from the Wij Land association which helps farmers transition to more sustainable production.
She says the rice being harvested now was a grain from northern Japan, which seems the best adapted to Dutch conditions.
The 27-year-old is one of the few people ever to have eaten Dutch-grown rice – from an experimental batch grown last year.
"It tasted delicious, to be honest," she laughs, saying the aim was to make sushi with it – and maybe sake.
"It was a bit chewy, but also great."

Would I want my child to study for a social media influencer degree? No, but it’s the way of the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:36 UTC
18:00:36 KST

Sometimes you read a story in the news that seems designed to wind up as many people as possible. This week, that story involves a degree in content creation from Nottingham Trent University. Otherwise known as the “influencer degree”, this three-year course comes with BA (Hons) status and a top-tier price tag of almost £10,000 a year, for which students will learn “hands-on technical production”, “analytics, branding and commercial strategy” and collaboration with brands and “industry partners”. Course leaders are at pains to point out it won’t turn them into overnight social media stars, but of course, while reading, I felt the cold drag of undertow forces pulling me towards world-gone-mad outrage.
We’ve been here before, obviously: media studies, women’s studies, anything that hasn’t been on the syllabus of the ancient universities for at least 500 years is vulnerable to accusations of dumbing down – and this is no different. The course was launched in 2022, meaning its first cohort of graduates are out there looking for jobs right now, while giving interviews about whether or not it was worth it. One very sensible-sounding graduate, talking to the BBC this week in what one assumes is an application of the all-publicity-is-good-publicity principle learned from her course, said that the £30,000 spend was worth it for the networking opportunities alone – an absolutely valid point and half the reason why people strive towards Oxbridge.
Still, there will be eyebrows twitching. That price tag seems punchy for a course that is currently in clearing. But the bigger issue is the triggering effect the words “social media” and “influencer” will have on parents mired in data supporting the view that their children’s lives are in constant peril from the forces unleashed by online platforms and the jobs that go with them. What next? A degree course in dropshipping?! How about an MPhil in manosphere studies? And so on and so on: all modern versions of the sinking spirits that have traditionally attended a child announcing they want to go to drama school.
In general, we’ve always been quite sniffy about vocational degrees in this country. Look at the prestige that comes, for example, from attending Columbia Journalism School in the US, despite much laughter from journalists in this country who think the best way to study journalism is to get a job in journalism. British friends with jobs in marketing hold similar views about degrees in that subject: “Get a job, it’s stupid to pay to study it.” If degree courses are supposed to teach critical thinking, so the argument goes, then these courses don’t qualify as suitably academic – not a concern anyone ever raises about medicine or law.
It’s snobbery, then, and in this case also conditioning. Influencing is empty, pointless, evil and grifty, underscored by narcissism and fulfilling no useful human or social need – an assessment that might just as easily be applied to the careers in banking that so many top graduates head towards. If anything, it seems to me that influencing is a clever spin from Nottingham Trent (and Brighton University, which also offers the course) in response to the terrible state of traditional media careers. Going forward, it’s fair to assume that for those going into the media, the smart move is to be an independent contractor rather than hold a traditional job without bonus structures or opportunities for profit-sharing.
In case you haven’t noticed, I’m trying hard here to argue against the gravitational pull exerted by my own experience of doing a traditional degree. I guess the real test would be what any of us parents would say if our kids came to us with an intention to apply for one of these courses.
In my own household, we’d have to go through a whole rigmarole in which I would definitely infuriate my children by suggesting their time might be better spent reading The Wife of Bath’s Tale or, like, the structure and function of proteins. I’d be forced to lecture them on the hollow interior life of anyone chasing fame and say the words, “Do we think the Kardashians are actually happy?” Then I’d look at the job market, at all the listings for social media managers, podcast producers and video editors and, if I could get over myself, might work my way to the conclusion that they could do a lot worse. (I’m kidding, I’d be devastated.)
- 
  Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

An organisation pushing the Green party to equate Zionism with racism has encouraged people to join the party specifically to support that agenda, and has links to activists who say that pro-Israel “infiltrators” must be rooted out of the UK, the Guardian has learned.
Some Green members are increasingly concerned that the party risks being manipulated by extremist outsiders over a motion to be voted on at the party’s annual conference this weekend, which states that “Zionism is racism”.
Some Jewish members have said privately they fear it will be difficult for them to remain in the party if the policy passes.
Zack Polanski, who leads the Green party in England and Wales, has come under pressure to take a definitive stance on the motion amid worries the controversy will harm the party in next week’s key Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where Polanski is seeking to win Keir Starmer’s former seat.
The motion came top of a members’ ballot of policy issues to be debated at the event in Brighton. It calls for a single Palestinian state and, if passed, it would mean members who support Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – could be disciplined for racism.
The controversy reflects a longstanding debate about the definition of Zionism, the political movement whose supporters see it as the necessary struggle for a Jewish homeland, and whose critics see it as a colonial project that has inevitably led to the dispossession of Palestinians. The term Zionist is, meanwhile, sometimes used as a synonym for Jew by antisemites.
Efforts to push the policy have been led by Greens for Palestine (GfP), a group not formally affiliated with the party. In repeated social media posts over recent months, GfP has urged backers of the idea to sign up as Green members specifically to get the motion debated at the conference and then adopted.
Polanski last week declared he was anti-Zionist, adding that Zionism was a form of racism because it involved the displacement and genocide of Palestinians. But he has supported amendments to tone down the motion. Lubna Speitan, a leading member of GfP who co-authored the motion, has rejected the amendments.
“It doesn’t matter what the leadership thinks,” Speitan said in a recent video, adding: “We are certainly not here to negotiate the terms of our liberation or oppression with any of our oppressors.”
GfP and Speitan have links to a group called the Anti-Zionist Movement (AZM), a more militant campaign group that argues that the “so-called Jewish state” should be dismantled, along with “Zionist organisations” in the UK and elsewhere.
A key member of AZM is David Miller, a former academic who was sacked by Bristol University over his criticisms of Israel, and subsequently won a tribunal case after it ruled he had been discriminated against because of his anti-Zionist views. He now presents a show for Press TV, the Iranian state channel.
In social media posts, Miller has argued that Zionists have, as “infiltrators and subversives”, gained access to not just all UK political parties but also “the media, entertainment industries, the law, financial institutions, sports and all sorts of apparently obscure parts of the UK”.
GfP and AZM have collaborated on a series of social media posts, and Speitan attended an AZM meeting in London this year. In a video posted by AZM about the meeting, Speitan said it was important for anti-Zionist groups to collaborate.
Speaking in the same video, Miller said his aim was to “dismantle Zionist organisations wherever they are in the world, including the 3,000 or 4,000 Zionist organisations in this country”.
Some senior Greens say they are deeply worried about the links. One said: “I just don’t understand why Zack hasn’t provided any leadership on this, especially when we have such a crucial byelection just days later.”
A spokesperson for the Greens said: “The Green party is a democratic party and membership has grown as more people join to support our full policy platform. The vast majority of members joined prior to a specific attempt at mobilisation.”
They added: “The Green party does not support the views of the AZM.”
A spokesperson for GfP cited Miller’s employment tribunal, saying it “concluded that anti-Zionist beliefs constitute a protected belief”, adding: “We reject all conflations of anti-Zionism with antisemitism, just as we reject the settler colonial project in occupied Palestine.”
Asked about the links to AZM, they added: “We welcome the adoption of our motion by all anti-racist organisations, political parties and unions.”
GfP, the statement added, “affirms the Palestinian people’s inalienable right to self-determination, including the right of the Palestinian people to resistance and liberation from Israeli occupation, domination and subjugation” via any means under international law.
