UK bookmakers that warned over illicit market had deal with offshore casinos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:35 UTC
18:00:35 KST

Three UK bookmakers that have repeatedly warned of the dangers of the illicit market have also benefited from a lucrative deal with one of the world’s largest offshore casinos, the Guardian can reveal.
Details of the arrangement emerged as a result of last week’s Casino Secrets leak, which saw the release of thousands of confidential files held by the gambling regulator on the Caribbean island of Curaçao, a haven for offshore betting sites.
One leaked file concerns the Santeda online casino network, which has been accused of illegally targeting vulnerable gamblers in the UK and has been fined in Spain for operating without a licence.
The file shows that Santeda signed a deal in 2022 with Sports Information Services (SIS) – a UK-based gambling content provider part-owned by Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done, the billionaire owner of Betfred.
The three bookmakers have repeatedly warned the government that excessive regulation or taxation could drive their customers into the arms of rogue offshore casinos with no licence to operate in Britain.
According to the leak, all three have also benefited from a share of tens of millions of pounds in dividends paid out by SIS after it signed the contract with Santeda.
The companies are understood to have been unaware of the deal at the time it was signed. Matt Zarb-Cousin, a prominent gambling reform campaigner, advised them to get their “house in order”.
The bookmakers collectively own more than 50% of SIS, which supplies gambling sites with live horse racing, greyhound and esports content, as well as data used to settle bets with customers.
The use of such data is critical to online betting companies, helping them serve customers and process their bets.
The leaked contract shows that SIS also agreed to provide Santeda websites with these services for two years, under a contract that auto-renewed unless either side opted to terminate it.
Under the terms of the deal, SIS received a percentage of revenues from losing bets placed via Santeda’s brands.
It is not clear whether the contract is still active, or how much SIS earned from it. SIS declined to say whether the deal had been terminated.
Industry sources said that Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done could not have known about the deal with Santeda, owing to controls designed to prevent them accessing commercially-sensitive information about industry rivals.
One source said the companies were “furious” with SIS for doing business with Santeda, at a time when licensed operators were stepping up their warnings about the illicit market.
Entain said it was “not a party to the commercial or customer arrangements SIS decides to strike. Now that this relationship has come to light, we take it very seriously and have raised our concerns to SIS”.
The contract with Santeda does not permit the use of SIS data in the UK.
But it appears to show that SIS supplied information to multiple Santeda websites that a previous Guardian investigation found was illegally targeting UK customers, including via promotional material apparently aimed at people trying to quit.
Santeda’s Curaçao licence does not permit it to operate in most leading jurisdictions that regulate gambling, such as the UK and US.
Companies House filings suggest that SIS’s shareholders – including Ladbrokes, William Hill and Done – have received at least £37m in dividends since the deal with Santeda was signed, including £30m in 2023.
Ladbrokes owns 23% of SIS, suggesting it has received £8.5m in payouts over the period.
Stella David, the chief executive of the Ladbrokes owner Entain, has criticised Premier League football clubs for “complicity” in fuelling illicit operators and warned that such firms could be boosted by any rise in taxes on licensed operators such as Ladbrokes.
William Hill appears to have received more than £7m from its near-20% stake in SIS.
Earlier this year, the bookmaker’s owner, Evoke, blamed the illicit market for weak online revenues.
Fred Done, who is also a director of SIS, holds an 8% stake, indicating his share of shareholder payouts was nearly £3m.
Done warned the chancellor this month that higher taxes on slot machines – under consideration as part of the upcoming budget – would drive punters to illicit market sites that don’t pay tax, contribute to horse racing or exercise regulatory controls.
Zarb-Cousin, the director of the gambling-blocking company Gamban and a longtime campaigner for tougher laws, said: “While the UK’s biggest gambling firms have been warning about the risks of growing the illicit market if the government increases tax and regulation, the very same firms are profiting from it.
“If the gambling industry is concerned about the black market, it needs to get its own house in order by cutting all ties with it.”
A spokesperson for SIS said all of its customers agreed to “only offer SIS products where it is legal to do so and where they have the necessary regulatory licences”.
They added: “Customers commit that they will comply with all such laws and licences at all times.
“Where SIS becomes aware that these terms are not being adhered to it takes corrective action to enforce the position, up to and including suspension or termination of contracts.”
The Guardian approached Evoke and Fred Done for comment.

‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:34 UTC
18:00:34 KST

He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.
Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.
But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez.
“[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas.
Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US.
Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast.
“I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him.
“They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.”
In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!”
Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January.
Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”.
Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!”
“The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said.
Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast.
Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently.
Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people joined a pro-government rally in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”).
“No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released.
The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear.
Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.”
But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power.
“If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.”
However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned.
So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests.
“Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”.
Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself.
The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told.
Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

‘They showed no mercy’: mapping the Rohingya villages being erased by rebel forces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:33 UTC
18:00:33 KST

There are at least 10 camps like the one on the paddy fields at Hnget Thay, built after the insurgent Arakan Army (AA) took control of most of northern Rakhine state in 2024. These are where many Rohingya people in the state now have to live. Others hide in the mountains, or flee abroad to the refugee camps of Bangladesh or make deadly boat journeys to Malaysia.
The arrival of more than 155,000 Rohingya in Bangladesh since 2024, which amounts to 25% of the 600,000 estimated to still be in Myanmar, has raised concerns about the very survival of a people who now mostly live abroad as refugees.
The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority group from western Myanmar who have faced decades of persecution and clashes with Buddhist nationalists. The word translates as from Rohang – the district that is now Rakhine State. Speaking a language similar to the Bengali dialect of Chattogram (formerly Chittagong) in Bangladesh, they are reviled by many in Myanmar as a foreign people and are denied citizenship by the regime.
In a military crackdown from 2016 to 2017 that led to Myanmar being accused of orchestrating ethnic cleansing, most of the Rohingya population, about 700,000 people, sought refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. The campaign of massacres unleashed against the Rohingya then is being investigated as possible genocide at the international court of justice (ICJ).
There are now 1.2 million Rohingya in Bangladeshi refugee camps. Since Myanmar’s civil war erupted in 2021, Rohingya remaining in the country have been caught in violence, forced displacement and oppression from both sides – the insurgent AA and government forces, which are fighting each other for control of Rakhine state.
Testimony received by the Guardian and reflected in recent UN reporting provides an insight into the “catastrophic” conditions that the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, says Rohingya are facing, including torture, gender-based violence, arbitrary arrests, confiscation of land, displacement, forced labour and conscription.
Many of the Rohingya are confined to a makeshift camp, Hnget Thay, to which the AA forced some survivors to relocate after a massacre at Hoyyar Siri. Human Rights Watch documented hundreds of unarmed Rohingya being killed at the village by AA forces.
“This is the end of the Rohingya in northern Rakhine, there is no question about that. It might take time, but the Arakan Army is working quietly to ensure the community has no future there,” says a UN specialist on Myanmar, who requested anonymity as they were not authorised to speak.
“The Rohingya can stay in prison-like camps in appalling conditions for as long as they can bear it, but they will not be permitted to return home,” they say.
An internal UN report has identified at least 800 hectares (2,000 acres) in 23 Rohingya villages that have been seized and repurposed as camps, settlements for other communities or for military infrastructure since 2024, describing this dynamic as linked to the AA’s consolidation of territory under its control.
Muhammad Ares, 18, a Rohingya who now lives in Bangladesh, says: “They used bulldozers to clear out entire residential areas, turning our villages into completely flat, empty fields.
“They cut down all the trees and cleared away every trace of our community, leaving nothing but barren ground. In the areas where they demolished our houses, they cleared the debris and set up their own military camps and outposts.”
The changes in the Buthidaung area of Rakhine happened after the AA took control of much of the region and active fighting abated. Data from the independent conflict monitor Acled shows 12 battles in Buthidaung in 2025, compared with 103 in 2024.
Mohammed Sadik, 26, from Ywet Nyo Taung, says: “They ordered us to stop farming and declared that the land no longer belonged to us; they confiscated the agricultural fields entirely.”
“They forced us to clear roads, dig trenches, and perform heavy labour inside their camps,” he says. “They forced us to work continuously. If anyone collapsed from exhaustion, they were left in the sun.”
All of their farm tools and land were confiscated and the AA authorities refused to return them, Sadik says, even when they explained they needed to grow food to survive.
Video shared with the Guardian by people from Ywet Nyo Taung appears to show the destruction wreaked on the area during this period. The footage was filmed by two locals riding on a motorbike southwards from the main school to the village of U Hla Hpay, which was completely destroyed.
In the footage, they point out landmarks such as schools, mosques, ferry docks, shops and homes. Towards the end of the footage, the person filming points out his own home. Scorched earth is visible and the structures are almost entirely demolished apart from a former bathroom that is partially intact.
Throughout the footage, bricks are seen lined up, often in neat piles, along the side of the road.
In multiple testimonies from Rohingya who were made to work by the AA, they said the forced labour included dismantling Rohingya property to use the materials to build new buildings for the insurgents, including the construction of military barracks, locally known as the AP Battalion, in Ywet Nyo Taung, for housing forcibly recruited Rohingya.
The AA claims to fight in the interests of all Rakhine state’s ethnic groups, and since 2024 has seized control of most of the region. Outwardly, it has proclaimed sympathy for the Rohingya’s suffering but conversely stands accused of emulating the policies of the Myanmar military when it destroyed and confiscated Rohingya land and subjected people to forced labour and conscription, including in the fight against the AA.
Last year, the UN-backed Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) released a report listing seven villages the Myanmar military had destroyed in 2017 and then built bases on. The ICJ, which is expected to deliver a decision in October on whether Rohingya were subjected to genocide in 2017, has previously considered the “systematic expulsion from and destruction of homes” to be an element of genocide.
The report highlighted that land in Myanmar is owned through a leasehold system and that the military exploited laws designed for natural disasters that allowed burned land to revert to the state, stripping away Rohingya ownership. Another law passed in 2018, after the Rohingya exodus, allowed uncultivated land to be taken by the state.
It was under these conditions that 250,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh in the early 1990s, first creating the refugee camps that became the world’s largest in 2017.
The IIMM’s head, Nicholas Koumjian, says: “Clearly, those that orchestrated the attacks on the Rohingya had the objective to create ‘facts on the ground’.” However, he adds that they have not confirmed the AA is responsible for the destruction of Rohingya land. “The Rohingya still inside Myanmar seem to be targeted by all sides of the ongoing conflict and caught in the middle of that conflict.”
Aung Kyaw Moe, who was until recently the only Rohingya member of Myanmar’s “national unity government”, a pro-democracy body in opposition to the 2021 military coup leaders that operates in exile, says the Rohingya are facing a “dangerous new phase” for those inside the country and for refugees hoping to return.
“The central issue is no longer whether Rohingya can survive in Myanmar,” he says. “It is whether conditions are being created that will make their permanent displacement and the erasure of their physical, political and historical presence irreversible.
“If villages are erased and land is being transformed while refugees remain outside of the country, then return becomes progressively more difficult.”
The UN report and testimony shared with the Guardian describe how Rohingya were not only displaced from their land but forced to provide men and women to work for, and to train for, the AA.
“I was forced to undergo military training against my will. I never volunteered to join any armed group,” says a 32-year-old Rohingya man conscripted by the insurgents. He described being initially held for a month, during which time he was repeatedly beaten.
“Throughout my detention, I endured constant physical abuse, psychological intimidation and forced labour.”
Another man said his 22-year-old daughter was taken by AA militia, who subjected her to physical and sexual abuse and made her carry out housekeeping duties for them. She also had to undergo military training.
As well as being forced to provide labour and conscripts, testimony from Rohingya who escaped to Bangladesh from Rakhine describe coercion to make regular payments of “taxes” to the AA, confiscation of land and livestock, and restrictions on their free movement. All of these were tactics enforced previously by the Myanmar military.
Tom Dannenbaum, a professor of international law at Stanford University in the US, says a combination of coercion and the dislocation of Rohingya, either internally or abroad, could amount to the war crime of population transfer.
“It’s devastating for any group to be socially dislocated, inflicted with destructive conditions of life, have their property destroyed and seized,” he says. “All of that is part of making the viability of that group socially, as well as physically, ultimately [impossible]. It clearly creates conditions for that group that make it very difficult to sustain.”
Salamat Khan fled from Rakhine state to Bangladesh in 2024. He feels it is impossible to return to Myanmar, as AA fighters ordered him to leave after attacking his village: “The fighters said to us: ‘go to Bangladesh, your homes are gone, go to the [refugee] camps’.”

Methodology
UN research identified land and property confiscation sites and camps created to confine displaced Rohingya. Interviews and additional testimony also provided information on where Rohingya villages were destroyed. Satellite imagery was used to analyse changes in these areas from before the Arakan Army’s takeover of these areas in April 2024 and after.
The photo and video of Ywet Nyo Taung were verified through the use of landmarks, notably the large school near the Mayu River, and the shape of the mountains behind the village. Nasa Fire Information for Resource Management (Firms) data was used to confirm the timing of fires in the area.

====================================================================================================

Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M Bender
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:33 UTC
18:00:33 KST

Amid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public.
The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was the Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public’s, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions.
The California governor, Gavin Newsom, issued a mandate to create an “AI kill-switch”; New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is similarly exploring the possibility of having “AI kill-switches”; and Senator Bernie Sanders and Congressman Greg Casar introduced legislation to “ban artificial superintelligence”.
While so many of us were focused on fictional superintelligent machines that we were told could hypothetically cause human extinction, however, there was a more serious story being reported.
A series of events almost got us to armageddon, not caused by “rogue, superintelligent AI”, but by government reliance on error-prone systems that are marketed by their manufacturers as being close to superintelligent.
A CNN report published on 18 September, which hasn’t been verified by other major outlets, describes how the US “almost started a war” with China, based on an intelligence report that claimed a Chinese ship was transporting components of nuclear weapons. Military personnel made plans to intercept the Chinese vessel, complete with aircraft and soldiers ready to board the ship. A military skirmish of this kind between China and the US could quickly escalate and spiral into world war three.
It was only moments before executing on the plan that American officials further investigated the intelligence report and found that it had been generated with the use of a chatbot and contained erroneous information about the vessel’s contents.
Unlike the terminator, “rogue AI”, scenario, this incident didn’t galvanize lawmakers into announcing calls for regulation so as to avoid potential human extinction. Media outlet after media outlet didn’t warn the public that we almost triggered a war against a nuclear superpower because of our military’s reliance on error-prone chatbots.
We describe the large language models (LLMs) powering these chatbots as stochastic parrots, that is, models that are designed to regurgitate the patterns of the data they are trained on. News coverage describing them as “powerful” “rogue” models that could render humanity extinct all on their own, bolsters perceptions of tools based on these models being infallible enough to merit usage in stakes as high as warfare.
Even CNN’s more critical coverage describes the chatbot used by the US military as presenting “profound risks” because it is “powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology”.
In fact, today’s LLMs and the chatbots they power are not poorly understood, nor are they powerful in the sense of being effective tools for this use case. They are systems for generating plausible-looking text, built out of enormous, haphazardly collected datasets and then “fine-tuned” (that is, further trained) to be especially appealing to their intended users.
CNN wasn’t able to learn which chatbot product was used in this case, but the LLM powering the product was probably fine-tuned to output text with the stylistic hallmarks of intelligence reports. Both the basic functionality and the risks of such a model have been well-understood and well-documented for years, including in our 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
Claims that system behavior is mysterious arise from deliberate mystification on the part of those selling those systems, and a misapprehension of what their output is by those procuring and using it.
Unlike the unscientific and fantastical claims of OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs and those who uncritically repeat their talking points, the harmful, and well-documented, impacts of these companies’ products have arisen because people believe that the products are superintelligent, not because they actually are.
From “AI” scribes used by hospitals erroneously classifying patients as illicit drug users, to governments killing children after relying on “intelligence analysis” systems which mistake schools for military facilities, we are seeing the predictable harms that come from misplaced faith in unreliable automated software.
Meanwhile, the marketing campaigns from the companies selling this software warn of impending superintelligence, directing our attention away from the real risk to their fantasies of doom.
It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high-stakes scenarios. Any automation used in military, medical or other life-and-death situations must be thoroughly evaluated within its use case and paired with usage norms that keep accountability with people who have actual power to make decisions.
As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption from the law when it comes to AI: there are existing laws that federal agencies and other regulators can enforce to protect the public against the AI industry’s unsafe and unscientific practices of pushing unsound products while marketing them as “magic intelligence in the sky”.
Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public. We call on journalists and lawmakers to hold companies accountable rather than parrot their marketing talking points.
- 
  Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February.
- 
  Emily M Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and co-author of The AI Con.

Beansprouts, nonya paste and kefir – whose fridge is this?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:32 UTC
18:00:32 KST

Curry leaves
I used to freeze fresh curry leaves, but then [the chef] Romy Gill said you lose all the aroma when you do this. So now I fry them and you get curry leaf oil, which keeps them fresh. You can then crumble them into things like dal.
Tofu
I’m addicted to tofu – I have firm, medium, soft, and puffy. But this is my breakfast tofu in ginger syrup; it’s like junket but made with soya beans. Someone taught me how to make this, but the secret ingredient was plaster of paris, so I get it from the Asian grocers. I’m not a big breakfast person, but I could easily eat a whole tub of this.
Chilli
This is my chilli box, which is on wheels – I’m short and need to get to the back of the fridge! I love Poon’s Everything Everywhere sauce: it’s all I need with poached prawns or chicken, or I might do a splodge on ramen with veggies and tofu. My ethos is: “always have two so you always have one,” although I do forget which one is open.
Lamb, mince, Chinese sausage.
My meat drawer has marinated lamb for the week, mince for mapo tofu, Chinese sausage, but also white anchovies and dried scallops. I also collect parmesan rinds [in a bag] in here, which I always think I’m going to make something with, but they sometimes just sit here.
Kiwi
I’m a two-kiwi-a-day person: one in the morning and one in the evening. It’s something sharp, sweet and puckery to freshen me up.
Black sesame paste
I have this from testing various recipes, but if I’m craving something chilled and sweet, then I make tang yuan [glutinous rice balls] filled with this paste.
Shawarma marinade
I used to make shawarma marinade from scratch, but it was such a pain. We do Friday night dinner instead of Sunday lunch, and last week I smothered a leg of lamb with this marinade from Ottolenghi.
Garlic shoots
When I’ve been away, I just want a load of greens, and quickly. I’m addicted to garlic shoots, which I blanch quickly and stir-fry with Chinese sausage, then I add rice and an egg and I’m so happy.
Kefir
I don’t drink kefir – I just couldn’t – but I use it like buttermilk, which is so good in cakes, but not easy to find here – plus, buttermilk is not always consistent. Kefir is so much better.
Salmon
My son is protein maxxing, so I’ve always got salmon. I squeeze in mayonnaise to oil and protect it, then I toss the fish in soy sauce, shoaxing wine, lemon juice or rice wine vinegar, sometimes wasabi paste, and grill for two minutes per side. That goes into poke bowls, to which I can also add some edamame.
Homemade elderflower cordial
I’ve been experimenting with how little sugar I can put in this. It has come out quite sharp, but it’s very refreshing.
Vanilla essence
Every time I use a vanilla bean, I pop it in here: my seven-year-old vanilla essence. Homemade vanilla essence, cheap vanilla essence, and a good vanilla paste are all different products to me. Sometimes I want that cheap, childish flavour, but this is somewhere in between.
Tamarind
I have both Thai and Indian tamarind. I love using tamarind in baking, if I’m caramelising something, otherwise I’ll add a squeeze to dal (instead of lemon) and curries.
Beansprouts
A friend from Malaysia sent me her World of Nyonya all-purpose spice paste, which if you add coconut milk turns into laksa. I then add beansprouts, fresh egg noodles, and my puffy tofu.

Lost in translation: Montenegro's EU accession faces a language barrier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

Montenegro may not be able to accurately translate all EU laws in time for accession, so the European Commission is currently weighing options for a derogation, including allowing Podgorica to use an existing EU language to fill the gaps. Croatian would be the most obvious choice.
Montenegro may fall short of translating all EU laws accurately before it joins the bloc. The European Commission is weighing several options for a temporary derogation, including letting the country use an existing EU language in the meantime.
Montenegro aims to become the EU's 28th member by 2028. But first it must adopt and translate the so-called acquis, the tens of thousands of EU laws that form the bloc's legal framework. Brussels is growing wary that it will not finish in time.
"Montenegro will need to produce translations of the acquis into its official language in good time before accession and will need to train a sufficient number of translators and interpreters required for the proper functioning of the EU institutions upon its accession," reads the country's negotiating framework with the EU.
Podgorica has invested significantly in its administrative capacity and assures that the work will be completed on time. But the EU executive has started looking at contingency plans, EU officials told Euronews.
The reason is that Croatia has been raising concerns about the quality of some translated legal texts. Zagreb is locked in a bilateral dispute with Montenegro that could delay the whole accession process.
Since Croatia, the bloc's most recent entrant, joined in 2013, the body of EU legislation has almost doubled.
Candidate countries must translate all relevant EU legislation into their future official language. The EU institutions are only responsible for a final check before publication in the Official Journal at the time of accession.
Translation is also only part of the linguistic preparation. Some laws need adapting to the candidate's institutional context, for instance by designating which authorities will be in charge of supervision.
"The Commission services are in regular contact with Montenegro and reviewing the pace of work in this regard," a Commission spokesperson told Euronews.
The Commission is assessing several options for a potential derogation, including allowing Montenegro to use another official EU language until it has time to fill the gaps and accurately translate the remaining legislation.
It would be up to Podgorica to choose, but Croatian is the obvious candidate. It is the only official EU language that shares the same core features and is understandable to a Montenegrin speaker.
"The Montenegrin standard language belongs to the same dialect continuum as the Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian standard languages, and that all are mutually intelligible," reads a recent study on the Montenegrin language.
Still, this is only one option among several, and it may not sit well with Montenegro. Identity politics runs deep in the Western Balkans, and Podgorica fought for years to have the Montenegrin language officially recognised internationally.
Derogations are not new. Malta set a precedent: short of qualified translators, it secured an exceptional, transitional derogation from the obligation to translate all EU acts into Maltese for three years after joining in 2004, with any backlog due by the end of 2008.
Ireland is another, with a key difference. Its derogation came decades after it joined, when Irish became a full official language, and it temporarily suspended the obligation to translate all EU acts into Irish.
In other words, Brussels has shown flexibility, not treating full translation of the acquis as an absolute condition for accession. Still, in this case, the most obvious fix may also be the hardest to sell politically.

‘Assassination plot’

“Neither Ivan nor I were explicitly told that we were the individuals whose names are concealed in the indictment against those accused of carrying out the assassination plot,” Kasparov said.

‘Bottle of gasoline’

“This may be part of a broader plan to destabilize the situation, intimidate people, and demonstrate the West’s inability to protect those it has committed itself to protecting,” Tyutrin said.
He said he was first warned by Lithuania that he was in danger after he helped raise money for Russians fighting alongside Ukrainian forces in 2023 and then visited the Ukrainian front the following year.
Then, during a visit to the United States in April 2024, FBI agents approached him at JFK airport in New York.

“They said, ‘We don’t want this to happen on the territory of the United States,” he said. “I was followed by FBI agents for two weeks.”
After returning to Lithuania, Tyutrin was placed under state protection. The security detail was withdrawn several months later.
He said Lithuania did not provide the same level of protection following the most recent warning. Nonetheless, he said he remained grateful to his host country.
“I am grateful to them for informing me,” he said. “Forewarned is forearmed.”

France's borrowing rate keeps rising, hitting its highest level since 2002
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:56:47 UTC
17:56:47 KST

The new rise in France's ten-year borrowing rate, now close to 5%, shows investors' mounting distrust of a public debt that keeps climbing.
Bad news keeps piling up for the government. France's ten-year borrowing rate climbed to 4.94% at 10 a.m. on Thursday 1 October, up from 4.85% at Wednesday's close. French government bonds on the secondary market last yielded a similar rate in 2002, when they reached 4.91%.
More importantly, the borrowing rate has just seen its largest quarterly increase in almost four decades, as well as its sharpest monthly rise since 2022.
This latest rise is a sign of investors' growing mistrust of French debt, just as the government presents on Thursday the outline of what could become the state budget for 2027. The task looks especially daunting for Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, all the more so as France has not had a balanced budget since 1973.
Yet this record surge hardly comes as a surprise. The day before, the prime minister had expressed regret that the warning had gone "almost unnoticed" in the public debate. "Energy tensions are pushing rates up in many countries. In France, political uncertainty ahead of the presidential election is adding to that pressure," he wrote on X.
"Let us not pile instability on top of these difficulties," he added.
"More interest to pay means fewer resources for the country's priorities. This reality applies to everyone: government, parliament, presidential candidates. Reality is catching up with us," said Lecornu, who had already announced his intention to deliver €54 billion in savings.
Beyond this rise, the seriousness of the situation can also be seen in the gap with Germany, whose borrowing rate serves as a benchmark in Europe. On Thursday, Germany's borrowing rate stood at 3.61%, around 1.30 percentage points lower than the French rate. This gap, known as the Franco-German spread, keeps widening and has now reached its highest level in 14 years.
European stock markets also opened lower on Thursday morning, with the CAC 40 stock index in Paris falling more than 1.4% by 11am, the FTSE 100 in London losing 1.8% and the DAX in Frankfurt trading 1.1% lower at the same time.
€3.596 trillion in debt
The government is under particular pressure, as public debt has reached record levels over President Emmanuel Macron's two terms, worrying investors and becoming one of the main issues ahead of next year's presidential election.
Debt now stands at €3.596 trillion, equivalent to 119% of gross domestic product (GDP), suggesting that the country's weakened public finances are likely to dominate the campaign.
One proposal to tackle the debt issue is proving particularly divisive. The La France insoumise candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has suggested cancelling French government bonds held by the European Central Bank in order to free up money for public spending, arguing that this would release resources for investment.
The idea was swiftly rejected by Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, who argues that it would be a "clear and simple violation" of the EU treaties, which forbid a central bank from financing states. She stressed that if France were to freeze its debt today, then when it returned to the markets its creditors could demand onerous terms or even flatly refuse to lend to it.
According to France's finance ministry, the country's debt is held by a wide range of investors. A quarter is owned by French investors, a quarter by investors from the eurozone and another quarter by investors based outside the currency bloc. The remaining 25% is held by the Banque de France, as part of purchases made under the European Central Bank's monetary policy.

Conflict has escalated between Afghanistan and Pakistan this year, with sporadic attacks continuing since a March truce failed to resolve security issues.
The latest strikes hit Helmand as well as Kunar, which borders Pakistan, killing 10 civilians, according to the Taliban government's deputy spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat.
Islamabad confirmed "planned and calibrated" strikes in Afghanistan, which it said targeted militants, without detailing locations.
Two Helmand residents told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that three airstrikes hit their village.
Pakistan's information ministry said its forces hit two locations in Afghanistan "based on credible intelligence, selective targeting of terrorist camps and hideouts."
Helmand in southern Afghanistan, along with neighboring Kandahar province, which an airstrike hit last week, is strategically important for the Taliban movement.
Speaking by phone from Helmand's Safar village, 50-year-old resident Abdul Wahid said the strikes killed four people and wounded seven.
Another villager, Qudrat Ullah, said he was home when strikes hit his neighbors' house.
"The whole area is destroyed," the 32-year-old said, adding that authorities kept residents away from the strike sites.
"There were civilians, children, women; they have killed them. There is no military or anything else," he told AFP by phone.
Pakistan's Information Ministry reported an initial toll of 22 militants killed and weapons and ammunition destroyed.
Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants behind frequent bomb and gun attacks in Pakistan.
The Taliban government denies this and criticizes Pakistan for violating Afghanistan's sovereignty and killing civilians.
In mountainous Kunar province, an AFP journalist saw the remains of stone houses in the remote Chugam Valley.
Mohammad Hashim, a farmer, said he rushed to rescue residents after the predawn attack.
"There was a woman, she was screaming for help to get her out of the rubble. She was having trouble breathing and told us that there are more people over there," the 30-year-old told AFP.
"We went there to dig, and there was a man with four children who were killed," he added.
The latest strikes follow bombardment last week on multiple Afghan provinces, which the Taliban government said killed civilians. Pakistan said it targeted militants.
Violence between the two countries has killed more than 500 civilians since October, according to figures from the United Nations mission in Afghanistan.

Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024), Valeriy Zaluzhny, has congratulated Ukrainian military personnel on Defenders Day, emphasizing that the future of not only Ukraine but also Western democracies depends on them.
"Our defenders are doing the impossible in extremely difficult conditions, even when it seems there is no hope left. Ukrainians are making history and standing up to a much more numerical enemy with all its resources and technologies of killing. Veterans play a special role for the future—those who know the real price of war and peace, life and freedom, for which they had to give their most precious possessions. Veterans remind society that peace cannot be bought with business deals by selling part of freedom and the memory of those who fell for it," Zaluzhny wrote on Facebook on Thursday.
In his column for the 24 Channel website, he noted that Russia's war against Ukraine is unique in its causes and forms of waging, but even more important will be its consequences, "which we will get precisely because of the mistakes of all opponents, rather than through the implementation of policies and strategies."
"The uniqueness lies precisely in the stubborn reluctance to understand the cause-and-effect relationships of this war in order to avoid the ability to influence this outcome. Despite a wide circle of country leaders involved in this process, a unique marketing also survives. Despite the unapparent reluctance to see future actions, it continues to make money that literally falls from the sky of Ukraine, killing civilians every day. And, of course, despite obvious threats, no one is even thinking of talking about the modern version of industrialization—technologization," Zaluzhny wrote.
According to him, the fate of the war "has been snatched from the hands of strategists and thinkers and handed over to the soldier on the battlefield," who is no longer a hostage to political ambitions, but becomes a participant in a "semi-marketing process, where they try to conclude some deals that were relevant yesterday in order not to think about tomorrow." "And it is this soldier who is the driving force that can stop everything," the former Commander-in-Chief emphasized.
Zaluzhny also expressed surprise at the position of the UN as an institution designed to protect freedom. "An organization that not only still protects the rights of the aggressor country that kills daily, but also, as it turned out, an organization that is unable to protect this very freedom and independence... Ukraine, despite everything, especially international law and the desire of modern politicians, began to change the rules by force, because it had no other way... All these UN charters, Helsinki Accords, the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the Budapest Memorandum and the associated non-proliferation treaty have ceased to act as safeguards against a possible outbreak of war—a Third World War," he stressed.
The diplomat emphasized that Ukraine does not trade, "and no diplomatic or business skills have anything to do with it, because the end of one war is the condition for the start of the next."
"It must be recognized that Ukraine's victory will be the victory of democracy. But this is difficult for some, because for this it is necessary not only to help survive, but also to fight. And it must begin with not being afraid to call the enemy an enemy, rather than a business partner... To lose the war to ourselves is also to lose civilization, by exchanging it, for example, for rare-earth materials for killer robots. Once and for all," Zaluzhny summarized.

OSINT analysts identify production facilities for the Russian Garpiya-A1 attack drone
OSINT analysts have identified the location of the production facilities for the Russian Garpiya-A1 attack drone, which was created based on the Shahed-136 concept.
Source: OSINT analyst Dnipro Osint ⟨ Harbuz ⟩ on Telegram
Details: Harbuz recalled how Almaz-Antey, a Russian state-owned company in the arms industry, recently posted a promotional video featuring the export version of the Garpiya-A1(E) and the UAV-D.
Promotional video featuring the export version of the Garpiya-A1(E) and the UAV-D
The analyst noted that externally, the Garpiya-A1 resembles the Russian Geran (Shahed-136), but it is manufactured by a different company within the Russian military-industrial complex – the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol.
Quote: "Coordinates: 56.852355° 53.276128°. Production facilities are located on the territory of the former 300th production site of the Izhevsk Mechanical Plant. In 2019, this site was acquired by the Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol."
Details: Harbuz emphasised that the video shows building No. 12. It is used as the final assembly shop for the UAVs.
The analyst also shared that in 2023, the Russian Ministry of Defence signed a contract with Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol worth over RUB 1 billion (about US$12 million) to begin production of the Garpiya-A1. On 13 September 2024, debris of this UAV type was recorded on the territory of Ukraine for the first time.
Harbuz also highlighted that these drones have already been repeatedly used for strikes against Ukraine. In particular, on 25 September, one of them struck a railway infrastructure facility in Poltava Oblast.
According to the OSINT analyst, the production site was geolocated through joint efforts with GEOINT analysts from project CyberBoroshno.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda along with the GEOINT project CyberBoroshno recently investigated Russian "droneports" (specialised drone launch facilities) and strikes against them.

Britain’s retired Hercules head to Türkiye in December
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:52:12 UTC
17:52:12 KST

- Türkiye's Defense Ministry said the first two of 12 former Royal Air Force C-130J transports will arrive in December after maintenance in the UK.
- Six pilots and six technicians are training in the United States, and 29 maintenance personnel are training in the UK.
Türkiye will receive the first two of 12 C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft it is buying from the UK in December, once maintenance on them is finished in Britain, the Turkish Defense Ministry said on Oct. 1, with the rest of the former Royal Air Force aircraft to follow in stages.
The ministry also said crews are already training to fly and maintain them. Six pilots and six technicians are training in the United States, and 29 maintenance personnel are training in the UK. It did not give a schedule for the remaining 10 aircraft or say where the first two will be based.
The aircraft are stretched C-130J-30 models that the Royal Air Force retired in June 2023, when the UK decided to rely on the larger Airbus A400M for its tactical airlift. Türkiye confirmed the purchase in October 2025, and the 12 aircraft were handed over to Marshall Aerospace in Cambridge, England, for overhaul and modernization before delivery. Turkish officials have said Türkiye plans to take over routine maintenance of the fleet itself once its personnel complete type training.
The UK government said in December 2025 that the sale and related work were worth more than £550 million ($727 million) to the British defense sector and Marshall Aerospace and would support about 1,400 skilled jobs in Cambridge, Turkish Minute reported.
The C-130Js will fill a gap in Türkiye’s airlift fleet. The Turkish Air Force operates about 10 A400Ms and a fleet of older C-130B and C-130E Hercules, many of them decades old. Those older C-130s were grounded after an accident in November 2025 near the border between Georgia and Azerbaijan, leaving the air force dependent on its A400Ms for heavy airlift, Aviation Week reported.
The C-130J is the latest version of Lockheed Martin’s long-serving four-engine turboprop transport, with a two-pilot glass cockpit, digital flight controls and more efficient Rolls-Royce engines than earlier Hercules models. The stretched -30 version has a longer cargo hold, letting it carry more troops, pallets or vehicles than the standard aircraft.
Türkiye is not the only buyer of the RAF’s surplus Super Hercules fleet. The UK has previously sold former RAF C-130Js to Bangladesh and Bahrain.

"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
11:52:00 EEST
17:52:00 KST

"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
When the Russian forces began stepping up their use of jet-powered drones, perhaps the most common question among Ukrainians was: "Why haven't we destroyed the launch sites yet?"
Although Ukraine's defence forces regularly attack Russian drone launch sites, the strikes have not produced an effect on the scale of Operation Spider's Web, in which a dozen Tu-95MS and Tu-22M3 bombers were destroyed.
The reason is that, over the past two years, Russia has built an extensive network of specialised drone launch facilities, capable of handling dozens of jet-powered and conventional drones every hour. In Ukrainian and Russian discourse, these facilities are dubbed "droneports" – a catch-all term for dedicated sites used to operate drones.
Ukrainska Pravda and CyberBoroshno, a Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) community, have looked into Russian drone launch sites and attacks on them. Read on to find out where Russian forces launch their UAVs from and why it is highly unlikely that these droneports will ever be destroyed.
Where does Russia launch its Shaheds from?
When the first Iranian-made Shahed loitering munitions arrived in Russia in autumn 2022, little preparation was needed before they could be put to use. The drones could be launched straight out of the box.
The only thing they needed was a site from which they could be launched.
Military airfields were among the first – and perhaps the most obvious – choices for launching the drones. They already had everything needed: secure perimeters, security personnel, ground staff, air defence systems and established logistics for receiving new drones. The airfields were also located away from civilian infrastructure and prying eyes.
Long runways also made it possible to use pick-ups and lorries as mobile launch platforms for Shaheds. Lightweight launchers were also deployed at the airfields. The UAVs took off from these launchers with the help of solid-fuel rocket boosters before switching to their piston engines for the rest of the flight. For the Russians, the existing airfield infrastructure was more than enough.
The first airfields used by Russian forces to launch Shaheds were in occupied Crimea and the border regions of Bryansk and Kursk oblasts. As the number of drones Russia received grew, so did the geographical scope of their deployment. Known launch sites included Cape Chauda, Yeysk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Kursk and Seshcha.
The Russians later began using sites other than airfields to launch Shahed drones, including positions around Balaklava on Crimea's southern coast.
This enabled Russian forces to launch dozens of drones every week. The locations were also far enough from the combat zone to keep the launch sites relatively safe, yet close enough to Ukraine for the drones to reach Ukrainian territory within a few hours.
The droneports
When Russia acquired the technology to produce Shahed loitering munitions, another problem emerged: there was a shortage of existing airfield infrastructure.
Unlike the Shaheds supplied by Iran, Russia's domestically produced versions, known as Geran drones, had to be not only launched but also maintained. They had to be assembled, stored, inspected and prepared for launch somewhere. Although the existing infrastructure could support an increase in the number of launch sites, it was still not enough.
Therefore, as Geran production got underway, the Russians began preparing new launch sites in parallel.
Garages for assembling and storing drones began appearing at airfields already used as launch sites. Russia also built underground storage facilities large enough to accommodate both the drones and their warheads. Launchers were also being installed in revetments – protected bays surrounded by earth banks or blast walls.
Alongside the expansion of existing sites, new ones have begun to appear across Russia. In just a few months, large drone bases capable of launching hundreds of drones a day have sprung up on land that was previously covered by fields or forests.
Perhaps the best-known of these is Tsimbulova in Oryol Oblast, about 180 km from the Ukrainian border. Russian sources describe it as "the world's largest droneport". And with good reason: the site covers 5 sq km.
OSINT analyst Dnipro Osint ⟨Harbuz⟩ told Ukrainska Pravda: "The Alabuga began building the site in August 2024, and by February 2025, the main facilities had been completed. Its construction was directly linked to the expansion of drone production at Alabuga. This droneport has, in essence, become the first facility whose infrastructure was designed entirely for storing, maintaining and launching drones."
Tsimbulova has been equipped with runways and fixed catapult launchers for drones. The site also includes hundreds of garages and dozens of underground shelters.
The base's facilities are spread out across the site, with each one separated from the others and surrounded by earthworks. The droneports were built on the assumption that they would eventually be attacked. The Russians therefore sought to ensure that only a direct bombardment could destroy them.
The drones themselves can be stored not only inside buildings but also outdoors. Satellite imagery shows both Shahed attack drones and Gerbera decoy drones, which are also launched from these droneports.
The sites are supported by the infrastructure needed for day-to-day operations: solar panels, diesel generators, fuel depots and radio and navigation equipment for drone control. Each facility has its own access roads, parking areas and additional exit routes. It is also protected by air defence and electronic warfare systems intended to counter Ukrainian attacks.
Harbuz says: "The droneports were initially built much larger than 'necessary'. By the end of 2024, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine estimated the production rate of Shaheds at 2,000 units per month – roughly 64 UAVs a day – yet the droneport infrastructure at Tsimbulova could store up to 3,000 combat drones and 100 UAVs simultaneously. It was clearly built with capacity to spare."
In 2026, the infrastructure at Tsimbulova has continued to expand. New hangars and warehouses were built at the droneport, alongside larger specialised launchers for Geran-4/5 jet-powered drones. These drones can also be launched from mobile platforms mounted on vehicles.
An analysis of satellite images by Ukrainska Pravda estimates that Tsimbulova has 23 launchers for different types of drones, 387 garages and 26 underground storage facilities. The site is still expanding: the Russians are preparing to build four more launchers for jet-powered drones, plus 83 garages and underground shelters.
Another well-known droneport has been established at the site of the destroyed Donetsk airport (DAP). Despite being 50 km from the front line, the site now has hangars and drone launch pads used to launch drones towards frontline areas and targets in the rear.
Up to 95% of drone launches take place from bases in Russia's Bryansk, Rostov, Smolensk and Oryol oblasts, as well as in Krasnodar Krai and occupied Crimea. There are also research droneports where Russia tests UAVs in flight.
Although these sites are smaller than Tsimbulova, they have much the same basic infrastructure.
Ukrainska Pravda has identified at least 63 launchers at the main droneports, but the total could be higher. The sites can accommodate hundreds of drones and tens of thousands of combat components for them.
Can droneports be destroyed?
Ukraine's defence forces could not ignore the fact that Russians were launching Shaheds across Ukraine. Therefore, they gradually began targeting the drone launch sites, choosing their targets according to the capabilities and resources available to them.
Some of the first known strikes on Shahed launch sites were carried out in 2024. Ukrainian forces hit a Shahed depot near Balaklava and a storage facility for the drones near Yeysk.
After the strike, the area near Balaklava ceased to be used for Shahed launches. Yeysk was the first – and so far the only – case in which the impact of a strike could be seen in the launch figures. For the first time, Russia then went 48 days without launching Shaheds on Ukraine.
Russia's droneports have also been struck whilst under construction. On 26 December 2024, at least three Storm Shadow cruise missiles hit a facility between Tsimbulova and Rudnevo. Russian media outlet Astra said two Russian service members were killed and seven others were taken to hospital as a result of the strike.
A month later, the same complex was once again targeted by Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles. Ukraine's General Staff reported that more than 200 Shaheds had been destroyed. The images show damage to one of the warehouses.
Donetsk airport is another well-known target that has come under repeated attacks by Ukraine's defence forces. In a separate article, Ukrainska Pravda details how Ukraine's drone forces have been destroying Shahed launchers at the airport.
Because the airport is so close to the front line, Ukraine's 1st Separate Centre of the Unmanned Systems Forces has been able to regularly destroy Russian weapons, mobile fire groups defending the airfield and infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used mid-range drones and even FPV drones to strike targets at the airfield.
(12) FP-2 drone strikes on the DAP. Video: Special Operations Forces
DAP itself is a good example of just how difficult droneports are to strike.
Harbuz says: "The Russians have built drone launch sites to make them as costly as possible for Ukraine's defence forces to destroy. Ammunition and fuel depots are concealed beneath concrete and earth. Conventional UAVs cannot penetrate these structures, and even if they do, the explosion is contained inside, preventing debris from reaching other depots and triggering a chain reaction.
If any facilities are destroyed, they can be rebuilt relatively quickly and cheaply. As the example of Donetsk airport shows, the Russians are adapting and expanding the drone launch site even there, despite constant Ukrainian strikes."
Therefore, the main objective of Ukraine's defence forces when striking drone launch sites is to disrupt Russia's ability to launch drones.
Falco, an officer with Ukraine's 1st Separate Drone Centre, tells Ukrainska Pravda: "The primary objective is to disrupt their ability to launch drones, so that they are unable to launch them for an extended period. This also affects the overall coordination of their actions and the cohesion of their units. It also makes it easier for our air defence units to engage aerial assets, because there are generally fewer of them."
There are several ways to disrupt drone launches: striking launchers and storage facilities, or creating an aerial threat over the droneport. The attacks can force launches to be postponed indefinitely, while the destruction of infrastructure can reduce the overall number of drones launched.
According to Falco, launch pads and storage garages are among the easiest targets to strike: they are stationary, and there may not always be personnel nearby. But the value of hitting static targets depends on the circumstances and the overall strategy. If a garage or warehouse is packed with explosives or drones, then it makes sense to strike it.
Over the past two years, Ukraine's defence forces have stepped up attacks on Russian droneports. Alongside DAP and Tsimbulova, they have repeatedly targeted sites at Navlya, Hvardiiske, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and elsewhere. The strikes have hit warehouses, launchers, garages and drones left out in the open.
In the latest attack on Tsimbulova, on 21 September, Ukrainian strikes hit a bunker used to store combat drones. One strike penetrated the bunker, and another caused an explosion on the surface. Separate strikes also hit drones near the launch sites.
The strategy behind the strikes has also evolved. Ukraine is no longer targeting only storage, preparation and launch sites, but has also begun striking relay stations used to control Geran and Gerbera drones. UAV ground control stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trubchevsk, Russia, and in the temporarily occupied settlements of Zaliznyi Port, Skadovsk, Chornomorsk and Olenivka.
These facilities are important too, but Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces have another target in their sights: the drone operators themselves.
"The most difficult target there is also the most valuable one: the operator," Falco says. "They don't stay near the launch sites for very long. So when you take out the people launching the drones, you're taking away a scarce resource. There aren't many operators to begin with, and the enemy then has to spend even more money training new crews."
Military personnel are not the only people involved in launching Russian drones. Staff from Alabuga take part in the process on a daily basis too. In its study of Russian drone launch sites, the Molfar Intelligence Institute released several classified Alabuga documents.
According to the documents, Alabuga employees complained about "unjustified risk" after a Ukrainian attack on a major droneport in Oryol Oblast in December 2024. They said they were expected to continue working even though Russian air defence systems could not prevent strikes on the launch sites. Many employees said they wanted to leave the sites – and Alabuga itself.
Employees were threatened that they would be shot in the knees if they did not come to work, and were forced to turn up. Apart from Alabuga staff, local residents are also enlisted to assemble drones. Staff at droneports, however, complain about the low efficiency of their work.
Meanwhile, keeping droneports out of operation requires constant pressure on Russian positions.
Falco concludes: "If we want to keep the pressure on, we need to increase the scale of our strikes. The more we can hit, the better. As a country, we are constantly moving towards the level we need. But it's not just about strikes. We also have to think about how the enemy may respond and plan our operations accordingly."
Another factor that could significantly disrupt the operation of Russian droneports would be the use of Ukraine's own ballistic missiles. Their speed and penetrating power could allow them to target drone operators during launches – as has already happened at Donetsk airport – and destroy underground depots.

Is the EU planning to freeze funds to German states that voted for the AfD?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:51:51 UTC
17:51:51 KST

Claims circulating online allege that the EU is threatening to block funds intended for the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, after the far-right AfD party won a recent election there. However, there's no evidence that this is the case.
Is Brussels trying to freeze EU funds to a German state that voted for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in an election in early September?
According to several social media posts amassing thousands of views, likes and shares, and often with a picture of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attached, it is.
They allege that millions, or even billions, of euros could be withheld from the state of Saxony-Anhalt, located in east-central Germany, after voters handed the AfD a landslide victory on 6 September.
However, the 39 seats it won were not enough to command a majority, even though the party secured more than twice as many seats as any other party.
The AfD has since struggled to establish a coalition, however, as the other parties have refused to collaborate with it.
Von der Leyen herself has repeatedly criticised the AfD in the past, and her own centre-right CDU party suffered a crushing defeat, winning just 17.2% of the vote and falling to 15 seats. This possibly fuelled the suggestions online that she is behind the scheme to freeze the EU funds.
However, there's no evidence that that's the case. Instead, the narrative seems to stem from a statement by German Green MEP Daniel Freund, who said after the state election that he would push to freeze EU money flowing to an AfD-led government if it violated any European values or misused funds.
Saxony-Anhalt is set to receive €2.95 billion in EU funding as part of the current 2021-2027 budget. This includes €1.3 billion from the European Regional Development Fund, €571 million from the European Social Fund, and €594 million from the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development.
On a per capita basis, Saxony-Anhalt benefits more from EU funding than any other German state, according to Freund, averaging over €650 per citizen over the full EU budget cycle.
He also highlighted that the EU had used similar freezing measures in the past in Poland and Hungary.
Brussels did indeed block money intended for those countries a few years ago, over rule-of-law and democratic backsliding concerns under previous governments.
Some of these funds have since been released following reforms. In Poland, for example, the European Commission formally unlocked €137 billion in cohesion and post-pandemic funds in 2024, after Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government brought in guarantees for judicial independence and the rule of law.
For Hungary, meanwhile, it has proposed unlocking a first tranche of €4.2 billion in cohesion funds and restoring access to programmes like Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe.
Billions of euros had been frozen over rule-of-law and corruption concerns under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, but recent legislative actions by Péter Magyar's administration have paved the way for the money to be unfrozen.
Nevertheless, for now, the idea that this could happen to Saxony-Anhalt appears to be the opinion of a few MEPs, rather than a concerted effort by Brussels.
Under the EU's rule-of-law conditionality mechanism, funding cannot be suspended simply because a particular party takes office. The European Commission says measures can only be proposed where breaches of the rule of law directly affect, or seriously risk affecting, the sound management of the EU budget or the EU's financial interests.
Such a measure would have to be proposed by the European Commission, with the Council of the European Union ultimately deciding whether to adopt it.
A spokesperson for the government of Saxony-Anhalt also told The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, that it was not aware of any plans to freeze the EU funds heading its way.
"In the current situation, there would be no legal basis for such a course of action," the spokesperson added, noting that a new state government has not yet been formed following the election on 6 September.
The European Commission meanwhile confirmed to us that it is not considering blocking EU funds for Saxony-Anhalt.
"As a matter of general practice, the Commission monitors the situation in all Member States and regions and takes action where necessary, in accordance with the legal frameworks governing EU funding," it said. "The election result itself does not constitute a legal basis for suspending EU funding."
In addition to that vote, the AfD also saw success in another election in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in the north a couple of weeks later. The Left meanwhile won in the Berlin state election.
- This article was updated to include a comment from the European Commission.

U.A.E. Opens Investigation Into FlyDubai Attack
Unknown

Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) has called off plans to attend the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) defence ministers meeting in Reykjavík on Thursday and Friday, due to his facing a confidence vote in Parliament.
The defence ministry announced the development in a press release on Thursday morning. Parliament is likely to take up the no-confidence motions against Häkkänen and the government on Friday.
Earlier this week, the opposition Greens' MP Atte Harjanne tabled a no confidence motion against the defence minister, with Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela seconding the proposal.
The parties have criticised Häkkänen's recent visit to Israel, where he met with his Israeli counterpart in mid September.
Deal with Israel
At the end of August, it was reported that Finland and Israel had quietly renewed a memorandum of understanding on defence materiel development and procurement cooperation.
The memorandum itself is not new. It was originally drawn up in 2013, and its previous period of validity was approaching its end. In early 2024, Finland proposed extending the agreement with Israel.
Meanwhile, the SDP has called for a vote of no confidence in the entire government. Parliamentary group chair Tytti Tuppurainen announced the move. According to the SDP, divisions within the government over Middle East policy are creating uncertainty about Finland's position.
Led by the UK, the Joint Expeditionary Force is a defence cooperation group made up of ten countries: Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the UK.
According to the Finnish defence ministry, JEF member countries aim to build military capabilities, prevent crises, and respond together when needed. The group mainly operates in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea region.
