Gunvor publicly condemned Russia’s war but continued to do business with Russian energy firms, records show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:48:52 UTC
17:48:52 KST

CHINA CAPITAL
Gunvor publicly condemned Russia’s war but continued to do business with Russian energy firms, records show
Even as the trading giant publicly claimed to be winding down its Russia business, Gunvor privately acknowledged the deals to its bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, saying they complied with sanctions laws.
Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, several major trading firms pledged to stop or reduce new dealings with Russian businesses, joining global efforts to weaken Vladimir Putin’s military machine.
One of them was Gunvor Group, a company co-founded by a Swedish businessman and a Russian oligarch close to the Kremlin. In 2014, a U.S. Treasury Department report said that Putin himself had investments in the energy trading firm and may have had access to its funds. Since then, Gunvor’s co-founders have exited, and the company, now valued at about $5 billion, has over the last decade sought to shake its image as a Putin investment tool.
Gunvor has publicly condemned Russia’s war in Ukraine, and in 2023 corporate filings stated that it had “largely wound-down the trade of Russian oil and products.”
Now, confidential records reviewed by Swedish daily Göteborgs-Posten and the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists show how, despite its public pledges, the trader, using some of its subsidiaries, continued doing business with sanctioned Russian oil and gas producers.
The records come from the archives of the U.K. operations of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the world’s largest bank by asset size and one of Gunvor’s lenders.
While likely not violating sanction laws, the deals found in the ICBC records are at odds with the trading giant’s public posturing following the start of the war. The dealings also go against a private reassurance Gunvor made in a 2022 email to ICBC saying that it had stopped new sales to Russian entities, the investigation found.
ICBC’s records were examined as part of China Capital, an ICIJ-led investigation that exposed the inner workings of the Chinese state-owned bank and its maneuvers to advance Beijing’s geopolitical goals. The project showed how ICBC’s London units routinely financed companies with opaque financial flows and murky corporate ownership, justifying the deals as part of its support for the Chinese government’s top priorities.
China Capital found, for example, that ICBC London provided loans to Norilsk Nickel, a Russian mining company partly owned by sanctioned oligarchs close to Putin, in breach of an internal branch policy forbidding dealings with clients linked to sanctioned people or entities. ICBC’s other branches also provided foreign exchange, deposits and cash management services to Norilsk Nickel, a key supplier to China’s booming electric vehicle and battery industries.
Justin Ko, a researcher at the University of Macau who studied China’s state banks, described China’s relationship to Russia as “opportunistic.” As mounting war sanctions have forced Western traders to stop dealing with Russian counterparts, Beijing has emerged as Moscow’s steadiest ally. “In that sense,” Ko told ICIJ, “there is going to be more business, more trade, and it’s only natural that ICBC and Bank of China, as [China’s] two leading international banks, will be leading the way for that.”
To be sure, ICBC London officers made an effort to ensure the bank complied with sanctions restrictions imposed following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, the records show.
But the bank’s continued dealings with Gunvor shows how ICBC chose to serve clients considered strategic by Beijing even when they did business with sanctioned Russian entities.
For ICBC, Gunvor was a special client. An internal memo dated 2016 said that a “China rationale” for financing the company was its ongoing expansion within China: “Gunvor is expanding its reach into the Chinese domestic market : by sealing supply contracts with new independent (teapot) refineries and supplying [specialty] ores.”
Confidential records provided by Gunvor to ICBC show that between 2022 and 2024 the company based in Geneva continued to deal with sanctioned Russian parties, using licenses and other forms of authorization.
In 2024, during an ICBC “client review” as part of a prospective $594 million credit line to support Gunvor’s “trade finance needs,” some bank officers raised concerns about the trader’s Russia dealings.
In a report marked “strictly confidential,” Gunvor had acknowledged to ICBC London that, through its subsidiaries, the “Group had dealings with Russian counterparties target of Sanctions,” including buying and selling oil, gas and other products to and from “entities part of Gazprom, Rosneft, Lukoil and Novatek groups.” But those transactions, the Gunvor report said, represented only 0.69% of the group’s revenue in the first quarter of 2024 — or about $234 million, according to Göteborgs-Posten’s estimates.
In an internal meeting, an analyst from ICBC’s Zurich office told his London colleagues that the Swiss branch found “Gunvor trading a bit more aggressive than other traders” and had chosen not to do business with the trader.
Still, ICBC London ultimately decided to keep serving its long-time client, classifying it as “high risk.” “The group remains vital part of ICBC London relationship,” a bank officer noted in an internal memo.
In response to reporters’ questions, Gunvor’s corporate affairs director, Seth Pietras, acknowledged that in 2024 the company “did undertake some limited sanctions-compliant trading of Russian commodities” and said that those activities are “disclosed transparently to our financial institutions and to relevant national competent authorities.” In his emailed statement to Göteborgs-Posten, Pietras added that all of Gunvor’s trading activity is performed in strict compliance with U.S., U.K., the European Union and other countries’ sanctions laws.
“Gunvor fully stands by its public statements relating to its decrease in trading and activities in Russia,” he said.
ICBC did not respond to ICIJ’s requests for comment.
Göteborgs-Posten’s Tobias Andersson Åkerblom and ICIJ’s Denise Ajiri contributed reporting for this article.

Trump Leaves Key US Allies Out of NATO Group Meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:43:52 UTC
17:43:52 KST

The Trump administration has excluded several major NATO allies, including the UK, France and the Baltic states, from an October meeting in Poland intended to discuss the alliance’s future.
The Pentagon-led gathering is being organized by US Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and will involve a select group of NATO countries, Politico reported on Wednesday, Sept. 30, citing six diplomats familiar with the planning.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The countries invited to participate are Norway, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. Colby has already held two similar meetings with representatives of those countries under a format known as the Bergen Group.
The exclusion of Britain, France and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania has caused confusion because the countries are among NATO’s most active defense contributors and play important roles in deterring Russian aggression in Europe.
“We’re doing everything that is being asked of us,” an official from one excluded country told Politico. “We’re trying to understand what the criteria is and what the purpose of these meetings are. Not much has been passed on to us yet.”
The White House did not respond to Politico’s request for comment, while the Pentagon declined to comment.
Pentagon creates select NATO group
Colby previously described the participants as NATO members that were quickly fulfilling their defense-spending commitments, possessed sufficient military scale and were prepared to focus on practical decisions.
Trump Again Blames Ukraine for Rising US Diesel Prices, Dismissing Middle East War Impact
A diplomat from one participating country said the Bergen Group was not intended to undermine NATO. Instead, members are expected to develop proposals that can later be tested and discussed by the full alliance.
“This can be an engine for transformation” for NATO, the diplomat said.
Denmark could become the next country invited to join following an agreement allowing the US to expand its military presence in Greenland, according to a person familiar with the planning.
However, even some invited countries have questioned why Washington selected particular participants while excluding major European military powers.
“If they try splitting NATO into the good ones and the bad ones, it is dangerous for the US,” another diplomat said. “But for Europe, this is existential.”
Trump increases pressure on allies
The initiative follows repeated threats by President Donald Trump and senior administration officials to reward what they describe as “model allies” while penalizing countries that resist US priorities.
Trump has criticized NATO members over defense spending and their refusal to support the US war against Iran. His administration previously considered creating what officials described as a “naughty and nice list” of allies based on their compliance with Washington’s demands, Politico reported.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has similarly said countries supporting US interests would be treated as model partners, while those that do not could face consequences.
The latest move comes despite NATO leaders’ public efforts to demonstrate unity at their July summit in Ankara. Previously, allies pledged €70 billion ($79 billion) in military assistance for Ukraine in 2026 and promised to maintain comparable support in 2027.
The summit also reaffirmed NATO’s collective-defense commitment and its target for members to allocate 5% of gross domestic product to defense and security-related spending by 2035.

Ukraine spots “whiskered” Shahed aimed at power lines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:42:35 UTC
17:42:35 KST

- Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko published video of a jet-powered Shahed fitted with whisker-like contacts, likely to detonate on power lines.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Russia appears to have used a jet drone carrying a 40-kg cutting warhead built for pylons and bridges.
A previously unseen version of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drone has appeared in Ukraine fitted with whisker-like rods on its nose, a modification that Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko says is designed to detonate the warhead on contact with high-voltage power lines.
Sternenko, a Ukrainian volunteer and activist who runs one of the country’s largest drone fundraising efforts, published video of the drone on X, saying the “whiskers” are most likely there to close an electrical contact and set off the charge when the drone strikes something as thin as a power cable. A similar modification has been seen at another location, though Sternenko did not say where either drone was found or whether it was intact.
“And this is a whiskered Shahed with a specialized warhead for attacks on high-voltage power lines. Most likely the whiskers were added to close a contact and initiate the warhead when hitting small targets such as power lines,” Sternenko wrote.
A standard impact fuse needs a solid surface to trigger, so a drone that clips a cable or the open lattice of a transmission tower may fly through or fall without exploding. Rods sticking out ahead of the airframe would let the drone detonate as soon as they touch a wire.
A second development points in the same direction. Serhii Beskrestnov, known as “Flash,” a specialist in drones and electronic warfare who serves as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s adviser on defense technology, said Russia appeared to use a special warhead on a jet-powered drone for the first time on Sept. 30. He identified it as a shaped-charge cutting payload, known by its Russian initials KRSN, designed specifically to destroy high-voltage transmission towers and steel bridge structures.
According to Beskrestnov, the KRSN consists of a 40-kg (88-pound) main charge and four additional strike modules. A cutting charge focuses its blast along a line to slice through metal, which makes it suited to severing the legs of a steel pylon or the girders of a bridge rather than causing broad blast damage. Beskrestnov did not say where the drone carrying it struck or what damage it caused.
Russia has attacked Ukraine’s power system throughout the war, mainly with missiles and Iranian-designed Shahed drones aimed at power plants and substations. Ukraine’s long transmission lines, which run across open country and are hard to defend, have been less frequent targets because individual towers and cables are small and difficult for a drone to hit and destroy. The jet-powered Shahed variants, which fly much faster than the original propeller-driven model, also give Ukrainian air defenses less time to react.

Could US sanction Netanyahu? Democrats push anti-settlement bill in House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:41:57 UTC
17:41:57 KST

Six Democratic members of the U.S. House are introducing legislation Thursday that would impose sanctions on foreign individuals and entities involved in building or expanding Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, a proposal that could potentially apply to senior Israeli government officials.
The Stop the Settlements Act is being introduced by Reps. Joaquin Castro of Texas, Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania, Don Beyer of Virginia, Greg Casar of Texas, Sara Jacobs of California and Veronica Escobar of Texas. More than 30 other House Democrats have signed on as original co-sponsors, including several longtime members of the party.
The bill would require sanctions against foreign individuals or entities involved in establishing new Israeli settlements or outposts in the West Bank or Gaza, including through infrastructure development, construction in the area known as E1 or facilitating the movement of Israeli civilians into settlements. It would also authorize measures targeting those involved in maintaining or expanding certain existing settlements and outposts.
E1 is a strategically sensitive tract of land east of Jerusalem between the city and the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim. Settlement construction there has long drawn international opposition because critics say it would make a contiguous Palestinian state more difficult to establish.
Potential penalties under the legislation include blocking assets and denying or revoking U.S. visas. The measure would also prohibit imports into the United States of goods produced wholly or partly in Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank and Gaza, moving beyond product-labeling requirements to an import ban.
Because the legislation applies broadly to foreign individuals and entities involved in settlement activity, Israeli government officials could potentially fall within its scope. U.S. citizens would be exempt from the sanctions provisions, including Israeli settlers who also hold American citizenship.
The proposal does not itself provide a comprehensive list of locations considered settlements, leaving implementation and sanctions designations to the executive branch.
The bill represents a broader approach than previous U.S. sanctions targeting individuals accused of violence or destabilizing activity in the West Bank. Its sponsors say they are seeking to use economic pressure against settlement construction and expansion itself.
Castro said the legislation was intended to give individuals and companies a choice between participating in settlement activity and maintaining access to the U.S. economy. He said he plans to continue pressing the issue “in the coming months and in the next Congress.”
Supporters of the legislation argue that settlement expansion displaces Palestinians and undermines the prospects for a negotiated Israeli-Palestinian settlement. Several sponsors also characterize Israeli settlements as violations of international law. Israel disputes some international legal characterizations of the settlements and has historically argued that the status of the territories should be resolved through negotiations.
The proposal comes amid growing criticism among congressional Democrats of Israeli settlement policy. J Street, a U.S. organization that describes itself as pro-Israel and pro-peace, endorsed the legislation, saying economic consequences were needed after decades of international opposition to settlement expansion.
The legislation faces significant obstacles in the current Republican-controlled House and under President Donald Trump, making enactment in the current Congress unlikely. Its sponsors, however, are framing it partly as groundwork for a future Congress.
A senior Democratic official said the prospects for such legislation would also be affected by the outcome of Israel’s elections and whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current governing coalition remains in power. The official said senior Democrats’ ability to block such measures “depends entirely on whether the current coalition continues. If it does, these laws will pass.” That assessment represents the official’s political judgment rather than a certainty about future congressional action.

Photos: Kashmir’s Dal Lake faces environmental and climate challenges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:41:57 UTC
17:41:57 KST

In Pictures
Photos: Kashmir’s Dal Lake faces environmental and climate challenges
Dal Lake’s fragile ecosystem is deteriorating amid pollution, unregulated construction and climate change in Kashmir.
Dal Lake in Srinagar, the heart of tourism and cultural life in Indian-administered Kashmir, is slowly giving way under mounting population and environmental pressures.
Once renowned for its clear waters, floating gardens and houseboats, the lake is now clogged with untreated sewage, plastic waste and rampant weed growth, even as thousands of residents and businesses rely on it for transport and their livelihoods.
Unregulated construction along its shores, land encroachment and the expansion of nearby neighbourhoods have reduced its surface area and further damaged its fragile ecosystem.
The impact of climate change, including erratic rainfall and rising temperatures, is accelerating the lake’s decline.
Despite periodic clean-up campaigns and official conservation schemes, the future of Dal Lake remains uncertain, reflecting a wider environmental crisis across the Kashmir Valley.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Thursday hailed the “expulsion” of the US from Iraq, saying the move marks the beginning of a broader US withdrawal from the region.
In a statement marking the completion of the US withdrawal from Iraq, the IRGC said the development was “the herald of West Asia’s liberation from the yoke of the Great Satan’s domination.”
The IRGC said the US departure from Iraq was the result of the “will of the Iraqi people,” as well as "resistance and action by the Iraqi government," describing it as a “historic victory.”

Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said the 12-year campaign “defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region.”
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the coalition’s military mission in Iraq under a timetable extending through the end of September 2026, with a transition to bilateral security relations between Iraq and member states.
The coalition was formed under US leadership in 2014 after ISIS (Daesh) seized large areas of Iraq and Syria, providing Iraqi forces with air, intelligence and training support during operations against the group.
Iraq announced in December 2017 that it had regained full control of territory seized by ISIS.
American forces first invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove Saddam Hussein, and withdrew at the end of 2011.

The world-leading internet and technology company this year agreed to a five-year lease across multiple Oracle data centers in south-east Asia amid an escalating AI race.
Neither Tencent nor Oracle has publicly revealed the reported deal.
Tencent's largest overseas deal empowered the company to access around 100,000 advanced AI chips, which were not available in China.
The agreement includes an upfront payment of about 30%.
The settlement follows a shortage of domestic supply and tightening American export controls that have led Chinese tech groups to seek more computing capacity overseas.
While Tencent is keeping pace with multibillion-dollar leasing deals, ByteDance and Alibaba remain the biggest clients of data centers in south-east Asia.
The tech group has increased its infrastructure spending over the past year as the company is also implementing AI agents in its ecosystem, particularly its WeChat superapp, which has more than 1.4 billion users.

U.S. Air Force taps BAE for pulsed laser research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:33:42 UTC
17:33:42 KST

- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded BAE Systems a contract worth up to $19.7 million for pulsed and solid-state laser research.
- Work will take place at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, through September 2031, with $1 million obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has hired BAE Systems to work out how pulsed lasers could be used for military missions and how to pair solid-state lasers with beam control systems the U.S. Air Force already has, under a contract worth up to $19.7 million.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, for a program called Laser Utilization for Military Innovation and Novel Applications, went to BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Broomfield, Colorado. The laboratory obligated $1 million in fiscal 2026 research funds at the time of award, and the work runs through Sept. 29, 2031. Six companies bid for it.
The contract notice describes two goals: finding ways to use the advantages of pulsed lasers, and integrating solid-state laser technology with existing beam control systems. A pulsed laser releases its energy in very short, intense bursts, while a continuous-wave laser, the type used in most laser weapons fielded so far, delivers a steady beam. Beam control is the set of optics, sensors and tracking equipment that points a laser, keeps it locked on a moving target and corrects for distortion in the air, and it is often the hardest part of making a laser weapon work.
The notice does not say what military applications the U.S. Air Force has in mind, whether the work is aimed at weapons, sensing, communications or something else, or what kind of targets or platforms are involved.
All of the work will take place at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, home to the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Directed Energy Directorate, which leads the service’s research on high-energy lasers and high-power microwaves.
BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems is the former Ball Aerospace, which BAE Systems bought in 2024. The Colorado unit builds spacecraft, satellite instruments and optical and sensor systems for the U.S. military and NASA.
As a cost-plus contract with a maximum ceiling, the deal reimburses BAE Systems for its costs plus a fixed fee, and the U.S. Air Force is not obligated to spend the full $19.7 million.

The Design Museum Gent , in the East Flanders' capital, is set to reopen this coming weekend after four years of renovations. The refurbished Design Museum Gent will showcase 500 objects, nearly half of which the museum has never exhibited before.
The refurbished Design Museum Gent now covers an area of approximately 6,500 square metres and has a total of around 3,700 square metres of exhibition space.
A new building has been added to the museum. This connects the existing buildings and provides space for lectures, workshops and events. On the 4th floor, there is an events space with a panoramic view over the fair city of Ghent.
The museum has a collection totalling 24,000 design pieces. 500 objects will be on display. Almost half of these have never been exhibited by the museum before.
10 unique loos
“I began a feasibility study in 2015,” explains director Katrien Laporte. “To identify what our needs were. And now, 11 years later, here we are in the new Design Museum Gent.”
“A great deal has changed. The building now fulfils a number of functions it didn’t have before. We didn’t have proper toilets, we didn’t have a lift, and we didn’t have a space for lectures, debates and events.”
“The new building is a very warm, accessible building, constructed entirely of timber. We also want it to make a statement. Design used to have an elitist image. This building will help to bring it down from its pedestal.”
‘You really do have to revisit the museum several times if only for the toilets. We have 10 different toilet cubicles, each with different tiles. It’s very tongue-in-cheek. And when you’re sitting on the loo, you can scan a QR code to find out how the tile was made.’
Opening festival
This coming weekend, the Design Museum Gent will reopen with a major opening festival lasting nine days.
There are more than 120 activities, including performances, music and workshops. Thirty-three shops and hotels in Ghent are transforming their shop windows into temporary exhibitions.
The festivities kick off on Friday evening with a performance by the Ghent-based brothers of 2manydjs. They will be playing from the balcony of the new building. On Sunday, between 10.00 and 16.00, local designers will be showcasing their work at 60 stalls at the Design Makers Market.

Corruption and EU reluctance: Ukrainians name key obstacles to EU membership – KIIS

Corruption and EU reluctance: Ukrainians name key obstacles to EU membership – KIIS
A total of 32% of Ukrainians believe corruption in the central government is the biggest obstacle to the country's EU membership, while 29% point to the reluctance of the European Union or some of its member states to admit Ukraine.
Source: a survey conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on 12-21 September
Details: Survey participants were asked to choose one of six answers to the question of what most hinders Ukraine's progress towards EU membership.
A total of 32% cited corruption in the central government, while 29% pointed to the reluctance of the EU or some of its member states to admit Ukraine.
Another 15% cited the war, while 10% pointed to the inadequate performance of the government and parliament.
Resistance to reforms by certain influential groups was selected by 5% of respondents, while 3% cited insufficient independence of the judiciary and law enforcement agencies.
For reference: The Kyiv International Institute of Sociology conducted its nationwide Omnibus public opinion survey, which included questions commissioned by the NGO Forum on attitudes towards holding an independent competitive selection process involving foreign experts to appoint the prosecutor general, as well as Ukraine's progress towards EU membership.
KIIS interviewed 1,002 Ukrainian citizens over 18 by telephone who were living in government-controlled territory. Respondents were selected using a random sample of mobile phone numbers.
The sample did not include residents of Russian-occupied territories or Ukrainian citizens who left the country after 24 February 2022. However, internally displaced people from occupied territories were included among the respondents.
The formal statistical margin of error, taking the design effect into account, does not exceed 4.1 percentage points. KIIS notes that additional systematic deviations may occur under wartime conditions.
Background:
- The European Commission has postponed until 6 October the presentation of its assessment of how future EU enlargement will affect the bloc's key policies and what changes the EU itself may need in order to admit new member states.
- Earlier, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos presented four areas for changes to the EU enlargement process: internal reforms of the bloc, stronger democratic safeguards, gradual integration and transitional measures.

design museum gent reopens with new wing built from locally made waste bricks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:30:02 UTC
17:30:02 KST

design museum gent reopens with new wing built from locally made waste bricks
carmody groarke and ATAMA lead the new extension, while RE-ST restores the historic buildings as part of a wider transformation that rethinks the museum’s collection, exhibitions and public spaces.
Design Museum Gent opens its collection to new perspectives
Design Museum Gent in Ghent, Belgium, reopens on October 3rd, 2026, following a four-year renovation and expansion led by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA, with the historic buildings restored by RE-ST. The project repositions the museum as an open civic space where design is used to examine how objects, cities and social systems are shaped. The new 2,200-square-meter wing completes the fragmented museum complex around its historic courtyard and introduces freely accessible spaces for exhibitions, workshops, lectures, events and community activity. The extension uses timber and white brick, with a facade made from Gent Waste Brick (find designboom’s previous coverage here), a lime-cured brick produced from locally sourced municipal waste. More than 82,000 bricks were produced locally at Het Arsenaal in Ghent, hardened through a low-energy lime-curing process.
Its new exhibition, Collection. Models from the Past for the Future, places around 500 objects from the museum’s 24,000-piece collection into contemporary themes including copy, comfort, migration, folds and connections, asking what earlier design ideas can still offer and what now needs to be reconsidered. Meanwhile, Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy treats democratic systems themselves as designed structures, while projects such as the AI-powered Searcher and the collaborative CO-LAB extend the role of the institution from displaying design to testing how it can operate as a tool for participation, debate and change.
completing a fragmented museum in ghent, belgium
The architectural project brings together a complex collection of buildings dating from the 16th to the 20th century, working to connect the existing parts into a more coherent whole. The new wing occupies a previously underused southern passage and an unused plot at the center of the site. Its addition allows the historic courtyard of Hotel de Coninck to become a garden and a central point of orientation, with views toward it running through the building and helping visitors understand the relationship between the different parts of the museum.
The building is organized around six zones: the basement art-handling area, the Stadskamer reception and shop, the Forum lecture space, the Atelier workshops, the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions, and the Loft, an event space on the fourth floor with views over Ghent. The Stadskamer, conceived as a freely accessible ‘city room,’ is intended as a place where local communities and neighborhoods can meet and present their own creations.
The white color of the new wing relates to the historic houses along Drabstraat, while the scale and rhythm of the facade draw from Ghent’s guild and merchant houses. Deep window reveals and pronounced copings give the contemporary building a civic presence without attempting to imitate its historic neighbors. Historic interiors have been restored, while later additions have been adapted to create additional space and improve climatic conditions. Materials are reused where possible, positioning the renovation as an exercise in working with what already exists.
looking at the collection differently
The renewed architectural framework of the Design Museum Gent is matched by a change in how its collection is presented. Collection. Models from the Past for the Future, curated by Evelien Bracke, returns to the institution’s origins as a ‘model museum.’ Founded in 1903, Design Museum Gent originally collected exemplary objects intended to inform and inspire craftspeople and visitors. The new display takes that premise and turns it into a contemporary question. Around 500 objects are organized around five themes, copy, comfort, migration, folds and connections, rather than being presented primarily through individual designers or chronological development. The curatorial goal is to make historical design less about established canon and more about changing interpretation. Objects once regarded as exemplary can now be reconsidered through contemporary concerns, while historical techniques and approaches can offer unexpected models for the future. Contemporary designers including Kana Arioka, OpenStructures and Victor Verhelst respond to objects and themes from the collection, bringing them into conversation with new work and showing how the archive can continue to inform contemporary practice.
The scenography of the exhibition by Nord + Laura Muyldermans also stages a conversation between different forms of making. Traditional clay-plastered walls are combined with the Belgian circular steel construction system Skellet, placing artisanal and industrial approaches alongside one another.
from objects to democratic systems
The museum’s most direct expansion of its design remit comes through Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy, the opening exhibition curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti. The premise is straightforward but consequential: democratic systems are designed. Ballot papers, parliamentary buildings and voting procedures are visible manifestations of that design, but so are the less tangible structures that determine who participates, who is represented and who is heard.
The exhibition considers questions of accessibility, including how people experiencing homelessness or visual impairments interact with electoral systems, alongside histories of women’s suffrage, civil rights and protest. Its Democracy Fitness Trail extends the exhibition into an interactive format. Visitors are invited to practice skills such as active listening, compromise and constructive conflict, treating democratic participation as something that can be exercised.
The approach grew partly from DE40, a citizens’ panel in which 40 residents of Ghent discussed how the museum could make design more accessible and relevant to people regardless of their background or prior knowledge. Their input was used as a framework for the museum’s transformation.
an institution that experiments with its own tools
 Technology becomes another way for Design Museum Gent to question how collections are accessed.
 Searcher, developed by Jon Stam, Valentin Vogelman and Boris Smeenk, uses AI to allow visitors to explore the collection of the museum through similarities in form, color and text. A museum archive can easily become a fixed narrative, organized around established classifications and historical hierarchies. Searcher presents it as a network that can be navigated through association and discovery.
The museum is also using its physical spaces as a platform for collaborative production. CO-LAB, curated by Siegrid Demyttenaere, brings Belgian and international designers, researchers and local communities together across eight historic period rooms in Hotel de Coninck. The projects address subjects including sustainable energy, queer archives, designing with nature and open-source tools.
project info:
name: Design Museum Gent | @designmuseumgent renovation and new wing
architects: Carmody Groarke | @carmodygroarke, ATAMA | @atama_architects, RE-ST
 location: Ghent, Belgium
 opening: October 3rd, 2026
 new wing area: 2,200 sqm
 historic buildings: 6,400 sqm
 structural engineer: Ney & Partners
 building services: Boydens Engineering
 acoustics: Daidalos Peutz

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- 'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' film in detailed response
'The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts,' IDF lambasts 'NAZA' film in detailed response
In a detailed rebuttal to the documentary "NAZA," the IDF said the film relies on anonymous, uncorroborated testimony from junior intelligence personnel to mischaracterize the IDF's strike process
The IDF published a formal response to the documentary "NAZA," saying it presents "a distorted, misleading, and disingenuous picture" of the military's target planning and strike process. The IDF said the film's narrative relies on testimony from anonymous individuals who generally describe only the initial, intelligence-gathering stages of a much longer targeting process, resulting in what it called "an incorrect and highly misleading description of reality."
The military noted that "NAZA" is the Hebrew acronym for "collateral damage," a standard term used by law-abiding militaries worldwide. It points out that the film paradoxically presents the IDF's detailed civilian harm estimation process as evidence of indifference to civilian life, when such assessments are in fact required under international law.
The IDF said the filmmakers did not submit their allegations for examination before publication and declined to provide the IDF a copy of the film after a public screening, despite the military's request. As a result, the IDF said it based its response on an account from a representative who attended a public screening, along with other public reporting and statements from the filmmakers themselves.
The IDF argued that the anonymous interviewees spoke about matters beyond their knowledge and competence, and testimony confined to preliminary stages does not establish the final assessments on which commanders relied. For example, an interviewee may recall a general, preliminary estimate of civilians present in an area around a military objective, but did not account for precautions decided later in the process.
Suggested articles
Additionally, the IDF claimed that besides the anonymous accounts, the film did not cite any military directives, contemporaneous records, or other corroborating evidence. The film's accounts of alleged strikes include no specific targets, dates, locations, or casualty figures, making the claims "general and unverifiable," the IDF claims.
Among the specific claims addressed, the IDF denied that artificial intelligence autonomously generated tens of thousands of human targets that were then struck, stating flatly that "in the IDF, artificial intelligence does not determine whether an object or a person is designated as a target, nor whether a target is struck." The military said human analysts identify targets under defined procedures, with decisions ultimately made by operational commanders.
Regarding allegations that soldiers fired on civilians near humanitarian aid distribution sites, the IDF said rules of engagement permitted fire only against armed operatives or suspects posing an immediate threat.
The IDF strongly rejected the film's suggestion that an interviewee's personal view constituted evidence of genocide, calling the allegation "outrageous and unfounded." It noted that genocide under international law requires specific intent to destroy a group, which it said, "never existed."
The military said its objectives in Gaza were to dismantle Hamas's military and governing capabilities and secure the return of hostages, not to harm Palestinian civilians. The IDF pointed to its warnings, strike cancellations, and facilitation of humanitarian aid, including more than 3.9 million metric tons of food delivered into Gaza since October 2023, as evidence against the claim.
The IDF said the film omits essential context necessary to understand its conduct during the war, including the October 7 massacre and Hamas's systematic embedding of military infrastructure within civilian areas such as hospitals, schools and mosques. It said the film's narrative is reinforced through "manipulative editing of interviews" and omits the professionals, including legal advisers and commanders, responsible for mitigating civilian harm throughout the targeting process.
"The tragic consequences of war do not justify distorting the facts," the IDF said, adding that "the IDF has acted and continues to act humanely, even if the filmmakers have done everything they can to conceal that fact."

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:27:36 UTC
17:27:36 KST

The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.
The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.
The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.
In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.
Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.
“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”
The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.
Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.
US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.
Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.
“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.
“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”
Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.
“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”
Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.
Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.
The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.
Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.
The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

Casio’s Crystal G-Shock Is the Most Expensive Ever Made
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:59 UTC
17:25:59 KST

At Madison Square Garden in New York City on November 9, 2017, at the G-Shock 35th Anniversary Celebration, G-Shock creator Kikuo Ibe showed off three sapphire-crystal prototype watches: one clear, one ruby, and one sapphire blue. Because machining sapphire was so difficult at the time, each watch took over a month to produce.
These were built with, for the time, high-end Casio features such as Tough Solar power and Multiband 6 radio-controlled timekeeping—but as they didn’t meet the G-Shock shock-resistance standards, the trio was never intended for sale. They were primarily a symbol of innovation for the Japanese brand, which started in 1983 specializing in super-tough performance timepieces.
Now, nine years later, in what Casio is calling the culmination of an “eight-year project” (so presumably the ball started rolling soon after the excited reception Ibe’s crystal concepts got on stage at MSG), G-Shock is launching a three-watch collection using blue sapphire as an expression of what happens when G-Shock toughness meets Japanese engineering. The flagship model, and by far the most expensive, is the $80,000 MRG-D5000, the first-ever retail G-Shock with an outer case and bezel hewn entirely from blue sapphire crystal.
The collection is called the “Blue Rose Project” because the blue rose is viewed as a symbol of making the impossible possible since it doesn’t exist in nature. It sees the super-expensive MRG-D5000 released alongside the $9,500 MRG-B5000SA-2, and the GMW-B5000SB-1A for $850.
Only 20 of the $80,000 MRG-D5000 full-sapphire G-Shocks will be made, putting these rugged “luxury” timepieces somewhat implausibly in the same price bracket as a Patek Philippe or Porsche Macan. This is quite the flex from a company that also sells its watches for less than $90.
The 2017 concept watches required metal bracing to hold the crystal sections together, which is partly why they couldn’t pass G-Shock’s rigorous toughness tests. The new MRG-D5000, however, is a fully functional G-Shock, taking construction lessons from the MR-G engineering team who found that dividing the outer case into multiple interacting components could disperse impact more effectively than a conventional single-piece construction.
G-Shock fans will have already seen this technique employed in the titanium MRG-B5000 from 2022, but this “Multi-Guard Structure” has now been reengineered specifically for sapphire crystal, with Casio claiming the construction takes inspiration from traditional Japanese timber-frame techniques, using interlocking pieces rather than placing stress around screw holes or other details that could result in cracking.
While the MRG-D5000’s bezel and outer case are entirely machined from blue sapphire crystal ingots grown over several months, sadly—unlike the 2017 concepts—the strap isn’t matching sapphire but instead a rubber strap that repeats the brick pattern seen on the watch face in raised detail. To round off the luxe makeover, the MRG-D5000’s MR-G mark, “Shock Resist,” and other lettering on the face are in 24-carat gold.
The G-Shock development team responsible for the new collection tells WIRED the fundamental challenge was building a “near-unbreakable” watch using an inherently brittle material. Making watch cases from sapphire is not new in the high-end watch world, and many distinguished makers, including Richard Mille and Hublot, have released pieces made of the crystal.
To make the sapphire case work for a G-Shock, however, Casio had to develop a brand-new, dedicated shock-resistant structure, with the Multi-Guard construction using virtually invisible seams, alongside a completely screwless assembly method to hit the required shock performance. To do this, the outer case assembly required the development of completely new, dedicated jigs and fixtures, a process apparently so demanding that only one person at Yamagata Casio (the primary “mother factory” for Casio) can currently perform it.
All three new watches, along with the proper G-Shock resistance to knocks and drops, are water-resistant to 200 meters, solar-powered, and feature radio-controlled timekeeping, world time, stopwatch, countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full-auto LED backlight.
If the $80K G-Shock is too steep an investment, the MRG-B5000SA-2 with two two-carat facet-cut blue sapphires and a grade-5 titanium exterior is limited to 500 pieces. The cheapest GMW-B5000SB-1A2 marries a full-metal black exterior with four round brilliant-cut blue sapphires.

U.S. Navy buys more 30mm guns to shoot down drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:25:56 UTC
17:25:56 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded MSI Defence Systems US a $197 million sole-source contract for MK88 MOD4 30 mm gun mounts and MK48 MOD2 sights.
- Most of the work will be done in Norfolk, England, with deliveries due by January 2031.
The U.S. Navy has awarded British-owned MSI Defence Systems a $197 million contract for 30mm deck gun mounts and the electro-optical sights that aim them, the weapons the service is fitting to its warships to shoot down small drones and fast attack boats.
The firm-fixed-price contract, issued by Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division in Maryland, covers MK88 MOD4 gun mounts, MK48 MOD2 electro-optical sights, related hardware and spares. The Department of War did not say how many systems it buys. Deliveries are due to finish by January 2031.
Together with an operator console, the gun mount and sight make up the MK 38 MOD 4 gun weapon system, which replaces the 25 mm MK 38 MOD 3 on U.S. Navy ships. The U.S. Navy has said the older system fell short of its requirements for countering drones, and the new version adds a larger 30 mm MK44 Bushmaster II cannon, with an optional coaxial .50-caliber machine gun. The mount holds 400 rounds in two separate ammunition bins, letting the crew switch between ammunition types.
Unlike earlier versions, the MOD 4 places its camera sight away from the gun rather than on the mount itself, so the system can track a target independently and pass aiming data to the gun. The design is based on MSI’s Seahawk DS30M A2 mount, a family of guns already used by the Royal Navy and other fleets.
The destroyer USS Mustin (DDG 89) became the first U.S. Navy warship to receive the system, with two mounts installed during a maintenance period in San Diego, Naval News reported in April 2024. The U.S. Navy plans to replace the 25 mm guns on its Arleigh Burke-class destroyers with the new system, and the U.S. Coast Guard also uses it.
The new contract is far larger than earlier orders. MSI received about $23.5 million in September 2023 for 15 gun mounts in low-rate production and about $34.5 million in late 2025 for 18 more, along with separate deals for the sight system. The company first delivered eight prototype systems for testing.
The U.S. Navy awarded the contract without competition under a legal exception for production that follows prototypes successfully completed under an other transaction agreement, a faster contracting route used for experimental work.
Most of the work, 73%, will take place at MSI’s facilities in Norfolk, England, with 19% at its U.S. subsidiary in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and the rest in Bozeman, Montana, and Eagleville, Pennsylvania. MSI Defence Systems is part of British company MS International.
The U.S. Navy obligated about $61.3 million at the time of award, drawing on weapons procurement and shipbuilding funds from fiscal 2023 through 2026, including money from accounts used to build new ships.

Immigration judge rules US can deport activist and community leader Salah Sarsour
An immigration judge ruled that the US government can deport Palestinian American Salah Sarsour, who is the president of Wisconsin's largest mosque and a US permanent resident, under a Cold War-era law.
Sarsour, who grew up in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was taken by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in late March and released in mid-June after a federal judge said he had raised a substantial free speech retaliation claim that would render his detention unlawful.
Chicago Immigration Court Judge Jayme Salinardi sided late on Tuesday with the government's argument that Sarsour posed a security and foreign policy threat under the Cold War-era Immigration and Nationality Act, while rejecting the government's allegation that he lied on his green card application.
The US Department of Homeland Security welcomed the ruling, saying the judge "sustained multiple grounds of removability" in the case.
Sarsour said his legal team will appeal the ruling, which he called "deeply disappointing."
"I will not stop standing up for what's right and for justice in Palestine," he said in a statement. Sarsour cannot be deported until all legal avenues available to him are exhausted. He says his life will be at risk if deported to the occupied West Bank.
Islamic Society of Milwaukee, Wisconsin's largest mosque, says Sarsour has lived in the US for over three decades.
The mosque has said Sarsour was "being targeted on the basis of his Palestinian and Muslim background, and his advocacy for Palestinian rights."
He has type 2 diabetes and lost more than 30 pounds in ICE detention, his legal team said.
Sarsour has no criminal record in the US and was convicted as a teenager in Israeli military court before he came to the United States, which the Trump administration noted to cast him as a threat. Sarsour says the government has known that information for decades.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem says military courts in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried for alleged crimes, have a 96% conviction rate and a history of extracting confessions through torture.
Sarsour denies committing crimes and says he was tortured and coerced into past confessions.
"This immigration proceeding has made it clear that I am being unfairly targeted by this administration for my advocacy on Palestinian human rights," he said in a public statement last month about the situation..
"I put my trust in God and my legal team to navigate this attack on me and the life I have built in America, and that I can continue to be with my family in Wisconsin as I have for the past three decades," he added.
Trump has attempted to deport foreign pro-Palestinian protesters, threatened funding freezes for universities where protests were held, enforced a social media screening of immigrants and sanctioned critics of Israel's genocide of the Palestinian people.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survives 2 lethal doses

08:25:00 UTC

A Tennessee woman convicted of murder survived two lethal injection doses and was hospitalized Thursday, prompting state officials to halt all executions this year after a second botched procedure in months.
Hours earlier Wednesday, the Supreme Court cleared the way for Christa Pike, 50, to become the first woman executed in the southern U.S. state of Tennessee in 200 years, but the attempt failed.
"This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said. "There is no precedent."
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol," adding Pike was taken to an "off-site medical facility."
Her attorneys said she was transported to a nearby hospital, adding they had not been informed of her condition.
"Tonight the state of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution," the attorneys said in a statement.
Tennessee halted the execution by lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after medical staff could not tap a vein.
Gov. Bill Lee called for a "comprehensive, third-party review" after Pike's failed execution.
"The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year," Lee said, apparently referencing the execution of convicted killer Gary Wayne Sutton scheduled for Dec. 3.
Pike was scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. (3 p.m. GMT) at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, where witnesses including journalists were present for the injections.
Kim Chandler, a media witness for The Associated Press, told CBS News, "Pike appeared notably awake as the execution began."
After the blinds of the execution chamber closed for the final time, Pike "could be heard loudly snoring, clearly very alive in the chamber until media witnesses were told to leave the area," Chandler said.
During a livestream, an ambulance with its lights flashing left the site of the execution. It was unclear whether it was transporting Pike.
The execution procedure went ahead hours after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled it could proceed, with liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissenting.
"The Court's decision ... unnecessarily prevents that lower court from giving Pike's claim due consideration," the dissenting justices wrote.
"Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the state to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts."
The case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.
Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.
The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.
Pike's lawyers argued she should be granted clemency because of her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing.
"She was 18 when she committed her crime and she was deeply mentally ill," they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.
The U.S. Supreme Court rejected Tuesday an application for a stay of execution, which argued Pike's history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause "needless suffering."
Independent United Nations human rights experts have urged the U.S. government and Tennessee authorities to "immediately halt" the execution and commute her death sentence.
In the U.S., only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Crete at the mercy of severe weather: Floods, landslides, power cuts and closed schools

Unknown Publisher

Heavy rain and thunderstorms have turned roads into torrents, causing landslides and power cuts, while authorities and civil protection are on high alert.
Severe problems in many parts of the Greek island of Crete have been caused by the powerful wave of bad weather that has been under way since Wednesday night.
The situation is particularly difficult in the mountainous Mylopotamos area, where the deluge has created serious disruption, mainly in Zoniana, Livadia and Axos.
In Zoniana, water entered homes, roads were flooded and in many places debris has been swept onto the carriageway. Crews from the Municipality of Mylopotamos and the Region of Crete have been working since the early hours, using machinery to restore access and tackle the damage.
At the same time, in Zoniana water is being pumped out of basements and other underground spaces. A similar operation is under way in Axos, where damage has also been recorded, while there are temporary problems on the Axos–Anogeia road.
Serious incident in Livadia
In Livadia, the force of the water flow caused damage to the Diskouri bridge. According to information available so far, a vehicle carrying a couple ended up in the river after part of the bridge collapsed.
The two occupants were injured and taken to the University General Hospital of Heraklion to receive medical care. Their condition has not yet been made known.
The bad weather has also caused problems to the electricity network. Zoniana, Anogeia and Axos are facing power cuts, while in Zoniana in particular there have been reports of fallen electricity poles.
Electricity grid operator HEDNO has been notified and crews are expected to carry out the necessary works to repair the damage.
So far there have been no reports of people being trapped or other situations posing an immediate risk to human life.
Travel warning
Because of the severity of the weather, a message has been sent via 112 advising citizens to avoid travelling to Zoniana, Livadia and the mountainous Mylopotamos area.
Authorities are urging people not to attempt to cross flooded roads and to exercise particular caution in areas where there have been landslides, rockfalls or damage to the road.
Municipal crews remain on standby, with the main priority being to secure safe access to the affected areas.
Problems in Heraklion
Heavy rainfall has also affected parts of Heraklion. Flooding has been recorded in areas of the city, while the Fire Service is receiving calls to pump out water.
Power cuts have been reported in the Agios Ioannis Chostos area, while problems are also being recorded in Tsalikaki.
Serious problems on the Lasithi Plateau
Rainfall is also intense on the Lasithi Plateau, where the bad weather has continued since the night.
According to the available data from meteo.gr, in Tzermiado by Thursday morning 174 millimetres of rain had fallen since the onset of the severe weather.
The mayor of the Municipality of Lasithi Plateau, Giorgos Athanasakis, is appealing to residents to limit their movements and be particularly careful, as the bad weather is still under way.
In Sitia, and in particular in the Palekastro area, large quantities of water have accumulated in a car park, leaving vehicles submerged in the water.
At the same time, the Kalogeropotamos stream in the Agkathia area has swelled significantly, with the increased flow causing concern in neighbouring districts.
Schools closed in many areas
The severe weather has also led to decisions to suspend the operation of schools.
In the Municipality of Mylopotamos, primary and secondary schools are not operating, nor are nurseries and crèches.
Similarly, in the Regional Unit of Lasithi it was decided to suspend the operation of all schools for the day, due to the hazardous weather conditions.
Schools also remain closed in the Municipalities of Sitia and Lasithi Plateau, while similar decisions have been taken in parts of Chania, Rethymno and the Municipality of Minoa Pediada. In Mylopotamos the decision also covers kindergartens and nurseries.
The decisions have been taken as a precaution, with the aim of limiting travel by pupils, teachers and other staff during the severe weather.

The battle for Kordofan: The corridor linking Sudan’s east and west
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:23:44 UTC
17:23:44 KST

The battle for Kordofan: The corridor linking Sudan’s east and west
Kordofan, which lies between the western Darfur region and central Sudan, is now a focal point of Sudan’s war.
Fighting in Sudan’s Kordofan region has intensified since late 2025, turning it into one of the main battlegrounds in the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), now in its fourth year.
The vast region, which comprises North, West and South Kordofan states, lies where the two sides’ areas of control meet, between the army-held central region and the RSF-controlled Darfur in the West. In recent months, the SAF has pushed the RSF out of much of North Kordofan.
The battle is increasingly being fought from the air. Drone strikes on towns in North Kordofan are growing more frequent and deadly, and civilian infrastructure has been hit across the region.
Since the war began in April 2023, one in five recorded attacks in Sudan has taken place in Kordofan.
Al Jazeera maps where the fighting is concentrated in Kordofan and across Sudan, and the displacement that has followed.
Who controls what on the ground?
Sudan is broadly divided between the two sides. The SAF controls the capital, Khartoum, and most of the north, east and centre, while the RSF controls the west, including almost all of Darfur and parts of Kordofan. Smaller armed groups, including the RSF-allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), hold pockets of territory in the south.
The army has the upper hand in the north, the RSF in the west, and South Kordofan remains contested.
Where have most attacks occurred?
According to an Al Jazeera analysis of data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor, there were 14,648 recorded attacks between the start of the war on April 15, 2023, and September 19, 2026.
The four most affected states include:
- Khartoum: The capital region has seen the most, with 5,719 attacks, or 39 percent of the total, almost three times as many as North Darfur, the second-highest
- North Darfur has witnessed 1,999 attacks (13.7 percent)
- Gezira state has seen 1,435 attacks (9.8 percent)
- Kordofan emerged as a major centre for fighting. North, South and West Kordofan together recorded 2,876 attacks, or about 19.7 percent of all recorded attacks, putting the region behind only Khartoum when considered collectively.
Who has carried out the most attacks?
The SAF is associated with the largest share of recorded attacks between April 15, 2023 and September 19, 2026, accounting for just over half (52 percent), compared with just over a third (34.7 percent) for the RSF and 13.3 percent for other actors.
The balance of attacks has shifted over time. The SAF was associated with more recorded attacks than the RSF in the first year and a half of the war, before the RSF overtook it in number of attacks from late 2024 to mid-2025.
Since August 2025, the two sides’ monthly attack counts have been closer, with the SAF generally recording slightly more, even as the overall number of attacks has fallen sharply.
Where have attacks in Kordofan occurred?
After the fall of el-Fasher, the last major Darfur city held by the army and its allies, in October 2025, attention shifted to Kordofan. The region sits between RSF-held Darfur and the army-held centre, north and east, forming a corridor between the two sides’ heartlands.
Kordofan’s three states recorded 2,717 attacks: North Kordofan had 1,205 (44 percent), South Kordofan 789 and West Kordofan 723. Adding Abyei, a disputed oil-rich area on the Sudan-South Sudan border that was historically part of Kordofan, brings the total to 2,878.
The concentration of attacks differs from state to state. In North Kordofan, Sheikan locality alone accounted for 497 attacks, or 41 percent of the state’s total. Sheikan is home to the state capital, el-Obeid, a commercial and administrative hub linking central Sudan with the west. Taking the city would open a route east towards Khartoum for the RSF.
On September 9, a drone strike on a college in el-Obeid tore the roof off the building and killed a security guard, the college’s dean, Abdel Aziz al-Sheikh, told Reuters.
“As you can see, the entire faculty is destroyed and we feel that our dreams are destroyed, our future is destroyed,” Omnia Aboul Gassim, a student who had sat her exams at the el-Obeid college just one day before the attack, told Reuters.
In South Kordofan, Dilling locality was the main hotspot, with 242 attacks (31 percent), followed by Kadugli with 107 (14 percent) and Al Quoz with 94 (12 percent).
Attacks in West Kordofan were spread more evenly across localities. Babnusa recorded the most, with 142, followed by En Nuhud (119), Al Khiwai (112) and Abu Zabad (111).
ACLED has recorded at least 12,314 reported fatalities in Kordofan since April 2023.
The SAF was associated with 1,323 attacks (46 percent) across all three states in Kordofan, compared with 920 (32 percent) for the RSF and 633 (22 percent) for other actors.
How many people are displaced?
About 8.6 million people remain internally displaced across Sudan, according to the latest United Nations figures, down from a peak of 11.6 million in January 2025 as millions returned home to areas retaken by the army. New displacement continues in Kordofan, Darfur and Blue Nile.
Darfur hosts the largest concentrations of internally displaced people (IDPs), particularly South and North Darfur.
Returns have steadily increased since 2025, reaching about 5.1 million by August 2026. Khartoum has seen a major return of displaced people, with about 2.7 million returnees.
Despite the decline, millions remain displaced more than three years into the war. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) says the number of people newly displaced in Kordofan since fighting escalated in October 2025 has risen 65 percent in four months, from more than 132,000 in February to at least 219,000 by late June.
The agency has warned that el-Obeid, which shelters about 500,000 people, including more than 83,000 displaced, faces a looming threat of a full-scale invasion.
“The warning signs are impossible to ignore,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope earlier this month. “Across Sudan, families are fleeing violence, losing access to water, electricity and healthcare, and now facing the added burden of destructive floods.”

The US has until 18 October to choose its Russia sanctions targets—if any. Kyiv’s wish list leads with the firms feeding Russia’s Starlink clone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:18:02 UTC
17:18:02 KST

Ukraine is about to tell Washington exactly which Russian targets it wants punished under America's new sanctions law, the Associated Press reported. A senior Ukrainian diplomat said Kyiv will hand the Trump administration and Congress a wish list of companies, ships, and people this week—and at the top are the firms supplying parts for Russia's answer to Starlink.
The law requires Washington to act but lets the president waive the sanctions if he certifies that doing so serves US national interests, and the first choice falls due in weeks. For Ukraine, a measure that names no targets changes nothing on the ground—which is why the fight now is over whose names make the list before the clock runs out.
A list topped by Russia's Starlink clone
Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said the priority is a group of Russian firms making components for Rassvet, Moscow's homegrown satellite network, which Russia hopes to complete by the end of the year—though its own officials have put the start of service in 2027. Bureau 1440, the firm building Rassvet, is not itself on US sanctions lists, but its parent company, ICS Holding, is under US blocking sanctions, according to Militarnyi. The suppliers feeding the network parts are not sanctioned, and those are the ones Kyiv wants added to the list.
Russia sped up the project after Ukraine and SpaceX cut off the Starlink terminals its troops had used without authorization at the front. If Russia completes the constellation, Sienik said, it could strike Ukraine at will with real-time information—a danger he warned would bite hardest this winter. "If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this program possible for Russia and that will be a game-changer," he told reporters, Reuters reported. Kyiv wants access to Starlink inside Russia, too, so it can strike targets there.
Euromaidan Press has reported how such a network would change the battlefield: the satellites transmit in high-frequency bands that are hard to jam, and a relay overhead would feed drones and missiles fresh coordinates mid-flight, letting them fly low under air defenses that struggle to see them.
Oil tankers and attacks on US firms
Ukraine is pushing for tougher action against Russia's shadow fleet, too—the aging tankers that sell its oil around Western restrictions—and is asking the administration and American industry to publicly condemn Russian attacks on US companies' operations inside Ukraine, Sienik said.
The deadline Washington is now facing
The requests arrive as the administration faces an 18 October deadline to decide which Russian entities, if any, to sanction under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which US President Donald Trump signed into law on 18 September. The law directs the White House to impose tariffs on Russia's biggest oil buyers and to block its banks, officials, and tankers—but lets the president waive those measures, which is why Kyiv is lobbying for the toughest list it can get.

U.S. Marine Corps orders 32 ACV-R armored recovery vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:17:35 UTC
17:17:35 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps awarded BAE Systems a $230.1 million contract modification for 32 full-rate production ACV recovery variants.
- Work will be performed mainly in York, Pennsylvania, with completion expected in November 2028.
The U.S. Marine Corps has ordered 32 recovery versions of its Amphibious Combat Vehicle from BAE Systems, the armored repair-and-tow vehicles that will haul broken-down or damaged ACVs off the battlefield and fix them in the field.
Marine Corps Systems Command awarded BAE Systems a $230.1 million firm-fixed-price modification on Oct. 1 to exercise options for the 32 full-rate production vehicles, along with production, fielding and support costs and spare parts. That works out to about $7.2 million per vehicle, though the figure includes support and spares as well as the vehicles themselves. The work is due to finish in November 2028.
The recovery variant, known as ACV-R, is the fourth and final member of the ACV family, which is replacing the U.S. Marine Corps’ decades-old Assault Amphibious Vehicles. It is designed to give field-level maintenance and towing support to other ACVs, and it replaces the AAV recovery variant, the AAVR7A1, which Marines have kept using while the new vehicle was developed.
The U.S. Marine Corps started paying for the recovery variant in March 2022 with a $34.9 million contract for its design and development, and BAE Systems was due to deliver production-representative test vehicles in 2025. The service said in 2023 that the ACV-R would not reach initial operational capability until early fiscal 2028, Defense News reported, meaning the first units could field it about a year before this order is due to be completed.
The rest of the ACV family is already in service or production. The basic personnel carrier, ACV-P, carries three crew and 13 Marines and has been in full-rate production since December 2020, followed by the ACV-C command and control version. A third variant, the ACV-30, carries a remotely operated 30 mm cannon. BAE Systems builds the eight-wheeled vehicle with Italian partner Iveco Defence Vehicles, whose design it is based on.
Most of the new work, 60%, will take place at BAE Systems’ plant in York, Pennsylvania, with 15% each in Aiken, South Carolina, and San Jose, California, and 5% each in Sterling Heights, Michigan, and Stafford, Virginia. The full order is paid for with fiscal 2026 U.S. Marine Corps procurement funds.
The underlying ACV contract is worth up to $4.1 billion if all options are exercised.

Russia's jury reform draws fire for handing verdicts back to the state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:16:20 UTC
17:16:20 KST

The Supreme Court proposals would allow presiding judges to "clarify" questions during deliberations and reduce jury panels from six or eight members to four, changes lawyers say undermine the independence of a system that acquits at 60 times the national average in non-jury trials.
Russia's Supreme Court is preparing legislation that would allow presiding judges to enter the deliberation room while a jury discusses its verdict and would reduce jury panels from six or eight members to four — changes that could greatly consolidate decision-making power in the hands of state-appointed officials.
Deputy Chair of the Supreme Court Nikolai Timoshin and Supreme Court judge Sergei Zelenin have outlined the main provisions of the planned reform, although the draft law has not yet been published.
Under the proposals, the presiding judge would not be permitted to vote on a defendant's guilt but would be entitled to "clarify" questions arising during deliberations.
Additional provisions would change the procedure for selecting jurors, allow citizens over 65 to serve, restrict the grounds for dissolving an already formed panel and give defendants the right to refuse a jury trial even after a hearing has been scheduled.
Jury trials are rare in Russia but produce acquittals at a rate sharply above the national average. Of more than 640,000 criminal cases heard in Russia in 2025, 643 were decided by a jury, or around 0.1%.
In the first half of 2025, 144 of 444 defendants in jury cases were acquitted, close to one in three, according to Professor Sergei Nasonov of Moscow State University of Law, cited by Current Time. Across the Russian criminal justice system as a whole, the acquittal rate is below 0.5%.
Less power to the people?
Zelenin has argued that Russia's current jury model draws heavily from the Anglo-American legal tradition and fits poorly with the continental legal system, and that closer interaction between judge and jury would make proceedings more stable.
The proposed model is closer to the European lay judge system, in which a professional judge and non-specialist members sit together as a single panel.
Supporters of the reform also cite the high rate at which jury acquittals are overturned on appeal — between 65% and more than 80% in different years, according to figures cited by the Supreme Court.
Critics argue that grounds for overturning verdicts are typically described as procedural breaches, which can be interpreted broadly: from paperwork errors to remarks by trial participants that courts treat as improper influence on the jury.
Lawyers' objections centre mainly on admitting the judge to deliberations, which they say undermines the jury's independence.
Reducing the panel to four also raises questions about how much weight public participation carries in verdicts.
One source cited by Current Time said the reform amounts to legalising practices already in use informally: "Judges on the ground do not want this, none of the law enforcers need these courts. They fight them as best they can. Now they are simply legalising what they are already doing anyway."
The same source said jurors had frequently exposed weaknesses in prosecution cases, showing that some were "stitched together with white thread," a Russian expression for crude fabrication.
Jury trials have existed in Russia since the judicial reforms of Tsar Alexander II in 1864. They were abolished in the Soviet period, restored in the early 1990s and have been revised several times since.
The Constitutional Court has previously emphasised the secrecy of deliberations and the independence of jurors as fundamental safeguards of a fair trial.
