Nearly month after controversy, IDF hits back at ‘NAZA’ film over ‘manipulative misrepresentations’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:15:53 UTC
17:15:53 KST

“The film 'NAZA' presents a distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process. The film's narrative is based on substantial factual errors stemming from manipulative misrepresentations of reality,” the military said Thursday morning, responding to the film by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Shor nearly a month after it sparked controversy.
The IDF then listed several points that it said contradicted claims made in the film.
In the first, the military said: “Binding IDF directives explicitly, comprehensively and clearly distinguish between military operatives and uninvolved civilians in Gaza. IDF targeting processes are fundamentally based on this distinction, prohibit intentionally directing strikes against civilians, and require mitigating the possibility of harm to them to the greatest extent feasible.”
In its second point, the IDF said: “The IDF has never planned, approved or carried out any strike in Gaza in which 500 civilians or anything close to that number were expected to be killed. Nor has anyone seriously alleged that an IDF strike caused deaths on that scale or anything close to it.”
“Artificial intelligence has never independently selected targets to strike in the IDF,” the military said in its third point. “The identification of targets to strike is done only by authorized intelligence officers, strikes are planned by relevant professionals, and the decision whether to strike is made by operational commanders.”
According to the fourth point, “Binding IDF directives have never granted automatic authorization for strikes against targets placing a fixed number of civilians at risk (such as 20 in a strike against a junior operative or 200 in a strike against a senior commander, as a person in the film claims).”
In its fifth point, the military said that “‘Lavender’ is not a database of targets approved to strike, but a database that assists intelligence analysts.”
“Binding IDF directives do not permit an evacuation warning for an area to be treated as authorization to carry out strikes there while disregarding civilians who remain,” the military said in its sixth point.
Finally, in its seventh point, the IDF said: “The IDF does not ignore the aftermath of its strikes but acts to assess them, including with regard to unintended civilian harm, contrary to the claim in the film. These assessments have prompted reviews of hundreds of incidents during the hostilities and provide a basis for lessons learned.”
‘Distortion of reality through manipulative editing of interviews’
The IDF Spokesperson’s Unit later said in a statement: “Had the filmmakers conducted adequate verification and corroboration of facts in good faith, as professional standards require, they could have identified the substantial errors presented in the film. The end result shows that they did not.”
“Many errors arise because the interviewees, described as having served in IDF intelligence roles, usually refer to only limited, initial stages dealing with intelligence, rather than the much broader process of planning and approving strikes. That process is not the responsibility of intelligence, but of operational bodies that manage and carry out targeting processes.
“Accordingly, it is apparent that in various cases interviewees raise speculation and assumptions without a factual basis.
“The filmmakers chose not to show many of the other individuals involved in the full targeting process – those responsible for planning that mitigates civilian harm, legal advisers who review proposed strikes, and commanders responsible for approving or rejecting them. The result, as noted, is an incorrect and highly misleading portrayal of reality.
“To fit the narrative the film seeks to promote, the filmmakers also omit context essential to understanding the war in Gaza and the IDF’s conduct during it.
“The film does not give due weight to Israel’s security reasons for operating in Gaza and the October 7th Massacre; to Hamas’ deliberate strategy of embedding itself within the civilian population, which is the root cause of harm to civilians; or the countless actions and methods the IDF employed to mitigate civilian harm, including warnings before strikes, selection of munitions and appropriate strike planning, facilitating humanitarian aid and more.
“The processes and decisions the film omits show what the IDF’s effort to protect civilians meant in practice – additional required intelligence, plans changed, strikes cancelled and military opportunities forgone. These decisions restricted the use of force solely because of assessed risks to civilians.
“Particularly troubling is the film's further distortion of reality through manipulative editing of interviews, irresponsible allusions to historical atrocities, and its false and baseless attribution of malicious intentions to the IDF.
“Even the film’s title inverts reality. “NAZA” is an acronym of the Hebrew term “Nezek Agavi”, which means “collateral damage” in English. This is a professional term used by every law-abiding military worldwide to describe incidental harm to civilians resulting from a strike on a military objective, which serves commanders to assess the lawfulness of the strike and adopt measures to mitigate harm to civilians to the greatest extent feasible.
“Paradoxically, the film portrays the exceptional effort and detail the IDF devotes to estimating civilian harm in strikes as indifference to civilian lives.
“In reality, assessing expected harm to civilians in strikes is a requirement under international law. The IDF conducts this assessment so commanders can determine whether a strike is lawful, direct additional precautions, modify the strike plan or cancel the strike, all to mitigate the possibility of harm to civilians to the greatest extent feasible, as IDF commanders did many times during the war.
“The IDF is open to hearing genuine criticism of its conduct and attaches importance to learning from substantiated allegations and continually improving its practices. It is bound by and committed to international humanitarian law, its operational procedures are designed to implement those legal obligations, and it operates dedicated units and mechanisms to mitigate civilian harm.
“The IDF does not disavow deficiencies and errors that occurred during the war; they do occur in complex combat situations. Suspected violations of the law or IDF directives are examined and, where warranted, addressed through disciplinary action, criminal investigation or other measures.
“Contrary to accepted practice, the filmmakers did not submit their allegations to the IDF for examination and response before publication, nor did they provide a copy of the film after its screening, although the IDF requested it. Therefore, in assessing the film’s contents, the IDF relied on a detailed account from a representative who attended a public screening, as well as other public accounts.”
The film “NAZA” presents what it describes as troubling testimony from 24 soldiers, allegedly from Unit 8200, the IDF's elite signals intelligence and cyber unit, about IDF operations during the war in Gaza.
The film, which was shot on rooftops in Tel Aviv during the war, includes interviewees who claim they were involved in “war crimes and genocide” and describe policies relating to collateral damage, bombardments and targeted killings.
One of the film’s central themes is the use of artificial intelligence, which interviewees claim was used, among other things, to recommend targets for assassination based on intercepted phone communications, including in cases in which a strike was expected to kill family members of targeted individuals.

Trump has not yet decided whether to ban diesel fuel exports

Trump has not yet decided whether to ban diesel fuel exports
Kyiv • UNN
Trump is considering restricting diesel exports due to record prices. Advisers warn that this could make gasoline and other fuels more expensive.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on September 30 that he had not yet decided whether to impose a ban on diesel fuel exports, despite fierce opposition to the idea in recent days from the oil and gas industry and some of his own advisers. UNN reports, citing Politico.
Details
The White House is facing mounting pressure to take action to lower record-high diesel fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, and Trump said last week that he would be open to restricting exports. But members of his Cabinet and senior industry officials argue that such a move would drive up prices for all types of fuel, including gasoline, and they have sought to present the U.S. president with alternative measures.
"I'm thinking about it," Trump said of an export ban at an event in the Oval Office. "I talk a lot with [Energy Secretary] Chris [Wright] and [Interior Secretary] Doug [Burgum] about it — they think it will help diesel, but it could raise the price of other things."
Trump said he was optimistic about prices coming down because oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz had increased in recent days, but he refused to rule out restricting diesel fuel supplies.
"It's something we're thinking and talking about every day," he said. "But it seems that it will negatively affect gasoline, so it will go up a little, while diesel fuel will go down a little."
Wright, who strongly opposes the ban and was with Trump in the Oval Office on Wednesday, said the administration would soon announce measures aimed at lowering diesel fuel prices. Europe will also announce steps to increase supply on the market, he said.
"You will hear announcements from our friends in Europe about new diesel fuel supplies that will come onto the market and significantly lower diesel fuel prices," Wright said.
The publication reported on Tuesday that the White House was considering asking European governments to release diesel fuel from their own strategic reserves.

High Court clears publication of identity of Gaza Division intelligence officer on Oct. 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:14:18 UTC
17:14:18 KST

The Gaza Division intelligence officer during the October 7 massacre can now be publicly identified, the High Court of Justice ruled on Thursday. It rejected Lt.-Col. Aryeh Amidror’s attempt to keep his name under a publication ban.
The IDF ended Amidror’s career service over what it said were professional failures surrounding the Hamas massacre.
An unidentified Gaza Division intelligence officer, Lt.-Col. “A,” had dismissed warnings from a female Unit 8200 noncommissioned officer about Hamas’s “Jericho Wall” invasion plan, The Jerusalem Post reported in the past.
N12 news site cited an email in which Amidror had described that scenario as “completely imaginary.” After the Unit 8200 noncommissioned officer had raised further concerns in late September 2023, Amidror said a raid was unlikely and scheduled a discussion for after Sukkot, KAN News reported.
Amidror has disputed the case against him, arguing that he entered the Gaza Division role only four months before the attack and had sought to challenge the military’s prevailing assumptions about Hamas.
No security concerns around releasing his name
Amidror is the son of Maj.-Gen. (res.) Yaakov Amidror, a former national security adviser and former head of the IDF Military Intelligence Research Division and IDF Military Colleges.
In Thursday’s ruling, Supreme Court President Isaac Amit said there was no longer a security reason to conceal Amidror’s identity, and that public interest justified publishing it.
Military officers had initially opposed publication under rules protecting the identities of Military Intelligence personnel.
They later reconsidered their position and told the court Amidror’s name could safely be published together with his former position in the Gaza Division.
Amidror said the proper authorities had not approved their revised position and that publication would endanger him and violate his privacy.
The state said the head of the IDF Information Security Department had approved the decision, and Amit said he found no reason to question that account.
Amit said the case had raised questions about the relationship between the IDF’s senior command, its internal investigations, its ability to enforce its conclusions, and public confidence in the defense establishment.
The October 7 massacre was a “traumatic event of biblical proportions,” he said, adding that the public interest extended to the identity of an officer whom the IDF was seeking to remove over an alleged professional failure.
Amidror’s identity had already been circulated widely online, Amit said. The case was similar to that of Brig.-Gen. Yossi Sariel, who was publicly identified as the commander of Unit 8200 before leaving military service, and there was no meaningful reason to treat the two officers differently, he said.
The appeal challenged a September 7 decision by the Tel Aviv District Court, sitting as an Administrative Affairs Court, to remove the publication ban. Amit dismissed the appeal and ruled that Amidror’s name and identifying details could be published immediately.
The ruling concerned only whether Amidror’s identity could be published. It did not determine whether he mishandled warnings before October 7, 2023, or rule on the merits of the IDF’s decision to end his career service.
IDF confirms Amidror was released from military service
The head of IDF Manpower Directorate, Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa, had decided to terminate Amidror’s commitment to career service, the IDF announced on September 17. It said Amidror could appeal the decision.
Amidror had asked the High Court to delay publication until his expected release from the IDF around December if the decision to end his service became final, the court said.
The process followed a decision by IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir last November 23 that several officers bore command responsibility for failures surrounding the October 7 massacre and should face command measures.
An IDF investigative team headed by Maj.-Gen. (res.) Sami Turgeman found that the Gaza Division had failed to maintain sustained intelligence and operational work on the “Jericho Wall” plan, conduct an orderly situational assessment, and raise the warning level in response to the information available on the night before the attack.
James Genn and Yonah Jeremy Bob contributed to this report.

Will Democrats move beyond rhetoric on Israel’s illegal settlements?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:13:15 UTC
17:13:15 KST

Will Democrats move beyond rhetoric on Israel’s illegal settlements?
A new E1 sanctions bill could test whether US objections are finally backed by consequences.
A shift is taking place in Washington. Senate Democrats are moving to sanction individuals and entities involved in Israel’s E1 settlement project, one of the most consequential efforts to reshape the occupied West Bank. The timing is significant. Reports that the project may have been put on hold raise the question of whether the pause represents a substantive policy change or merely a tactical delay. Meanwhile, the Senate is preparing to leave Washington this week, narrowing the immediate window for action. The question is no longer simply whether Democrats object to illegal settlement expansion, but whether they are prepared to turn those objections into consequences.
The legislation, introduced on September 23 by Senators Chris Coons, Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden and Ruben Gallego, would target individuals and entities involved in facilitating settlement construction in E1. It has at least 10 Democratic cosponsors and was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
E1 lies between occupied East Jerusalem and the major illegal settlement of Maale Adumim. Its development has long been viewed by Palestinian officials, foreign governments and advocates of a two-state solution as particularly consequential because construction there could disrupt territorial continuity between northern and southern parts of the occupied West Bank while further isolating East Jerusalem. The issue, therefore, is not simply another settlement project, but whether the geography of the West Bank is being altered in ways that could make Palestinian territorial self-determination increasingly difficult.
From condemnation to accountability
The proposed legislation would impose sanctions on foreign individuals and entities determined by the Treasury Department to have facilitated settlement construction or related activity in E1, including participation in tenders. It would also target those involved in organising, financing or facilitating the transfer of Israeli civilians into illegal settlements in the area.
That would represent a departure from the traditional Washington response. A government can dismiss a diplomatic protest; sanctions affecting companies, individuals or access to the US financial system are harder to ignore. Yet the measure remains a proposal, its prospects are uncertain, and the House of Representatives is out of session. The Senate’s impending departure means the immediate political opportunity is narrowing, although the legislation will remain alive during the recess.
Its significance, therefore, may depend as much on what happens when Congress returns as on what happens before it leaves.
What does an E1 pause actually mean?
Reports that the E1 project may have been put on hold deserve attention, but also caution. A suspension, delay in tenders or postponement would not necessarily amount to abandonment. Nor would it reverse settlement expansion already approved or resolve the broader question of the West Bank’s territorial future.
If E1 has merely been deferred, Washington should not mistake a pause for a policy change. But if the project has genuinely been halted, the moment presents an opportunity to test whether US pressure can help turn temporary restraint into a durable decision.
That is where sanctions could matter. Their significance would not necessarily lie in punishing a project after the fact, but in establishing that settlement expansion can carry consequences before the process becomes irreversible.
The Democratic contradiction
The Democratic debate must also confront the Biden administration’s record. The administration repeatedly stated that settlements were inconsistent with international law and harmful to the prospects for a two-state solution. Yet those objections coexisted with continued military assistance and a broader strategic relationship with Israel. Washington thus continued to articulate support for Palestinian statehood while doing relatively little to prevent developments that could make such a state increasingly difficult to realise.
That contradiction has not been confined to one administration. Successive US governments have often treated settlement expansion as an obstacle to peace while stopping short of using significant leverage to prevent it.
The political environment within the Democratic Party, however, is changing. A growing number of Democratic lawmakers are challenging aspects of Israeli policy, including settlement expansion and pogroms. The E1 legislation reflects a broader debate over whether support for Israel must also mean insulating Israeli government policies from meaningful US consequences.
What would meaningful change require?
For the E1 initiative to become more than symbolism, Congress would have to establish clear criteria for sanctions, consistent enforcement and the political willingness to sustain them. More fundamentally, Washington would have to confront the larger framework of its relationship with Israel.
If Palestinian self-determination remains a US policy objective, a basic question follows: what happens when an ally pursues policies that American officials themselves say undermine that objective?
For decades, the answer has mostly been diplomatic objection without corresponding leverage. The proposed sanctions would introduce something largely missing from US settlement policy: the possibility that settlement activity could carry a tangible cost in the United States.
That does not guarantee passage, nor would sanctions by themselves resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. But they would alter the terms of the debate by linking Washington’s stated policy to an instrument capable of imposing consequences.
The test comes after the headlines
The E1 initiative should therefore be neither exaggerated nor dismissed. It remains at the beginning of the congressional process, with the House out of session and the Senate preparing to leave Washington. The immediate prospects for enactment may be uncertain. But the more important test is whether its sponsors continue to press the issue after the current political moment has passed.
If E1 has been temporarily put on hold, Washington has an opportunity to press for a permanent halt rather than treating the pause as sufficient. “If the project proceeds, Congress will face a clearer choice over whether settlement activity should continue to be met with statements of concern or tangible consequences.
Ultimately, E1 is about more than a strip of land between Jerusalem and Maale Adumim. It is a test of whether US foreign policy means what it says. Washington has spent decades declaring that settlement expansion undermines Palestinian self-determination and the prospects for a negotiated peace, while rarely attaching a meaningful cost to it.
The E1 legislation offers Democrats an opportunity to begin closing that gap. The decisive question is not whether Washington can issue another warning, but whether it is finally prepared to make its own stated principles matter and make clear that a US commitment to Palestinian self-determination cannot remain a diplomatic phrase while the realities on the ground move in the opposite direction.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Eviction: Where are tenants most and least protected across Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:12:47 UTC
17:12:47 KST

The eviction of a disabled 87-year-old woman in Madrid from a flat she lived in for 70 years has sparked outrage and comparisons of renter rights across the continent.
The Spanish pensioner's ordeal put Europe's housing crisis back in the spotlight. So what happens when landlords want their property back?
The reality is that owners can still terminate the contract with the tenant ahead of schedule if they want, but with a few caveats and important differences depending on where you live in Europe.
In general, if tenants are paying regularly, landlords need an important and legally recognised reason, such as if they are selling the property; they need it for themselves or close relatives; or, in some cases, if the house needs major renovation.
No force majeure is needed if the tenant isn't paying regularly; however, there may be legal exceptions and challenges in some cases if the tenant is vulnerable.
Spain: Short notice period, potential suspension for vulnerable people
Spain has one of the shortest notice periods — only two months — according to the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos. However, the terms apply only after the first year of tenancy.
The landlord must be a physical person, not a company. Of course, non-payment is grounds for eviction through a legal procedure called desahucio por falta de pago.
"Economically vulnerable" tenants can request a suspension while social services evaluate alternative housing options. Suspensions can be rejected if the landlord owns fewer than three properties.
The suspension can last for up to three years and is re-examined every 12 months.
France: Winter truce and longer notice for unfurnished properties
In France, tenants are a bit more protected. Landlords can't terminate the lease halfway through; the notice period starts only three months before the end of the contract if the house came furnished, and six months before if it was unfurnished.
Also, evictions are banned during what's known as the "winter truce", between 1 November and 31 March, inclusive.
Tenants who are late with payments have six weeks to clear their arrears after receiving a commandement de payer (order of payment).
However, a judge can give a tenant up to three years to repay rent arrears through a payment plan, provided that they have resumed paying their current rent and are considered capable of clearing the debt.
Germany: No minimum period before the termination notice
In Germany, tenants can legally challenge a termination if they face hardship risks, according to the country's civil code, the Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch.
Otherwise, the notice is three months, extending to six months after five years, and to nine months after eight years.
But, unlike in France and Spain, there is no minimum period before the termination notice is sent.
Also, failure to pay rent for at least two months is enough to open a termination procedure — fristlose Kündigung.
The judge decides the delay to vacate the property, up to a maximum of one year. The tenant has two months to repay the debt and void the procedure after the termination order is issued.
However, this mechanism can only be used once every two years.
Italy: No termination before four years if there's no serious breach
In Italy, notice is given six months before the end of the contract, which usually lasts for a minimum of four years, as regulated by the country's law 431/98.
During that period, landlords cannot ask their tenants to move out for any reason, unless the tenant is in severe breach of their obligations.
The course of action is shorter in case of payment failure. The grace period goes from a minimum of three to a maximum of four months if the tenant faces issues such as unemployment or sickness after entering the property.
If the tenant still fails to pay, eviction takes place within a maximum of two months after the end of the grace period.
UK: New protections for tenants
From May 2026, in England, as it already was in Scotland, landlords are no longer allowed to terminate the contract before the end of the tenancy without a specific ground for possession — like selling or moving in — following the repeal of Section 21 of the Housing Act, where no-fault eviction was allowed.
The notice period was set to four months, and it cannot be triggered in the first year of tenancy.
In case of arrears, landlords can seek mandatory eviction if a tenant owes at least three months' rent. If the debt is below three months, eviction may still be possible, but it's up to the judge to decide whether there are reasonable grounds.
The picture is slightly different in Wales and Northern Ireland, where it is still possible to terminate the contract for no particular reason. In Wales, the landlord needs to give six months' notice and cannot force the tenant to move out before the first year elapses.
The notice period is much shorter in Northern Ireland. Only four weeks, if the tenancy has been going on for less than a year. For tenancies of over a year, the notice is two months, rising to three months for contracts of more than 10 years.
The background: What happened to Maricarmen Abascal?
Europe's housing crisis came back into the spotlight when wheelchair-bound Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly evicted from her apartment in Madrid last week, after refusing to honour a more than €1,000 hike on her monthly rent.
Her pension is around €1,300, and she was paying €500 for her apartment, where she had lived since 1956.
The price hike was set by an investment fund, Urbagestión, which acquired the building where the flat is located in 2018. The eviction led to huge protests across Spain, including in Madrid and Barcelona, prompted donations and even sparked an appeal from the United Nations.
Luckily for Abascal, the story ended positively. She was offered a new eight-year contract capped at 30% of her income, following negotiations between Urbagestión and Madrid's housing authority.
However, the backlash had far-reaching implications, prompting Spain's government to swiftly introduce new housing support measures, in particular a ban on evictions for vulnerable people until 2030.
It also brought in further restrictions and controls on investment funds buying building complexes, such as stricter scrutiny of contract termination procedures against elderly tenants and increased tax penalties for holding empty units.

Data belonging to thousands of people were leaked after a bank was hacked in South Korea, Yonhap News reported Thursday.
Shinhan Bank said data including annual income, names and phone numbers of some 25,000 customers were compromised a day earlier.
The country’s Financial Supervisory Service launched an on-site investigation into the data leak at the bank on Thursday.

South Korea has suffered several leaks of personal data in recent months, and authorities last month increased penalties for those found responsible.
Those found guilty of leaking data involving 10 million or more people could face fines of up to 10% of their total revenue under the revised Personal Information Protection Act.

According to broadcaster KBS, some 48 million people were affected by personal data breaches last year, with leaks concentrated in the private sector.
Between 2021 and 2025, the country’s spy agency found more than 100 cases of industrial technology leaks overseas.
Of 107 such cases, leaks involving the semiconductor sector accounted for nearly 40%, according to data submitted to parliament by South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources.

U.S. Air Force buys 40 electronic warfare kits for F-15EX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:09:09 UTC
17:09:09 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded BAE Systems a $146.7 million sole-source contract for 40 EPAWSS hardware sets for F-15EX Lots 7 and 8.
- Work will take place in Nashua, New Hampshire, through August 2030, with $58.8 million obligated at award.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded BAE Systems a $146.7 million contract for 40 sets of the electronic warfare suite that protects the F-15EX Eagle II, covering jets in the fighter’s seventh and eighth production lots.
The sole-source contract, announced by the Department of War, buys 40 production hardware sets of the Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System, known as EPAWSS, along with magazines and retainers for the jet’s countermeasure dispensers. BAE Systems will do the work in Nashua, New Hampshire, and expects to finish by Aug. 31, 2030. The U.S. Air Force obligated $58.8 million in fiscal 2025 and 2026 procurement funds at the time of award, and the full value works out to roughly $3.7 million per set.
EPAWSS is the F-15’s built-in self-protection system. It warns the crew when enemy radars are tracking the jet, works out where those radars are, jams them, and controls the release of chaff and flares to decoy incoming missiles. Every F-15EX is built with EPAWSS installed at Boeing’s St. Louis factory, and the U.S. Air Force is also retrofitting the system into part of its older F-15E Strike Eagle fleet, where it replaces an analog electronic warfare suite in use since the 1980s.
The award follows a U.S. Air Force move to add a capability EPAWSS does not cover. On Sept. 29, the F-15 program office asked industry for an already-qualified missile warning system that could be fitted into six sensor locations built into the F-15EX for that purpose, The Defence Blog reported. EPAWSS focuses on radar threats, while a dedicated missile warning system looks for the heat or light of an incoming missile’s motor, including heat-seeking missiles that give off no radar signal.
The F-15EX is a two-seat, heavily modernized version of the F-15 that the U.S. Air Force is buying mainly to replace its aging F-15C and F-15D fighters. The order for Lot 7 and Lot 8 hardware means EPAWSS supply is being lined up for jets that will be built over the next several years, and the service’s fiscal 2027 budget request asked for 24 more F-15EX aircraft.
EPAWSS cleared full-rate production in early 2025, and the U.S. Air Force has since opened a dedicated installation line at Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex in Georgia to speed upgrades of F-15Es outside their regular depot maintenance.

Not much has been passed on to us yet."
Diplomatic circles fear that Washington’s selectivity could lead to a transformation of the alliance as a whole, while acknowledging that US actions have disappointed its allies, many of which have reached the defense spending targets set by US President Donald Trump’s administration. "If they try splitting NATO into the good ones and the bad ones, it is dangerous for the US," another diplomat told Politico. "But for Europe, this is existential."

Gimmick or recipe for success? Japan's convenience stores test AI flavours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:07:13 UTC
17:07:13 KST

Japanese convenience store chains are turning to AI for dessert ideas. Some are unexpected mashups.
A pickle-flavoured lemon tart might seem an unlikely dessert, but Japanese convenience store chains are betting that artificial intelligence (AI) can help them find combinations customers never knew they wanted.
Popular convenience store chains FamilyMart and Lawson are using the technology to develop new food products, looking for ideas that go beyond familiar flavours.
The experiments come amid wider concerns about AI replacing workers and increasingly powerful systems slipping beyond human control.
Here, the technology’s role is more modest — suggesting what might go into your next snack.
AI supplied the ideas, but humans still had to turn them into something worth eating. Companies used the technology mainly for brainstorming, with human specialists involved in developing the final products.
FamilyMart fed sales data into AI to help develop a French-style canelé made with dough containing sweet potato purée and topped with caramel sauce. The chain said it wanted to create something new but likely to sell.
In July, the chain test-launched its first AI experiment with a biscuit sandwich filled with thick milk cream.
Rival chain Lawson took a different approach, asking AI for unexpected combinations without feeding it past sales figures or market data to generate ideas “unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends," according to a statement from the company.
One suggestion was to pair lemon tart with pickles.
For Shingo Shiina, a 64-year-old who works in architecture, the combination came as a surprise.
“I was like ‘huh’ at first, but it actually goes pretty well, doesn’t it? The pickles. I’m surprised,” he said after tasting the tart.
“It’s a strange flavour, but it’s tasty. It really is delicious.”
Shiina was also impressed by the idea itself.
“You’d probably never come up with this, right? Pickles and this. I don’t think a human would ever think of that. That’s AI for you,” he said.
Lawson’s other AI-inspired products include a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yoghurt cream, and a Japanese-style salad presented like a parfait.
The pickle-flavoured lemon tart is being launched in Tokyo and surrounding regions in September, according to Lawson.

Ukraine Appeals to OSCE as Civilians Face Starvation in Temporarily Russian-Occupied Oleshky
Ukraine has initiated urgent consideration of the humanitarian crisis in temporarily Russian-occupied Oleshky at the OSCE Permanent Council, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote on X on September 30.
The issue, titled “On the catastrophic humanitarian situation in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky, temporarily occupied by the Russian Federation,” is expected to be addressed on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Oleshky, a city on the left bank of the Dnipro in Ukraine’s Kherson region, has been under Russian occupation since February 2022
The humanitarian situation in Oleshky has deteriorated sharply in recent weeks. Ukrainian officials have reported severe shortages of food, medicine, clean water, electricity, and medical care, while evacuation remains extremely dangerous because of mines and Russian military activity.
Sybiha stated that Ukraine’s delegation would brief participating states on conditions created by Russian occupation authorities.
“The delegation of Ukraine will inform participating States about the appalling situation created by the Russian occupation authorities, who are holding civilians, including children, hostage,” Sybiha wrote. “This is nothing less than a man-made humanitarian disaster.”
He added that Ukraine would continue challenging Russian narratives and informing international partners about conditions in the city.
“The situation in Oleshky is critical and requires urgent action by the international community,” Sybiha wrote. “I call on the Swiss OSCE Chairmanship and all participating States to condemn the aggressor and exert the strongest possible pressure on Russia.”
Sybiha also called for immediate humanitarian access to the occupied city.
“Oleshky needs urgent humanitarian relief. Russia must be compelled to allow it immediately,” he wrote.
Days earlier, the UN reported that Russia had still not guaranteed safe humanitarian access to Oleshky and nearby Hola Prystan, despite requests from Ukrainian authorities.
UN Humanitarian Coordinator Matthias Schmale noted that civilians were facing food and medicine shortages and that occupying forces are required under international law to facilitate humanitarian assistance.

Turkish intelligence captures suspect in 2013 Reyhanli terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:02:57 UTC
17:02:57 KST

Merve Berker
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Türkiye's National Intelligence Organization (MIT) captured Omer al-Khatib, one of the Syrian suspects in the 2013 terror attack in Reyhanli that killed 53 people, as he was preparing to flee to Europe by sea, security sources said on Thursday.
According to the sources, al-Khatib, who was wanted under an Interpol Red Notice, was involved in planning and organizing the attack in the Turkish town and coordinated between the perpetrators and intelligence officials affiliated with Bashar al-Assad.
Al-Khatib brought Yusuf Nazik, who was planning operations targeting Türkiye, together with Kifah Melhem in 2013, with details of the attack determined during the meetings.
Al-Khatib and Nazik first entered Türkiye through Hatay in February 2013 before the attack and identified the locations to be targeted. They received approval from Melhem, who was in Latakia, according to the sources.
Before the attack in May 2013, al-Khatib went with Temir Dukanci to the Latakia branch of military intelligence and received materials to be used in the explosive device.
The bomb-laden vehicle was taken to Reyhanli by Dukanci and Nazik and detonated using a remote-controlled explosive device.
Immediately after the attack, al-Khatib took Dukanci and Nazik, who had fled to Syria, to the Latakia branch of military intelligence.
Al-Khatib and others who carried out the attack were financially rewarded by the Bashar al-Assad regime, the sources said.
MIT tracks suspect step by step
MIT began efforts to capture those responsible immediately after the Reyhanli attack and closely monitored al-Khatib's activities in Syria, as it did with other suspects.
MIT captured al-Khatib as he was preparing to flee to Europe by sea and subsequently brought him to Türkiye.
Nazik, one of the perpetrators and planners of the attack, was captured in 2018; Cengiz Sertel in 2024, and Muhammed Dib Korali and Dukanci were captured in 2025.
Maj. Gen. Kifah Melhem in Syria, who gave the order for the Reyhanli attack, was appointed by Bashar al-Assad as head of the National Security Bureau in February 2024.
Melhem is known to have fled abroad following the fall of the Assad regime.

Here are some past examples of plane hijackings and attempted hijackings potentially involving pilots or crew members:
An off-duty Alaska Airlines pilot tried to cut the engines of a Horizon Air jet travelling from Everett, Washington, to San Francisco while riding in an extra seat in the cockpit. The plane was diverted and landed in Portland with more than 80 people. Joseph Emerson told police he was despondent over a friend’s recent death, had taken psychedelic mushrooms and hadn’t slept in days.
A China Eastern Airlines flight from Kunming in southwest China to Guangzhou, near Hong Kong, slammed into a mountain, killing all 132 people aboard. Chinese authorities have yet to release their final investigative report, but data released by American investigators earlier this year suggests the jet’s engines were deliberately shut off and there was a cockpit struggle before the plane nose-dived.
The co-pilot on a Germanwings jet traveling from Barcelona, Spain, to Duesseldorf, Germany, locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately crashed the plane into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board. Andreas Lubitz had struggled with depression and suffered from sleeplessness and fear of losing his vision.

The co-pilot on an Ethiopian Airlines flight from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to Milan, Italy, hijacked the jet and rerouted it to Geneva, Switzerland. Hailemedhin Abera Tegegn, the co-pilot, surrendered to local police and sought political asylum. None of the 193 passengers were harmed.
The pilot of a Mozambique Airlines plane traveling from the southern African nation to Angola deliberately downed the jet in a national park in Namibia, killing all 33 people on board. Authorities said at the time that Herminio dos Santos Fernandes, the pilot, locked the cockpit door and set the plane on course to crash when the co-pilot went to the bathroom.
An EgyptAir flight from Los Angeles to Cairo plunged into the Atlantic Ocean off Nantucket, Massachusetts, killing all 217 passengers and crew on board. American investigators concluded the copilot, Gameel Al-Batouti, set the plane on course to crash while the captain was in the bathroom. Egyptian authorities, however, disputed the findings, concluding in their own investigation that mechanical failure was to blame.
A SilkAir flight from Jakarta to Singapore crashed near the Indonesian town of Palembang, killing all 104 people on board. Indonesian investigators concluded that “unlawful interference” likely caused the crash of the new model Boeing jet in good weather. Their report found the pilot, Tsu Way Ming, “was in the process of, or intending to, leave the cockpit” before the cockpit voice recorder cut out. Authorities also said the pilot was “facing financial problems, and had experienced several company disciplinary actions”, including a demotion.
A pilot crashed a Royal Air Maroc flight from Agadir, Morocco, to Casablanca into the Atlas Mountains just 10 minutes after takeoff, killing all 44 people on board. Investigators determined Younes Khayati switched off the autopilot and sent the plane hurtling to the ground as the co-pilot tried in vain to intervene. The Associated Press reported at the time that it was “the deliberate wish of the pilot to end his life”. A union representing pilots disputed the findings.
An off-duty FedEx flight engineer attempted to hijack a company cargo plane traveling from Memphis, Tennessee, to San Jose, California, while riding as a jump seat passenger. Auburn Calloway attacked the flight crew armed with a hammer and a spear gun. The crew subdued him and safely landed the plane, despite those who confronted Calloway suffering extensive injuries. Investigators said Calloway had intended to crash the plane after facing possible disciplinary measures.
A Japan Airlines flight from Fukuoka to Tokyo crashed in Tokyo Bay just as it was landing, killing 24 of the 174 people on board. Investigators said there was a fight in the cockpit as the pilot, Seiji Katagiri, put the engines into reverse thrust. They also later determined Katagiri, who survived the crash, had been deemed fit to fly even after having a history of mental illness, including paranoid schizophrenia.

Europe injects only 70% of gas needed for winter into storage by end-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:00:34 UTC
17:00:34 KST

MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. Europe managed to inject only 70% of the gas volumes needed for the coming winter into its underground gas storage facilities by the end of the first month of autumn, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Net gas injections - the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes - into underground storage facilities in EU countries have exceeded 47.5 bln cubic meters since the start of the summer season in April 2026. Thus, Europe has so far managed to inject only 70% of the volumes needed for the coming winter.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is allowed in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. Thus, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bln cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the storage target.
Average gas injection rates into EU storage facilities in September remain the highest in the past four years amid warm weather. At the same time, gas prices at European hubs are at their highest since late 2022, indicating the European Union’s urgent efforts to fill its storage facilities for the winter even at very high prices. However, Europe has already missed the summer months that offered the most favorable conditions for injections.
As of September 29, European storage facilities were 71.54% full, 15.53 percentage points below the five-year average for that date, compared with 82.6% a year earlier. This is the lowest level for that date since records began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold around 78.3 bln cubic meters of gas, 12.7 bln cubic meters less than a year earlier and the lowest level since 2013. Gazprom has forecast that gas inventories in European storage facilities may not even reach 75% by the next heating season.
TASS reported earlier that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas inventories. EU countries may have their storage facilities only 70-75% full by the traditional start of the autumn-winter season, which would be the lowest level ever recorded at the start of the heating season.

Outage schedules have been canceled, but this may change - which regions should prepare
Kyiv • UNN
The outage schedules for October 1 have been canceled, but the situation may change. Due to Russian attacks, some consumers in five regions are without power.
The electricity outage schedules introduced against the backdrop of renewed Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have currently, as of the morning of October 1, been canceled, but the situation may change. Kyiv, Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions need to conserve electricity during the evening hours. Enemy attacks have caused power outages in five regions. UNN reports this, citing the Ministry of Energy and NPC Ukrenergo.
Russian attacks
"The enemy continues to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure," Ukrenergo said.
"As a result of hostilities and Russian shelling of energy infrastructure, some consumers in the Kirovohrad, Rivne, Sumy, Kharkiv and Chernihiv regions remain temporarily without electricity," the Ministry of Energy said in a statement.
Where the security situation allows, crews are already working to restore power, the ministry said. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore electricity to Ukrainian homes as soon as possible. Restoration work is continuing around the clock, the ministry emphasized.
What is happening with the schedules
"The use of outage schedules has currently been canceled. At the same time, the situation in the power system may change in certain regions," the Ministry of Energy said.
Ukrenergo clarified that "the hourly electricity outage schedules and capacity limitation schedules for industrial consumers, whose forced implementation had been forecast the previous day, are not currently being applied".
However, in certain regions, including Kyiv, Kyiv and Zhytomyr regions, electricity must be consumed sparingly during the evening hours. Please limit the use of high-powered electrical appliances from 17:00 to 22:00. This will reduce the load on the power system and the likelihood of forced restrictions due to overloading of equipment damaged by enemy shelling
Consumption
Electricity consumption, Ukrenergo said, has increased. Today, October 1, as of 09:30, it was 2.1% higher than at the same time the previous day—Wednesday. The reason is cloudy weather in parts of the southeastern regions. This is resulting in lower efficiency of household solar power plants and a corresponding increase in the amount of electricity consumed from the general grid.
Yesterday, September 30, the daily peak in consumption was recorded in the evening. It was at the same level as the previous day’s peak—Tuesday, September 29.
"Today, it would be advisable to shift the use of high-powered electrical appliances to the period when industrial solar power plants operate most efficiently—from 10:00 to 16:00," Ukrenergo said.

A New Lens on Modern Heritage: ArchDaily Partners with World Monuments Fund
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

What makes a building worth preserving? Age is the most common answer, but not always the best one. A building from the 1950s or 70s may carry as much historical significance as a medieval cathedral; it simply demands a different framework, one that weighs political context, cultural meaning, and architectural innovation over the mere passage of time. This is especially true for modernist architecture across the so-called Global South, where the movement took on unique forms of expression.
It is precisely this conversation that ArchDaily and World Monuments Fund are now opening together. WMF brings on-the-ground conservation expertise across the world, and ArchDaily brings the editorial capacity to contextualize that work and connect it to a global audience. The goal is to do both at once: preserve places and tell their stories, shaping how modernist heritage is understood far beyond the field of preservation itself.
To mark the start of this collaboration, we spoke with Javier Ors Ausín, Director of Thematic Programs at World Monuments Fund, and Christele Harrouk, Editor-in-Chief of ArchDaily. Read the full conversation below.
Related Article
United Nations’ Africa Hall Restoration in Ethiopia Receives 2026 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize
Romullo Baratto [Managing Editor]: What does this partnership mean to World Monuments Fund and ArchDaily? Javier, would you like to begin?
Javier Ors Ausín: This is a new partnership for World Monuments Fund, and we are genuinely exploring what it means as it unfolds. But what strikes me as particularly special is how complementary our roles are. At WMF, we engage directly with sites, implementing conservation projects, advocacy initiatives, and documentation of heritage preservation work. We work with governments, communities, local NGOs, and professionals in the field. Having ArchDaily as a partner — a platform that communicates architecture to an international audience through a broad network — means we can both engage with sites and preserve them, while also explaining why this work matters and why these places are globally relevant. The ability to pursue preservation and narration in parallel is very valuable.
Christele Harrouk: I really like what Javier said about this complementarity. We represent two complementary forms of responsibility toward architecture. WMF works with communities, places, and physical conservation. We work on narration, giving the world access to these stories. What makes this collaboration so meaningful is that it brings both capacities together and makes the work accessible to a global audience, while also contributing to safeguarding it.
 Because talking about something, documenting it, is itself a form of conservation. For ArchDaily, this partnership is particularly significant because we see ourselves as active participants in architectural culture. This collaboration gives us a chance to reflect that — to help shape what conservation is, what heritage is, and how people understand and engage with it.
JOA: Exactly. By doing the editorial and communication work, you are making communication itself part of the conservation process. In the conservation field, we sometimes limit ourselves to before-and-after photographs. But communicating the work from beginning to end is also conservation; it builds visibility, awareness, and ultimately support for the initiatives and field projects we undertake.
RB: Christele, why World Monuments Fund, and why now?
CH: ArchDaily has been around for 18 years. Almost two decades documenting and doing more than what a platform typically does. Our role goes beyond documentation and narration: we contextualize, connect information, make knowledge available, and we explain why it matters. Over those years, heritage has been a recurring thread. So when WMF came along, the timing felt exactly right — we had, in some sense, built everything toward it. They brought conservation knowledge, on-the-ground expertise, and active projects. We brought our editorial team, our global audience, and our archive. It was the best timing.
JOA: When I joined World Monuments Fund as an architect, almost ten years ago, I realized how segregated our field was. A lot of experts working in heritage preservation were not really part of the broader architectural conversations and discourses. Partnering with ArchDaily is a way of reconnecting the specialized discussions happening in the heritage field with the broader architectural discourse. There is no better partner for that: ArchDaily is genuinely shaping and actively participating in the global architectural conversation.
CH: I'd add one more dimension: what World Monuments Fund and ArchDaily together make possible is not just ensuring that the architecture that matters survives physically, but that the knowledge around it also survives. That, for me, is the core of this partnership.
RB: One of the defining features of the partnership is the focus on modernist architecture, with a particular emphasis on the Global South. Javier, why do you think that is the right frame for this collaboration?
JOA: What initially drew me to the field of preservation and documentation of modernist architecture was the opportunity to tell a larger story about 20th-century architecture. In my experience as an architect, the established narrative around modern architecture heritage remains quite narrow, focused primarily on the United States and Europe.
 But modernism was not confined to those regions. It took different shapes in South America, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East, adapting to different climates, materials, and technologies. Since joining WMF, part of my mission has been to tell that larger story through our sites and projects.
To give concrete examples: we developed a conservation management plan for the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium in India, a brutalist structure designed by Charles Correa and Mahendra Raj during the post-independence period. The urgency was heightened after the demolition of modernist sites in India, but also because these buildings are aging and require expert conservation management. In Africa, we are currently working in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, in a remarkable and relatively unknown example of modernist architecture deeply grounded in the local climate and vernacular construction traditions, using earthen materials and natural ventilation. The partnership with ArchDaily is an opportunity to expand that global narrative while also addressing the real technical challenges these buildings face.
RB: Christele, you've mentioned ArchDaily's coverage on heritage throughout the years. How do you see WMF's work fitting into ArchDaily's agenda?
CH: Being global is foundational for ArchDaily, but what we've been working toward is becoming more intentional about what "global" actually means. It is not just about publishing projects from many countries. It is about understanding architecture in its full context: shaped by climate, culture, politics, materials, economies, communities, and histories. That applies directly to modernism. We have long questioned the idea that architectural movements radiated, unchanged, from one center outward. We know that they were transformed, became hybrid, were appropriated, and challenged. Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, Central Asia — all of these places produced distinct histories of modernism.
 When we choose what to publish and how to contextualize it, we are participating in the construction of architectural history. We are adjusting the narrative. That has been central to our work for at least a decade.
With WMF, we have the opportunity to take it further: to discover more places, more contexts, more projects, and to push forward the idea that preserving modernism also means shaping what becomes visible and what is taken as a reference.
RB: When we think about heritage, modernist buildings don't enjoy the same prestige as, for instance, a Gothic cathedral or a medieval town when it comes to preservation. Javier, how do you build the case for this kind of work? How do you approach governments, communities, and other stakeholders?
JOA: That is the fundamental challenge. A medieval building, a castle, a cathedral, a mosque, is automatically recognized as a place of historical value and significance. A building from the 1950s, 60s, or 70s has to constantly prove that it embodies heritage values, historical significance, and architectural innovation. That is frustrating for anyone working in this field, but it is also the central challenge we all contribute to overcoming.
 Our approach is grounded in interpretation and education. We work to show — to communities living near these sites, to governments, to the broader public — that the value of these places is not based solely on age, but on the political and historical context in which they were built and the architectural innovation they represent.
Take the United Nations' Africa Hall in Addis Ababa, recognized by WMF in 2026 for its restoration project. Its importance is not that it dates to a particular decade. It lies in what it represents: decolonization, institution-building in Africa, the creation of a continental platform for political discussion. The fact that it was built in Ethiopia — the only African country never colonized — is, itself, a layer of historical significance. There is also remarkable architectural innovation in its use of reinforced concrete. Much remains to be done in terms of interpretation and knowledge dissemination to overcome the perception that these buildings are too recent to be preserved. In fact, many of them are approaching a century of age. Interpretation, ultimately, is where the opportunity lies.
RB: Many of the cities where these buildings are located are facing rapid urban growth. How do conservation and urban development coexist? How do we balance civic interest, land value, and the preservation of buildings that, as you've said, are not measured by age alone?
CH: I don't see them as opposing forces. We tend to forget that cities are living systems, and that heritage, the buildings we're discussing, was always part of those systems and evolved alongside them. The question we should always be asking is how we allow our cities to change, to grow, to evolve, while also understanding what they already carry culturally, socially, and in terms of heritage value.
And not just what that value is, but who gets to define it. That question is crucial. WMF is doing important work in redefining which buildings can be considered to carry value, not necessarily because of specific construction techniques, but because of their place in the urban fabric, the stories they hold, and how they are embedded in the lives of the communities around them. In rapidly changing cities, the communities living in these places must be part of determining their future. Heritage cannot be defined only institutionally or architecturally, without understanding its collective and lived value. It is not a question of conservation or urban growth — it is a question of how our cities can evolve with a greater awareness of what already exists, what we need to preserve, and what we might lose in the process.
JOA: I agree entirely. People tend to see conservation and development as opposing forces, but they shouldn't. The question for me is: how can architecture and conservation serve as vehicles for informing the decisions we make about how our cities grow? Cities have always changed — and modernism itself was a force of urban transformation in the 20th century. So the question is not conservation versus growth, but rather how heritage preservation can provide the tools to ensure that when cities change, those decisions are informed by community needs, by the cultural and historical places embedded in the built environment.
 Conservation, rather than being imposed, should be one more tool in the toolkit — helping us make informed, sustainable decisions. I prefer to see it as a tool to manage change, not resist it.
This is also why I advocate for architects to be more actively involved in government, in institutions like WMF, in platforms like ArchDaily — because that is where these ideas need to be present to have real impact.
CH: That's something I say constantly: architects need to be in decision-making positions, especially in politics. Change happens faster, and with greater impact, when it comes from there.
RB: What will ArchDaily readers find on the platform that they wouldn't without this partnership?
CH: We're digitizing WMF's projects and creating an online library that will document them through project features, narratives, interviews, stories, and accounts of specific conservation processes. What we want to do is turn WMF's archive into active architectural knowledge and situate it within ArchDaily's ecosystem of architectural knowledge.
JOA: This is a genuine opportunity for WMF to present our work in a completely different way: to tell a comprehensive story about what we've been doing in modern architecture since the early 2000s, not just through completed projects but through new material we'll generate together. We will speak about projects currently underway and begin working on a new project next year, with ArchDaily as a partner. What excites me most is the idea that the editorial angle can be an integrated part of our work — not something that happens after the fact, but something that runs alongside the conservation process from the beginning.
RB: Could you tell us more about this new project for next year?
CH: This is the most exciting part. We always say architecture matters, and this is our chance to demonstrate that in practice. This will be the first ArchDaily-supported conservation project, and the financial commitment matters because it marks a shift from documenting value to actively supporting it.
 We'll follow the process from beginning to end, showcasing how the project evolves — the stages, the phases, the story behind it. It's an educational process in itself. It extends what ArchDaily is already doing; I see it as the next step, a natural continuation.
JOA: Absolutely. This is really an opportunity to go beyond a conventional communications partnership and put everything we've been discussing into real practice. WMF is constantly engaging new sites, and the scope varies enormously — from physical restoration to conservation planning, adaptive reuse, advocacy campaigns for sites under threat. We don't yet know exactly what shape this project will take with ArchDaily, but that's also part of the excitement: exploring how editorial and communications expertise can be integrated into a project from the very beginning. Knowledge sharing and visibility are also forms of advocacy — and many of these sites urgently need that.
CH: What I find most compelling is using an individual site as a reference point for larger questions. How has modernism been transformed across continents? How have political and social histories shaped architecture, and how do they continue to shape it today? How have communities changed these buildings, and what can those transformations teach us? How might all of this change our contemporary practice? Using this site to answer larger questions — about heritage, about modernism, about the world, about the narratives we tell — that is what this is really about.

Russia’s state arms giant claims a new drone-missile class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:59:51 UTC
16:59:51 KST

- Russian state conglomerate Rostec said its S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T jet-powered strike drones perform the role of cruise missiles at lower cost.
- Rostec said the weapons are already used in Ukraine and should become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec says three of its newest jet-powered strike drones, the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, can now do the job of cruise missiles at a fraction of the cost, and that all three are already being used against Ukraine.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda published on Sept. 30, describing the weapons as a new category that sits between attack drones and missiles. The company did not give prices, production numbers or performance figures for any of the three, and its claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
“In fact, a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle. However, not every UAV of this type is a cruise missile. Nevertheless, in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased,” Rostec said in its statement.
The company said the drones have the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles while being significantly cheaper than conventional missiles, and that the gap between the two kinds of weapon will keep shrinking as drone production matures. Rostec said it expects the new jet-powered drones to become a standard weapon for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside the glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023.
The S-71M and S-71K are designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Rostec told the state news agency TASS. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57’s internal weapons bay, which lets the jet carry them without spoiling its radar-evading shape, and Russia’s arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has examined debris from both. It says the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance, and that the S-71M, called Monokhrom, contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small U.S.-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board, Militarnyi reported. Some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets and can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones, which suggests the company is aiming it at export buyers. Accounts of where the Dan-T comes from differ: some analysts describe it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt, while Ukrainian experts have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T’s range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, citing Ukrainian intelligence officials who said Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025 and is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region. Ukraine’s military intelligence says the Banderol contains a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly U.S.-made electronics, Euronews reported.
Cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build, the same logic behind Russia’s mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons that includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group’s KUB loitering munitions.

KU Leuven warns of invoice fraud with tuition fee payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
07:59:18 UTC
16:59:18 KST

Leuven University is warning students and parents about fraud relating to tuition fee payments. A number of parents received an invoice that looked genuine, but the account number had been altered to that of fraudsters. The university is now urging everyone always to check payment details before transferring any money.
At present, only a few cases are known. Nevertheless, KU Leuven is warning all students and parents, as many students have yet to pay their tuition fees.
In cases of invoice fraud, fraudsters intercept a genuine invoice or bank statement and alter the account number. The document itself therefore appears legitimate, but anyone making the payment transfers the money to the fraudsters’ account.
It is possible that fraudsters have gained access to the recipient’s email inbox. KU Leuven’s own systems have not been tampered with by the fraudsters.
Check the account number
KU Leuven is asking students and parents to check the details on the bank transfer before making any payment. You can do this using the personal verification code shown on the document. On the university’s verification page, students can compare the amount, the account number and the reference number.
The official account number is also listed on KU Leuven’s website. Anyone paying via a banking app should enter ‘KU Leuven’ or ‘Katholieke Universiteit Leuven’ as the beneficiary’s name.
If the banking app displays a warning alerting you to the fact that the name does not match the account number, the university advises you to stop the payment immediately.
Paid already? No need to panic
Anyone who has already paid their tuition fees and has not received a warning email from KU Leuven may, according to the university, assume that the payment has gone through correctly.
KU Leuven is currently investigating whether it can take further legal action. The university also says it will remain vigilant against other forms of online fraud and abuse.
The UCLL University of Applied Sciences is also warning about emails containing fake invoices. So far, one person has fallen victim to that scam.

Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization (MIT) has captured Omar al-Khatib, a Syrian suspect accused of helping plan the 2013 Reyhanli bombings near the Turkish-Syrian border that killed 53 people.
Al-Khatib, who was wanted under an Interpol Red Notice, was intercepted while attempting to flee to Europe by sea and brought to Türkiye, security sources said on Thursday.
The sources said he helped plan and organise the attack and coordinated contacts between its perpetrators and intelligence officers loyal to ousted regime leader Bashar al Assad.
MIT had been monitoring his activities in Syria as part of efforts to track down those responsible for the bombings in Türkiye’s southern Hatay province.
Planning and preparation
According to the sources, al-Khatib arranged meetings in 2013 between Yusuf Nazik, another planner of the attack, and Syrian intelligence official Kifah Melhem, during which details of the operation were decided.
Al-Khatib and Nazik entered Türkiye through Hatay in February that year to identify targets, subsequently obtaining approval from Melhem, who was based in Latakia, the sources said.
In May, before the attack, al-Khatib accompanied Temir Dukanci to the Latakia branch of Syrian military intelligence to collect materials for the explosive device, they added.
The sources said Dukanci and Nazik transported the bomb-laden vehicle to Reyhanli, where it was detonated remotely.
After the attack, the pair fled to Syria, where al-Khatib took them to the same military intelligence branch in Latakia. The sources alleged that the ousted Assad regime rewarded al-Khatib and the other perpetrators with money.
Efforts to track down suspects
MIT began tracking those responsible immediately after the bombings and closely monitored al-Khatib’s activities in Syria, the sources said.
His capture follows the arrests of Nazik in 2018, Cengiz Sertel in 2024, and Muhammed Dib Korali and Temir Dukanci in 2025.
Melhem, whom the sources identified as the major general who ordered the attack, was appointed head of the National Security Bureau by Assad in February 2024.
He fled abroad after the fall of the Assad regime, according to the sources.
