Can Myanmar’s New Government Revive the Stalled Dawei SEZ Project?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Myanmar’s military-backed administration is again trying to put the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) project on the agenda. This time, Russia has emerged as a potential partner for some of its port and energy plans, but it remains unclear whether it can turn the area into a functioning economic zone.
The Dawei SEZ, with its proposed deep-sea port, sits on Myanmar’s Andaman coast. It faces the Indian Ocean and has an overland connection to Thailand and the wider Mekong region. The 138-kilometer-long Dawei-Htee Khee road, opened in 2013 but still requiring major upgrades, could connect the SEZ to the Southern Economic Corridor through Bangkok, Phnom Penh, and Ho Chi Minh City. For Thailand and the wider Mekong, Dawei could offer a westward route to the Indian Ocean that bypasses the Strait of Malacca. This position has long underpinned the project’s strategic and economic significance.
Dawei was an ambitious project from the beginning. Launched in 2008 under Myanmar’s military regime, it combined a deep-sea port, an industrial estate, power generation and utilities, and a road link across the border to Thailand. The early estimates for the entire project exceeded $50 billion. However, financial and development problems led to major restructuring in 2015–16, during Myanmar’s democratic transition. The challenge was raising enough capital and moving different parts of the project forward together.
The industrial zone needed power, water, transport, and access to a seaport. The port, in turn, relied on cargo and industrial activity. Investors also needed confidence that the wider infrastructure would be built. Much of Dawei’s regional potential also rested on having a reliable connection to Thailand. Yet the Dawei-Htee Khee road on the Myanmar side was poorly suited to serve as a major industrial corridor. Limited border facilities and cargo transfer capacity created additional bottlenecks.
Successive governments tried to address these constraints during Myanmar’s decade of political and economic opening. Myanmar and Thailand created a joint development vehicle in 2013, and Japan joined in 2015. Later, the government recast the Dawei project into initial and full phases. The first, smaller phase was estimated to cost about $1.7 billion. Financing remained difficult. In January 2020, under Myanmar’s elected civilian government, the Dawei SEZ Management Committee revised the concession terms to allow staged financing and reduce extra government risk.
By December 2020, it had terminated all nine initial-phase contracts with Italian-Thai Development after repeated delays and unmet financial obligations. The committee said the termination would allow it to rethink the project and seek new partners. The decision came just weeks before the February 2021 coup.
Dawei was hard to manage even when Myanmar had more access to international investors and development partners. Its problems with coordination and financing now exist in a much tougher economic, political, and security environment.
An ISP-Myanmar report based on official investment data shows recorded FDI falling from more than $28.7 billion in 2016-2020 to $7.4 billion in 2021-2025. Targeted post-coup sanctions remain in place, but the fall in investment reflects a wider deterioration that also includes armed conflict, policy uncertainty, difficult business conditions, and major corporate exits. Inflation and foreign-exchange pressure further complicate long-term investment.
The SEZ now effectively sits in a conflict zone. The fighting between military forces and local resistance groups has reportedly intensified around the project area, with reports of violence against civilians by military forces. The road toward Thailand crosses conflict-affected parts of Tanintharyi Region. The Htee Khee border trade area has also been controlled by the Karen National Union and its allied resistance forces since May 2025. For a cross-border SEZ, reliable access and security will remain central to long-term investment and development.
In this tougher setting, the Myanmar military-backed administration began making efforts to revive the project last year. Closer post-coup ties with Russia have brought Dawei back into active investment talks on power plants, oil refineries, and seaports. In June 2026, the Russian state-owned firm Inter RAO and the Myanmar military-controlled Launglon Economic Development Company signed an agreement for a 660-megawatt coal-fired power plant. Russia is seeking majority stakes during the project payback period to meet its banks’ lending conditions. The broader project plan is under discussion. Financing remains unsettled and undisclosed.
Beyond Russia, Dawei is reappearing in regional economic diplomacy. In August, Thailand also held bilateral talks on the Htee Khee-Dawei corridor under its policy of “calibrated re-engagement” with Myanmar. A month later, when coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing visited Vietnam, Myanmar’s military-backed administration promoted Dawei to Vietnamese investors at a business forum in Hanoi. Dawei appears to be part of the new administration’s regional re-engagement talks, despite unresolved issues around financing, security, and implementation.
Alongside these challenges, the project’s revival raises concerns about its impact on local communities. A 2014 survey of more than 1,500 households reported concerns about land loss, limited consultation, and incomplete compensation. These concerns are now compounded by questions about ownership, transparency, environmental safeguards, and local benefits.
Dawei’s viability depends on more than building individual assets, but even that will be difficult under current conditions. The seaport, power plant, and transport links must support industry while also creating economic opportunities and benefits for communities. Without that wider ecosystem, Dawei could remain a scattered collection of infrastructure rather than a functioning and sustainable economic zone.

Many of the texts you encounter seem to do nothing other than make an argument for a particular…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:27:00 UTC
10:27:00 KST

Many of the texts you encounter seem to do nothing other than make an argument for a particular conclusion. The conclusion is supposed to follow from the premises according to the usual rules of logic. As you read, you determine whether or not the machinery of logic successfully leads to the conclusion. The value of such a text then seems to be coextensive with its logical success or failure.
But it is always possible that even the most logical text is also about something else. This is not the conclusion named in the text but something revealed through the process of reading openly. Here, the text is not just a logical argument but a pretext to some further possibility. It is a call to notice a particular insight, an idea that drives the text itself. And it is this driving force that you might also discover can drive you.

The new tariffs will take effect on October 1, 2026, and remain in force until January 1, 2027.

Five things to know ahead of the NRL and NRLW grand finals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:10:48 UTC

Fri, 18 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Tigers 0, Raiders 6
When is the NRL and NRLW grand finals, what time is it with daylight savings time, and how to watch
The final day of the NRL and NRLW season is almost here. The grand finals for the men and women will be held on Sunday.
In the women's decider, the Sydney Roosters and Brisbane Broncos face off in a rematch of last year's grand final.
In the men's grand final, the Sydney Roosters are facing the Newcastle Knights.
Here's everything you need to know about the NRL and NRLW grand finals day.
What time are the NRL and NRLW grand finals?
The NRL and NRLW grand finals will be held on Sunday, October 4, the first day of daylight saving time in many states and territories across the country.
Here is when each grand final begins in each state and territory.
NRL grand final
- 7:30pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania
- 7pm ACDT: South Australia
- 6:30pm: Queensland
- 6pm: Northern Territory
- 4:30pm: Western Australia
NRLW grand final
- 4pm AEDT: NSW, ACT, Victoria, Tasmania
- 3:30pm ACDT: South Australia
- 3pm: Queensland
- 2:30pm: Northern Territory
- 1pm: Western Australia
How can you watch and listen to the grand final?
The game will be on Channel 9 and 9Now, but be very aware that it will not be shown on Kayo or Fox Sports. It is the only game of the entire NRL season that is exclusive to Channel 9.
To listen to the grand final, join your local ABC Sport radio team, and follow along with the ABC Sport live blog at abc.net.au.
Where are the NRL and NRLW grand finals being played?
The NRL and NRLW grand finals are being played at Stadium Australia in Sydney.
Stadium Australia has hosted every NRL grand final since 1999, with the exception of the 2021 decider which was played at Brisbane's Lang Park during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Since the NRLW's inception in 2018, all grand finals have been played at Stadium Australia, again with 2021 being the exception. That decider was played at Dolphin Stadium in Redcliffe.
Who is playing in the NRL grand final?
The Sydney Roosters face the Newcastle Knights for the NRL premiership.
The Roosters finished the season fourth on the ladder, and lost their opening match of the finals before victories over Cronulla and the Dolphins.
The Newcastle Knights finished seventh on the ladder. After defeating Souths in the first week of the finals, the Knights went to Auckland and defeated the Warriors, then beat Penrith while being down to 12 players for all of the second half.
Who is playing in the NRLW grand final?
The Sydney Roosters are undefeated in 2026, winning all 11 matches in the home-and-away season, then defeating the Canberra Raiders in last week's preliminary final.
It mirrors Sydney's fantastic NRLW season in 2025, where they were undefeated until losing in last year's decider to the Brisbane Broncos.
The Broncos finished third on the table, with a record of 8–3 in the home-and-away season. The Broncos suffered a three-game losing run in the middle of the season, but have won their past five matches, including last weekend's preliminary final win against the Gold Coast Titans.

This week, the Chinese military opened a new logistics and training facility at an airport in Laos, further expanding its regional security presence and establishing the first overseas presence of the Chinese air force.
In a statement, China’s Ministry of Defense said that the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center was inaugurated on Tuesday, in a ceremony that was attended by Lao Defense Minister Khamlieng Outhakaysone and a delegation from the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
The facility, which is based at Ban Keun Airport, which sits close to the Nam Ngum River around 50 kilometers north of the capital Vientiane, also includes a China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
“The center, jointly maintained and operated by both sides, is aimed at helping Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots,” the Ministry said, but offered no details about what personnel or equipment would be based at the airport.
“The construction and use of the center reflect mutual respect and equal consultation between China and Laos, comply with both countries’ domestic laws, relevant international law and common practice,” it said. “It is not directed against any third party and contributes to enhancing practical military cooperation as well as promoting regional peace and stability.”
Satellite imagery of the Ban Keun facility shows it also includes the construction of an extensive airfield. According to Reuters, work began on the new airfield in late 2025 and work was ongoing as of early September. “In place of green fields,” it reported, “a large paved runway and a parallel taxiway and apron were visible, along with a number of new buildings.”
The airport was built on the site of an airfield known as Lima Site 44, one of a network of airstrips that were used by the U.S. military and Central Intelligence Agency during the Vietnam War, when the U.S. secretly supported an insurgency by anti-communist Hmong rebels. However, satellite images show that the new airfield expands far beyond the narrow, red-earthed strip established during the Vietnam War.
The new center adds to the handful of overseas facilities now operated by the PLA, since the opening of its first official overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017. It also complements a similar training and logistics facility that has been established at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand. The Cambodian facility was officially inaugurated by Prime Minister Hun Manet in April 2025, after three years of Chinese-funded refurbishments that include a 300-meter-long deep-water pier, a 5,000-ton dry dock, and a 1,000-ton slipway.
China’s involvement at Ream has attracted the suspicion of Western, and particularly American, security officials, who fear that the base may evolve into a full-blown Chinese base. Cambodia has sought to allay these fears by inviting foreign navies, including those of Japan, Vietnam, and the U.S., to visit the base.
Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said in a post on X that unlike Ream, the base in Laos is “more ostensibly similar to the one in Djibouti.” He added, “It may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA overseas base in Southeast Asia.”
The development at Ban Keun is perhaps unsurprising given the rapid expansion of China’s influence in Laos over the past 15 years. During that time, the north of the country has become economically fused to southern China, as new highways and an impressive China-built railway have improved overland connections. The Chinese investment presence is clearly visible in most parts of the country, and there is a large Chinese expatriate community in Vientiane and the provincial towns of northern Laos.
Defense relations have proceeded more slowly, perhaps due to the sensitivities of Vietnam, Laos’ traditional defense patron, which has had close ties with Laos dating back to the communist struggle of the 1960s and 1970s. In June, however, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith visited Beijing for meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping, during which the two leaders agreed to enhance defense cooperation.
Xi also suggested that China and Laos should establish a “3+3” strategic dialogue mechanism involving their foreign, defense, and public security ministers, “as an opportunity to strengthen law enforcement and security cooperation and crack down on cross-border crimes.” (A similar mechanism was established with Cambodia earlier this year.) Last month, Beijing and Vientiane also concluded “Peace Train 2026,” a 16-day joint military exercise aimed at “humanitarian assistance and military medical services.”
One Chinese security analyst told the state-run Global Times that the base at Ban Keun was a means of providing the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force, which operates a small and obsolescent fleet of Chinese and Russian craft, with a “systematic training system for pilots, maintenance crew and flight personnel” that will reduce its reliance on overseas training. More broadly, the analyst said, the facility will deepen “practical exchanges” between the two militaries, “upgrading from simple equipment assistance to long-term integrated cooperation in talent training, joint exercises and equipment support.”
Perhaps most tellingly, the analyst drew an explicit parallel between Ban Keun and the facility at Ream Naval Base, noting that together they “cover inland airspace in the Indochina Peninsula and the maritime direction in the Gulf of Thailand.”
In both cases, the Chinese military has emphasized that the facilities have been established on the basis of “mutual respect” and are not directed at any
Nonetheless, the Ban Keun facility has the potential to alter the strategic map of mainland Southeast Asia, pulling Laos and Cambodia further out of the Vietnamese sphere of influence.
Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told Bloomberg that in light of the recent expansion of China’s military presence in Cambodia and the South China Sea, Vietnam in particular could have “serious grounds for concern” if the Ban Keun facility becomes a foothold for a more permanent PLA presence in Laos.
“These developments could give Beijing greater leverage over strategic access routes around Vietnam, raising concerns about its ability to monitor, and potentially constrain, Vietnam’s room for maneuver in time of crisis,” Giang told the newspaper. “Much depends on how the facility is used.”
Vietnam has not yet officially commented on the opening of the new facilities in Laos.

FACTBOX - Canada’s residential schools: Over 150,000 Indigenous children, thousands dead, searches still underway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:05:18 UTC
10:05:18 KST

Canada marked its National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, commemorating Indigenous children who died or disappeared while attending residential schools and survivors of a system that separated more than 150,000 children from their families over more than a century.
For Canada’s more than 1.8 million Indigenous people — about 5% of the population according to the 2021 census — Sept. 30 is also Orange Shirt Day, symbolized by an orange shirt taken from six-year-old residential school survivor Phyllis Webstad in 1973.
Webstad had arrived at St. Joseph Mission Residential School in British Columbia wearing a new orange shirt bought by her grandmother. School staff took the shirt along with the rest of her clothes, and she never saw it again.
Orange Shirt Day began in 2013, while Sept. 30 became the federal National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021. The government says the orange shirt now symbolizes the loss of culture, freedom and self-esteem experienced by many Indigenous children.
The residential school system stretched back to the 19th century and continued into the 1990s. Canada’s federal government recognizes 140 former residential schools under the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, and at least 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Metis children attended the institutions.
The schools were funded and regulated by the federal government but largely operated by churches. About 60% were run by Roman Catholic organizations, about 30% by the Anglican Church and roughly 10% by the United and Presbyterian churches, according to records cited in a report on the residential school system.
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) said the residential school system was designed to assimilate Indigenous children by separating them from their families, languages and cultures and replacing Indigenous ways of life with European-Canadian Christian norms, a policy it calls “cultural genocide.”
In 1920, residential school attendance became compulsory for many First Nations children between the ages of seven and 15. Authorities could prosecute parents who refused to send their children and, in some cases, police were used to return children to the schools.
Canada’s first prime minister, John A. Macdonald, laid out the assimilationist reasoning in Parliament in 1883, saying a child educated while remaining with an Indigenous family was “simply a savage who can read and write.” He argued that Indigenous children should instead be removed from parental influence and placed in industrial schools.
The system was chronically underfunded and overcrowded. Survivors described physical and sexual abuse, harsh punishment for speaking Indigenous languages, inadequate food and medical care, and prolonged separation from their families.
The exact number of children who perished at the schools remains unknown.
The NCTR’s National Student Memorial Register includes more than 4,000 named and unnamed children identified through records and family and survivor accounts. In September 2025 alone, researchers verified 1,143 additional names and updated information on more than 1,000 other students, underscoring that the record remains incomplete.
Former TRC Chairman Murray Sinclair estimated that 6,000 or more children may have died. Disease, malnutrition, neglect, fires, accidents, violence and other causes were among the factors documented in residential school deaths.
Many children who died were not returned to their families.
The TRC found that students were often buried in cemeteries on school grounds or in nearby church, reserve or municipal cemeteries. Indian Affairs officials opposed transporting bodies home in many cases because of the cost, leaving some children buried hundreds or thousands of kilometers from their communities.
Records of some cemeteries were incomplete, while markers — often made of wood — disappeared over time and some burial grounds became overgrown, abandoned or difficult to locate.
That history has driven a new wave of Indigenous-led searches using archival research, survivor testimony, ground-penetrating radar, LiDAR scanning, human-remains detection dogs and other methods.
The issue drew international attention in 2021 when the Tk’emlups te Secwepemc announced preliminary findings indicating more than 200 potential burials, initially reported as 215, at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School in British Columbia.
The First Nation stressed that the investigation was continuing. In February 2026, it said ground-penetrating radar, LiDAR and detection-dog findings overlapped in several areas and that investigators had found signatures resembling burials, while some other locations had been ruled out.
Ground-penetrating radar does not by itself identify human remains. It detects disturbances or features beneath the soil that can warrant further investigation, meaning radar anomalies and potential burial sites should not be reported as confirmed graves without additional evidence.
Search work is now taking place across Canada.
As of January 2026, Ottawa had 164 funding agreements worth about C$280 million ($196.7 million) with Indigenous communities and partners for efforts to locate, document and memorialize burial sites.
Federal briefing material said ground searches reported under funded projects in seven communities had identified more than 370 subsurface anomalies and confirmed 88 unmarked graves. Those figures cover reported work under the program and are not a national total.
In the 2025-2026 fiscal year alone, the federal community support fund approved 52 projects worth C$37.4 million, including 24 involving technical field investigations.
The work has also led to the return of remains. In October 2025, the remains of a child who attended the Fort Resolution residential school in the Northwest Territories in the 1940s were identified and repatriated to her home community for reburial beside her mother.
But communities say access to records remains crucial. The NCTR continues to build its National Student Memorial Register and a repository of residential school burial sites, while Indigenous communities seek government, church, hospital and other records that could help establish what happened to children who never returned home.
Tk’emlups te Secwepemc said this year that its investigation was still being hindered by restrictions on government records and slow access to Roman Catholic Church material covering the Kamloops school’s 88 years of operation.
The broader reckoning grew out of the TRC, which gathered nearly 7,000 survivor and family statements and examined about 5 million documents before ending its mandate in 2015. It issued 94 Calls to Action, including six specifically addressing missing children and burial information.
Those efforts continue beyond formal government programs.
At Loyalist College in Belleville, Ontario, near Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory, the school this week unveiled a large timeline installation called Truth Before Reconciliation, tracing colonial policies, their effects on Indigenous peoples and Indigenous resistance.
“This timeline was created to help us tell a story about how colonial policies have shaped Indigenous experiences in Canada,” Indigenous Studies professor Katharine Davis said.
On Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Wednesday, First Nations, Inuit and Metis residential school survivors raised the Survivors’ Flag in memory of the children who never returned home — five years after Canada first formally observed the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Japan Has Been Here Before: The 1987 Persian Gulf Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:03:00 UTC
10:03:00 KST

The Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed following the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in February, leaving oil tankers unable to transit the strait, which is both the entrance to the Persian Gulf and one of the world’s most critical trade arteries. Japan imports more than 90 percent of its crude oil from the Middle East. Gasoline prices have surged, and the effects on daily life have been wide-ranging. The current crisis has a precedent. During the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, the Japanese government actively debated whether to send Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) minesweepers and Japan Coast Guard (JCG) patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf — and ultimately chose not to.
Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980, beginning the Iran–Iraq War. Around 1984 the conflict spread to the sea, and passage through the Persian Gulf became hazardous for tankers as missile attacks and mines proliferated. In July 1987, at Kuwait’s request, the U.S. government dispatched warships and began escorting tankers, but a tanker still struck a mine. Washington then asked Western countries, including Japan, to send minesweepers. The U.K., France, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium all subsequently contributed to the minesweeping effort.
The Japanese government began exploring how it could contribute to navigational safety in the Gulf. Prime Minister Nakasone Yasuhiro was personally in favor of deploying personnel via MSDF minesweepers. On August 27, 1987, speaking before a Lower House committee, he argued that while he did not intend to order the dispatch, the act of removing mines would not, in his view, constitute the use of force, and that sending vessels to the Persian Gulf would not constitute the overseas dispatch of troops.
Naval mines constitute weapons of naval warfare, and laying them is an established means of naval combat. Under international law, minesweeping operations conducted during an armed conflict are themselves considered a use of force. This posed a legal challenge to Nakasone’s position: his argument applied only to the removal of abandoned mines in peacetime, after a ceasefire had been reached — not to active operations in an ongoing conflict.
Within the Japanese government, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs led efforts to identify feasible forms of contribution. It became clear that any MSDF minesweeper dispatch would require a destroyer escort, and amid strong public opposition the government decided against sending minesweepers. Instead, it developed alternative proposals: providing economic cooperation in the Gulf region, sharing the costs of ensuring safe passage, increasing Japan’s host-nation support for U.S. forces, and dispatching JCG patrol vessels as a means of contributing personnel.
A senior Foreign Ministry official argued that dispatching JCG patrol vessels would circumvent constitutional constraints while signaling Japan’s proactive stance to the world. Under then Transport Minister Hashimoto Ryutaro, the Ministry of Transport and the JCG continued to explore this option. The JCG faced no statutory geographic limits on its activities, and operations in the Persian Gulf would have been legally permissible. The problem was operational: the Gulf was a war zone, and the safety of any JCG vessels deployed there could not be guaranteed.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Gotoda Masaharu would later describe Nakasone as one of the most outstanding postwar Japanese leaders, noting that they rarely differed in their political judgments — with one exception. That exception was the proposed dispatch of JCG patrol vessels to the Persian Gulf. Gotoda risked his position to oppose it, telling Nakasone that while the Cabinet would make the final decision, he personally would not sign off on it regardless.
Gotoda’s stand proved decisive. At U.S. urging, Japan instead agreed to fund the installation of high-precision radio navigation aids known as Decca chains. The resulting Decca Navigator stations allowed vessels to chart safe routes through the Gulf while avoiding the war zone, a practical and politically viable contribution that did not require deploying personnel into a combat area.
The 1987 episode established a precedent: Japan would not send vessels into an active conflict zone. That caution carried forward. Those 1987 deliberations directly shaped Japan’s approach to the subsequent Gulf War, and continue to shape its response to the current Strait of Hormuz crisis. During the Gulf War, Japan dispatched MSDF minesweepers to the Persian Gulf only after the ceasefire agreement took effect.
When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, the U.S. again asked Japan to dispatch minesweepers and supply vessels. Senior Foreign Ministry officials resisted, citing the 1987 precedent against sending vessels into areas of armed conflict. Japan instead provided $13 billion in financial support, a contribution that drew a cold response from the international community, as it was widely viewed as checkbook diplomacy without strategic commitment. After the Gulf War ceasefire took effect in April 1991, with the Persian Gulf no longer a combat zone, Japan dispatched MSDF minesweeper units that same month. The pattern established in 1987 held: deployment was permissible, but only once hostilities had ceased. As Japan weighs its options in the current Strait of Hormuz crisis, that calculus — and the political constraints behind it — remain fundamentally unchanged.

Contemporary Istanbul art fair draws 38,500 visitors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
00:59:43 UTC
09:59:43 KST

Aişe Hümeyra Akgün, Beril Çanakcı
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Contemporary Istanbul, Türkiye’s international contemporary art fair, brought together 70 galleries from 16 countries, 736 artists and 1,372 artworks for its 21st edition.
Organized with Akbank as its main partner, the five-day fair attracted 38,500 visitors, with international attendance rising 50% from the previous edition, according to the Contemporary Istanbul Foundation for Art, Culture and Education.
Twenty-two galleries joined the fair for the first time, while Istanbul hosted VIP guests from 37 countries and representatives of 148 institutions.
The fair featured galleries from across Asia including Hong Kong, Shanghai, Tokyo, Seoul, New Delhi and Singapore through its Focus Asia section alongside the Newcomers and New Grounds sections.
Ali Gureli, chairman of Contemporary Istanbul, said the fair helped establish new international connections and announced that Germany would be the focus of next year's program.
A sculpture route at Tersane Istanbul, a historic former shipyard complex located along a 2-kilometer (1.24-mile) shoreline on the northern coast of the Golden Horn in Beyoglu, Istanbul, featured 12 works by artists including Jaume Plensa, Arne Quinze, Bahadır Baruter, Bernar Venet, Ecem Yerman and Johnny Depp.
The fair also saw Oddviz's "Istanbul City Walls" added to the collection of the Istanbul Governorship.
To encourage young people to engage with contemporary art, the fair offered free admission to university students, with 1,250 students taking part. More than 300 students from fine arts high schools also joined special guided tours organized by Akbank.
The 22nd edition in 2027 will feature Focus Germany, bringing together art communities from Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Stuttgart and Cologne with Türkiye's art scene.

U.S. President Donald Trump offered his own extraordinary account Wednesday night of the drama aboard the flydubai flight to Israel, saying he had spoken "at length" with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and recounting how, according to what he was told, an Israeli plumber with no flying experience helped prevent the aircraft from crashing.
"I think it’s an incredible story," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "I did speak to Bibi Netanyahu at length about this event." Trump said the information he received suggested that "the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot."
He said the wounded captain was in ‘very bad shape,’ but praised his actions after the attack. Trump said the pilot managed to open the reinforced cockpit door despite his injuries, allowing others to enter.
"In a way, he was a hero," Trump said, noting that cockpit doors are designed so they cannot be opened from outside. According to Trump’s account, the injured pilot managed to open the door and scream for help.
Trump then turned to the Israeli passenger who intervened, apparently referring to Yaniv Hayun. "An Israeli plumber saw what was happening," Trump said. "And you know, when you lift pipe all day, you’re strong."
Trump said Hayun was near the front of the aircraft when he heard the screams and saw what was unfolding. At that point, Trump said, the plane was already descending rapidly. "The plane was going sharply down at an unbelievable angle," he said, adding that the aircraft was traveling far beyond its normal operating limits.
Trump also claimed that the dive was so extreme that "the rudder ripped off the back of the plane." He said the Israeli passenger then confronted the co-pilot. "He ripped this guy out of the seat, threw him back," Trump said, adding that other passengers then grabbed and restrained the man.
Then came the part of the story that appeared to impress Trump most. "Having never flown a plane, he took the stick, lifted it up, and leveled out the plane before it crashed," Trump said.
But Trump immediately stressed that he was recounting information given to him rather than presenting an independently verified version of events. "Now this is the story that I heard. I don’t know if it’s true, but that’s the story that I got from Bibi," he said.
Trump said other pilots and security personnel subsequently reached the cockpit and took control of the aircraft. "I think it’s the most amazing story," he said.
Trump also recounted what he had been told about how Hayun knew what to do with the controls. "When asked why he did that, he said, 'He watches that show Air Disasters,'" Trump said.
Trump called Air Disasters ‘the craziest show’ and said Hayun had apparently told Netanyahu that he watched it frequently.
"He said he watches it a lot, and he learned from watching that show sort of how to fly," Trump said.
Trump joked about the series, saying watching programs about aviation catastrophes made him uncomfortable because ‘bad things happen,’ before returning to the improbability of a passenger drawing on a television show during an actual midair emergency.
He also repeated his caution about the suspected attacker’s intentions. "They said he wanted to crash. They don’t know that. They don’t know that kind of information," Trump said.
The president later again described Hayun as a plumber, referring to him at one point as a "Jewish plumber."
flydubai Flight FZ1073 was traveling from Dubai to Israel Wednesday morning with 174 people aboard, most of them Israelis, when a violent incident erupted in the cockpit. The Omani co-pilot attacked the Indian captain and the aircraft rapidly lost altitude before passengers and crew members entered the cockpit and subdued him.
Two other pilots traveling aboard the flight later took control of the aircraft and landed it safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The passengers subsequently returned to Israel aboard a replacement flyDubai flight.
The precise motive for the attack remains under investigation. Not all elements of the dramatic account Trump said he received from Netanyahu and others have been independently confirmed.

He said the attacks "constitute a grave violation of international humanitarian law and the principles of civilian protection."
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the army's claims.
The statement came as fighting between government forces and the Houthis intensified on several fronts, including in Taiz and Lahj provinces near the Bab al-Mandab Strait in southwestern Yemen, Marib in the east, Al-Jawf in the north and Al-Bayda in central Yemen.
The latest fighting is part of a military escalation that began in early July, described as the largest since the relative calm that followed an April 2022 truce.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.

The Woman Who Held Mahathir’s Hand For 70 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
00:42:00 UTC
09:42:00 KST

Dr. Siti Hasmah Mohamad Ali had just one complaint about her husband, Dr. Mahathir Mohamad: that he was very shy about holding her hand in public. The man, who remained loyal and faithful to her for more than 70 years, felt a little embarrassed about showing his love for the Malay girl he met at King Edward VII College of Medicine in Singapore in 1947.
On Mahathir’s 93rd birthday, in an interview with Channel NewsAsia conducted by 10-year-old Kashika Selvam, Siti Hasmah narrated a funny incident about holding hands. She said that he was so shy that once, while driving through a highway toll booth, he pulled back his hand because he didn’t want the toll operator to see them holding hands.
Mahathir ruled Malaysia ruthlessly between 1981 and 2003, during which his critics and detractors were the subjects of sometimes furious political vendettas.
But when it comes to his fidelity and faithfulness to Siti Hasmah, even his critics cannot raise a finger against him.
At home, Mahathir was a loyal husband and an affectionate father, thanks in large part to Siti Hasmah. His daughter, Marina Mahathir, says her mother insisted that the siblings show their love and affection for each other openly by hugging and kissing.
Unlike many other politicians’ wives, Siti Hasmah’s conduct in public never gave a hint that she was the prime minister’s wife. Narrating a poignant incident in the 2019 documentary “M for Malaysia,” Siti Hasmah says: “I was taking my husband to the hospital, not the Prime Minister of Malaysia,” when Mahathir suffered a heart attack in 1989. Like any other devoted spouse, she was more concerned about her husband than the post he occupied.
Six years ago, on November 23, 2019, Malaysians saw a rare sight in Kuala Lumpur: the 94-year-old prime minister taking his 93-year-old wife out on a date. Driving Siti Hasmah in a Proton car, with no protocol or usual entourage, the couple went to a café on Jalan Bukit Bintang, where they had coffee and cake. It looked as if the two students who met at the medical college in Singapore were reliving those moments when they took a bus to Marine Parade to eat their favourite tauhu bakar, kangkong, and squid. The pictures touched such a chord with Malaysians that when Mahathir posted them on his official Instagram page, they received 55,000 likes and 2,000 comments.
Whenever the couple was asked about the secret of their marriage, both said in unison: tolerance. They married after a nine-year courtship. Both were in their thirties when they married. By that point, they were mature enough to understand each other’s goals in life. They never tried to portray themselves as the “perfect couple.” On many occasions, Siti Hasmah insisted that their marriage was like anybody else’s. There were happy moments and sad moments. They fought, made up and went on holidays together, she said.
Unlike others, there was nothing glamorous about this First Couple. They continued working towards their goals and made this marriage very endearing to Malaysians because they showed that accommodation and tolerance are a recipe for a lasting marriage.
On September 28, 2026, Siti Hasmah let go of Mahathir’s hand forever. On physical separation, Rumi once said: “Goodbyes are only for those who love with their eyes. Because for those who love with heart and soul there is no such thing as separation.” For 70 years, they were inseparable, and even death cannot separate them.

Morocco: Whistleblower reveals how authorities used a web of surveillance to silence journalists and activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
00:30:00 UTC
09:30:00 KST

- Ex-security agent provides rare first-hand insight into how Morocco surveillance system works from the inside.
- Targets secretly recorded in detention, offices, homes, cars and airports
- Intelligence services conspired with phone shop owners to sell phones pre-infected with spyware
Authorities in Morocco operate an expansive and vast surveillance apparatus that combines digital and analogue tools to track, monitor and ultimately silence journalists, activists and other critical voices, Amnesty International said in a new report.
We start with the verdict: Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine reveals how Moroccan authorities use unlawful surveillance to target human rights defenders, journalists and other dissenting voices and subject them to criminal prosecutions, judicial harassment and other forms of repression in violation of their rights to privacy, liberty, and freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly.
“Morocco has wholly embraced techno-authoritarian practices, acquiring a wide range of surveillance technologies to establish and enable a repressive system specifically designed to instill fear among human rights activists and journalists, silence their voices and obstruct their work inside and outside Morocco,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
Morocco has repeatedly denied using spyware to spy on its citizens. However, new evidence obtained by Amnesty International including whistleblower testimony, leaked surveillance data, government spyware targeting records and material from companies selling surveillance tools proves the opposite. Drawing on this evidence, the organization documents not only the range of tools and techniques used to target dissent, but the web of international vendors providing them.
“Our report provides the most detailed picture to date of the tools deployed by the Moroccan authorities, such as high-tech spyware, audio bugging systems and trackers to spy on journalists, human rights defenders and other individuals. Morocco’s surveillance tools are purchased from corporate actors based in Israel, the EU and the United States of America, and including NSO Group, the now defunct Italian spyware company Hacking Team, now known as Memento Labs, and the British-German network of companies Gamma Group and FinFisher.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“This is another demonstration of a global economy of techno-oppression, enabled by companies and States failing to uphold their obligations under international law.
“This repressive ecosystem makes it difficult, and dangerous for people in Morocco to exercise their rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly. Even after they have been released from prison, they continue to live under the shadow of surveillance and are subject to smear campaigns with private details that can only be obtained through surveillance. Moroccan authorities must immediately end the unlawful surveillance of human rights defenders and journalists,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
Forensic evidence unearthed by Amnesty International demonstrates how human rights defenders were targeted using multiple infection methods, including physical infection of devices; 1-click attacks, which typically rely on the victim clicking on a malicious link; zero-click attacks, which can infect a target without them having to click a link, or take any action; and network injection attacks, delivered via the state-owned Maroc Telecom network.
A whistleblower at the heart of Morocco’s surveillance system
Amnesty International had previously published the first ever forensic evidence confirming Pegasus spyware infections of the mobile phones of human rights defenders and activists in Morocco.
This new report now identifies the Direction Générale de la Surveillance du Territoire (DGST), as the entity responsible for the deployment of Pegasus spyware in Morocco, and the extensively documented abuses of Pegasus against activists and journalists between 2017 and 2021 despite previous denials by Moroccan authorities.
A whistleblower, known by the pseudonym Safir, is a former DGST employee. In multiple interviews conducted over several years, he described the inner operations of the DGST and detailed the wide range of surveillance tools and techniques used by the agency. Amnesty International corroborated key aspects of Safir’s testimony with independent sources, technical evidence and interviews with human rights defenders.
By combining the first-hand accounts of the DGST insider with digital forensics research, interviews with ten targets of surveillance, and leaked data on both surveillance operations in Morocco and range of surveillance technology suppliers, Amnesty International is able to provide one of the most detailed and revealing accounts of state surveillance operations, while contextualizing spyware abuses as one tactic situated inside a wider system of surveillance and control.
Safir described how personal devices are compromised. Targeted individuals are secretly filmed and audio recorded while in detention, in their offices and cars, at cafes, and even inside their bedrooms. Phone calls are routinely intercepted. Location data is tracked, exposing the daily movements of activists and their associates. Safir described how phone shops were co-opted to sell mobile phones pre-infected with spyware by DGST agents, and how neighbours of targeted human rights defenders are recruited as informants.
These tactics do not only affect the targeted activists, but also extend to families, friends and professional networks. Agents operate without judicial oversight or accountability and target activists in secrecy and with impunity.
“The tools they use are wide-ranging, but the goal is clear: to blackmail, discredit, shame and, if necessary, unjustly imprison those who speak out in defence of human rights in Morocco,
Rebecca White, Amnesty International Security Lab Researcher.
“Ultimately, for human rights defenders in Morocco, there is virtually nowhere to hide and no way to escape the state’s all-encompassing web of surveillance, which even extends beyond Morocco’s borders.”
How the DGST targets activists
Morocco’s surveillance operations are primarily executed by the DGST. While many advanced digital surveillance techniques can be conducted remotely, the DGST has also relied on physical infection of devices as a key surveillance method against journalists and activists.
In his testimony, Safir said these methods were routinely deployed against individuals transiting through Morocco’s airports, as well as through arrangements to covertly supply “new” devices to targeted individuals via secondhand phone vendors. These phones appear new and unused, but when activated give authorities full access to the individual’s entire communications.
“We infected so many internet cafés with Remote Controlled Spyware (RCS). The field agents tell us which cybercafé the target is visiting, and we had visibility on what they were doing because we had previously infected all the machines there,” Safir said.
RCS spyware allows the operator to track calls, read messages, access photos and record audio.
Once a person is marked as a surveillance target, the DGST has an array of tools at its disposal, including advanced digital targeted and mass surveillance technologies. Beyond telephone surveillance, authorities covertly planted microphones and other recording devices in private spaces to capture conversations.
Journalist Omar Radi, who faced years of harassment and later imprisonment because of his work on corruption and human rights violations, was targeted using this method. Safir described them as small microphones operating wirelessly via encrypted radio transmission, implanted in his apartment’s light fixtures.
Human rights defenders also face surveillance, criminal prosecution and smear campaigns based on information they believe has been obtained through surveillance. These campaigns are deployed through state-aligned media platforms, often meant to delegitimize or stigmatize activists in Moroccan society.
“As soon as I speak in public, as soon as I write a Facebook post, as soon as I put something out on Instagram, they scrutinize my every move, they insult me. They’re not media – they’re tools of terror,”
Omar Radi.
The suspicion that private and domestic spaces have been intruded has a profound psychological impact on human rights defenders.
In 2021, veteran human rights activist Fouad Abdelmoumni was covertly filmed at home with his fiancée and the video circulated on WhatsApp.
“When I saw the videos of me and my partner in bed, the location and angle of the recording were clearly visible. It must have been the air-conditioning unit. I went to look but I didn’t find anything, so I deduced that they’d been able to easily install and remove it. The quality of the image and sound was very good, despite the fact it was dark, so the equipment must have been very sophisticated,” he said.
Safir confirmed Abdelmoumni’s testimony describing it as a “textbook case” of DGST’s surveil and clean-up operation designed to leave no trace.
The investigation was conducted as part of a collaboration with 14 media organizations coordinated by Forbidden Stories, and builds on the work of Moroccan investigative journalist Hicham Mansouri – himself a victim of Morocco’s surveillance machine and now exiled in France. In 2015, he was imprisoned under trumped-up charges of “adultery” and “sexual exploitation” after a trial which did not meet international standards. He told Amnesty International how surveillance leads to self-censorship.
“It’s very violent. A friend told me that, after years of this, the day he went into prison, it was a kind of relief,” said Mansouri
In October 2019, Amnesty International forensically documented the first Pegasus infection attempts in Morocco, targeting Abdessadak El Bouchattaoui, a human rights lawyer involved in defending Hirak El-Rif movement protesters. Pegasus Project records show that his phone number was entered into Morocco’s Pegasus system on 19 September 2017 and repeatedly selected for spyware targeting on multiple occasions, including on 23 October 2017, shortly before he received an SMS infection link. This confirms that Morocco’s Pegasus spyware operations were fully operational by October 2017.
Pegasus spyware evolution and use against human rights defenders and journalists
Based on analysis of legal documents, leaked surveillance records, open-source intelligence and Safir’s testimony, the report provides further evidence that from September 2017, the DGST began deploying and using Pegasus, with NSO Group staff conducting demonstrations or dry runs of the system during visits to Morocco. NSO Group develops the notorious and highly invasive Pegasus spyware.
Further evidence, drawn from previously unpublished internal NSO Group materials disclosed as part of a long-running US civil court case against the company initiated by WhatsApp and Meta, indicates that NSO staff conducted trainings and performed tests demonstrating new capabilities of their spyware product for the benefit of Moroccan authorities, a customer who NSO Group internally codenamed Morgen.
An analysis of all target phone numbers entered in the Moroccan Pegasus system between September and December 2017 by Amnesty International provides further evidence that human rights defenders and independent journalists were the DGST’s priority targets.
Amnesty International matched 103 Moroccan phone numbers to specific individuals selected as potential Pegasus targets. Sixty-five were identifiable as civil society members (including 34 human rights defenders, 22 journalists and media workers, five lawyers, and four academics), 25 were political representatives or officials, and five were diplomats or representatives of international organizations. The remaining eight included business people, religious figures and others whose identity or categorization was unclear.
“These records show the phone numbers of prominent human rights defenders and journalists were among the first to be entered into the Pegasus system, indicating that this was the priority purpose for which the DGST had acquired the highly invasive spyware system,
Donncha Ó Cearbhaill, Head of Amnesty International’s Security Lab.
“The report also evidences and forensically attributes numerous cases of Pegasus abuses to the DGST based on technical analysis of Pegasus attacks. Together, these findings provide strong evidence that Morocco was responsible for an extensive cross-border Pegasus surveillance campaign against critical journalists, activists, lawyers and politicians.”
Four weeks prior to publication of its report, Amnesty International wrote to Moroccan authorities but did not receive any response.
Prior to publication, Amnesty International wrote to the companies featured in the report with our key findings related to their operations.
Verint replied to stating that “Verint divested this line of business on Feb. 1, 2021. Media inquiries should be referred to Cognyte Software Ltd.”
Memento Labs stated that “We can confirm to you that there isn’t any active contract with any Morrocan Agency,” adding that “Memento Labs in the last years has dramatically changed the way of doing business and has already implemented an Internal Compliance program in order to carefully monitor Countries’ situations.”
Amnesty International did not receive a reply from any of the other companies.
For the purposes of our report, Amnesty International considers surveillance to be unlawful where it is conducted in violation of domestic laws and procedures governing the use of surveillance. Surveillance may also be unlawful even when undertaken in accordance with domestic legal procedures if it is used in ways that contravene international human rights law and standards.
Morocco’s surveillance practices and many of the tools it uses violate international human rights law and standards. Morocco must urgently cease the surveillance of human rights defenders and journalists lawfully exercising their human rights. Moroccan judicial authorities must ensure an independent and effective investigation into all reported cases of unlawful surveillance by the DGST.
States must stop the export of spyware, digital forensics tools, and other privacy-invasive technology to Morocco until there’s a system of human rights safeguards in place capable of preventing human rights abuses in practice.

Netanyahu says it's too early to determine motive in FlyDubai cockpit stabbing incident
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu indicated to CBS News Wednesday that the motive of the co-pilot accused of stabbing his fellow pilot on a passenger jet bound from Dubai to Tel Aviv was still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil.
"I think it looks like a suicide attempt simply because of what this hero Yaniv described when he went in," Netanyahu speculated, referring to Yaniv Hayoun, one of the passengers on the FlyDubai flight who has been credited with entering the cockpit and helping to subdue the attacker.
"This guy was trying to jam the equipment between the two flight seats, the pilot seats," Netanyahu said of the co-pilot, whose identity has not been revealed. "He wasn't sitting in the pilot seat trying to stabilize the plane, he was trying to jam the equipment."
Speaking Thursday to Fox News, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. In He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
According to Israeli officials, on Wednesday morning local time, the FlyDubai jet was about two hours into its flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when the co-pilot stabbed the captain.
Per data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News, the plane then plunged about 17,000 feet, climbed 5,000 feet, and then fell another 7,000 feet before stabilizing.

====================================================================================================

Israel's next government faces heavy debt, high defense costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
00:19:02 UTC
09:19:02 KST

Israel’s next finance minister will inherit an economy with a tight labor market, a resilient shekel and a technology sector that continued to operate through nearly three years of war. At the same time, the government will face roughly NIS 350 billion (around $114 billion) in estimated war-related fiscal costs and a public-debt ratio approaching 70% of gross domestic product.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The next government will therefore confront a different economic environment from the one Israel faced before October 7, 2023. The economy has absorbed repeated military shocks without entering a financial crisis, but the fiscal room available to respond to future shocks has narrowed.
Longstanding structural problems also remain unresolved, including weak productivity in parts of the economy, educational gaps and low labor-force participation in some communities.
Public debt on the rise in Israel
The Bank of Israel estimates the fiscal cost of the war from 2023 through 2026 at about NIS 350 billion, with roughly half financed through borrowing. By the end of 2025, public debt had risen to 68.5% of GDP from 60.5% at the beginning of 2023, while the government deficit stood at 4.7%.
The central bank separately estimated that the economy produced about NIS 177 billion less between the start of the war and the end of 2025 than it otherwise would have.
Prof. Elise S. Brezis, a macroeconomist at Bar-Ilan University, cautions against treating the rise in debt as Israel’s most urgent economic problem.
“When you look at that compared to many OECD countries, our situation is not so bad,” Brezis told The Media Line.
She pointed to the exchange rate and Israel’s continuing ability to finance itself as indications that markets do not currently view the country as facing an imminent fiscal crisis.
“It is a problem,” she said, “but that’s not the first thing that a new government should take care of.”
Recent Bank of Israel indicators offer some support for that assessment. In September, the bank said Israel’s risk premium was around levels seen before October 7, 2023, while the labor market remained tight.
Economic activity also rebounded sharply during the second quarter of 2026, although the bank cautioned that part of the increase reflected recovery from disruption caused by earlier fighting with Iran.
Adrian Filut, chief economic commentator at the Israeli financial newspaper Calcalist, takes a more cautious view.
'Little fiscal room' for Israel's next government
Filut told The Media Line that Israel’s next government, regardless of its composition, will enter office with “very little fiscal room.”
In his view, comparisons with heavily indebted large economies can be misleading because Israel faces unusually high geopolitical risk and therefore requires larger fiscal reserves.
“Israel is not Switzerland,” Filut said. “You need buffers. You need space and cushions of protection that other governments perhaps do not need.”
For Filut, a debt ratio of about 70% is therefore more consequential for Israel than the headline figure alone might suggest. The country entered the war with fiscal space accumulated over previous years, he said, and has since used much of it.
Defense spending will make rebuilding that fiscal space more difficult.
Before the war, military spending was about 4.5% of GDP. The International Monetary Fund estimated that it reached roughly 8% in 2025 and could remain near 6% in 2026. Even if wartime spending declines, defense would still consume a larger share of the economy than it did before Oct. 7.
The Bank of Israel’s July forecast projected a 2026 deficit of 4.9% of GDP and public debt of about 69%. The projection already incorporated additional defense spending but did not account for every possible increase.
The bank said that adding as much as 25 billion shekels to the defense budget, bringing it to roughly 183 billion shekels, could push the deficit to about 5.5%.
That would leave policymakers with a limited range of options.
“If you can’t touch defense, you don’t have that much room left in civilian and social spending,” Filut said.
The alternatives, he said, include increasing government revenue, broadening the tax base, reducing sectoral spending, cutting other expenditures or borrowing more.
Higher value-added or income taxes would raise substantial revenue but could also weigh on consumption and growth. Filut said he would first examine taxes associated with negative externalities, including pollution and products that generate future public-health costs.
Will workers have the skills needed in a modern economy?
Brezis places greater emphasis on education and human capital.
For her, the more serious long-term risk is whether a growing share of Israelis receives the education needed to participate productively in a modern economy.
She challenges the common framing of the Haredi economic problem as simply one of workforce participation. Some employment, she said, may not be fully reflected in official statistics. The deeper issue, in her view, is whether workers have the skills needed to enter productive sectors of the economy.
“They don’t know English, they don’t know math,” Brezis said, arguing that publicly funded schools across Israeli society should provide the same core academic curriculum while allowing communities to add religious, cultural or other subjects.
Asked what she would prioritize during the first year of a new government, Brezis proposed ending budget allocations based on family size or sectoral affiliation, redirecting funding toward education reform and beginning a major effort to improve public transportation.
She estimated that changes to sector-based spending could save roughly 20 billion shekels, although that figure was her own estimate.
Filut reaches a similar conclusion on human capital, but from a more restrictive fiscal starting point.
Israel, he said, cannot address its demographic challenge simply by increasing the number of people in employment if many of those jobs remain low-skilled and low-paid.
“The game changer is the productive and skilled labor market,” he said.
Israel’s economic advantage, Filut argued, rests overwhelmingly on its people rather than natural resources. Maintaining that advantage requires workers who can enter technology, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and other high-productivity industries.
That makes education and labor-market integration among Haredi and Arab Israelis an immediate economic and budgetary issue rather than one that can be deferred to future governments.
Brezis also sees high tech as the sector capable of sustaining Israel’s relative economic strength.
“The locomotive in the 21st-century economy will be high tech,” she said, arguing that Israel’s capacity for entrepreneurship and technological innovation remains intact despite the war.
The two economists differ less on the need for structural reform than on the order in which the next government should act.
Brezis believes Israel has enough underlying economic strength to focus first on education, institutional quality and the allocation of public resources.
Filut wants the next government to begin with a medium-term fiscal plan that puts the debt ratio back on a downward path, followed by education and labor-market reform and measures addressing Israel’s high cost of living.
For Filut, delaying a decision on how to finance permanently higher defense spending could carry substantial long-term costs.
If the money comes from civilian budgets, he said, education, universities, research and public health will face greater pressure. If it comes from additional borrowing, a larger share of future budgets will go toward servicing debt.
“Interest is the worst payment,” Filut said. “You pay billions of shekels and receive nothing. You are only financing the debt.”

Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-01
01:08:23 BST
09:08:23 KST

Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
- Published
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.
Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."
The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer, affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.
"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.
This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.
"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.
"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levels… which could affect billions of people living along the coast."
Additional reporting by Dominic Bailey
- The before and after images showing glaciers vanishing before our eyes
