====================================================================================================

Fitbit data reveal a link between teens’ erratic sleep and how they handle emotions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
22:00:47 UTC
07:00:47 KST

Adolescents who get less sleep, go to bed later, and have inconsistent sleep schedules tend to experience more inward-directed distress, such as anxiety and depression. A new study published in npj Mental Health Research indicates that highly variable sleep patterns are also linked to a greater reliance on suppressing emotions, with sleep inconsistency showing an especially strong connection to distress in teenage girls. These findings suggest that establishing stable sleep routines might help support the emotional well-being of adolescents.
Adolescence represents a sensitive developmental phase characterized by the emergence of new emotional challenges and the refinement of emotional coping skills. During this time, many young people begin to experience internalizing symptoms, which are emotional and behavioral difficulties directed inward, such as feelings of anxiety, depression, and social withdrawal. To navigate these feelings, adolescents rely on emotion regulation, a process of managing emotional responses.
Two common strategies for regulating emotion are cognitive reappraisal, which involves reframing a situation to change its emotional impact, and expressive suppression, which involves hiding or inhibiting the outward display of feelings. Physical health behaviors, particularly sleep, play a role in how adolescents manage these emotional processes. A 2026 study of teenagers indicated that later bedtimes and shorter sleep periods are linked to poorer self-control and increased impulsiveness.
Another 2026 study of adolescents suggested that sleep problems and emotional coping strategies influence each other over time, and that these patterns can differ between boys and girls. Much of the past research on adolescent sleep and mental health relies on self-reported survey data, which can sometimes overestimate sleep problems or reflect a person’s perceived sleep quality rather than their actual time asleep.
“Sleep problems and mental-health difficulties are known to influence one another, but much of the existing research relies on parental report or adolescents’ own statements about how they sleep,” explained study authors Andrea N. Goldstein-Piekarski and Sarah Izabel. Goldstein-Piekarski is an assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Stanford School of Medicine and director of the CoPsyN Sleep Lab, and Izabel is a graduate student at Stanford.
“We wanted to investigate whether different aspects of sleep derived objectively from a Fitbit device were associated with symptoms such as sadness, worry, and anxiety and with the strategies adolescents use to regulate their emotions,” the researchers said.
To explore these questions, the research team analyzed data from 1,371 teenagers, with an average age of 14, participating in the ongoing Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study. They gathered sleep data using Fitbit devices worn by the participants for up to three weeks. To ensure accuracy, the team only included data from adolescents who had at least three weekdays and one weekend day of usable sleep tracking per week.
The researchers categorized the participants into two groups based on the average amount of sleep they received each night, based on their Fitbit. The short sleep group consisted of adolescents who slept just over seven hours or less, while the non-short sleep group consistently slept more than seven hours.
The authors also calculated sleep duration variability, which measures how much a participant’s sleep length fluctuated from night to night on weekdays, and sleep onset time, which was the average time a participant fell asleep. To assess mental health, the adolescents completed standardized questionnaires. The Brief Problem Monitor measured internalizing symptoms by asking teenagers how often they felt fearful, guilty, self-conscious, or sad, while the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents evaluated how frequently the participants used cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression to manage their feelings.
The data revealed connections between several sleep measures and emotional distress. Adolescents who slept around seven hours or less reported greater internalizing symptoms than those who slept longer, and later sleep onset times were similarly associated with higher levels of internalizing symptoms.
Inconsistent sleep schedules also played a role in emotional well-being, as higher variability in sleep duration was linked to more internalizing symptoms. The researchers found that this association was stronger in teenage girls than in teenage boys, suggesting that adolescent females might be especially sensitive to irregular sleep patterns.
Sleep irregularity was also linked to expressive suppression. Adolescents with highly variable sleep durations were more likely to report suppressing their emotions, whereas neither short sleep duration nor late sleep onset times were associated with expressive suppression.
“Taken together, these findings emphasize that sleep is important to mental health, but they also show that the relationship is nuanced,” the researchers noted. “It depends on which aspect of sleep and which mental health outcome you examine, as well as factors such as sex.”
When looking at cognitive reappraisal, however, the researchers did not find a relationship with any of the sleep measures. Whether teenagers slept adequately, fell asleep late, or had irregular schedules, their tendency to mentally reframe emotional situations remained unaffected.
“From past literature, we anticipated that a greater tendency to use adaptive emotion regulation strategies, including cognitive reappraisal, would be associated with better sleep, but this was not borne out,” the researchers told PsyPost.
“Cognitive reappraisal is a more complex skill that continues to develop through adolescence, so our older teens may have had relatively stable reappraisal abilities that were less sensitive to short-term sleep patterns,” they explained. “It is also possible that links between sleep and reappraisal emerge over longer periods than the one-week window we assessed.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which observed that irregular sleep patterns are linked to increased internalizing symptoms in 14-year-olds. The results also align with another study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicating that poor teen sleep is linked to anxiety and depression, though the new research expands on this by using objective sleep tracking devices instead of self-reported sleep surveys.
The connection between sleep variability and emotion regulation reflects patterns seen in younger children. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 linked objective sleep variability to emotional regulation difficulties, though that earlier research observed behavioral regulation during frustration tasks in six-year-olds rather than self-reported coping strategies in adolescents.
Broadly, these insights complement research covered by PsyPost in 2025 showing that sleep problems top the list of predictors for teen mental illness within this same nationwide cohort.
But the new study, like all research, includes some caveats.
“Our study looked at sleep and mental health at one point in time in an adolescent’s developmental journey (the average age of our participants was about 14 years old), so we cannot conclude that irregular, shorter, or later sleep causes mental-health difficulties across all of adolescent development,” the researchers noted.
It is possible that irregular sleep causes emotional distress, but it is equally possible that experiencing internalizing symptoms leads to a disrupted sleep schedule.
“Another caveat is that sleep was measured with a consumer wearable device (the Fitbit), which gives us an estimate of sleep behavior based on movement rather than a direct measure of brain activity during sleep, which is more precise,” they said.
“In addition, the group of adolescents included in our study was more likely to include White teens and teens with parents who had education beyond high school, so the findings may not apply equally across all groups of adolescents,” the authors added. This demographic skew means the findings might not fully represent the experiences of adolescents from different socioeconomic or racial backgrounds.
“An important next step is research that follows adolescents over time and across different developmental periods to better clarify the timing of the relationships between sleep and mental health measures,” the researchers said. “For example, we want to learn if changes in sleep variability can predict later changes in emotional well-being for early adolescents (around 10-13 years old) and if these changes are different at different stages of adolescence (middle adolescence (14-17 years old) and late adolescence (18-21 years old)).”
They added that future work should also explore the direction of these associations, including whether emotional difficulties lead to sleep disruptions. “We also need studies that test whether helping adolescents get enough sleep, keep more consistent schedules, and fall asleep earlier can improve emotional symptoms and well-being,” they noted.
“Our study emphasizes that different facets of sleep including sleep duration, sleep duration variability, and sleep timing, are each linked with adolescent mental health,” the researchers concluded. “This is encouraging because these are modifiable sleep behaviors that can be improved. Supporting sustainable sleep routines that include all these aspects of sleep health may be a practical way to support adolescent mental health.”
The study, “Associations between objective sleep duration, sleep duration variability, and sleep onset with emotion regulation and internalizing symptoms in adolescents: findings from the ABCD® study,” was authored by Sarah Sampaio Izabel, Orsolya Kiss, Adam J. Krause, Ethan T. Hunt, Sarahjane L. Dube, Nicholas Allgaier, Alexandra S. Potter, Micah E. Johnson, Hugh Garavan, Fiona C. Baker, and Andrea N. Goldstein-Piekarski.

What are the differences between job vacancies and job ads?
How are the ABS job figures so different to the other ANZ / SEEK / IVI?
- C
Hi C,
You can read about the conceptual differences on the ABS website on this page.
The ABS defines "job vacancies" in the Job Vacancies Survey (JVS) as employee jobs available for immediate filling on the actual survey reference day and for which employers have undertaken recruitment action.
It says "recruitment action" includes efforts to fill vacancies by advertising, by on site or online notices, by notifying employment agencies or trade unions, and many other things.
It then explains the differences between the three job ads measures:
ANZ-Indeed Australian Job Ads
The ANZ produces a series of job advertisements based on counts of internet advertisements on selected employment internet sites.
Counts of job advertisements can differ from counts of job vacancies for several reasons, including the multiple advertising of a single job. Further, recruitment through word of mouth, on site notices, etc., are included in JVS but are out of scope for the ANZ-Indeed Australian Job Ads.
SEEK Employment Index
SEEK produces a monthly Employment Index, which measures the number of new job ads posted on their website in a particular month. The series is adjusted to ensure that multiple postings count as one ad.
Jobs and Skills Australia's Internet Vacancy Index
The Internet Vacancy Index (IVI), based on a count of newly lodged online vacancies on selected employment internet sites (from secondary sources).
Mr Ottley from CBA was pointing out how interesting it was that there's now a large divergence between the ABS's job vacancies measure and the three job ads measures, given they all used to track closely together in the years before COVID:
Different job vacancies outcomes
CBA's economics team has circulated a note on the job vacancies data from the Bureau of Statistics today.
They says the vacancy stock has declined by 31.2% from its May 2022 peak of 472,700, consistent with a gradual normalisation in labour demand.
This is what the ABS data looks like in a graph today:
But CBA's team says there's an interesting difference between the data coming from the ABS and data that's coming from Jobs and Skills Australia, SEEK job-ad, and ANZ-Indeed job ad measures.
See below:
They say ABS vacancies still remain materially above 2019 levels, while the alternative job-ad measures are much closer to their pre-COVID positions:
"Conceptual and coverage differences may explain part of this divergence," CBA's Harry Ottley says.
"Still, all three indicators show substantial easing from their 2022 peaks and suggest broadly stable conditions in recent quarters with the exception of ANZ-Indeed job ads which have strengthened."
China's resales of Australian LNG strengthens case for prioritising domestic users
Last week, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), an independent think tank, published a report that estimated that China had earned $6.6 billion (US$4.6b) from reselling LNG sourced from Australia and the United States between 2021 and 2026.
And yesterday, the Queensland government raised concerns about the Albanese government's proposed domestic gas reservation scheme (which will redirect some of the gas production from Australian LNG exports to the domestic market on Australia's east coast).
So today, Amanda Denis-Ryan, IEEFA Australia CEO, and Joshua Runciman, lead analyst of Australian Gas at IEEFA, have argued that their research from last week actually strengthens the case for prioritising Australia's domestic gas users.
In commentary published on IEEFA's website today, they argue that:
China resold an estimated 17-19 million tonnes of LNG abroad in 2025, from the US, Australia and other global suppliers. This volume is similar to China’s total LNG imports from Australia, and more than twice eastern Australia’s gas demand.
Chinese companies are estimated to have made at least $1.6 billion in arbitrage profits since 2021 on resales of Australian LNG, with 2026 on track to significantly exceed previous years.
With Australia’s two largest LNG buyers – Japan and China – both reselling large volumes of Australian gas, there is a strong case for prioritising domestic users when it comes to utilising eastern Australia's cheapest gas.
The Queensland government has warned against redirecting existing gas production from LNG exports to the domestic market, despite it being the cheapest source of gas available to alleviate forecast shortages in eastern Australia.
ACCI says small business will carry burden for end of credit, debit card surcharges
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) says the end of credit and debit card surcharges will create a significant burden for millions of small businesses.
As of today, Australian businesses are banned from charging customers credit, debit and prepaid card surcharges.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has welcomed the change, saying the "annoying" charges would ease pressure on people in a tough economic environment.
But ACCI chief Andrew Mackellar says it could cause some businesses to reprice their services to meet the provider payments.
"These surcharges are not going away. Somebody still has to pay this. The payment service providers, the credit card issuers, they're not working for free. They're continuing to charge the same fees through whatever means they can do that to their business customers," Mackellar says.
"It's just now much more difficult for those small businesses to work out how they wear that expense."

Thanks Phillip.
The specific section on households and businesses goes into a lot of interesting detail on this topic.
For example, the RBA says it uses scenario analysis to inform its assessment of how negative shocks could affect the financial condition of Australian households.
In an "adverse downturn" where a shock originates from overseas, the unemployment rate rises to 6.3%, inflation hits 7%, and the cash rate rises to 5.4%, the RBA says the share of mortgagors at a higher risk of defaulting on their loans is estimated to increase to about 5%, which is only a little higher than the peak in 2023 (that looks like they've modelled for a modern variety of stagflation). So even in an extreme scenario, the financial condition of Australian households is still expected to remain manageable.
Overall, it says despite recent declines in housing prices, most borrowers still have large housing equity buffers.
"Housing prices have declined in recent months as housing market sentiment has weakened, reflecting the somewhat restrictive stance of monetary policy and changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax discount policies," it says.
"Despite this, most household balance sheets remain strong, with less than 1 per cent of borrowers estimated to owe more on their loan than the value of their property (negative equity).
"Recent buyers and those who took out higher LVR loans are more likely to be in negative equity. This includes first home buyers participating in the Australian Government 5% Deposit Scheme.
"However, the potential risks to financial stability from these borrowers are mitigated by the structure of the scheme and the typical low-risk characteristics of most first home buyers.
"While downside risks to housing prices remain, the RBA’s Securitisation System data suggest that even in a scenario involving a large uniform fall in housing prices of 20 per cent from current levels, only around 5 per cent of mortgages would fall into negative equity," it says.

What does this all mean?
Basically, if you want to receive those barrels of oil now, with all those supply disruptions caused by the Middle East war, you'll have to pay a huge premium. Hence the more expensive spot price.
But if you're buying a futures contract, to accept delivery of the oil at a later date, it's cheaper if you're willing to wait a little longer.
It's because traders are betting the US-Iran conflict will de-escalate soon and the supply crunch will be resolved.

Robots won’t replace armored vehicles, says Ukrainian company that builds both. It reveals one job they can’t do
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:48:46 UTC
06:48:46 KST

Robots will not replace armored vehicles on the battlefield, says a company that builds both. Ground robots are a new tool that lets Ukraine distribute risk more smartly, but they cannot do everything a crewed armored vehicle can, above all pulling wounded soldiers out under fire, says Ukr Armo Tech's chief executive Hennadii Khirhii, in an interview with RBC-Ukraine.
Ukraine has a serious shortage of armored vehicles, from evacuation carriers to tracked fighting vehicles, with the focus shifting to hulls that offer heavy mine protection and built-in electronic warfare. For medical-evacuation armor alone, Khirhii says, the deficit is often put at 80 percent.
Robots can ease some of that, hauling ammunition and supplies to the front without risking a crew, but they are a complement, not a substitute, a view frontline commanders also confirm.
Robots share the load, not replace it
Where a robot can do the job, Khirhii says, there is no sense sending in heavy armor and the people inside it to face danger. For carrying ammunition or food, unmanned ground vehicles are useful. But evacuating the wounded is different: that usually needs, at least for the second leg, a protected medical vehicle in which care can begin on the move, with room for transfusions and resuscitation that a robot's capsule cannot provide.
"A UGV doesn't cancel the armored vehicle, just as the drone didn't cancel artillery," he says.
The limits show at evacuation
Ukraine has leaned hard into robotic logistics and casualty evacuation, running more than 100,000 such missions this year to keep medics and crews off exposed roads, but the robots themselves now draw Russian drone and artillery fire, and they cannot replace medical personnel.
One commander has called ground robots too slow for evacuation and easy targets, arguing brigades still need staffed evacuation teams and light-armored vehicles.
Commanders want both
The lesson from the front is not robots instead of armor, but robots alongside it. What matters, Khirhii says, is a smart combination of machines for each mission, with people's safety and the task's practicality first. The front today needs both armored vehicles and ground robots, he continues, and it needs a great amount of both.

Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:47:35 UTC
06:47:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a 20 percent cut to the number of generals and admirals in the US military, intensifying concerns that the Trump administration is reshaping the armed forces around its political and ideological agenda.
Hegseth portrayed the cuts as an exercise in "accountability", suggesting that officers who failed to embrace his drive to purge what he calls "woke" policies from the military had been removed.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base on Wednesday.
"We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent."
"So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board," he added. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
The announcement comes amid mounting concerns among Democratic lawmakers and some current and former military officials that the Trump administration is eroding the traditionally non-partisan character of the US armed forces and making adherence to its political agenda increasingly important for senior officers.
Since returning to office last year, President Donald Trump and Hegseth have removed a succession of senior military leaders, often without publicly explaining the reasons for their dismissal.
They include former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Charles "CQ" Brown, who Trump fired without explanation in February 2025, as well as the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, a Navy admiral assigned to NATO and three senior military lawyers.
Hegseth has also fired or blocked the promotions of scores of generals and admirals during his tenure, according to US media reports.
The upheaval has prompted warnings from some former senior officers about the potential creation of a loyalty culture within the military.
H.R. McMaster, a retired Army general who served as Trump's national security adviser during his first term, recently warned against creating "a climate in which everything's a loyalty test".
Hegseth rejects accusations that the changes amount to a political purge, insisting that Trump is entitled to select the military leadership he wants and that his reforms are intended to restore an apolitical force focused on combat effectiveness.
In Wednesday's address, however, he explicitly linked the fate of senior officers to their response to his previous efforts to reshape military culture.
Hegseth said officers who "responded positively" to a speech he delivered to senior commanders last year were now "leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations", while those who did not "no longer work here".
"We are no longer the woke department, or the weak department," Hegseth said.
"Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors -- just tough, ready, committed troops."
Hegseth ordered major cuts to the military leadership in May 2025, including a 10-percent reduction in the overall number of generals and admirals and a 20-percent cut to the highest four-star ranks.
During his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon bureaucracy was top-heavy and that resources should instead be directed towards combat capabilities.
"It's going to be my job, working with those that we hire and those inside the administration, to identify those places where fat can be cut, so it can go toward lethality," he told lawmakers.
His campaign has extended beyond the military's senior ranks. The Pentagon has dismantled diversity programmes and Hegseth this week moved to end tenure for future civilian faculty at US military academies, saying the institutions should refocus on their "warfighting" mission.
Critics argue that the combination of ideological changes and unexplained dismissals risks encouraging officers to tailor their conduct to the political preferences of the administration.
Hegseth, meanwhile, has cast the changes as necessary to reverse what he regards as years of misplaced priorities at the Pentagon.
"The media calls that a purge," he said on Wednesday. "I call it accountability."

Ohio woman sues hospital for allegedly amputating wrong leg during surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:47:06 UTC
06:47:06 KST

An Ohio woman is suing a hospital after doctors allegedly amputated the wrong leg during a scheduled operation last year.
Sharon Jacks, 74, of Meigs county, alleged that she went to Selby general hospital in September 2025 to undergo a planned below-the-knee amputation of her right leg. Instead doctors removed her left leg during the procedure, according to the lawsuit, which was filed earlier this month in Washington county court in Marietta, where the hospital is based.
Her attorney, Brad Layne, said the error ultimately left Jacks, an army veteran, a double amputee after doctors at another hospital in Ohio had to remove the correct leg four months later.
According to the 32-page complaint, Jacks “suffered physical injury, permanent disability, pain and suffering, emotional distress, humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, medical expenses and other damages”.
Jacks and her husband named nine defendants in the lawsuit, including the hospital and Jacks’s medical and surgical teams, accusing them of gross negligence, battery and reckless conduct.
“Defendants acted willfully, wantonly, recklessly, maliciously, and with conscious disregard for the substantial certainty of catastrophic injury,” the complaint alleged.
The amputation of Jacks’s lower right leg was recommended as part of a treatment plan for a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, according to the lawsuit, and she “consented only to surgery involving her right lower extremity” and “never consented to amputation of her left lower extremity”.
According to the complaint, medical records show that the surgical team conducted two “time-outs” before the procedure. In surgery, these pauses are supposed to be used to confirm the patient’s identity, the planned procedure and the correct surgical site. But “despite multiple opportunities … to identify and correct the error”, the team proceeded to amputate the wrong leg, it alleged.
“The performance of surgery upon the wrong extremity constituted a complete failure of basic safety procedures,” the lawsuit said.
In a statement to WBNS-TV, the hospital acknowledged that “this was an avoidable event, and that our expected operating room procedures were not followed.”
The statement added: “Those involved were held accountable for their actions and are no longer in their positions.
“We are saddened by what occurred, and our team continues to keep this patient and their family in our prayers.”
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages on behalf of Jacks.

The US Blacklists Alleged Venezuelan Cyber Crime Mastermind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:38:00 UTC
06:38:00 KST

Reported by
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Wednesday announced it had placed on a special blacklist Aníbal Alexander Canelón Aguirre— a Venezuelan who appears on the FBI’s "Ten Most Wanted" list—identifying him as a key link in a financial network for the notorious crime group Tren de Aragua.
Canelón Aguirre is wanted by the Justice Department for allegedly leading a multi-million dollar ATM fraud scheme. Authorities accuse him of masterminding a jackpotting operation involving malware that when installed allows thieves to direct the bank machine to spew out money.
The alleged Venezuelan hacker topped a list of six Venezuelans and three Mexicans whose names were announced Wednesday as having been added to a group of specially designated nationals. It effectively locks them out of the global financial system. Six of the named are co-defendants of Canelón Aguirre in a U.S. prosecution.
The accused hacker has been on the run, lending his tech skills to the likes of a Romanian mafia operating along Mexico's white-sand beaches and became the cyber "engineer" of the infamous Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang.
Appearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee two weeks ago, the FBI Director Kash Patel announced that federal authorities had apprehended a long-sought fugitive, claiming the arrest effectively cleared the agency’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list.
"Just this past weekend, we captured a thug down in Venezuela who is on our most wanted list and on the run for years. He has been captured, apprehended, and is on his way back to the United States of America. That's ten of ten," Patel told lawmakers.
Patel did not formally identify the suspect or provide operational details, offering no information on how the operation was carried out and whether Venezuelan authorities assisted. He only said that the arrested person was en route to the United States to face prosecution.
OCCRP reached out the Venezuelan government for comment but did not get a response.
An FBI spokesman declined to elaborate on the director’s remarks and as of Wednesday afternoon Canelón Aguirre, 49, remains on the agency’s website for the current 10 Most Wanted Fugitives.
He was added to the list on March 12, 2026, becoming the first alleged cybercriminal ever to appear on it. The agency was offering up to a million dollars for information leading directly to his arrest and described him as armed and dangerous.
Known as "El Ingeniero," "Prometeo" or "Prometheus," Canelón Aguirre is accused by the FBI of being the alleged creator of a malware tied to Tren de Aragua (TdA), a Venezuelan gang that has spread to half a dozen South American countries after emerging from a Venezuelan prison around 2012.
The scheme allowed a network to loot millions of dollars from ATMs across several U.S. states starting at least in January 2024. The technique is known as jackpotting: malicious software takes control of the ATM and forces it to dispense all the cash it holds.
“Within TdA, the jackpotting proceeds would then be transferred among members and associates of the organization in an effort to conceal the fact that they are illegally obtained proceeds,” according to the indictment of Canelon and colleagues.
Prosecutors claim that the proceeds were then moved through a money-laundering network tied to Tren de Aragua, an organization Washington has designated a foreign terrorist group. U.S. authorities describe the structure as combining high-level cybercrime with financing for a transnational criminal organization. OCCRP was among the first to warn of the nascent criminal organization spreading into the U.S. in its November 2023 series Narcofiles: The New Criminal Order.
The arrest warrant against Canelón Aguirre was issued in Omaha on December 9, 2025, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Nebraska, as part of a case that already includes dozens of defendants. He was charged with conspiracy to commit bank fraud, conspiracy to commit bank burglary and intentionally damage a protected computer system as well as to commit money laundering and provide material support to a foreign terrorist organization.
Also charged in the same indictment is Jimena Romina Araya Navarro, known in Venezuela as "Rosita" from a Venezuelan comedy show, who is accused of playing a role in the 2012 prison break of the leader of the Tren de Aragua, Héctor Rusthenford Guerrero Flore. His alias is "Niño Guerrero," and he escaped from the notorious Tocorón prison. The broader jackpotting case now totals 87 defendants nationwide across the United States. Araya Navarro was not among those placed under the Treasury blacklisting.
Before becoming Tren de Aragua's "engineer," Canelón Aguirre had already been flagged in connection with a different kind of criminal structure. According to an intelligence brief from Mexico's Security Cabinet (Gabinete de Seguridad), dated October 30, 2020, and a report from Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) on Romanian criminal groups, Canelón was identified as the developer of the malware known as Ploutus.D.
This software, the intelligence brief suggested, was used by the organization known as the Riviera Maya Gang, led by Romanian national Florian Tudor, alias "El Tiburón" ("The Shark"), to empty ATMs in the tourist zone of Quintana Roo, which includes Cancún, and in the United States.

"The enterprise AI solutions market, including cloud capacity, is expected to exceed $1trn by 2028, and we think Meta's consumer data and communications apps could give Meta's advantages for AI enterprise sales to consumer-focused companies," BofA Global Research analysts wrote in a Monday note. "We would expect distribution of Meta's model APIs on leading hyperscaler platforms."
September was also the fifth best month on record for Meta. The stock outperformed all of its mega-cap peers and trounced the Nasdaq, which gained almost 2% over that stretch.

German chancellor vows to press ahead with gradual economic reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:34:34 UTC
06:34:34 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told business leaders Wednesday that his government would gradually press ahead with fundamental economic reforms. 
“The need for structural reforms is great,” Merz said during a meeting in Berlin with business representatives from the “Made for Germany” initiative.
The federal government has set a number of initiatives in motion, but they are not yet where they actually wanted them to be at this point in time, he added.
Merz said that no one should doubt “my determination” to continue implementing reforms step by step, according to the German Press Agency (dpa).
He cited as an example efforts to increase flexibility in the labor market.
“We have some catching up to do there,” he said, adding this is to be discussed next week in the coalition committee, and a whole series of labor market laws still need to follow.
The chancellor also referred to the deepening of the EU single market and planned pension reform in Germany.
This reform is controversial within the coalition, however. Merz’s junior coalition partner, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), wants to discuss the planned abolition of the full pension after 45 years of contributions. Measures to make the labor market more flexible are also controversial.
Merz pointed out that economic research institutes have raised their economic forecasts for this year. A key driver is the government’s investment of billions in infrastructure modernization through a debt-financed special fund. He said there is not yet a self-sustaining economic upswing for the coming years.
The chancellor made it clear that Germany has great opportunities in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) but at the same time issued an appeal to small and medium-sized enterprises.
“Small and medium-sized enterprises in Germany must make better use of their data,” he said.
If these businesses tap into this treasure trove of data and put it to use, Germany will have one of the greatest competitive advantages in the world, he said, adding that no other country in the world has such a diverse and deeply stratified industrial small-and medium business sector as Germany.

Israeli lawmaker Naama Lazimi named among Time Magazine's 2026 Influential Rising Stars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:32:56 UTC
06:32:56 KST

Democrats lawmaker Naama Lazimi was included Wednesday in TIME magazine's 2026 TIME100 Next list, which recognizes 100 rising figures the magazine says are shaping the future and the next generation of leadership.
Karl Vick, a TIME editor who wrote Lazimi's profile, described her as a "superstar" of an embattled Israeli left and highlighted her focus on poverty, public housing and what he described as the deepening divisions in Israeli society and an "authoritarian shift" under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Vick pointed in particular to a speech Lazimi gave in July on poverty and public housing that moved the Knesset's right-wing presiding officer to tears. He also noted Lazimi's support for a negotiated peace with the Palestinians and wrote that she hopes to serve in a future government that distributes Israel's "resources and burdens evenly."
Responding to the recognition, Lazimi said in a post on X that she was "deeply moved" and thanked TIME, describing the honor as recognition not only of her own work but of "an entire camp in Israel" fighting for democracy, solidarity and social justice.
"This is not just a personal achievement, but a badge of honor for an entire camp in Israel – a proud and determined camp fighting for the democratic character of our country and for solidarity and social justice," she wrote. Lazimi said the recognition gave her renewed momentum ahead of what she called "the most important elections the State of Israel has ever known."
Democrats chairman Yair Golan also congratulated Lazimi on X, citing TIME's description of her as a "charismatic leader" and "superstar of the Israeli left."
"This year in TIME100 Next. Next year in the government," Golan wrote.
Lazimi has become one of the most prominent figures in Israel's Zionist left. She first drew national attention in 2022, when she unexpectedly finished first in the Labor Party primary, and her standing has grown since Labor merged with Meretz to form the Democrats.
In the party's primary in July, she received more than 90 percent of the vote and secured the top spot on its slate behind chairman Yair Golan.
The primary drew more than 97,000 voters, with Lazimi finishing ahead of fellow incumbent lawmakers Gilad Kariv and Efrat Rayten. The Democrats have sought to consolidate Israel's Zionist left while also incorporating prominent figures from the anti-government protest movement.
Lazimi's political profile has been built around social-democratic issues including public housing, food security and economic inequality, alongside a highly visible role in protests against Netanyahu's government and the judicial overhaul. She has also become known for combative speeches in the Knesset and for confronting coalition members directly.
Lazimi has increasingly become a target of attacks from coalition lawmakers. Likud MK Nissim Vaturi recently called her "worse than Hamas" and an "enemy from within," while United Torah Judaism MK Yitzhak Pindrus said protesters blocking roads should be shot in the legs, adding: "But start with Naama Lazimi." Lazimi filed complaints over both remarks and accused members of the government of inciting violence against her.
TIME's annual TIME100 Next list aims to spotlight emerging figures across politics, culture, business and other fields whose influence the magazine expects to grow.

Ukraine’s training facilities get boost: EU is funding centers where its army prepares soldiers, with Denmark putting in €33 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:31:50 UTC
06:31:50 KST

The EU is putting money into the places inside Ukraine where the army trains its soldiers. The bloc will fund the modernization of several military training centers in Ukraine, upgrading facilities, housing, and equipment, with Denmark administering the funds and the Come Back Alive charity carrying out the work, the Defense Ministry said.
The Ministries of Defense of Ukraine and Denmark previously signed a Letter of Intent to implement a project to modernize one of the Armed Forces of Ukraine's training centers. Under this agreement, Denmark allocated about €33 million to training infrastructure, living and sanitary conditions, equipment, and drones for training defenders.
The money goes into the centers
The support will pay to modernize several training sites: better living quarters for the troops who cycle through them, upgraded facilities, and improved infrastructure, the ministry says.
The project runs under the EU's diplomatic and military-planning bodies, the European External Action Service, the Military Planning and Conduct Capability, and the bloc's military-assistance mission for Ukraine, with the Come Back Alive foundation carrying it out alongside the Defense Ministry.
Halan calls training a foundation
The aim is a modern environment for preparing soldiers.
"Modernized centers let us train the military on real combat experience," Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan says, thanking the EU and every partner country.
Training inside Ukraine, she says, is as fundamental to defense as ammunition and equipment, because weapons do not work without people trained to use them. The modernized sites, the ministry says, are meant to let Ukraine prepare its own forces to a higher standard, faster, and closer to the front.
Denmark administers the funds
The project is an EU initiative, open to any partner willing to contribute, with Denmark as the fund administrator. The ministry thanked the EU, Denmark, and Come Back Alive for support it says raises the quality of Ukraine's training.

Trump administration files complaint against judges over media comments
Seven Minnesota judges face ethics complaint after speaking publicly about the US president’s immigration crackdown.
The United States Justice Department has filed a misconduct complaint against seven federal judges in Minnesota who spoke publicly about the pressure their courts came under during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
The judges spoke to The New York Times this month about dealing with a flood of cases during Operation Metro Surge, an immigration crackdown that led to thousands of arrests in the Minneapolis-St Paul area from December to February.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release
- list 2 of 4White House bars CNN from Air Force One for Trump’s upcoming trip
- list 3 of 4US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue third-country deportations
- list 4 of 4US judge rules Wisconsin mosque leader Salah Sarsour can be deported
The Justice Department says it crossed an ethical line by talking publicly about the cases.
Attorney General Todd Blanche accused the judges of showing “obvious bias” against the Trump administration and called on them to step aside from any cases involving the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
“When we have a situation like we have now, where you have a judge, a couple of judges, just not only violating the canons in our view but also showing bias in what they’re saying, we have no choice but to act,” Blanche told reporters.
The judges say they did nothing wrong. A spokesperson for Minnesota’s federal court system said legal experts had found that the judges were “well within the ethical rules” when they spoke to the newspaper.
The complaint is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and the judiciary, which has blocked some of the president’s policies and, in several cases, accused government lawyers of failing to follow court orders.
One of the judges named in the complaint, Patrick Schiltz, alleged that the government did not comply with nearly 100 court orders related to immigration enforcement in January alone.
In one ruling, he wrote that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “is not a law unto itself”.
Schiltz was nominated by Republican President George W Bush and previously clerked for conservative Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia.
He later told The New York Times that what happened in Minnesota’s federal courts during the crackdown “created a grave threat to the rule of law”.
Schiltz also pointed to guidance issued by a federal judicial ethics panel in February, saying that judges can speak publicly about issues such as the rule of law and judicial independence.
“That is exactly what I did,” he said.

War at the expense of orphans and pensioners: Russia’s regions cut social spending — CPD
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

War at the expense of orphans and pensioners: Russia’s regions cut social spending — CPD
Kyiv • UNN
In Tula Oblast, more than 54 million rubles in social assistance were allocated to military personnel. In St. Petersburg, they plan to cut the budget by 70.2 billion rubles.
Russian regions are being forced to sacrifice key social expenditures to satisfy the Kremlin’s growing wartime demands. This is reported by the Center for Countering Disinformation of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (CCD), according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that, for example, the authorities of Tula Oblast took more than 54 million rubles ($637,000) allocated for social support for residents and redirected them to payments for military personnel. In particular, payments to foster parents for the upkeep of orphaned children, as well as funds for low-income families, pensioners, and labor veterans, were cut.
An even larger budget sequestration is being carried out in St. Petersburg: officials are proposing cutting budget expenditures by 70.2 billion rubles ($828 million). The city is reducing funding for education, healthcare, and housing and utilities. At the same time, expenditures on payments to war participants and their families are being additionally increased by 6.4 billion rubles ($75.5 million)
They point out that the regions are taking such steps against the backdrop of a significant deficit in local budgets.
"To maintain the flow of "cannon fodder" for the Kremlin, regional authorities are effectively taking money away from orphans, medical workers, and pensioners," the CCD concludes.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has praised the profound solidarity between Türkiye and Palestine following an emotive friendly football match hosted in the central Turkish province of Konya.
"Tonight in Konya, the friendly match between Konyaspor and the Palestine national football team was an exceptional example of the brotherhood, solidarity and unity of hearts between our countries," Erdogan stated in a message shared on the X platform.
The Turkish leader conveyed his "most heartfelt greetings and affection" to the visiting Palestinian squad members who travelled to Türkiye for the encounter, as well as to the wider Palestinian population enduring ongoing conflict.
Erdogan thanked local supporters in Konya who packed the 42,000-capacity stadium to welcome the Palestinian national squad and openly show collective backing for the Palestinian cause.
Tributes to Palestinian children
The president noted that the fixture served as an urgent reminder to the international community regarding the ongoing "tragedy and genocide" unfolding in Palestine and Gaza.
"As Türkiye, we will continue to stand united and in solidarity with our Palestinian and Gazan brothers and sisters, defend their rights on the international stage, and demonstrate our solidarity with them in the strongest possible way," Erdogan added.
The fixture took place on Wednesday evening as the centrepiece of dedicated "Palestine Day" commemorations in Konya, featuring emotional tributes and ceremonies designed to draw global attention to the thousands of children who have lost their lives in Palestine.
On the pitch, the match delivered competitive drama.
Konyaspor opened the scoring inside two minutes courtesy of Melih Ibrahimoglu, before the Palestine national team responded with two clinical goals from Mohammed Sandouqa in the 12th and 25th minutes to seize a 2–1 advantage.
Konyaspor striker Mostafa Mohamed found an equaliser in the 28th minute to level the scoreline before the break.
Despite persistent attacking opportunities created by both sides throughout an energetic second half, neither team could break the deadlock, concluding the historic friendly in a 2–2 draw.

Exclusives
Intelligence and technology
Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest. Chains of Russian drones keep crossing near the Belarus border, Ukraine's Air Force says.
Ukrainian combat simulator, used to train more than 500,000 troops, can now be ordered from NATO’s supply catalogs by single code. Each trainer assigned a 13-digit NATO Stock Number.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges. Russia opens a massed assault on the grid.
Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach. A Ukrainian robot drives to the front, then swims.
Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module. The Mangal launcher carries two cameras, picks out drones on its own, and mounts on a vehicle or a fixed post.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters. Ukraine can jam Russian drones into drifting off course—a satellite relay overhead would let them fly straight through the jamming and strike.
International
EU wants reforms before more money. Kyiv wants Europe to touch Russia’s frozen billions. The push comes as Ukraine seeks access to €210 billion in immobilized Russian central-bank assets to help cover its needs.
Humanitarian and social impact
Ukraine brings 14 more children home from Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast. One of them was being forced onto Russia’s military rolls. This year's returns from the occupied south now reach 204.
Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram bomb while children in grades 1–4 were studying there. The bomb hit as about 40 children sheltered inside, one of many Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities and villages over the past 24 hours.
Kyiv’s supermarkets are the new front line as Russia hunts civilian life before winter. Officials say the Kremlin is blending drone strikes, sabotage, and bot-farm propaganda to break the capital before the cold arrives.
Russian troops seize drone-dropped food in occupied Oleshky, accusing recipients of cooperating with Ukraine. Some people go missing, a local official says. One family in Oleshky was taken "to the basement" and has since disappeared without a trace, an Oleshky official says.

Pete Hegseth confirms cutting 20% of US military generals and admirals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:20:58 UTC
06:20:58 KST

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military.
Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates.
The defense secretary pointed to those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. About “80% of the force” onboard was retained, he said.
Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration.
“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”
He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”
Generals “who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”, Hegseth said.
Eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, it emerged last week.
Hegseth appeared to reference the carrier while attacking the media on Wednesday, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.
The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid Trump’s war on Iran.
During his speech in Quantico, Virginia, the defense secretary announced several new initiatives, including a a new Pentagon project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with the department to study the “future of warfare”.
The Guardian previously reported on how Luckey’s company, Anduril Inudstries, a major defense technology company, has received billions in government contracts over the last year.
Hegseth also took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges during his speech – which Trump has targeted routinely since he returned to office. The defense secretary branded the institutions as “DEI-worshipping woke factories”. Notably, Hegseth is a graduate of Harvard and Princeton Universities – both members of the Ivy League.
Hegseth said the Pentagon would now partner with other institutions as part of its educational pipeline. Some of these schools, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College, are known for conservative values.
Others joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.

Lithuania Moves to Ban Russian, Belarusian Artists Who Performed in Occupied Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:18:48 UTC
06:18:48 KST

Lithuania’s government has approved a proposal to bar Russian and Belarusian artists and other cultural figures from performing in the country if they had previously worked in occupied or annexed Ukrainian territories.
The government backed the measure on Wednesday, Sept. 30, Lithuanian media LRT reported. The ban would also cover anyone who has directly or indirectly supported Russia’s war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Exemptions would apply to those who have “clearly acted against aggression, occupation or annexation, publicly demonstrated their opposition to these actions and whose activities objectively did not contribute to the implementation of the interests of the occupying authorities,” according to the proposal.
Awaiting parliament’s approval
The amendment must still pass Lithuania’s parliament, the Seimas. If approved, it would take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. The government has not yet set out the specific criteria for determining who would fall under the ban.
Until now, Lithuania has handled such cases individually, barring several performers who support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime and have performed in Russia or in occupied Crimea from entering the country.
Around the same time on Wednesday, the Lithuanian government also backed a separate measure to ban Russian and Belarusian nationals from owning property near strategic sites.
The restrictions, however, would not apply to ownership acquired through inheritance.
Russian Attacks on Kyiv Continue Into Thursday as Drone Crashes Near Playground and Fires Erupt
The move follows similar steps by both Finland and Latvia, who had already restricted property purchases by Russian and Belarusian citizens, exempting those who hold residence permits.
Meanwhile, Estonia is working on comparable legislation.
Possible risks for anti-war artists
Under the proposal put forward by Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry, artists and cultural figures would be required to sign a publicly available declaration condemning Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and supporting its territorial integrity.
Those who refuse would be barred from working in Lithuania completely.
However, signing such a declaration poses significant risks for Russian citizens. Since the full-scale invasion, Russia has prosecuted numerous civilians for anti-war statements and has also moved against Yabloko – its only registered liberal party – whose ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in August along with an 11-year prison sentence for its deputy chairman.
In July, Turkey deported a 24-year-old anti-war activist Ariadna Litvinova to Russia, where she faces up to seven years in prison for writing slogans such as “Peace to Ukraine” on banners at a pro-war exhibition in St. Petersburg.
Rights advocates said the case was part of a wider pattern of transnational repression targeting Russian anti-war exiles.
Moscow courts have also ordered the arrest in absentia of anti-war pop singer Monetochka, who now lives and performs in Europe, and sentenced novelist Boris Akunin to 14 years in prison in absentia after he voiced support for Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported.
Such sentences would take effect if the exiled artist returned to Russia or were extradited.
Rising tensions with Moscow
The measures come amid heightened tensions between NATO members, particularly the Baltic states, and Moscow.
On Sept. 11, Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Lithuania would “disappear from the map of the world” if it lifted its long-standing ban on nuclear weapons.
Russia’s embassy in Belgium warned on Sept. 28 that Moscow was ready to use its entire arsenal if NATO countries tried to isolate Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave bordering Lithuania.
NATO dismissed the warning, condemning Russia’s irresponsible nuclear rhetoric while reiterating that it is a defensive alliance. Vilnius rejected the threat by framing the warnings as a form of psychological pressure.
The warning came days after Putin claimed on Sept. 25 that the rights of Russian speakers were being violated in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, while insisting that Russia had no plans for military action against Europe.
The Kremlin used similar unfounded claims to justify its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:18:19 UTC
06:18:19 KST

Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so-called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.
A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.
The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.
Unlike Musk’s role at Doge – which drew heavy public criticism and costly boycotts of his products – the scope and goals of Project Meridian appear as if they will be much less time-consuming for the tech mogul. The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release.
“We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.”
Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare. Both have extensive defense department contracts through their companies, with Anduril’s business centered on the government purchasing products that it advertises as the latest advance in warfare.
Gingrich was appointed as a member of the defense policy board in December 2020 during the first Trump administration but was dismissed less than three months later after Joe Biden became president. Going back to the 1990s, he has been warning about the threat of an electromagnetic pulse attack that could knock out US power grids.

Trump demands Powell resign from Fed board over headquarters renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:17:01 UTC
06:17:01 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday demanded that Jerome Powell immediately resign from the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors over cost overruns in the central bank's headquarters renovation.
Trump said he had asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to review an inspector general's report on the project.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump cited findings of deficiencies in the management of the Washington, DC, renovation project and accused Powell of failing to control its costs.
"This is Jerome Powell's fault, and he should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!" Trump wrote.
He said he had instructed Blanche to study the report and determine what action to take over a project that, according to his post, would cost at least $2.5 billion.
Trump threatened legal action if Powell refused to step down, saying the US government should sue him "for either corruption or incompetence."
The inspector general's review, however, found no grounds for a criminal referral and no administrative misconduct, while identifying significant shortcomings in the Fed's oversight of the renovation.
Powell remains a Fed governor after his term as chair ended in May.
Trump highlighted passages stating that the Fed board did not obtain a project cost estimate from its construction manager until January 2026, three-and-a-half years after construction began and after more than $2 billion in construction costs had been awarded.
According to the passages quoted in his post, the board had also failed to establish a guaranteed maximum price by July 2026, leaving it without cost certainty and without transferring material risk to the construction manager.
Trump predicted that the final bill could reach $3.5 billion or $4 billion and claimed he could have completed the renovation for $25 million while preserving the buildings’ historic appearance. 
Dispute over interest rates
The renovation has become a focal point of Trump's broader dispute with Powell over interest rates and the central bank's independence.
In January, Powell disclosed that the Justice Department had served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas threatening a criminal indictment related to his June 2025 Senate testimony about the renovation.
Powell said the threat stemmed from the Fed setting interest rates according to its assessment of economic conditions rather than the president's preferences.
He described the renovation and his congressional testimony as pretexts for the pressure.
In April, Powell said the Justice Department had provided assurances that it would not reopen the investigation without a criminal referral from the Fed's inspector general. 
Renovation of 2 historic buildings
The project covers the Marriner S. Eccles Building, the Fed board's headquarters, and the neighboring 1951 Constitution Avenue Building.
The Fed has listed the board-approved renovation budget at $2.46 billion.
It said the work aims to modernize building systems, remove asbestos and lead contamination, improve safety and accommodate modern workplace technology.
Construction costs alone rose from an estimated $921 million in February 2020 to $2.018 billion by December 2024, according to the watchdog's findings.
The Fed has attributed overruns to inflation, unexpected remediation expenses and additional requirements from agencies reviewing the project.

Keogh defends record as minister following backdown on veterans' allied health cap
Matt Keogh says he looks forward to staying on as veterans' affairs minister despite backing down on the veterans' allied health care cap.
The federal government bowed to pressure last month and scrapped a budget plan to cap allied health services for veterans at $5,000 a year.
The proposal was criticised by veteran advocacy groups and the Coalition, who said it would create barriers for ex-servicemen and women.
But Keogh defended his record as veterans minister and says he still thinks he can work collaboratively with the sector.
"I've been so proud and humbled to be the Veterans' Affairs minister under the Albanese Labor government," Keogh says.
"There's still more to do and I look forward to delivering on those better outcomes."
Labor MP 'shocked' over Shoebridge's comments on Jewish community
Labor MP Josh Burns has accused the new Greens leader of "prejudice" over comments he made about his relationship with the Jewish community.
Soon after being elected as leader yesterday, David Shoebridge was asked how he would repair the party's relationship with the Jewish community.
The Greens leader said he has strong connections with Jewish Australians who are "fighting genocide", referring to the crisis in Gaza.
"I'd ask those in the media who are covering this issue to actually listen to these powerful, principled voices coming from the progressive Jewish Australian community," he said.
Today, Burns says Shoebridge's answer to the question was "shocking" and that people shouldn't be placed into categories based on their views.
"Senator Shoebridge's answer yesterday when asked about his thoughts and his message to the Jewish community upon taking the leadership, I thought was pretty shocking," Burns says.
"Senator Shoebridge decided to give an answer that said that he has relationships with some members of the Jewish community who agree with him on their perspective of the Middle East.
"That is not progressive leadership, that's prejudice and I would say to Senator Shoebridge that he should reflect on his answer. He is now in a leadership position and having public statements like that actually will send chills up the spines of many people in the Jewish community."
Taylor commends NSW premier for swipe at federal Labor's spending
The opposition leader has praised NSW Premier Chris Minns for calling on governments to moderate their spending.
Yesterday, Minns said he had "long" heard advice from the Reserve Bank to rein in spending and, when asked, declined to support the federal government's fiscal approach.
Angus Taylor has commended the NSW premier for pointing out Labor's "failures" on government spending.
"Well done to Chris Minns to call out the federal Labor government on their failures when it comes to government spending because he knows and we know," Taylor says.
"This is not how money should be spent during a cost-of-living crisis. And good on Chris Minns for calling that out."
Taylor backs Bell Bay bailout 'only because it is necessary now'
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says the government's bailout of the Bell Bay aluminium smelter is a result of Labor's energy policy.
But he has initially skirted around questions about whether the Coalition supports the $200 million joint Commonwealth and Tasmanian government investment.
Taylor says the cost of producing aluminium is driven mostly by the cost of electricity, which he says has been driven up by Labor's net-zero policy.
"We need a government prepared to scrap net zero and scrap all the embedded carbon taxes they've put into our energy system. That is what we will do," Taylor says.
"We'd prefer that it was not necessary to have to do this. That's the whole point. The government keeps putting bandaids on bullet wounds, and sometimes you have to do that."
But pressed again on whether he backs the bailout, Taylor says he does support it but "only because it's necessary now".
TIME names Anika Wells a 'rising star'
Communications Minister Anika Wells is one of the "world's most influential rising stars", according to TIME magazine.
Wells, who spearheaded Australia's under-16 social media ban and is now targeting Big Tech's algorithms, made the TIME100 NEXT annual list.
In a blurb penned by former Labor prime minister Julia Gillard, Wells was described as "one of the most significant voices in a growing global movement to reframe the relationship between technology and the well-being of our children".
“Even in the face of intense opposition from some of the world's largest tech companies, she remains steadfast," Gillard wrote.
"Future generations will look back on her landmark changes as courageous and trail-blazing."
Wells wasn't the only Aussie to make the list — Bridgerton star Yerin Ha and musician Troye Sivan made the cut, with pop icon Kylie Minogue saying of the latter:
"We so would’ve been friends in school."
"Troye doesn't just make pop music to love. He makes pop music to believe in."
Analysis: David Shoebridge wants to woo the same angry voters as One Nation — but from the left
The elevation of NSW Senator David Shoebridge to the Greens' top job is the clearest indication that the party is prepared to swing further to the populist left and fight harder to demolish Labor, especially in its inner-city heartland.
He wasn't the only contender to lead the party — Sarah Hanson-Young and Mehreen Faruqi also put their hands up for the top job.
Faruqi is reportedly divisive inside the party and Hanson-Young, despite being the longest-serving Greens senator, is seen as too moderate, according to sources.
Greens leadership talks are usually done under a cloak of secrecy, driven by consensus. But yesterday's contest broke convention.
