ACCI says small business will carry burden for end of credit, debit card surcharges
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) says the end of credit and debit card surcharges will create a significant burden for millions of small businesses.
As of today, Australian businesses are banned from charging customers credit, debit and prepaid card surcharges.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has welcomed the change, saying the "annoying" charges would ease pressure on people in a tough economic environment.
But ACCI chief Andrew Mackellar says it could cause some businesses to reprice their services to meet the provider payments.
"These surcharges are not going away. Somebody still has to pay this. The payment service providers, the credit card issuers, they're not working for free. They're continuing to charge the same fees through whatever means they can to their business customers," Mackellar says.
"It's just now much more difficult for those small businesses to work out how they wear that expense."
Analysis: Chalmers promised action on inflation and productivity. The scorecard on both is grim
On the morning after last year's landslide Labor election win, Jim Chalmers declared a shift in priorities for the government's second term.
"The first term was primarily inflation without forgetting productivity," the treasurer told Insiders. "The second term will be primarily productivity without forgetting inflation."
At the midway point of this term, the scorecard on both is grim.
As Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock put it this week: "Inflation is too high and has been driven by domestic capacity pressures."
As for productivity, Bullock was even more blunt: "Productivity is doing nothing."
Read the full analysis from ABC political lead David Speers in the link below.
Master Builders Association projects Housing Accord to fall short of home build goal
The Master Builders Association says construction forecasts have deteriorated following May's federal budget.
The industry body says 62,000 fewer home constructions have started in Australia compared with forecasts six months ago.
It expects Australia to build 262,000 fewer homes under the National Housing Accord, which aims to build 1.2 million homes by 2030.
Chief executive Denita Wawn says that while the Middle East war is having an impact on project feasibility, Labor's budget tax changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing are not incentivising people to spend.
She's called for the government to reverse its tax changes.
"We are saying to the government fix the economy, ensure that inflation is kept in check. Make sure that we have a stable economy so people can feel confident in investing large amounts of money into the building and construction industry," Wawn says.
Government taking NDIS concerns 'seriously', Chalmers says
Phase one of Thriving Kids, the new NDIS alternative for children under nine with developmental delay or autism who have "low to moderate" support needs, begins today with the launch of a phone line and online resource hub for families.
More intensive supports such as group therapies and playgroups will be rolled out by states and territories over the next 15 months.
The changes are happening alongside cuts to the NDIS passed by the parliament in August, which are expected to remove 240,000 participants over the next four years, saving about $38 billion.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged this morning that, while families still have many questions and concerns, the government believes it will be able to "take care of" those who need disability support while also making sure the NDIS is financially sustainable.
"When you are changing programs like this there is a level of concern and there is a level of anxiety. We take that seriously," he told reporters in Brisbane.
"But we're confident that we will come up with the best combination of services and care and support for some of our most vulnerable people."
You can read more about Thriving Kids and what's changing when in the link below.
Chalmers says GST overhaul comments are a 'distraction'
The federal treasurer has taken a swipe at his Queensland counterpart, David Janetzki, after the state treasurer called for a GST overhaul in a speech at the National Press Club yesterday.
In that speech, Janetzkisaid the current GST distribution is unfair and the current carve-up, which benefits Western Australia, "threatens the fiscal stability of the federation".
"I think David Janetzki's looking for a distraction from the fact he just lost Queensland's triple A credit rating," Jim Chalmers said.
"I do try and say this as respectfully as I can because I know that every state treasurer is dealing with the sorts of pressures that we are dealing with at the Commonwealth level. I would rather work collaboratively and cooperatively with him and with others, but I think everyone knows what he's doing here."
In an interim report earlier this year, the Productivity Commission called WA's GST arrangement a "costly mistake", but the prime minister ruled out any changes to the deal.
Falling house prices due to a 'number of factors', Treasurer says
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is being asked about the government's housing tax changes amid falling house prices.
ICYMI, house prices fell for a sixth straight month in September, bringing cumulative declines to 5.2 per cent below March's peak.
Experts say house prices could drop about 15 per cent in the coming months amid rising inflation and interest rate hikes.
Chalmers has been asked if the government's reforms are working as intended.
He said house prices were at a similar level to November last year — suggesting prices had flattened — and added that multiple factors contributed to lower prices, including interest rates and broader economic conditions.
The changes in the budget are designed to make it more afforable for first home buyers, he said, adding that extraordinary price growth over the past 20 decades had locked young people out of the market.
"Housing is the defining intergenerational challenge," he said. "Prices started to come off before the budget, and that's because there are a number of factors at play."
Treasurer asked about Minns's comments on government spending
Treasurer Jim Chlamers has been asked about comments from NSW Premier Chris Minns yesterday about government spending.
Minns, a Labor premier, yesterday said his own government had been "careful with public money", and he declined to defend Chalmers when asked about the accusation that federal spending was contributing to rising inflation and interest rates.
Chalmers appeared to suggest Minns was speaking in general terms about all governments.
"The premier of NSW made the same sorts of points that we have been making, which is that there is an onus on all governments at all levels to manage their budgets in the most responsible way that they can," Chalmers said.
"As I understand it, he was referring to demand in the economy."
He said public demand growth had "slowed considerably".
"And so Chris, as I understand it, was talking about demand, talking about the role that every government has to make sure they're managing the budget in the most responsible way they can, and that's what we're doing. "
Treasurer hails ban on 'annoying' surcharges
Jim Chalmers is spruiking the end of "pesky" credit and debit card surcharges incurred when consumers tap to pay.
He said the move would ease pressure on people in a tough economic environment, adding that surcharges cost $1.6 billion a year.
"What you see on the menu is what you pay when you tap your card," he said.
"This is about easing the cost of living … this is about the end of those annoying, pesky surcharges that everyone has paid in one way or another."
Chalmers said the Reserve Bank of Australia would implement the change, while the small business ombudsman would help small businesses adapt.
"We'll make sure that everybody's doing the right thing. The ACCC's got an important role to play in that regard," he said.
But he said if small businesses raise prices in response, they'll need to justify it and put it on the menu.
Treasurer announces $134m investment in crisis housing
The government will invest $134 million in crisis transition housing for families experiencing domestic and family violence, and for young people at risk of homelessness, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said today.
Speaking at a press conference earlier while the PM was speaking, Chalmers said there had been some difficult reminders recently about the "horrific impact" of domestic and family violence in the community.
He said that issue was tightly linked to housing and homelessness.
He says the scheme will give people a "safe and secure place to rebuild their lives".
He said the funding would build more than 200 homes across Queensland, and was expected to help 20,000 families and 5,000 young people at risk of homelessness over the next 20 years.
PM sidesteps question on union plan to levy AI companies
Unions and researchers are pushing for tech giants that want to build data centres in Australia to be slugged with a levy to help fund a local artificial intelligence (AI) industry.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has sidestepped the question and says the government is engaging constructively with AI companies, including internationally based ones.
"AI does have risks, but it also has potentially enormous benefits for humankind to lift the quality of life, to boost productivity of businesses, including ones here," the PM says.
And that's the end of the PM's press conference from Tasmania.
Albanese says rising fuel prices have wider inflationary impact
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says rising fuel prices due to the war in the Middle East have a flow-on effect on other goods and services.
Headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent in August, from 3.5 per cent in July, driven by higher housing costs and automotive fuel prices.
The Reserve Bank of Australia on Tuesday raised interest rates for the fourth time this year to 4.6 per cent.
"It has an inflationary impact … right around the world, which is why we continue to call for a de-escalation," Albanese says.
Albanese says it's 'concerning' new Greens leader has attacked Labor
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has congratulated new Greens leader David Shoebridge for his election to the party's leadership.
Following his election, Shoebridge says he wants the Greens to replace Labor and doesn't want to help the government improve.
The PM says it was "somewhat concerning" that Shoebridge used the opportunity to criticised Labor amid the rise in One Nation.
"Sounded a lot like some of the people who didn't win their seats at the House of Representatives election last May," the PM said, referring to the three Greens MPs who lost their seats at the last election.

DOHA, September 30. /TASS/. Flydubai has temporarily suspended flights to and from Israel pending the completion of an investigation into an incident aboard a plane bound for Tel Aviv, an airline spokesperson told TASS.
"Following the incident involving flight FZ 1073 on September 30, and in coordination with the relevant authorities, Flydubai flights to and from Israel will be suspended while the investigation continues," the spokesperson said. The airline emphasized that "this temporary suspension will allow the relevant authorities to continue their work and establish all the facts surrounding the incident."
The spokesperson added that Flydubai is "fully committed to supporting the ongoing investigation and maintaining the highest safety standards" across all its routes. "We remain in close coordination with government authorities, regulators and airport stakeholders and will review the suspension as more information becomes available," the airline said. Flydubai also apologized to passengers whose travel plans had been affected, saying it is "working to provide support and alternative arrangements where possible."

Gas pipeline explodes in Syria, knocks three power plants offline

Gunmen kill 7 on bus in Syria as pipeline blast knocks out 3 power plants
Gunmen attack bus in Homs province hours after a pipeline explosion knocked out three power plants near Damascus.
Gunmen have opened fire on a bus in western Syria, killing at least seven people, according to state media, hours after an explosion and fire at a gas pipeline near Damascus forced three power plants offline.
The Sana news agency said “unknown assailants” attacked the bus on Wednesday as it crossed the Masyaf bridge in Homs, killing and wounding a number of people. It said security forces have opened an investigation and published photographs of officers examining a small bus.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3‘Opening a new chapter’: Syria reopens embassy in Libya after talks
- list 3 of 3Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery
Brigadier General Bassem Muhammad Shaaban, the Homs internal security chief, said the vehicle was a civilian bus carrying employees of a company home from work.
He offered his “deepest condolences” to the victims’ families and promised accountability.
“We view this cowardly attack as an attempt to undermine the security and stability of the province of Homs,” he was quoted as saying. “This crime will not go unpunished. Internal security will continue to pursue the perpetrators until they are arrested and brought before the judiciary to receive their due punishment.”
The violence underscored the security challenges facing Syria’s authorities since the fall of President Bashar al-Assad’s government at the end of 2024. Damascus and its outskirts have been hit by a number of attacks during that time.
Shortly before the bus shooting, state media reported an explosion at a gas pipeline in eastern Ghouta, near Damascus, close to one of the country’s main power plants. The blast came two days after another pipeline was sabotaged in eastern Syria.
The Syrian Electricity Company said the Deir Ali, al-Nasiriyah and Tishreen power plants were out of service because of inadequate gas supplies following the explosion. A fire also broke out at the Tishreen power plant after the explosion.
Mohammed al-Bashir, the energy minister, said at the site late on Wednesday that the fire was now under control and that civil defence crews were conducting cooling operations.
“The cause of the Tishreen power station explosion is still unclear,” he told state media. “It could be a technical malfunction, an attack or an act of sabotage. Specialised teams will inspect the site after cooling to determine the exact cause.”
Al-Bashir said the Tishreen power plant would need repairs and maintenance once the damage was assessed. Gas pressure would be raised gradually to restart the Deir Ali plant after work at Tishreen was completed, he said.
The Syrian Electricity Company meanwhile warned that the shutdown of the three power plants would increase power rationing hours due to dwindling electricity supplies.
Wednesday’s blast was the third to hit Syria’s gas network in six weeks. The Syrian Petroleum Company said the two earlier incidents were sabotage.
No one has claimed responsibility for any of the explosions.
Syrians have complained about rising energy costs in recent months, with protests breaking out across the country two weeks ago after the government increased diesel prices by as much as 40 percent and petrol prices by 28 percent.
It said the increases were temporary and caused by a sharp rise in global energy costs.

The White House Is Starting to Panic Over the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

President Donald Trump has told aides that he thinks Republicans could still outperform expectations in the midterm elections this November, seemingly unwilling to confront the worsening political climate for the GOP.
But aides acknowledge privately that the national polling for Trump is shockingly bad, and the White House, in recent weeks, has begun to contemplate for the first time losing both the House and Senate majorities.
One longtime Trumpworld operative, who correctly predicted weeks before the 2024 presidential election that Trump was on course to win every battleground state, summed it up for Inner Loop: “Oh, yeah, we're going to get creamed.”
Trump's approval rating recently dropped to 37 percent in a Wall Street Journal poll, the lowest of any president heading into a midterm election dating back to 1990, when these polls first began. Trump’s more positive outlook has been informed in part by internal polling that shows Republicans down by less in individual House races, the sources say.
“No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle tells WIRED. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
To counter the deeply negative political environment for Republicans this cycle, Trump's team started looking for foreign policy wins last month that he would be able to tout to voters in order to encourage turnout from his MAGA base, sources say.
That led Trump to quickly sign an agreement between the US and Denmark that allows more American forces on Greenland, even though it stopped short of a US takeover that the president has long desired.
Trump also proclaimed an oil deal with Venezuela. However, that deal is likely to need renegotiating because it asserts a 100-year concession on oil production that contravenes Venezuela's national hydrocarbons law barring such practices.
But while Trump sees foreign policy as a legacy-defining issue, voters have been far more focused on domestic issues like high grocery and gas prices.
Diesel prices hit a record high this month and regular gasoline reached a national average of $4.43 a gallon, according to the AAA, while Trump has been on the opposite side of public opinion on tech issues like AI regulation and data centers.
Now, with their election chances that much slimmer, Trumpworld is much more concerned about planning a response to what will likely be an immediate crush of subpoenas from Democrats in Congress, the sources say.
Broadly speaking, the White House expects a dual track of Trump asserting executive privilege and attorney-client protections, the bedrock legal principle designed to protect confidential discussions with lawyers, to shield senior aides from oversight probes.
Attorney-client privilege is set to be supercharged when it involves government lawyers, after the US Supreme Court ruled in the so-called Trump immunity decision in 2024 that not even federal courts could “peel back the curtain” to examine discussions that involve deliberations central to the presidency.
One unique aspect of Trump's second term has been the conversion of his personal lawyers into government lawyers, producing a consistent network of overlapping legal protections around himself and his top aides.
Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche, for example, has become the attorney general. Many of Trump's aides were previously represented by the current number three at DOJ, Stanley Woodward, who also was a Trump 2024 campaign lawyer. Trump's former appellate lawyer, Will Scharf, recently moved from White House staff secretary to White House counsel, replacing former Trump lawyer David Warrington.
Trump's aides are hoping that the double protections will stymie Democrats for years. And they have some precedent: Trump's White House counsel from his first term, Don McGahn, only testified to Congress about the Mueller investigation after Trump had already left office.
After November 3, the midterms will end in the minds of most Americans. But for Trump’s White House, it’s all just beginning.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Stefanchuk discusses return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia with Costa Rican parliament speaker
According to Ukrinform, Stefanchuk announced this on Facebook.
“The first meeting between the speakers of the parliaments of Ukraine and Costa Rica is a good start for much closer interparliamentary cooperation,” Stefanchuk noted.
He thanked Costa Rica for its consistent support of Ukraine.
“We specifically discussed the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken by Russia. Costa Rica was the first Latin American country to join the relevant international coalition, and I particularly appreciate the President’s willingness to personally devote attention to this issue,” Stefanchuk emphasized.
In addition, Stefanchuk and Jiménez discussed increasing sanctions pressure on Russia, the possibility of Costa Rica joining the Shelter Coalition, and participation in the Fifth Parliamentary Summit of the Crimea Platform.
“We agreed to continue the dialogue and strengthen cooperation between our parliaments. I invited Yara Jiménez to visit Ukraine—such a visit would be another important step in the development of our bilateral relations,” Stefanchuk noted.
He expressed gratitude for the candid conversation, solidarity with Ukraine, and the willingness to work together to secure the return of Ukrainian children and achieve a just peace.
As reported by Ukrinform, Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk and European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos discussed further financial support for Ukraine and the adoption of the necessary decisions to that end.

Australia strikes back to avoid ODI whitewash ahead of Test series
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:56:57 UTC
05:56:57 KST

Australia avoided a whitewash in their ODI series in South Africa, with Pat Cummins's encouraging comeback and the return to form of Adam Zampa and Alex Carey inspiring them to a rain-interrupted win in Potchefstroom.
The final day-nighter was eventually called off under the lights on Wednesday as rain ruined the finale, but Australia could still celebrate a satisfying 45-run (DLS method) victory on a day when they were vastly improved after their capitulation in chases in the first two matches.
Half-centuries from the rejuvenated Carey (74 off 88 balls) and captain Mitch Marsh (56 off 42 balls), plus 48 from Ollie Peake, helped propel Australia to 9-322 after they had been put in, with South Africa at no point then threatening to pull off the highest successful ODI chase ever at the ground.
By the time the rain, which had also delayed the start by half an hour, returned to quite spoil the fun, Australia were already in full control.
Zampa (2-34 off six overs) rediscovered his best after recent struggles and Xavier Bartlett earned a couple of key early wickets (2-25 off five) as only Ryan Rickelton (71no off 81 balls) looked likely to trouble the visitors with South Africa limping to 4-145 off 28 overs.
Cummins may have returned as bowler only, not as the captain, with Marsh keeping the job for the third and final match, but his return seemed to enthuse everyone, with his 0-17 off five probing overs suggesting he'll be in fine shape to lead his troops in the first Test in Durban on October 9.
Stand-in Marsh again did his bit, leading from the front, as he powered to his third half-century of the series following his 60 and 84 in Durban and Johannesburg.
He and Travis Head (24 off 20) again provided an electric start with a 78 stand at nine runs an over, and this time the middle-order built much more assiduously against a Proteas side who weren't helped by resting key spinner, player-of-the-series Keshav Maharaj, and captain Temba Bavuma among four changes.
Cameron Green had an eventful time, taking a fearful beamer from Bosch straight into his box, but recovering to hit the next delivery, also a fast full-toss, courageously for six, only to then be bumped out next ball by a short one, seemingly suffering a muscle injury in the process.
Zampa was back to his squeezing, probing best, luring the dangerous first-match centurion Matthew Breetzke to be stumped on 25 and trapping Tristan Stubbs lbw for 14.

Cristiano Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after coach says he will not start against Denmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:56:15 UTC
05:56:15 KST

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Cristiano Ronaldo left Portugal’s national team camp Wednesday, hours after head coach Jorge Jesus said the veteran forward would not start the UEFA Nations League match Thursday against Denmark.
Ronaldo confirmed his departure in a social media statement after speaking with Portuguese Football Federation President Pedro Proenca.
“Following the national team coach’s press conference, and after having a conversation with the Portuguese Football Federation president, I decided to leave the national team’s training camp,” said the 41-year-old.
“In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated,” he added, wishing his teammates luck.
Jesus said Ronaldo would again start on the bench against Denmark, with Goncalo Ramos expected to lead the attack.
“If I need him, he’ll come on. If I don’t need him, he won’t,” said Jesus, denying there was a rift between the pair.
Ronaldo was an unused substitute in Portugal’s 2-1 Nations League victory Sunday against Norway, the first competitive international in more than 18 years in which he was available but did not play.
He subsequently missed team training sessions and did not join Wednesday’s session in Copenhagen despite arriving at the stadium with the squad.
Jesus acknowledged Ronaldo had been disappointed after warming up but remaining on the bench against Norway, while insisting selection decisions were his responsibility.
Ronaldo is Portugal’s record appearance holder and goal scorer, with 146 goals in 234 internationals.

MOSCOW, September 30. /TASS/. European countries’ production of weapons for Ukraine only delays prospects for a settlement to the conflict, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a briefing.
"European countries are directly involved in the Ukrainian conflict. They are not simply providing assistance. By opening weapons production plants and forming joint ventures with Ukraine’s defense industry, they are fully involved," the diplomat said, commenting on statements about Patriot production in Poland.
According to Zakharova, "this only delays a settlement to the conflict rather than bringing it closer, as some forces in Europe think or claim."
Earlier, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said that Warsaw had proposed Washington establish joint production with Ukraine of missiles for Patriot air defense systems in a "safe location."

Hurricane Rachel strengthens to Category 1 off Mexico's Pacific coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:54:59 UTC
05:54:59 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
 Hurricane Rachel strengthened to Category 1 early Wednesday off Mexico's Pacific coast, according to the National Civil Protection Coordination.
“Rachel evolved into a Category 1 hurricane at 00:00,” the agency said in a post on the US social media platform X, as the storm continued moving offshore.
Rachel was located 365 kilometers (227 miles) south-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, a coastal area in the western state of Jalisco, and 495 kilometers west of Lazaro Cardenas, a port city on the Pacific coast of southwestern Michoacan.
The hurricane was moving northwest at 19 kilometers per hour (12 miles per hour), with maximum sustained winds of 120 kilometers per hour and gusts reaching 150 kph, said the agency.
The system was expected to maintain a northwestward trajectory and gradually move farther from the Pacific coast, according to the National Civil Protection Coordination.
Authorities were monitoring the storm as it moved parallel to the country's Pacific coastline, with its projected path expected to keep it offshore.
The National Civil Protection Coordination urged authorities and residents to remain attentive to updates on Rachel's development and movement.
The storm's strengthening comes during Mexico's Pacific hurricane season, which runs from May through November and regularly brings tropical storms and hurricanes to the western coastline.
Authorities have continued to monitor Rachel's location, intensity and projected trajectory to assess any potential effects on coastal areas.
Based on its current trajectory, Rachel was not expected to make landfall in Mexico, according to information released by the National Civil Protection Coordination.
The agency advised residents in potentially affected areas to follow weather updates, as the conditions and trajectory of tropical systems can change as they develop.
Rachel's development will continue to be monitored as the hurricane moves northwest over the Pacific, with authorities expected to issue updates on its strength and trajectory.

Global steel forum agrees joint action to tackle rising excess capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:51:46 UTC
05:51:46 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Members of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity agreed Wednesday on a comprehensive framework for joint action to tackle rising excess capacity and its impact on steel producers and workers.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer chaired the ministerial meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where participants reached consensus on the "Milwaukee Framework," according to a statement from his office.
The framework outlines measures countries intend to implement under their national laws, reflecting domestic circumstances and international commitments.
These include reducing market-distorting subsidies, strengthening monitoring of steel imports and coordinating efforts to detect and address circumvention of trade restrictions.
Members also intend to pursue antidumping, countervailing duty and safeguard investigations where appropriate, alongside other trade measures targeting steel and steel-containing products from sources of global excess capacity.
The framework calls for greater transparency on where steel is first melted and poured to help identify suspicious trade patterns and prevent imports displaced from one member's market from entering through another.
Greer said US tariffs, trade agreements, tax policies and energy measures were supporting a revival in the American steel industry, urging partners to adopt similar policies.
"If like-minded partners adopt similar policies, they can hold accountable those countries that are contributing to the problem of global overcapacity in steel," he said.
Excess capacity projected to hit decade high
Despite increased national action and trade remedies, global steel excess capacity continues to rise, according to the ministerial statement.
It is projected to increase from 601 million tonnes in 2024 to 745 million tonnes by 2028, reaching its highest level in a decade and exceeding the forum members’ current combined production by 319 million tonnes.
Ministers warned that their steel industries could not compete on a level playing field without further collective intervention.
They tasked the forum with reviewing implementation of the framework and reporting progress at its next ministerial meeting.
Türkiye, the US, EU, UK, Japan, Canada, Brazil and other economies participated in the meeting.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined an invitation to appear at a Senate subcommittee hearing on Wednesday on the risks of rogue artificial intelligence, according to Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
Hawley, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subpanel that held the hearing, sent a letter to Altman on Sept. 25 requesting his presence to "help shed light on 
the Subcommittee's ongoing investigation into recent rogue AI incidents involving OpenAI models." NBC News first reported that Altman did not accept the invitation to testify.
"He turned us down," Hawley said of Altman at the hearing. "I think that's unfortunate because I think the American people deserve to know exactly what's going on at all of these companies. And to give us the sort of transparency that I think is needed for not just comfort, but to have an understanding of what these companies — that are the most powerful companies in the world — are doing right now with the most powerful technology ever known to man."
A spokesperson for OpenAI noted that Altman received the invitation to testify on Friday, just five days ahead of the hearing. Altman on Tuesday appeared at the company's annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco as other AI officials — including OpenAI President Greg Brockman — were in Washington meeting with President Donald Trump.
"OpenAI is deeply engaged with Congress on federal policies to advance AI safety, including through dozens of meetings in recent weeks with members of both parties in both chambers," the spokesperson said. "We look forward to continuing to work constructively and proactively with Senator Hawley and members of Congress on federal AI safety legislation that materially raises the safety bar."
Hawley's overture to Altman comes weeks after he opened an investigation into OpenAI earlier this month. Hawley sought information on a cyberattack involving hundreds of OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of another AI company called Hugging Face.
The cyber attack was one in a series of recent hacks involving frontier AI models that have raised alarms and prompted calls for Congress to act to rein in the rapidly evolving technology.
Hawley requested information from Altman on the cyber attack and on the existential risks of the technology and set an Oct. 1 deadline. A spokesperson for Hawley said OpenAI is expected to provide additional documents by the end of the week.
"The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue. This investigation will seek those answers," Hawley said in the Sept. 10 letter.

"Decisive victory over ISIS": Trump announces the end of the 12-year U.S. mission in Iraq
Kyiv • UNN
The United States has finally withdrawn its troops from Iraq as part of Operation "Inherent Resolve." American forces have remained in the region and continue their mission in Syria.
The United States has completed its mission in Iraq and fully withdrawn its troops as part of Operation "Inherent Resolve." U.S. President Donald Trump announced this on the Truth Social network, reports UNN.
Details
According to him, the end of the American presence is a "victory for the United States, a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over ISIS."
Unlike Afghanistan, where a great deal of military equipment and everything else was left behind, where 13 service members were killed and many others were seriously wounded, this organized withdrawal of coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marks the end of a very expensive journey to hell
At the same time, according to the U.S. Central Command, American troops remain in the region after leaving Iraq. The headquarters of the operation against ISIS was moved to Jordan, while U.S. forces continue their mission in Syria together with coalition partners.
Background
The United States invaded Iraq in 2003 to overthrow Saddam Hussein's regime. After that, American troops remained in the country, supported the new government, and waged a years-long fight against insurgents.
At the end of 2011, the United States withdrew its forces. However, less than three years later, American troops returned to Iraq, this time to support Iraqi forces in the fight against ISIS. The main combat operations against the group lasted from 2014 to 2017.
Over more than two decades of war in Iraq, the United States lost 4,500 Americans. This year, 18 American service members were killed in the war against Iran, seven of them in Iraq.

Russia’s Geran-5 Is Jet-Powered—Ukraine Built P1-SUN JetKiller to Hunt It
A Ukrainian-made P1-SUN JetKiller interceptor drone has destroyed a Russian jet-powered Geran-5 attack UAV, Ukrainian manufacturer SkyFall told Ukrinform on September 30.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the outlet, the Russian drone was intercepted by operators from Lasar’s Group, a unit of Ukraine’s National Guard specializing in unmanned systems.
“The target was destroyed by unmanned systems operators from Lasar’s Group of the National Guard of Ukraine,” SkyFall said.
During the interception, the crew also used a remote-control system that allows operators to control the interceptor from any location worldwide, Ukrinform reported.
According to Militarnyi, tthe interceptor can reach speeds of up to 370 kilometers per hour, has a range of up to 30 kilometers, operates at altitudes of up to nine kilometers, and can remain airborne for up to 15 minutes. It carries a 500-gram warhead.
The interceptor can be equipped with daytime or nighttime cameras, as well as an AI module for automatic target detection, tracking, and lock-on. Its guidance system can detect targets at distances of up to one kilometer.
The Geran-5, meanwhile, is a Russian strike UAV with a maximum takeoff weight of approximately 850 kilograms and a cruising speed of 450 to 600 kilometers per hour, making it considerably faster than the Geran-3. According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the drone can remain airborne for around two hours and has a range of up to 950 kilometers.
The interception comes as Ukraine expands the use of specialized drones against Russia’s jet-powered UAVs. On September 28, the Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation reported that Ukraine’s 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade had received new interceptor drones designed to pursue and destroy Geran-5s.
According to the foundation, the brigade’s “Yastrub” crew used one of the newly supplied interceptors to shoot down a Geran-5 over Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.

Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:49:52 UTC
05:49:52 KST

MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, Va.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide drive to field autonomous systems, as the Pentagon’s takes a bullish approach towards artificial intelligence and drone warfare. He also unveiled five other initiatives during what he promised will become an annual “State of the Force” address here Sept. 30.
Hegseth plans to launch the Autonomous Warfare Command within a year as a combatant command endowed with “service-like authorities, built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” he said. Its portfolio will include drones, artificial intelligence, and command and control systems.
Hegseth also announced the creation of a new program office, led by a two-star officer, to ensure military installations can generate their own power to isolate themselves from attacks on public grids. Bases in the homeland are increasingly seen as possibly contested environments where the U.S. military must be able to operate while under threat in a age of increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and so-called hybrid warfare activities by America’s adversaries.
And he confirmed plans to slash the total number of generals and admirals across the military by 20 percent, a move Air & Space Forces Magazine and other outlets had reported would be part of Hegseth’s speech.
Other initiatives include:
- A new group, dubbed “Project Meridian,” to study the future of warfare led by tech leaders Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, who were in attendance.
- An initiative, called the “Next Great American Base,” to build a new military installation to host 15,000-25,000 service members. Hegseth said governors and adjutant generals from every state will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch locations.
- The creation of five new corps of cadets at Hillsdale College, Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Mississippi State University, and Tuskegee University, which will all be given priority in officer commissioning.
- A new “Office of Religious Affairs” reporting directly to the Secretary of Defense to give chaplains better access to senior leadership.
Exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of senior officers and enlisted from commands across the globe to Quantico for an address outlining his vision for the U.S. military, he spoke this time to an audience of around 600 E-6 enlisted members and O-3 officers, who the Pentagon said were selected by their units for their performance and leadership potential.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force Gen. Dan Caine briefly addressed the crowd and introduced Hegseth.
Autonomy
The new Autonomous Warfare Command will drive the design, development, and fielding of autonomous and semi-autonomous capabilities and systems.
“The autonomous and robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades,” Hegseth said. “Civilian leaders can provide direction and urgency, but lasting change must be anchored in military command structures and operationalized by leaders across our joint force.”
The Pentagon is already leaning heavily into autonomy, and the new command is designed to significantly accelerate that effort. Lawmakers in the Senate had proposed the creation of such a combatant command during deliberations for the 2027 defense policy bill. The measure cleared the committee, but the bill is still pending. To be authorized, the House would also have to approve the measure.
It is not yet clear how the new four-star command will be structured, who will lead it, or how it will work with the autonomy efforts already underway within the different services. In a memo, Hegseth wrote the Pentagon plans to work with Congress to stand up the command by October 1, 2027, a year on from the announcement.
Hegseth said it will start with an interim step, dubbed “Project Agincourt,” named for the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Project Agincourt will draw from existing efforts like the Defense Innovation Unit and the Drone Dominance program, Hegseth said, and pair “operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units.”
Project Agincourt will be guided by DIU director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser, the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School. Creating Autonomous Warfare Command will take place “over the course of several months,” Hegseth said.
The Air Force and Navy are already developing Collaborative Combat Aircraft: semi-autonomous drones designed to work alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force is also pursuing a lower-cost intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drone with autonomous capabilities under its Massed Modular Aircraft program, and the Navy is working to field an unmanned tanker drone, the MQ-25.
The growth of autonomomy and the Penatagon’s future plans to harvest technology with its new command represent the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” Hegseth said.
“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he added, using an acronym for so-called super intelligence, President Donald Trump’s favored term for AI.
At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference earlier this month, Air Force leadership made it clear they see autonomous systems as central to the service’s future. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference that while true autonomous aircraft are a “few years off,” the service is leaning heavily into autonomy in its current future Force Design model.
“The FQ-42 and the FQ-44 [Collaborative Combat Aircraft] are autonomous fighters, and then we’re going to have perhaps other platforms that are autonomous, where you don’t actually need a crew to do a fighter mission,” Wilsbach said during a session with reporters. “You just send the aircraft off, and it does its mission because it’s automated.”
The Pentagon has deployed uncrewed surface vessels operationally in the Middle East for a few years for maritime surveillance. This summer, a U.S. Navy drone boat was even able to rescue two downed Army Apache pilots near the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Southern Command, which has been conducting strikes on boats suspected of smuggling drugs for over a year, recently established an autonomous warfare branch that will employ its own uncrewed vessels and aerial intelligence-gathering platforms. On the southern border, the U.S. military is now using 10 uncrewed surface vessels to patrol the Rio Grande River, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs M. Roosevelt Ditlevson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview.
“We’re moving into next-generation tools here that we’re going to employ to make sure that we hold these narcoterrorists at bay,” Ditlevson said, referring to drug smugglers. “I’m very excited about what is going to happen in the autonomy space and how we’re going to employ these different systems.”
But the Pentagon is automating more than aircraft, ships, and vehicles.
The Pentagon’s Maven Smart System has become a key tool for the U.S. military, a system aggregating sensors, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and command and control as part of the targeting process. Maven is used for operations ranging from targeting assistance in the Middle East to, more recently, counter-drone and anti-smuggling efforts on the southern border.
Ditlevson said AI, through Maven, will also feed into the Pentagon’s sweeping Golden Dome missile defense shield. “Maven Smart System is going to feed into the Golden Dome picture,” he said.
At the border, the Defense Department also uses autonomy software called Fortress, an adaptation of Anduril’s Lattice, which integrates data and sensors using AI. “All of our systems must be compatible with Maven Smart System,” Ditlevson said. “Everything that we have, that data needs to be integrated into Maven and into Lattice.”
To support all these new autonomous systems, Hegseth said, each military service will phase in new military occupational specialties for autonomy.
“We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters,” he said.
Fortress America
Hegseth also said the Pentagon is creating a new initiative called “Fortress America” to ensure military installations are able to generate their own power. The Pentagon has been working on building nuclear microreactors at key U.S. bases in the homeland and has previously said it plans to field a nuclear reactor at a military base by September 2028.
The Air Force in particular is working on a microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, with plans to build more at other bases in the coming years. The service has also explored using alternate power sources like solar panels, geothermal plants, and more to create so-called “microgirds” for bases so they’re not entirely reliant on local civilian power grids.
The drive to give bases their own energy sources is driven by concerns that adversaries may target critical infrastructure, around 80 percent of which is currently in the commercial sector, to kneecap the military’s ability to generate forces. The Pentagon chief referred to the program as “nation’s insurance policy” in a memo directing the establishment of Fortress America.
“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit, our aircraft keep flying, our command centers never go dark,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth is also slashing the number of general and flag officers, cutting billets by 20 percent. That doubles down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.
“The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said. “And I know because I directed it that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent. So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.”
Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.
The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.
The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and has plans to continue to grow that number.
A year ago, most senior military leaders gave stoic reactions during politically charged speeches from Hegseth and Trump, keeping with the military’s apolitical tradition. The troops at this year’s addres gave Hegseth a more vocal reception, particularly during his reference to Musk, Luckey, and Gingrich, and Hegseth exited to applause from the troops, though service members appeared to avoid visual reactions to Hegseth’s more ideological comments. Attendees were separated by branch, and were given a “War Department Field Manual,” a collection speeches by Hegseth with a forward written by Trump. Earlier in the day, the service members in attendance participated in a physical training session with Hegseth on the grounds of the Pentagon.

where le corbusier’s plan voisin sought to organize paris, chtcheglov chose to drift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:45:01 UTC
05:45:01 KST

where le corbusier’s plan voisin sought to organize paris, chtcheglov chose to drift
a clash between urban order and the unpredictable experience of wandering, where efficiency gives way to mood, chance and discovery.
le corbusier’s plan voisin reorganizes paris
Le Corbusier’s Plan Voisin imagines Paris as a highly ordered urban system, replacing a large section of central Paris with cruciform office towers, residential blocks, open space and a hierarchical road network. The 1925 proposal responds to congestion and poor sanitary conditions, but it also advances a particular idea of urban life, where functions are separated, movement is organized, and the city becomes legible as a complete system. The scheme would have removed much of the existing fabric of the Marais and surrounding areas while preserving monuments including the Louvre, Palais-Royal and Place Vendôme. Eighteen cruciform office towers would rise from an open landscape, with residential buildings arranged separately from the business district. Plan Voisin was never built, but its principles became part of a wider modernist approach to urban planning. The separation of functions, concentration of buildings vertically and prioritization of circulation and open space continued to shape architectural thinking through the development of the Ville Radieuse and the Athens Charter.
then chtcheglov starts somewhere else
Almost three decades later, French philosopher Ivan Chtcheglov looks at the modern city and sees boredom as the main problem. In his Formulary for a New Urbanism, written in 1953 under the pseudonym Gilles Ivain, he calls for ‘new, changeable decors’ that can alter with the people living in them. He is not particularly diplomatic about Le Corbusier. Chtcheglov describes his architecture as suitable for ‘factories and hospitals’ and, eventually, prisons, before accusing him of destroying ‘joy’ and ‘love, passion, freedom.’
In the place of cities based on Plan Voisin, he imagines architecture that can alter moods, generate dreams and change the way people experience their surroundings. He describes houses that move with the sun, sliding walls that allow vegetation to enter, and buildings whose appearance changes according to the wishes of their inhabitants. He also proposes an entire city divided according to feeling, with a Bizarre Quarter, Happy Quarter, Noble and Tragic Quarter and even a Sinister Quarter.
a city built for getting lost
While Le Corbusier’s proposal begins with the idea that the city can be reorganized according to a rational structure, Chtcheglov is interested in what happens when the experience of moving through it is not as organized. The Situationists described this wandering through the city as the dérive, allowing streets, buildings and changing surroundings to determine where the journey goes. For Chtcheglov, a building or street did not have to serve one purpose. It could change the mood of a walk, pull someone in another direction or make a familiar part of the city feel strange. Getting somewhere was only part of the experience; the journey could be the point. Drifting runs against the logic of optimization. The shortest route gets you there faster. Chtcheglov was interested in what you might find by taking the long way. ‘The main activity of the inhabitants will be CONTINUOUS DRIFTING,’ he writes. The landscapes of the city would change from one hour to the next, producing what he calls ‘total disorientation.’ The point is not simply to arrive somewhere, but to see where the city takes you.
For Chtcheglov, even a familiar street could become something else. A building might draw you in, a change in atmosphere might send you in another direction, or an unexpected space might make an ordinary part of Paris feel unfamiliar. It is difficult to imagine anything further from Plan Voisin. Le Corbusier’s city is drawn from above, with its functions and circulation worked out in advance. Chtcheglov’s city only really comes alive once people start wandering through it.
the value of taking the long way
Plan Voisin was responding to real problems. Paris was dealing with overcrowding and poor sanitary conditions, while modernist architects were looking for ways to bring more light, air and open space into the city. But the more completely those problems are solved through planning, the more the city becomes predetermined. If every building has a function, every road has a purpose and every movement has been accounted for, there is less room for the detours and unexpected uses that make a city feel alive. This is what Chtcheglov finds troubling. He is drawn to things that are difficult to measure, such as the mood of a place, the attraction of a particular street, the feeling of discovering somewhere by accident. He takes the idea much further than simply making cities more entertaining. His imagined city is full of spaces designed around those feelings. The Sinister Quarter, for instance, would be unsettling without being dangerous. Elsewhere, there are rooms for dreaming and places intended to bring back a sense of secrecy or exoticism.
There is something almost funny about putting these two visions side by side. Le Corbusier wants to make the city more efficient; Chtcheglov wants people to wander through it and see what happens. His city does not need every space to have a clear purpose, a strange idea to put against the logic of convenience and efficiency.
The fastest route may be useful, but it is also predictable. Chtcheglov is interested in the things that happen when you take the wrong turn or come across a place you were not looking for. Plan Voisin leaves little room for that kind of accident. Chtcheglov envisions it in the city.
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

US stocks closed mixed Wednesday, the final trading day of September, as rising Treasury yields weighed on sentiment despite softer-than-expected inflation data.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 443.87 points, or 0.86%, to 50,906.05, while the S&P 500 declined 19.30 points, or 0.25%, to 7,651.54.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq composite gained 63.52 points, or 0.24%, to 26,861.06.
Investors assessed the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, which increased 3.4% year-on-year in August, below market expectations of 3.7%.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, stood at 3%, also below expectations. Both measures remained above the Fed's 2% inflation target.
Stronger-than-expected employment data accompanied the inflation release.
Private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, according to payroll processing firm ADP, exceeding expectations of 68,000.
"After a three-month slowdown, job creation rebounded and pay growth remained solid," ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said.
Traders reduced bets on an October interest rate increase following the inflation figures.
The probability of a quarter-point hike fell to around 35%, from 51% a day earlier, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Attention now turns to Friday's September employment report, with nonfarm payrolls expected to increase by 84,000.
Meanwhile, the yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury rose about 4.3 basis points to a 24-year high of 5.306%.
European stocks close lower
European stock markets finished Wednesday lower as investors monitored developments in the Middle East, their implications for energy prices and inflation, and elevated bond yields.
The benchmark Stoxx Europe 600 index fell 0.5% to 634.89.
Britain's FTSE 100 declined 0.29% to 10,606, while Germany's DAX 40 dropped 0.79% to 25,199.19.
France's CAC 40 lost 0.89% to 7,964.51, and Italy's FTSE MIB retreated 0.84% to 51,371.98.

The U.K. has sanctioned four Georgians—including the brother-in-law of Tbilisi’s mayor—for “legitimising Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory” after they met with the head of a Russian-backed separatist republic.
The designations are part of a broader British sanctions package announced in response to intensifying Russian drone strikes against Ukraine in September. According to a press release Thursday, the wider measures target Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Kremlin propagandists, and individuals allegedly involved in human rights abuses against Ukrainian civilians.
“The U.K. will not flinch in our support for Ukraine,” said Europe Minister Lord Wood of Anfield.
The U.K. sanctions notice states the four men “joined a delegation of Georgian politicians who met with the head of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, and subsequently publicised the visit.” All four now face U.K. asset freezes and travel bans.
The sanctioned delegates include political commentator Paata Abuladze, Mamuka Pipia, leader of the minor Solidarity for Peace party, party member Giorgi Iremadze, and Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, founder of a Georgian Russian-language TV channel.
Separatist leader Denis Pushilin praised the September 2025 meeting on Telegram, referring to the delegation as “likeminded people from Georgia.”
“It was pleasant to hear words of support for our region’s residents from the Georgian guests, who wished for the swift liberation of all the territory of the Donetsk People’s Republic,” he wrote.
According to a video of the meeting, Pipia told Pushilin: “We hope in the very near future the Donetsk People’s Republic will be free.”
Abuladze added: “You won't be able to show me a single country in the world that is such a small country, yet has endured and is doing whatever it takes to restore diplomatic relations.”
Three of the four delegates have so far responded to the U.K. measures, some using profanity and insults.
Mamuka Pipia told the Georgian TV channel Pirveli that he considered the sanctions a “reward” and that he was “very happy.” Mzhavanadze told his Facebook followers that the decision was “shameful,” and said the U.K. was “afraid that the positions expressed by a person will harm their politics.” Iremadze did not respond to Monitori’s request for comment.
Abuladze also took to Facebook following the news of his designation. “Britain sanctioned me… and congratulated me,” he told his followers, “I am grateful to the British for sanctioning me.”
Contacted by Monitori, he added: “So what? Like I won’t go to Donbas now?”
“I have never been to [Britain] in my life,” he said. “It’s just a formality.”
In his Telegram post, Pushilin referred to Abuladze as a “member” of the ruling Georgian Dream party. While Monitori was unable to verify his formal party membership and he holds no elected office, Abuladze has family ties to an influential Georgian Dream figure: he is the brother-in-law of Kakha Kaladze, the Mayor of Tbilisi.
Manana Toqmajishvili, the head of the Tbilisi City Hall Press Service, confirmed to Monitori that Abuladze is Kaladze’s “half-sister’s husband” but that he has “absolutely no connection to Tbilisi City Hall.” She did not comment further.

Telcos seek to 'rebuild trust' with mobile roaming during disasters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:32:06 UTC
05:32:06 KST

Telcos activate temporary disaster roaming agreement for mobile coverage
In short:
From October 1, telcos will activate temporary disaster roaming (TDR) when one network goes down during a severe weather event.
It will only be available outside major cities, and not if a network goes down in large parts of regional Australia where there is only one provider.
What's next?
The telcos will decide when to switch roaming on and off, but neither the industry nor government has outlined accountability measures.
After years of testing, Australia's three major telcos are ready to switch on a system that would give customers access to a rival network if their own goes down during a weather emergency.
Known as temporary disaster roaming (TDR), Telstra, Optus and TPG will work together to decide when to activate it in regional areas where a mobile service has been disrupted by severe weather.
"You'll continue to be able to make phone calls, send text messages, and you'll have limited capacity data services," the chief executive of Australian Telecommunications Alliance, Luke Coleman, said.
"You can't expect to have your full usual high-speed data, but you will still have enough data to send a WhatsApp or an iMessage, maybe even to check an emergency service website like Fires Near Me, for example."
For TDR to work, another network must be available in that area that mobile users can roam onto.
That means it will not work if a network fails in large parts of regional Australia served by only one provider.
Telstra has indicated it would also be willing to consider allowing Optus and TPG customers to roam onto its network during disasters in Telstra-only areas, if they were satisfied it would not affect network capacity.
Regional Independent MP Helen Haines has long been advocating for such a service, which she described as a "game changer".
"When disaster knocks in regional communities and pulls out a mobile network, people shouldn't have to wait for their own provider to restore that service before they can reconnect," she said.
"This is existential in times of disaster."
Telcos in charge
TDR is already available in some form, either mandated or agreed to by industry, in several countries including the United States and Japan.
In 2023, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission found TDR technically feasible, and in 2024 the Regional Telecommunications Review recommended mandating it "at the earliest possible opportunity".
Ms Haines previously tried to have this legislated through a private members' bill and amendments, but it did not have government support.
"I'll keep pushing to make sure that the telecommunications companies ensure that there's enough network capacity to facilitate temporary disaster roaming, that the telecommunication companies ensure that there's power backup to our mobile network," she said.
Mr Coleman said the telcos were best placed to be the custodians of the initiative as they "have full visibility of the network's capacity" and could make sure the "surviving network continues to operate".
He said telcos would monitor its progress but did not specify any benchmarks or framework to measure success.
"The telcos are being good corporate citizens here and this is part of rebuilding trust with Australians to show that there is no additional charge for this,"
"If you're a consumer, your phone will just automatically start using another available network where it is safe to do so."
Under the terms of the agreement, the service will be available only outside major cities and will be implemented in up to three different disaster areas at any one time.
There can only be up to 15 towers within each area, and those areas must be at least 400 kilometres apart.
When asked how a decision would be made in a situation where multiple areas in the same region might be affected, Mr Coleman said telcos were best placed to make a choice.
"Those areas do need to be spaced a certain distance apart because there is a risk otherwise of the network being overloaded," he said.
Communications Minister Anika Wells was not available for interview.
A statement quoting a ministerial spokesperson did not answer the ABC's questions, including whether there would be any accountability around the initiative.
"The government will continue to engage closely with industry to make sure TDR is working as intended to keep communities safer," the statement said.
No change to Triple Zero
Mobile roaming differs from an existing permanent provision known as "camp on," which allows mobile users to call Triple Zero (000) no matter what network they are subscribed to, as long as at least one network is available.
For TDR, Mr Coleman said "most modern smartphones" would have settings to enable VoLTE technology, which would allow them to roam when activated.
He would not confirm if there would be subsidies for anyone needing to upgrade their phone, but encouraged people to approach their telco for advice.
TDR is also different from domestic roaming, which the ACCC is currently reviewing to see if it should be mandated on a permanent and more widespread basis.

====================================================================================================

Thriving Kids launches today. Here's what parents should know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-30
20:30:24 UTC
05:30:24 KST

In brief
- The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended.
- The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.
On 1 October, the first stage of Thriving Kids begins to roll out. This new program, announced just over a year ago, is part of the federal government’s sweeping changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).
It means children aged eight and under, who have developmental delay or autism and low to moderate support needs, will increasingly receive support outside the NDIS, through Thriving Kids. The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.
But this doesn’t mean children are being moved off the NDIS today. Changes to NDIS access won't begin until January 2028.
So, what will Thriving Kids provide? And — after more than a year of negotiation, consultation and controversy — what questions remain?
How did we get here?
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended, and the scheme’s budget is growing too quickly.
One group the government says is particularly over-represented is children under 15. They make up just under half of all NDIS participants. One in two new entrants to the scheme is under nine — many with autism or developmental delay — and across the country one in ten six-year-olds receives NDIS support.
There is also mounting concern the scheme doesn’t serve all these young children well.
The government has argued these children would benefit more from strong, mainstream and community services, rather than an individual NDIS package.
But there wasn’t much initial detail
When Thriving Kids was announced in August 2025 there was relatively little detail. This caused considerable anxiety among families and disability advocates.
Since then — after an advisory process, a parliamentary inquiry, and lengthy negotiations between the Commonwealth and states and territories — we know more about the program.
The proposed national model will combine broad, or universal, supports with more targeted assistance for children who need additional help. Support will respond to children's needs rather than simply depend on a diagnosis, recognising that children's developmental and support needs are not static but can change over time.
So, how will Thriving Kids work?
Currently, children on the NDIS are assessed individually and receive a certain amount of funding their family can use to access services such as speech therapy or visits to a psychologist.
But Thriving Kids will provide supports where children are already going about their lives: in schools and early childhood centres, as well as community spaces (such as libraries or organised sport) and health care. These are known as foundational supports.
Some foundational supports will be universal, meaning they are available to all children and families. These include providing information about child development and linking families to services.
Some universal supports will begin on 1 October — such as supported playgroups for children aged five and under — or shortly after, such as the Medicare-funded health check for three-year-olds, done by GPs and rolling out in November.
Some supports will be targeted to kids' specific needs and provided by allied health professionals, such as occupational therapists, speech pathologists and physiotherapists. These will require some form of assessment to access.
Children with permanent and significant disability, including children with high support needs, will continue to be eligible for the NDIS.
State and territory governments will take the lead on designing and commissioning services that are appropriate to their local population. But Queensland is yet to sign up, so important questions remain about how this will work.
What have some of the sticking points been?
Important questions about Thriving Kids' implementation remain.
One of the biggest challenges has been working out who is responsible for providing and paying for supports outside the NDIS. This problem predates Thriving Kids.
In 2023, the NDIS Review argued the NDIS had blown out its estimates so much because states and territories had moved away from providing disability supports, forcing people to seek NDIS support.
Foundational supports — jointly funded by all governments — are meant to be part of the solution. Thriving Kids is the first program of this kind to be launched.
But while states and territories initially signed up to the federal government’s new model, the relationship has become more fractious as plans have developed.
And while the other states and territories have signed on to deliver Thriving Kids and are developing plans about what these will look like in their communities, Queensland is yet to sign up.
At the moment we don’t know what this will mean for younger children with low-to-moderate needs in Queensland. For example, some aspects of Thriving Kids’ first stage will be rolled out, focusing on general supports. But it’s unclear whether targeted services will be developed.
What do we still need to know?
The Queensland minister for disability services, Amanda Camm, has previously said the federal government has not sufficiently defined what it means by developmental delay or different levels of support needs. She argues the federal government simply wants to shift costs to the states and territories.
The Queensland government shares a concern with a number of disability advocates: that children and families might fall between gaps in services if they’re no longer eligible for the NDIS but can’t get the specific support they need through Thriving Kids.
NDIS eligibility is set to tighten, with the government seeking to cut 160,000 participants from the scheme over the next four years.
So what will happen for families whose children age out of Thriving Kids — at nine — but aren’t eligible for NDIS support? This is a key concern.
The kind of early intervention offered by Thriving Kids is important, but for most children their support needs won’t disappear as they age.
The government has floated the idea of a Thriving Teens scheme, but there are no solid plans yet.
What happens next?
This first stage of Thriving Kids focuses on general universal supports, such as information and advice for families who have concerns about their child’s development, and supported playgroups for children aged five and under.
From January 2027, states and territories will start to develop and roll out targeted supports. These are for children who need additional support, for example, low-cost assistive technologies or speech therapy.
The NDIS will not change its eligibility criteria until January 2028, meaning children will continue to be admitted to the scheme until these changes take place.
Helen Dickinson is a professor of public service research and director of the Public Service Research Group at the School of Business, University of New South Wales, Canberra. She receives funding from ARC, NHRMC, MRFF, NDRP and Australian governments.
Catherine Smith is a senior lecturer of wellbeing science at the Melbourne Graduate School of Education at the University of Melbourne. She receives funding from the NDRP and Australian governments.
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.
